title: ‘And you will be the People’s Earl’ – Charles Spencer’s Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, digested by John Crace | Diana, Princess of Wales | The Guardian
description: The earl on his globally lauded eulogy for Diana, King Charles’s sausage fingers and toxic Raine, topped off with a lavish sprinkling of adverbs
Author: John Crace
Headline: The earl on his globally lauded eulogy for Diana, King Charles’s sausage fingers and toxic Raine, topped off with a lavish sprinkling of adverbs
Content: A customer holds a copy of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer at Waterstones Piccadilly in London.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/GettyView image in fullscreenA customer holds a copy of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer at Waterstones Piccadilly in London.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/GettyDigested readDiana, Princess of Wales‘And you will be the People’s Earl’ – Charles Spencer’s Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, digested by John CraceThe earl on his globally lauded eulogy for Diana, King Charles’s sausage fingers and toxic Raine, topped off with a lavish sprinkling of adverbsJohn CraceWed 23 Sep 2026 12.18 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCheers were heard up and down the land. Halley’s comet made an unscheduled appearance in the ethereal night sky. In very heaven, angelic choirs rang out. A saviour had been born. A light to lighten the world. But enough about me. For this paragraph at least.In my universally acclaimedfuneral address, I aimed to speak for my sister. The real Diana. For only I truly knew her. She had the heart of a lion. And I had a glut of cliches. Yet when Diana had swept so triumphantly into the arena of royal life, I was but a callow youth awash with hormones and gripped by the self-centredness of adolescence. Nothing much has changed. Yet I know, with all my heart, that Diana would have wanted me to tellour story.Why now, you may ask? The answer is simple. I could do with the money. And with the 30th anniversary of the most tragic death in human history approaching, I wanted to get in before someone like Amol Rajan did.Quite simply, the Diana I knew is not the Diana that has been portrayed up till now. We have been told she had an unhappy childhood. But let me say, we were both the secure recipients of parental love.Earl Spencer apologises to Piers Morgan over ‘incorrect assumption’Read moreNever were we more content than when our parents separated. Or when we were carted off to boarding schools that thrived on neglect. And we adored the way our father was miserable for so much of our lives, his latter years made still more miserable by marrying the venomousRaine.Back to me. I was in Cape Town when I heard Diana had died. At first I could not comprehend what had happened. I was stunned, watching the TV as the story unfurled.The initial reports had been more hopeful. She was merely slightly injured. My lips curled as the commentators implied that she had got what she deserved for betraying the royal family.Then, when her death was announced, they had to change their tone. That will teach the media to be mean about my sister, I thought. My lips grimly broke into a grim smile.Quick pause as I go into yet more unimaginably dull guff about our privileged childhood and how we were always happy except when we weren’t. Then to remember how Prince Charles had sounded so giddily elated when he had phoned me to offer his congratulations. “Get in there,” he had said. “Finally I can be left in peace with my top bit on the side.”With that, the cold finality of death struck home. Never again would my heart soar at seeing my beloved Diana alive again. On the plane back to London, my thoughts turned to her eulogy. We would need someone utterly brilliant. Someone who could capture the vibrant essence of Diana and represent her true blood family. One of far more noble lineage than the House of Windsor.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Earl Spencer, Prince William, Prince Harry and King Charles, who was then the Prince of Wales, at the funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales, in 1997.Photograph: Adam Butler/PAWith that, I realised it could only be me who could be entrusted with such a solemn duty. And I would do a lot better thanNorman St John-Stevas, who had ruined my father’s service with his crass middle-class antics.Time now for a digression into some pointless filler about the Spencer family history. How for many centuries we had fulfilled our duty of opening fetes and losing money because working for a living was beneath us. How Diana and I had once gone swimming with Prince Andrew. Even then he had been even more stupid than the average member of the royal family, and I remember thinking that one day he would get into trouble for hanging around with a paedophile.Such carefree lives we all led back then. Apart from the eating disorders and the other undiagnosed mental health conditions. Little did I know that Diana’s life would be ended by a tabloid press. The paparazzi who chased her down the Alma tunnel were all wearing Piers Morgan masks. How ironic that Diana, the goddess of hunting, should be the most hunted woman on the planet. By the way, that’s a line you might recall I wrote in my superb oration. Genius, isn’t it?I’m not sure who nominated me point man for liaising with the royal family – I’m guessing it might have been me. I recall other disturbing conversations with the prince. “You’re so lucky your dad has died,” he confided. “I wish my mum would. They just treat me like a child. I even have a footman to lay out my electric train set each morning. I’d love to do it for myself.” I cut short the conversation, my mind once more returning to the magnificence of the eulogy I was shortly to deliver to a stunned world.View image in fullscreenDiana in London in December 1993.Photograph: Princess Diana Archive/GettyBut the pressure from the palace was relentless. Time and again we were told that the Spencers had always been too common for the Windsors. The funeral arrangements soon took on a darker, more sombre tone.“William and Harry must walk behind Diana’s coffin,” Colonel Ross insisted. That wasn’t going to happen, I firmly replied, firmly. “I think you will find it will,” Ross snapped menacingly with menace. The Prince of Wales needs a human shield in case people heckle him. One of my happiest memories of the funeral procession was a lone piper in the crowd playing the ancient lament, “Who’s that wanker in the crown?”“Don’t worry too much,” said Prince Charles. “Everyone will have forgotten about her soon enough.” I couldn’t believe my ears.“No one will ever forget Diana,” I tartly snapped, tartly.“Diana who?”All such a long way from the fairytale that had begun in 1980. Then the country had been in thrall to the fact that the future Earl Spencer was about to become brother-in-law to the next king of England. Diana, though, was already a broken butterfly, crushed by a man who had told her he would never love her but would marry her because he couldn’t really get out of it. “Thing is,” he said. “Not only do I adore Camilla with all my heart but you’re actually a bit podgy.” How I wish I had been there to say: “You’re no oil painting yourself, sausage fingers.”Diana later told me she had sobbed, sobbingly to my father that she could never marry a man who didn’t love her. But my father wouldn’t countenance such a thing. The Spencers always do their duty dutifully. Till death us do part.And so the inevitable train of events that would lead to her death were put in train. She was to be the royal family’s sacrifice to an insatiably, ravenous tabloid press who would not relent until she lay dying in the back of a car in Paris.“Oh Carlos,” Diana said to me.“Oh Duch,” I replied, replyingly“Oh Carlos.”“Oh Duch.”I find it almost too unbearably unbearable to recall some of the all too fleeting moments we had together. Though I sincerely believe that Diana was always at her happiest when she was with me. And we were so in tune with each other that silently we often didn’t need to talk.Only once did I try to dissuade her from getting a divorce, but she quickly shut me up. I like to think that Diana, like me, would be on to her fourth marriage by now, had she lived. Then we could have had a good old moan about our exes. And how expensive they are.View image in fullscreenElton John, ‘the warm-up act’, plays a specially rewritten version of Candle in the Wind at Diana’s funeral service.Photograph: Paul Hackett/APNow we get to the most solemn moment of the entire book. I find it incredible that no one in all these years has stopped to enquire how I felt when making the most celebrated eulogy in the history of mankind. Do I not count for something?Only Tony Blair fleetingly acknowledged the nation’s debt of gratitude to me. “Diana will always be the People’s Princess.” He paused, for effect. Clearly he had learned from my oratorical oratory. “And you will be the People’s Earl.”My years as a journalist for NBC filing meaningless stories that no one had ever watched was the perfect training for someone about to write a eulogy to end all eulogies. Have I mentioned that I was writing the eulogy?Once I was satisfied that I had achieved perfection, a car drove me to the chapel where Diana’s coffin was resting. It was almost as if she was tired of life. There I read her my eulogy. And at that moment, the sun shone through the stained glass and crowds bowed down in the streets, and from the coffin came Diana’s disembodied voice: “You’re a leg, Carlos.”The funeral passed almost in a daze. I remember Elton John singing Candle in the Wind and thinking: “Who is this idiot who has been brought in as my warm-up act?” After all, this was a day for me as much as for her. As for the eulogy? Let’s just say that the whole world bowed down to remember both me and Diana. Though let’s be clear, I was doing this for William and Harry. In the same way that this book is dedicated to them too.And so we come to the end of this book. Who knows what lies ahead for me? More divorces probably. But I can face the world knowing I have done right by my sister. Her memory will live for ever. Who knows what she might have become? The first lady of the US? Nelson Mandela’s wife? But at least she can rest in peace knowing that in death, at least, she had my eulogy. The eulogy which is mine.AAAGH. MAKE THIS STOP.Digested read, digested: Swanning AroundSwan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer is published by Michael Joseph (£28). title: Britain’s far-right violence comes to us direct from the 1970s. But so does the solution | Taj Ali | The Guardian
description: Young men punched in the street, mosques attacked: Britain badly needs an anti-racist uprising. Let 70s Asian youth movements provide the inspiration, says Taj Ali, author of Come What May, We’re Here to Stay
Author: Taj Ali
Headline: Young men punched in the street, mosques attacked: Britain badly needs an anti-racist uprising. Let 70s Asian youth movements provide the inspiration, says Taj Ali, author of Come What May, We’re Here to Stay
Content: ‘It was because of their heroic efforts that many of us  have grown up in safer environments.’ A protest in Southall, west London, in June 1976.Photograph: Bill Cross/PRView image in fullscreen‘It was because of their heroic efforts that many of us  have grown up in safer environments.’ A protest in Southall, west London, in June 1976.Photograph: Bill Cross/PROpinionRaceBritain’s far-right violence comes to us direct from the 1970s. But so does the solutionTaj AliYoung men punched in the street, mosques attacked: Britain badly needs an anti-racist uprising. Let 70s Asian youth movements provide the inspirationWed 23 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTShareThere it was: a pool of blood spreading across the pavement. A section of the high street had been cordoned off and a uniformed police officer gestured for bystanders to move along. It was the long hot summer of 1976, and a racist murder had stunned Southall in westLondon.“What has happened here, officers?” askedSuresh Grover, then a curious 22-year-old, later to be widely known as a leading racial justice activist. “Go away, it’s just Indian blood,” was the response. Grover was soon to learn that 18-year-oldGurdip Singh Chaggar, an engineering student, had been stabbed to death by racist thugs the night before.The late 1970s was the era of “Paki-bashing”: homes, shops and places of worship were attacked, while south Asians – young and old – were murdered on the streets. That day, Grover acted instinctively, taking some paint and daubing the pavement near the blood with the words: “This racist murder will be avenged. We’ll get you racist scum.”View image in fullscreenProtesters against a National Front rally in Southall town hall are detained in April 1979.Photograph: PA/PA Archive/PA ImagesThis is the story of working-class youth who refused to turn the other cheek. From Southall to Sheffield and from Brick Lane to Bradford, theAsian youth movementswere set up to physically defend communities from racist attacks. It was because of their heroic efforts that many of us in diverse towns and cities have grown up in safer environments.But more than 50 years on, that racist violence has returned with shocking ferocity, a deterioration traceable to the summer of 2024, which marked some of the worstracist riotingin living memory.In Hartlepool, a young south Asian man was walking down a street when he waspunched in the face. Onlookers cheered, laughed and yelled racial slurs. “A Paki got banged,” one shouted, as those around him began to smash the windows of small businesses and kick down the door of a nearby house. In Middlesbrough, a group of white men stopped motorists and questioned them about their ethnicity, asking whether they were “white” before letting them through. InRotherham and Tamworth, racist mobs tried to burn down hotels housing refugees.And now? A seemingly relentless rise.Every five days, a mosque in Britain is attacked. The rhetoric of the far right has been mainstreamed.After years spent researching and writing a book on the rich and proud tradition of political activism in the south Asian community, it seems clear to me that we cannot fight racism in silos. We must build broad movements that transcend racial and religious divides.View image in fullscreenChildren playing at school in Southall, London, in 1972.Photograph: Tony Henshaw/AlamyThe Asian youth movements had a belief in the concept of political blackness as a banner that people of colour could unite under. ToTariq Mehmood, an Asian youth movement member who was born in Pakistan but raised in Bradford, there was no real difference between south Asian, African and Caribbean people: they were all the same to those who wanted to harm them. “We were called ‘black bastards’ on the streets,” he recalled. “We were commonly united with our African and Afro-Caribbean friends. They didn’t know they were black until they came here — I didn’t know I was a ‘Paki’ until I came to Bradford. We were united on those common issues of our oppression.”They saw themselves as part of a broader working class. TheSheffield Asian Youth Movementand the Indian Workers’ Association, for instance, sent minibuses of their members to picket lines during the 1984-85 miners’ strike. They stood with white working-class communities fighting to save their industries, providing much needed financial support while challenging prejudice in these communities. Grover tells me that more than a decade after that strike, Kent miners were still attending Punjabi Sikh weddings in Southall because of the links that were built during that dispute.These were movements rooted in their communities and strategic in their organising. They monitored the far right and mapped out who was most vulnerable to racist attacks. The Sheffield Asian Youth Movement had a big thick folder called the “fascist file”, in which they would compile information on local racists.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA Sheffield Asian Youth Movement stall in the early 1980s.Photograph: Matloub Husayn Ali KhanBut things changed. As the 20th century wore on, anti-racist activism was increasingly institutionalised as the struggle moved from the streets to council chambers and boardrooms. Where we once had grassroots anti-racist movements rooted in communities, we now have a race-relations industry in which a few people are paid to tackle discrimination. We also have the rise of self-proclaimed community leaders under the policy of state multiculturalism who often speak on behalf of entire communities. Too often, they become the prism through which authorities engage with ethnic-minority communities.A revival of grassroots anti-racist movements is long overdue. But it must be of this time, attuned to the changing circumstances of 2026. Racism is not experienced equally. Class, gender and geography all matter. A hijab-wearing Muslim woman is more likely to be a victim of Islamophobia than a Muslim man. Those living in smaller, more isolated ethnic-minority communities are more vulnerable to racist attack. First-generation migrants have greater insecurity than the grandchildren of migrants. An effective anti-racist movement must reflect on these challenges and prioritise those most vulnerable to racist violence.The good news is that we are starting to see a revival of this approach. A few months ago, I spoke alongside Grover at the launch of the Nottinghamshire Solidarity Network, which is taking a strategic approach to anti-racism by organising county-wide to ensure smaller ethnic-minority communities are not left isolated. A week later, I spoke at the launch of the Greater Manchester Workers’ and Tenants’ Association. Its members understand that the far right feeds on deprivation and despair in working-class communities, and they are seeking to organise on the basis of class in an attempt to offer a counter-narrative to that of division and hate.All of these movements, past and present, understand that racism will not be defeated from above. It will only be defeated by us – ordinary citizens who refuse to look away.Taj Ali is a journalist and historian and author ofCome What May, We’re Here to Stay: the Story of South Asian Resistance in BritainDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsRaceOpinionProtestLondonFar rightActivismImmigration and asylumReligioncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Watermelons’: Zack Polanski and the rise of the ‘green outside, red inside’ eco-populists | Zack Polanski | The Guardian
description: Author Russell Warfield argues the Green leader’s brand of politics is not new but has evolved in the party over time
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Author Russell Warfield argues the Green leader’s brand of politics is not new but has evolved in the party over time
Content: Zack Polanski on the campaign trail for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in LondonPhotograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenZack Polanski on the campaign trail for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in LondonPhotograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press/ShutterstockZack Polanski‘Watermelons’: Zack Polanski and the rise of the ‘green outside, red inside’ eco-populistsAuthor Russell Warfield argues the Green leader’s brand of politics is not new but has evolved in the party over timeMatthew PearceWed 23 Sep 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWatermelons: the term used to describe the members of theGreen partyof England and Wales who are green on the outside and red on the inside. People in this faction are environmentalists but bleed socialist ideologies.Of the roughly 160,000 people who haveflocked to the partysince Zack Polanski became leader last year, most are thought to be in this camp, drawn to a political space on the left that they see as vacated by the Labour party.But the author of a new book – The Green Socialist:Zack Polanskiand the Battle for Britain’s Future – says this flavour of Green is nothing new. “What you’ve got to understand is that the party has been watermelon for at least 10 years,” says Russell Warfield, a former party staffer who has worked on election campaigns, including Polanski’s.“There’s often this dichotomy presented that there’s this ‘real core’ Green party who are these ecologists who really just care about conservation of the environment, then there’s this new cohort of hard leftists,” Warfield says. “Actually, this has been both an organic process but also one which reaches much more deeply into the past of the party, where a lot of the fundamental positions of the party can be traced back to the early 1970s.”His book unpacks the history of the party to explain how Polanski fits into it, arguing that the leader and his“eco-populist” packageis not a departure from Green tradition but the culmination of a 50-year evolution that has turned the party into the main electoral force on the British left.Not everyone agrees. During the leadership contest between Polanski and co-runners Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns in 2025, a senior Green source described Polanski’s rise as a“hostile takeover”. Even Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ first MP and a former party leader, has said, when pressed, that she wouldlove him to talk about the environment more.“It’s just obvious nonsense,” Warfield says of the hostile takeover comment. “Look at the mandate, it was 85%,” Polanski’s landslide leadership win. “He won across every wing of the party.”View image in fullscreenRussell Warfield.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianBut how green are the Greens? Since Polanski took over, he has been splashed across newspapers and TV screens discussing subjects ranging from Gaza to wealth taxes – progressive politics, but not necessarily or overtly green.Warfield responds with a statistic: 34% of voters trust the Greensmore than any other partyon the environment, according to YouGov polling – the highest level of trust recorded for any party on any issue. “There is not a voter in this country, leftwing, rightwing, old, young, rural, urban, whatever, that does not strongly associate the Green party with taking action on the environment.”Because of that starting point, he argues, the sensible move forward was to evolve into a broader message – one previous leaders paved the way for. “The reason the party exists is in recognition of the fact that just having a bunch of environmental conservation movements isn’t addressing the root political and economic causes of environmental degradation.“We tried 50 years of that. And it got us so far, but the manifest moments of material advancement have been tied to moments where we’ve been able to be more responsive to the actual political context of the day.”Warfield points out that many of Polanski’s positions are not his alone. Green party members vote on policy and the leaders are constitutionally duty bound to advocate for it. “Take thewealth tax,” Warfield writes. “He did not arrive at this policy personally. A ‘wealth tax’ is called for as ‘a means of limiting large accumulations of wealth’ in a Green party manifesto published long before Polanski’s leadership.”The book finds links between the party’s past and present, even in unlikely places. It’s unavoidable, Warfield writes, that there were “some distinctly rightwing people present at the formation of the Green party”. The first key figure was Teddy Goldsmith, an environmentalist part of afamous Tory family. His writings formed key texts for People, the political party from which the modern Greens descend.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut even Goldsmith – whose “deep ecology” philosophy leaned into Malthusian concerns about human population and misanthropic views that blamed humanity as a monolith for ecological degradation – shares threads with Polanski’s Greens, Warfield says. Both share the golden Green rule that infinite economic growth and endless extraction are impossible on a planet with finite resources. Both reject the idea that capitalism can simply carry on with business as usual, green or otherwise.As the party has shifted towards social ecology over the years, Warfield says Polanski’s eco-socialism simply represents a modern evolution: arguing that capitalism and the 1% – not all of humanity – are the root cause of environmental destruction.But Polanski’s tenure has also brought controversies. There was his criticism of the police response to the Golders Green attack, which the Met commissioner, Mark Rowley,called “inaccurate and misinformed”. There was thefalse claimhe was a British Red Cross spokesperson and the sharing of a photo of a man with aT-shirt showing a guillotineand the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”, a reference to Nigel Farage. YouGov polling shows Polanski’s approval rating has slumped since he became leader, whileGreen voting intention has droppedfrom 21% of the electorate in March to 11% this month.Should the partytake Polanski’s social media away? “Golders Green was a misstep,” says Warfield. “But what you don’t want to do is to get to a situation where every post needs double-tick signoff from different members of staff and you can’t just let Zack engage with social media in the way that allows him to reap the political points of authenticity.”Polanski was criticised for his refusal to apologise for sharing the Farage guillotine picture. “Reform were trying to goad him into apologising for incitement to murder,” Warfield says. “If you do that, you legitimise the claim that they’re making. I think there’s a lot of strength in not succumbing to the pressure of playing that game.”On 8 October, Polanski will contest theHolborn and St Pancras byelectionafter Keir Starmer announced his decision to vacate the seat. Warfield thinks Polanski can win. “You could vote Labour again and you get another backbencher who is one among literally hundreds of Labour MPs and that doesn’t make much difference to anything,” he says. “Or you can put a really prominent, independently minded Green in there and continue to put pressure on the Burnham project from its left.”Explore more on these topicsZack PolanskiGreen partyEnvironment policyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Something in your eye? Here’s how to get it out – without making it worse | Well actually | The Guardian
description: It’s natural to want to soothe eye irritation, but mishandling could lead to more problems, experts warn. We asked them for advice on how to deal with it properly
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It’s natural to want to soothe eye irritation, but mishandling could lead to more problems, experts warn. We asked them for advice on how to deal with it properly
Content: ‘Be mindful of what you’re doing, react quickly, and don’t do something silly like trying to fix the problem yourself when something does go wrong,’ says Avnish Deobhakta, an ophthalmologist.Photograph: PixelsEffect/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Be mindful of what you’re doing, react quickly, and don’t do something silly like trying to fix the problem yourself when something does go wrong,’ says Avnish Deobhakta, an ophthalmologist.Photograph: PixelsEffect/Getty ImagesWell actuallySomething in your eye? Here’s how to get it out – without making it worseIt’s natural to want to soothe eye irritation, but mishandling could lead to more problems, experts warn. We asked them for advice on how to deal with it properlySarah SloatWed 23 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt may feel like a gritty, annoying sensation, or a sharp pain. Either way, you may have the same problem: something is stuck in your eye and needs to come out.Addressing the situation incorrectly can lead to biggerissuessuch as infection, scarring, an ulcer or corneal scratches, which are abrasions on the clear covering of your eye. Ignoring the dilemma can lead to similar consequences.Experts explain how to handle this predicament, when it’s time to see a medical professional, and some of the most common mistakes.What can get stuck in the eye – and what does it feel like?As innocuous as they may seem, eyelashes are some of the most common foreign bodies to get stuck in eyes. If an eyelash ends up under an eyelid, it can be quite painful, explained Dr Douglas Lazzaro, an ophthalmologist and professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Other common examples Lazzaro encounters include dust and other small debris kicked up on a windy day and glue from attaching false eyelashes. Those working in construction may encounter flecks of industrial materials such as fiberglass, metal and wood.Contact lenses are another frequent culprit, he said. These can roll up and hide under the upper eyelid, break in the eye, ormay be forgotten and not removedbefore another is put in.The feeling of having something in your eye can depend on the object, but generalsymptomsinclude burning and irritation, blurred vision, a scratchy feeling or sensitivity to bright lights.How do you get something out of your eye?For some small objects, like eyelashes, sand or mascara flecks,blinking and your own tearsare often all you need to get them out.But if that doesn’t work, you may need to do more.Wash your handsfirst and work in a well-lit area. Lazzaro recommends carefully examining your eye to locate whatever may be stuck. This may include gently pulling down your lower eyelid with clean fingers, or using a cotton-tipped swab to slowly lift your upper lid.If the object is small and not penetrating your eye, blinking and irrigating the eye with artificial tears may flush the object out. If irrigation doesn’t work, then it’s likely best to seek professional attention, said Lazzaro.‘I suck at breaks’: a day in the life of an aerial cellistRead moreWhat about liquids?If a foreign liquid gets in your eye – such as detergents and disinfectants – you’ll want to act quickly, said Dr Keith Baratz, an ophthalmologist at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. He recommends rinsing your eye with tap water as soon as possible.A general rule of thumb is that liquids with ahigh pH(for example, bleach, ammonia and most drain cleaners) are more damaging than those with a low pH – but you should hasten to rinse your eyes with tap water regardless.“Speed is the important thing,” said Baratz. “You want to do it right away, not wait a half hour while you drive to the emergency room.”After you rinse the eye, you should then go to the emergency room, said Dr Avnish Deobhakta, an ophthalmologist at the New York Eye and Ear Infirmary of Mount Sinai.“There can still be ongoing damage even if you flushed it,” he said.When should you see an eye doctor?Experts’ advice falls into two categories. On some occasions, you should go to the doctor to remove something from your eye. There are also times when you should go even if you have been able to remove the object.A common mistake is assuming that something in the eye will come out on its own, said Lazzaro. According to theMayo Clinic, avoid removing anything embedded in the eye or sticking out between the lids. Doctors have tools that make the process easier: numbing drops, magnifying devices (for instance, aslit lamp microscope) and sterile tools such as forceps or needles, which are used to dislodge particles. You should not use these tools at home, said Lazzaro.But let’s say you removed the object and your eye still hurts. For the first 24 hours, you can continue to irrigate the eye with artificial tears, Lazzaro said. Cold compresses can also make the eye feel a little better, but don’t provide any healing benefits.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy it’s important to protect your hearing as you age – and what experts suggestRead moreIf irrigating your eye doesn’t work, and you still have “something that’s bothering you, causing vision problems, or is hard to reach”, then you “really do need to seek professional care”, said Deobhakta.Generally, the rule is that if you don’t feel better within 24 hours – there’s still inflammation, redness, tearing or vision changes – then you should seek medical attention, said Lazzaro.It’s possible that, when removing the object, either you caused harm or injury had already been inflicted by the object, explained Deobhakta. Another likelihood is that the injury exposed the eye to infection. A doctor can examine the wound and provide the correct aftercare, he said.Medical care can help you avoid more than just pain; even if the foreign matter is removed, there can still be downstream effects, Lazzaro said. For example, a removed piece of wood or vegetable matter could leave behind afungal infection. Or if a piece of metal is on the eye, rust can accumulate and become stuck to the cornea. If left untreated, this can lead to infection and scarring that can affect vision. Doctors have special instruments that brush away rust, and can follow up with an antibiotic treatment, said Lazzaro.What are some common eye care mistakes to avoid?Rubbing the eye is heavily discouraged, said Lazzaro. If the object is still in your eye, you can “actually rub it further into your cornea”, he said. Rubbing can introduce bacteria from your hands into the eye and can also increase inflammation.People should not use metal tools at home, like tweezers, to remove something from the eye. This can cause further injury.“One of the worst-case scenarios is that the individual goes to a mirror and tries to pick at the foreign object with a toothpick or tweezers,” said Deobhakta.You also don’t want to try to use your fingers to pick something out of your eye, said Baratz, adding that “this is the number one mistake we see”.Skip the run: here are six joint-friendly cardio alternatives suggested by expertsRead moreCulprits often include people who wear contact lenses and, in turn, are used to touching their eyes, he explains. But using your fingers can increase the risk of infection and injury.Patients who wear contact lenses also tend to leave their contacts in, even if something is irritating their eyes. Another tendency is to put contacts back in immediately after an eye injury, sid Deobhakta.“Do not put a contact lens on an eye that is already sore,” he advises. “If it’s getting better and you feel OK, use lubricating drops and wear your glasses.”Generally, people can underestimate the inherent danger some activities pose to their eyes, said Deobhakta. He has seen patients use their glasses instead of safety goggles during a debris-causing activity such as mowing the lawn. In this case, grass can still fly up under the glasses into the eye, or a rock could hit and break the glasses, causing injury.“Be mindful of what you’re doing, react quickly, and don’t do something silly like trying to fix the problem yourself when something does go wrong,” he says.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyHealth & wellbeingHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is where I live now, the back of a truck’: a day in the life of a grandmother in Gaza | Global development | The Guardian
description: As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. At 76, Mansoura’s most precious possession is the key to her former home
Author: Tess McClure
Headline: As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. At 76, Mansoura’s most precious possession is the key to her former home
Content: Mansoura. Art direction by Guardian DesignGaza: a week in the lifeGlobal development‘This is where I live now, the back of a truck’: a day in the life of a grandmother in GazaAs the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each tells the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the conflict. At 76, Mansoura’s most precious possession is the key to her former homeSupported byAbout this contentSeham Tanteshin Gaza andTess McClureWed 23 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTShareAs the war inGazaapproaches its fourth year, this week, the Guardian follows five ordinary Palestinians as they go about their lives. Each will tell the story of their day, revealing the terrible toll of the ongoing conflict.The flat-bed truck is open to the hot summer air, its metal frame covered on two sides by draped tarpaulins, the rear by a pegged-up bedsheet. On the tin floor lies a squab mattress and pillow with a yellow frilled cover.Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem balances a thin cushion at the truck bed’s metal edge to protect her knees as she crawls in and out. She lowers her foot to the plastic chair below, then drops to the ground, staggering slightly as she gets her balance. Mansoura is 76 years old. The truck is her home now. All around her, her family live in tents, the fabric ripped and fraying.This is a day in the life of a grandmother living in Gaza.Daybreakdouble quotation markLast night, I stayed awake until 2am. I barely sleep during the night because of the mosquitoes and the heat. I fall asleep for a short while, I wake up early in the morning, pray to God, and wait to hear the call to dawn prayer. When I wake up, I call for my grandson to bring over the white plastic chair that I need to climb in and out of the truck.This is where I live now: in the back of a pickup truck. This truck, we brought it with us when we were fleeing for our lives fromBeit Lahia[a city innorthern Gaza]. Its owners had abandoned it, so we took it with us, displaced from place to place – untilwe ended up here. When we finally arrived, there was no space for me anywhere else – the tents that we have are small, torn and overcrowded, they fall down on the children – so I was forced to live in the truck. I sleep in it to escape the sand, dirt and insects. That is the story of the truck.After I wake up, I fold up the mattress and prop it with the pillows against the wall, then use a cloth to sweep the dirt and sand from the tarpaulin floor. I sit with my grandson, and we try to make the tiny gas stove work, to boil water for coffee. It’s an old stove – inherited from my own grandfather – and it’s hard to get it to light, as there isn’t enough gas, but eventually we get a flame. I boil water in a small pot and brew coffee for my sons and I – a few spoonfuls for each person. The coffee is filled with the taste ofparaffin.Mansoura climbs out of the truck where she livesMiddayMansoura’s son holds up the phone for a video call with one of her grandsons, who left Gaza and is now living overseas, and she chats to him for a while. For lunch, Mansoura takes a few basil leaves from a plant the family have grown in a tin can, and grinds them with garlic in her mortar and pestle. She adds a chopped tomato and eats it with a little bread.double quotation markThis is the salad I used to make at home – back then I would add rosemary, green thymeand mint. When I see vegetables growing, it reminds me of Beit Lahia, of our farming, crops and land.Before the war, I lived like a queen. I had a beautiful life. I was a farmer. I planted and harvested my land. I had animal shelters where I raised livestock, chickens, rabbits and ducks. I lived a very beautiful life, but it has changed for me.Now, we have no home, no source of income and no good food. Life in tents is terrible – actually unbearable. There are insects everywhere, mosquitoes, sand, dirt, garbage and torn tents. And the wind. In winter, it blows everything away. In summer, we die from the extreme heat. We do not even have enough space to build a proper bathroom – a person who showers in a tent comes out dirtier leaving the bathroom.My feeling is that for people my age, death is more honorable than living this life. This isn’t life. We are not living. We are dead. Everything beautiful is gone. It has disappeared, and I have disappeared with it.Top: Mansoura cuts basil to prepare a simple lunch; below: clothes have to be washed by hand in a bucketAfter eating, I wash the clothing for my family. Back home, we lived in a two-storey house, and had a washing machine – I used to run it on the long cycle, rinsing the clothes once, twice, even three times. Now, even though I am an elderly woman, I wash all the clothes by hand in a plastic bucket.AfternoonAfter lunch, Mansoura sits on the ground outside, gathers her grandchildren around her, and quizzes them about their old lives. Some are young and can barely remember a time before the war: they have spent nearly three years living in tents amid the rubble.“Where did we live, Mohammed?” Mansoura asks.“In northern Beit Lahia,” he answers.“Where in the north?”“Near 36th Street.”“Tell them what Beit Lahia was like before the war.”“Honestly, it was good, better than these days.”“We will return there,” Mansoura says.She draws her leather satchel toward her, looking through the pockets.“Look at what I have in my bag. What is this?” Mansoura asks, dangling an object in front of her.They answer: “The key of the house.”double quotation markThis is the most precious thing I own – the key to our house in the north. It is the key to the house that the occupation forces bulldozed.They flattened it: the house, the trees, the well, even apen full of animals – they bulldozed it all. We couldn’t take anything with us, no money, no livestock.I lived through wars before this.None was as bad as this one. During the 52-day war, we sheltered in schools, and we were OK– there wasn’t bombing like this, not the level of killing, and not the destruction of homes. But this war is extremely difficult. The destruction is enormous, the devastation is enormous – and all without any benefit. All of this is for nothing.Mansoura shows her grandchildren the key to their former home, which was destroyedLife has become very different. Our family never knew hunger before, never knew displacement, bombardment, missiles, killingand destruction in this way or on this scale. The other thing I keep in this bag is a bullet – it was pulled from my son’s back. During the famine, he had nothing to eat and nothing to feed his seven children, so he went to get a bag of flour to feed his children from the aid stations, and they shot him. I keep this as a reminder of what happened – all for the sake of getting food.Honestly,every day is the samefor me now. I wake up, arrange the place around us and our sleeping area, clean it, eat, sit, and sleep.The things that make me smile are when I wake up in the morning and find my children safe, when I hear that my grandchildren are well, and when I myself am OK, thank God … This is the greatest life for me and the greatest happiness for me.At night, I call my grandson to bring the chair. Then I crawl back into the truck to sleep.CreditsVideo: Tantesh Media ServicesArt direction: Harry Fischer, Anaïs Mims, Barry Ainslie and Alessia AmitrianoVideo editor/producer: Joshua JacobVideo executive producers: Temujin Doran and Augusta AnthonyAdditional research: Harriet Barber

title: ‘They smell of urinal cakes!’: 100 unusual crisp flavours, ranked – from truly awful to totally scoffable | Food | The Guardian
description: Move over ready salted, salt and vinegar and cheese and onion. Gourmet crisps are everywhere, but which are actually worth trying?
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: Move over ready salted, salt and vinegar and cheese and onion. Gourmet crisps are everywhere, but which are actually worth trying?
Content: Ammar Kalia gets to grips with his crisps.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAmmar Kalia gets to grips with his crisps.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianTaste testFood‘They smell of urinal cakes!’: 100 unusual crisp flavours, ranked – from truly awful to totally scoffableMove over ready salted, salt and vinegar and cheese and onion. Gourmet crisps are everywhere, but which are actually worth trying?Ammar KaliaWed 23 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt seems the era of the “holy trinity of flavours” – ready salted, salt and vinegar, cheese and onion – is over. Gourmet crisps are everywhere. Caviar and truffle flavours are on corner-shop shelves, while supermarket brands now include everything from glazed meats to blue cheese. We tasted 100 of the strangest crisp options available to find out which are worth coming back to and which should have stayed in the test kitchen.100.Grouseandwhinberry, Taste of GameFor someone who has tasted neither grouse nor whinberry before, after eating these crisps I never want to. Smelling as meaty as a butcher’s but tasting sweet, this is truly the worst of all worlds.Taste: 0/10,texture: 2/10,novelty: 10/1099.Sparkling wine, TorresView image in fullscreenShould crisps taste of sparkling wine?Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianCrisps are an excellent accompaniment for sparkling wine, but should they actually taste of it? The answer is a resounding no. These actually have the fizz of prosecco – strange and vile at the same time.Taste: 0/10,texture: 3/10,novelty: 9/1098.Blueheat, TakisThese cylindrical Takis leave a luminescent blue powder on your fingers, smell of urinal cakes and taste of synthetic lime and chilli.Taste: 0/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 8/1097.Sweet andsaltybuttercaramel,PringlesA sweet crisp is a brave idea, but it only serves to confirm that they are meant to be savoury, rather than taste like a pat of butter and sugar.Taste: 1/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 9/1096.Bubbly andserrano, SavoursmithsWe must stop putting booze in crisps – especially ones that promise serrano ham but still end up tasting like flat prosecco.Taste: 1/10, Texture: 4/10, Novelty: 9/1095.Fried egg, TorresThe sulphurous smell that greets you when you open the pack is quite something. They taste so similar to a bite of a fried egg that they are almost guaranteed to bring on the egg ick.Taste: 2/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 9/1094.Truffle androsemary, SavoursmithsTruffle is a pungent flavour, as is rosemary – together they create an odd and overpowering combination of pure herbaceousness.Taste: 3/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 8/1093.Haggisand cracked black pepper,Taylor’sA hint of pepper hums through, but the haggis seems more marketing ploy than reality. Maybe that’s a blessing in disguise.Taste: 2/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 8/1092. Padronpeppers and salt,Mr Filbert’sPromises sophistication but lacks in delivery. Vegetal and vinegary are the lingering aftertastes.Taste: 2/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 8/1091.Hothoney, WalkersMore sweet honey than hot, this trendy flavour only serves to underscore the point that crisps should remain a savoury experience.Taste: 2/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 8/1090.MarmitecrispsView image in fullscreen‘You’re better off seeking out a Twiglet’ … Marmite crisps.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianAs the old adage goes: you either love it or you hate it. Except, these don’t taste of Marmite at all. You’re better off seeking out a Twiglet.Taste: 2/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 7/1089.Hotkickketchup, McCoy’sTastes like the stale, rubbery nubbin of ketchup you find crusted on the rim of the bottle, accompanied by a dash of pepper.Taste: 2/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 7/1088.Crunchips Xcutkebab, LorenzPromises hangover-curing doner meat on the packet, but a sad disappointment taste-wise. The only doner-like authenticity is the grease it leaves behind.Taste: 3/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 8/1087.Frenchstylechickentwister, PringlesA remarkable feat: these manage to taste of nothing at all. The moreish texture saves the day, dissolving on the tongue, but they might as well be marketed as Italian-style beef ragu.Taste: 2/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 6/1086.Lamb andmint, SeabrookMove over roast chicken, there’s a new Sunday lunch flavour on the market and it’s dull. Mainly minty rather than meaty.Taste: 2/10,texture: 3/10,novelty: 6/1085.BBQ, BretsFrench gourmand brand Brets has legions of fans, but their BBQ flavour smells more of the sauce than tastes of it.Taste: 2/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 5/1084.Hot chilli hoops, CofreshThe south Asian brand Cofresh should know better when it comes to chilli. These Hula Hoops knock-offs are tasty, but not hot enough.Taste: 3/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 4/1083.Honeydijon, Kettle ChipsThe honey overpowers the dijon here, threatening a dangerously sweet eating experience.Taste: 3/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 4/1082.Garlicand olive oil, LidlAll the garlic burn without the flavour, eating these crisps is a masochistic experience sure to linger on the taste buds and trail on the breath for hours to come.Taste: 2/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 7/1081.Roastox, RealWhat makes something taste like ox meat? In this case, a vague and underwhelming savouriness.Taste: 2/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 8/1080.Italian cheese and wine, SavoursmithsView image in fullscreen‘The Italian origins are a mystery’ … Savoursmiths’ Italian cheese and wine flavoured crisps.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianMercifully there is more cheese than wine here, although the Italian origins are a mystery.Taste: 2/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 8/1079.Jalapeño pepper, RealMildly spiced and subtly earthy, these taste more like the stem of a jalapeño than the thing itself.Taste: 3/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 7/1078. Yakitori, BretsConjuring Japanese meat skewers grilled on an open flame, but tasting like nondescript meat.Taste: 3/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 8/1077.Chippiesgravy, Golden WonderThe real star of these crisps is their fiendish texture; they’re chopped and fried into tiny shards, waiting to lodge themselves in your throat.Taste: 2/10,texture: 8/10,novelty: 7/1076.Glutenfreecurvies, SchärGluten-free Pringles knock-offs that underpromise on flavour but deliver a convincing texture.Taste: 3/10,texture: 8/10,novelty: 4/1075.Dragonsweetchilli, TakisCome for the Takis signature heat, stay for the strange, subtle sweetness that might tempt you to go back for more.Taste: 3/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 5/1074.Steak &peppercorn, Taylor’sThis has neither steak nor pepper to it. Like a ready salted that’s flirted with the idea of meat-eating.Taste: 2/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 5/1073.Sun dried tomato, WalkersClose to an actual ketchup flavour but still lacking the tangy sweetness of the bottled stuff.Taste: 3/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 5/1072.Mushroom, BretsSmelling like a can of soup, this mushroom flavour is convincingly fungal – for better or worse.Taste: 3/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 6/1071.Chilli and lime grills, CofreshOnce again, Cofresh fails to deliver on the chilli front, although there is a pleasantly mouth-watering citrus tang to the combination.Taste: 4/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 5/1070.Tomatoketchup, Golden WonderEdging ever closer to the Heinz ketchup golden standard, this variation tastes more like the stale remnants at the bottom of the bottle.Taste: 4/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 5/1069.Sweetchilli &sourcream, Kettle ChipsWhat this combination lacks in chilli it makes up for in the pleasantly cooling sensation of sour cream. It’s nothing on the Pringles standard though.Taste: 4/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 5/1068.Chorizo, InessenceIs there such a thing as tasting too meaty? This thick-cut crisp seems to argue yes, tasting overwhelmingly and somewhat repulsively of cured, fatty pork.Taste: 3/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 5/1067.Aberdeen Angus beef and Suffolkale, LidlPerhaps some alcohol is passable in a crisp flavour – the unobtrusive taste of ale lends these a pleasant savoury tang.Taste: 3/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 6/1066.Chicken curry, M&SMore like coronation chicken than chicken curry, but still a worthy effort, with lashings of turmeric.Taste: 3/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 6/1065.Thai stylegreencurry, Co-opThe most Thai thing about this flavour is the hint of coconut that comes through the otherwise salty taste. Still, not altogether disgusting.Taste: 3/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 6/1064.Thaisweetchicken, McCoy’sNot sure where the poultry comes into the equation, but there is a touch of sweetness mercifully balanced by a peppery heat.Taste: 4/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 4/1063.Roast beef, Monster MunchView image in fullscreen‘A textural marvel’ … Monster Munch’s roast beef crisps.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianNo match for the classic pickled onion Monster Munch, this maize-based treat is still a textural marvel, both crunchy and liable to dissolve on the tongue.Taste: 4/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 5/1062.BBQ loverspizza, PringlesThe “pizza” element remains a mystery, but the barbecue and a mild cheesiness comes through.Taste: 4/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 6/1061.Carolinareaper, Herr’sDefinitely more bark than bite here. The packet shows a scotch bonnet on fire, but the flavour profile is more peppery than scorching.Taste: 5/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 4/1060.Hotdogs, TaytoTheIrish brand Tayto has its loyal followers, but this frankfurter flavour is neither meaty nor salty enough.Taste: 5/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 6/1059.Sweetcorn, SeabrookSweet and strange is the only way to describe this crisp, which has recently come back on the market at the discount store Home Bargains.Taste: 4/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 8/1058.Wagyu beef and honey mustard, SavoursmithsMore mustard than beef hits the tongue here and you’re left wondering what exactly makes this “wagyu”?Taste: 4/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 8/1057.Redleicester Quavers, WalkersThe thinking person’s Quaver: a classy new take on a classic that tastes much the same as the original.Taste: 4/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 7/1056.Sticky glazed pork, M&SSlightly umami and somewhat sweet. A mild option for the meat lovers.Taste: 4/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 7/1055.Rib ‘n’saucy, Nik NaksI’m not sure what makes this “saucy”. Still, it has a nice umami tang and unique texture.Taste: 4/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 6/1054.Spiced venison with capersand fennel, Taste of GameThankfully, no game in sight here. Instead, this tastes of pepper and vinegar, with the capers adding a nice zing.Taste: 5/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 8/1053.Chipshopcurry, Golden WonderView image in fullscreen‘Curry sauce on the nose but absent from the palate.’Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianSmell is the sense that comes out on top here, with curry sauce on the nose but somewhat absent from the palate.Taste: 5/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 7/1052.Caviar, TorresConsidered the gold standard of luxury crisps, but in fact tastes like the breaded outer layer of a fish finger.Taste: 4/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 9/1051.Pecorino andsummertruffle, WaitroseWhat makes a truffle taste of summer? Eat these and you are unlikely to find out. The lingering flavour is cloying cheese.Taste: 4/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 7/1050.Dillpickle, Co-opSo acidic it’ll burn the roof of your mouth off, although the salty aftertaste is surprisingly moreish. One for the intrepid flavour explorers.Taste: 5/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 7/1049.Intensenacho, TakisThe cheese flavour here is nowhere near as “intense” as it should be. It will still leave your fingers coated in luminescent dust, though.Taste: 5/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 6/1048.Pickle, TorresErrs more on the side of a sweet than a salty pickle. Convincing, but could do with more vinegar for balance.Taste: 5/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 8/1047.Truffleandseasalt,TyrrellsAn overpowering, overwhelming taste of truffle. A smell that will linger for days.Taste: 5/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 7/1046.Smokedrib andanchochilli, WaitroseThe marketing copy is doing a lot of heavy lifting here, as there is neither smokiness nor rib present. But a pleasant, bacon-adjacent experience.Taste: 5/10,texture: 5/10,novelty: 6/1045.Hot ‘nhoneycheese curls, Herr’sDelivers an emphatic kick, as well as capitalising on the hot honey trend. Not sure about the cheese though.Taste: 5/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 8/1044.Pouletbraisé, BretsChicken is somewhat absent, but the slightly charred taste of a roast comes through.Taste: 5/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 7/1043.Saltandchillichicken, Golden WonderA similarly chicken-free experience, although with added salt to make it moreish.Taste: 5/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 8/1042.Britishham and hot mustard, M&SA nice nose-burning hit of mustard comes through with each mouthful, although the ham is so subtle it’s almost undetectable.Taste: 6/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 6/1041.Slow roasted beef, WalkersSlightly tangy and enjoyably savoury, these are more meaty than most crisps, although the oven-baked texture will suck all the moisture from your mouth.Taste: 6/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 6/1040. Smokedpaprika,TyrrellsMore smoke than paprika but the light fry and heavy crunch makes these very scoffable.Taste: 6/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 6/1039.Stickyteriyaki, WalkersMore sweetness than smoky teriyaki, although there is a hint of flame-grilled char still present.Taste: 6/10,texture: 4/10,novelty: 7/1038.Southern style BBQ, BuglesThese little ridged cones are a textural wonder and super moreish. Not sure, though, what makes the barbecue “southern style”.Taste: 6/10,texture: 10/10,novelty: 6/1037.Yellowmustard, McCoy’sAiming for the mildness of American mustard and leaving a lingering tang on the palate. Unusual and enticing.Taste: 6/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 8/1036.Chorizo and cider, Mr Filbert’sAn acceptable level of meatiness, but could do with the added acid of extra cider flavour.Taste: 6/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 7/1035.Texas BBQ sauce, PringlesFinally, a full smoky barbecue experience. All you need is a beer and someone burning a sausage to complete the scene.Taste: 6/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 7/1034.Scampifries, SmithsThis pub classic deserves its status thanks to its distinct crunch and puckering acidity.Taste: 7/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 7/1033.Flame grilled Aberdeen Angus, TaylorsWe’re getting closer to steak with the salty, charred flavour here, although it could do with added umami bite.Taste: 7/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 7/1032.Hot smoked paprika, TorresNot much heat, but the paprika does deliver a smoky barbecue sensation.Taste: 7/10,texture: 6/10,novelty: 7/1031.Chipshopcurrysauce, TaylorsDeeply ridged, super tangy and spiked with turmeric, these lack the flavour of your typical chip shop sauce, but they are salivatingly moreish.Taste: 7/10,texture: 8/10,novelty: 5/1030.Extra virginolive oil andserrano ham, M&SA convincing dupe of the Torres Iberian ham flavour (see below), but with a slightly synthetic aftertaste.Taste: 7/10,texture: 8/10,novelty: 7/1029.Masalachicken, WalkersWe’re nearing real curry flavour here, although it’s more curry leaf than layered spice.Taste: 7/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 8/1028. Sizzlingkingprawn, McCoy’sA gourmet prawn cocktail with added salt, but sadly no sizzle.Taste: 7/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 7/1027.Worcester sauce, M&SView image in fullscreen‘So tangy it’ll make your mouth water.’Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianOne for the thrill-seekers: so tangy it’ll make your mouth water and cheeks burn.Taste: 7/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 8/1026.Hotsmokin’ BBQribs, PringlesAt last, some actual heat. Tongue-scorching chilli action only somewhat subdued by the smoky barbecue.Taste: 7/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 8/1025.Springonion, TaytoOnly the lightest hint of onion, combined with a thicker-cut Tayto texture. A classy choice for cheese and onion fans looking to try something new.Taste: 7/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 5/1024.Vinegar, TorresA worthy effort to consciously uncouple salt and vinegar, which mainly serves as a reminder of why they should remain together.Taste: 7/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 8/1023.Blackgarlicandsourcream,TyrrellsA lovely balance of garlic burn and creamy coolness. Although beware of your breath after eating.Taste: 7/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 8/1022.Tigerprawn,chilli andlime, Brown BagAn even classier take on prawn cocktail, with that zingy hint of lime making these extra moreish.Taste: 7/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 8/1021.Maxstronghotchickenwings, WalkersMuch like the Pringles, these have an actual kick to them, along with the vague taste of chicken. A pleasant combination.Taste: 7/10,texture: 8/10,novelty: 9/1020.Tomatoketchup, WalkersHats off to Walkers for making these taste like a bottle of Heinz dumped over a bag of ready salted.Taste: 8/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 8/1019.Hotcheeseandchilli, PringlesEven hotter than the hot smokin’ BBQ ribs: mouth-numbingly spicy, blended with pungently overpowering cheese. Not for the faint-hearted.Taste: 8/10,texture: 7/10,novelty: 7/1018.Fuego, TakisThe classic Takis flavour – full of preservatives, artificial colouring and a mouth-watering heat that somehow keeps you coming back for more. The perfect hangover crisp.Taste: 8/10,texture: 8/10,novelty: 8/1017.Beef andonion, TaytoA hardy pub crisp, with enough onion and meaty umami flavour to head off any accompanying drink.Taste: 8/10,texture: 8/10,novelty: 7/1016.Bleu d’auvergne PDO, BretsThese come with the authentic pong and pleasantly salty tang of blue cheese.
