title: UK shares findings of damning climate crisis national security report suppressed under Starmer | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: El Niño poses critical threat to nations’ defences, says Ed Miliband in presentation to global foreign ministers
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: El Niño poses critical threat to nations’ defences, says Ed Miliband in presentation to global foreign ministers
Content: Miliband at the UN security council on Wednesday. The UK’s foreign secretary later briefed fellow foreign ministers about the UK climate report.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMiliband at the UN security council on Wednesday. The UK’s foreign secretary later briefed fellow foreign ministers about the UK climate report.Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty ImagesClimate crisisUK shares findings of damning climate crisis national security report suppressed under StarmerEl Niño poses critical threat to nations’ defences, says Ed Miliband in presentation to global foreign ministersFiona HarveyEnvironment editorWed 23 Sep 2026 17.21 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK has warned countries around the world that the climate and nature crises and the coming El Niño threaten their national security and defence, presenting foreign ministries with the findings of an explosive report suppressed under Keir Starmer.Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, made a presentation to the foreign ministers of the EU as well as Kenya and other countries on Wednesday night at a private meeting during the UN general assembly in New York, based on thereport by the UK’s spy chiefsthat found the collapse of natural systems around the world would lead to conflict, migration and food shortages.Miliband told the meeting, the first such discussion among foreign ministers, that thecoming El Niño, which has beensupercharged by climate breakdown, would test the world’s food systems as never before.“We face an El Niño that is already set to be the most intense in living memory,” he said. “This will intensify climate shocks that compound and cascade across borders, threatening food and water security, displacing communities, putting pressure on markets and scarring economies.”el nino deaths mapThis year’s heatwaves,bad harvestsandfood price inflationshowed governments what they were in for, he said, and must be dealt with at the highest levels.“Climate change and nature loss have never been issues for climate and environment ministers alone,” he said. “They are defining challenges for our citizens, our economies, our foreign policy and our national security.”With the backing of Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, Miliband presented the research that found the collapse of global ecosystems such as in the Amazon and Congo rainforests, driven by the climate crisis and the destruction of nature, would have impacts on national security around the world.Thejoint intelligence committee (JIC) report, revealed by the Guardian, was scheduled to be published last October, but was suppressed on the eve of its launch by Downing Street. Aredacted version was issuedin January under the Freedom of Information Act, but ministers have continued to resist calls for the full report to be made public.Richard Nugee, a retired general and security expert, told the Guardian governments must treat the climate as they would other threats to national security, such as sabotage by hostile states.“If a bridge is washed away, it has the same impact whether it’s done by [a foreign power] or the climate,” he said. “The climate crisis will affect food security, energy security, water security, and lead to migration and potentially the recruitment of farmers to [terrorist organisations such as] Isis. Countries should absolutely be treating this as a national security issue.”He said it was not surprising that the JIC report was suppressed and redacted, as it was “very rare” for security reports to be published.El Niño food insecurity chartMiliband will appoint a new special representative for climate security, as well as a new ministerial taskforce on “the national security and resilience risks of a changing climate and nature loss”, with military and security experts as well as climate scientists.He also announced £330m for theGlobal Environment Facility, the main international fund for protecting nature, that will go towards protecting forests, oceans and other critical ecosystems in developing countries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe closed-door meeting among foreign ministers was convened after Miliband made apublic speechon Monday at the UN general assembly that touched on the links between the climate and national security. Soon after taking office in July, the former energy secretary told the Guardian he wouldput the climate at the heart of UK foreign policy.On Wednesday night, Miliband said: “The countries fit for the future will be those that see climate and nature as intrinsic to economic and national security. Countries that anticipate risks and invest in resilience before crises hit.“Countries that seize the incredible opportunities the clean energy transition presents. Countries that don’t just see the connections but act on them.”He added: “That is why the UK is placing climate and nature security at the heart of our national security and foreign policy decision-making.”Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, who has campaigned for the JIC report to be made public, said: “It’s good that the foreign secretary is presenting the findings of this crucial report to ministers from other governments.“But it begs the question, why are MPs in this country still being denied access to the full report? And, most importantly, why has our government still not published its response to how it will address the stark findings?”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisEd MilibandUnited NationsEl Niño southern oscillationEnvironment policyForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Millions in England unaware they have ‘silent killer’ condition, research reveals | High blood pressure | The Guardian
description: Approach to treating high blood pressure ‘not fit for purpose’, say researchers, with 59% of cases undiagnosed
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Approach to treating high blood pressure ‘not fit for purpose’, say researchers, with 59% of cases undiagnosed
Content: According to a new study by Oxford University, only half of people being treated by their GP for high blood pressure have it under control.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PAView image in fullscreenAccording to a new study by Oxford University, only half of people being treated by their GP for high blood pressure have it under control.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PAHigh blood pressureMillions in England unaware they have ‘silent killer’ condition, research revealsApproach to treating high blood pressure ‘not fit for purpose’, say researchers, with 59% of cases undiagnosedAndrew GregoryandWill ParmanWed 23 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnly half of people being treated by a GP for high blood pressure in England have it under control, and millions more are completely unaware they have the “silent killer” condition, research reveals.Most people with hypertension (59%) are in the dark and undiagnosed, raising their risk of stroke, heart attack and early death, according to the largest ever study of its kind.Even among those who are diagnosed and receiving medication via their family doctor, in 50% of cases their blood pressure is out of control, the Oxford University study of 1.4 million adults suggests.Researchers said the findings,published in journal BMJ Public Health, suggested the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure in England was “not fit for purpose”.The study used data from theOur Future Health programmeand looked at people enrolled between 2022 and 2025 with high blood pressure, defined as 140/90 mmHg or higher.‘People should not feel guilty’: weekend lie-in may be good for you, experts sayRead moreResearchers calculated that more than a third of adults (37%) had high blood pressure, with six in 10 of these oblivious to their condition.Hypertension was almost 50% more common in men than women (42% compared with 29% across all ages), and more common in older people, according to the research.Despite substantial improvements in high blood pressure detection and control during the 2000s, progress had plateaued since about 2011, the researchers said.There were also “indications of worsening trends following the Covid-19 pandemic, possibly because disruptions to healthcare delivery may have had lasting effects”.Wenyu Liu, a medical statistician at Oxford PopulationHealthand lead author of the study, said: “While hypertension is largely a ‘silent killer’, the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure is not fit for purpose.“Our study highlights the prevalence of hypertension across demographics. This underscores the need for population-wide prevention strategies alongside targeted treatment for people at high cardiovascular risk.”The researchers said “the most striking finding” of the study was the high absolute number and the high proportion of people with undiagnosed hypertension. It also found only half of adults with high blood pressure treated by a GP were adequately controlled.Dr Iain Turnbull, a GP, deputy chief medical officer at Our Future Health and a clinical research fellow at Oxford Population Health, said it was not clear why 50% of patients who said they were taking blood pressure-lowering drugs had uncontrolled hypertension.“Blood pressure varies considerably between people, and some people need changes in dose or two or more different medicines before it is brought under control. Other health conditions and medications can affect blood pressure, too.AI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggestsRead more“There are also practical and social factors: side effects, complicated treatment regimens and competing health or life pressures can make medicines difficult to take consistently. Weight, diet, salt intake, alcohol and physical activity can also influence blood pressure.“So a high reading can have many explanations and shouldn’t be seen simply as a reflection of what an individual patient or healthcare professional has done.“There are also some important caveats … we did not have prescribing records available to independently confirm medication use, and a blood pressure measurement on one day does not necessarily represent someone’s usual blood pressure.“Even with those caveats, I wouldn’t regard 50% as a satisfactory figure. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of stroke and heart disease, and bringing it under control reduces that risk.”Prof Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, said the study “paints a concerning picture of the scale of undetected high blood pressure in the UK, and the challenges of keeping blood pressure under control in those already receiving treatment”.“Better detection and treatment could help tens of thousands of people to avoid a preventable heart attack and stroke,” he added. “But to achieve this, we will need to rethink how we identify, treat and support those at risk so that blood pressure checks and effective treatment can benefit everyone.”Explore more on these topicsHigh blood pressureStrokeHeart attackHeart diseaseHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham signals he may lift ban on alcohol in football stands | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Prime minister says measure is discriminatory when fans of other sports are not similarly restricted
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Prime minister says measure is discriminatory when fans of other sports are not similarly restricted
Content: Andy Burnham with Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, at Everton’s stadium last week.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, at Everton’s stadium last week.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesSoccerAndy Burnham signals he may lift ban on alcohol in football standsPrime minister says measure is discriminatory when fans of other sports are not similarly restrictedPippa CrerarandTom GarryWed 23 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has signalled he may lift the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, suggesting it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports.The prime minister, a committedEverton fanwho still attends matches, said there was a case for trialling an end to the ban to bring football in line with rugby and cricket.The move was welcomed by the Football Supporters’ Association and the English Football League, but police warned it would be “incredibly rash” to make changes without considering their impact on safety.Burnham has long opposed the ban, saying it is discriminatory and out of date, harking back to an era when football violence was fuelled by drinking within view of the pitch.Asked by reporters on the planeto New Yorkabout lifting a ban, Burnham said: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination.“There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”The Sporting Events (Control ofAlcoholetc) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales.The fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the ban to be re-examined and suggested piloting the sale of alcohol within sight of the pitch in lower-tier English football.A spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit, which coordinates football policing policy in England and Wales, said: “The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.“Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor report [of 1990 into the causes of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster] for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster. It would be incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area.”A spokesperson for the English Football League said it would be “receptive” to a review of legislation that “was introduced more than 40 years ago and has not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding”.Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters’ Association, said: “The FSA has always argued that it’s unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We welcome the prime minister’s comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed. We look forward to being part of that consultation.”Supporters at Women’s Super League and WSL2 matches have been permitted to drink alcohol in view of the pitch since the start of this season, after a successful 18-month trial period led to a change to the WSL’s regulations this summer, allowing clubs – but not obliging them – to give fans that option.Since that rule change, 25 of the 26 clubs across the two divisions of English women’s football have decided to take up the option at all of their home games. The only exception is Brighton & Hove Albion’s home matches at Crawley’s Broadfield Stadium, but Brighton have permitted fans to drink in view of the pitch when the team play their home matches at the Amex Stadium, such as last Sunday when they hosted Aston Villa. Women’s matches have typically seen fewer incidents of crowd trouble.Explore more on these topicsFootballAlcoholPoliceAndy BurnhamLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Pupils to be offered vocational GCSEs in radical shake-up of system in England | GCSEs | The Guardian
description: Courses such as finance and construction form part of PM’s push for education ‘that offers a path for everybody’
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Courses such as finance and construction form part of PM’s push for education ‘that offers a path for everybody’
Content: The new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England.Photograph: Peter Muller/Getty Images/Image SourceView image in fullscreenThe new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England.Photograph: Peter Muller/Getty Images/Image SourceGCSEsPupils to be offered vocational GCSEs in radical shake-up of system in EnglandCourses such as finance and construction form part of PM’s push for education ‘that offers a path for everybody’Richard AdamsandSally WealeWed 23 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeenagers are to be offered a range of new vocational GCSEs under a radical shake-up of the school system inEnglanddesigned to tackle a crisis that has left nearly a million young people out of work or training.From 2029, pupils will be able to supplement compulsory GCSE subjects such as English, maths and sciences with courses such as construction, creative media production and child development, marking the biggest changes to the qualification for more than a decade.The Department for Education (DfE) said the newGCSEswould be two-year courses taken in year 10 and 11, “with nationally set content, grading and assessment” and regulated by Ofqual, England’s qualifications watchdog, to the same standards as academic GCSEs.England’s teenagers outperform peers in most countries in maths, reading and scienceRead moreThe courses are part of an effort by Andy Burnham to fulfil his pledge of “an education system that offers a path for everybody, academic and technical, in equal balance”, madethe day after his electionas MP for Makerfield.Announcing the new courses, the prime minister said: “We’ve all heard someone say ‘school wasn’t really for me’ because they were not given the chance to study vocational courses as well as traditional subjects.“That one-size-fits-all approach isn’t working, so we’re building an education system that values both academic and technical paths. I want to give all young people across Britain the hope that their future will be brighter, whether it starts at university or not.”Whitehall sources said the courses were expected to be offered from September 2029 but that the education secretary, Lucy Powell, wanted to move more quickly if possible, with schools given the option to add vocational GCSEs to their existing subjects.Powell said: “Time and again young people, parents and employers tell me they want schools to do more to help them understand and prepare for the jobs of the future. Our new vocational GCSEs will give young people a stronger connection to the careers and industries shaping our economy, helping them discover and develop their talents while maintaining high standards across our education system.“This is not about creating different routes for different children. It is about ensuring every child has access to a rich and ambitious education that opens doors, creates opportunity and prepares them for life beyond the classroom.”View image in fullscreenThe new courses would be designed to lead into further study including A-levels.Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesThe change is part of a range of measures that Burnham has announced since coming to power to tackle the Neets crisis, with a call to “value the hard hat as much as the graduation cap”. It follows plans togive local businesses a rolein setting curriculums in their areas.In a review published in May, Alan Milburn said that without significant change the number of young people not in work or education couldgrow by 25%by the early 2030s, opening up a “generational fault line” between the young and old.Critics, however, say the focus on technical education risks widening the gap between richer and poorer children. Sam Freedman, a policy adviser to Michael Gove when he was education secretary,wrote last month: “The more we ration a full set of academic GCSEs to children from better-off families, the more we will bake in existing inequalities.”The shadow education secretary, Laura Trott, said the courses would mean lowered expectations for disadvantaged children who had benefited most from high standards.“Labour are sabotaging young people’s futures,” she said. “Just weeks after thelatest Pisa resultsshowed England’s pupils climbing into the world’s top 10 for reading, maths and science, they want to rip up the system and review existing GCSEs.“Soaring up international league tables didn’t happen by accident. It followed years of evidence-led reform built around knowledge, rigour and high expectations.Labourrisks throwing that progress away and if English, maths and science become merely a ‘common entitlement’, not a requirement for new qualifications, we risk repeating the mistakes of the past.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe DfE said the subjects offered could include management and finance, creative media production, digital technology and building and construction, and would be designed to lead into further study including A-levels.The new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England, with travel and tourism and health and care courses among the most popular. About 350,000 technical awards and certificates were issued this year, compared with more than 5m GCSEs.Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needsRead moreSchool leaders said the success of the new courses would depend on having the resources and staffing to teach specialist subjects.The general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, Pepe Di’Iasio, said: “Reshaping and rebadging vocational and technical qualifications is well intentioned but will not in itself address the barriers to more young people taking these subjects. Reform needs to be accompanied by a strategy to ensure that schools have the staffing and resources to deliver them, and a campaign to raise public awareness of vocational and technical routes.”The general secretary of the National Education Union, Daniel Kebede, agreed. “These proposed changes will fall at the first hurdle unless there is sufficient investment in schools and the workforce,” he said.The general secretary of the NAHT school leaders’ union, Paul Whiteman, said: “In recent years, the content behind too many GCSEs became unwieldy and the over-reliance on final exams did not play to the strengths of all students.“It will be crucial these pitfalls are avoided in developing these qualifications and that the government works closely with educators, local leaders and employers to ensure they offer high-quality learning which sets young people up for future training, education or employment.”The government has also said it will launch a “national mission” by calling on employers to provide an additional 200,000 work experience placements to give young people exposure to the workplace by age 16. No 10 North will offer work experience for students aged 14 to 16 this academic year.Explore more on these topicsGCSEsVocational educationEducation policyLabourSecondary schoolsSchoolsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 years | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chances
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Andy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chances
Content: A YouGov poll conducted in June found Labour vowing to seek membership of the EU would help unite progressive voters behind the party.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA YouGov poll conducted in June found Labour vowing to seek membership of the EU would help unite progressive voters behind the party.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press/ShutterstockBrexitTony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 yearsAndy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chancesKiran StaceyPolicy editorWed 23 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain should work towards rejoining the EU in the next decade, Tony Blair has said, adding to growing pressure onAndy Burnhamto abandon Labour’s reluctance to revisit the 2016 referendum.The former prime minister has urged Burnham to use his 10-year plan in November to put the country’s membership of the union back on the table, a decade after it voted to leave.In a paper entitled A Path to Rejoining a Reformed Europe, theTony BlairInstitute (TBI) calls for the UK to accept free movement of people and make a financial contribution as the price of entry.The intervention comes after Burnhamdeclined to rule outpromising to rejoin the EU in the next Labour manifesto, though it also threatens to reopen the deep rifts caused by the vote 10 years ago.In a foreword to the paper, Blair argues: “Britain should signal an intention if the terms are right to enter into a structured formal relationship with Europe and initiate a process of negotiation where everything is on the table but nothing agreed until everything is agreed.”TBI researchers say in the paper itself: “Over the next decade, Britain should work towards the ambition of rejoining a significantly reformed EU.”View image in fullscreenTony Blair speaking at a Board of Peace conference in New York on Wednesday.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesBlair is the latest in a series of Labour figures to back rejoining the EU. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary,has calledthe Brexit vote a “catastrophic mistake” and said the party should aim to rejoin the bloc, while Burnham himselftold the Guardianlast year: “I hope in my lifetime I see this country rejoin the European Union.”But Burnham has said he does not wish to pursue membership of the union in the near term. When asked by reporters this week if it could be in the next election manifesto, he said it was a question “for another day”.Others are sceptical of the electoral wisdom of giving the appearance that the party wants to undo the result of the 2016 referendum, especially in areas of the country where Reform UK has made inroads in recent years.Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary,dismissed the ideaearlier this year as she warned against “reopening the circular arguments that we ended up in as a country”.However, pollsters suggestLabourcould benefit electorally by promising to rejoin. A new megapoll conducted by YouGov on behalf of the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain suggests the party could more than double its seat total if it goes into the next election promising to rejoin.The survey of more than 13,000 people, undertaken in June before Burnham became prime minister, found that a pledge to seek membership would help unite progressive voters behind Labour while doing nothing to boost Reform’s vote.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe results suggested the move could take Labour from a projected 136 seats to 321 – though those totals will have changed since Burnham came to office, which has given the party a poll lead for the first time in months.The TBI paper calls for Britain to try to accelerate European market reforms using possible re-entry as leverage. It argues that pro-reformers in Brussels would have a significant incentive to work with Britain on a project to make the EU more economically liberal and to reform its regulations on energy and technology.It adds that Burnham should scrap the government’s red lines of not rejoining, not allowing free movement and not entering the single market or a customs union. The paper argues that the prime minister should replace them with a single promise only to sign up to rules and initiatives that prove of economic or strategic benefit to the UK.TBI has advocated in recent years for the UK to slow down its push to achieve net zero carbon emissions and is a heavy backer of increased use of artificial intelligence in government.Its policy positionshave brought scrutinyon some of the institute’s most high-profile funders, who include the technology billionaire Larry Ellison, and its clients, which include the government of Saudi Arabia.Explore more on these topicsBrexitTony BlairAndy BurnhamLabourForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Tories target universal credit claimants in plan condemned as ‘fast track to poverty’ | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Proposals aim to push people into work, but charities say families are still paying price of austerity cuts and rise in cost of living
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Proposals aim to push people into work, but charities say families are still paying price of austerity cuts and rise in cost of living
Content: Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said welfare had to be a safety net, ‘not a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered’.Photograph: Jacob King/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said welfare had to be a safety net, ‘not a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered’.Photograph: Jacob King/PAConservativesTories target universal credit claimants in plan condemned as ‘fast track to poverty’Proposals aim to push people into work, but charities say families are still paying price of austerity cuts and rise in cost of livingPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentWed 23 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople claiming universal credit (UC) would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan condemned by one charity as “a fast track to increased poverty”.Under the proposals, those who receive this “subsistence allowance” would have it paid into a dedicated debit card that would prevent from them buying alcohol or tobacco, based on an Australian system that was scrappedafter trials foundlimited evidence it changed behaviour.While the proposals are billed by theConservativesas a way to push people into work, the poverty charity Trussell said trimming incomes so that people struggled with rent and transport was likely to make it even harder for them to find and keep a job.Pay rent, eat or keep warm? Growing numbers face hard choices as housing benefit gap growsRead moreUnder the plan, UC claimants would receive the full amount to which they are entitled for six months, but after this point the sum would be tied to how long they have worked at a level that triggers national insurance payments.This would have to happen for at least twice as long as the claimant period, meaning someone who has amassed two years of NI payments would qualify for another 12 months of full UC, before falling to the lower rate.Set at 70% of the standard amount, this would leave a single claimant aged under 25 living on £237 a month, or just over £7.50 a day. For a couple aged 25 or over, under the plan they would lose £200 a month, falling to £466 in total.Anyone placed on the reduced level would have their UC payments put on to a “back to work card”, which would block purchases of alcohol, tobacco and gambling, or cash withdrawals.The plan would exclude those already in work – about a third of UC claimants have jobs – and those who are assessed as having what is called limited capability for work and work-related activity, because of a health condition or disability. Separate payments connected to housing or dependant children would be unaffected.The Conservatives said the plan would affect about 350,000 people in England, Scotland and Wales and save £538m a year.Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the aim was to be “tough on those who exploit the system”, adding: “Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered.”The party argues that in some countries such as Germany and the Netherlands, unemployment payments are contingent on sufficient contributions having been made and can be time-limited.Those payments, however, are notably more generous and can be between 60% and 70% of someone’s previous monthly wage. There is also separate support for those who have not paid in sufficiently, with single people in Germany receiving about £480 a month.Sara Ogilvie, the director of policy at ChildPovertyAction Group, said: “The reality is that families are still paying the price of austerity cuts to our social security safety net. With living costs continuing to rise, these proposals are a fast track to increased poverty and are the last thing people need as they try to get back on their feet.”Helen Barnard, the head of policy at Trussell, called the idea “deeply misguided”, saying UC already had strong conditions to ensure people seek work.She said: “If you’re struggling to afford food and rent, childcare or the bus fare to an interview, then finding and keeping a job becomes harder not easier. Cutting support would only make things worse.”Explore more on these topicsConservativesUniversal creditWelfareBenefitsPovertynewsShareReuse this content

title: Three charged with assault after anti-migration protests in Hampshire | UK news | The Guardian
description: Hundreds gathered on Tuesday night in anticipation of a small boat arriving in Gosport
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Hundreds gathered on Tuesday night in anticipation of a small boat arriving in Gosport
Content: Police faced protesters in Gosport on Tuesday night.Photograph: Lab Mo/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice faced protesters in Gosport on Tuesday night.Photograph: Lab Mo/SOPA Images/ShutterstockUK newsThree charged with assault after anti-migration protests in HampshireHundreds gathered on Tuesday night in anticipation of a small boat arriving in GosportHarry CockburnWed 23 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 17.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree people have been charged in connection with anti-migrant protests that drew hundreds of demonstrators to a marina in Hampshire on Tuesday night.Six people were arrested by police, as anti-migrant activists who mistakenly believed a small boat was due to arrive at Gosport gathered in an attempt to disrupt the arrival of any asylum seekers.Those charged are Shannon Dodds, 32, of Leonard Road in Gosport, who has been charged with two counts of assault by beating of an emergency worker, Sally Pearson, 31, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with assault by beating of an emergency worker and a racially aggravated public order offence, and Toby Matthews, 33, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with common assault of an emergency worker.Dodds and Pearson have been remanded in custody and will appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on Thursday 24 September.Matthews was bailed but must appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 9 November.Hampshire police said in addition to these charges, a 19-year-old man and a 36-year-old man from Salisbury who were arrested on suspicion of aggravated trespass had been bailed with conditions until 22 December while inquiries continued.They added: “A 67-year-old man from Gosport was also given a fixed-penalty notice for driving without due care and attention. He was also arrested on suspicion of assaulting an emergency worker and has been bailed with conditions until 22 December while enquiries continue.”The protests in Gosport followed a social media push by far-right activist Daniel Thomas, who styles himself Danny Tommo, who called for action to disrupt the potential arrival of asylum seekers as he livestreamed efforts to apprehend small boats crossing the channel to more than 100,000 followers on Tuesday afternoon.He is also now facing a police inquiry after he used a knife to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard.His livestream showed him approaching an empty dinghy which had contained about 50 migrants who had reportedly left from a beach in Normandy. They had been picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area, but a French official then got on to the craft.The footage showed Thomas taking out a knife and slashing at the vessel in the channel, shouting at the French rescue worker: “Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more.”“Traitor,” Thomas shouted as his boat motored away.The protesters in Gosport, many of whom wore black clothing and face coverings, chanted “send them back”, wrongly assuming the boat would arrive on the Hampshire coast.Instead of heading for Gosport, the RNLI transferred the asylum seekers to a Border Force vessel which landed in Dover early on Wednesday.Hampshire police said they had deployed officers to the town on Tuesday evening “to help facilitate peaceful protest, ensure the safety of the local community and support partners in the event of any emergency at sea”.A Home Office spokesperson said: “We have been clear that groups creating fear and intimidating communities cannot be allowed to operate with impunity.“Police should make full use of the powers available to them to deal robustly with criminality and ensure communities, staff and those in their care are protected.”Campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the incident as “disgusting” ina post on X, and said Thomas’s supporters in Gosport had blocked ambulances during the protests.The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, was forced to order an urgent security review after the failure by the Border Force to intercept two other migrant boats in two days before they reached the Kentish coast this week.She said on Wednesday: “This was not acceptable. Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare. But even one is one too many.“The new tactics adopted by the smugglers, like launches from much further west in France, are a reminder of two things. Firstly, these gangs have no regard for human life. They are putting people on increasingly long and dangerous crossings.“Secondly, our efforts are having an impact. We are making it much harder for gangs to launch vessels, forcing them to change their approach, and as a result we are significantly reducing the numbers coming here by small boat.”The total number of migrants who have crossed the Channel by boat so far this year is 17,784, according to the government – a figure 45% lower than at the same point last year.The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Tuesday’s “chaos” showed the UK was seeing “illegal immigrants crossing at will over ever larger distances and in ever larger boats”.“This latest fiasco shows that the French are not even trying to stop the illegal immigrants’ boats,” he added.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Michael Kiwanuka says he faces ‘long, tough journey’ to recovery from stroke | Music | The Guardian
description: Mercury prize-winner reveals ‘quite severe’ bleed was why he’d missed support slots with Mumford & Sons this year
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Mercury prize-winner reveals ‘quite severe’ bleed was why he’d missed support slots with Mumford & Sons this year
Content: Michael Kiwanuka onstage at London’s Eventim Apollo in Hammersmith on 10 March 2025.Photograph: Joseph Okpako/WireImageView image in fullscreenMichael Kiwanuka onstage at London’s Eventim Apollo in Hammersmith on 10 March 2025.Photograph: Joseph Okpako/WireImageMusicMichael Kiwanuka says he faces ‘long, tough journey’ to recovery from strokeMercury prize-winner reveals ‘quite severe’ bleed was why he’d missed support slots with Mumford & Sons this yearHarry CockburnWed 23 Sep 2026 16.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British singer-songwriterMichael Kiwanukahas said he has suffered a stroke and faces a “long tough journey” on the road to recovery.The 39-year-old singer from London, whose hits include Cold Little Heart and Home Again, said the “quite severe” bleed in his brain was the reason he had missed some tour dates this year when he was due to support Mumford & Sons, and that the stroke had been brought on by high blood pressure.Kiwanuka, who won the 2020 Mercury prize, said inan Instagram postpromoting his new album, recorded before the stroke, that there was still “a lot of rehab to be done”.He said: “I’m very happy to be announcing to you my new album Fudge. I’m especially happy because the last few months I’ve been battling some health problems which would heavily hinder and get in the way of me making music for the foreseeable future.“A few months ago I suffered a stroke brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure,” the post reads. “It’s a long journey recovering from a stroke, which is why I missed some gigs recently out in the US, but I look forward to seeing you all soon.”He added: “I’m not sure when I’ll be back out on the road or what that will look like, the brain injury I suffered was quite severe.”Describing the period as “a difficult few months”, he said he had a “long tough journey ahead, but I’m fighting to get better”.Millions in England unaware they have ‘silent killer’ condition, research revealsRead moreHe also thanked the “incredible” NHS staff who have cared for him.He said: “This has definitely been one of the toughest challenges I’ve faced and I’ll be happy to be on the other side of it when the time comes.“Until then I wish you all well and look forward to seeing you further down the road.”The news has prompted an outpouring of support from fans, artists and other celebrities.6 Music presenter Lauren Laverne responded: “So sorry to read this, Michael. What a time you must have had. Really glad you have good care and wishing you a full recovery asap. One day at a time. Xx.”Singers Olivia Dean and Self Esteem, comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Radiohead guitarist Ed O’Brien also sent supportive messages.Kiwanuka released his debut album, Home Again, in 2012, followed by his chart-topping record, Love & Hate, in 2016.The singer said more details on his forthcoming album Fudge will be announced this week.Explore more on these topicsMusicMichael KiwanukaStrokeMercury prize 2020newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It sent a message’: anti-migrant feeling pervades Hampshire town where hundreds protested | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Far-right posters go up around Gosport, but some residents say there’s ‘another side’ to life in the town
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Far-right posters go up around Gosport, but some residents say there’s ‘another side’ to life in the town
Content: An anti-immigration sticker and poster on a lamppost in Gosport.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn anti-immigration sticker and poster on a lamppost in Gosport.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianImmigration and asylum‘It sent a message’: anti-migrant feeling pervades Hampshire town where hundreds protestedFar-right posters go up around Gosport, but some residents say there’s ‘another side’ to life in the townBen QuinnPolitical correspondentWed 23 Sep 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlan Dale was in two minds as he gazed across at Portsmouth harbour in the late September sunshine and reflected on the latest show of force by far-right activists on the south coast against a supposed disembarkation of asylum seekers.A stone’s throw away, masked followers of the anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas had been cheered on Tuesday night by hundreds of people, many of them local, who had gathered after social media posts suggested authorities planned to land the migrants in the nearby town of Gosport.The gathering had at least “sent a message”, said Dale, a retired Royal Navy veteran who echoed a common local sentiment that Gosport and Britain more widely had changed, and that migrants were being put “to the front of the queue” for public services.“Is it going to be heard though? I don’t think so. It’s almost like the government is sticking its fingers in its ears and saying: ‘We are not listening to you.’”View image in fullscreenAlan Dale, a Royal Navy veteran, in Gosport’s Falkland Gardens.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAs for the masked vigilantes who answered the call from Thomas – who calls himself “Danny Tommo” and was filmed earlier in the dayusing a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channelwhile a rescue worker was onboard – Dale admitted to feeling uncomfortable about their face coverings, but insisted: “With any protest you are always going to get troublemakers.”Many local people from a block of flats close to Gosport’s marina indeed appeared have swelled the numbers of those who turned up in what senior Reform UK figures, including theHampshireMP and former home secretary Suella Braverman, had cheered on as a show of “people power”.But a far-right presence – and hostility towards migrants – was discernible in the town in a part of England where organised activists from their ranks have been building links for a number of years with anti-migrant campaigns.Most shockingly to outsiders unfamiliar with the depth of vitriol towards migrants among some here, children had been seen and heard chanting “let them drown” into a megaphone.Red and white far-right posters emblazoned with the word “resistance” and slogans such as “protecting our children’s future” were plastered on lampposts around the bench where Dale sat in Gosport’s Falkland Gardens.At least two outsiders were among thesix people arrested on Tuesday night by police: a 19-year-old and a 36-year-old, both from Salisbury, who were detained on suspicion of aggravated trespass.In the end, the small boat carrying 51 people docked in Dover, Kent, at about 12.30am on Wednesday after spending 33 hours at sea.While there was no plan to land them in Gosport, Home Office sources have insisted, the events have once again placed Thomas in the spotlight – even as he faces the prospect of a police inquiry into his knife-wielding at sea – and saw a blurring of the lines between his activities and local protesters who were praised by Reform.View image in fullscreenGosport churchgoer Tyler Palmer said fearmongering on social media was having a negative impact on local people.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian“It’s a depressing situation that so many people turned up but there is another side here as well and you have people in Portsmouth who are organising gigs to raise funds for the RNLI [Royal National Lifeboat Institution],” said a local man who had worked with young people in the area where the protest took place but declined to give his name.He also cited the fact that Gosport’s nearby Rowner area had been allocated money – as much as £20m – from thegovernment’s Pride in Place initiative, a long-term strategic effort launched under Keir Starmer’s premiership to counter the electoral threat posed by rising nationalism and the far right in areas where such sentiment finds some sympathy.A diversity of views could be found again on Wednesday morning among those gathered for a Bible study group inside Gosport’s Holy Trinity church, a short stroll from the seafront.They included the retired priest Margaret Hay, who said the first thought that came to her mind was that Jesus was an immigrant too, while at least one other participant voiced discomfort that many of those crossing the Channel appeared to be men.The group also included Tyler Palmer, a young churchgoer who watched the protests on Tuesday night from the edge of the crowd.“We’ve always been diverse here in Gosport and it’s forgotten. Turkish sailors who fought alongside us in the second world war were housed here,” he said.“But we’re also a naval town and people are very proud. They’re reading things that scare them – whether that’s GB News or fearmongering on social media.“These are everyday people, your plumbers, your plasterers, who you wouldn’t expect to be at protests.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumFar rightHampshireMigrationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Republican jitters grow as unpopular Trump fuels midterm ‘bloodbath’ fears | Republicans | The Guardian
description: Iran war, rising prices and president’s low ratings give Democrats advantage, but Republicans have poured cash into key races – could it be decisive?
Author: Chris Stein
Headline: Iran war, rising prices and president’s low ratings give Democrats advantage, but Republicans have poured cash into key races – could it be decisive?
Content: Trump attends a rally for Michael Whatley, the Republican Senate candidate in North Carolina, in Gastonia last week.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenTrump attends a rally for Michael Whatley, the Republican Senate candidate in North Carolina, in Gastonia last week.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersRepublicansRepublican jitters grow as unpopular Trump fuels midterm ‘bloodbath’ fearsIran war, rising prices and president’s low ratings give Democrats advantage, but Republicans have poured cash into key races – could it be decisive?Sign up for The Stakes 2026: your weekly guide to the US midtermsChris Steinin WashingtonWed 23 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump pulled out all the stops at the Republican party’s midterm convention two weeks ago. In speeches aimed at the voters who will soon decide whether to keep Republicans in control of Congress for the final phase of his presidency, the president dangled$5,000 checks, and warned the United States would turn into a “communist country” if Democrats are elected.Theunprecedented political gatheringamounted to a Hail Mary pass at retaining control of Congress, whichhistory indicatedTrump’s Republican allies had always been likely to lose in the 3 November vote. Two weeks later, with election administrators in several states already sending out mail ballots, there is no indication the gambit has worked.Polls have continued to show Democrats with an edge on the generic ballot, a key indicator of voter sentiment in congressional races, as well as in some key Senate contests such as North Carolina and Georgia, both states where Trump won two years ago. Forecasters have moved their ratings of other battleground racesalmostuniformlyin Democrats’ favor, despite Republican-led states’ concerted effort toredrawHouse districts in the party’s favor.Trump’s approval ratings remain low, withsomesurveysfinding him plumbing new depths. Prices for gasoline and diesel have started climbing again amid the ongoing war with Iran, prompting the Republican Senate stalwart Chuck Grassley of Iowa topublicly encouragethe president to do more for farmers, whose businesses have been particularly hard hit by the conflict’s economic shocks.Chart of Donald Trump’s approval ratingTop Republicans suddenly appear worried about the fortunes of incumbents standing for re-election in some of the reddest states in the country. Last week, vice-president JD Vance campaigned in Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, but whereAdam Hamiltonis seen as a strong challenger to the Republican incumbent Roger Marshall.Back in Washington, the extent of the House GOP’s jitters became clear when Democrats forced a vote on a war powers resolution to end the fighting with Iran, andthree Republicanswho had not backed the previous five efforts supported this one, ensuring its passage.“This midterm is going to be a fucking bloodbath,” said Nancy Mace, theoutgoing congresswomanwho was among the trio of new converts, and predicted that her party would not keep control of the Senate and House of Representatives when ballots are tallied in a month and a half.In the days that followed, moreRepublicansin competitive races came out against the Iran war.“The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for Michigan’sopen Senate seat, said in a campaign ad released on Monday. Ashley Hinson, the congresswoman who is running to represent Iowa in the Senate, wrote on social media “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end”. She had voted against the Democratic war powers resolution, as had John James, the congressman who is the Republican nominee for governor of Michigan, but on Tuesday, the Detroit News reported he told reporters: “We need to end this war quickly. Because war is terrible, and no one likes war.”Democratic operatives have long maintained that Trump was leading the GOP’s congressional majorities into oblivion, and are now being joined in that prediction by veteran politics watchers, who see the toxic combination of rising prices, poor approval ratings and dampening enthusiasm among voters as likely fatal for Republicans’ hopes of keeping control of the House, if not the Senate.“We are seeing a dramatic souring and just overall level of anger at the broken promises of Trump and House Republicans, like, issue after issue after issue. Like, people are just unhappy right now,” said a Democratic strategist who did not want their name to be used.Talk has even re-emerged of a “blue wave” in November that will see Republicans lose in deep-red corners of the country.“Republicans should brace themselves: the three most plausible outcomes are that it will be bad, really bad, or truly horrible,”wrotethe veteran analyst Charlie Cook.View image in fullscreenRepublican attendees at the midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month.Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersYet not everything is necessarily going Democrats’ way. In the battle for the Senate, Republicans have grown increasingly optimistic abouttheir Senate candidatewinning in New Hampshire, which somemajorforecasters now view as a toss-up. The party may also have come out ahead in the mid-decade redistricting push, and definitely has more financial resources this year than the Democrats – a reversal from most midterms prior.“House Republicans are running with a more favorable map, historic fundraising, stronger candidates, and a commonsense agenda, whileDemocratsare burdened by unelectable far-left nominees and deeply unpopular policies that make their path to the majority far more challenging than the pundits suggest,” said Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee.After much speculation about when he would act, Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac has started spending its $400m war chest, buying $15m in advertisements to support the RepublicanKen Paxtonin the Texas senate race. Fairshake, a Super Pac connected to the cryptocurrency industry, willreportedlyspend $30m against Sherrod Brown, the Democratic former senator from Ohio andcryptocurrency adversaryseeking to returnto the chamber, after the industry spent $40m to see him defeated in 2024.Republicans and their allies have thus far put $384.5m into Senate races, to Democrats’ and their supporters’ $112.7m, according to datacompiledby political analyst Rob Pyers. In the House, Republican supporters have spent nearly $65.7m to the Democrats’ $51.1m, but Politico hasreportedthat much of that money has gone to districts where Trump won two years ago, a sign that the GOP is playing defense.Winning the Senate will require Democrats to oust at least four Republicans in states that Trump won in 2024. The House seems an easier target for the party, since the GOP controls it by a low single-digit majority.House Republican leaders including the speaker Mike Johnson nonetheless insist that voters will expand rather than disband their majority in November. They note that 23 Democrats represent districts that voted for Trump in 2024, a number that has increased due to GOP-led states’ redistricting, while only eight Republicans represent districts that backed Kamala Harris. The party also believes that voters are stilltoo disenchantedwith Democrats overall to put them back in charge in the Capitol.“Voters might not like Trump. They might not even like Republicans. But the polling shows that they hate Democrats even more,” a Republican strategist said on condition of anonymity.In a statement, Julie Merz, the executive director of the House Democrats’ campaign arm, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, acknowledged the party’s fundraising struggles but said they were still on track for a return to power.“We are confident we’re poised to win the majority, and that’s why Republicans in deep red territory are running scared,” Merz said. “If Democrats want to break the Republican gerrymanders in the south and get the largest majority possible, more resources ensure we can flip those seats too. We need more cash.”Money isn’t everything, as Democrats know – Harris and her supporters outspent Trump and his allies in 2024, a year of resounding Democratic losses. And many of the factors that will decide the election outcome may already be baked into the result, said John T Woolley, co-director of the American Presidency Project at the University of California, Santa Barbara.“Inflation, employment rates – they’re just not going to change a whole lot. So the kind of thing that’s left, the seats, those are fixed, [you] can’t change that stuff. So the only thing that’s left is the president’s approval,” Woolley said.“What that means is the president has to shift swing voters, independent voters, voters who don’t identify as either Republican or Democrats.”But that group, too, appears to have soured on the GOP: a New York Times and Siena University poll released last week found 57% of independent voters were planning to vote Democratic in the midterms, and just 34% for Republican candidates.Explore more on these topicsRepublicansUS midterm elections 2026US politicsDonald TrumpDemocratsUS SenateHouse of RepresentativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair | Cyberwar | The Guardian
description: Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are being used to spread deceitful narratives
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are being used to spread deceitful narratives
Content: Deepfake image from the fake documentary Olympics Has Fallen, produced by Russia-affiliated influence actor Storm-1679. It advanced pro-Kremlin disinformation and used the image and likeness of Tom Cruise, who did not participate in any such documentary.Illustration: Storm-1679/Microsoft Threat Analysis CenterView image in fullscreenDeepfake image from the fake documentary Olympics Has Fallen, produced by Russia-affiliated influence actor Storm-1679. It advanced pro-Kremlin disinformation and used the image and likeness of Tom Cruise, who did not participate in any such documentary.Illustration: Storm-1679/Microsoft Threat Analysis CenterDisinfo black opsCyberwarAnalysisHow the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despairDan MilmoandRobert BoothWhether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are pushing multiple false narrativesWed 23 Sep 2026 15.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 17.53 EDTShareRussian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies.The narratives range froma deepfake Tom Cruise criticising the Paris Olympicsto portrayinga recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland borderas a false-flag operation.Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo ona video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorskfour years ago.New UK agency to fight ‘information warfare’ from likes of Russia, Burnham tells UNRead moreThe tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots.It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough,announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence.“We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said.Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”.Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research atAlliance4Europe,a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats.“You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says.Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”.Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks”, this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning.It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption.The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says.It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both useddeepfake newscasterstoadvance their goals.Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguardsRead moreOne recent study, conducted mostly in February by theSocial Market Foundation, a British thinktank, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic.The UK governmentdefines misinformationas the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect.Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”.Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service.Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest bylaunching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unitafter the Southport disturbances in 2024. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”.The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns.One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News.Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accountsOne of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024.The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity | EditorialRead moreRobert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them.He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather, he said, Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it.“What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka.AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns.The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models.The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.Explore more on these topicsCyberwarDisinfo black opsDeepfakeAI (artificial intelligence)InternetTechnology policyRussiaChatbotsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Bats originated in Europe, rewriting mammals’ family tree, study reveals  | Mammals | The Guardian
description: Biggest study of its kind provides insights into bats’ evolution – a potential gamechanger for research into human virus and cancer treatment
Author: Gloria Dickie
Headline: Biggest study of its kind provides insights into bats’ evolution – a potential gamechanger for research into human virus and cancer treatment
Content: A hammer-headed fruit bat in DRC, where scientists collected bat DNA swabs as data for the study.Photograph: Sarah Olson/Wildlife Conservation Society CanadaView image in fullscreenA hammer-headed fruit bat in DRC, where scientists collected bat DNA swabs as data for the study.Photograph: Sarah Olson/Wildlife Conservation Society CanadaThe age of extinctionMammalsBats originated in Europe, rewriting mammals’ family tree, study revealsBiggest study of its kind provides insights into bats’ evolution – a potential gamechanger for research into treating viruses and cancer in humansThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentGloria DickieWed 23 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the northern forests of the Congo-Brazzaville, as the sun slips away, a distinctive honking fills the dusky sky. Every evening, thousands of hammer-headed fruit bats depart their daytime roosts in search of mates, calling out through large, box-shaped snouts that give the flying mammals the appearance of a winged moose. Here, along the Congo River, scientists have been collecting DNA swabs and tissue samples from the bats for years, working deep into the night in spacesuit-like protective gear.Those hard-won samples are now among the thousands of specimens gathered from bats across the world that have helped to reshape what we know about the bat family tree.View image in fullscreenA bat fossil found in Messel oil shale in Germany, that is about 47-48m years old.Photograph: Matthew F Jones/HandoutIn a landmark studypublished today in the journal Nature, a team of more than 130 international researchers combed through ancient bat fossils and genomic data from living species to establish that bats likely originated in Europe about 65m years ago – not in Africa, Asia or North America, as had previously been thought.Rather, it seems that the earliest ancestors of modern bats dispersed from Europe into Africa, then expanded onwards to Asia, the Americas and Australia. The findings also reveal that echolocation, like flight, also evolved near the dawn of bat evolution.“Bats, on a scale of amazing to amazing, they’re super amazing,” said Sarah Olson, one of the study’s authors and director of health research at the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Society. “It’s fun to have part of that puzzle piece in the block, and then we can keep finding and adding other puzzle pieces to it now.”View image in fullscreenThe Honduran white bat, or Caribbean white tent-making bat, one of more than 1,500 bat species.Photograph: Daniel Whitby/HandoutThe work is part of a larger global effort known asBat1K, launched in 2017, which seeks to sequence the genomes of all the living 1,500 bat species – the second most diverse mammal species in the world, and accounting for one-fifth of all mammals. Genomes are an organism’s complete set of genetic constructions, containing all the DNA needed to build, grow and live.The Naturestudy ultimately drew on 103 bat genomes from 21 bat families, alongside 44 fossil bats – mostly their teeth – unearthed across the globe.Olson said their findings lay the groundwork for better understanding bat physiology and, critically, how the mammals have evolved to be so resistant to disease. Bats are often identified as reservoirs of fatal zoonotic viruses, includingEbola,NipahandMarburg– but the bats don’t get sick themselves.“How are they living with these viruses that, when they get into us, they cause so much damage?” Olson said. “What we have now is a kind-of code book of life.”View image in fullscreenA wooly horseshoe bat. The mammals have evolved to be particularly resistant to disease.Photograph:   Manuel Ruedi/HandoutA2025 studybased on the Bat1K genomic work found that early bat ancestors seemed to have excessive immune gene adaptations. “We showed for the first time that these adaptations associated with viral tolerance and disease resistance probably evolved at the same time that all bats evolved,” said the evolutionary biologist Ariadna Morales, who worked on both studies.Bats are also unique among mammals in that they live exceptionally long for their size, showing few signs of ageing or cancers. Now, scientists say they will be able to investigate the genes driving those traits. What they learn could be a gamechanger for research into human ageing, immunity and disease resistance.“With the genetic information that we can find in bats, it could be used to develop therapeutics associated with zoonotic disease. And they could also be models to develop treatments for cancer,” Morales said.Olson added that the research can also strengthen our understanding of “what makes a healthy bat a healthy bat, and what are bats going to be susceptible to?”About half of the knownbat specieshave unknown or decreasing populations, with 18% of species considered threatened by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature.View image in fullscreenA lesser horseshoe bat. Almost a fifth of bat species are considered threatened.Photograph: Daniel Whitby/HandoutBats are at risk from the climate crisis, habitat loss, and bat persecution and harvesting, said study co-author Liliana Dávalos, a conservation biologist at Stony Brook University in New York. At the same time, bats play an important role in ecosystems, helping to pollinate plants, spread seeds, and keeping insect numbers – particularly mosquitoes, another spreader of disease – in check.“Unlike most small mammals, all but one bat species have very small litters of one or two pups, so when individuals drop dead from scorching temperatures, or get killed through persecution or harvesting, populations cannot quickly recover their numbers,” Dávalos said.And while bats have shown resilience to Ebola and Marburg, in Canada and the United States bats have perishedby the millionsfrom a fungal pathogen calledwhite nose syndrome, which grows on the skin of hibernating bats.“This research can help us go back and look at what makes the myotis bat species more susceptible to these fungal diseases,” Olson said. “There may be some interesting findings that other researchers can take from this study … to go back and piece together what’s happening with white nose syndrome.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsMammalsThe age of extinctionMedical researchZoologyBiologynewsShareReuse this content

title: Sleep payments: could they lead to better rest – and better health? | Sleep | The Guardian
description: We all need a good night’s rest, but regular, sufficient sleep is hard for many of us to come by. Students in Pittsburgh have been offered a novel incentive
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: We all need a good night’s rest, but regular, sufficient sleep is hard for many of us to come by. Students in Pittsburgh have been offered a novel incentive
Content: Snooze you (don’t) lose.Photograph: Maria Korneeva/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSnooze you (don’t) lose.Photograph: Maria Korneeva/Getty ImagesPass notesSleepSleep payments: could they lead to better rest – and better health?We all need a good night’s rest, but regular, sufficient sleep is hard for many of us to come by. Students in Pittsburgh have been offered a novel incentiveWed 23 Sep 2026 11.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Sleeppayments.Age:A new strategy for an age-old problem.Appearance:Nice work if you can get it.Paying people to sleep?I’m in.The idea is not without precedent – there is such a job as aprofessional sleeper, for research purposes.Sounds good. Where do I sign up?A new study has taken a slightly different approach: they rewarded students with money whenever they managed more than seven hours’ sleep.What kind of students?University of Pittsburgh undergraduates, with an average age of 19.How much money?Not a lot – about five bucks (£3.76) each time.Why would they do that?To see what happens.And whathappened?The students who received the money got on average 19 more minutes of sleep per school night than the ones who didn’t.I’m no research scientist, but 19 minutes doesn’t sound likefive dollars worth of sleep to me.It’s enough that those students hit the seven-hour target – considered to be an optimal amount – on 26% more nights.Does that really make a difference?The rewarded students also saw an improvement in their marks – their GPA rose by an average of 0.08 points.I don’t even know what GPA stands for.It stands for grade point average – imagine a scale where an A equals 4, a B is 3, and …No maths, please. What you’re saying is, academic improvement was modest but significant.It was even more marked among first-year students.And all it took was money?The students were also given sleep trackers that issued bedtime reminders and morning feedback, but without the monetary incentive, these had little effect.While I like the idea of cash as a form of therapy, I worry it could get expensive in the long run.Interestingly, some of the effects of the incentive persisted: students still slept an additional eight minutes on average in the weeks after the money stopped, and their grades remained higher through the following semester.How has news of this intriguing study been received by the British public?“Great preparation for the UK benefits life,” read one comment under the MailOnline article on the subject.Honestly, that sounds like a wilful misreading ofthe study’s aims and its …“Great training for the next generation,” read a comment under a similar Times article. “Get paid $ for doing nothing.”Do say:“Modest incentives may improve sleep and improved sleep can improve performance.”Don’t say:“I’m going to a nightclub, so I’ll be needing this week’s sleep money upfront.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
