title: Sindhu Vee: ‘Makeup, music to feel reckless, two pieces of milk chocolate – and then I go on’ | Stage | The Guardian
description: The banker turned standup turned actor shares her preshow rituals, what’s behind her ‘very swanky hairstyle’ and her joke about Indian Santa Claus
Author: Liam Pape
Headline: The banker turned standup turned actor shares her preshow rituals, what’s behind her ‘very swanky hairstyle’ and her joke about Indian Santa Claus
Content: ‘One day I may get a facelift because never say never’ … Sindhu Vee.Photograph: Matt CrockettView image in fullscreen‘One day I may get a facelift because never say never’ … Sindhu Vee.Photograph: Matt CrockettComedy Q&AStageSindhu Vee: ‘Makeup, music to feel reckless, two pieces of milk chocolate – and then I go on’The banker turned standup turned actor shares her preshow rituals, what’s behind her ‘very swanky hairstyle’ and her joke about Indian Santa ClausInterview byLiam PapeWed 23 Sep 2026 09.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow did you go from investment banker to standup comedian?I didn’t go on purpose from one to the other. I transitioned from banking to stay-at-home mother to standup comedian. There was absolutely no previous thought process. I got on stage almost by chance, and a lot of alcohol was involved. Standup found me, and I’ve never left it alone.What inspired your latest show, Swanky?It’s just the continuing story of Sindhu Vee! The trials and tribulations, the victories and losses. My parents passed away in quick succession recently and, in their absence, I realised I had to champion myself. I took a long hard look at my life and I thought: actually it’s not going that badly. A word my father used for things that were good but kind of like mysterious and cool was swanky. I suppose one could say that my life is swanky. Why not? Then I got a very swanky hairstyle and a dress for the poster. In the absence of my parents, I had to do it. They were big champions of me.Do you have any preshow rituals?I don’t typically wear a lot of makeup, but for shows I have a very small, neat makeup routine. I listen to a playlist which is made up of primarily old music that I’ve always loved, nothing new. It’s music that makes me feel reckless. I’ll always have two pieces of milk chocolate before going on. That’s it.Did you decide to become an actor, or did it happen to you?I think a lot of standups will tell you, as you start becoming known, sooner or later your agent will get a call and say: “Would you like to read for this part?” That’s how I got everything from Sex Education to Matilda to Feel Good to Starstruck. I didn’t think I was an actor. I genuinely thought, “This is a diversity casting issue.” It turns out I can act, and a number of people who have absolutely no upside in lying to me about it have said, “No, no, you can act.” So that’s been fantastic.Standup now is very familiar. I understand it. Acting is like being in some seductive foreign country where you want to try the food and wear the clothes. It’s all very cool, but you don’t really know what’s going on. So I’ve been lucky to have directors who have been very generous.View image in fullscreen‘You can be funny without punching down’ … Sindhu Vee.Photograph: Matt CrockettWhat’s one of the strangest fan encounters you’ve had?One happened a couple of weeks ago in an airport lounge. We were all getting in the lift to go to our flight and suddenly someone said, “Oh no. Really?”, then started sobbing. We all turned to this woman. She was staring at me, so everyone then turned to stare at me. Because it was in America, I thought, “Have I said something and she’s offended?” She was crying and she said, “It’s you and I have been trying to see your shows.” Then she asked, “Can I give you a hug?” And I could not, in front of 30 people, be like: maybe that’s a step too far. So she walked across the hallway and hugged me and sobbed. I told her it was fine, wished her well, and she calmed down. I would be nowhere without fans and without my audience, but I find this a little disconcerting.Whatwas one of your all-time favourite gigs?There was a gig in a big marquee in St Albans one Christmas many years ago. We got there and it was cosy but gross because everyone had been stuffed in. It didn’t have glass windows, but if it did, they’d have fogged up from everyone’s breath. I remember I was trying out a joke about Santa Claus. I was sort of commenting on poverty in India and how that made Indian Santa Claus very skinny, so it was difficult for children to believe in him. It was a little bit tricky because I think it’s not easy to make fun of poverty. But again, as a comic, I think: this could be funny. It went down really well, and that’s when I realised how you can bring people into seeing that something is funny without punching down.Can you recall a gig so badit’s now funny?I gigged in Delhi early on in my career. I had to do 20 minutes and for some reason the MC brought me on and said, “Here’s Sindhu, who left India to go to the UK and become a comic there.” It really alienated me and everyone was furious. I started some of my best material and someone said, “Why don’t you fuck off back where you come from?” I was like, “Bro, I’m from Delhi.” Everyone hated me. People jumped on stage, stood in front of me, and said, “Look, we can tell jokes better than her.” I went home and drank half a bottle of whiskey.What have you learned from standup?If you can make people laugh, no matter how divided they are, they will feel all part of the same humanity while they’re laughing. Human beings have a capacity for that. I’ve always known it, but now I’ve experienced it. My audiences are from 20 to 80 years old. Politically, I think, they’re quite varied. But they can all laugh at the same thing. I think that means I’ll never be cynical about what human beings are capable of.What’s next for you?There’s this skin treatment called XERF. It’s a kind of a radio frequency thing on your face. One day I may get a facelift because never say never. But before that, you can try this and see what it does to your face. I’m going to try it – I’m so excited. So if you see me in the papers with a super sharp jawline, it’s because I’ve done XERF. And I’m in The Split Up, coming out on the BBC.Sindhu Vee: Swanky is on tour in the UK until 17 AprilExplore more on these topicsStageComedy Q&AComedy (Stage)Sindhu VeeComedy (Culture)featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘I find myself weeping after almost every scene’: how seminal show 7 Up has touched your lives | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s inspired careers, moved you deeply and helped you reevaluate your own journeys. As the series that began in 1964 comes to an end with 70 Up, Guardian readers explain the impact of the decades-spanning tale
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: It’s inspired careers, moved you deeply and helped you reevaluate your own journeys. As the series that began in 1964 comes to an end with 70 Up, Guardian readers explain the impact of the decades-spanning tale
Content: ‘Changed my life’ … The participants gather for 7 Up’s final season, 70 Up.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Changed my life’ … The participants gather for 7 Up’s final season, 70 Up.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockTelevision‘I find myself weeping after almost every scene’: how seminal show 7 Up has touched your livesIt’s inspired careers, moved you deeply and helped you reevaluate your own journeys. As the series that began in 1964 comes to an end with 70 Up, Guardian readers explain the impact of the decades-spanning taleGuardian readersandAlfie PackhamWed 23 Sep 2026 05.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 07.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleITV’s landmark 7 Up documentary series has launched its final outing after 63 years. The show started following the lives of 10 boys and four girls in England when they were seven years old, and has returned every seven years since.‘It’s the Bayeux tapestry of TV!’ After six decades, the seminal series bows out with 70 UpRead moreAs the final season 70 Up reaches its conclusion, seven people tell us what it has meant to them over the decades – along with pictures of themselves contrasting their appearance now with their childhood selves.‘Life is a sum of experience, even if seemingly mundane’View image in fullscreenJudith Barton.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenJudith Barton, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityThe sadness of Suzy as a teenager and seeing her become more content and confident was a standout moment. As was Bruce becoming a “missionary” in his own way by teaching. And, of course, Neil, whose life has often been troubled but is probably the most interesting. It has been a privilege to be able to compare myself with the participants and look at my own journey. It has made me realise that life, whether you’re rich or poor, is a sum of experience, even if seemingly mundane. In many ways, it’s not education or privilege that makes life interesting, but what you do with opportunities as they present themselves. The most engaging characters have been those who have challenged themselves, pursued an ambition or who have had difficulties to overcome.Judith Barton, 69, Surrey‘Deeply moving’View image in fullscreenSheila Lambe.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenSheila Lambe, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityThat Neil, who was the most adorable, magical-thinking seven-year-old, would have mental health crises had a deeply moving effect on me. His challenge was one that could have affected any of the participants, regardless of class and background. And Nick achieved so much despite relatively humble beginnings but gave one of the most impactful statements – that the birth of his son was his greatest moment. As the series progressed, it seemed that the real measure of success was not academic or material achievements after all, but familial love and finding peace.Sheila Lambe, 63, Scotland‘The series fired my imagination’View image in fullscreenMartin Forsey.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenMartin Forsey on his first day of school.Photograph: Guardian CommunityIt was Bruce I related to most. His disposition, his search for meaning. I was an overseas volunteer and related strongly to his search for local connections later in his life. Different, but the same. The series changed my life. I first encountered it through a sociology of education class, as part of a graduate diploma I was studying part-time in the evenings, while working as a science teacher. I was from a working-class background and had no idea what sociology was when I left school. The Up series fired my sociological imagination; I retrained and became a sociologist and anthropologist because of it. It was exciting in the ways it helped explain myself to myself, as well as the broader world in which I lived. My research focused on education and I have written a number of papers focused on the structural and cultural effects of class on life trajectories and the choices people make.Martin Forsey, 65, Fremantle, Western Australia‘The best TV series ever’View image in fullscreenShirley.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenShirley, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityI’ve watched the whole series. It resonated with me because I am of a similar age. I was not surprised to see that the girls seem to have a lesser part, with emphasis during interviews on their roles as wives and mothers, rather than their careers. I experienced the same kind of thing. I think the teenage years showed a lot of vulnerability in girls who wanted to appear grown up to the world. I believe it is the best TV series ever, showing how times have changed from the 60s to the present and the progression through a person’s life. I think perhaps every seven years it should be repeated in its entirety, with tributes to those involved who have passed.Shirley, 68, London‘Unexpectedly overwhelming’Lyle JacksonPhotograph: Caitlin Steva/Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenLyle Jackson, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityWatching 70 Up has been unexpectedly overwhelming. I have found myself weeping after almost every scene. Over the past three years, I have lost several close friends and family members, so grief is always near the surface. The series brings back not only the years that have passed, but also what was lost, what endured and what was learned along the way. When I started watching in 1975, documentaries were almost absent from commercial television in the US. It was intimate, patient and honest about ordinary lives. It showed that a person’s story could unfold slowly, with all its disappointments, contradictions, resilience and surprise.That recognition changed the arc of my life. I became a documentary photographer and producer, winning 18 regional Emmys. My work has often focused on people who were overlooked, marginalised or simply not often given the space to be seen.Documentarywork kept me grounded through hard periods in my own life. I will always be grateful for what the series gave me: a belief that ordinary lives are never ordinary when someone has the patience and compassion to keep looking.Lyle Jackson, 72, Nashville, Tennessee‘As I grow older, I identify with the participants more and more’View image in fullscreenKhalid Dajani.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenKhalid Dajani, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityI most identify with Paul, who is first seen at the foster home and establishes a family of his own with his lovely wife in sunny Australia while remaining the sensitive, gentle and intelligent boy he was when we first saw him in 1964. He struggled with his self-confidence, even though there was no apparent reason for that, and bravely acknowledged it as an ongoing issue. I would have liked to have been his friend, had I been a seven-year-old there with him back in 1964.I first heard of the series about eight years ago, through a Roger Ebert book where he marked it out as the best documentary he had ever seen. I watched all the episodes on YouTube over two weeks just in time for the 2019 release and it was amazing to see the children grow into middle age. By pure luck, I also got a chance to see [the now late director] Michael Apted and his wife in Dubai who were here for a movie showing at that time. As I grow older, I identify with the participants more and more while also noticing what different lives we all lead but with the same, shared core of wanting to spend our limited time as best as we can. If only we knew how.Khalid Dajani, 54, Dubai‘I became a documentary film-maker in my 20s and the 7 Up films set a gold standard’View image in fullscreenAlan Reich.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenAlan Reich, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityIn 1970, when I was seven, my brother and I went to a Jewish summer camp. I cried for the first few nights missing my parents and home. In the first week, the original 7 Up film was shown on a noisy film projector and I sat transfixed, watching these other seven-year-olds from such a different world to my sheltered religious Jewish bubble. I continued to seek out the following films wherever I lived and catch up with these familiar children, who were like friends that were always seven years ahead of me in my own life journey. With the edit back to their younger selves, I could understand how the little boy and girl can still be seen in that grown up. I became a documentary film-maker in my 20s and the 7 Up films set a gold standard for me to have a deeper connection with interviewees, and where possible maintain contact with them.In 2018, at the Sheffield documentary festival, I met Michael Apted and told him that the 7 Up films had influenced me to become a documentary film-maker. In his intense, inquiring questioning style that I recognised from all those films, he flashed back: “And how is that going for you?” The truth is that by then my career in films had petered out and I had retrained as a psychotherapist. I am now 63 and I still enjoy the deeper connection with people, helping them to explore and shine a light on how our past still plays out in our adult lives.Alan Reich, 63, LondonExplore more on these topicsTelevisionDocumentaryFactual TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Eric Idle has had tons of celebrities staying at his house. God, it must be exhausting | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: Whether it’s an A-lister or an old schoolfriend emerging blearily from the spare room, those first moments of the day are tricky, writes Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: Whether it’s an A-lister or an old schoolfriend emerging blearily from the spare room, those first moments of the day are tricky, writes Adrian Chiles
Content: A man of wisdom … Eric Idle.Photograph: Nina Prommer/EPAView image in fullscreenA man of wisdom … Eric Idle.Photograph: Nina Prommer/EPAOpinionEric IdleEric Idle has had tons of celebrities staying at his house. God, it must be exhaustingAdrian ChilesWhether it’s an A-lister or an old schoolfriend emerging blearily from the spare room, those first moments of the day are trickyWed 23 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareFirst thing in the morning, that’s the hardest time.Eric Idletold me this. A wise man, is Eric. Actor, comedian, songwriter, musician, screenwriter and playwright and, when it comes to mornings, a man of wisdom.I interviewed him about his new book, which is a love letter to his house in Provence. He bought it more than half a century ago, before he hit the big time. It didn’t cost him much, because it was tiny, tumbledown and without water or electricity. Slowly, as the money came in from this job or that, he made improvements. By hook or by crook, the water and electricity started to flow, and with them a steady stream of guests coming to stay. These weren’t just any old guests: they were superstars, among them David Bowie, Art Garfunkel, Penny Marshall, Lauren Hutton, Brian Cox (the professor and the actor too, I think, although possibly not at the same time), Paul Simon, Carrie Fisher, Robin Williams and George Harrison. Also Michael Palin and assorted Pythons; Ronnie Wood and assorted Stones. And so on. There are photos of Wood sitting on the floor strumming his guitar; Bowie mooning about clad only in short shorts. Quite something, but all I could think about was how tiring it must have been to have so many guests turning up all the time. Let’s be honest: guests are a bit of an effort. A-lister or Joe Bloggs, a guest’s a guest.This isn’t an issue raised in the book, which I should say is a moving, elegiac affair, and not just a torrent of name-drops as I’ve rather implied. But the guest question nagged away at me until I plucked up the courage to interrogate Mr Idle on the matter. Who was the best guest? Who was the worst? And what did he do if they were getting on his wick? After all, since they’d gone all that way, he could hardly turf them out.Sensibly, Eric wouldn’t be drawn on any of these questions, although much as he plainly loved them being there, he did tacitly admit that having guests in your space – even guests of this calibre – does have its challenges, and that it’s the mornings that are hardest.He’s dead right. It doesn’t matter who it is emerging blearily from the spare room. Be it Bowie, Fisher or an old schoolfriend, those first moments of the day are tricky. When you’re a kid, a teenager, a student, sleepovers happen all the time, and they’re kind of normal, so you know the drill. But as you get older, they happen less and less. I have close friends who I’ve known since primary school, but I can’t remember the last time we had a sleepover – a word we obviously no longer use now we’re middle-aged. However well you know your guest – or, in Eric’s case, however well the world knows your guest – you’re unlikely to have spent much time with them straight after they’ve got out of bed. And in this phase of the day, we’re all different animals.Morning. Oh, hi. Morning. What’s for breakfast? Awkwardness, that’s what’s for breakfast. Tea? Coffee? Toast? Can I get you an, erm, egg? Cereal? Oh, right, granola. I’ll have a look. Skimmed? No, sorry, no skimmed. Decaf? Sorry, no. Earl Grey? Hang on, I’ll check. Er, no, sorry. Silences of various lengths punctuate what passes for conversation. Sleep OK? Good. Silence. Clink of cutlery. Slurp of tea. Silence. An embarrassed request. What? No toilet paper in the loo? How embarrassing! So sorry. I’ve left some on the stairs. Then there’s another silence while whoever it was who lacked the toilet paper waits for a little time to pass before sloping off for a poo. Awkward, awkward, awkward.All are welcome at mine, but don’t mind me if I slip out and take the dog for a walk first thing, leaving you enough time to sort yourselves out.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous  | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like Trump
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like Trump
Content: ‘Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment.’Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment.’Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersOpinionUS newsTrump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerousKenneth RothIt is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like TrumpWed 23 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 13.33 EDTShareDonald Trump’sspeechon Tuesday to the United Nations general assembly was an object lesson in his lawless rule and remarkable capacity for self-delusion. Disregarding the UNcharter’semphasis on the peaceful resolution of disputes, he doubled down on his violent unilateralism while denigrating the global issues that the UN is designed to address.For many, the headline remark was his musing about whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” ofIran. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”But it was probably less a genuine threat than a clumsy effort to influencenegotiationswhere he has little leverage. Trump is in desperate quest of some face-saving gesture that will allow him to feign “victory” and extract himself from his disastrous war of choice.He spoke of destroying the “Islamic Republic”, which might imply the Iranian military, a legitimate military target. But his reference to precluding future generations suggests he meant to threaten the Iranian people. Attacking them would be a blatant war crime.In July, he alreadyvowedto destroy Iran’s bridges or power plants – itself athreatto commit war crimes. The international criminal court (ICC) has charged four Russianmilitarycommandersfor doing precisely that in Ukraine.Trump didn’t even bother to offer a coherent rationale for his threat. Once more, he proclaimed: “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” But Tehran has long disavowed that goal.He claimed that other American presidents “just wanted to ignore” the issue. But Barack Obama negotiated adealto constrain Iran’s ability to build a nuclear weapon. Trumprippedit up, preferring his utterly counterproductive military solution, which has brought Iran farcloserto a nuclear weapon than ever before.Preposterously, Trump claimed, “when it comes to Iran,” the midterm election “doesn’t even enter my mind.” No one believes that. If the Republicans face the disastrous showing that the polls nowpredict, he knows the election will be seen as a repudiation of his arbitrary tariffs and Iran war which have fueled inflation and aggravated the affordability crisis that hebelittles.Trump also spotlighted his other acts of aggression. He celebrated the seizure of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro, emphasizing how some political prisoners have now been freed, althoughhundredsremain. But while Trump lauded his coerced deal with Venezuela’s remaining autocratic leaders to take a large chunk of the country’s oil, he said nothing about a democratic future. Instead, touting hismight-makes-rightbeliefs, he proclaimed: “To the victor belong the spoils.”He noted the newagreementon Greenland without mentioning his earlier threat to seize the territory by force even though it has long been administered by Denmark, a fellow Nato member.He raved about slaughtering drug suspects at sea, claiming they are “at war with civilization” and “should be killed … as enemy combatants”. But there isnoreal war, only a rhetorical one.Drug traffickers form a criminal cartel, not an organized force in armed conflict with the United States. They should be arrested and prosecuted, not summarily executed by drone. The killings are murders and arguablycrimes against humanity.Many of the victims were on boats registered in Columbia or Venezuela – both at the time members of the ICC. That would give the court jurisdiction over these crimes, which may bewhyTrump reprised his attack on this important institution of justice. Trump wants to be restrained only by his own warped “morality”.It has beenreportedthat Trump may soon supplement his sanctions against 13 ICC personnel – judges and prosecutors – with sanctions against the court as a whole. But that would only compound the criminality of his conduct, because retaliation against court personnel for the performance of their official duties is obstructing justice under article 70 of the court’sstatute.Trump emphasized his role as a peacemaker. “I have made peace,” he declared, as he claimed to have “settle[d] eight wars”. Yet the reality is more complicated.He said he had “ended the war in Gaza”. In fact, despite the “ceasefire”, Israel’s continuing attacks continue to raise thedeath toll. Trump mentioned his 20-point peace plan for Gaza without noting that virtually none of it has been implemented. Israel continues tokillPalestinians andblockneeded supplies, while Hamas has notdisarmed. He didn’t even bother to mouth the word “Palestinian”.Indeed, the Trump administration hasrejecteda leading candidate for the next UN secretary general because she has publicly recognized that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, suggesting that Trump will accept only future UN leaders who are willing to deny thisreality.He claimed to have “contribute[d] to peace” between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, without noting that Rwanda’s M23 militia continues tooccupylarge swathes of eastern DRC. Trump seems fine with that, so long as the murderous M23 brings the region’smineralriches to the western market.He claimed to be making progress in securing peace in Ukraine, without acknowledging his prior suggestion to reward Vladimir Putin’s aggression by having Ukraine not only cede territory already illegally occupied by Russia but tohand overadditional chunks of its territory as well.Meanwhile, Trump belittled the problems that the UN, able to convene the world’s nations, is ideally suited to address. He called the existential threat of climate change a “hoax”. Ignoring the enormousrisksposed by artificial intelligence, he attempted to relabel AI as “superintelligence” and derided efforts to regulate it as “globalist.”This week Trump meets with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Yet rather than outline the important issues to be addressed, Trump chose to self-promote: “We’re leading now over China by a lot”.Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment. It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president who excels mainly in disseminating self-promoting fantasies while flouting the most basic rules of decency. His UN speech put that all on painful display.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionUS politicsDonald TrumpUnited NationsUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyIrancommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham survived his first Trump meeting. His nice hair may have had something to do with it | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: The PM’s shiny newness could explain the easy ride he got this time. But who would dare predict the ever-shifting weather in the president’s head? asks Guardian columnist, Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The PM’s shiny newness could explain the easy ride he got this time. But who would dare predict the ever-shifting weather in the president’s head? asks Guardian columnist, Emma Brockes
Content: Andy Burnham and Donald Trump held their first face-to-face meeting in New York.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Donald Trump held their first face-to-face meeting in New York.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamBurnham survived his first Trump meeting. His nice hair may have had something to do with itEmma BrockesThe PM’s shiny newness could explain the easy ride he got this time. But who would dare predict the ever-shifting weather in the president’s head?Wed 23 Sep 2026 07.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareWatching footage ofAndy Burnham at the UN general assemblyon Tuesday was like watching your child from behind a tree in the playground. Are they making friends? How normal do they seem relative to the average? How will they react when they come into contact with that hulking great child who seems to be running things? Burnham’sfirst face-to-facewith Donald Trump was billed as a knife-edge encounter that, due to the latter’s capriciousness, could go either way. In the event, it was drama-free, leaving observers to ask: was it Burnham’s brilliance or simply the weather in Trump’s head?To viewers at home, Burnham’s performance at the press conference looked like that of a man who had worked out his best approach was to go for the sheepish, slightly cheeky air of the junior partner. Burnham is 24 years younger than Trump, on top of everything else – which can afford a certain licence to the less powerful person in any exchange. At the last minute, the meeting had been moved behind closed doors and afterwards, in a windowless room at the UN, the two men appeared side by side, mirroring each other’s body language: just two guys, legs akimbo, shoulders hunched, hanging on a bench in the locker room.It was intriguing to guess what Trump saw when he looked at the UK’s new prime minister. British people can’t always parse class or regional difference in Americans and one assumes Trump can’t distinguish Burnham’s accent from that of someone from Melbourne, or Torquay. Still, something in the British prime minister’s bearing clearly appealed to him. “Thank you, Mr President,” said Burnham after Trump praised this country as “special” and Burnham’s tone – “That’s wonderful. We really appreciate that. This relationship matters so much to us” – hit just the right note of warm condescension that probably struck the president as flattery.Other factors in play: it seems ridiculous to mention, but knowing how superficial Trump is, it seems to me that Burnham’s extremely impressive coiffure for a man of his age – which appears to exist without augmentation – won’t have been missed by a US president who spends an awful lot of time on his hair.There were also a couple of contextual factors that may have given Burnham an easier ride than some other, less fortunate world leaders. First, the run-up to the meeting had seen Trump on absolutely top chaotic form while addressing delegates at the UN,threatening the destruction of Iranand going on a whimsical detour to try to get the acronym SI (“superintelligence”) as opposed to AI off the ground. Perhaps, by lunchtime, he had burned himself out and was ready for a bit of quiet time.We know Trump gets bored quicker than a toddler spoilt for toys and Burnham’s shiny newness will have, briefly, diverted him. The replacement of Keir Starmer in relatively brutal fashion also gave Trump an opportunity to do something he loves more than anything else in this world, which is to kick a person when they’re down. When asked about recent rockiness in US-UK relations, the president replied, “No, I thinkthey’re up … well, they’re more up now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.” In that moment, one saw a tiny endorphin rush of meanness light up his face.And finally, I guess, the president is fresh out of friends at the moment, as thefight with Canada continuesand he falls out with his European friend Giorgia Meloni,formerly known as the “Trump whisperer”. As a result, Burnham was lavished with the highest praise Trump can summon, namely: “I think he’s a natural businessperson.” An astute reader of weakness, he perhaps sensed in Burnham someone more sure of himself than Starmer was. And the prime minister passed Trump’s do-you-think-you’re-better-than-me? test, in which anyone who displays any kind of overt intellectual curiosity is instantly a threat to be vanquished. Even his name, Andy, gives regular-guy vibes that probably helped.Burnham weathered all this with equanimity, although it was tempting to detect behind his poker face the shadow of a smirk while, surely, he thought to himself, “God, this guy”. “News is fake!” said Trump, and,in reference to the Chagos Islands, “they’re a very important piece of real estate!” Meanwhile, Burnham smiled slightly as if appeasing a lunatic. “He gets it,” said Trump and for once, one had to agree.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionDonald TrumpUnited NationscommentShareReuse this content

title: Does Airtel Money mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yet | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: The biggest flotation in five years was a bit of a shoo-in. Let’s see what happens when overseas competition is tougher
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: The biggest flotation in five years was a bit of a shoo-in. Let’s see what happens when overseas competition is tougher
Content: Airtel Money is a 78%-owned subsidiary of Airtel Africa, an established FTSE 100 firm.Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/ReutersView image in fullscreenAirtel Money is a 78%-owned subsidiary of Airtel Africa, an established FTSE 100 firm.Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/ReutersNils Pratley on financeLondon Stock ExchangeDoes Airtel Money mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yetNils PratleyThe biggest flotation in five years was a bit of a shoo-in. Let’s see what happens when overseas competition is tougherIndian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in yearsWed 23 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareAwin is a win, but we should probably contain our excitement aboutthe biggest flotation in London for five years. Airtel Money, a payments processor that operates in 13 African countries and should be worth between £6bn and £7bn, is a welcome addition to the stock market but it would be a stretch to say the event marks a definitive change in the weather to end the listings drought.Why? Because, in a sense, Airtel Money is already here. It is a 78%-owned subsidiary of Airtel Africa, an established FTSE 100 firm with a market value of £11.3bn ultimately controlled by Bharti Enterprises under the Indian billionaireSunil Bharti Mittal, also known for his 25% stake in BT.London Stock Exchange to lose three more firms after takeover offersRead moreThat means this was a home fixture for London in the competition with other venues. The Airtel/Bharti collective still had a look at the Middle East, the US and the rest of Europe, we’re told, but London will have started as a heavy favourite. It is simply easier to spin off a subsidiary on a market where the parent is already known – and, indeed, a market where Airtel Africa was a top-performing Footsie stock last year.Ian Ferrao, the chief executive of Airtel Money, still made all the right noises to please exchange officials. London got the nod on account of its deep capital pools plus investors’ enthusiasm for fintech firms and their general understanding of African companies, he said. All true, but it’s also the case that it would have been simply odd to list Airtel Money on a different market to Airtel Africa.The latter is likely to remain the largest shareholder for years yet, and the two businesses are closely linked operationally. Airtel Money has grown out of Airtel Africa’s telecoms business, and one of its key growth opportunities is to persuade even more of the telephony customers to join the payments service. There are 75 million potential recruits to go at, on top of the established 53 million monthly active users, so there is a decent story to tell.It is one reason why the listing should go well, assuming the wider stock market environment remains calm. Airtel Money is capital-lite, converts a chunky proportion of its earnings into cash, carries the buzzy fintech vibe and is growing at about 20% a year. The cash-generative qualities mean no new equity is being raised, so it is really an opportunity for existing shareholders – including minority owners including TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding – to cash in a few chips. As long as they don’t get greedy on price, it looks a relatively easy pitch for the promoters.For London, the listings game is really about winning a few high-profile names where the competition from overseas markets is tougher. The biggie remains Norway’s Visma, one of Europe’s biggest software companies. A listing was delayed earlier this year because of the so-called“Claude crash”– the sell-off in data-related sectors deemed to be under threat from AI tools – but private equity-backed Visma remains a top target given its valuation a year agowas put at almost €20bn(£17.2bn).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe listing venue for Visma looks to be a shootout between London, Stockholm and Amsterdam. Win that one and it may be time to turn more cheerful about the UK’s pulling power. We’re not there yet.Explore more on these topicsLondon Stock ExchangeNils Pratley on financeFTSEStock marketsIPOsEmerging marketsFintechFinancial sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Our message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s end | Open letter | The Guardian
description: As the UN gathers, signatories from Bernie Sanders to Yeb Saño issue an open letter calling for clean power for all
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As the UN gathers, signatories from Bernie Sanders to Yeb Saño issue an open letter calling for clean power for all
Content: ‘Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most.’Photograph: Visoot Uthairam/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most.’Photograph: Visoot Uthairam/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisOur message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s endOpen letterAs the UN gathers, signatories from Bernie Sanders to Yeb Saño issue an open letter calling for clean power for allThe climate fight has one great ally. You just can’t look at it directlyWed 23 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 06.08 EDTShareWe the undersigned writethis letterout of great fear and great hope.Over the last few months, we’ve seen the world set ablaze by both war and warming. From the conflict in Iran, which has claimed thousands of lives and disrupted billions more, to the series of ever worsening climate disasters, from wildfires in Europe to collapsing glaciers in Nepal, the world seems to be falling apart exactly when it needs to be coming together.We know that these crises are connected. The oil that governments fight over is also the carbon pollution that is warming our climate. The bad air quality in Delhi, the high price of fuel in Vietnam, the cost of electricity in the United States, the terrifying floods in the Himalayas – they all connect back to fossil fuels.Until we end that dependence, we’ll never be able to address the climate emergency and stop fighting these endless oil-soaked wars. That’s why today we are inviting the world to unite around a common cause: repowering the world with cheap, clean energy.We are callingon governments, businesses, institutions and the public to work together to provide clean, affordable energy to everyone, everywhere by 2030.From the nearly 1 billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more of us who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels.We know this world is within reach.Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most.With cheap solar, wind and batteries, we can create huge and rapid change.California is already using just half as much natural gas to generate electricity as it did three years ago, thanks to solar and batteries. In Pakistan, people have put up millions of solar panels in just months, relying on social media for instruction. Each month, millions more people across sub-Saharan Africa are getting electricity for the first time with home solar kits.This energy transition is already moving quickly – but we need it to go much quicker. And so we come together to urge two steps.First, we must build clean power for everyone. For the first time ever, we can reliably bring electricity to the one in 10 people on earth living without regular access.We ask everyone who can afford it to donate something so that others can turn the lights on for studying, cooking and medical care – and never have to think about a gallon of diesel or gas again. It takes just $15 to give access to clean electricity for one person for a generation.Second, we need to build clean power everywhere, and to make that happen, we need to build a movement powerful and beautiful enough to force governments to take large-scale action.Individual steps alone are not enough: too many of our leaders will resist action until we demonstrate together how much we want them to move. We must demand that governments stop building coal, oil and gas projects we no longer need, and start building the clean-energy systems that works – no pollution or wars required.One important day along this path will be 20 June, as the summer solstice approaches in the northern hemisphere, generating the most solar power of any day on earth yet. We will celebrate that day as Sun Day, coming together to celebrate and accelerate this great shift.The path forward is difficult, but the way is clear. We want solar for everyone, everywhere, before the decade is out.We know that standing up to the powerful can be scary. But if there is one thing that unites us, it is that we live beneath the same sun. That unity is our strength, and we must use it to act now.Signed,Muhammad Mustafa Amjad, director of programs, Renewables FirstAlyssa Barber, content creator, @NewLifestyleABBLauren Bash, content creator and film-makerRachel Bender, disability rights advocate, @rachcutiepieTzeporah Berman, chair, Fossil Fuel Treaty InitiativeCaitlin Blunnie, content creator, 2Liberal JaneJessica Craven, content creator, @jesscraven101Nick Cutsumpas, founder, Farmer NickSummer Dean, founder, Climate Diva MediaChristiana Figueres, former UN climate secretary and founding partner, Global OptimismJane Fonda, actor, activist and founder, Jane Fonda Climate PacNela Cadinanos GonzalezSaul Griffith, engineer and co-founder, Rewiring AmericaMalynda Hale, actor, film-maker, creatorFletcher Harper, executive director, GreenfaithAlex Honnold, professional climber and founder, Honnold FoundationDanny Kennedy, chair, Global Solar CouncilCatherine McKenna, founder, Climate and Nature Solutions & Women Lead on ClimateBill McKibben, author, climate activist and co-founder, Third ActKumi Naidoo, president, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty InitiativeKy Polanco, co-Founder, @FeministSean Taylor Pugerude, creator and community Organizer, @heyseantaylorAbbie Richards, researcher and educator, @abbiesrTom Rivett-Carnac, founding partner, Global OptimismBernie Sanders, US senator for VermontYeb Saño, board chair, Laudato Si’ MovementJacob Simon, creator and educator – @jacobsimonsaysLaurence Tubiana, CEO, European Climate FoundationExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionSolar powerWind powerEnergyRenewable energycommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s easy to ignore the Lib Dems, but they could soon hold the balance of power | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: Ed Davey’s strategy is meant to build a ‘firewall’ of MPs to prevent Reform UK entering government. The stakes are high if he gets it wrong, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: Ed Davey’s strategy is meant to build a ‘firewall’ of MPs to prevent Reform UK entering government. The stakes are high if he gets it wrong, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Ed Davey in a speedboat at Rampion offshore wind farm, off the Sussex coast, 21 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEd Davey in a speedboat at Rampion offshore wind farm, off the Sussex coast, 21 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionEd DaveyIt’s easy to ignore the Lib Dems, but they could soon hold the balance of powerRafael BehrEd Davey’s strategy is meant to build a ‘firewall’ of MPs to prevent Reform UK entering government. The stakes are high if he gets it wrongWed 23 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.45 EDTShareNo politician craves obscurity, but it is better to be unknown than despised. That is consolation forLiberal Democrats, gathered in Brighton for their annual conference, fretting about Ed Davey’s low profile and wondering whether a more prominent leader would hoist their flagging poll ratings.Renewal by decapitation is a concept that has succeeded twice this parliament for other parties. Labour’s fortunes were transformed when Andy Burnham entered No 10. The Greens enjoyed a polling surge last year when Zack Polanski was elected leader. In the fidgety culture of British politics, Davey’s six-year reignfeels like an aeon. But the experience of other parties has little to teach the Lib Dems.Keir Starmer didn’t suffer from underexposure. The country watched a showcase of his abilities and didn’t like what it saw. Polanski’s talent for harvesting clicks on social media has expanded his audience, especially among younger voters, but the Green leader hasn’t shown that he can sustain that interest. Increased scrutiny may not do him any favours. The chart mapping hisfavourability ratingssince taking the job shows a stable core of fans beneath a steadily rising line of disapproval, suggesting that, outside a Green comfort zone, the more people see of Polanski, they less they like. The equivalent picture for Davey tells a story of flat indifference.Voters don’t have a clear sense ofwhat the Lib Dem leader stands for, but they don’t feel threatened by him, which is an underrated value in a leader whose prospects depend on tactical voting. His supporters aren’t relaxed about a polling slump but they argue that the party’s tally of seats in parliament and on local councils is evidence that more has gone right than wrong in recent years.They have a point. There are 72 Lib Dem MPs – a record high – and reasons to expect that number to grow at the next election. The party prides itself on tenacious incumbency, digging in deep and fortifying each seat with local activism. Lib Dems are resented by rivals for the same reason, compared to cockroaches for their stubborn resistance to removal. Those tactics can’t protect a popular local candidate if a national tide turns against the party, as happened in 2015 when the Lib Dems were crushed almost to death by the weight of amassed resentment over their coalition collaboration with the Tories. But sometimes the party finds itself swimming with the current.To the extent that any forecast can reliably be made about Britain’s choppy political waters, it looks likely that a decisive factor at the next general election will be the question of Reform UK’s suitability for power and, assuming he is still the leader, Nigel Farage’s candidacy to be prime minister. The result will then depend on the organisation of tactical anti-Farage voting (and levels of dysfunction in any putative Reform-Conservative pact) at constituency level.That dynamic can work in Davey’s favour if the question of who is best placed to stop the radical right is unambiguous. Conservatives are the challengers in nearly all of the Lib Dems’ current constituencies and the incumbents in most of the party’s target seats. Given how porous the ideological membrane is between Tories and Reform, Lib-Dem campaigners in key battlegrounds can correctly argue that a vote forLabouror Greens serves only to enable Faragism.View image in fullscreenEd Davey delivering the keynote speech at the Lib Dem party conference, Brighton, 22 September 2026.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPADavey is already building that case. He presents his party’s bloc of MPs as a “firewall” to stop British politics being captured by a brand of demagogic nationalism that is inspired by Donald Trump and bankrolled by unsavoury billionaires.An obvious inference from that position is that Davey would facilitate Burnham staying on in Downing Street in a hung parliament. Speculation on that question, years before an election is even due, is tedious but necessary for the Lib Dems. They find it demeaning to be cast as parliamentary handmaids waiting to serve a grander political master, but at least that status keeps them relevant. Coalition is the mechanism by which Davey can plausibly get manifesto commitments enacted. It is an important point of distinction from what Lib Dems see as sideline pressure-group politics practised by the Greens.The strategy gets trickier if the Lib Dems already maxed out the anti-rightwing tactical vote in 2024, when there was the pressing matter of a Tory government to evict. Where do they go next?A suite of victories in that campaign established a base for the party in the “blue wall” of affluent southern towns and suburbs. These are places that once dependably voted Tory but where the old allegiance has been sundered by a combination of demographic change (younger voters moving in), rank incompetence (Boris Johnson; Liz Truss) and unhinged Brexit fanaticism.The cultural shift is not superficial, but nor is it baked in so hard that the Lib Dems can afford to lean too far to the left. Consolidation and growth depend on expansion into the vacant space on the political spectrum where moderate “one nation” Tories once dwelt and that Kemi Badenoch is not reclaiming.That risks causing discomfort to Lib Dems in the party’s orthodox social-democratic tradition, or who campaign in seats where the opposition is Labour. They want to compete in radical colours – a reddish shade of orange, not a pale orangey-blue. They don’t see themselves as a party of the centre-right.Davey has abalance to strike. He needs to signal progressive credentials to reassure tactical voters and Lib Dem activists that his anti-Farage firewall will be suitably robust. He also needs to consolidate and expand his support among former Tory voters who might be liberal on social matters but are still classically conservative on the economy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHis conference speech on Tuesday was crafted with those twin tracks in mind. He led with impassioned denunciation of far-right thuggery on British streets, connecting it to Reform’s anti-immigration agenda, but the headline retail offer was abig income tax cut– raising the personal allowance and the 40p threshold. The latter would be a gift to people who, like everyone else, feel squeezed by inflation and stagnant wages but are far from the neediest end of national income distribution.There is a racism and cohesion crisis in Britain, and someone needs to lead us out of it. His name is Andy Burnham | Polly ToynbeeRead moreIt is an expensive gamble. In theory, the £17bn cost to the exchequer would be recovered once the British economy was restored to the EU single market and thriving as a result. Spending a reverse-Brexit dividend on tax cuts is a cute political message for middle-class remainers. It wouldn’t pass a Treasury test of fiscal neutrality given the complexity and upfront cost of the accession process.Davey is prepared to take heat in accusations of sketchy budgeting, verging on denial of fiscal reality, if the row also sheds light on his pro-European, tax-cutting ambition for the benefit of people who care about both of those things.It is a targeted bet on raising the Lib Dems’ profile with the specific voters who will decide how many seats the party wins. That number can’t be extrapolated from midterm opinion polls.Local elections next year will give some indication of whether Davey’s method is working. A byelection in a winnable seat may settle Lib Dem nerves. But the plan only comes to fruition as the sum of tactical choices made in polling booths in a general election, once voters confront the prospect of Reform in government.Right now, it may not be obvious what purpose the Lib Dems serve, but if they hold enough seats to thwart a Faragist majority, their utility to British democracy won’t be in doubt. That is the uncertainty inherent in a firewall. You only find out whether it works when you need it most, and then you don’t get a second chance.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEd DaveyOpinionLiberal DemocratsLabourReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: I tried to become a gay tradwife – and failed abysmally | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: My sourdough starter died and my lone tomato nearly ruined me financially and emotionally. How did domestic drudgery and hard labour become an aspirational aesthetic, asks Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: My sourdough starter died and my lone tomato nearly ruined me financially and emotionally. How did domestic drudgery and hard labour become an aspirational aesthetic, asks Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Should have gone to Aldi … gardening is just too hard.Photograph: Darya Komarova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShould have gone to Aldi … gardening is just too hard.Photograph: Darya Komarova/Getty ImagesOpinionWomenI tried to become a gay tradwife – and failed abysmallyArwa MahdawiMy sourdough starter died and my lone tomato nearly ruined me financially and emotionally. How did domestic drudgery and hard labour become an aspirational aesthetic?Wed 23 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTShareI have just eaten what may be the world’s most expensive tomato. It comes from a little region of Philadelphia better known for sports culture than horticulture and was cultivated by yours truly. I spent only a few dollars on the plant, but then I had to buy a tomato cage and a few companion plants to keep it company. Then I had to spend an ungodly amount of time watering it and hacking away at weeds. In short: I put a huge amount of emotional investment into that tomato. Was it worth it? Absolutely not. I should have just gone to Aldi.Of course, the tomato growing wasn’t really about saving money, it was about saving my sanity. Earlier this year, my wife and Igot a plotat our local community garden; buoyed up by this development, I decided to ward off existential angst by throwing myself into tradwife-adjacent hobbies such as gardening and baking. I don’t know if it’s possible to be a gay tradwife but, after Googling the subject, I did find amagazine pieceentitled The Curious Case of the Bisexual Tradwife. Alas, I can’t tell you much more about the phenomenon because there was a paywall. There are a lot of walls to pay in this life and this one did not make the cut.While bisexual tradwives may be on the rise, my sourdough isn’t. I acquired some sourdough starter at a community garden fermentation and pickling workshop and, channelling my inner tradwife, I fed it religiously for a couple of weeks before I forgot about it and it died a pungent death. Nary a loaf was baked; the closest I got was buying some bread flour in the supermarket.My interest in growing my own seems to have perished, too. Gardening is not the relaxing hobby it’s made out to be; it’s extremely hard work. I would go to the allotment feeling perky and return exhausted, covered in dirt and mosquito bites with bits of twig stuck in my hair. After I neglected my duties for a couple of weeks due to a heatwave, the weeds took over and I received an official violation warning from the garden’s Plot Monitoring Committee. If you get two warnings you get kicked out, and now I, a diligent rule-follower, live in fear of the dreaded second one.Anyway, good on the tradwives for making domestic drudgery and hard labour into an aspirational aesthetic, but I think I’ll pass. Forget touching grass, it’s back to doomscrolling on the couch.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the future of the UN: more embattled, but more necessary, than ever | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: As the secretary general, António Guterres, prepares to step down, the general assembly is highlighting the scale of the organisation’s challenges
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: As the secretary general, António Guterres, prepares to step down, the general assembly is highlighting the scale of the organisation’s challenges
Content: The UN headquarters in New York City, US. ‘It remains an essential forum, not least for smaller countries to coordinate and campaign.’Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UN headquarters in New York City, US. ‘It remains an essential forum, not least for smaller countries to coordinate and campaign.’Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesOpinionUnited NationsThe Guardian view on the future of the UN: more embattled, but more necessary, than everEditorialAs the secretary general, António Guterres, prepares to step down, the general assembly is highlighting the scale of the organisation’s challengesWed 23 Sep 2026 13.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareThe United Nations was created,its charter states, to “save succeeding generations from the scourge of war”. Donald Trump used his address to the general assembly tothreaten Iran, another member state, with annihilation again. The charter also speaks of the obligations of international law. On Venezuela, Mr Trumpgloatedthat “to the victor belong the spoils”. His speech in New York on Tuesday might be regarded as an improvement onlast year’sonly in that it was not an explicit, full-scale attack on the UN itself, merely on its founding principles.The absences this year are perhaps as telling as the US president’s hostile presence. Vladimir Putin has not attended for more than a decade. Nor has Xi Jinping – but the snub is more striking ashe is in Washingtonto meet the US president. India’s Narendra Modi is not present; nor are Cyril Ramaphosa, Bola Tinubu or Abdel Fatah al-Sisi – the leaders of Africa’s three giants, South Africa, Nigeria and Egypt. While their reasons are various, the gaps speak collectively to Mr Trump’s wrecking capability and the broader challenges faced by the UN.View image in fullscreenAntónio Guterres.Photograph: Bianca Otero/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockIn a world where “cracks have become canyons”,to quote António Guterres, the body is more necessary than ever, and under greater strain. The outgoing secretary general has struggled with a “might is right” world: an authoritarian resurgence, the rising tide of conflict and a deadlocked security council. Mr Trump sought to supplant the UN with his “Board of Peace” for Gaza before largely losing interest. Even the biggest champions of multilateralism, such as Canada’s Mark Carney, are looking primarily to other mechanisms rather than UN reform.With extremely limited powers, secretary generals usually fall into mediator or activist roles. Critics argue that Mr Guterres should have beenmore hands-onin diplomacy, in conflicts such as Sudan, as he was in brokering aBlack Sea grain dealin 2022. But he has been a powerful voice of conscience: early to raise the threats posed by AI, passionate in calling for climate action and heartfelt on the suffering in Gaza, Ukraine and beyond. He has also kept the organisation on its feet – no mean feat given the disappearance of essential US funding (though Washington is nowpaying some of its debt).The first female secretary general is long overdue and the informalregional rotationwould suggest that a Latin American or Caribbean figuremay succeed him; Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana have been frontrunners. But major powers may be biding their time, with serious contenders still to emerge. Observers think that there is a real possibility that a successor may not be agreed before Mr Guterres’s departure date of 31 December, underlining the UN’s challenges.Yet it remains an essential forum, not least for smaller countries to coordinate and campaign – resulting in important action on issues from landmines to global heating and its consequences. And major powers will eventually have to recognise that the case for security council reform, stressed again by Mr Guterres, cannot be ignored for ever. The charter reminds us that the UN was born from the desperation engendered by two world wars rather than a utopian dream. It endures not because of glorious successes, nor because it has avoided glaring failures, but because a world without it would be far worse. The troubles it faces are all the more reason to defend it.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Andy Burnham’s accusation against the Kremlin tells half the story. Domestic extremists amplified by US big tech are part of the same problem
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Andy Burnham’s accusation against the Kremlin tells half the story. Domestic extremists amplified by US big tech are part of the same problem
Content: Elon Musk addressing crowds at a rally organised By the far-right activist Tommy Robinson in London in 2025.Photograph: Grant Rooney Premium/AlamyView image in fullscreenElon Musk addressing crowds at a rally organised By the far-right activist Tommy Robinson in London in 2025.Photograph: Grant Rooney Premium/AlamyOpinionCyberwarThe Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicityEditorialAndy Burnham’s accusation against the Kremlin tells half the story. Domestic extremists amplified by US big tech are part of the same problemWed 23 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareIn November 2020, Barack Obama warned of an “epistemological crisis” facing western democracies. Polarisation and radicalisation were corroding trust in established information sources. “If we do not have the capacity to distinguish what’s true from what’s false, then by definition the marketplace of ideas doesn’t work,” the former US president said.That vulnerability has grown since then. Democracy’s enemies have become more determined to exploit it. This is the threat that Andy Burnham highlighted in a speech at the United Nations this week. The prime ministeraccused Russiaof waging an “industrial-scale assault” on the UK’s information environment using bot armies and fake websites to spread falsehoods, interfere in elections, foment discord and poison inter-community relations.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetThe prime minister announced the creation of a National Centre for Information Defence to thwart campaigns of epistemological sabotage by hostile actors. It is an overdue enhancement of Britain’s civil defence capabilities.Mr Burnham is right to highlight the threat, but he told only part of the story. The Kremlin would be wasting its money pumping out disinformation if large US tech platforms didn’t provide convenient channels for the toxin to spread, if there weren’t a complicit audience in Britain sharing the offending material and if the market for spreading pernicious propaganda weren’t so lucrative. Information warfare is only effective when it exploits structural vulnerabilities in the target society. Far-right material sowing hatred against migrants is most fruitful where the terrain has been fertilised by domestic politics.Earlier this year,analysis by the Guardianfound that more than half of accounts on X that were posting about racially aggravated riots in Belfast and civil disorder in Southampton were based outside the UK. Seven of the most-read tweets originated in the US, including one posted by X’s proprietor, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man.Mr Musk has been assiduous in promoting a warped, dystopian idea of Britain as a failed state whose culture is being corroded by mass migration. His platform has been invaluable to far-right activists who have mustered gangs of masked men into mobs that obstruct roads, intimidate people and threaten asylum claimants at British ports. Last year, Mr Muskaddressed a rallyorganised by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, where he called for the Labour government to be removed. Earlier this year, Mr Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon,travelled to Moscowon a trip funded by the Musk Foundation. He said the purpose of the trip was to “see the beauty of a civilised society”.Mr Burnham did not address that side of the anti‑democracy equation in his speech, perhaps because he felt that it would be impolitic to impugn US big tech under the president’s nose. Mr Trump is also an originator and disseminator of falsehoods online, but the nature of transatlantic diplomacy prevents a UK prime minister confronting him with that record.Under the circumstances, it made sense for Mr Burnham to concentrate his remarks on the threat from the Kremlin, but that must not signal the limit of his policy focus. British democracy is indeed under attack fromRussia, but an effective campaign to build resilience has to recognise also the complicity of domestic extremists and the digital privileges they enjoy thanks to US technology companies.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Stop the Ofsted inspections that are harming teachers | Ofsted | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers on the new grading regime that is causing more stress and health issues for school staff than ever before
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers on the new grading regime that is causing more stress and health issues for school staff than ever before
Content: ‘Accountability without humanity serves neither school leaders nor the children whose education depends on them.’Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreen‘Accountability without humanity serves neither school leaders nor the children whose education depends on them.’Photograph: Yui Mok/PAOfstedLettersStop the Ofsted inspections that are harming teachersReaders on the new grading regime that is causing more stress and health issues for school staff than ever beforeWed 23 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareYour report (New Ofsted inspection regime is damaging our health, headteachers say, 21 September) reflects what those of us supporting school leaders are hearing. As a volunteer withHeadrest, a school leader wellbeing helpline, I cannot discuss individual cases. I can, however, describe the disturbing patterns we encounter.We have spoken to headteachers whom mental health professionals considered suicide risks following their experience of theOfstedprocess. We have spoken to leaders whose physical or mental health has been seriously damaged by inspections. We have heard from headteachers who successfully navigated inspections but then chose early retirement rather than face that level of stress again.We have also heard from school leaders facing serious personal circumstances who have sought inspection deferrals and had their requests refused. Whatever the administrative requirements of an inspection system, there must surely be circumstances in which compassion and humanity take precedence over process.These are not arguments against inspection.Schoolsmust be accountable and children must be safeguarded. However, accountability without humanity serves neither school leaders nor the children whose education depends on them.Thedeath of Ruth Perryshould have represented a watershed. Thecoronerconcluded that an Ofsted inspection contributed to her suicide. Yet we continue to hear accounts that should be unacceptable to every politician and education policymaker.Nobody should wait for another tragedy before asking whether the system has genuinely changed enough. Accountability is necessary. An inspection system that places those leading our schools at avoidable risk is not.Pete CrockettRoyal Wootton Bassett, WiltshireSchool leaders are sounding the alarm about the mental health impact of the new Ofsted regime. As a researcher on accountability in the education sector, I have contributed to the parliamentary consultation on the work of Ofsted, and the evidence on the impact of poor Ofsted outcomes on teachers’ careers is overwhelming.Although the new framework was designed to create greater nuance, it has not dealt with the underlying issues of validity: do inspection outcomes accurately reflect the quality of education? England has arguably the most stringent school-inspection regime in the world, yet little attention has been given to how well the system works. The lack of serious empirical scrutiny that Ofsted has come under is at odds with the power it wields. To make Ofsted truly fit for purpose, we need hard evidence on basic questions such as whether children gain more from enrolling at a school that is highly rated by inspectors.Dr Iftikhar HussainUniversity of SussexThe education secretary, Lucy Powell, is proposing major changes to the education system. To achieve these, she needs the support of school leaders. There would be no better way to help secure that support than by agreeing to re-examine the Ofsted regime. It has lost the confidence of leaders in its overall direction and management, in its detailed operating procedures and, in particular, its ability to inspect schools without causing undue harm to the health and wellbeing of headteachers and staff.The education secretary should welcome the National Association of Head Teachers’ proposals as a first step to reforming a deeply flawed inspection regime, but needs to go much further.Colin Richards and Frank NorrisFormer HM inspectors of schoolsIt’s a sad and shocking indictment of our school-inspection system when an article about Ofsted ends with the Samaritans’ phone number.Toby WoodPeterboroughIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsOfstedEducation policyTeachingMental healthSchoolslettersShareReuse this content

title: Picking a side on Ed Sheeran, Israel and Palestine | Ed Sheeran | The Guardian
description: Letters: Celebrities like Ed Sheeran should not shy away from expressing political opinions, writes Dr Richard J Goy, while Anna Emms praises the singer’s commitment to his fans. Plus a letter from David Parry
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Celebrities like Ed Sheeran should not shy away from expressing political opinions, writes Dr Richard J Goy, while Anna Emms praises the singer’s commitment to his fans. Plus a letter from David Parry
Content: Ed Sheeran performing in New York in 2025.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Kevin MazurGetty Images for iHeartRadioView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran performing in New York in 2025.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Kevin MazurGetty Images for iHeartRadioEd SheeranLettersPicking a side on Ed Sheeran, Israel and PalestineCelebrities like Ed Sheeran should not shy away from expressing political opinions, writesDr Richard J Goy, whileAnna Emmspraises the singer’s commitment to his fans. Plus a letter fromDavid ParryWed 23 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareNadia Khomami provides an excellent analysis of current dilemmas regarding political songs and engagement (‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a full-blown culture war, 19 September).However, I do feel that it lacks a longer timeframe. Outspoken, overtly political singers and songwriters have been active for decades. My own generation was brought up on Bob Dylan and Joan Baez. A bit  further back were Woody Guthrie and Billie Holiday. Who would dare to writeStrange Fruittoday? In all, far too many are being deterred by fears of censorship by media billionaires and their like. They need to get out there and shout and scream about the world’s appalling injustices. We need a hundred Billy Braggs, not just one.Dr Richard J GoyCambridgeMost world leaders do not have sufficient understanding of the history and complications of the Arab-Israeli conflict or organisations such as Hamas to make informed decisions; Ed Sheeran certainly doesn’t, and I commend him for trying not to “pick a side” (Dear Ed Sheeran, fence-sitting is so last century: musicians can no longer opt out of politics, 17 September).There’s nothing wrong with Ed admitting that his fans just want to have a fun time dancing and singing along. He is right to put these people first and acknowledge the importance of this work to all of the people backstage in the music industry. Terrible crimes are committed all over the world every second of the day, but it shouldn’t be a crime to try to bring people together through music.Anna EmmsIpswich, SuffolkJason Okundaye is absolutely right to chastise artists for failing to speak out, particularly in these times of assault by the extreme right on our liberal societies (Ed Sheeran thought fans didn’t want artists to be politically engaged. He’s finding out how wrong he was, 19 September). The failure of many to speak out against the rise of nazism in Germany and against fascists in Italy during the 1930s certainly allowed a fatal normalisation of dictatorial fascism. Let us not allow the same thing to happen again. We artists have a positive duty to speak out.David ParryAntingham, NorfolkHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Folk or AI could be a winner for the UK at Eurovision | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers have advice for a cross-party committee of MPs looking into the UK’s poor record at the song contest
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers have advice for a cross-party committee of MPs looking into the UK’s poor record at the song contest
Content: The UK’s Eurovision 2026 entry, Look Mum No Computer, on stage in Vienna, Austria in May this year.Photograph: Christian Bruna/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UK’s Eurovision 2026 entry, Look Mum No Computer, on stage in Vienna, Austria in May this year.Photograph: Christian Bruna/Getty ImagesEurovisionLettersFolk or AI could be a winner for the UK at EurovisionReaders have advice for a cross-party committee of MPs looking into the UK’s poor record at the song contestWed 23 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareI agree with Laura Snapes that the very last thing we need is MPs’ questionable tastes entering the murky waters of the UK’s Eurovision song choice (What do you think of the MPs’ inquiry into UK Eurovision song contest failure? I give it nul points, 21 September).However, one thing I can’t believe hasn’t happened is for the UK to draw upon our ridiculously rich folk tradition. Loads of other countries do it – Ukraine won it a few years back with a song that infused Ukrainian folk with pop – so why can’t we?And who’s to say it even need be sung in English? A Welsh, Cornish or Scots entry would freshen things up, and no one could accuse us of a Europop facsimile.Tim ThorntonLondonZoe Williams’ article on the proposed inquiry into “why are our Eurovision entries so bad?” was very amusing (Britain loves its underdogs. We should be celebrating our Eurovision flops, not investigating them, 21 September). It also made me think that the House of Commons select committee could save time and money by asking AI. It would probably take it 10 minutes, and it might even produce a winning song.Linda KarlsenWhitstable, KentHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
