title: Farewell, nimbys of Piddington… | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the news that an Oxfordshire village has voted to leave the UK over plans to house asylum seekers nearby
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the news that an Oxfordshire village has voted to leave the UK over plans to house asylum seekers nearby
Content: Local residents unveil a ‘Principality of Piddington’ sign after a symbolic referendum.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenLocal residents unveil a ‘Principality of Piddington’ sign after a symbolic referendum.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAImmigration and asylumLettersFarewell, nimbys of Piddington…Readers respond to the news that an Oxfordshire village has voted to leave the UK over plans to house asylum seekers nearbyWed 23 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTShareSo the people of Piddington have spoken – an overwhelming majority want to leave the UK (English village votes to leave UK in protest over migrant housing plan, 16 September). They didn’t really consider the consequences, did they? We can say goodbye, but to protect our borders we would need to erect a solid barrier around the village. Obviously anyone who works in the UK outside Piddington’s borders would need a work visa now, and travel visas will be needed by people wanting to visit supermarkets – or relatives. I note that there’s a small river running through Piddington. Any attempt to leave on small boats should be dealt with like any other attempted illegal entry.I’m not sure they really thought through the reality of leaving, preferring instead a mix of populist soundbites and protest votes. It’s going to go badly. Where have I heard this before?Neil KnowlesLondonLisa Nandy rightly pointed out that all communities should shoulder the burden of asylum seekers, not just those areas with cheap accommodation as was the policy under the Conservative government.We are all susceptible to a bit of nimbyism, but this “vote” was based on ignorance of the facts and on prejudice whipped up by the rightwing media.Linda KarlsenWhitstable, KentI note with interest that Piddington has voted to leave the UK. But if they can have a vote, why can’t the rest of us get a say in this? If given the chance, I’d vote for the nimbys of Piddington to be expelled from the UK. It would be interesting to see how long they’d last without us.Chris JonesYorkHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Harry Kane admits England’s World Cup 2026 exit ‘hurt more than any other’ | England | The Guardian
description: The striker, who will lead England against Spain in the Nations League, said World Cup defeat hurt ‘even more than when I missed the penalty in Qatar’
Author: David Hytner
Headline: The striker, who will lead England against Spain in the Nations League, said World Cup defeat hurt ‘even more than when I missed the penalty in Qatar’
Content: Harry Kane and England are preparing for four Nations League matches in 11 days.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenHarry Kane and England are preparing for four Nations League matches in 11 days.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAEnglandHarry Kane admits England’s World Cup 2026 exit ‘hurt more than any other’‘It wasn’t the team that we wanted and said we’d be’England host Spain in Nations League on SaturdayDavid HytnerWed 23 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Kane has described England’sWorld Cup semi-final defeatagainst Argentina as his most painful tournament exit because of how the team lost sight of who they were.The captain is determined to move on as quickly as possible and is chasing a statement performance against Spain at Wembley on Saturday night in theNations League. But he admits he is yet to get over the Argentina game and knows it is something he and his England teammates must work to process.Branthwaite reveals brain study helped him conquer injuries and earn England callRead more“It felt like it wasn’t us as a team,” Kane said, as he reflected on howEnglandlost their way in the 2-1 defeat, barely touching the ball after they went ahead in the 55th minute. “It wasn’t the team that we wanted to be and said we’d be. When you maybe go against your beliefs and you lose, it feels 10 times worse than just losing in a way where … if we lose doing it our way you accept it, take it on the chin and move on. It’s tough and it will still be tough.“I’m so passionate about England and especially because I’ve been on this journey … been to finals, semi‑finals and been so close. Each one hurts in a different way and this one hurt, for sure, more than any other one. I’d say even more than when I missed the penalty in Qatar [in the2-1 defeat by Francein the 2022 World Cup quarter-finals] because of just the manner that it happened.”It was put to Kane that it was a healing process. “It kind of is,” he replied. “But you have to heal while getting on with it. In football, you don’t have time. Before you know it’s the next one. It’s a hard balance because you’re trying to get over it and learn from it but also we play the world champions on Saturday and it’s a big, important game.”Kane knows England must identify why they have repeatedly fallen short against the toughest teams when it matters most. “How can we be better in those moments? How can we be ourselves more in those moments? Through qualifying campaigns and a lot of games in tournaments, we play with a certain intensity, we play in a good way. It’s something that we haven’t quite been able to do in latter stages of tournaments against the bigger and better nations.“It may be a mixture of things. It may be personalities, mentality. It may be just the direction and how we want to play in those games. It’s conversations that we need to have as a group.”Kane accepts it was not only against Argentina that England were not at their best. “Taking away the big loss at the end, there were still games at theWorld Cupwhere we didn’t quite reach our potential, the way that we train,” he said.But the message – as articulated by Thomas Tuchel when he addressed the squad at St George’s Park on Tuesday – was of the need to fine-tune. “The general messaging is that we continue what we’ve been building,” Kane said. “Sometimes after a tournament, it’s easy to say it’s a new start but I don’t think it is that. It’s a continuation because we have done a lot of good things.”View image in fullscreenHarry Kane asked: ‘How can we be better in those moments? How can we be ourselves more?’ after England’s World Cup heartbreak.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersTuchel has beenrocked by the withdrawalsof Declan Rice, Cole Palmer, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento for the upcoming Nations League fixtures; after Spain, England play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia. Rice’s absence has attracted attention because it is for load-management reasons rather than an injury that would immediately rule him out. Kane understands the move, given Rice’s well-documented problems with nerve pain in a hamstring.“I spoke to Dec,” Kane said. “I know Dec goes far and beyond for the club and country. I know he’s been struggling for a while with his issues. Dec reached out to me, he voice-noted me. Everyone has to look after themselves and I trust all the boys.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is a seismic time for Kane. He is four caps shy of Peter Shilton’s all‑time England record of 125; he could be level with him by the end of this international window. Kane is also tipped to win the Ballon d’Or on 26 October and is poised to extend his contract at Bayern Munich. “We’re fairly close,” he said. “I’m happy there. It won’t be too long before there’s some sort of announcement.”The 33-year-old allowed his thoughts to drift to the longer term and as he mused about his ambition to become an NFL kicker, there was a clear hint he saw himself finishing his football career in Major League Soccer.“I take penalties and it [being an NFL kicker] is a very similar pressure and technique. If I was to do it, it is something I would take seriously. I would take six months to a year to try and practise before. Maybe if I am in the MLS in the future or somewhere like that, it might be a thing where you could connect the two maybe with the seasons.”Kane has previously said he would be interested in becoming a professional golfer. He loves to play and revealed he did not watch the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina because he went for a round of golf in New York.“I watch golf and think: ‘I could be there.’ Then I go out and play and I am like: ‘There’s no way.’ I play off two. But I am a member at Wentworth and I shoot 10 over. Then I watch the pros, who played there last week, and 20 under wins it. I think I’ll stick to football.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandHarry KaneWorld Cup 2026World CupNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Warwickshire ‘in the groove’ as County Championship destiny calls | County Championship Division One | The Guardian
description: Going into the last round 11 points clear, the bowler Olly Hannon-Dalby is confident the favourites can clinch the title
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: Going into the last round 11 points clear, the bowler Olly Hannon-Dalby is confident the favourites can clinch the title
Content: Olly Hannon-Dalby (third from right) has been vital in Warwickshire’s push for County Championship glory.Photograph: Jacob King/PAView image in fullscreenOlly Hannon-Dalby (third from right) has been vital in Warwickshire’s push for County Championship glory.Photograph: Jacob King/PACounty Championship Division OneWarwickshire ‘in the groove’ as County Championship destiny callsGoing into the last round 11 points clear, the bowler Olly Hannon-Dalby is confident the favourites can clinch the titleTanya AldredWed 23 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlly Hannon‑Dalby, 6ft 7in of medium‑fast heritage craft, has just come out of training at Edgbaston. The last round of County Championship cricket is about to startand slow‑burn Warwickshire are nailed-on favourites. Hannon‑Dalby tries to pinpoint what has made the team tick this summer.“Our bowling has massive depth,” he says. “Ethan Bamber has had an outstanding year with 60 wickets, and then Chris Woakes has been around the majority of the season. To be able to throw an English legend the ball every now and then is unbelievable – and his demeanour when he plays, how he carries himself is amazing. In fact our depth in general is great, everyone has played and contributed.”Somerset are poised to finish second again – and after 136 years it still hurtsRead moreWarwickshire, after starting the season as if they had a nail in their shoe with two wins from their first eight games, have stepped up when it mattered. With four wins from the last five matches – and the past two victories, against Essex and Glamorgan, notched up in two days – they have leapt over the 2025 champions, Nottinghamshire, and causedthe usual heartbreak to Somerset.After being ahead before the penultimate round, Somerset stumbled at Headingley last week, leaving Warwickshire 11 points clear. Win their last match, at homeagainst the relegation-threatened Leicestershire, and they are champions. A draw with six bonus points would also get the job done.Hannon-Dalby has more than played his part and, having spent the first four games of the summer on loan to Worcestershire, he now tops the Edgbaston averages with 27 wickets at 18.“I’d never been on loan before. It wasn’t the way I would have designed my season but we have a really strong bowling attack and my opportunities were limited. To be able to get some overs in my legs in those early weeks of the season was brilliant and I’m really grateful to Worcestershire for taking me.View image in fullscreenBen Cliff is bowled by Hannon-Dalby on day four of the County Championship match between Yorkshire and Warwickshire at Edgbaston in May.Photograph: PA/Alamy“I could have stayed at Edgbaston and played for [Warwickshire’s] second team but it is different to championship cricket. To know that I was playing, bowling well, contributing for Worcestershire, meant I was ready to hit the ground running.” And whenWarwickshirerecalled him, he did.An unfancied Warwickshire last won the championship in Covid‑affected 2021, and went on to win the Bob Willis Trophy at Lord’s the same year, a match that dragged on until a properly autumnal 2 October. Hannon‑Dalby was injured for the second part of that season, supporting in the dressing room but desperate to get on the pitch.“This time around is very exciting from a personal point of view, to be fully involved,” he says.When this last batch of games started five weeks ago, we just wanted to give ourselves the chance to be in the hunt, and now we have destiny in our hands going into the last game.“We’ve just got to bat and bowl and field well and if we can do all those things, well, hopefully … also, everyone is fit for the last game of the season, I’ve certainly been involved in campaigns when there are only one or two fit bowlers still standing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWarwickshire’s Will Rhodes lifts the County Championship trophy alongside his teammates in 2021.Photograph: Harry Trump/Getty ImagesIs the body hurting after 12 matches – eight for Warwickshire, four for Worcestershire? “The season is hard, it has ebbs and flows, but by this time of year you are used to the workloads and we’ve helped ourselves by shovelling a few four-day games into two-day games and manufacturing more rest for ourselves. When you get to this stage you are in the groove a bit.”Hannon-Dalby is able to empathise with Leicestershire – he has experience of last-round blues. On the final day of the 2022 season he was bowling at the other end (one for 40) when Liam Norwell’s nine for 63 blew away Hampshire and saved Warwickshire from relegation.“At the end there was absolute elation but the day itself was horrific, the feeling that you were going to get relegated the entire time. The last couple of hours were pandemonium – I wouldn’t want to do that again.”After taking 50 championship wickets in 2022, 2023 and 2024, and enjoying a fruitful 2026, Hannon‑Dalby signed a new three‑year contract this summer, which will make him a Bear as he moves into his 40s. “A brilliant club that have been very kind to me,” is how he describes Warwickshire.View image in fullscreenChris Woakes takes a catch to dismiss Essex’s Paul Walter this month.Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty ImagesHis long career gives him the perspective to see how the game has been transformed, and what matters. “Cricket has changed a little bit, there are lots of offshoots, and the franchise world of course. But on a day-to-day basis, the measure of you as a cricketer is either Test cricket if you can play it, or otherwise the County Championship.“To do well in county cricket is incredibly satisfying, and being able to win the championship is a great marker in your career. It says a lot that the great Chris Woakes could have sailed off into the sunset, but he has stayed for weeks like this.” By Sunday, we will know how the die fell.Explore more on these topicsCounty Championship Division OneWarwickshireSomersetCounty ChampionshipNottinghamshireCricketfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kaptein fantastic strikes as Chelsea battle to WCL win over Austria Vienna | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Wieke Kaptein’s goal after 11 minutes was enough to secure victory for Chelsea in their league-phase opener, with Keira Walsh’s early withdrawal a concern
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Wieke Kaptein’s goal after 11 minutes was enough to secure victory for Chelsea in their league-phase opener, with Keira Walsh’s early withdrawal a concern
Content: Wieke Kaptein (left) and Veerle Buurman celebrate after the former’s decisive goal.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenWieke Kaptein (left) and Veerle Buurman celebrate after the former’s decisive goal.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersWomen's Champions LeagueKaptein fantastic strikes as Chelsea battle to WCL win over Austria ViennaSuzanne Wrackat the Cherry Red Records StadiumWed 23 Sep 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWieke Kaptein’s early goal gave Chelsea a winning start to their Champions League campaign proper against Austria Vienna, but it was a far from comfortable evening for them.“Probably the performance is not the one we wanted to have,” Chelsea’s manager, Sonia Bompastor, said. “We could have controlled the game a little bit better in terms of scoring a second goal to kill the opposition’s hope, but sometimes you need to focus on what is most important and tonight that was to win and to take the three points from the game.”Caldentey’s late penalty provides WCL relief for struggling Arsenal against KøgeRead moreA David v Goliath endeavour welcomed the visiting team at the Cherry Red Records Stadium and they rose to the challenge. The mammoth financial gulf between the two teams was highlighted in the buildup by the Austrian broadcaster ORF, which reported: “Chelsea Women’s personnel costs alone for the 2024-25 season, at a cool €17m, were higher than those of the entire Austria club (€14.9m) – including the men’s department, by far the largest item.” Meanwhile, Uefa noted that the manager, Stefan Kenesei, has a full-time job in state pensions insurance.Ultimately, the gap in quality on the pitch looked far smaller than the finances suggested. Aware of that possibility, Bompastor did not take any risks and made only three changes to the team that secured a 2-0 win against Birmingham on Saturday, despite Arsenal up next on Sunday at Stamford Bridge.It was a statement of intent from a team desperate to get their hands on the only club trophy to elude them and they were right to be cautious. As the Danish side HB Køge showed against Arsenal on Tuesday night, Champions League minnows can cause big problems.“The physicality from those [lower-ranked] teams is good,” Bompastor said. “The players are able to match the intensity of the Champions League games from the beginning of the game until the end, as you could see tonight. I also think the coaches who are coaching those teams are good in terms of the tactical aspects. When they come into this game, they are really well prepared and they have a good game plan. So, nothing is easy.”A moment of magic from the Dutch midfielder Kaptein gave the host side the breathing space of an early lead 11 minutes in. The 21-year-old was quickest to the loose ball after a slick sliding tackle from Katharina Schiechtl dispossessed Melvine Malard and she sent a rising strike in off the underside of the bar from 25 yards.View image in fullscreenSonia Bompastor, the Chelsea manager, shouts instructions from the sidelines.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAAustria Vienna responded rather than folding, threatening until the final whistle while supported vocally by the small block of travelling fans who appreciated the efforts of the underdogs. Set pieces and the forward Modesta Uka were their best outlets. Uka’s close control provided both an attacking threat and gave her teammates a reprieve from chasing.The threat from Uka had been evident in the Austrian side’s qualifying campaign. The Kosovan scored in their 3-2 win against Hajduk Split and scored another two in their 5-0 victory against Farul Constanta in the second qualifying round, before grabbing a hat-trick in a 4-0 win against the Norwegian side Brann to overturn a 2-1 away defeat in the third round and secure their place in the league phase.“She’s a great player and she deserves to play at this level, just as the whole team does,” Kenesei said. “She deserves to play in the Champions League and we’ve seen today how much potential there is.”The longer the game went without Bompastor’s side building on their lead, the more confident the players in white became. Just shy of the 70th minute there was another tense moment for the host side, when pressure from the ever-bright Uka forced Veerle Buurman into an error. Katie McCabe looked to have clipped the Austria Vienna player, who seemed to have beaten her to the ball, but a pause after the ball went out of play did not lead to an intervention from the video assistant referee.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrustrations boiled over a little at the close, when Almedina Sisic re‑entered the field without waiting a minute after receiving some treatment, with Bompastor forced to hold back her enraged assistant, Camille Abily, before giving the fourth official a piece of her mind.Quick GuideRoundup: Lyon hit eight, Barça rally past Paris FCShowMarie-Antoinette Katoto [pictured] scored a hat-trick asLyonnesthrashedServette8-0 in their opening league phase game of the Women’s Champions League. Katoto’s treble, Melchie Dumornay’s double and two own goals from the Swiss hosts saw Lyonnes go top of the early standings with a crushing display.The eight-times winners went ahead eight minutes in through Laia Balleste’s own goal before Katoto took control. The France striker bagged her first of the night in the 28th minute and added a second 12 minutes later. Dumornay’s chipped finish gave Lyon a four-goal advantage at the break and just two minutes after the restart, Katoto completed her treble from Lily Yohanes' backheeled pass.Dumornay added her second in the 54th minute and Laura Strik’s own goal piled more misery on Swiss champions Servette, who conceded again in the 89th minute when Ines Benyahia struck. In Wednesday's other early kick-off,Romasubstitute Marta Pandini hit the post with a stoppage-time penalty as they were held to a 0-0 draw atOH Leuven.Ewa Pajor’s double helped holdersBarcelonaget off to a winning start as they came back from behind to beatParis FC5-2. Barça were handed an initial scare when Evelyne Viens put Paris in front only five minutes in, but Kerolin replied for the hosts with a tidy finish in the 18th minute.Clara Serrajordi put Barca ahead 10 minutes later, kicking off a destructive 15 minute-period for the hosts, which saw Pajor and Caroline Graham Hansen strike.Pajor struck again in the 70th minute, before the visitors pulled one back through Clara Mateo as Barça comfortably saw out the win.Lyonnes host Chelsea next Wednesday in their second league-phase game, while Barcelona visit Roma and Paris FC welcome Arsenal.PA MediaPhotograph: Pierre Albouy/REUTERSWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.In the end, it is a testament to the visiting team that they will leave London extremely disappointed not to have taken anything from a game that gave them opportunity after opportunity to do so.“Yes, we’re proud,” Kenesei said. “We were brave as we’d planned, really, but to be honest I’m also disappointed that we didn’t get at least one point. We saw what you all saw today, that we performed at almost the same level as Chelsea.”Chelsea can breathe easy, although Keira Walsh’s precautionary early withdrawal with a quad issue will be a concern, but they have a job to do to snuff out those chances before they face teams that will capitalise and punish them.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueChelsea WomenAustria Vienna WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Prem agrees to revamp refereeing in boost for England’s Rugby World Cup hopes | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: Steve Borthwick has secured a boost for the World Cup next year, with an overhaul in the refereeing of Prem matches for the coming season designed to help England’s hopes
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Steve Borthwick has secured a boost for the World Cup next year, with an overhaul in the refereeing of Prem matches for the coming season designed to help England’s hopes
Content: Steve Borthwick is seeking to mount a challenge to the supremacy of South Africa at the World Cup in Australia.Photograph: Alex Livesey/The RFU Collection/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSteve Borthwick is seeking to mount a challenge to the supremacy of South Africa at the World Cup in Australia.Photograph: Alex Livesey/The RFU Collection/Getty ImagesRugby unionPrem agrees to revamp refereeing in boost for England’s Rugby World Cup hopesLeague agrees new interpretations to help BorthwickScrum and breakdown targeted as areas of inconsistencyExclusive byGerard MeagherWed 23 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSteve Borthwick has secured a boost to his preparations for the World Cup next year, with an overhaul in the refereeing of Prem matches for the coming season designed to help England’s hopes in Australia.The Guardian understands that in the formal absence of relegation from the Prem for the first time this season, agreement has been reached over a number of law interpretations that will better align officiating in club matches with the international game.Prem Rugby 2026-27: the essential club-by-club guide to the new seasonRead moreThe areas that will be policed differently include the offside line as well as the scrum – specifically the brake-foot law – as England’s head coach seeks to mount a challenge to the supremacy of South Africa at the World Cup in Australia next year. Borthwick has also previously lamented how differently the breakdown is refereed in the Prem – in which there tends to be less of a contest – than the international stage. Indeed, the breakdown was a frequent problem during England’s miserable Six Nations campaign, whilethe four-Test series between South Africa and New Zealandover the summer highlighted the ferocity with which elite nations are contesting that area of the game.It is understood that Borthwick met the directors of rugby last month and a presentation was given by the Rugby Football Union’s refereeing team on the intended law interpretations. England’s scrum has markedly improved since the appointment of Borthwick, under the guidance of the assistant coach Tom Harrison.Borthwick, however, will be mindful of how dominant South Africa, who have won the past two World Cup tournaments, are in that facet of the game and how influential it was in their series win against New Zealand.Interestingly it was Karl Dickson, one of the RFU’s professional officials, who twice penalised the All Blacks hooker Codie Taylor for brake‑foot infringements in the fourth Test in Baltimore. The brake-foot law was introduced in 2022 as a safety measure and requires the hooker to position one foot forward before engagement at the scrum. The New Zealand assistant coach Neil Barnes said afterwards that it is a law “which no one really gives a shit about, but the referees are concentrating on”.View image in fullscreenNew law interpretations around the breakdown and scrum will aid England players such as Northampton’s Henry Pollock.Photograph: Garry Bowden/ShutterstockIn February it was announced that the coming season, which begins on Friday with Northampton hosting Newcastle and Harlequins facing Bath, would bethe first in which the Prem is formally a closed league. It is understood that the absence of the jeopardy of relegation has been a significant factor in allowing for the aligned law interpretations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Prem director of rugby told the Guardian: “The standard and the intensity of the Prem has increased. At international level the speed is quicker than it is in the Prem. The physicality is more intense and then there’s the nature and style and strategy of the game. That comes down in part to how it’s refereed and we had a conversation around the product we want to get out there and the nuances and interpretations of the laws. Can we align that with international refereeing?”Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSteve BorthwickEngland rugby union teamPrem RugbynewsShareReuse this content

title: Netherlands v Germany: Klopp and Xavi begin revival projects with derby | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Jürgen Klopp and Xavi Hernández face each other in Nations League as they take the reins following disappointing World Cups
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Jürgen Klopp and Xavi Hernández face each other in Nations League as they take the reins following disappointing World Cups
Content: Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp (left) and Netherlands head coach Xavi Hernandez.Composite: Getty Images; EPAView image in fullscreenGermany head coach Jürgen Klopp (left) and Netherlands head coach Xavi Hernandez.Composite: Getty Images; EPANations LeagueNetherlands v Germany: Klopp and Xavi begin revival projects with derbyJürgen Klopp and Xavi Hernández face each other in Nations League as they take the reins following disappointing World CupsNick AmesWed 23 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore the latest instalment of a time-honoured international rivalry gearing up for two distinct new beginnings,Jürgen Kloppcould not resist sprinkling a little of the old mischief. “The good thing is that we both have the exact same situation,” he said of Xavi Hernández, his counterpart when Germany visit the Netherlands on Thursday night. “We met on Monday and play on Thursday. And the coach knows the players from television. I actually know more of the Dutch players personally than Xavi does. Whether that’s an advantage, I don’t know, but it’s still a fact.”Jürgen Klopp vows to change Germany but threatens to quit if family hounded by mediaRead moreIn his public appearances Klopp has been on irrepressible form since taking the role in July. The task of whippingGermanyback into shape has visibly and audibly topped up the energy levels that had drained by the time he departed Liverpool. Klopp, his wit sharp and appetite piqued, looks a far cry from the character who, to most trained eyes, was going through the motions upon his unveiling as Red Bull’s head of global soccer early last year.Securing Klopp was a coup for the German football federation even if it came with a caveat, issued within seconds of his introduction to the media, that he would not be seen for dust if his family were hounded by the media. Xavi’s arrival in Amsterdam is no less fascinating even if, in the Dutch way, no bones were made by his employers about the fact Pep Guardiola and Arne Slot had been higher in their sightsafter Ronald Koeman’s departure. He is the Netherlands’ first foreign manager since Ernst Happel’s 10-month stint ended in 1978 but the fit is instinctively pleasing. Even if Guardiola was out of reach, they could land upon another product of the Johan Cruyff school that created modern-day Barcelona.View image in fullscreenXavi’s captain is Virgil van Dijk, who considered international retirement after the World Cup.Photograph: Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP/Getty ImagesIf Xavi is to take theNetherlands, occasionally exciting but frequently unstable during a World Cup run that shuddered to a halt in the last 32, back to their roots it will require a measure of patience. The pool of players does not allow much else; the recall of Borussia Dortmund’s Joey Veerman, who has not played international football for more than two years, speaks of the need for a technically adept midfield fulcrum but otherwise Xavi has scant scope for surprises. Virgil van Dijk will continue as captain despite considering international retirement during the summer; the head coach’s options may feel more complete when Frenkie de Jong and Donyell Malen have returned from injury.Xavi has resisted any temptation to engage in analysis of the Netherlands’ performance in the United States. “I don’t talk about the past,” is the standard line, ironically an easier one to roll out if theNations Leagueopener in Amsterdam brings a performance redolent of headier times. The revolution may have to be conducted with minimal effusive pronouncements from the coach. It is certainly a less dramatic shake-up than the one Klopp, acting like a man licensed to break a few moulds, has enacted before the next fortnight’s four-game baptism.It raised eyebrows when Klopp named a squad of 44 players for the matches against the Netherlands, Serbia and, home and away, Greece. The expanded unit will be split into two: half will play on Thursday and in Germany’s next game, at home against the Greeks, and the remainder will be involved in the second two games. Only Finn Dahmen, the Augsburg goalkeeper, will be required across the set.“I want to get to know as many players as possible,” Klopp said. “There is no A or B team. The squads are put together in a way that makes sense on the pitch and in terms of character and experience.”View image in fullscreenThe goalkeeper Finn Dahmen (centre) is the only player on call for all four Germany matches.Photograph: Federico Gambarini/DPA/APClub managers feeling squeamish at their players’ workloads during this expanded break will immediately have warmed to Klopp’s split selection. But the priority is to discover who best fits his vision for an intensely committed, front-footed, enthusiasticNationalmannschaftthat places round pegs, even unexpected ones, in round holes. Four players from Freiburg have made his sprawling selection; so has Felix Keidel from promoted Elversberg. Mika Baur of Celtic and the Hoffenheim winger Bambasé Conté were both stunned to receive first call-ups. The Brentford midfielder Vitaly Janelt joins his teammate Kevin Schade in the fray. Sixteen are uncapped.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCanale and Gill the heroes as Paraguay hand Germany first World Cup shootout defeatRead moreLast weekend Klopp and his coaching staff convened at their headquarters in Herzogenaurach to watch as many of their charges’ domestic games as possible in one go. Freiburg’s Max Rosenfelder, one of the new brood, acknowledged the aura surrounding Klopp and described him as “a very, very special person”. Even if the mixed lineups prove to lack experience and cohesion, Klopp hopes his charges’ sheer thirst for the task will lift Germany from the doldrums of their most recent World Cup flop.If he can unite 44 players, why not a whole country? Among Klopp’s many recent pronouncements was the timely intervention in favour of “positive patriotism” that followed an election victory by the anti‑immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party in Saxony‑Anhalt. If it is some time since Germany’s football team have been at their best, perhaps the same may be said for the nation too.In the Dutch capital, two big‑name managers will take their first steps towards bringing the good times back. “It could be a bit wild, but I accept that, it just has to be lively,” Klopp said. That comes with something approaching a cast‑iron guarantee.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueNetherlandsGermanyJürgen KloppfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I want to go’: Lewis Hamilton hopes F1 is able to end season in Middle East | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The seven-time F1 world champion said of the proposed final two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi: ‘I personally want to go. I love going to the Middle East’
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The seven-time F1 world champion said of the proposed final two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi: ‘I personally want to go. I love going to the Middle East’
Content: Lewis Hamilton spoke to the media before the Azerbaijan Grand Prix this weekend.Photograph: Michael Potts/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton spoke to the media before the Azerbaijan Grand Prix this weekend.Photograph: Michael Potts/ShutterstockFormula One 2026‘I want to go’: Lewis Hamilton hopes F1 is able to end season in Middle East‘I love going to the Middle East,’ says Ferrari driverQatar and Abu Dhabi races could still be cancelledGiles RichardsWed 23 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton said he hopes the Formula One season can still end at the two scheduled rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, with the finale still in doubt because of the war in the Middle East.Formula One is pressing ahead with its original plan, although a contingency is understood to be in place to host a final round in Imola if the volatile situation means both meetings have to be cancelled.Speaking before this weekend’s grand prix in Azerbaijan, which borders Iran, Hamilton said he trusted the sport to make the right decision, given the unease among many in the paddock of racing in the region while the conflict continues.Spanish GP plans to change Madring after fierce criticism from F1 driversRead more“I personally want to go. I love going to the Middle East,” he said. “From what I have read, things seem OK out there, but I don’t have all the information and I don’t know what the risk levels are. I trust in Stefano [Domenicali, F1’s chief executive] to make the right decision for the sport. And I do hope we get to go there.”Whether the races take place or not could affect the world championship.Kimi Antonelli leadshis Mercedes teammate George Russell by 81 points with nine meetings remaining. If that number was reduced to eight the Italian could close it out even sooner than might be expected. As things stand a lead of 100 points after Mexico, in five races time, or 75 after Brazill would suffice.A decision is unlikely to be forthcoming until after Antonelli has the championship won, however, at the very least to keep the title fight alive as long as possible.In March the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian grands prixwere called offbecause of the ongoing US-Iran conflict. The Bahrain race has been moved to next weekend at Sepang in Malaysia and it is believed F1 must deliver at least 23 races to meet its commitments to broadcasters, meaning the cancellation of Qatar and Abu Dhabi would make a finale at Imola imperative.The promoters of the races are bullish that they will go ahead but are always reluctant to cancel as they would still be liable for the race fee payable to F1. If the sport cancels, the fees do not have to be paid.Abu Dhabi organisers have gone as far as confirming musical acts set to perform including Zara Larsson, the Script, Imagine Dragons and Lewis Capaldi. However, that the situation was far from settled was illustrated this week when Larsson said she would not be performing.Responding to a post on social media asking her: “Please read about what UAE is doing to Sudan then cancel your Abu Dhabi show,” the Swedish singer posted: “I will not be going to Abu Dhabi.”This was later deleted but Larsson did go on to confirm she would not perform at the meeting. “Maybe it came off as a impulsive response to a comment,” she said. “But I have spent some time thinking about everything and decided that to not do the show aligns with me the most right now, for many different personal reasons beyond politics.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Lewis HamiltonFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I had a headache for days’: Hrgovic reveals brutal toll of Itauma world title fight | Boxing | The Guardian
description: The Croat, who shocked Moses Itauma to win the IBF heavyweight title last month, said: ‘I didn’t celebrate. I went home to rest. It was such a hard fight’
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: The Croat, who shocked Moses Itauma to win the IBF heavyweight title last month, said: ‘I didn’t celebrate. I went home to rest. It was such a hard fight’
Content: Filip Hrgovic said he ‘received a lot of shots and was bruised’ during his win against Moses Itauma.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenFilip Hrgovic said he ‘received a lot of shots and was bruised’ during his win against Moses Itauma.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersBoxing‘I had a headache for days’: Hrgovic reveals brutal toll of Itauma world title fight‘I didn’t celebrate. I went home to rest. It was a hard fight’Hrgovic stopped Briton to win the IBF heavyweight titleDonald McRaeWed 23 Sep 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilip Hrgovic, the new IBF world heavyweight champion, has offered a candid insight into the ordeal he endured beforebeating Moses Itaumain a shock stoppage victory last month, revealing he absorbed so many heavy punches in the first eight rounds that he felt headaches for a number of days afterwards.“I felt fucked up,” said the 34-year-old Croat. “I received a lot of shots and I was bruised. I had a bit of a headache for a few days. On the Wednesday after the fight I was back in the gym, working out already, but for a few days I felt really tired and bruised, with some headaches.”Jack Dempsey v Gene Tunney at 100: when a great champion met his greatest inquisitorRead moreHrgovic, who aims to unify the heavyweight division, said there was a chance he would faceRico Verhoeven, the Dutch fighterwho used to be a world kickboxing champion, on the undercard to the much-delayed bout between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury that is expected to finally take place in Cardiff on 11 December.But revisiting the aftermath of the brutal Itauma bout which changed his life, Hrgovic said: “I didn’t celebrate. I just went home to rest. It was such a hard fight I didn’t even do my tradition after I win, when I go to McDonald’s. I didn’t have the strength.”Hrgovic believes Itauma is so skilful that, if he learns from his painful defeat, the 21-year-old British prodigy can become unbeatable: “He’s really good. He’s special. Very fast, very talented and he countered whatever I tried with his speed and timing. I never was in the ring before with such a talented kid, with such a fast guy. You have some fast guys but they’re small heavyweights. You can handle them with your power but this kid is fast and big. He’s got great IQ and great talent. If he recovers from this loss, mentally, it will be hard for anyone to ever beat him again.”View image in fullscreenFilip Hrgovic said ‘it will be hard for anyone to ever beat him [Moses Itauma] again’ if he recovers from his first defeat.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersItauma is a complex character and Hrgovic suggested that doubts remain about his mentality. “We’ll see. It was a big shock for him, a big humiliation, so maybe it’s the end of his career if he’s not mentally tough.“A lot of people, after that kind of loss, never come back. It will be a hard journey for him to come back but if he recovers and he does not lose his confidence then, with this experience, I think no one will ever beat him again.”Since his shattering defeat, attention has focused on a comment Itauma made before the fight which implied that he has never sparred for 12 successive rounds. Hrgovic said: “It’s not about physical preparation. It’s about experience and mentality. If we go for a run now, or we’re in the gym together, he’s in tremendous shape. He will beat me in every exercise, running, hitting the heavy bag. I think he was physically ready but it’s the mental part. It’s experience.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHrgovic, however, compared his own preparation with the less hard-edged approach of Itauma. “You have to go through a ruthless, hard training camp. You need to go through hell to be mentally ready for this shit. Old school is the best school. I told Itauma this before the fight. He’s drinking water, hugging trees in the morning, saying hello to the sun. He does a lot of this bullshit. He’s surrounded by 10,000 yes-men, nutritionists and a coach for sleeping. You can’t get ready for a war this way.”An exhausted Itauma ran out of energy, after setting a blistering pace, and he was overwhelmed in the ninth round. But the new champion said: “I’m still kind of angry because he outboxed me. In my whole career, in 20 years of boxing, I was never outboxed in any sparring or any fight. I was always competitive. But this kid outboxed me. On that night, I think he will beat anyone apart from myself. But that night I refused to lose.”Hrgovic is relishing his rise to world champion: “If I knew it would be so good I would have won the championship before. It’s amazing to be world champion. I want to unify the division and stay here as long as possible. I feel great.”Explore more on these topicsBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former NFL star Antonio Brown to avoid possibility of 30 years in prison with plea deal | NFL | The Guardian
description: Former NFL star Antonio Brown plans to accept a plea deal on an attempted murder charge in Miami, his lawyer said Wednesday
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Former NFL star Antonio Brown plans to accept a plea deal on an attempted murder charge in Miami, his lawyer said Wednesday
Content: Antonio Brown played in the NFL for 12 seasons.Photograph: Corey Sipkin/APView image in fullscreenAntonio Brown played in the NFL for 12 seasons.Photograph: Corey Sipkin/APNFLFormer NFL star Antonio Brown to avoid possibility of 30 years in prison with plea deal38-year-old had been facing attempted murder chargeFormer player will accept aggravated assault chargeGuardian sportand agenciesWed 23 Sep 2026 15.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer NFL star Antonio Brown plans to accept a plea dealon an attempted murder chargein Miami, his lawyer said Wednesday. Doing so will mean the former wide receiver avoids prison.Brown is scheduled to appear in court next Wednesday to make the deal final. He could face up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the current attempted murder charge.“They made [Brown] an offer he couldn’t refuse,” Brown’s attorney, Mark Eiglarsh, said in a statement. “There is a profound difference between believing you can win a case and deciding that you and your family cannot afford to spend another year, or potentially several years, wearing an ankle monitor and fighting it.”Brown is accusedof grabbing a handgun from a member of security after a celebrity boxing match in Miami in May 2025. The 38-year-old is then alleged to have fired two shots at a man he had gotten into a fistfight with earlier, according to an arrest warrant. Zul-Qarnain Kwame Nantambu told investigators that one of the bullets grazed his neck.Nantaumbu’s attorney, Richard L Cooper, said this month that his client has forgiven Brown and would no longer take part in the case against the former player.“We believe that the ends of justice are accomplished with this plea deal, and my client wishes Mr Brown good health,” Cooper told ESPN on Wednesday.Eiglarsh said Brown would accept a charge of aggravated assault as part of the plea deal.“There’s no prison, there’s no jail, there’s no house arrest. There’s only straight probation,” Eiglarsh told ESPN. “And no alcohol or drug evaluation, no psychological evaluation, no letter of apology, no community service hours, no fines. Just stay away from the victim.”TheMiaminative played 12 NFL seasons for the Pittsburgh Steelers, New England Patriots and Tampa Bay Buccaneers, becoming one of the most prolific receivers of his era. He caught 928 passes for 12,291 yards and 83 touchdowns over 146 career games and was named to the Pro Bowl seven times, earning first-team All-Pro honors in four consecutive seasons from 2014 to 2017.Brownwon a Super Bowl with Tampa Bayin the 2020 season, catching a touchdown pass from Tom Brady in the game. His career ended in 2021 after hedramatically exited a game mid-play, removing his jersey and jogging off the field.Explore more on these topicsNFLMiamiUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Florian Wirtz does not look like a £116m player but it’s too early to write him off | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: The 23-year-old playmaker has been disappointing for Liverpool but has he really been that bad?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 23-year-old playmaker has been disappointing for Liverpool but has he really been that bad?
Content: The numbers show that fans and pundits should give Florian Wirtz more time.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe numbers show that fans and pundits should give Florian Wirtz more time.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesGuardian Sport NetworkLiverpoolFlorian Wirtz does not look like a £116m player but it’s too early to write him offThe 23-year-old playmaker has been disappointing for Liverpool but has he really been that bad?ByOpta AnalystDavid SegarWed 23 Sep 2026 09.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 16.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenFlorian Wirtz signed for Liverpoolin the summer of 2025, there was only one logical assumption. The Premier League champions at the time had recruited one of the hottest young talents in world football – a key player in the Bayer Leverkusen team that had won the double in 2023-24 and a star in the Germany team. An exciting and productive young attacking midfielder being added to the best team in England? How could this notwork?Football has a habit of flipping the script, though. Last season was difficult forLiverpoolfor several reasons, and Wirtz, along with other new arrivals, struggled to make the impact expected of a player costing up to £116m. There were conversations among fans this summer about how long he and his fellow nine-figure signing Alexander Isak should be given before difficult questions needed be asked. The consensus was until Christmas.As it turned out, the real answer was after the opening game as Wirtz and Isak laboured inLiverpool’s 2-2 draw at Newcastleand loud doubts began to surface. Jamie Carragher spoke on the first Monday Night Football of the season about Wirtz’s signing in 2025 potentially being part of the “worst transfer window in Premier League history”.The former Liverpool defender was criticising a few players – and Isak has since gone on to score four times in hislast four league appearancesto quieten his doubters – but Carragher focused his ire on Wirtz again on Sunday in a new podcast for Sky Sports.“The reason I worry is, I don’t think Wirtz is in poor form since he came to Liverpool. I think what we’re seeing is what he is,” he said. “The worry for Wirtz now is that what he’s given Liverpool is so low. Where we were expecting him was to take Liverpool to another league title, to take Liverpool to a Champions League. The gap he’s got to close to justify what people were expecting I almost think is too big. You can’t get there. Even if he improves a bit, it’s still not what Liverpool thought they were getting. AndoniIraola’s got a decision to make here. Wirtz would not be in my Liverpool team.”Carragher derided Wirtz – who has just one assist in six games this season – for his performance in the team’s1-0 win at Bournemouth, calling it “one of the poorest I’ve ever seen him in a Liverpool shirt”. Iraola was more generous, though, and accepted that the German had struggled in the first half. “He started the game slowly,” Iraola said. “After that first phase, we improved. Florian has helped us also to improve. Second half he was playing much better, he was finding better spots to receive and turn. I’m much more happy with his second half.”Wirtz’s numbers from the game were not that bad. He created three chances, the joint-most of any Liverpool player along with Cody Gakpo; he won six of his eight duels; and he won possession four times: only Alexis Mac Allister (seven), Ronald Araújo (six), and Jérémy Jacquet (six) won the ball more often for the visitors.Perhaps we should not be saying this, being Opta and all, but data does not always tell the whole story. Anyone watching the game could see a player struggling to impose himself, with several passes not finding the target. Only 26 of Wirtz’s 37 attempted passes reached a teammate (70.3%). That is not unusual for a creative midfielder but there were too many simple balls sloppily overhit or played too close to Bournemouth defenders.View image in fullscreenWirtz received a lot of criticism for giving the ball away; he lost possession 15 times before leaving the pitch in the 71st minute. Only Araújo (24) and Gakpo (16) did so more often, though they both played the whole game. That said, “possession lost” is a tricky statistic to hang your hat on, as creative players who play risky passes in the busiest areas of the pitch often find themselves losing the ball the most.He also made a near-post run in the second half that led to the ball dropping kindly for Isak to score the winner. It did not go down as an assist as it touched a defender on the way to Isak but, without Wirtz’s run, the goal would not have happened. He also showed some nice moments, even in the first half. He drifted through defenders before winning a free-kick on the edge of the Bournemouth penalty area early on, while a classy one-touch layoff to Isak could have been a nice assist if the striker hadn’t sent his shot high and wide.Expectations were greater for Wirtz, though. He was meant to take games by the scruff of the neck and decide them with moments of brilliance like he did at Leverkusen. Suggestions that Wirtz maybe just isn’t good enough to be the player he was expected to be in the Premier League seem harsh, though. There was hype around his arrival for very good reason.View image in fullscreenAfter joining Leverkusen from Cologne at the age of 16, he recorded 18 goals and 21 assists in 69 games in his first two full seasons. Wirtz tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his left knee in March 2022, though, and missed 10 months of action.He showed no ill effects on his return, playing a central role in one of the most incredible campaigns by a team in recent years. Leverkusen won their first Bundesliga title, becoming the first team to go unbeaten over a league season in the German top flight. They also won the DFB-Pokal, and reached the Europa League final, where adefeat to Atalantawas their only loss in any competition across the entire campaign.Wirtz recorded 18 goals and 19 assists in 47 games that season; the only player from Europe’s top five leagues to record at least 16 goals and 16 assists in all competitions. He produced 16 goals and 14 assists in his final season before heading to England, with only Mohamed Salah (18) and Lamine Yamal (13) getting more than his 12 assists from open play among players from Europe’s top five leagues.However, he recorded only seven goals and eight assists in 49 games in his first season at Liverpool, and it took until late December to register his first league goal as the champions struggled, ultimately limping home in fifth place and ending the campaign without a trophy. To be fair, it was a hard environment to come into. The death of Diogo Jota cast a dark cloud over the club and Arne Slot struggled to get his team playing anywhere near as coherently as they had the previous year.View image in fullscreenWirtz was far from terrible, though. He was by some considerable distance Liverpool’s most creative outlet in open play, which helped after the loss of Trent Alexander-Arnold. He created 95 chances from open play in all competitions, at least 27 more than any other Liverpool player. But there was no denying that it was a disappointing debut season for him.The World Cup was a chance to show he could do it on the big stage and he managed three assists in four games for Germany before they wereeliminated on penalties by Paraguay in the last 32. Only two players at the tournament had more assists at the end of that round, and only five players created more chances from open play than his nine. Despite that, he still bore the brunt of criticism from many in Germany for their underwhelming showing, such are the standards expected of him.View image in fullscreenWith a pre-season under Iraola, though, there was hope that a new system and a fresh start would help. You could argue he has played pretty well in at least two of his six appearances so far this season. Liverpool were not great in the2-2 home draw with Nottingham Forest, but Wirtz was their main threat, denied what would have been a well-taken goal by an offside call against Jeremie Frimpong, and playing a neat pass into Víctor Muñoz for their second equaliser.He was also impressive in the2-1 home win over Atlético Madridin the Champions League, and would have had another assist had Bradley Barcola not dragged his shot wide when sent through on goal by some sharp play by Wirtz.While he struggled to make much of an impact in games against Newcastle, Ipswich Town and Fulham, those “what if” moments have been a theme. Wirtz was not great in the 2-0 win at Ipswich, but he did produce a fine turn and cross for Isak to score what would have been his hat-trick goal, only for the flag to deny him by the narrowest of margins.Wirtz has at least been trying to make a difference in possession. He has made 19 progressive passes in the league this season (joint 16th), level with Martin Ødegaard and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. He has also made 43 line-breaking passes at a rate of 9.6 per 90, almost double his 5.2 per 90 in the Premier League last season.Another area where there has been an increase, numbers-wise, from Wirtz this season is off the ball. He has won possession in the opposition’s final third six times in the Premier League; only five players have done so more often, while only five have applied more pressures than him (419) and only six have received more pressures (260), showing that he is doing his work out of possession and is occupying defenders in possession. He ranked joint 12th, 21st and 27th in the Premier League for each metric, respectively, last season.Wirtz has also covered the most distance of Liverpool players in three of his five Premier League games, but it is his lack of impact on the ball that seems to have most people taking aim. He has been underwhelming, but six appearances into a new season seems early to be making damning conclusions. Things have barely got going under Iraola, and Liverpool as a team are clearly still several rungs below their potential.Slip sliding away: football season-ticket holders fear falling down pecking orderRead moreWirtz is a 23-year-old trying to find his feet in the strongest league in the world and, while there is no denying that he’s far from his best, that doesn’t mean improvement is impossible, or even unlikely.The eye-watering fee is undoubtedly a factor for the critics. Whether fair or not, players are judged against how much they cost. Paul Pogba was hardly a success story at Manchester United, but the criticism often felt over the top, mostly because of his £93m fee and the hype that followed his return to Old Trafford in 2016.The big question is can Wirtz ever show more in England? Undeniably world-class players have failed to do so in the past, including another highly rated former Bayer Leverkusen midfielder in Michael Ballack, who never really found his best form in a Chelsea shirt after his move from Bayern Munich in 2006. Patience has been shown, and more is required for now. It still feels too soon for sweeping statements and loud conclusions.This is an article byOpta AnalystExplore more on these topicsLiverpoolGuardian Sport NetworkAndoni IraolaJamie CarragherEuropean club footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: RAF jet crashes and explodes in Anglesey moments after pilots eject  | Royal Air Force | The Guardian
description: Witness says T2 Hawk aircraft, which was being used for a training flight, ‘was basically on fire’ on takeoff
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Witness says T2 Hawk aircraft, which was being used for a training flight, ‘was basically on fire’ on takeoff
Content: The Hawk T2 aircraft was trailing smoke before it crashed near houses and agricultural buildings, sending a fireball into the sky.Photograph: John Heyworth/FacebookView image in fullscreenThe Hawk T2 aircraft was trailing smoke before it crashed near houses and agricultural buildings, sending a fireball into the sky.Photograph: John Heyworth/FacebookRoyal Air ForceRAF jet crashes and explodes in Anglesey moments after pilots ejectWitness says T2 Hawk aircraft, which was being used for a training flight, ‘was basically on fire’ on takeoffHarry CockburnWed 23 Sep 2026 14.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn RAF jet crashed and exploded moments after two pilots ejected during a training flight over Anglesey (Ynys Môn) in northWaleson Wednesday.The aircraft, a Hawk T2, had just taken off from RAF Valley on the west of the island when the incident occurred, witnesses said.RAF pilots eject from training plane before crashBoth pilots parachuted to the ground and were reportedly treated for minor injuries.A video of the crash shows the aircraft appearing to climb unevenly before the pilots eject. The plane then nosedives towards the ground while trailing smoke and crashing near houses and agricultural buildings, sending an enormous fireball into the sky.An RAF spokesperson said: “An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley, occurred near Anglesey. An investigation is under way and we will not comment further at this time.”The site of the crash, at Pencarnisiog, is less than two miles from the airbase. RAF Valley is home to the air force’s No 4 Flying Training School, which trains fighter pilots using Hawk T2 and Texan T1 aircraft.A spokesperson for North Wales fire and rescue service said: “Crews and officers attended an incident involving an aircraft in the Pencarnisiog area of Anglesey, working alongside colleagues fromRoyal Air Force, North Wales police, Welsh ambulance service and Wales air ambulance. The fire is now under control.”They added: “Members of the public are asked to avoid the area while emergency services continue their work safely.”Due to the crash, local train lines were closed and replacement buses were running between Bangor and Holyhead.View image in fullscreenThe jet, moments before it crashed.Photograph: John Heyworth/FacebookPete Bennett, a local resident,told Wales Liveit appeared the plane was in trouble as soon as it left the runway. He said: “I knew straight away that it was in trouble. Right on takeoff there was an orange flame, and as it accelerated it was basically on fire.“As it gained altitude the flame disappeared but it was clearly in trouble. It climbed at an aggressive pitch – like the pilot was trying to gain altitude. It pitched twice violently in the air and then there were two clear, loud bangs. It was probably at around 800ft at this point. The pilots ejected and both parachutes opened.”He said the explosion caused a “huge wall of fire and black smoke”. He added: “The aircrew came down around halfway between the runway and where the plane crashed, which I’m guessing was around a mile inland from RAF Valley.”The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said in apost on X: “My thoughts are first and foremost with the pilots. We will provide further updates in due course.”North Wales police said: “Two pilots are being treated for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage there are no reports of any wider damage or injuries.”Explore more on these topicsRoyal Air ForceMilitaryWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: No signs Chagos deal can be adapted to suit Trump, say UK officials | Chagos Islands | The Guardian
description: Agreement with Mauritius over Diego Garcia unlikely to be revived unless president changes his mind, insiders believe
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Agreement with Mauritius over Diego Garcia unlikely to be revived unless president changes his mind, insiders believe
Content: The Chagos Islands host the strategically important Diego Garcia base.Photograph: CPA Media Pte Ltd/PAView image in fullscreenThe Chagos Islands host the strategically important Diego Garcia base.Photograph: CPA Media Pte Ltd/PAChagos IslandsNo signs Chagos deal can be adapted to suit Trump, say UK officialsAgreement with Mauritius over Diego Garcia unlikely to be revived unless president changes his mind, insiders believePeter WalkerandAletha AduWed 23 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheChagos Islandsdeal is on hold for as long as Donald Trump objects to it, UK officials believe, with no immediate signs it can be adapted to suit the US president.After Trump savaged the three-way plan as “a terrible deal” during ameeting with Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly, the prime minister said he was “confident” the UK would be able to find a solution to revive the idea.But while efforts are still taking place to do this, there is an acceptance in the government that it is extremely unlikely unless Trump has another change of heart. “Until the president changes his mind there will not be any progress,” one official said. “We are where we are. We were waiting for the president to present a view, which he has.”The UKsigned a treaty last yearto transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, part of the Indian Ocean archipelago, under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year.map graphicWes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said on Wednesday morning that payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius were on hold given the dealcould not go ahead without US support.“This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support,” Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today’s programme. “So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government ofMauritiusand our government.”The US had supported the plan, but Trump changed his mind amid a wider deterioration of relations with Keir Starmer over the lack of UK support for the US attacks on Iran.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat are the Chagos Islands – and why is the UK returning them to Mauritius?Read moreSpeaking after their first in-person meeting at the UN in New York on Tuesday, Trump praised Burnham but gave no ground on his scepticism about the Chagos deal.“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible,” Trump told reporters. “It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before, after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous.”Burnham later said he had “inherited the situation” and had told Trump “that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides”. He added: “It was clear that we need to come to that agreement, but I’m confident we can find it working with our US partners.”Given Trump’s objections appear based on the core element of the deal – the transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius – there appears to be no immediate way forward. The UK government has previously made clear that Washington’s approval is a prerequisite for the plan.UK officials stress, however, that while Burnham inherited the impasse from Starmer, there is no intention to deprioritise a plan, begun under Rishi Sunak, that the government says is vital to ensure the future of the strategically vital Diego Garcia base, given Mauritian claims to sovereignty of the archipelago.“It’s not back to the drawing board, as we do need to find a diplomatic solution to this,” another UK official said. “Everyone agrees something has to be done, which is why several prime ministers and even more foreign secretaries have tried to get it over the line.”Streeting stressed the same point to the BBC, saying: “The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand … I would caution is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world.”Explore more on these topicsChagos IslandsTrump administrationForeign policyMauritiusUS foreign policyDefence policyDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Six Flags Magic Mountain sued over alleged ‘catastrophic brain damage’ from X2 rollercoaster | California | The Guardian
description: Lawsuit joined by more than 100 others claims they experienced traumatic injuries from the ride
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Lawsuit joined by more than 100 others claims they experienced traumatic injuries from the ride
Content: Six Flags Magic Mountain theme park in Valencia, California.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSix Flags Magic Mountain theme park in Valencia, California.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesCaliforniaSix Flags Magic Mountain sued over alleged ‘catastrophic brain damage’ from X2 rollercoasterLawsuit joined by more than 100 others claims they experienced traumatic injuries from the rideDani AnguianoWed 23 Sep 2026 15.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCalifornia’s Six Flags Magic Mountain is facing lawsuits from three people who alleged they suffered “catastrophic brain damage” after riding the X2 rollercoaster.More than 100 other people also claimed that they experienced traumatic brain injuries from the attraction at the Valencia amusement park, according to the law firm representing the plaintiffs.“These people went to Magic Mountain for some entertainment. For some family fun. And they suffered catastrophic brain damage,” Gary Dordick, an attorney, said during a press conference on Tuesday.Rollercoaster at LA’s Six Flags shut after two riders suffered brain injuries, inquiry findsRead moreThe ride has facedincreased scrutinyin recent months amid reports of riders becoming gravely injured.In July, two women experienced brain hemorrhages and had to undergo emergency surgery after going on the X2 – one of whom, 25-year-old Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, remains hospitalized. Attorneys say that doctors attributed the injuries to a “rapid acceleration-deceleration event” they experienced on the X2.AnAugust CNN investigationfound that over nearly 20 years there have been more than a dozen reports of serious injuries, including two deaths, associated with the X2 coaster.Six Flags said in a statement that it does not comment on pending litigation and the X2 had been closed since mid-July. According to the park website, Six Flags has a “comprehensive safety program” with “rigorous inspections [and] industry-leading standards”. There are daily inspections as well as regular evaluations by third-party ride inspectors, state and insurance inspectors, and company engineering and safety experts, according to Six Flags.The park describes the X2 as a “fifth-dimension wing roller coaster [that] will have even the most hardened thrill seeker screaming” and that is “downright scary”. It features seats that rotate 360 degrees and flip as the ride reaches speeds of up to 76mph, racing through half loops that suddenly become “sheer drops”.More than 300 people contacted Dordick’s firm to report injuries, he said. Attorney Christopher Bulone said that experts have said the ride was built to be more dangerous than others, and it has more variables and forces.“It’s the design of this ride that makes it inherently dangerous and makes it dangerous in a way that no reasonable rider would expect,” he said. “Time after time innocent people are coming off the ride with permanent brain damage.”Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaWest CoastLaw (US)Theme parksLos AngelesnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to join EU ocean science scheme to better predict extreme weather events | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Cooperation on OceanEye, which aims to better anticipate climate events, comes amid efforts to boost ties with bloc
Author: Karen McVeigh
Headline: Cooperation on OceanEye, which aims to better anticipate climate events, comes amid efforts to boost ties with bloc
Content: Melting sea ice in the Arctic Ocean at Svalbard in Norway.Photograph: Lisi Niesner/ReutersView image in fullscreenMelting sea ice in the Arctic Ocean at Svalbard in Norway.Photograph: Lisi Niesner/ReutersClimate crisisUK to join EU ocean science scheme to better predict extreme weather eventsCooperation on OceanEye, which aims to create ‘real-time’ model of world’s oceans, comes amid efforts to boost EU tiesKaren McVeighWed 23 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain is to join a major new ocean science programme, led by the EU, to better forecast extreme weather and climate events, the environment secretary is to announce in New York.The announcement on Wednesday will come as Andy Burnham’s government aims to rebuild the UK’s relationship with Europe, and follows warnings this year’s“supersized” El Niño, tracked in the Pacific Ocean, will fuel more extreme weather globally.Scientists have warned that the global marine monitoring system, which is vital to predict extreme weather events and ultimately to save lives, is under strain afterthreats by the US administration this yearto dismantle its substantial share of global ocean observations.In June,the EU launched a €92m (£78m) initiative called OceanEye, to boost its role in ocean observation and to provide data-backed marine intelligence to deepen understanding and management of the ocean. It plans to create a digital “real time” replica model of the ocean, collected by satellites, sensors and other models by 2030, to help decisions on ocean protection and security. The EU introduced aninternational alliance with Canadaas part of OceanEye, to address critical gaps in under-monitored regions and strengthen cooperation between nations.In addition to weather and climate predictions, ocean observations also underpin national security, global trade and marine protections.Angela Eagle will announce the UK is to join the scheme at a meeting attended by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, at the UN headquarters in New York.Britain will share more data from the Met Office and other agencies with the EU and Canada than before.The environment secretary will tell the event: “As an island nation and a global leader in climate science, we know that data from ocean monitoring is essential to our ability to protect and restore our oceans, and anticipate and respond to the huge threats they face, because we cannot save our oceans if we do not understand them.”“Changing weather patterns and currents are fuelling the extreme weather which is already impacting all of our nations – through floods, droughts, storms and extreme heat. That’s why the UK is so committed to maintaining our vital global network of observation systems, which span coastal waters, shelf seas and the open ocean, including some of the longest-running observations in the world.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJoining the alliance to support and provide data to the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) would help better protect Britain from the impacts of climate change, said the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Currently, the global ocean observing capacity has significant gaps, at the poles, the deep ocean and of biological measurements.The US, which provides over half the ocean observing platforms and much of the technology, has reversed a proposal to scrap its$368m (£275m) funding for its Ocean Observatories Initiativeafter a backlash from scientists. However, moves to cut funding for US ocean agencies have left GOOS vulnerable to changing priorities of the US administration.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisOceansEuropean UnionForeign policyBrexitEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Beluga whale rescued from closed Canadian marine park dies in US | Illinois | The Guardian
description: Osiris, one of 30 belugas removed from Ontario’s shuttered Marineland, struggled to acclimate to her Illinois home
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Osiris, one of 30 belugas removed from Ontario’s shuttered Marineland, struggled to acclimate to her Illinois home
Content: Osiris at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium on 20 August 2026.Photograph: Rachel Mittelstaedt/Shedd Aquarium/APView image in fullscreenOsiris at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium on 20 August 2026.Photograph: Rachel Mittelstaedt/Shedd Aquarium/APIllinoisBeluga whale rescued from closed Canadian marine park dies in USOsiris, one of 30 belugas removed from Ontario’s shuttered Marineland, struggled to acclimate to her Illinois homeRichard Luscombeand agencyWed 23 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnIllinoisaquarium has said that a third beluga whale it rescued from a closed marine park inCanadathis summer has died after it struggled to acclimate to its new environment.Osiris, a 26-year-old female, was one of30 belugasremoved from Ontario’s shuttered Marineland amusement park, and among 10 rehomed at the Shedd aquarium in Chicago, which said the whale died there on Monday.Over the last month two other rescued belugas, named Peekachu and Rain, have died at the Shedd;
