and a 19-year-old male, Jelly Bean, one of two relocated to Oceanogràfic de València in Spain, died “suddenly and unexpectedly” last week.“When Shedd was asked to help with this rescue, we understood that these animals arrived with significant vulnerabilities and that the outcome for every individual could not be guaranteed,” the aquarium said in a statement.Beluga whales are particularly vulnerable to changes in their environment, such as climate change, pollution and other sources of stress, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).Native to Alaska’s Cook Inlet, belugas are classified as an endangered species, and their numbers have declined by almost 80% from 1979 to 2018.The 30 whales, and a number of bottlenose dolphins, became the subject of what marine activists said was akin to a hostage situation following the 2024 closure to the public of Marineland, atroubled theme parkon the southern shores of the Niagara river.More than 20 whales and dolphins had died there since 2019, and a calamitous drop in visitor numbers and income forced the owners to abandon the venture. The Canadian government blocked the sale of the surviving animals to China, leaving them facing the threat of euthanasia.A complex international operation moved 30 whales to aquariums in the US and Spain over the summer, but many did not take well to their new surroundings. The deaths were sudden and unexpected as their health wavered amid the challenges of adjusting to a new home, according to statements from the aquariums.The rescued belugas were moved in custom-made slings and temperature-controlled containers, Shedd staff told the Associated Press. Aquarium personnel traveled to Marineland to examine their health records in preparation for the move. They have monitored their health minute by minute since they arrived, staff said.Peekachu and Rain died at the Shedd in late August and early September after arriving fromCanada. Another beluga, at the aquarium for decades, died around the same time.Osiris was a “whale of clinical concern” since she arrived, according to the aquarium. The whale did not eat as consistently as her fellow animals, which complicated the efforts to keep her well-fed and hydrated, according to the statement.“Osiris experienced periods of meaningful progress, both nutritionally and socially, but her overall condition remained closely monitored,” the aquarium stated.Osiris’ caretakers noticed sudden changes in her behavior and breathing patterns the morning of her death, according to the aquarium. She was moved to the medical habitat, but “her condition declined rapidly,” and she “passed away despite lifesaving efforts”.José Rafael Serra Díez, spokesperson for Oceanogràfic de València, said Jelly Bean’s death was also unexpected. The whale “experienced feeding difficulties, prompting the veterinary team to intensify her monitoring”, despite periods of improvement, the spokesperson said in an email to the AP.The Georgia aquarium and SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio have also accepted whales from the Canadian park.The two rescued whales at the Georgia aquarium showed decreased appetites and were examined, but no issues were found, the aquarium said in a social media post on Friday. The whales at SeaWorld are in “stable health”, according to AnneMarie Iturrizaga, a spokesperson for the company that owns the parks.The Shedd aquarium notified Noaa of Osiris’s death Monday, according to John Chu, a spokesperson for Noaa Fisheries. Within 30 days of the whales’ deaths, the aquarium must formally submit their names and causes of death, and on request, provide copies of necropsy reports, Chu said.The Shedd aquarium said it will conduct necropsies and share the confirmed results.The Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsIllinoisCanadaWhalesMarine lifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Save the Children officially warned by regulator over staff put at risk in Yemen | Charities | The Guardian
description: Warning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Warning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023
Content: Children displaced by war wait to collect food aid at a camp for internally displaced people near Aden, Yemen, on 23 September 2026.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenChildren displaced by war wait to collect food aid at a camp for internally displaced people near Aden, Yemen, on 23 September 2026.Photograph: ReutersCharitiesSave the Children officially warned by regulator over staff put at risk in YemenWarning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023Patrick ButlerSocial policy editorWed 23 Sep 2026 14.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe international aid charity Save the Children has been issued with an official regulatory warning over management failures and misconduct that put staff at itsYemenoffice at serious risk.Thewarningconcluded a two-year investigation by the Charity Commission for England and Wales into the running of the office after the death of its safety and security director, Hisham Al-Hakimi, in October 2023 after he was detained by the Yemeni authorities.The commission said weak governance meant staff at the Yemen office were not properly safeguarded in response to what it called a “live security concern”, and incidents of poor conduct by staff were not addressed.The warning letter refers to “substantial policy breaches and a lack of accountability” at the office, and said local charity bosses failed to adequately assess and escalate complaints and reports made by whistleblowers.An internal Save the Children investigation in 2024 after the death of Al-Hakimi found a “negative working culture” in the Yemen office had left staff “disillusioned and marginalised”.It apologised to staff after admitting it had let them down by failing to properly appreciate the risks facing them amid the deteriorating security situation in the country.In a statement to the Guardian, Save the Children International said that since 2024 it had made significant changes under new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve support for staff and rebuild trust. The charity has closed its north Yemen office because of security concerns.It said despite its best efforts to understand the circumstances around Al-Hakimi’s detention and his death the challenges in Yemen meant it may never know what happened and why. Another Save the Children member of staff is understood to currently be in detention.The commission’s warning comes amid a growing humanitarian crisis in Yemen, where the charity has been providing emergency medical help, shelter and drinking water to displaced families.Official warningsare relatively rare, and are issued when the commission decides breaches of trust or mismanagement in a charity put its staff or beneficiaries at risk. They can be issued where charity trustees are deemed to have acted recklessly or without proper care.The commission ordered Save the Children International to ensure sufficient resources are in place to safeguard and protect staff and other individuals working with the charity.Stephen Roake, assistant director for high-risk compliance at the commission, said: “It can be incredibly difficult for charities operating in high-risk, volatile environments and we know that circumstances can change rapidly. However, it is for this very reason that trustees must ensure they have sufficient oversight of their overseas operations.”In a statement, Save the Children International said it had accepted the commission’s findings of serious shortcomings in governance, management, oversight and compliance with policies and procedures in the Yemen office at the time.Since 2024, it had installed new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve staff support and rebuild trust. It had also introduced detention risk assessments, taken steps to improve incident management procedures and strengthened crisis management.It said: “We remain committed to learning from this tragedy and ensuring a safe, supportive environment for our colleagues.“We will continue to work closely with the Charity Commission to address any outstanding matters, while continuing to support our colleagues in Yemen and deliver for children in extremely challenging contexts.”Save the Children’s Yemen officewarned last weekthat the country faced a “catastrophic humanitarian situation” as a result of escalating conflict, collapsing health services and outbreaks of disease.More than 1,000 people have been killed or wounded, and tens of thousands displaced byfighting in recent weeksbetween the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.Explore more on these topicsCharitiesYemenVoluntary sectorMiddle East and north AfricaAidHumanitarian responsenewsShareReuse this content

title: Bentley launches first fully electric car – with fake engine sounds to replace classic growl | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Torcal SUV can travel up to 375 miles on a single charge and is part of a £350m investment in the VW-owned carmaker’s UK business
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Torcal SUV can travel up to 375 miles on a single charge and is part of a £350m investment in the VW-owned carmaker’s UK business
Content: Bentley’s new Torcal SUV aims to appeal to younger buyers, with prices starting at £173,000.Photograph: BentleyView image in fullscreenBentley’s new Torcal SUV aims to appeal to younger buyers, with prices starting at £173,000.Photograph: BentleyAutomotive industryBentley launches first fully electric car – with fake engine sounds to replace classic growlTorcal SUV can travel up to 375 miles on a single charge and is part of a £350m investment in the VW-owned carmaker’s UK businessAlex DanielWed 23 Sep 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBentley is launching its first fully electric car – complete with a drum soundtrack to replace the growl of a combustion engine – as part of a £350m investment in its UK business.The vehicle, an SUV called the Torcal, is Bentley’s cheapest, starting at £173,000, and will be built at its factory in Crewe, securing the jobs of the 4,000 workers there.Bentley hopes to win over both EV refuseniks and younger customers with a new synthetic engine noise built from drum recordings based on its old eight-cylinder engines. The feature is designed to give “emotion to the car” and “bridge the gap” to new buyers, said Bentley’s chief executive, Frank-Steffen Walliser.“We expect a younger clientele,” he added, pointing to a more muscular vehicle body shape than previous models and the comparatively low price, which gives “easier access” to the brand, whose cars can cost up to £1.7m forone-off vehicles built to be showstoppers for billionaires.The Torcal launches into a thin market for fully electric luxury SUVs. Arch-rival Rolls-Royce’s only EV is a two-door coupe called the Spectre, which starts at about £330,000. Therecently announced Range Rover Electric– considered part of the premium segment rather than luxury – begins retailing at £154,070.It also marks a more tentative entry into the EV market than Bentley once predicted. In 2024, it was forced to abandon plans to launch new electric cars each year from 2025 to 2030, citing poor demand.Walliser said that while early indications showed demand would be strong in the UK, Europe and the Middle East, he admitted: “We managers always say we know but to be honest we don’t know [how much demand there will be].”There are “no plans at the moment” for a second EV launch, he added. “I revised so many long-term plans in the last 10 years that one has to be careful of it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Torcal is to be built in Bentley’s Crewe factory.Photograph: BentleyIt is the third big funding announcement in just over a week for Britain’s automotive sector. Nissan has said itwill invest £170mto build a new model at its factory in Sunderland, whileMcLaren will spend £500m on a new factory, creating 1,000 jobs and its first SUV.However, carmakers remain under significant pressure from US tariffs, competition from Chinese rivals andhigh industrial energy costs. Jaguar Land Rover recently said it wouldcut 4,000 jobs, citing “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”, while Bentley’s owner, Volkswagen, iscutting 100,000 jobsby 2030.Asked if Bentley was immune from the cuts at VW, Walliser said: “Immune would be the wrong wording. But there’s a very simple rule in Volkswagen. If you’re successful you can run your business. And we consider we are a successful business … it doesn’t bother me too much at the moment.”Bentley itself cut 245 jobs in Crewe earlier this year to reduce costs, and sales have fallen by a third since a 2022 peak of 15,200 cars. Walliser said a period of strong margins after the pandemic was a “post-Covid boom … now we are back to normal”.Walliser said headcount in Crewe will not grow with the investment “for profitability reasons”, but he insisted that “the statement cannot be clearer” about investing in the UK and that the money will partly go towards a new assembly line.Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said it was the “third win in just seven days for our world-class automotive industry, which truly shows the confidence that businesses have in Britain”.But Walliser said the landscape remained “difficult” for Bentley suppliers. “We see a lot of impact on especially the smaller businesses,” he said, citing new EU rules of origin and high industrial energy prices both in the UK and Europe. “There’s a lot of pressure,” he said.The Torcal can travel up to 375 miles on a single charge, and can power up from 10% full to 80% full in 20 minutes using an ultra-fast charger. The car marks the fourth model in Bentley’s lineup, alongside the Continental, Flying Spur and Bentayga.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryMotoringVolkswagen (VW)Luxury goods sectorManufacturing sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC to axe sports bulletins on its TV news channel | BBC | The Guardian
description: Cuts are part of plan to save £500m and lose as many as 2,000 staff by 2028
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Cuts are part of plan to save £500m and lose as many as 2,000 staff by 2028
Content: The BBC Sport booth before a Six Nations rugby match at Murrayfield.Photograph: Harry Murphy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe BBC Sport booth before a Six Nations rugby match at Murrayfield.Photograph: Harry Murphy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesBBCBBC to axe sports bulletins on its TV news channelCuts are part of plan to save £500m and lose as many as 2,000 staff by 2028Michael SavageMedia editorWed 23 Sep 2026 12.33 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC is to axe sports bulletins on itsTV newschannel and make more senior journalist roles redundant, as the corporation begins to unveil a series of painful cost-saving measures.Lunchtime and overnight bulletins on theBBCNews channel will no longer be shown, according to internal announcements made to staff.It is understood staff were told that compulsory redundancies would have to be made, as there had not been enough applicants for a voluntary programme. Across BBC Sport, it is understood there will be a net reduction of 36 jobs, including four senior producer positions.The cuts are part of a BBC-wide plan to save £500m and lose as many as 2,000 staff by 2028.BBC boss concedes real prospect of strikes over pay and job cutsRead moreStaff morale was already low and many suspect a strike is inevitable at the broadcaster, given the size of the cuts and an ongoingdispute over pay.The axing of sports bulletins has been seen as part of a wider shift in how sports news is consumed. Senior BBC figures believe that many sports fans have already seen crucial goals and developments on social media long before they appear on bulletins.As a result, they have been directing the BBC’s limited resources towards making content for growing online audiences, especially the insatiable appetite for Premier League football analysis.Alex Kay-Jelski, the BBC’s director of sport, has made clear that he is prepared to make unpopular decisions in order to adapt its coverage. Insiders say he has been focusing on online analysis and building digital audiences via social media and YouTube.However, his approach has divided staff. Some believe he has moved too far away from providing bulletin updates for general viewers, who are often older, while other staff members see the changes as painful but necessary.Further cuts are expected to be announced across the corporation in the next few days, ensuring a grim fortnight for staff. Redundancy rounds are expected to rumble on for months.Philippa Childs, the head of the broadcasting union Bectu, said the “slow-motion pace of the announcements will also be adding to the anxiety of those who have yet to hear their fates”.“It seems clear that cuts will have a direct impact on what sport the BBC can cover and the worry is that the quality and breadth of coverage will suffer as a result,” she said.The cuts follow an acute financial crunch at the BBC, as rising costs of making television have combined with the falling value of the licence fee and the fact that a rising number of households are opting not to pay it.Last week,the Guardian revealedthe BBC had spent hundreds of millions of pounds of its cash reserves in a single year, increasing concerns over the perilous state of its finances.Financial pressures and changing viewer habits are even more acute in the world of sport, where the rights to show sporting events are expensive and social media provides acres of content for fans.The BBC has taken radical action, axing long-running programmes and coverage of a series of minority sports. It announced earlier this month it wasending Ski Sunday. That decision came after it had already dropped the Commonwealth Games, the Boat Race, the World Indoor Bowls Championships and the Rugby League World Cup.Football Focus, its Saturday lunchtime show, was brought to an end last season.A new BBC Football YouTube channel has reached 100,000 subscribers in four months. Kay-Jelski has also highlighted the reach of BBC coverage of the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham over the summer.“The BBC faces difficult choices and significant financial challenges, and we cannot do everything,” he said last month. “Some sports will understandably prioritise the revenue they need to survive and thrive, and every situation is different.“But the value, visibility and scale that free-to-air broadcasting can provide remains something we’re incredibly proud of.”The BBC declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsBBCSport TVBBC licence feeTV newsMedia businessPublic service broadcastingTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Trans row nurse tells tribunal she ‘felt discriminated against’ by her union | Transgender | The Guardian
description: Sandie Peggie accuses RCN of failing to adequately support her in dispute over sharing women’s changing room with trans doctor
Author: Eve Livingston
Headline: Sandie Peggie accuses RCN of failing to adequately support her in dispute over sharing women’s changing room with trans doctor
Content: Sandie Peggie worked for NHS Fife for more than 30 yearsPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSandie Peggie worked for NHS Fife for more than 30 yearsPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianTransgenderTrans row nurse tells tribunal she ‘felt discriminated against’ by her unionSandie Peggie accuses RCN of failing to adequately support her in dispute over sharing women’s changing room with trans doctorEve LivingstonScotland correspondentWed 23 Sep 2026 11.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA nurse who objected to sharing a changing room with a transgender doctor has said she felt “discriminated against” by her union after raising the complaint.Sandie Peggie, who worked for NHS Fife for more than 30 years, won a partial victory against her employer after a tribunal in December 2025, when a judgeupheld her harassment claimagainst the health board but dismissed claims of discrimination, indirect discrimination and victimisation.Now Peggie has begun a new tribunal proceeding, this time against her trade union, theRoyal College of Nursing(RCN), which she accuses of failing to adequately support her in her original employment dispute. The union denies all allegations.Giving evidence on the first day of the tribunal, Peggie said she had originally spoken to her RCN representative, Stuart Fraser, in January 2024 after being placed on special leave by NHS Fife. She told the tribunal: “I felt like he thought I was being disciplined because I had done something wrong.”Peggie said Fraser was “non-committal” in their first conversation, and did not seem to agree with her that Dr Beth Upton should not be allowed in female changing areas. She said she felt she was being discriminated against and that she was not being supported, but acknowledged she did not say this to Fraser at the time.She told the tribunal that by February 2024 she had “lost faith” in the RCN, because Fraser had not mentioned legal support in their earlier conversation.Of the circumstances surrounding her original tribunal claim, Peggie said there had been “general chit chat” among NHS Fife staff about the use of a women’s changing room in Kirkcaldy’s Victoria hospital by Upton.When asked why no colleagues had given evidence to support her case she said: “I think possibly it was fear … They had seen the way I had been treated at the hospital by senior staff members.”Peggie’s case further claims that the union refused a request for legal support in January 2025, and that it did not provide adequate support when she asked NHS Fife to commit to ensuring changing facilities should be single-sex.She argues that the union discriminated against her because of her “gender-critical and sex realist” beliefs. Peggie said: “I felt unsupported. Mainly because I felt I had been discriminated against.”The nurse has also appealed against the decision from her original tribunal proceedings. That case is expected to be heard in the first half of next year.The tribunal, taking place in Dundee before judge Melanie Sangster, is expected to continue for seven days.Explore more on these topicsTransgenderRoyal College of NursingNursingTrade unionsDiscrimination at workEmployment tribunalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction | Harvey Weinstein | The Guardian
description: Sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in case involving former TV production assistant Miriam Haley
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in case involving former TV production assistant Miriam Haley
Content: Former Hollywood film producer Harvey Weinstein appears in Manhattan criminal court for the retrial of his rape case on 15 May 2026 in New York City.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFormer Hollywood film producer Harvey Weinstein appears in Manhattan criminal court for the retrial of his rape case on 15 May 2026 in New York City.Photograph: Getty ImagesHarvey WeinsteinHarvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault convictionSentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in case involving former TV production assistant Miriam HaleyMarina DunbarWed 23 Sep 2026 11.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarvey Weinsteinwas sentenced to 15 years on Wednesday after being convicted of sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006 at his Manhattan apartment.Haley appeared in court on Wednesday morning and delivered a victim impact statement.In her statement, Haley spoke about the harassment and humiliation she has endured over the past seven years, saying she was publicly smeared by Weinstein, his defense team, and podcasters she suspects were paid to damage her image.Haley added that her experience following the assault has “already been a life sentence” for her, and asked the judge to take all of this into consideration.New York assistant district attorney Nicole Blumberg addressed the court on behalf of the prosecution. She asked the court to sentence Weinstein, 74, to 20 years with five years of post-release supervision, stating he never showed any type of remorse for his crimes.Weinstein said in his statement he has remorse for Haley. “I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize for my actions,” he said.Weinstein’s defense had also argued that their client is too sick to serve a long sentence following a diagnosis of several health conditions includingblood cancerandheart disease. The defense asked for a nine-year sentence.Before sentencing, Judge Curtis Farber acknowledged that Weinstein would be remembered not just for producing films, but for being the face of the #MeToo movement. Farber said Weinstein took advantage of Haley’s dreams of working in the film industry.“You had it all,” Farber said. “Your legacy could have been cemented with greatness. But you threw it all away by assaulting Miriam Haley.”The latest sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in the closely watched case.Weinstein was sentenced to 23 years in prison in 2020 after a jury convicted him of sexually assaulting Haley and raping aspiring actor Jessica Mann.But in 2024, New York’s highest court overturned the convictions, saying Weinstein’s trial had been prejudiced by the judge allowing woman who alleged they were sexual assault victims of Weinstein to testify, despite not being plaintiffs in the case.Weinstein went on trial again in 2025 and was once more convicted of a criminal sexual act involving Haley.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJurors acquitted Weinstein of a separate sexual assault charge involving former model Kaja Sokola but could not reach a verdict on the rape charge involving Mann. Prosecutors retried the Mann charge earlier this year, but the jury deadlocked in May. The charge was later dropped after Mann said she could not endure another trial.Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separateCaliforniarape case.In June, a California appeals courtupheldWeinstein’s 2022 rape and sexual assault conviction. He was found guilty of assaulting an Italian model in her hotel room during a film festival.He could serve the California sentence before beginning the sentence imposed in New York. Farber said at Wednesday’s sentencing that California will have the final say on whether Weinstein’s sentences run consecutively or concurrently.The accusations and subsequent charges against Weinstein were one of the biggest factors in launching the #MeToo movement. More than 80 women have come forward with allegations of sexual assault or misconduct against him.Explore more on these topicsHarvey WeinsteinUS crimeNew YorkCaliforniaSexual harassmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid home | Spain | The Guardian
description: Housing rights campaigners decry landlord’s ‘barbaric behaviour’ after apartment Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years was bought by a developer
Author: Stephen Burgen
Headline: Housing rights campaigners decry landlord’s ‘barbaric behaviour’ after apartment Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years was bought by a developer
Content: Maricarmen’s case was taken up by Madrid’s tenants’ union in city where the right to housing is a live issue.Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMaricarmen’s case was taken up by Madrid’s tenants’ union in city where the right to housing is a live issue.Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/ShutterstockSpainPolice use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid homeHousing rights campaigners decry landlord’s ‘barbaric behaviour’ after apartment Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years was bought by a developerStephen Burgenin BarcelonaWed 23 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere were violent scenes in Madrid on Wednesday as riot police fought with protesters trying to prevent the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her apartment in the Retiro district.Hundreds of protesters had gathered, many of them overnight, in an effort to block the fourth attempt to carry out the eviction. Activists from the Madrid and Barcelona tenants’ union, and celebrities including the actor Carlos Bardem and the singer and actor Ana Belén, joined the protest.Police fired rounds of teargas and made repeated baton charges as they tried to open a path for a judicial committee to carry out the eviction order, which was eventually executed on Wednesday morning. The tenant, known simply by her first name, Maricarmen, is about to turn 88.View image in fullscreenMaricarmen is overwhelmed by emotion at an event organised by housing activists the day before her eviction.Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/ShutterstockDemonstrators chanted “Ayuso’s attic for Maricarmen”, a reference to the scandal surrounding the Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso’salleged purchase with public moneyof a €6.3m residential apartment for her use as a temporary office.Behind the building’s locked door, more protesters occupied the staircase leading to Maricarmen’s flat while neighbours handed out snacks and offered the demonstrators the use of their bathrooms.When a developer bought the building Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years, she was offered the chance to buy her apartment for €247,000 (£212,000), an impossible sum for a pensioner.They then raised her rent from €500 to €1,650 a month, while she receives a state pension of €1,350. An unnamed “prominent” writer offered to pay the €1,150 difference indefinitely but their offer was ignored.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators rally against Maricarmen’s eviction in Madrid’s El Retiro neighbourhood.Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/ShutterstockIn a video recorded by the local tenants’ union before the eviction, a tearful Maricarmen said: “Good morning, everyone, I thank you for the action you are taking, spending the whole night sleeping in the street. Please, keep going, but don’t hurt one another. This has to be peaceful.“I can still hear all your noise. A hug to everyone and to all the people who are supporting me in this cruel struggle against a person who wants to make money but who should not forget that they have parents and that one day they could find themselves in the situation that unfortunately I am in.”The most beautiful act of resistance I’ve seen: Madrid tenants fighting landlords with art | Leah PattemRead moreThe original 1956 contract for the flat was in Maricarmen’s father’s name. When he died, the apartment passed to his wife, and on her death in 2008 it was then sublet to Maricarmen. The landlords, Urbagestión SL, successfully argued in the supreme court that this subletting was invalid and that the contract was no longer valid. Urbagestión SL has been approached for comment.Speaking at the scene, Aldo Reverte, a spokesperson for the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions, said: “Maricarmen’s case is just one more example of what happens when housing is put in the hands of landlords. The difference is that a lot of people have become aware of her situation and the tenants’ union has shown that we can fight this type of barbaric behaviour.”However, for all their efforts, the protesters were unable to stop the eviction. Beatriz Duro, the lawyer representing Maricarmen, said: “The owner isn’t prepared to negotiate or accept any sort of offer. We have asked for a place where we can take Maricarmen’s personal belongings.”So far this year, 4,000 evictions have been carried out inSpain.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Texas executes death-row prisoner over 2005 triple killing | Texas | The Guardian
description: Ker’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection, the sixth person to be executed by Texas officials this year
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ker’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection, the sixth person to be executed by Texas officials this year
Content: The Texas execution chamber in Huntsville.Photograph: Pat Sullivan/APView image in fullscreenThe Texas execution chamber in Huntsville.Photograph: Pat Sullivan/APTexasTexas executes death-row prisoner over 2005 triple killingKer’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection, the sixth person to be executed by Texas officials this yearAssociated PressWed 23 Sep 2026 19.52 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man found guilty of fatally shooting three people during a 2005 attempted robbery at a ruralTexashome was executed Wednesday, a week after the other man convicted in the killings was put to death.Ker’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection at the state penitentiary in Huntsville. He isthe sixth person executed so far this year in Texas, with three more people scheduled over the next two months.A jury convicted Ramey of capital murder and sentenced him to death over the shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, in the home they shared in the small city of Edna, about 100 miles (160km) south-west of Houston.Ramey and LeJames Norman believed there was cocaine in the house and hoped to steal it, according to court records. They found none and killed the three victims, who lived across the street from Norman.View image in fullscreenKer-Sean Ramey in 2022.Photograph: Texas department of criminal justice/APNorman was put to death on 16 September, also in Huntsville. He had no last words, and no relatives or friends of the victims witnessed that execution.The US supreme court rejected a final appeal from Ramey hours before Wednesday’s execution.Ramey’s attorneys had argued that jurors never heard about how he suffered physical abuse as a child and grew up in poverty. State prosecutors told the court the appeal was “meritless” and argued that evidence showed Ramey had “an escalating pattern of criminal behavior”.Norman testified at Ramey’s trial nearly two years before being sentenced to death by a jury after pleading guilty to capital murder. He testified that he and Ramey shot the victims. Ramey’s attorneys blamed the shootings on Norman.Ramey’s former girlfriend testified that she was with him when he threw two pistols into a lake after the killings, and that he told her in detail about his involvement.Lopez was shot four times, including in the back of the head; Peacock was shot twice in the head; and Roberts was shot five times in the chest, neck and head.Explore more on these topicsTexasCapital punishmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three international bodies warn of risks of rising debt and soaring borrowing in major economies | Global economy | The Guardian
description: IIF highlights challenges facing US, France, UK and Japan, while OECD and IMF also voice global concerns
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: IIF highlights challenges facing US, France, UK and Japan, while OECD and IMF also voice global concerns
Content: The City of London. The OECD said the global economy had withstood the Iran war better than first feared but the recent resurgence in oil and gas prices posed risks.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe City of London. The OECD said the global economy had withstood the Iran war better than first feared but the recent resurgence in oil and gas prices posed risks.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAGlobal economyThree international bodies warn of risks of rising debt and soaring borrowing in major economiesIIF highlights challenges facing US, France, UK and Japan, while OECD and IMF also voice global concernsHeather StewartandPippa CrerarWed 23 Sep 2026 05.27 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree heavyweight international bodies have issued stark warnings about the risks of rising debt levels and soaring borrowing costs across large economies.The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the International Institute of Finance (IIF), the voice of global banking, on Wednesday highlighted the dangers of soaring interest rates on $365tn (£275tn) in global borrowing.In its quarterly debt monitor, the IIF predicted a “structurally debt-intensive future” as governments and companies scramble to invest in new technologies and bear the costs of ageing societies.“The buildup in global debt is set to accelerate as governments and corporates compete to boost growth and secure their positions in an economy reshaped by structural changes,” it said.It compared the current status of some of the world’s largest economies, including the UK, with crisis-hit emerging countries.“The US, France, the UK, and Japan face persistently large deficits and rising interest expenses – challenges long associated with debt-distressed emerging market sovereigns.”UK minister warns of impact of Trump’s Iran war on next month’s budgetRead moreWith many politicians facing elections in the coming months, and belt-tightening unlikely to be popular with voters, it said: “The risk is that already-unsustainable debt trajectories continue to deteriorate.”While in New York this week for the UN general assembly, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, denied reports that he had been shocked by the parlous state of the public finances since he came to power in July.“It’s not the case that we were surprised when we came in, not least because I was in access talks and understood very clearly the position,” he told reporters. “The truth of the matter is that because of the situation in the Middle East, the position changed, and has changed over the time I’ve been in. That’s just the reality of the situation that we’re in.”The IIF’s warning came as theOECDhighlighted the rising cost of servicing government debts as one key risk to the global economy in the coming months.In its interim economic outlook the OECD said global growth had been more resilient than expected given the strains of theUS-Israel war on Iran.However, presenting the report, its secretary general, Mathias Cormann, warned: “Fiscal and financial risks have grown. Thirty-year government bond yields are at their highest in 15 years or more in six of the G7 economies. That means higher debt-servicing costs for governments whose budgets are already under strain, and it means higher borrowing costs for businesses and households.”His words echoed a warning by the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, Kristalina Georgieva, who told the BBC the world’s advanced economies must take action to reduce their borrowing and bring down debt levels.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGeorgieva said a succession of global economic shocks had been “pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven”, with governments taking “no action to contain that service cost. [It’s] time to take that action,” Georgieva said, adding that courage was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.In its quarterly forecast update, the OECD highlighted the better-than-expected growth performance of the global economy this year but warned that the recent resurgence in oil and gas prices posed risks for the coming months.“Global economic prospects remain heavily dependent on whether a durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is achieved,” it said.It projected global economic growth of 2.9% this year – a modest 0.1 percentage point upgrade from the 2.8% it forecast in June. At the same time, it trimmed the outlook for next year slightly, from 3.1% to 3%.It also identified the record-breaking El Niño weather system –expected to be the strongest in 1,000 years– as a “significant downside risk” to the global economy, warning that it could hit agricultural production and push up food prices.Looking at the UK, the OECD significantly cut its inflation forecast for this year, from 3.7% to 3.1%, after prices rose less dramatically than expected.Economic growth for the UK is forecast at 1.1% for 2026,up from the 0.9% it had forecast in Juneand 0.7% in March, “with consumption expected to be supported by newly announced government support measures”.Explore more on these topicsGlobal economyOECDInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)EconomicsUS-Israel war on IranInternational tradeOilnewsShareReuse this content

title: Legal & General to cut 1,000 jobs by mid-2027 | Legal & General | The Guardian
description: Programme will initially involve voluntary redundancies in the UK but the insurance and pensions firm will consider mandatory job cuts depending on the take-up
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Programme will initially involve voluntary redundancies in the UK but the insurance and pensions firm will consider mandatory job cuts depending on the take-up
Content: Most of Legal & General’s 10,000 employees are based in the UK.Photograph: Alessia Pierdomenico/ReutersView image in fullscreenMost of Legal & General’s 10,000 employees are based in the UK.Photograph: Alessia Pierdomenico/ReutersLegal & GeneralLegal & General to cut 1,000 jobs by mid-2027Programme will initially involve voluntary redundancies in the UK but the insurance and pensions firm will consider mandatory job cuts depending on the take-upJulia KolleweWed 23 Sep 2026 07.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLegal & General plans to cut 1,000 jobs by the middle of next year, about a tenth of the British insurance and pensions firm’s workforce.António Simões, the chief executive, is wielding the axe as part of his attempts to create a “leaner organisation” since taking over from longtime CEO Nigel Wilson in January 2024. L&G described the move as “the next stage of that transformation”.The London-headquartered firm told staff on Wednesday that it had begun moves to eliminate about 1,000 roles by mid-2027, which had first been reported by Bloomberg News. Most of L&G’s 10,000 employees are based in the UK.The programme will initially involve voluntary redundancies in the UK but L&G will consider mandatory job cuts depending on the take-up.The fund management division, which oversees £1.2tn in assets, is excluded as it has its own restructuring plan.Simões, who previously worked for Santander and HSBC,announced a sharper focus on L&G’s booming pensions armin June 2024 and reduced the group’s four businesses to three, by merging its asset management divisions. It sold several “non-strategic” assets, the biggest of which was the housebuilder Cala Homes, along with legacy land and real estate.He also brought in a new executive team and pledged to return more than £5bn to shareholders between 2025 and 2027 through dividends and share buybacks.Simões told employees in an email:“Over the past two-and-a-half years, we have made significant progress executing our strategy, simplifying L&G, establishing three core businesses, and creating a more focused business.“However, over the last decade, different structures, processes and ways of working have developed across L&G, making us more complex than we need to be… we need to change how we work today and, through this, become a leaner organisation.”An L&G spokesperson said the changes “will help us focus our resources and investment on the areas where we see the strongest opportunities for long-term growth”. The spokesperson added: “We recognise and take seriously the impact on colleagues and are committed to supporting our people throughout the process and consulting with our unions.”The company expects £500bn of transactions in the UK pensions market over the next decade, as employers transfer their old defined benefit pension plans to insurers and pension companies. L&G said it was also benefiting from strong auto-enrolment of staff in their companies’ pension schemes, with about £1bn of new inflows each month.Explore more on these topicsLegal & GeneralJob lossesInsurance industryPensions industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years | London Stock Exchange | The Guardian
description: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market
Content: Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but it wants Airtel Money to be listed separately.Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/ReutersView image in fullscreenAirtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but it wants Airtel Money to be listed separately.Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/ReutersLondon Stock ExchangeIndian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in yearsSunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock marketNils Pratley: Does this mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yetJoanna PartridgeWed 23 Sep 2026 07.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the strugglingLondon Stock Exchange.Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that hasfaced a string of recent departures.The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-SaharanAfrica, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.View image in fullscreenSunil Bharti Mittal controls Bharti Enterprises.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesIt operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 butdelayed itto the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAirtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result ofoverseas takeovers of UK companies.Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wisefloated in 2021with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from Londonto New York.Explore more on these topicsLondon Stock ExchangeIPOsEmerging marketsStock marketsAfricaIndiaLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: A blood-splattered surgeon after an emergency horse op: Andrea Modica’s best photograph | Photography | The Guardian
description: ‘You’d have to be out of your mind not to want to photograph this incredible woman. And I only realised afterwards that she looks like a medieval statue, a madonna’
Author: Amy Fleming
Headline: ‘You’d have to be out of your mind not to want to photograph this incredible woman. And I only realised afterwards that she looks like a medieval statue, a madonna’
Content: ‘The floor was covered in the contents of the horse’s intestines. We went outside’ … Modica’s shot taken at the horse hospital.View image in fullscreen‘The floor was covered in the contents of the horse’s intestines. We went outside’ … Modica’s shot taken at the horse hospital.My best shotPhotographyA blood-splattered surgeon after an emergency horse op: Andrea Modica’s best photograph‘You’d have to be out of your mind not to want to photograph this incredible woman. And it was only afterwards that I realised she looks like a medieval statue, a madonna’Interview byAmy FlemingWed 23 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter my first job in the 80s, I had a little money and set off for Italy with my camera and a backpack. I had grown up hearing about Italy, where my family is from, and so began 40 years of travelling back and forth – at times to teach photography, or for a relationship, and always to make photographs with no real agenda, just being in the moment.My new book and the show that this image appears in spans my many visits. It was taken about six years ago. I becamevery interested in a horse hospital outside Bologna.I made a large body of work there and this first appeared in a book called Theatrum Equorum, Latin for Horse Theatre, all caught on an old-style large-format 8x10 camera.I photographed horses that had been taken out of surgery, and put into these wonderful recovery boxes filled with shredded paper and beautiful light. To give you a sense of the size of the camera, it takes 8x10 inch negatives – a lot bigger than the tiny negatives from 35mm cameras. The large format meant I couldn’t photograph a horse galloping across a field.double quotation markEveryone in my work is posing – but hopefully not appearing to be posing. That is where the skill comes inIn my work everybody knows they’re being photographed. They are reacting to me and the camera, and in a sense posing, but hopefully notappearingto be posing, which is where my skill comes in. With the horses in recovery, I had a few minutes before they came to. I also made pictures of the surgical tools, before and after surgery. Then I focused on the devices that stud horses mount to have sperm collected – that’s big business. The device is a stand-in for a female horse, but first the male smells an actual horse which they keep in heat for 365 days a year. Then there were some one-off images, and this is one of them.Two people operated there: a head surgeon(the owner), and this woman,who I liked very much and connected with. In this image, she had just done emergency surgery on a horse with an obstruction in its gastrointestinal tract. The floor was covered in blood and the contents of the intestines. Many of the procedures I photographed were keyhole surgeries and the tools were very tidy, whereas this was really dramatic.She came out of surgery looking like this. I asked if I could make her portrait – you’d have to be out of your mind not to want to photograph this incredible woman. We went outside into the shade where I knew the detail would showin all its glory,as opposed to in the sun.Where punk meets Catholicism: Andrea Modica’s portraits of 1980s schoolgirlsRead moreI didn’t do it on purpose, but I like that her feet are covered so she looks like a column, and I think her hands resemble those I often saw on medieval wooden statues of saints and madonnas. This was all very unconscious, but I could see after that she looks like a statue, and I also think a very beautiful and very powerful woman. I like the picture for so many reasons that maybe somebody else wouldn’t consciously notice. But photographs can work on viewers without them knowing why.I don’t title my work.Photographyis so tied to the facts. The way the blood drips down from each one of the folds, each one becomes its own little painting. Those are facts that really existed. What we do with the facts can create an interesting story, which the viewer can ideally interpret for themself. Of course the photographer has to make the image seductive, so that a viewer actually wants to get to that point. I think this picture is at once elegant and yet has elements of horror. She’s powerful but she’s also covered in blood. There’s conflict.Andrea Modica: Italian Story is atAlice Austen House, Staten Island, New York, until 20 FebruaryAndrea Modica’s CVView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jerry SpagnoliBorn:Manhattan, 1960High point:I don’t look back and think something’s higher than what I’m doing now, even though it may have been a bigger accomplishment. I’m shooting a portrait today at 3 o’clock – that’s what I’m excited about right nowTop tip:The best work can be made if you disregard audience completely – an important message now, with people shooting and posting on social media directly. There’s something lost in the joy of the process of shooting if one thinks about the productExplore more on these topicsPhotographyMy best shotHorsesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We live in a world of extreme consumption and waste’: Magali Reus, the artist reimagining rubbish | Art | The Guardian
description: Making vast versions of sardine tins and fishing lures, the Dutch sculptor explains how she imbues disposable objects with autonomy and meaning
Author: Sam Moore
Headline: Making vast versions of sardine tins and fishing lures, the Dutch sculptor explains how she imbues disposable objects with autonomy and meaning
Content: ‘Our understanding of objects is one of a quick transaction’ … Magali Reus with her works.Photograph: Gerrit Schreurs/ BaZView image in fullscreen‘Our understanding of objects is one of a quick transaction’ … Magali Reus with her works.Photograph: Gerrit Schreurs/ BaZArtInterview‘We live in a world of extreme consumption and waste’: Magali Reus, the artist reimagining rubbishSam MooreMaking vast versions of sardine tins and fishing lures, the Dutch sculptor explains how she imbues disposable objects with autonomy and meaningWed 23 Sep 2026 09.03 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMidway through my conversation with Magali Reus, we are interrupted by a courier. They’ve arrived at the artist’s studio to deliver an important package – one of the final components of a sculpture being finalised for Reus’s show Swimming By Night at the Perimeter in London.The studio is filled with such sculptures, all in various stages of completion. Reus likes to take everyday, often disposable, items – pizza boxes and sardine tins among them – and recreate them on a larger-than-life scale. One of them – vast looming fish hook lures made to look like uncanny cupcake cases or severed skeletal limbs – looms nearby, resting against a studio wall.View image in fullscreen‘Let’s Hang’ … Rig (All Eyes On), 2025.Photograph: Courtesy of the Artist and Mai 36 Galerie, ZurichBorn in the Netherlands and now based in London, Reus has shown in institutions across Europe and the US over the last few years, with her sculptures often responding to the specific details of buildings such as the Kunstverein Freiburg in Freiburg im Breisgau, Germany, and Kunsthalle Wien in Vienna, Austria. Her practice comments on our world of overconsumption and the fast disposing of objects that have served their purpose. “Our understanding of objects is one of a quick transaction,” she says.Reus tells me that when someone is first confronted by her sculptures, her hope is that they will seem simultaneously familiar and alien. Often, her work takes objects that would normally be briefly used then thrown away, and turns them into something more physically robust and imposing.At first glance, works from her series Subs are made to look like discarded pizza boxes – but their aluminium construction and meticulously ripped and hand-hammered edges reveal something much less disposable. “We live in a world of extreme overproduction, consumption and waste,” Reus says. Inside the “pizza boxes” that make upSubs are images of discarded Christmas trees, objects that have a brief, but meaningful, space in our lives.“In December, we gather around it, decorate it and sing beside it,” says Reus. “For a brief period of time it is a totemic, almost monumental presence in our home. By January, it lies forlorn in the street or has been thrust headfirst into a bin.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStreamers (Sprout), 2025.Photograph: Courtesy of the Artist and Mai 36 Galerie, ZurichEven when she’s describing these objects, Reus imbues them with a sense of humanity that is at odds with their disposable nature. There’s a deliberateness in the way that the work is slowly made: sheet metal is bashed into shape; multiple layers of paint are applied to resin. “The transformation,” Reus says, “changes the way that people relate to the object or the image.”Reus tells me that her aim is to give them “autonomy as objects”, allowing these things to occupy a new space, serving a purpose other than the one that might be foisted on them. These objects then become, to borrow the artist’s phrasing, “active agents,” rather than passive things to be manipulated or cast aside by people. At the centre of Rig (All Eyes On) is a recreation of a candy heart, blown up in size, with the words “Let’s Hang” emblazoned across it. This object, in its normal context, would be smaller and much more fleeting, dissolving on the tongue of whoever might consume it.View image in fullscreenFamiliar and alien … Merlin (The Tide), 2024.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Galerie Greta Meert, BrusselsReus wants these objects to “refuse to serve us, [establishing] their own parameters”. She tells me that people don’t often clock the fact that her pizza boxes are made from aluminium rather than cardboard. “I like listening to and allowing the material to dictate how things come together,” she says.Reus’s world might seem surreal, sharp and dangerous around the edges. But the more time you spend surrounded by it, the more the artist’s real aim comes into focus: allowing people to slow down and reimagine the world around them.Magali Reus: Swimming by Night is at the Perimeter, London, 25 September to 16 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArtSculptureExhibitionsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wonka’s Golden Ticket review – this bleak reality show is all nausea, no sugar rush | Television | The Guardian
description: Netflix’s new series is the ruthless, hyper-capitalist competitive take on a kids’ book that no one needed. AI-generating Gene Wilder’s voice for it just feels wrong
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Netflix’s new series is the ruthless, hyper-capitalist competitive take on a kids’ book that no one needed. AI-generating Gene Wilder’s voice for it just feels wrong
Content: ‘Watch if you must – but brush your teeth afterwards’ … Wonka’s Golden Ticket.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreen‘Watch if you must – but brush your teeth afterwards’ … Wonka’s Golden Ticket.Photograph: NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewWonka’s Golden Ticket review – this bleak reality show is all nausea, no sugar rushNetflix’s new series is the ruthless, hyper-capitalist competitive take on a kids’ book that no one needed. AI-generating Gene Wilder’s voice for it just feels wrongPhil HarrisonWed 23 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the sad-faced Oompa-Loompas who acted in Glasgow’s famously catastrophicWilly’s Chocolate Experiencein 2024 will testify, if you come at Willy Wonka, you’d better not miss. There’s always a risk involved when trying to recreate fantastical, fictional worlds: if you fall short – or miss the point – the bathos is all the more devastating. Roll up, then, for Wonka’s Golden Ticket, Netflix’s twist on Roald Dahl’s confectionary phantasmagoria, which reimagines the story as Squid Game: The Sugar Headache. It gets messy.As we join our contestants, they’ve assembled outside Wonka’s factory, having found Golden Tickets in apparently random bars of chocolate – although, as a group, they seem fortuitously demographically mixed and able to bring a range of disparate yet complementary backstories to the table. A lucky break. But wait! Is that the voice of beloved Wonka-proxy Gene Wilder?Almost. As it turns out, the show’s producers (with the approval of Wilder’s estate) have rendered the late actor’s voice in AI form. It sounds stilted, indefinablywrongsomehow. Like so much AI, it feels like a solution to a problem that doesn’t really exist – Wilder’s “presence” adds nothing beyond a sort of uncanny-valley queasiness that, of course, should be present in any rendering of Wonka anyway. The sickly scent of decay is already close at hand.For a group of grown adults who haven’t even ingested anything sweet at this point, the group seem wildly excited. However, the true meaning of the enterprise is about to be revealed: “Whoever reaches the end will walk away with a lifetime’s supply of money. A six-figure salary for 30 years.” Oh, the romance and wonder! In the spirit of the moment, the fact that GeneGPT doesn’t tell them if this money is taxable feels like an omission. From this point on, this bunch have their eyes firmly on the prize. What follows is a weird mixture of infantilisation (Charlie and the Chocolate Factory is a kids’ book, guys!) and hyper-capitalist, last-person-standing ruthlessness.View image in fullscreenLess Charlie Bucket, more Veruca Salt … Wonka’s Golden Ticket.Photograph: NetflixBut first, chocolate. Yes, there is a river of it, surrounded by edible grass, edible flowers and presumably, though we don’t actually see anyone on their hands and knees licking the floor, edible paving stones, too. The set-pieces are actually very well realised, even if the show’s value system feels somewhat bleak and desperately recycled.The first task involves gumballs, some of which cause contestants to disappear. But everything unfolds too slowly. The first time a contender vanishes in a puff of dry ice, it’s deliciously bracing; by the sixth, the producers are just offering you another bottom-of-the-tin Quality Street on Boxing Day evening. This rug-pulling surrealism needs a frantic pace to work, but for the most part, this show wanders around sluggishly. Worse still, it relies on the kind of reality competition alliance-building that keeps everything earthbound. It would have worked better as pure, crazy experience; a metaphorical sugar-addled eight-year-old charging giddily around a candyfloss playground. As it is, we get the nausea without the sugar rush; the cavities without the crunch.Eventually, everything just feels too familiar and prosaic. The living quarters are nicer than the austere Squid Games bunks but there isn’t room for everyone. This means negotiation. Emotional blackmail. Plenty of boilerplate competition show sequences in which people sit around scowling mistrustfully at each other. Contestant Ziad bellows “Daddy’s home!” upon entering the bedrooms, presumably prompting a shudder of regret and self-loathing in everyone who voted to save him from gumball oblivion. He also has thoughts on where this might be heading. “Going into Wonka-vision 2.0, I want to be prepared,” he solemnly states. He doesn’t appear to be joking. Lighten up, mate, you’re not on The Apprentice. Although actually, maybe you are. So much of this stuff is basically the same fondant fancy in a slightly different wrapper. The prize money raises the stakes but, paradoxically, it often removes the fun.And so it goes on. There’s a TV show within a TV show. A challenge so gut-churning that one contender threatens to regurgitate their samples of the chocolate river. Another paints a target on their back right from the start, but others (a grandfather and grandson; a devoted father-and-daughter combo) are reality TV-cute.But finally (much like the challenge version of Squid Game), Wonka’s Golden Ticket seems to point in the opposite moral direction to the creation which spawned it. Don’t expect Charlie Buckets here – doing the right thing, resisting the everlasting gobstopper. Instead, resign yourself to a factory full of Veruca Salts: blithe, easily manipulated, wanting everything right now. Watch them if you must – but brush your teeth afterwards, and keep the Rennies handy.Wonka’s Golden Ticket is on NetflixExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewRoald DahlReality TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Manhunter review – Michael Mann serves up a bold and queasy starter to the serial killer spectacle | Movies | The Guardian
description: Before Anthony Hopkins’ Dr Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, Brian Cox played a cannibalistic killer in Mann’s pioneering Red Dragon adaptation
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Before Anthony Hopkins’ Dr Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, Brian Cox played a cannibalistic killer in Mann’s pioneering Red Dragon adaptation
Content: Downbeat and deadly … Brian Cox as Dr Hannibal Lecktor in Manhunter.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenDownbeat and deadly … Brian Cox as Dr Hannibal Lecktor in Manhunter.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMoviesReviewManhunter review – Michael Mann serves up a bold and queasy starter to the serial killer spectacleBefore Anthony Hopkins’ Dr Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, Brian Cox played a cannibalistic killer in Mann’s pioneering Red Dragon adaptationPeter BradshawWed 23 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive years before The Silence of the Lambs, there was writer-director Michael Mann’s pioneeringThomas Harrisadaptation Manhunter, now on re-release in a director’s “final cut” for its 40th anniversary. It was his version of Harris’s 1981 novel Red Dragon, a movie which features Dr Hannibal Lecter (here spelt Lecktor) in a relatively minor part, and played in a much more coolly matter-of-fact and downbeat way by Brian Cox, who is first discovered in his cell lying down with his back to the camera.It has long been a haughty, hipster film-bro affectation to claim that Cox is better in the role than Anthony Hopkins. (Lecktor’s early acoustic stuff was great, you see, before he went electric as Lecter.) I think that’s a bit obtuse, for all that Cox is of course very good. Hopkins in The Silence of the Lambs is the definitive version: face it. But I will concede that Cox is more interesting than Hopkins by the time the latter came to make the 2002 adaptation of Red Dragon, at which stage the franchise had become a bit tired. Manhunter itself is a very interesting and watchable movie, but feels a little unevolved compared to Jonathan Demme’s masterly guignol spectacle, although Demme clearly inhaled Mann’s excitement at jets, ’copters and military hardware deployed at speed to bring down just one man.As in Lambs, the idea is that Dr Lecktor has to be creepily consulted in prison by a law enforcement officer who needs his help bringing down another serial killer, in this case the Tooth Fairy. (Unlike that monster or Lambs’ Buffalo Bill, Lecktor himself does not suffer the vulgar indignity of a nickname, and is always respectfully addressed by his name and academic title.) But there is an interestingly hostile charge in the fact that the person coming to see Lecktor is not a demurely polite young woman, but the guy who actually brought him down in the first place: careworn but brilliantly intuitive FBI profiler Will Graham (William Petersen). The cold dislike in Cox’s face, and his subsequent evil plan, is a marvel.After the trauma and burnout of tracking down Lecktor, Graham has been persuaded back on to the job by FBI chief Jack Crawford (Dennis Farina), desperate for his expert help; this has obvious implications for what no one in 1986 called Graham’s “mental health”. Graham is brilliant at the job because he can think his way into the serial killer’s twisted mind, and doing this all over again could send him over the edge. Right now, he has a very 80s-looking luxury sunkissed beachfront home in Florida in which to spend his retirement.The Tooth Fairy himself is Francis Dollarhyde (Tom Noonan) who has a Frankenstein’s-monster type tendresse with a blind co-worker called Reba, played byJoan Allen. It is with her that the film has the strange and rather amazing, if preposterous, scene; somehow Dollarhyde has connections at the zoo which lets him get Reba in behind the scenes to stroke a sedated tiger in one of the most startling “first date” scenes in cinema.The film also features an obnoxious tabloid journalist, Freddy Lounds (Stephen Lang), whose terrible fate at the hands of the Tooth Fairy is pretty plain from the outset: we see how creepy loser Lounds in his way has something in common with serial killers: pathetic, inadequate and predatory, projecting his failings into compulsive behaviour, but evidently without the satanic glamour and imagination of the alpha-male psycho murderers. Manhunter is a brash, queasy, bold thriller; yet for me, it is a curtain-raiser for the main event.Manhunter is in UK and Irish cinemas from 25 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmThrillersMichael MannJoan AllenBrian CoxFilm adaptationsThomas HarrisreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Boorman and the Devil review – enjoyable re-evaluation of the disaster that was Exorcist II: The Heretic | Movies | The Guardian
description: John Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly panned
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: John Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly panned
Content: Oh the horror … John Boorman in Boorman and the DevilView image in fullscreenOh the horror … John Boorman in Boorman and the DevilMoviesReviewBoorman and the Devil review – enjoyable re-evaluation of the disaster that was Exorcist II: The HereticJohn Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly pannedPeter BradshawWed 23 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Kittredge gives us a thoroughly enjoyable, detailed account of the catastrophe that was John Boorman’s 1977 film Exorcist II: The Heretic, the deeply ill-conceived and widely derided follow-up to The Exorcist, a bizarre but ambitious fantasy supernatural rhapsody, brimming with unintentional comedy. Yet it was visually bold and even brilliant, pioneering in its use of Steadicam; Linda Blair and Max von Sydow were persuaded to return; Richard Burton was cast as a troubled priest, and Louise Fletcher as a psychiatrist whose weird “mind-reader” contraption was entirely ridiculous. At the first film, people screamed. Now they screamed with laughter.According to an apocryphal tale gleefully repeated by William Friedkin, director of the first film, the sequel resulted in an enraged audience one night turning round and booing Warner Brothers executives in the back row of the cinema, and then chasing them out of the building and down the street. Boorman desperately recut the film with the sillier bits removed. But the damage was done.Boorman is interviewed here and generously goes into great detail about his painful and mortifying experience with the film, how he had originally been offered the first Exorcist, disliked the story and turned it down, but was induced to take on the sequel. Perhaps Kittredge could have made it clearer how risky it was for Boorman to have taken on a project which he fundamentally didn’t believe in and was somehow creatively working against. He hired a kind of script-and-direction consultant, his friend Rospo Pallenberg, whose influence with Boorman annoyed the cast.This, after all, was the era of sequels, and Coppola’s Godfather II had shown that they could be as good or better than the original. It was also an era when brilliant directors were trusted by studios to follow their instincts, cushioned from risk by something called “blind bidding” from movie theatre chains who would pay upfront for films on the basis of known quantities like stars, story and director, a practice which this disastrous film ended. But it was also an era when, after Mel Brooks’s The Producers, the media’s chattering classes were alive to the hilarity of so-bad-it’s-good. There was something else, too, something rarely acknowledged by reviewers: the pressure to follow extravagant praise with disparagement, so that the critical-superlative economy does not go bankrupt. And finally, like William Friedkin’s Sorcerer that same year, like all films good and bad of the time, Exorcist II: The Heretic had to go up against Star Wars, which blew everything else out of the water.It’s another proof of William Goldman’s maxim that nobody knows anything. If people had laughed at the spinning head in the first Exorcist, industry sages would have shrugged and said: yes, of course, obviously, it’s absurd. But the stars were aligned for that one. Now in retrospect we can make a case for Exorcist II: The Heretic being an interesting and misunderstood film. Kittredge quotes some mean reviews but doesn’t mention that the New Yorker’s Pauline Kaelactually made a contrarian case for it at the time, on the basis of its delirious experimental visuals. Perhaps the truth is that Heretic was, like Boorman’s sci-fi adventure Zardoz with Sean Connery in the crazy red mankini: weird, surreal, challenging, a shapeshifting creature vulnerable to mockery, at once monstrous and terribly fragile.Boorman and the Devil is in UK and Irish cinemas from 25 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsHorror filmsThe ExorcistJohn BoormanFilm industryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s about being loudly visible’: Ahadadream, the British-Pakistani dance star defanging racist slurs | Dance music | The Guardian
description: Like many south Asians in the UK, he kept creativity separate from a corporate career. But after co-signs from dance music’s A-list, he’s releasing a defiant – and daringly titled – debut album
Author: Tara Joshi
Headline: Like many south Asians in the UK, he kept creativity separate from a corporate career. But after co-signs from dance music’s A-list, he’s releasing a defiant – and daringly titled – debut album
Content: ‘The intention is pride, confidence, and self-love’ … Ahadadream photographed this month in Lahore, Pakistan.Photograph: Marshall LawrenceView image in fullscreen‘The intention is pride, confidence, and self-love’ … Ahadadream photographed this month in Lahore, Pakistan.Photograph: Marshall LawrenceDance musicInterview‘It’s about being loudly visible’: Ahadadream, the British-Pakistani dance star defanging racist slursTara JoshiLike many south Asians in the UK, he kept creativity separate from a corporate career. But after co-signs from dance music’s A-list, he’s releasing a defiant – and daringly titled – debut albumWed 23 Sep 2026 08.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Ahad Elley was 12, his family moved from Karachi to the UK. Quickly, he discovered his Pakistani identity was the basis of a slur. “Growing up inPakistan, I never knew that was a bad word, because why would it be? The word ‘pak’ means clean, it has no negative connotations.” Elley’s childhood response was to disconnect from his heritage, and what followed was “potentially shrinking or hiding parts of myself to fit into society”. It’s likely a familiar story for many diasporic south Asians who, at some point, have felt the call to assimilate.Twenty years later, Elley is better known as Ahadadream, an integral architect of the current British south Asian music scene, as well as a DJ, producer, label head, A&R and promoter shining a light on dance music from around the world. His tracks are favourites in sets by A-list dance artists such as Fred Again, Caribou, Peggy Gou and Four Tet, and with the release of his debut album, P★KI (pronounced “pee-star-kay-eye”) Elley’s star is set to rise further.The album’s title has caused some upset, given the word is laced with hurt and histories of racist violence, but Elley wants to reframe a slur used against him. “The intention is pride, confidence, and self-love,” he explains over video call from his home in east London. “There’s no intention to cause anyone any hurt or pain. But I totally understand everyone’s perspectives, and it’s also about sharing perspectives with each other, which I think is your responsibility as an artist.”Music wasn’t always an obvious journey for Elley. Like many desis, he thought of creativity as a hobby. “Music had always been drilled into me as something you did on the side,” he says. It was dance producer Skrillex who, in 2023, encouraged Elley to pursue his dreams. “He said to me: ‘No, you’ve got to quit your job. If you can’t make enough money, you can come and sleep on my sofa.’”Elley had spent a decade working full-time corporate jobs while establishing himself at the forefront of British underground dance music in his spare time.
