While studying chemistry at university, Elley had discovered club culture: attending Elijah and Skilliam’s infamous grime raves, Butterz; listening to Mini Mixes on Annie Mac’s Radio 1 show; running his own nights. He felt the pull of percussion early on, he says: “Rhythmic music has probably always been in my blood, going to weddings and being exposed to the dhol [drums]. Maybe I was drawn to UK funky because it’s more rhythmic, and that was almost a gateway to discovering things like gqom from South Africa, [Brazilian] baile funk, [Angolan] kuduro … I don’t understand why those sounds aren’t given as much importance as house and techno.”View image in fullscreen‘Rhythmic music has probably always been in my blood’ … Ahadadream.Photograph: Marshall LawrenceAnd so his own sets and productions began weaving together kinetic global polyrhythms. In 2017, he co-founded the label More Time, releasing tracks by artists from Trinidad to Taiwan. Simultaneously, he worked behind the scenes at DJ livestreaming company Boiler Room, all while making space for south Asian DJs who couldn’t easily be categorised: whether at his club night No ID, or Dialled In, the platform he co-founded. Though it started as a London-based festival, Dialled In has scaled up, with parties across the Indian subcontinent, international shows for south Asian artists, mentoring and, most recently, a record label – through which Elley is releasing P★KI.Capturing the bold energy of his DJ sets, with drums leading the melody throughout, P★KI is a thrilling love letter to Elley’s constituent parts, marrying a bright, borderless mesh of sounds that feel like being free. There’s a euphoric shout-out to inclusive clubbing on Make Space, alongside dark, boisterous nods to grime, slinky UK funky, skittering bass. The album’s visual identity, created with Elley’s wife, architect Esha Sikander, is a nod to the Radio Pakistan logo, with Elley dressed in brash colour combinations to embody his journey. He grins: “It’s about being loudly visible.”It’s fitting, then, that P★KI opens with Elley’s edit of transcendent qawwali singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, arguably the greatest icon of Pakistani music. Tere Bin is a gleaming rework that’s become a fan favourite – at least one couple have played it down the aisle at their wedding and, at Dialled In’s fifth birthday in London this summer, a rapturous, misty-eyed crowd sang along.“It’s always so emotional,” says Elley. “Sometimes I question where those emotions come from: like, why are there tears on the dancefloor when we’re all singing Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan at the highest possible volume we can? There’s some sense of healing, and part of that is because in our day to day lives we are maybe a little bit disconnected from our heritage or identity.”On P★KI, Ahadadream is proudly facilitating that healing for a new generation, rejecting the urge to shrink away.P★KI is out now via Dialled In/Island. Ahadadream plays Electric Brixton, London, on 27 NovemberExplore more on these topicsDance musicClub cultureFolk musicPakistanElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Roomful of Teeth/Kahane review – twisty and tuneful songs with a darkly comic edge | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Gabriel Kahane’s whimsical song cycle about grief, divorce and death brings irresistible melodies and moments of comic brilliance to the virtuoso US vocal ensemble
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Gabriel Kahane’s whimsical song cycle about grief, divorce and death brings irresistible melodies and moments of comic brilliance to the virtuoso US vocal ensemble
Content: Mesmeric … Roomful of Teeth at LSO St Luke’s, London.Photograph: Ed Maitland SmithView image in fullscreenMesmeric … Roomful of Teeth at LSO St Luke’s, London.Photograph: Ed Maitland SmithClassical musicReviewRoomful of Teeth/Kahane review – twisty and tuneful songs with a darkly comic edgeLSO St Luke’s, LondonGabriel Kahane’s whimsical song cycle about grief, divorce and death brings irresistible melodies and moments of comic brilliance to the virtuoso US vocal ensembleErica JealWed 23 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBetween having aclarinet concerto at the Promsand a duo project with violinist Pekka Kuusisto this autumn, the singer, songwriter and composerGabriel Kahaneis touring withRoomful of Teeth, the virtuoso US vocal ensemble whose founding members include Caroline Shaw.Elevator Songs, which he wrote for them in 2023, is a darkly whimsical piece somewhere between a concept pop album and a song cycle. We are in a wormhole of a hotel, where the elevator – cue chimes – takes us to what seem like parallel worlds. Kahane’s songs deal deftly with grief, divorce and death, but within his style – tuneful, melancholic, full of twisty harmonies – it was the comedic ones that hit most immediately here.Each singer got their moment, accompanied by the others – all using mics – and with some doubling up to play violin, vibraphone or, in Kahane’s case, piano and guitar. Thann Scoggin brought stentorian poise as the man whose hot-tub session is disturbed by a paranoid drunk, the ensuing exchange set as a quasi-operatic duet in Bergian style. Holcombe Waller was the silky-smooth influencer pronouncing on cabin baggage and its emotional counterpart, his spoken advice segueing into 1980s soul choruses as catchy as a perfect disposable pop song.View image in fullscreenDarkly whimsical … Roomful of Teeth at LSO St Luke’s, London, with Gabriel Kahane.Photograph: Ed Maitland SmithBefore this, Kahane had accompanied himself in a handful of songs from his Book of Travelers – songs about a dis-United States written during a cross-continent rail trip – and one of his Craigslistlieder, setting a personal ad in severe, Bartókian style. Then a sequence fromBits Torn From Words, by Peter Shin, showcased Roomful of Teeth in their usual guise: a cappella, drawing on abundant vocal techniques. Syllables pulsed around the semicircle of singers, raw and vibrant or with sine-wave purity, and the overtones on Cameron Beauchamp’s bass notes skittered up and down the harmonic series mesmerically.Strictly speaking, this was the evening’s most arresting music – but the earworms all came from Kahane.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Another taste of honey: Shelagh Delaney’s long-lost play about a teenage truant is a little gem | Audio drama | The Guardian
description: The playwright’s daughter found Catch Me Who Can after her mother’s death. Now it has become a compelling audio drama with Toby Jones and Rita Tushingham
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: The playwright’s daughter found Catch Me Who Can after her mother’s death. Now it has become a compelling audio drama with Toby Jones and Rita Tushingham
Content: A remarkable gift for dialogue … Shelagh Delaney pictured in 1960.Photograph: Tom Stuttard/the GuardianView image in fullscreenA remarkable gift for dialogue … Shelagh Delaney pictured in 1960.Photograph: Tom Stuttard/the GuardianAudio dramaAnother taste of honey: Shelagh Delaney’s long-lost play about a teenage truant is a little gemThe playwright’s daughter found Catch Me Who Can after her mother’s death. Now it has become a compelling audio drama with Toby Jones and Rita TushinghamMichael BillingtonWed 23 Sep 2026 04.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 04.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWas Shelagh Delaney a one-hit wonder? Absolutely not. Aside from A Taste of Honey which, in the words of Dominic Dromgoole, “has a rock-solid heart and the gleam of the natural”, she wrote the screenplays for the films Charlie Bubbles and Dance With a Stranger, TV series including The House That Jack Built and several radio plays. But now a 30-minute piece,Catch Me Who Can, has come to light, been released as an audio drama and turns out to be a little gem.Its origins are fascinating. It deals with a teenage truant and was discovered by Delaney’s daughter, Charlotte, after her mother’s death in 2011. But why did it lay hidden for so long? According to Charlotte, who has adapted it for audio: “It imagines my last few hours on the lam having run away from home and school when I was 14 in 1978. I was gone for three days and two nights. I’d suggest it’s a racing certainty that the reason nothing has ever been heard of it is that it’s about me and my mum had rules about that kind of thing.”The bulk of the play consists of a testy confrontation between the runaway Hattie (Ivy Sheehan) and her maths teacher (Toby Jones) who tries to persuade her to return home. Although the teacher is only out jogging in a park because he is on strike, he stands for a world of order, discipline and control; Hattie, on the other hand, embodies the need for freedom, anarchy and self-expression. But Delaney imbues the situation with its own ironies. The teacher argues for the sanctity of family life but is himself a conspicuous loner; Hattie’s urge for self-discovery conceals a total disregard for other people including her anxious parents.View image in fullscreenRita Tushingham, far left, with Robert Stephens, Murray Melvin and Dora Bryan in the 1961 film version of A Taste of Honey.Photograph: Ronald GrantSeveral things make the play worth listening to. One is the ease and naturalness of the dialogue. Hattie, not unlike the teenage Jo in A Taste of Honey, asks endless questions. At one point she taxes the teacher as to whether he ever did anything to find out what it was like just for the sake of it since “you once told us curiosity was divine”. Delaney also introduces an itinerant bag lady – played by none other than Rita Tushingham who was Jo in Tony Richardson’s film of A Taste of Honey – who says of a relative: “They took him into hospital and took his leg off – just like President Tito.”The best theatre to stream this month: Bryan Cranston cranks up the tension in All My SonsRead moreAs well as a collision between self-restraint and teenage truancy, the play offers – in Charlotte Delaney’s words – a snapshot of London life in 1978, with oblique references to the IRA, the Vietnamese “boat people” and Rock Against Racism: a reminder of the turbulence of the times.Deftly produced by Polly Thomas, the piece is very well acted by Jones as the audibly repressed teacher and by Sheehan as the experience-hungry Hattie. What you come away with is a reminder of Delaney’s remarkable gift for dialogue and her equal understanding of the value of education and the exuberance of youth.Catch Me Who Can is on SpotifyExplore more on these topicsAudio dramaTheatreShelagh DelaneyToby JonesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fire in My Mouth review – Wolfe’s multimedia oratorio tells its tragic story with focus and power | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Marin Alsop, the Philharmonia and three outstanding choirs gave the London premiere of Wolfe’s work about the deaths of 146 workers in a New York garment factory fire in 1911
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Marin Alsop, the Philharmonia and three outstanding choirs gave the London premiere of Wolfe’s work about the deaths of 146 workers in a New York garment factory fire in 1911
Content: Scissors snapped shut in unison with metallic bite … Fire in My Mouth at Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Pete WoodheadView image in fullscreenScissors snapped shut in unison with metallic bite … Fire in My Mouth at Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Pete WoodheadClassical musicReviewFire in My Mouth review – Wolfe’s multimedia oratorio tells its tragic story with focus and powerRoyal Festival Hall, LondonMarin Alsop, the Philharmonia and three outstanding choirs gave the London premiere of Wolfe’s work about the deaths of 146 workers in a New York garment factory fire in 1911Alexandra CoghlanWed 23 Sep 2026 08.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Saturday 25 March, 1911, Greenwich Village’s Triangle Shirtwaist Factory caught fire. One hundred and forty-six garment workers – mostly recent Jewish and Italian immigrant women – died, many prevented from escaping the flames by stairwells and exits locked by the management.The disaster is the catalyst for Pulitzer-winning composer Julia Wolfe’s 2019 multimedia oratorioFire in My Mouth: the third in her series of large-scale works drawing on the history of the American worker, and a punchy opener to the Southbank Centre’s autumn season.This isn’t the first protest-work we’ve seen from Wolfe in London this year; 2026 opened withunEarth at the Barbican– an earnest homily on the climate emergency. But where the latter preached, Fire in My Mouth dramatises. Succinct and direct, told largely in verbatim words from survivors and contemporaries, the piece’s strength is its refusal to widen the lens, to turn a tragedy into a touchstone or individuals into everywomen.View image in fullscreenMassed protest song … the Philharmonia, London Voices, the RSNO Youth Chorus and Farnham Youth Choir perform Fire in My Mouth.Photograph: Pete WoodheadThe score churns and whirs with kinetic energy: the clack of the sewing machines or the swell of the ocean we first meet the women crossing “without passports or anything”. Text is fragmented and superimposed, layered in motoric patterns until consonants become verbal pistons and levers. Underneath, a large orchestra (here a keenly expressive Philharmonia conducted by Marin Alsop) shapes more sustained soundscapes, occasionally fascinatingly alien: the pitchless grind of bows into strings creating a flickering Geiger counter effect, or the scissors raised high above the chorus’s heads, snapped shut in unison with metallic bite.With so many moving parts – an all-female professional chamber choir and youth chorus; a slow-strafing slideshow of black and white photographs and archive film footage created by Jeff Sugg; ritual gestures and movements by director Anne Kauffman – it would be easy for the music to turn into a soundtrack. The distilled clarity of Wolfe’s score ensures it doesn’t, aided here by outstanding performances fromLondon Voicesas well as theRSNO Youth ChorusandFarnham Youth Choir– all crisply and undemonstratively marshalled by Alsop.The work ends (echoes of John Adams’ 9/11 homage On the Transmigration of Souls) with a litany of the names of the dead. It’s a statement that would have been impossible until 2011, when the final victims were at last identified, just a year before a fire in a Bangladesh garment factory killed 124.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicThe Philharmonia OrchestrareviewsShareReuse this content

title: John Green got an astronomical following from his books. What came next? ‘I’m still competing for clicks’ | John Green | The Guardian
description: Returning with his first-ever adult novel, the bestselling author reflects on fame, YouTube and his brother’s AI controversy
Author: Carter Sherman
Headline: Returning with his first-ever adult novel, the bestselling author reflects on fame, YouTube and his brother’s AI controversy
Content: John Green: ‘I suspect that young people want to be famous for the same reason I wanted public attention, which is that I thought it would fill a hole inside of me.’Photograph: Marina WaterView image in fullscreenJohn Green: ‘I suspect that young people want to be famous for the same reason I wanted public attention, which is that I thought it would fill a hole inside of me.’Photograph: Marina WaterJohn GreenJohn Green got an astronomical following from his books. What came next? ‘I’m still competing for clicks’Returning with his first-ever adult novel, the bestselling author reflects on fame, YouTube and his brother’s AI controversyCarter ShermanWed 23 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.28 EDTShareBy his mid-30s,John Greenhad done pretty well for himself. His debut novel, Looking for Alaska, had won a prestigious award for young adult literature. He and his brother, Hank, had launched a popular YouTube channel, where they regularly posted videos about their lives. With their combined incomes, Green and his wife were able to cobble together a living, buying a house and starting a family in Indianapolis.And then, in 2012, he published The Fault in Our Stars.“The week that book came out, it sold more copies than all of my previous books had sold in hardcover combined,” Green recalled in a recent interview with the Guardian podcastStateside with Kai and Carter. “Up until that moment, I’d been very cavalier about sharing my life online and offline, and it was only in the wake of that that I started to realize the cost of that. People started coming to our house, sometimes quite late at night. We had young kids – babies – back then. People don’t always have the best boundaries.”The Fault in Our Stars follows the story of Hazel, a 16-year-old living with cancer, who falls in love with a fellow cancer patient. Powered in part by Green’s online fandom, the book sold more than 20m copies – enough for every person in the state of New York to have a copy, and then some. In 2014, Hollywood adapted it into a movie starring Shailene Woodley and Ansel Elgort. After the film became a blockbuster, raking in more than $300m at the global box office, Hollywood started adapting Green’s other books, too.double quotation markYou have a choice about how public to make your life. You don’t really have a choice about the public’s response to thatJohn GreenToday, Green is as famous as an author can probably get. He has published another young adult novel and two nonfiction books – all of which also became bestsellers. HisYouTubechannel with Hank, Vlogbrothers, now has north of 4 million subscribers. The brothers have posted about practically every topic imaginable, from giraffe mating to presidential tax platforms to what it feels like to spend 15 hours in a Target.But he remains decidedly ambivalent about his popularity. It doesn’t feel nourishing, he said. It feels like empty calories.“It was uncomfortable to talk about, because how do you not be grateful for this overwhelmingly wonderful thing in your life?” Green said. “I have a friend who’s a very successful author, and I remember she said to me once: ‘Of all the good things that ever happened to me, fame was the worst.’ I think that’s a pretty good way to think about it.”View image in fullscreenHollywood, Ending by John Green.Green decided to work through his mixed feelings in his new book, Hollywood, Ending. Released this week, the book follows two young actors who make a movie about Andy Warhol, fall in love, and try to stay sane as they sell pieces of themselves to the internet and the Hollywood publicity machine. It’s Green’s first novel in nearly a decade, and his first-ever for adults. But it still feels like a classic John Green book – thanks, predominantly, to its ardent belief that art, and other people, can help us survive anything. In an era in which more and more people must market themselves on social media, courting the dizzying highs and crushing lows of fame, Green still hopes we’ll find something better.I spoke with Green about the moral complexity of the attention economy, what he wishes he had done differently as a pioneering YouTuber and his brother Hank’s recent AI controversy.This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. Watch the Stateside podcast episode in fullhere.CS:This book is so much about fame and the various machines that create and perpetuate celebrity culture: journalists, social media, movie studios. Why was this something you wanted to write about?JG: It used to be that this was a question mostly for celebrities, mostly for actors and to a lesser extent novelists. Now, it is a question for everyone because we all participate in this attention economy. We all transform our private lives into publicly consumable goods, whether that’s posting about our dog’s death on Facebook or our marriage on Reddit or whatever. These questions about how best to handle the publicization of one’s private life are no longer rarefied.I guess the overriding question was: is it worth it to make art in an age where art will inevitably be so commodified and will cost us so much in the making?I feel like the moment your fame really kicked into a different gear was with the publication of The Fault in Our Stars in 2012. When did you realize:“Wow, I have really hit something new here?”I remember I was on the road for about a month touring. I got home, and I called my agent and I said: “When does this end?”And she said: “You don’t really choose.”How did you feel in that moment?Both excited and trapped, which I think is the nature of celebrity a little bit – that it’s exciting and also claustrophobic. You have a choice about how public to make your life. You don’t really have a choice about the public’s response to that.View image in fullscreenAnsel Elgort (left) and Shailene Woodley in the film adaptation of The Fault in Our Stars (2014).Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Sportsphoto/AllstarOn the other hand, it was wonderful to have the book reaching so many millions of people. Living with all that at the same time was both exciting and challenging, like it is for the young people in Hollywood, Ending.It’s much harder for them because I was 35 years old and married and had kids and the foundational relationships in my life were pretty set. When this happens when you’re 22, as it happens to a lot of people, whether they’re influencers or actors, you often don’t have those relationships. It can be really disorienting.It sounds to me like you’re saying:“This thing that was happening around my house, around my family, that was more real.” Why did the excitement around the book feel unreal?I don’t think it ever feels real, to be honest with you. I think it always feels like that’s happening to someone else. One of the things that [Andy] Warhol saw coming is that people don’t really see famous people as people. They see them as both more than people and less than people. They objectify them in every imaginable way. They feel free to comment on their bodies, they feel free to comment on their work as if they weren’t people, and so on.The other thing is that I wanted really badly to be successful. I think I wanted much more than would be healthy to be successful. I had no concept of what it would actually feel like. It was really rewarding to have so many people respond to the books and the story so generously. But the fame part of fame was quite empty.Why did you want fame in the first place?I don’t think I was liked very much in middle school. I really struggled with making friends. I thought that if I was famous, then everyone would be my friend and like me. That turns out to be a little bit of an oversimplification.A lot of people don’t like you, right? The nature of being famous is that everybody has an opinion about you, but not everybody has a positive opinion about you. That’s one thing that I hadn’t really thought very hard about.The other thing is that compliments simply don’t penetrate. I believe people in the abstract when they say that my work has been helpful to them or that it has been meaningful for them, and I’m extremely grateful for that. I don’t want to disbelieve them because that would dishonor the gift that they’ve given me by investing in my work and by bringing their deepest selves to it.But the criticism just penetrates in a different way. I believe it, because deep down there’s something about me that believes I don’t deserve any of this and I’m an impostor and I’m not a very good writer.47:50John Green wanted to be famous. Now what? – Stateside with Kai and CarterYou and your brother Hank have been creating videos for YouTube since 2007. How do you feel about your legacy as a pioneer of the social internet?Hank and I try really hard to do interesting, useful, fun, meaningful stuff in online spaces that build community and also make the world suck less. I hope that we’ve been able to do some of that. But there’s no question that just participating in an algorithmically generated internet is morally complex.You’re competing with Mr Beast for clicks. Even if I’m making an educational video that’s intended for high school students to be able to understand US history or physics or organic chemistry or whatever, I’m still competing for clicks with people who will do or say literally anything for clicks.Do you think, feeling the way you feel now about the social internet, you would have started making YouTube videos if you had to do it all over again?I’d do it again because it’s been an amazing experience and it’s been such a gift in my life.I might do it without my face in the videos, to be honest with you. That’s the big difference. A lot of my educational video friends don’t have their faces in their videos, and I find that admirable.But so much of the community you build is, frankly, parasocial.Yeah, it is. It is face-based. It’s hard to imagine not doing it that way.Actually, the time when Hank and I both realized that we weren’t actually in control of what we share was when Hank got cancer a couple years ago. We realized one of two things was gonna happen.One: Hank was going to, for the first time in 20 years, take eight months away from making Vlogbrothers videos without an explanation. Or, two: he was going to be forced to talk about having cancer in public.Hank ended up dealing with it beautifully by not just talking about having cancer, but by sort of science-communicating his way through cancer treatment, which is a very Hank Green thing to do.What do you make of the fact that in the age of the social internet, so many people, particularly young people, really just wanna be famous? The fame itself is a goal.Not only is the fame itself a goal, fame has become so decoupled from wealth that no longer is fame a guarantee of financial security. I have a friend, for example, who was a famous TikToker and also worked at the Gap. People would come to the Gap where they worked and be like: “Why are you working?” They would be like: “For money. Because this is where I work.”double quotation markI do think we have to build meaningful relationships with each other in meat space, as they say onlineJohn GreenI suspect that young people want to be famous for the same reason I wanted public attention, which is that I thought it would fill a hole inside of me. What fills the hole is real connection, which is the relationships that are gonna sustain you through everything you have to survive.It’s interesting that you’re saying this. In an interviewyou did last year with the New York Times, you talked about feeling like people believe the internet fills a hole – but then, you didn’t really want to tell young people not to try to use the internet to heal themselves. I’m wondering if you have different advice for young people now.It’s so hard. I’m going through this now with one of my godchildren, where when you don’t have the relationships that you want to have in your community because you’re different – as I was – or because your interests are too niche or whatever it is, you find connection online. I was part of the first generation of people who found that, in 1993 on CompuServe. It was revelatory, to be able to not be stuck inside of a body that was frail and embarrassing and full of failure, and instead to be this creature online where I could really connect with people. Some of the people I connected with, I’m still connected to. I’m so grateful for that.Yet at the same time, it can’t replace what we experience with real life connection. I do feel a little differently than I did a year or two ago. I do think we have to build meaningful relationships with each other in meat space, as they say online.I think it’s very helpful to be reminded that my body is made out of meat, that even the thinking parts are made out of meat. It’s very easy online to lose track of the fact that you’re a mammal. You’re much, much, much closer to being a squirrel than you are to being an artificial intelligence.I feel like in the book and in this conversation, you are suggesting that fame is corrosive to us and that the online attention economy is not good for us. But having a social media platform, having a personal brand, being on camera – that is all stuff that more and more people just have to engage with, not in order to necessarily be famous,but to have a professional life. How are we supposed to move forward?What the book concludes, I hope, is that we have to seize the reins of power and understand that we have more power than we think we have as internet citizens, as creators online.I remember suddenly becoming conscious on the set of The Fault in Our Stars that everyone cared what I thought. The reason they cared what I thought was not because I’m an incredibly compelling person, but because I had millions of followers on Twitter and at any moment I could blow up the movie. Understanding that with the sacrifices involved in participating in the social internet – there is also an exchange of power. Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk don’t have all the power, as evidenced by the declining role of X in society. They have a lot of power. They have too much power. Way, way, way too much power. But, combined, we have more.View image in fullscreenJohn Green (left) and Hank Green speak at VidCon at the Anaheim convention center on 23 July 2015 in Anaheim, California.Photograph: FilmMagicHollywood, Ending is to some extent about how much you have to feed the content beasts in order to succeed. So I did want to ask about a recent dust-up that Hank was involved in, where he was accused of using AI to write part of a script for a video. He addressed the controversy. He said that AI did not write the script but admitted to relying on AI more and more to research his work. That’s honestly understandable to me, because he really produces a lot. Hank suggested that you and he had spoken and that you had some criticism of his AI use. Are you comfortable telling me about those criticisms?Yeah, it’s more than being critical of his AI use in particular. I have my own opinions. I don’t use LLMs and don’t see a need to use them in my work.It was more about the fact of what you just said, which is Hank makes a lot of stuff. I think especially in the last couple of years, Hank has been obsessively trying to get everything in his head out into the world and I think that is not healthy. We’ve had that conversation and that’s part of being a brother. Hank’s had those conversations with me many times before.Hank Green: ‘I used all my power to make YouTube powerful, good and strong’Read moreTrying to get everything out of your head seems like a pretty reasonable response to a bad health scare.Yeah, I think it is a reasonable response to mortality. I think the more reasonable response – not that I’m here to lecture my brother – is to invest in your core relationships.You have expressed mixed feelings about people seeing too much of you in the art you make. I have spent this interview very much reading you into Hollywood, Ending. How do you feel about that?You haven’t read into it in a way that makes me uncomfortable, so I feel fine about it. There are other things you could have read into it that would have bothered me.It’s uncomfortable to be read into the book because I don’t want to be a character in the book. I have written two nonfiction books now and six novels, and writing fiction is so much more vulnerable and intimate than writing nonfiction.Why is it more vulnerable?It just is. Because I have to go to deeper places within me. I have to go to places that nobody else knows about, not even the people closest to me. That’s really hard work, but it’s good work because I’m asking the reader to do the same. I’m asking them to bring their deepest selves to the story, to bring their own particular traumas and fears and loves and losses to the story in a way that no one else can. That’s asking a lot. So I have to do the work on the other side to make that worth it. Hopefully.Hollywood, Endingby John Green is out now via Dutton Books

title: Britain’s Slave Traders by William A Pettigrew review – the inconvenient truth | History books | The Guardian
description: This revelatory history shows just how deeply embedded slavery is in the foundations of modern Britain
Author: Joe Moran
Headline: This revelatory history shows just how deeply embedded slavery is in the foundations of modern Britain
Content: The statue of Edward Colston in Bristol, before its toppling in June 2020.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe statue of Edward Colston in Bristol, before its toppling in June 2020.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesBook of the dayHistory booksReviewBritain’s Slave Traders by William A Pettigrew review – the inconvenient truthThis revelatory history shows just how deeply embedded slavery is in the foundations of modern BritainJoe MoranWed 23 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 05.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne tedious aspect of Britain’s post-imperial melancholia is the number of amateur historians who would rather we stopped going on about our role in the slave trade. Isn’t it all in the past? Weren’t we the first to abolish it anyway? In April, the Reform party announced anew policyof halting visas to people from countries seeking slavery reparations from Britain. “The United Kingdom is not an ATM for ethnic grievances from the past,” the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said.Unfortunately for those who would rather forget, the slave trade, as William Pettigrew argues in this grimly important book, can be found “in the depths of Britain’s grain”. Ninety per cent of the enslaved Africans transported to America went on British ships, and slave traders’ actions transformed Britain in ways that still resonate today.The erasure of this history began with the abolitionists, who quickly realised that identifying and shaming slave traders might harm their cause. They chose instead to argue that abolition would confirm Britain’s superior moral righteousness. Lauding abolition obscured what Pettigrew calls “slave gain”: Britain’s gigantic profiting from the trade. Wilkie Collins and Charles Dickens, in a jointly authored article of 1857, blithely suggested that the gains of slavery had evaporated “as the Arabian Wizard’s money turned to leaves”. Thus began a general tendency to downplay Britain’s role, offshoring slavery’s causes and effects to the Americas or localising them to port cities such as Bristol and Liverpool.Since April 2021, Pettigrew has led a group of nine academic historians identifying all the known investors – about 13,000 of them – who financed Britain’s brutal trafficking of 3.3 million enslaved Africans, of whom about half a million died during the Atlantic crossing. The traffic began in the 1560s with a syndicate of city merchants, naval and state officials. It soon earned royal approval, because of the role it played in humiliating the Spanish, increasing influence in the New World, establishing a foothold in west Africa, and enlarging the royal purse.After the Glorious Revolution of 1688, English slave merchants loosened their ties with the monarchy and embraced a free market. The trade expanded beyond political and commercial elites, and out from London to the regions. Bristol and Liverpool shared out the trade in the 18th century, the latter perfecting and industrialising it.In Pettigrew’s account, hardly an event in this period of British history – the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the rebuilding of London after the Great Fire of 1666, the 1707 Act of Union between England and Scotland – wasn’t impacted directly or indirectly by the slave trade. Slave gain funded the physical structures, from docks to canals, that helped make Britain a global force. The conventions of mercantile philanthropy also meant that it greatly improved the lives of the sick and poor, mainly through huge endowments to London’s hospitals. Institutions such as the British Museum and the Royal Academy of Music were founded with the help of slave traders’ donations. The Royal Society was not only a pioneer institutional investor in the slave trade but developed the racist “science” that perpetuated its inhuman practices.Civilised Britons justified participating in the slave trade with what Pettigrew calls “an impressive degree of societal cognitive dissonance”. Daniel Defoe, an uncompromising satirist of his own society, promoted the slave trade in countless articles, arguing that it “exports nothing but what we want to part with, and it imports nothing but what we cannot be without”. Samuel Taylor Coleridge won the Browne Medal for classical poetry for a Greek composition condemning the slave trade; his education at Christ’s Hospital School and Jesus College, Cambridge had been funded by slave traders. Thomas Southerne, author of the successful play Oroonoko, with its unflinching account of the cruelties of slavery, invested £2,000 of the money it generated in slave stocks.Pettigrew tells the story straight, with little reference to today’s culture wars. The most recent politician cited is Tony Blair. There is no mention of the opprobrium heaped on the National Trust for exploring its historic links to slavery; nor of the toppling of Edward Colston’s statue in Bristol in 2020, although Pettigrew does point out that he was a far less significant slave trader than other Bristolians.But Pettigrew’s careful tone is ultimately more effective than stridency. In this argument, slave traders cannot be conveniently separated out; they become central to the British project of economic and technological progress and cultural enlightenment. The slave trade, for instance, was at the forefront of effective treatments for smallpox, the concern to save human cargoes from this deadly disease being a simple commercial imperative. Virtually any behaviour could be justified if it supported free trade, including the violent trafficking of children. “Those who fetishise economic advancement,” Pettigrew writes in a rare moment of acerbity, “must confront the role that self-interpreting economics has played in undermining African humanity.” Nigel Farage has said that he is “tired of this endless conversation about the UK’s complicity with slavery”. As this deeply researched and revelatory book demonstrates, the conversation has barely begun.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The Complex by Karan Mahajan review – a superb family saga set in Delhi  | Fiction | The Guardian
description: At once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty squabbles, this tale of corruption and betrayal is packed with drama
Author: James Smart
Headline: At once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty squabbles, this tale of corruption and betrayal is packed with drama
Content: Karan Mahajan.Photograph: Briscoe SavoyView image in fullscreenKaran Mahajan.Photograph: Briscoe SavoyFictionReviewThe Complex by Karan Mahajan review – a superb family saga set in DelhiAt once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty differences, this tale of corruption and betrayal is packed with dramaJames SmartWed 23 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe learn about the murder of the Chopra clan’s shifty, crude, charismatic patriarch Laxman in the opening pages of The Complex. Twenty-five years have passed, but the stain on this once-respectable Punjabi family remains. The man who did it, Laxman’s nephew Brij, has served his jail time and is about to be released. Some relatives think Brij is too dangerous, too shameful to return to the family home, but his son Mohit decides the pair will live together – and rewinds the clock to tell the story of the decades leading up to the crime.Karan Mahajan’s warmly received first two works, Family Planning andThe Association of Small Bombs, explored individual lives alongside larger forces – urban development in the former, a car bomb’s traumatic aftermath in the latter. His excellent third novel has Delhi at its heart, but also visits Indian villages and cities, the American midwest and London, its short chapters flitting between different members of the Chopra family. You start by nodding in appreciation at Mahajan’s observant character portraits; before you know it you’re waist-deep in frustration, corruption and betrayal, as the book ranges through politics, faith, migration, infidelity and entrepreneurship.The main stage for Mahajan’s epic yet grubby tale is the residential compound that gives the novel its name. This sun-eaten collection of flats and bungalows in the Delhi suburbs became the family’s base in the post-independence glory days of SP Chopra, a freedom fighter turned politician and businessman. Since his death from a boardroom heart attack, his nine children and their descendants have never quite lived up to his reputation, and the complex has become the increasingly ramshackle home of several couples and their offspring. Family members swap gossip, chide their servants and tussle for the best apartments, flouting building regulations and each other’s wishes as they go.double quotation markMahajan’s skill at getting into his characters’ heads means The Complex is a wonderfully immersive and in-the-moment workSP’s elder children are mostly distant figures, and instead we follow the youngest, Laxman, who half-heartedly runs a bobby pin factory and a local temple; Brij, a military pilot turned paper-mill manager; and Brij’s younger brother Sachin, who moves to Michigan to develop squeezable plastic sauce bottles. Around these would-be giants of industry, women find what power and release they can. Laxman’s wife Archana sneaks on to the complex roof for cigarettes and privacy, while Brij’s wife Karishma walks the weedy garden. In the US, Sachin and his wife, Gita, have both more space and more isolation, but the rest of the Chopras are never far away: on visits they demand tea at all hours and comment on the pair’s problems conceiving. The swaggering, entitled Laxman makes grim lunges at both Gita and Karishma.As the 70s become the 80s, Sachin and Gita return to Delhi while Laxman, Karishma and Brij join forces to produce a line of ayurvedic balms. Children cram for exams and play cricket; adults bicker, hatch plans and do their best to ignore the increasingly blatant infidelity in their midst. Outside the complex, socialist governments become increasingly pro-business, Indira Gandhi is assassinated and Hindu nationalism rises. Laxman at first tries to mollify tensions, before becoming a vital player in a fledgling party that seeks to inflame them: the BJP.This is a novel at a constant simmer, packed with characters who are all deeply flawed and often deeply awful. Everyone plays the game to one degree or other, confident problems can be solved by money, force of personality or the right favour from the right person. But the Chopras are fraying, and the Complex is at once a palace and prison, with its “glum black water tankies; the clotheslines savagely crossing the roofs; everything sloping toward death”.Mahajan’s skill at getting into his characters’ heads means The Complex doesn’t feel as bleak as that image might suggest: it’s a wonderfully immersive and in-the-moment work. There’s beauty here, in marble temple floors “the colour of a thunderstorm”, or the image of Gita tightening her shawl to protect her “inky Banarasi silk sari from the cinders whizzing like miniature glowing kites” – as well as kindness, particularly in the sweet relationship between Gita and her nephews.But the darkness is rendered just as vividly: cruel conversations around the snack table, vengeful nationalism, caste snobbery, the almost surreal horror of communal violence, Laxman’s grasping hands. This is a fine piece of work, at once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty squabbles. Mahajan drops enough breadcrumbs as he goes that the Chopras’ journey towards murder and radicalism feels less like a twist and more like a procession – but one packed with drama and life.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Why fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplay | Games | The Guardian
description: From highlighted ledges to characters telling you what to do, blockbuster games are increasingly taking the challenge out of playing – and players are pushing back
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: From highlighted ledges to characters telling you what to do, blockbuster games are increasingly taking the challenge out of playing – and players are pushing back
Content: No friction … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyView image in fullscreenNo friction … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWhy fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplayFrom highlighted ledges to characters telling you what to do, blockbuster games are increasingly taking the challenge out of playing – and players are pushing backDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 23 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarvel’s Wolverine, the latest action game from Sony’s stable of expensive blockbuster-factory studios, has had an unfortunate launch.Reviews were decent, if not stellar, but a series of viral video clips from reviewers and streamers have made it the scapegoat for a patronising flavour of game design that gamers have hated for decades.This clip, from Skill Up’s review, shows the player entering a beautiful wintry landscape before being overwhelmed by visual cues telling them what they’re supposed to be doing there. Sonar pulses point you in the direction of objectives. Targets – which, it bears emphasising, areshaped like targets– get an extra reflective visual effect so you know you’re supposed to pay attention to them. A trail shows you not just where to go, but where the level’s sole hidden collectible is.It is hand-holding to the point of parody. Indeed, it reminded me of the sniggersomeMario in Unreal Enginesatiricalvideosthat makes the social media rounds every few months (“A mushroom? I should take a look at this”). Skill Up’s clip has been followed by hundreds of others, gleefully ripping into Wolverine with ironic savagery. In one much-copied clip, a streamer simply lays down his controller during a motorbike chase sequence and watches as Wolverine speeds on regardless, bouncing off the scenery as the game plays itself.People really detest this kind of thing. It’s impossible to pinpoint exactly when big-budget games started assuming that players were irredeemably stupid, but throughout the late 00s and 2010s it became more and more common to see obvious GPS trails showing you where to go, and for characters to talk to themselves to remind you what to do. At the same time, there’s been a cyclical discussion over the difficulty of games: every time a notably challenging game comes out, we rehash the same talking points about whether all games should have easy modes. Is it acceptable for games to shut players out if they aren’t prepared to “git gud”?I am not a game designer, but as a critic wholoves challenging gamesand has thought a lot about them, for me there is a difference between a game’s difficulty and its friction. A game might be difficult for all kinds of reasons, intentional or otherwise: perhaps the controls or camera aren’t great; perhaps there’s a mid-game boss with a bafflingly massive health bar and one devastating unblockable attack; perhaps the balancing is off. But a game’s friction is always an intentional part of its design. Friction is about how much a game helps you achieve its tasks. Games with perfect friction are clear about showing you what to do, but not overbearing about helping you do it: there is intentional distance, distance that you must broach with agency, strategy and skill. Friction leaves space for frustration and learning, and a sense of achievement.View image in fullscreen‘A game is only fun if you have to do something’ … 007 First Light.Photograph: IO Interactive A/SA lot of modern blockbuster game design seems hellbent on removing this friction. Not sure where to go? Here – follow this brightly coloured trail of fart gas. Not sure how to climb that building? We’ve helpfully painted the ledges yellow. Have you stood still for 30 seconds? We’ll have another character talk in your ear and tell you exactly what you need to do. Playing through the opening hours of007 First Lightrecently, I was dismayed when Bond inevitably acquired a watch that magically highlights important things in his vicinity with the press of a button.At its best, game design like this helps players avoid becoming irrevocably stuck. At its worst, it totally removes agency and challenge – you know, the reasons that many of us play games in the first place. Fundamentally, a game is only fun if you have to do something. I don’t play games for passive entertainment. That’s what binge-watching Netflix is for. If you don’t have to invest anything to reap the rewards, the experience just washes over you.Games can be difficult and have high friction. InHollow Knight: Silksong, you are constantly figuring out what to do, where the next boss might be, how to open that tantalisingly blocked path. Achieving those goals is then also very challenging, requiring practice and mastery of whip-fast fighting and precise jumping. Or they can be high-friction, low-difficulty:Blue Princetells you literally nothing about how to make your way to its mansion’s secret 46th room, but it’s not difficult to walk around and try out ideas. An example of a low-friction, high-difficulty game, meanwhile, would be a combat-focused one likeDevil May Cry(or most shooters), where the aim is always “kill all the guys to open the next area” but actually killing all those guys is majorly demanding.Low-friction, low-difficulty games hold very little interest. Many mobile games fall into this category, where you barely have to do anything save prod the screen to provoke a dopamine-shower of flashy visual effects (I’m looking at you, Monopoly Go). It’s unfair to lump Wolverine in with these almost entirely valueless games – but it is instructive that it has been subjected to such ridicule.The infamously challengingDark Souls, a dramatically influential game that turned 15 years old this week, seemed to remind the entire games industry that you canactually trust players: that they won’t drop the controller and storm off as soon as they get skewered by a skeleton. That there’s immense and unique pleasure in participatingin a game, unravelling it, conquering it little by little with skill and understanding. I hope that the reaction to Wolverine will serve as another reminder of that fact, for any executives who need to hear it.What to playView image in fullscreenPsychosocial dread … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnKonami’s horror series is on a roll lately. The Silent Hill 2 remake was very well received (with a few exceptions,including our critic), last year’s feminist, small-town Japanese horror story Silent Hill: f was excellent, and nowSilent Hill: Townfallhas succeeded in sending the series to a new setting: an island off the Scottish coast. Per our reviewerLewis Gordon: “This is a taut, smart tale, less about psychosexual terror than psychosocial dread… Townfall seems to understand that some things should remain shrouded in fog. The fate of St Amelia naturally festers in our imagination. How very Silent Hill.”Available on:PS5, Xbox, PCEstimated playtime:12-15 hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenPikachu in spaaaaaace … a toy Pikachu floats inside the International Space Station.Photograph: S Adenot/ESA/NASA/SWNSPikachuisnow an astronaut, thanks to a collaboration between Pokémon and the European Space Agency as part of the franchise’s seemingly endless series of 30th birthday celebrations. Human astronaut Sophie Adenaut brought a Pikachu plush up to the International Space Station, where it spent 67 days in orbit.According to Sonic Team boss Takashi Iizuka, Sega was once poised to kill off the wholeSonicfranchise. It was the success of 2020’s live-action Sonic movie that saved it. “I had to fight within the organization to keep the franchise as long as possible,” he toldOne More Game.The newResident Evil movieis out, and it’sgoing down well. Aftermathdescribesit as like watching your inept stoner roommate play the games; certified horror-game enjoyer Keith Stuart says it’s one of the best video game adaptations he’s seen.The Tokyo Game Showhad to wrap up one day early last week due to an incoming typhoon. Gamesindustry.biz has a slightly depressingrundownof the show, which was heavily dominated by AI.There have been yet moredramatic changesat Microsoft’sXboxdivision. The company is all but closing Halo Studios and moving Halo’s development to Activision, which will also now be in charge of storied British studio Rare. Multi-BAFTA-winning studio Ninja Theory is starting consultations on a proposed closure, having failed to find a funding deal to return itself to independence.What to clickSilent Hill: Townfall – shame and suffering on the Scottish coast | ★★★★☆Resident Evil – Zach Cregger’s rebooted action horror is a wild rollercoaster ride | ★★★★☆Control Resonant – save New York from paranormal phenomena | ★★★☆☆Roman Sands RE:Build – marooned in a crumbling vaporwave dream | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenSurreally European … Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.Photograph: Kepler InteractiveReaderMikeasks:“I just finished reading your article about the GameCube, which ironically got me thinking about the PS1 & 2, marvellous machines which I remember fondly. The game I got bundled with my PS2 was ‘Shadow of Memories’ which sticks with me to this day, the story was magnificent and also beautifully rendered, with multiple endings. Are there any similar ‘timeywimey’ games set in beautiful European villages, evoking memories of this game, out there today? Either on Android or PS5?”This question unearthed a bunch of half-remembered fragments from the early days of the PS2 – I definitely played Shadow of Memories as well. It’s a Konami game about a young German travelling through time, trying to solve his own murder. You mentioned games available on PS5, so here are a few that have some of the same elements. TheLife is Strangeseries is set in the US but has a similar time-travel and murder-solving premise;Clair Obscuris a very different kind of game but is as uniquely and surreally European; this year’s Japanese RPGThe Adventures of Elliotinvolves travelling through different eras to prevent a catastrophe. None of these have the same strange adventure-game atmosphere as Shadow of Memories, though – that’s something that felt really specific to the PS2 era. Readers, have you any more suggestions for Mike?If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter –email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterMarvelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Romeo and Juliet review – Russell Kane and Natalie Casey turn love’s young dream into a midlife fling | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Cacophonous and comedic staging sees an experienced, older duo engage in an enthusiastic liaison rather than a rebellious first romance
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Cacophonous and comedic staging sees an experienced, older duo engage in an enthusiastic liaison rather than a rebellious first romance
Content: Certain in her desires … Russell Kane and Natalie Casey in Romeo and Juliet at the New Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme.Photograph: Patch DolanView image in fullscreenCertain in her desires … Russell Kane and Natalie Casey in Romeo and Juliet at the New Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme.Photograph: Patch DolanTheatreReviewRomeo and Juliet review – Russell Kane and Natalie Casey turn love’s young dream into a midlife flingNew Vic, Newcastle-under-LymeCacophonous and comedic staging sees an experienced, older duo engage in an enthusiastic liaison rather than a rebellious first romanceMark FisherWed 23 Sep 2026 06.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs in any production of Shakespeare’s tragedy of star-crossed lovers, the nurse can tell Juliet’s age “unto an hour”. In this collaboration between the New Vic and Not Too Tame, however, that age is older than most. The Capulets’ upcoming party – a barrage of Balearic beats around a swimming pool with Tybalt (Patrick Knowles) on the decks – will mark her 40th birthday.Played by Natalie Casey, Juliet gets ready to the sounds of a chamber orchestra playing Like a Virgin. If you believe the nurse (Louise Haggerty), she is anything but.This Juliet is no innocent girl waking up to the possibility of love, but an assertive woman, certain in her desires. She has her adult insecurities, but she knows what she wants and argues forcibly to get it. Not so mature that she won’t do the splits or dance on the spot, she is as impulsive and lovable as anyone.That suits the similarly seasoned Romeo, played by comedian turned actorRussell Kane, dressed as a scaffolder in hi-vis jacket and shorts, his belt stuffed with spanners and wrenches. With impressive command of the language, he is no headstrong youth but just as lovestruck.View image in fullscreenTweakments … Lizzie Hopley as Lady Capulet, right, with Natalie Casey as Juliet.Photograph: Patch DolanIn all the cacophony of Jimmy Fairhurst’s staging, their relationship feels more like an enthusiastic fling than a meeting of soulmates. You miss a sense of profundity even as you will them on.Age in itself, however, is not an impediment to the story. What is lost is the sense of the new order trying to overthrow the old, a young generation recognising the folly of family feuds and the old generation closing ranks. For all its passion, this love is not rebellious. The tragedy is more private than political.And while there is a lot to enjoy in Fairhurst’s production, with its Botox injections for Lady Capulet (Lizzie Hopley), updated gags and chirpy audience interaction, it also strains too hard to persuade us we are enjoying ourselves. The extraneous business accounts for a longer-than-average running time and, for all the ebullience and heart of the cast, a little more trust in the play would be no bad thing.AtNew Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreRomeo and JulietRussell KanereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threats | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Star’s estate granted restraining order against Bryan Seaver, who publicly announced Parton’s death, over alleged intimidation that he denies
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Star’s estate granted restraining order against Bryan Seaver, who publicly announced Parton’s death, over alleged intimidation that he denies
Content: Dolly Parton performing at Glastonbury festival in England in 2014.Photograph: Ian Gavan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDolly Parton performing at Glastonbury festival in England in 2014.Photograph: Ian Gavan/Getty ImagesDolly PartonDolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threatsStar’s estate granted restraining order against Bryan Seaver, who publicly announced Parton’s death, over alleged intimidation that he deniesBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 23 Sep 2026 06.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe estate of the lateDolly Partonis involved in a dispute with the country music star’s nephew and former head of security, and was granted a restraining order against him and his private security company amid allegations of threats.Bryan Seaver was responsible for Parton’s security, and was tasked with announcing herdeath on 25 Augustwith a video, “something Dolly asked of me years ago”, he said.But since the singer died, her estate, which is run by Parton’s manager Danny Nozell, has reportedly fired Seaver from his security job, and has now alleged that he made “relentless” threats against Nozell and others.According toBillboard, the lawsuit filed in aTennesseecourt reads: “These were not ordinary workplace disputes or heated words; they were deliberate threats from a self-proclaimed heavily armed, former security operative with a military-contractor background. Many of [Parton’s staff members] are now afraid to come to work or have resigned entirely because they do not feel safe.”Wednesday’s restraining order says theTennesseejudge took into account the repeated threats cited in the complaint, as well as the alleged demands for payment and Seaver’s “claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate”.As part of the order, Seaver and his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, must refrain from talking with or being within 1,000ft (300 meters) of employees, attorneys and business partners of She’s Alive, the entity founded to manage Parton’s estate. The order is also meant to keep Seaver from interfering with its business relationships.A hearing is scheduled for 7 October.Seaver is alleged to have written to a lawyer for Parton, “I’m a killer”, and separately told Nozell: “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” He is also alleged to have claimed that he made a $27m arms and ammunition deal with Haiti.He allegedly claimed he would “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or fucking pay me.”Seaver repeated some of those claims in comments to TMZ while defending his actions, saying: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.”Regarding the messages to Nozell, Seaver said: “I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster. A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.”In another message, Seaver reportedly said: “I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratfucking anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”Speaking to TMZ, Seaver said of that comment: “I was talking about people that have done bad to Dolly in business – a specific company that scared her and intimated her. Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeaver’s security contract was terminated on 15 September, with a leaked termination letter saying the decision was made “for the protection of the trust and beneficiaries as a whole”, though it reassured Seaver it was “not a termination of your personal interest in the trust”.Seaver put out a statement after the termination, saying: “We remain unshakably resolved to fulfil her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much.”The Guardian has contacted Seaver and lawyers for Parton’s estate for further comment.Parton left behind considerable financial assets: not only her songbook featuring hits such as 9 to 5, but also a broad business empire including the entertainment resort Dollywood in Tennessee.She had no children, and her husband, Carl, died in 2025, but she is survived by other family members including six siblings and an uncle. Seaver is the son of her sister Cassie.Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountryLaw (US)CelebrityTennesseenewsShareReuse this content

title: The living dead: we can watch ‘Janis Joplin’ perform or reunite the Beatles, but who are the real winners here? | Music | The Guardian
description: Advances in digital technology mean that avatars are ever more realistic, and zombie concerts are coming our way. Exciting as it might be to witness the Fab Four, or Maria Callas on stage, I’d rather have flesh and blood live experiences any day.
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Advances in digital technology mean that avatars are ever more realistic, and zombie concerts are coming our way. Exciting as it might be to witness the Fab Four, or Maria Callas on stage, I’d rather have flesh and blood live experiences any day.
Content: A trick of the light … you think you’re seeing Abba in 3D but you’re not.Photograph: Johan Persson/Abba Voyage/PAView image in fullscreenA trick of the light … you think you’re seeing Abba in 3D but you’re not.Photograph: Johan Persson/Abba Voyage/PATom Service on musicMusicThe living dead: we can watch ‘Janis Joplin’ perform or reunite the Beatles, but who are the real winners here?Tom ServiceAdvances in digital technology mean that avatars are ever more realistic, and zombie concerts are coming our way. Exciting as it might be to witness the Fab Four, or Maria Calla on stage, I’d rather have flesh and blood live experiences any day.Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.01 EDTShareIt seems that AI’s powers – terrifyingly – know no bounds. But can it raise the dead? Here’s what Avatar concert producer Unit1 Studio’s CEO Barney Wragg said in a recent interview. “We [are] talk[ing] aboutusing AI to simulate the way that tears evaporate in your eye between blinks, or subcutaneous blood flow, so that when one of our [digital] characters laughs or opens their mouth or smiles, areas of their flesh will change colour as it would do in a real human”. Digital avatars are already part of our entertainment landscape – fromTupacandAbbatoMaria Callas– but now that an avatar’s cheeks can change colour mid-set, is it game over for humans?double quotation markIn the 21st century’s equivalent of the magic lantern,  audiences will pay to witness a very expensive LED screen showing phantom musiciansWragg last week reported a massive investment in his company to makehyper-realistic avatar-entertainment.Unit1 plans to roll out avatars of musicians living – and dead – so that the success ofAbba Voyageis just the start of a slew of “hybrid” concerts. In other words, flesh-and-blood audiences paying massive amounts of human money to witness a very expensive LED screen showing phantom musicians in the 21st century’s equivalent of the magic lantern. (The tech is a 2D illusion: you think you’re seeing Abba’s Agnetha in 3D, but you’re not; it’s all just a new-fangled but fundamentally old-fashioned trick of the light.)And the frontiers for Wragg and his team are endless: recreating Live Aid, Hendrix at Woodstock, the Beatles at the Cavern Club, and doing so in multiple locations simultaneously.View image in fullscreenPart of our entertainment landscape … Snoop Dogg performs at Coachella in 2012 with a digital avatar of Tupac.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Getty ImagesIt’s the logical endpoint of a culture of nostalgia epitomised for Wragg byhis teenage nephew, who, having discovered and fallen in love with Janis Joplin’s music, wanted to see her live, but the unfortunate fact of her death in 1970 meant that this was impossible. But why should that tiny hiccup be an impediment? Unit1 can bring her back, potentially resurrecting all your other favourites of yesteryear in what Wragg calls “time-travel tourism” – assuming that they receive permission from the musicians’ estates.Wragg talks about the tech not in terms of its creative use, but its documentary capacity: “We are re-engineering a moment in time, absolutely to fidelity. It’s not a case of interpreting what somebody said, it’s just representing exactly what they said.” Unit1’s vision goes far beyond any of classical music’s attempts to recreate the musical cultures of the past withhistorically informed performance practice. Wragg talks in terms of absolute fidelity to what happened, a perfect simulacrum not of a song, a symphony, or an aria, but of an actual “moment in time”, rendered as precisely as possible, to be repeated indefinitely.double quotation markIsn’t fiction the whole point of the technology? Why not have Mozart in a keyboard battle with Beethoven?Wragg admits there are limits: “We have been approached where people say, ‘What about if this person met this star?’ We’ve said, ‘Look, you’re straying into a world of fiction.’” But surely, seeing Joplin’s avatar perform as if she were still alive today is the height of science fiction. Isn’t fiction the whole point of the technology? Why not imagine Freddie Mercury singing with Ella Fitzgerald, Nat King Cole with Marlene Dietrich, or how about Mozart in a keyboard battle with Beethoven?The problem with Mozart, Beethoven or Bach, say, is that they didn’t, alas, leave much of a digital record to work with to make their avatars, unlike Abba or Joplin. As opposed to recreating, faithfully, actual moments in time, this seems to actually be about making advanced-level digital exhibits that people will pay to see every night in spaces once reserved for human musicians to perform in but that will now be consecrated to these digital homunculi: zombie concerts, opiates for an apocalyptically nostalgic age. Try throwing an apple at the stage; try interrupting the setlist; try making them perform an encore; try to get their autographs; try to find empathy and connection with this digital playback.View image in fullscreenA hologram of Maria Callas (1923-1977) performs during a concert at the National Auditorium of Mexico City in April 2019.Photograph: José Méndez/EPAOr maybe I should get with the programme and embrace the theme-park immersion of this wondrous age of technology that helps keep us stuck in a permanently perfected past. But if Unit1 could find enough digital traces out there in the ether, I’d love to have been there for the premiere of Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro in Vienna in 1786; to have witnessed Louise Bertin’s Fausto in Paris in 1831; to be overwhelmed by Mahler’s Eighth Symphony when it was first performed in Munich in 1910; or to have been in the crowd for the premiere of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring in Paris in 1913 to find out if there really was a riot at the ballet.But here’s the thing. Even if Unit1 could accurately represent not only the performers but every detail of these events, it would still be meaningless as a creative project.Classical music, at least, is all about interpreting what somebody wrote in the context of our times, not recreating the same thing night after night. That’s true time travel, and there’s no AI required.This week Tom has been listening to:Keir GoGwilt and friends’The Zarabanda Variations, which takes a simple question – what are the origins of the dance known as the sarabande in European repertoires? – anddiscovers and unearthsa network of stories that connect Africa to the Caribbean, European salons to the realities of colonialism, and turns all of those histories into a teeming, thrumming, retuned present tense.Explore more on these topicsMusicTom Service on musicClassical musiccommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia banned this anti-fascist play in 1936 at the request of the Nazis. Ninety years on, it’s being staged again | Australian theatre | The Guardian
description: A new production of Clifford Odets’ agitprop work Till the Day I Die is being remounted on the back of a truck in a Melbourne car park – rekindling its activist intent
Author: Tim Byrne
Headline: A new production of Clifford Odets’ agitprop work Till the Day I Die is being remounted on the back of a truck in a Melbourne car park – rekindling its activist intent
Content: Theatre-makers Mark Wilson and Katie Sfetkidis are directing Till the Day I Die, an anti-Nazi play that was banned in Australia in 1936, and is making a return during the Melbourne fringe festival in October.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTheatre-makers Mark Wilson and Katie Sfetkidis are directing Till the Day I Die, an anti-Nazi play that was banned in Australia in 1936, and is making a return during the Melbourne fringe festival in October.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The GuardianAustralian theatreAustralia banned this anti-fascist play in 1936 at the request of the Nazis. Ninety years on, it’s being staged againA new production of Clifford Odets’ agitprop work Till the Day I Die is being remounted on the back of a truck in a Melbourne car park – rekindling its activist intentTim ByrneWed 23 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 20.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt might be difficult to imagine these days, but there was a time when theatre in Australia was so politically incendiary it could cause an international diplomatic scandal. A year after it premiered on Broadway in 1935,US playwright Clifford Odets’ Till the Day I Die found itself at the centre of controversy in Australia when it wasbanned by the federal governmentat the request of the Nazi party’s consul general, on the grounds it was offensive to a “friendly foreign nation”.Odets’ play, about a communist Berliner arrested by the Nazis for producing leftwing political pamphlets, was a companion piece to his more famous Waiting for Lefty, which was staged the year before by Sydney’s New Theatre – one of a branch of theatre companies that sprang up around the globe in the 1930s that was heavily affiliated with communism. The ban was counterproductive, leading to a massive public outcry and a cobbled, surreptitious production performed on the back of a truck at Collingwood town hall in Melbourne.Sylvia Plath Stole My Boyfriend: the 95-year-old who has turned her romance with Ted Hughes into a playRead moreThat truck is a galvanising symbol of rebellion and resistance for theatre-makers Mark Wilson and Katie Sfetkidis, who have been inspired to revisit the play as an act of leftist solidarity with the past and a spur for future activism. They’re staging a new production of it for this year’sMelbournefringe festival in the car park of the Trades Hall building on the back of their own truck. “We got excited by these artists refusing to be banned, about the idea of a necessary theatre,” Wilson says.Sfetkidis was intrigued by the story of Till the Day I Die, but concerned the play itself might be painfully didactic and outdated. “I found a copy in the library, read it and went straight to Mark: have you read this?”Wilson, who recently directed a production of The Glass Menagerie for Melbourne Theatre Company, has long been interested in Odets as a key antecedent of Tennessee Williams and Arthur Miller. His plays burn with political conviction, but they’re also surprisingly considered and psychologically astute. “Odets was a method-trained actor,” Wilson says, “so he can’t help but write extraordinarily complex and well-rounded characters.”View image in fullscreenWilson and Sfetkidis have marshalled a professional cast of almost 30 actors for their restaging of Till the Day I Die.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The GuardianTill the Day I Die is concerned with the battle between idealism and pragmatism, and asks if one activist’s martyrdom is worth the price when the fruits of that activism remain apocryphal. Sfetkidis also sees a direct parallel with our own culture of trepidation: “We’re in this weird time now where people don’t want to discuss things politically, because they’re scared they’re going to upset someone.”double quotation markFighting against the forces of fascism is going to be much larger than anybody’s lifetimeMark WilsonOdets’ work fell into obscurity not from any lack of merit, but because the times changed around him. “As soon as the world accepted the abuses of Stalinism,” Wilson explains, “it became very difficult to put these plays on as light entertainment.” Overtly political theatre hasn’t exactly been in vogue recently, but Wilson argues that all theatre is political, especially when it pretends not to be. “A lot of rightwing theatre is made in this country that we pretend isn’t rightwing. There’s that old saying: if you think you’re neutral, you’re on the side of the oppressor.”Wilson and Sfetkidis aren’t simply remounting the original Melbourne production; they are attempting to rekindle its activist intent. They have marshalled a professional cast of almost 30 actors. “We only rehearse on weekends, so people can go to their jobs and earn money,” Sfetkidis laughs. While it may have been tempting to apply for government funding, Sfetkidis felt that might compromise the project somehow: “That also comes with the kind of political interrogation we don’t need. Sometimes you want to be independent so you can be free.”View image in fullscreenThe directors were inspired to revisit Till The Day I Die as an act of leftist solidarity.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The GuardianTill The Day I Die is an example of agitprop – a portmanteau of agitation and propaganda – that took hold in the Soviet theatre as a way of manipulating and harnessing public opinion towards the party cause. It’s hard to see theatre shifting much of anything these days, but Wilson and Sfetkidis see value in simply putting up a fight.“The work is long and the work is ongoing, and fighting against the forces of fascism is going to be much larger than anybody’s lifetime,” Wilson says. Sfetkidis quickly agrees: “I feel that’s true for the characters in the play; they also feel the work will go beyond them.”Agitprop tends to retreat in times of economic prosperity only to reappear in times of crisis, and this production aims to ride a wave of anti-fascist discourse while linking itself with the political and theatrical movements of the past.“The joy of this piece,” Wilson says, “is that it’s both an agitprop play that is unapologetically anti-Nazi and it’s an extraordinary drama about human beings. It’s ultimately about the personal cost of political commitment.”Till The Day I Dieis on as part of Melbourne fringe festival, Festival Hub: Trades Hall – The Car park, 1-4 OctoberExplore more on these topicsAustralian theatreMelbourneNazismfeaturesShareReuse this content
