title: Create a ‘donation station’ and never buy round containers: professional organisers’ tips for a tidy home | Homes | The Guardian
description: Whether it’s streamlining shoes or being strict with toiletries, we asked the experts for the home organisation hacks they swear by
Author: Isabelle Aron
Headline: Whether it’s streamlining shoes or being strict with toiletries, we asked the experts for the home organisation hacks they swear by
Content: Clear intentions: a designated basket can stop unwanted clothes from becoming another pile to deal with.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenClear intentions: a designated basket can stop unwanted clothes from becoming another pile to deal with.Photograph: GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHomesCreate a ‘donation station’ and never buy round containers: professional organisers’ tips for a tidy homeWhether it’s streamlining shoes or being strict with toiletries, we asked the experts for the home organisation hacks they swear byHow to get rid of household clutter – without sending it to landfillIsabelle AronWed 23 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew things conjure a sense of achievement quite like a clearout or bringing order to that cupboard of doom you’ve been ignoring for months. But how best to tackle this beast of a job?To help you make a start, we asked professional organisers and declutterers for their tips and tricks, as well as the products they recommend to help streamline the areas everyone struggles with. From never buying round storage containers to getting the kids to help tidy up, these are the solutions they swear by.How to keep your home tidyHave a simple system to organise toysI have a one-year-old, and a lack of toy storage meant our living room was becoming increasingly chaotic. I finally got some fabric baskets from Amazon that fit perfectly in our built-in cupboards – they’ve been a revelation. Each one is loosely categorised into things such as blocks and cuddly toys, which makes tidying up super easy. My daughter often plays in our kitchen while we prepare food, so I also got a seagrass basket from Dunelm for that space – every night, I swoop everything up and chuck it in.View image in fullscreenSeagrass storage basket£12 at DunelmView image in fullscreenMangata large storage box, set ofthree£26.99 at AmazonCreate a donation stationView image in fullscreenBox clever: keep a designated donation basket ready for things you no longer need.Photograph: Pressmaster/GettyDonating things you no longer need is a great way to declutter sustainably, but you need a system so that you don’t end up with random charity shop piles around your home. “If you’ve got a designated space where you can gather things until you’ve got enough to go to the charity shop, that’s super helpful,” says Lesley Spellman, who, with Ingrid Jansen, is co-founder ofthe Declutter Hub, host ofthe Declutter Hub podcastand co-author ofReset Your Home. “Have a donation station – a box or basket somewhere easily accessible where you can put things.”Stack your TupperwareIf you’ve got a food storage container drawer or cupboard that’s in a constant state of disarray, you’re not alone. “The worst thing in the kitchen is Tupperware,” says Simon Wigzell, founder ofLet’s Get It Sorted. “I put the lids on everything and stack them. It’s not the best use of space, but you can see exactly what you need and get it out easily.”Vicky Silverthorn, founder ofYou Need A Vicky, also stores her food storage containers with the lids on. If that’s not for you, she recommends Joseph Joseph’s nesting system, which neatly stacks together.View image in fullscreenJoseph Joseph NestLockfood container set,five pieces£26.60 at John Lewis£26.60 at DunelmMake tidying toys into a gameView image in fullscreenPlay away: make putting toys back part of the fun.Photograph: Catherine Falls Commercial/GettyIf your children are old enough to help, get them involved in the tidying too, says Wigzell, who has a four- and six-year-old: “Before bed, we put on a song and make it so it’s fun to put everything away.”Lucy Mansey, founder ofOrganised by Lucy, makes decluttering toys into a game, too. “I encourage my kids to think about 10 things they’re currently playing with, 10 things they haven’t thought about in a while and 10 things they’re happy to let go of.” She’ll then work out what to take to a charity shop or pass on to friends and family.Decant your most used ingredients into containersDon’t get sucked in by picture-perfect pantries on Instagram, says Silverthorn. “Everyone gets carried away with storage containers and buys 100 of them for every bit of dried food they’ve got. My tip would be to use them only for products you use frequently. Never buy round ones. It’s all about square edges that slot together.The Organizing Warehousehas a range called Fitt – they’re really good quality. I don’t put labels on mine – they’re clear, so you don’t need to.” If you have containers of easily confused items – such as plain and self-raising flour – just label those, says Silverthorn.View image in fullscreenFitt airtight food storage canister, medium£8.45 at the Organizing WarehouseUpgrade your wardrobe hangersTo maximise space in your wardrobe, Silverthorn recommends slimline, non-slip rubberised hangers. “[You can get them] for knitwear, which is a hanger with a curved shape that protects the shape of the garment. Traditional hangers are typically made for a broader shoulder, which can stretch the fabric of smaller sizes. You can use nonslip hangers for everything in your wardrobe, including items such as silk camisoles, which would slide off a normal hanger on to the floor. The other brilliant ones are trouser hangers with an open side – they lift everything higher than your normal triangular hanger,because the hanger itself is shorter, giving you more space underneath. And because they’ve got one side missing, you don’t have to thread your trousers through,” she says.View image in fullscreenThe Hanger Store nonslipcoat hangers, 10 pack£12.99 at B&Q£12.34 at AmazonView image in fullscreenAmazon Basics trouserhangers, 10 pack£14.24 at AmazonStreamline your shoes in the hallway (and put them away)“Have a minimal amount of shoes in your hall – only what you’re wearing day-to-day needs to live downstairs,” says Mansey. All other shoes should be stored elsewhere (under the bed is a good spot). When it comes to hallway storage, Wigzell recommends a slimline shoe cabinet. “A lot of people think they can’t fit furniture in, but you can get slimline shoe racks where you open the front drawers and your shoes slot in. You can probably get about 12 to 15 pairs in a standard one. Ikea has one that’s reasonably priced.”View image in fullscreenStäll shoe cabinet£129 at IkeaBring some order to your wiresGot a box of miscellaneous wires? First, sort through them and work out which ones you need and recycle the rest. “They shouldn’t go in the bin – you can recycle any wires, not just electrical goods. There’s a website calledRecycle Your Electricalswhich is great,” says Silverthorn. Wigzell suggests organising the remaining ones with Velcro cable tidies to keep them in place so they don’t unravel. If you want to be super organised, you can get specific cable labels, too. For cables and extension leads that are being used every day, tryorganisers that cover up the plugsand separate wires to stop them from becoming a tangled mess.View image in fullscreenReusable cable ties, 50 pack£3.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenCable labels, 240 pack£4.95 at AmazonMake your spices accessible“If space allows, the best way to store spice jars is in a drawer, by using an organiser –this one is brilliant. Or you could put a large turntable in a cupboard, so you can see them all and you’re not having to reach into the back,” says Mansey. Another option Wigzell recommends is a spice rack with different levels. “You can get spice steps where they’re elevated on each level so you can see what you’ve got,” he says.View image in fullscreenThe Organizing Warehouselazy Susan, 28.5cm£13.75 at the Organizing WarehouseView image in fullscreenExtendable bamboo shelf organiser£19.99 at Lakeland£19.99 at AmazonFind a home for your water bottlesReusable water bottles tend to hang around on your kitchen worktops or in random spots about your house. The key is to have a place for them, says Spellman. “Typically, people have multiple bottles, and if you try to stack them all upright in a cupboard, they can fall over. Instead, keep water bottle lids separate from the bottles themselves, ideally in their own box or tub,” she says. “Lids left screwed on can trap moisture and lead to mould, and it’s much easier to rummage through a separate box to find the right match.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor more, read our guide to thebest water bottles for leaks, looks and sustainabilityRethink how you store pots and pans“Don’t keep pots and pans with the lids on; store the lids separately,” says Mansey. “Joseph Joseph does great lid organisers that stick on the inside of your drawer or cupboard, so you’re not using up any space.” Another option is a drawer divider with plastic spikes that you can position to create designated places for pots and prop up pan lids on their sides. Do an audit, too. “Do you really need six frying pans?” says Wigzell.View image in fullscreenCupboardStoregrey pan lid holders, set of 4£10.80 at LeekesView image in fullscreenUppdatera pegboard drawer organiser£10 at IkeaUse the dead space in your kitchen cupboardsWhen cupboards get crammed with tins and packets, it can be easy to lose track of what’s in there. Wigzell recommends Ikea’s metal shelving inserts. “If you’ve got deep enough shelving, you can put in an additional layer, which means you can see exactly what you’ve got. It does clip-on metal baskets too,” he says. “Joseph Joseph also does something that hooks underneath a shelf, and you put your clingfilm and tinfoil on that.”View image in fullscreenVariera shelf insert£5 at IkeaView image in fullscreenPålycke clip-on basket£4.50 at IkeaView image in fullscreenCupboardStore film, foiland bag organiser£7.70 at Dunelm£12.50 at Joseph JosephGet creative with home office storageMany of us now work from home in communal living spaces, but no one wants to look at their work stuff when they’re not on the clock. “Stackers has a product called Office in a Box – you have it on your desk or table, and you open it up, and it has your laptop, notepad and other things in there. Then at the end of the day, you just close it all back up,” says Mansey.View image in fullscreenStackersOffice in aBox£120 at Stackers£120 at John LewisSwap vacuum bags for fabric boxesPeople often swap out their clothes seasonally and store the excess on the top shelves of their wardrobes. While vacuum bags might seem like the obvious solution, they can end up being an awkward shape and a bit of an eyesore. “I don’t love a vacuum bag in plain sight, or even in a wardrobe. I think they should be for giant coats and ski-wear only,” says Silverthorn. Instead, she recommends Muji’s fabric storage boxes. “They’re a plain beige colour, and they come in different sizes. They’re good-quality and sturdy. And they look so much nicer.Total Wardrobe Carehas some fantastic mothproof options, too.”View image in fullscreenMuji fabric storage box with lid£14.95 at MujiKeep bath toys containedKids love bath toys, but parents often struggle to keep them dry and mould-free, and with where to put them. This basket from Munchkin can help with that. “It’s a toy basket that sticks on the inside of the bath, so the toys can drip dry into the bath after use and not end up on the side in a bucket of mouldy, gross water,” says Mansey.View image in fullscreenMunchkinbaby bath toybasket£15.99 at Amazon£18.49 at John LewisDon’t overbuy toiletries“If you’ve got three drawers full of spare toiletries, you need to have a word with yourself,” says Silverthorn. It’s OK to have some spares, but keep them somewhere that isn’t a prime space for everyday products, perhaps in a bottom drawer in the bathroom, or a cupboard that’s somewhere else in your home. Depending on what built-in storage you have, a caddy can also be useful for everyday items to free up cluttered sink space. Dunelm makes a great slimline rattan caddy.The Edited Life Rattan caddy£50 at DunelmBe ruthless with paperworkView image in fullscreenPaper chase: scan what you can, file what you need and ditch the rest.Photograph: fermate/Getty/iStockphoto“A lot of people don’t need all their paperwork,” says Wigzell. “You can scan it and save it in the cloud or on a hard drive. With bank statements, I always say: keep two years’ worth. Go through your household manuals – you’ll find you don’t have that lawnmower any more, or do you really need a manual for a toaster or kettle?” If you want to keep physical copies, he suggests using box or lever-arch files, and labelling them to keep things organised.“Have a place to put your post when it comes in. This could be an open in-tray by the front door, on your desk in the study, or next to the fruit bowl in the kitchen,” says Wigzell. “Then, spend half an hour once a week processing the paperwork, getting it into a filing cabinet or expandable folder. Once you get into that routine, paperwork becomes easy.”Store your baking trays vertically“One of the things I always recommend to clients is an upright baking tray holder. If your trays are stacked vertically, not horizontally, you can get them out much more easily. You can put other things in them like cake tins, too,” says Spellman.View image in fullscreenSpectrum kitchen organiser£22.01 at AmazonCreate a makeshift gallery for your children’s artworkView image in fullscreenWall of fame: give children’s artwork a rotating place of honour.Photograph: Jupiterimages/Getty“If a child’s created a piece of artwork and it’s sitting on the side for weeks, that can be disheartening for them,” says Mansey. “Get a pegboard or pinboard and put it up. I’ve used a shower curtain wire that went across the length of the wall, and wooden pegs – it became a gallery of what they had created. Even if it changes week on week, at least they’re seeing the fruits of their labour being celebrated.” They’re also useful for hanging up your children’s creations while they dry.For more, read thebest home storage hacksandhow to get rid of household clutter – without sending it to landfillDo you have any ingenious ways to keep your home tidy, stay on top of cluttered drawers, or organise your cupboards? title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: in praise of slightly silly clothes | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The push to buy lasting, sustainable clothes is a good thing, but every wardrobe need a bit of mischief
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: The push to buy lasting, sustainable clothes is a good thing, but every wardrobe need a bit of mischief
Content: Video: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Melanie WilkinsonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley on fashionFashionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: in praise of slightly silly clothesThe push to buy lasting, sustainable clothes is a good thing, but every wardrobe need a bit of mischiefJess Cartner-MorleyWed 23 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdo hope you are wearing your zebra stripe trousers today. Anyone who is anyone is wearing zebra stripes this month, you know. If you haven’t yet got with the programme, I suggest you nip to the shops and snap some up before they are all gone. It would be mortifying to be the last one without a pair. Hurry!Only teasing. Fashion doesn’t work like that any more. The days when people like me bullied everyone else into wearing banana yellow one season and puffball sleeves the next are over. Looking trendy is over. Timeless chic is the only show in town. Peacocking has been phased out in favour of understatement and personal style.This is a very good thing. The fashion playbook that minted a whole new look every six months has a lot to answer for, seeding a sense of clothes as disposable that has got us into the right old mess that the industry is now in, with a glut of poorly made garments. Clothes that you never tire of, that you look after and repair because you want to wear them for ever, are obviously the holy grail of a sustainable wardrobe. When a look has the timestamp of a specific season – like Brat green in the summer of 2024 or Barbie pink the year before – it becomes a sell-by date. Clothes have a longer shelf life when their appeal isn’t based on novelty.double quotation markThe zebra stripes are a flag planted in the ground for the idea of an outfit that isn’t scared of being a lotBut. There is a but, I’m afraid. Which is that in the eminently sensible process of making fashion less frantic, I do sometimes find myself wondering whether we have lost some of the fun along the way. Fashion should not be disposable, but it is quite nice for it to be slightly silly now and again. These are heavy times and we need a little levity. Are we missing a trick here in our ageless button-down shirts and tasteful straight-leg jeans and classic loafers? The aesthetics that have dominated style recently – from the cashmere neutrals of Quiet Luxury fashion to the doe-eyed wholesomeness of Clean Girl beauty – have been so polite, so well behaved. There is a drift toward a generic upscale smart-casual aesthetic, the unspoken dress code of hotel lobbies, which is frankly a little bit dull. An epidemic of unimpeachable good taste. Have we lost our edge?View image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The GuardianWhich brings us back to the zebra stripes. Not specifically – think of the zebra as the mascot, not the mandate. The zebra stripes are a flag planted in the ground for the idea of an outfit that isn’t scared of being a lot. For standing in front of your wardrobe and deciding that Out of Africa meets Studio 54 is your vibe for the day, because why not? That instinct to reach for the loud thing instead of the safe thing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: swot up with these lessons in back-to-school dressingRead moreThis is harder than it sounds. We have become more thoughtful about evaluating new purchases with a coherent, lasting wardrobe in mind. We want to buy pieces that will work seamlessly for weekends as well as work and not date too quickly. And this is great, in the way that a really dependable boiler is great. But wardrobes need a bit of mischief in them. The earring or bag that catches your eye in the lift mirror and makes you smile is a functionally important part of your Monday morning outfit.Edge doesn’t have to mean excess. It can be a single quirky piece in an otherwise sensible ensemble. You can wear a practical grey coat with statement shoes. One necklace too many. A jazzy sock. None of this requires abandoning the principles of buying less and buying better. The clothes that earn their keep are not necessarily the ones that blend into the background, but are sometimes the charming oddballs you have owned for 15 years.So no, I am not telling you to buy the zebra trousers. I am telling you that somewhere in your wardrobe, wedged behind the neutrals, there is a garment you stopped wearing because it felt unfashionably frivolous. Get it out. Fashion doesn’t need another trend – it just needs to get its nerve back.Stylist: Melanie Wilkinson. Styling assistant: Charlotte Gornall. Model: Moli at Milk. title: The best cheap smartphones in 2026: nine budget buys for £600 or less, tested | Mobile phones | The Guardian
description: A new smartphone needn’t cost a fortune. From Samsung, Google, Apple and more, these are the lower-cost models we rate most – and how to buy a refurbished handset
Author: Thomas Deehan
Headline: A new smartphone needn’t cost a fortune. From Samsung, Google, Apple and more, these are the lower-cost models we rate most – and how to buy a refurbished handset
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterMobile phonesReviewThe best cheap smartphones in 2026: nine budget buys for £600 or less, testedA new smartphone needn’t cost a fortune. From Samsung, Google, Apple and more, these are the lower-cost models we rate most – and how to buy a refurbished handsetHow to make your smartphone last longerThomas DeehanWed 23 Sep 2026 10.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBuying a flagship phone in 2026 makes little sense unless you’re really going to use all the features at hand. By comparison, the budget smartphone market has come on leaps and bounds in the past few years, and you can now get most of the features you’d want, including a high-quality OLED screen and a well-performing chipset, all for a reasonable price.There’s more choice than ever for shoppers who don’t want to spend too much on their next upgrade, but many models simply aren’t worth your time. That’s where this guide comes into play. I’ve tested the latest models and pinpointed the nine best budget phones available right now – all you have to do is pick the one that best suits your needs.Due to the ongoingRam shortagefuelled by AI development, smartphones have become increasingly expensive recently, but nothing in this guide costs more than £600 – and many cost less.At a glanceBest budget phone overallSamsungGalaxy A37£349 at AmazonBest cheap phone for battery lifeMotorolaEdge 70 Fusion£379 at John LewisBest cheap phone for cameraGooglePixel 9a£349 at ArgosBest cheap iPhoneAppleiPhone 16e£599 at John LewisBest phone under £150TCL60R 5G£129.99 (new) at eBayWhy you should trust meI’ve been a tech journalist for almost a decade, and I’ve had the pleasure of testing many phones across the price spectrum in that time. From flagship-leveliPhonesto budget-friendly Samsung handsets, I know exactly what makes a phone worth buying and, more crucially, how each one compares with the other options on the market.How I testedPicture this: putting the phone’s camera to the test.To find out if these phones are truly as good as the marketing jargon suggests, I used each one as my daily mobile for the better part of a week, with my sim card in tow. I tested 11 in total.With each phone, I split my testing into two categories: real-world use and benchmarking. For the former, I used the phones as normal, noting how well they perform in everyday tasks such as checking Google Maps for directions, scrolling through social media, and streaming YouTube. I also monitored the battery drain over time.View image in fullscreenPlay on: testing the phones’ performance with demanding mobile games.Photograph: Thomas Deehan/The GuardianTo benchmark and see the raw performance capabilities of each phone, I put each device through gaming sessions in Call of Duty: Mobile and the more demanding Honkai: Star Rail, followed by tests in PCMark and Geekbench 7. In both tests, the higher the score, the better. Many of these phones are able to beat flagships when it comes to battery life due to having larger cells, but on raw horsepower (which is where Geekbench 7 comes into play), you can expect pricier options to have a single-core and multi-core score of more than 1,500 and 5,500, respectively. For context, the single-core score (as its name suggests) shows us what just one core of the CPU is capable of, while the multi-core score brings them all into play.Every phone featured here did a brilliant job at passing these tests, so no matter which one you pick, you’ll be getting a great-performing device.If not returned to the manufacturer, these review units were donated to charity after testing.The best budget phones in 2026View image in fullscreenDialled in: our top budget phone picks.Photograph: Thomas Deehan/The GuardianBest budget phone overall:Samsung Galaxy A37SamsungGalaxy A37from£349£399 at Samsung£349 at AmazonWhat we loveUpdates until 2032 and a slick software experienceWhat we don’t loveIt’s a minimal update over the Galaxy A36View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Thomas Deehan/The GuardianFrom £399 at Samsung£349 at AmazonSamsung doesn’t really do itself any favours by having so many phones on the market – it’s hard work just to understand how each one is different from the next, particularly at the more affordable end. But if all you need is a great all-rounder that’s designed to last, then you can’t really go wrong with the Samsung Galaxy A37.Why we love itWith a promised six years of software and security updates from the time of launch in April 2026, the Galaxy A37 offers far better long-term value than most. Samsung’s One UI Android overlay has come a long way in recent times, too, and it now rivals the stock Android experience of Pixel phones when it comes to everyday usability.Thanks to the glass backing, the A37 doesn’t feel like a budget phone in the hand either. To the untrained eye (that wouldn’t notice the slightly smaller lenses), the phone could be mistaken for the far more expensive Galaxy S26+. Durability has been tightened up against its predecessor, the A36, with a higher IP68 dust and water resistance rating, and the newer Exynos 1480 chipset performs well as you jump from one app to another.For repairability, the phone only has a C rating in the EU’s EPREL database, and while Samsung does offer a recycling service for handsets, they must be taken to the Samsung KX store in London’s King’s Cross.It’s a shame that …as much as I rate the Galaxy A37, it is almost identical to its predecessor, the Samsung Galaxy A36, which nowcosts less.Screen:6.7in AMOLED 120HzProcessor:Samsung Exynos 1480Ram:6/8GBGeekbench 7 CPU results:990 single-core, 3,357 multi-coreStorage:128/256GBOperating system:AndroidSecurity updates available until:2032Battery size:5,000mAhPCMark tested battery life:16hrs 37minsCamera:50MP wide, 8MP ultrawide, 5MP macro, 12MP selfieConnectivity:Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 6Dust and water resistance:IP68Dimensions:78.2 x 7.4 x 162.9mm (WDH)Weight:196gSamsungGalaxy A37from£349£399 at Samsung£349 at AmazonWhat we loveUpdates until 2032 and a slick software experienceWhat we don’t loveIt’s a minimal update over the Galaxy A36For more, readSamuel Gibbs’s guide to thebest Android phones, compared and rankedBest cheap phone for battery life:Motorola Edge 70 FusionMotorolaEdge 70 Fusionfrom£379£379 at John Lewis£379.99 at MotorolaWhat we loveThe phone can last for up to two days at a timeWhat we don’t loveThe larger-battery model only comes in one colourView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Thomas Deehan/The Guardian£379 at John Lewis£379.99 at MotorolaEver since getting my hands on the mid-range Motorola Edge 60 Pro last year, I’ve been increasingly impressed with the brand. Not only is it offering a genuine alternative to the likes of Samsung and Google, but it’s doing so with phones that make the competition look boring. The Motorola Edge 70 Fusion deviates from this strategy slightly, but the massive battery more than makes up for any misgivings.Why we love itWith its sizeable 7,000mAh battery, the Edge 70 Fusion can outlast almost any budget phone on the market–even the Honor Magic 8 Lite below, despite its larger battery. And the 70 Fusion trumps Honor’s phone for software: Motorola hasn’t tinkered with it too much, for an experience that feels a lot like stock Android. With that battery in tow, you can easily get the phone to last for up to two days at a time.That kind of longevity is great when you’re having a night out on the town and need to use your phone for directions, payments, train tickets and more. Speaking from experience and the fact that I now regularly carry apower bank, being able to avoid any battery anxiety is worth the price of admission alone. There is a version of this phone with a 5,200mAh battery thatcosts £20 less, but I would avoid that.If you need any repairs, Motorola’sReplaceBase websitesells replacement parts for devices, and there are helpful video tutorials available to help you fix your phone.It’s a shame that …for whatever reason, Motorola has kept all of the exciting colours to the 5,200mAh version of the Edge 70 Fusion, so anyone who wants the larger battery has to make do with a rather unexciting Pantone silhouette. There are also just three years of software updates (until 2029), although you do get five years of security patches (until 2031).Screen:6.78in AMOLED 144HzProcessor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 3Ram:8GBGeekbench 7 CPU results:989 single-core, 2,764 multi-coreStorage:256GBOperating system:AndroidSecurity updates available until:2031Battery size:7,000mAh (tested unit)PCMark tested battery life:24hrs 35minsCamera:50MP wide, 13MP ultrawide, 32MP selfieConnectivity:Bluetooth 6, wifi 6EDust and water resistance:IP68/IP69Dimensions:75.6 x 7.99 x 162.8mm (WDH)Weight:193gMotorolaEdge 70 Fusionfrom£379£379 at John Lewis£379.99 at MotorolaWhat we loveThe phone can last for up to two days at a timeWhat we don’t loveThe larger-battery model only comes in one colourBest cheap phone for camera:Google Pixel 9aGooglePixel 9afrom£349£349 at Argos£349 at John LewisWhat we loveHigh-quality photos with helpful editing featuresWhat we don’t loveThe Tensor G4 chip isn’t great for gamingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Thomas Deehan/The Guardian£349 at Argos£349 at John LewisAlthough it’s been supplanted by the newerPixel 10a, Google has rather smartly kept thePixel 9aaround and slashed its price to just £349. It can be found for even less if you shop around. Aside from making the camera flush with the phone, upping the brightness and durability of the display and introducing faster charging, the Pixel 10a is practically identical to its predecessor – they even use the same chipset. You’re better off picking up the previous-gen tech at a discount.Why we love itThe Pixel 9a shows you don’t always need high-end camera hardware to take great pictures. Google’s computational processingremains among the best on the market. Colours are vibrant, while skin tones are naturally replicated, and each photo looks like it could have been taken on a much pricier phone. The abundance of AI-driven features such as Magic Eraser and Best Take make it easy to edit on the go, too.With its clean Android interface, this is the least cluttered software experience you’ll find outside Apple’s ecosystem, with no annoying bloatware to contend with when you switch the phone on for the first time. Alongside Samsung, Google leads the charge on long-term support, too, with a committed seven years of updates (until 2032). This means the phone will last you for quite some time to come. At least 23% of the device is made from recycled materials, and when it reaches the end of its life, Google offers a free devicerecycling service.It’s a shame that …for all its prowess elsewhere, the Pixel 9a isn’t a great phone for gaming: the Tensor G4 isn’t as powerful as comparable Snapdragon chips. Charging at 23W is also quite slow for a modern phone.Screen:6.3in pOLED 120HzProcessor:Google Tensor G4Ram:8GBGeekbench 7 CPU results:1,479 single-core, 4,206 multi-coreStorage:128/256GBOperating system:AndroidSecurity updates available until:2032Battery size:5,100mAhPCMark tested battery life:20hrs 39mins (refurbished unit)Camera:48MP wide, 13MP ultrawide, 13MP selfieConnectivity:Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 6EDust and water resistance:IP68Dimensions:73.3 x 8.9 x 154.7mm (WDH)Weight:186gGooglePixel 9afrom£349£349 at Argos£349 at John LewisWhat we loveHigh-quality photos with helpful editing featuresWhat we don’t loveThe Tensor G4 chip isn’t great for gamingBest cheap iPhone:Apple iPhone 16eAppleiPhone 16efrom£599£599 at John Lewis£599 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable iOS; great performance and battery lifeWhat we don’t loveOnly one camera and a slow 60Hz refresh rateView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Thomas Deehan/The Guardian£599 at John Lewis£599 at AmazonDesigned as the spiritual successor to the iPhone SE, theiPhone 16ewas something of a head-scratcher at launch. Despite its £599 price, there were a number of missing features, such as Apple’s MagSafe technology, and only a single camera on the back of the phone. Those issues were softened when Apple reduced the phone to £499 after the release of the iPhone 17e, but the price has since jumped back up as a result of the ongoing memory crisis. However, becausethe phone can be picked up for less when going down the refurbishedroute and I anticipate plenty of deals for the iPhone 16e during major sales events like Black Friday, I’ve decided to keep the iPhone 16e in this list.Why we love itIt might sound a bit obvious, but the best thing about the iPhone 16e is the unfettered access to iOS and the entire Apple ecosystem for a reduced price. Apple News remains one of the better non-Kindle reading apps available, while Find My is helpful for tracking down your keys or anything else with an AirTag attached, as well as offering peace of mind on whether your iPhone-toting friends or family have made it home safely.Apps are also better optimised for iPhones, with less variety between models to develop for. I struggled to get the Edits app to run smoothly on myPixel 10 Pro, but had no such issues with the iPhone 16e and its super-efficient A18 chipset. It’s also a better long-term investment, since Apple has a good track record of supporting older phones. The recent iOS 27 update extends all the way back to 2019’s iPhone 11. More than 30% of the iPhone 16e’s overall composition is made from recycled materials, and while there is scope for home repair, Apple does provide (admittedly fairly costly)screenandbatteryrepairs for handsets that are out of warranty.It’s a shame that …the single 48MP sensor means you’re limited with the types of photos you can take. It can take solid shots with enough light, but the shutter speed is noticeably slower than pricier iPhones, and there’s no ultrawide capability.Screen:6.1in 60Hz OLEDProcessor:Apple A18Ram:8GBGeekbench 7 CPU results:2,881 single-core, 7,618 multi-coreStorage:128/256/512GBOperating system:iOSSecurity updates available until:2032Battery size:4,005mAh (estimated)Average battery life:up to two days (PCMark battery test unavailable on iPhone)Camera:48MP wide, 12MP selfieConnectivity:Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 6Dust and water resistance:IP68Dimensions:71.5 x 7.8 x 146.7mm (WDH)Weight:167gAppleiPhone 16efrom£599£599 at John Lewis£599 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable iOS; great performance and battery lifeWhat we don’t loveOnly one camera and a slow 60Hz refresh rateFor more, read our guide to thebest iPhonesskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBest phone under £150:TCL 60R 5GTCL60R 5G£129.99£129.99 (new) at eBayWhat we loveCovers the smartphone basics on a budgetWhat we don’t loveLimited software support hampers long-term useView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Thomas Deehan/The Guardian£129.99 (new) at eBayAs much as I would recommend saving a bit more for the Samsung Galaxy A17 or the Pixel 9a, if you need a lower-budget phone, then the TCL 60R 5G is worth a look. At £99.99, the 60R 5G is very affordable, and you still get some impressive features for the price.Why we love itIt’s fair to expect a compromise for a phone as cheap as this, but I was surprised by what TCL had managed to include, particularly the display. It’s a 6.7-inch IPS LCD panel (so you won’t be getting the deeper contrast in colours that OLED can provide), but it’s very bright and packs a decent 120Hz refresh rate – higher than the pricier iPhone 16e’s. Plus, with stereo speakers onboard, it works well for entertainment.I was also impressed with the performance of the MediaTek Dimensity 6300 chipset. I did notice the occasional bit of lag when scrolling through certain websites too quickly, but I played a few rounds of Call of Duty: Mobile without issue (even if the graphics were downplayed to improve performance). There’s a sizeable 5,200mAh battery to get you through long days, and the ability to expand storage viaa microSD cardis always welcome.TCL has agold EcoVadis ratingfor a more responsible manufacturing process, and the company runsa repair servicefor faulty handsets.It’s a shame that …the big compromise with the TCL 60R is that it includes just one major OS update that came out this year, and only two years of security updates (until 2027), so it won’t last as long as other phones here.Screen:6.7in IPS LCD 120HzProcessor:MediaTek Dimensity 6300Ram:4GBGeekbench 7 CPU results:652 single-core, 1,828 multi-coreStorage:128GBOperating system:AndroidSecurity updates available until:2027Battery size:5,200mAhPCMark tested battery life:19hrs 17minsCamera:50MP wide, 8MP selfieConnectivity:Bluetooth 5.4, wifi 5 dual-bandDust and water resistance:IP54Dimensions:76.2 x 8.2 x 165.6mm (WDH)Weight:190gTCL60R 5G£129.99£129.99 (new) at eBayWhat we loveCovers the smartphone basics on a budgetWhat we don’t loveLimited software support hampers long-term useThe best of the restView image in fullscreenClose contenders: the best of the rest.Photograph: Thomas Deehan/The GuardianSamsung Galaxy A17SamsungGalaxy A17from£155.39£169.99 at Argos£155.39 at AmazonWhat we loveHas longer support than most sub-£200 phonesWhat we don’t loveThe camera is lacking compared with the Pixel 9AView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Thomas Deehan/The Guardian£169.99 at Argos£155.39 at AmazonBest for:a phone under £200If the Galaxy A37 is out of your price range but you still want long-term software support, then it’s worth considering the Samsung Galaxy A17. Despite costing only £169.99, Samsung has committed to supporting the phone for six years from release (until 2031), so you’re getting far more bang for your buck than with any other budget smartphone below £200.Samsung’s One UI software is better than ever, with a very sleek interface that’s fun to use. As a longtime tech reviewer, I’ve endured my fair share of bloatware-riddenAndroid phones, but this isn’t one of them. Unlike the A37, the A17 uses a slightly cheap-feeling plastic backing, but the Exynos 1330 chipset works well under everyday use.It didn’t make the final cut because …the Galaxy A37 is a better buy overall, and doesn’t cost that much more. The Pixel 9a is only a bit pricier, too, and you’ll get far better camera performance.Screen:6.7in AMOLED 90Hz;processor:Samsung Exynos 1330Ram:4GB;Geekbench 7 CPU results:619 single-core, 1,851 multi-core;storage:128GB;operating system:Android ;Security updates available until:2031;battery size:5,000mAh;PCMark tested battery life:17hrs 24mins;camera:50MP wide, 5MP ultrawide, 2MP macro, 13MP selfie;connectivity:Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 5, dual-banddust and water resistance:IP54;dimensions:77.9 x 7.5 x 164.4mm (WDH);weight:192gSamsungGalaxy A17from£155.39£169.99 at Argos£155.39 at AmazonWhat we loveHas longer support than most sub-£200 phonesWhat we don’t loveThe camera is lacking compared with the Pixel 9ANothing Phone (4b)NothingPhone (4b)from£299£299 at Nothing£299 at AmazonWhat we loveBudget phone with better looks than most flagshipsWhat we don’t loveSamsung offers better long-term support for lessView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Thomas Deehan/The Guardian£299 at Nothing£299 at AmazonBest for:a well-designed phone on a budgetOne of the unfortunate compromises at the budget end of the market is that design is often an afterthought. There are some fun colourways, sure, but very few options are what I would deem to be eye-catching. But the Nothing Phone (4b) is different. Regardless of the price tag, Nothing endows all of its phones with an engaging, space-age aesthetic – many big-brand options seem boring by comparison.That philosophy also extends to the software, with Nothing OS featuring exclusive widgets that go beyond the standard Android fare. On the back you’ll find the Glyph Bar, a small strip of LED lights that can display all manner of information, including the impending arrival of your Uber driver and the countdown of a timer. Admittedly, it’s a bit scaled back compared with the Glyph lights on previous Nothing phones, but it still works rather well.It didn’t make the final cut because …the (4b) pales in comparison to Samsung and Google phones for long-term support, getting just three years of OS updates (until 2029), although its lifespan is lengthened by six years of security patches (until 2032).Screen:6.77in AMOLED 120Hz;processor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 6 Gen 4;Ram:8GB;Geekbench 7 CPU results:956 single-core, 3,145 multi-core;storage:128GB;operating system:Android;Security updates available until:2032;battery size:5,200mAh;PCMark tested battery life:20hrs 8mins;camera:50MP wide, 8MP ultrawide, 16MP selfie;connectivity:Bluetooth 6, wifi 6;dust and water resistance:IP64;dimensions:78.2 x 8.6 x 164.4mm (WDH);weight:210gNothingPhone (4b)from£299£299 at Nothing£299 at AmazonWhat we loveBudget phone with better looks than most flagshipsWhat we don’t loveSamsung offers better long-term support for lessHonor Magic 8 LiteHonorMagic 8 Litefrom£329£329 at Currys£329.99 at ArgosWhat we loveBattery lasts for days; screen made for streamingWhat we don’t loveOS is cumbersome; ultrawide camera is lackingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Thomas Deehan/The Guardian£329 at Currys£329.99 at ArgosBest for:entertainmentWith so many of the brand’s phones occupying space at the budget end of the market, it can be tricky to know where the Honor Magic 8 Lite sits among them. If you want a long-lasting phone with a great screen for streaming, though, then this is the one to go for.The 7,500mAh battery can stretch to multiple days of use, making it great for a long journey, and the display’s peak brightness of 6,000nits makes flagship phones look dim by comparison. The 6.79in panel provides plenty of space for wide-screen films to sprawl out. There is a fair amount of bloatware to deal with when you first boot up the phone, but it’s not a major issue.It didn’t make the final cut because …Honor’s MagicOS overlay is a bit too cumbersome to use, especially when compared with the cleaner Android experience on the Motorola Edge 70 Fusion or the latest Pixel phones.Screen:6.79in 120Hz AMOLED;processor:Qualcomm Snapdragon 6 Gen 4;Ram:8GB;Geekbench 7 CPU results:958 single-core, 3,040 multi-core;storage:512GB;operating system:Android;Security updates available until:2031;battery size:7,500mAh;PCMark tested battery life:19hrs 56mins;camera:108MP wide, 5MP ultrawide, 16MP selfie;connectivity:Bluetooth 5.2, wifi 6;dust and water resistance:IP68/IP69K;dimensions:76.1 x 7.76 x 161.9mm (WDH);weight:189gHonorMagic 8 Litefrom£329£329 at Currys£329.99 at ArgosWhat we loveBattery lasts for days; screen made for streamingWhat we don’t loveOS is cumbersome; ultrawide camera is lackingTCL Nxtpaper 70 ProTCLNxtpaper 70 Profrom£289£289.99 at Argos£289 at AmazonWhat we loveThe ideal budget phone to help curb doomscrollingWhat we don’t loveJust two years of OS security patches and bug fixesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Thomas Deehan/The Guardian£289.99 at Argos£289 at AmazonBest for:displayIf you’re an avid reader of online articles and books, and don’t want to carry around a separatee-reader, then the TCL Nxtpaper 70 Pro is well worth a look. The phone features a matt display that minimises reflections, and a slider toggles a book-style Ink Paper mode for easy reading.For those who prefer a dumb-phone approach, there’s also the Max Ink mode that limits distractions and puts an emphasis on using the Nxtpaper 70 Pro for reading. It’s reminiscent ofFairphone’s Moments toggle, and I wish more manufacturers offered it. Anything that diverts my attention away from social media and towards something more fulfilling gets a big thumbs up from me.It didn’t make the final cut because …the screen doesn’t feel quite as sharp without the E-Ink-style modes activated, and there are only two years of OS security patches and vulnerability fixes (until 2028).Display:6.9in IPS LCD 120Hz;processor:MediaTek Dimensity 7300;Ram:8GB;Geekbench 7 CPU results:905 single-core, 3,280 multi-core;storage:256GB/512GB;operating system:Android;Security updates available until:2028battery size:5,200mAh;PCMark tested battery life:19hrs 10mins;cameras:50MP wide, 8MP ultrawide, 32MP selfie;connectivity:Bluetooth 5.4, 802.11ax wifi 6E;dust and water resistance:IP68;dimensions:80.1 x 8 x 169.4mm (WDH);weight:208gTCLNxtpaper 70 Profrom£289£289.99 at Argos£289 at AmazonWhat we loveThe ideal budget phone to help curb doomscrollingWhat we don’t loveJust two years of OS security patches and bug fixesWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenBeyond the specs: what matters is how a phone performs in everyday use.Photograph: Thomas Deehan/The GuardianWhat to look for when choosing a budget phoneForget about branding and all the marketing that goes with the latest phones, and instead consider the features that you prioritise from your current handset. After all, in order to hit a budget price for a phone, manufacturers are forced to compromise in one way or another.A phone may have a great battery and a bright screen, but the chipset might be lacking. A phone that performs as well as a much pricier handset might lack another feature, such as fast charging. Decide ahead of time which features matter the most to you, so you won’t find yourself regretting your purchase.It’s also worth considering how long the phone will be supported in terms of software and security updates. If you don’t want to fork out again in three or four years, then opt for a phone with longer support.What to avoid when choosing a budget phoneAs with any phone, don’t be swayed by the specs on paper: they don’t always translate to a better experience. For instance, the Honor Magic 8 Lite packs a 108MP main camera, but its photos aren’t as pleasing to the eye as those captured on thePixel9a: Google’s computational processing works its technical wizardry despite the phone’s 48MP sensor.This guide is based on real-world use, so these recommendations will help you avoid these marketing pitfalls.When you should replace your phoneTo maximise the value of your phone (and cut down on waste), it’s worth holding on to your existing phone for as long as it’s officially supported with software and security updates. But if your phone is irreparably damaged or the battery has aged to the point that it can no longer be replaced or mitigated with apower bank, it might be time to upgrade.How to buy a good refurbished phoneIf you’re looking for a bargain on a phone, there’s never been a better time to choose refurbished. Reputable retailers such asGiffgaff,Back Marketandthe iOutletsell professionally refurbished devices with clear gradings and warranties.Keep an eye out for incentives, too. Giffgaff provides a 24-month warranty with phones bought in “like new” condition, while Vodafone’s Battery Refresh scheme lets you get a new battery for your phone, free of charge, for up to three years from the point of purchase, depending on your plan.I would strongly advise against buying a refurbished phone through private or unverified sellers, however. Unverified sellers aren’t held to the same standards as those aforementioned retailers, so the quality of the phones they’re selling cannot be guaranteed.For more, read Samuel Gibbs’s guide onhow to find the best refurbished phoneFor more:How to make your smartphone last longerThe best Android phones: flagship smartphones compared and rankedThe best iPhones: which Apple smartphone is right for youThe best phone straps: our favourite stylish and practical picksThomas Deehan is a technology and entertainment journalistwith almosta decade’sexperience.He’s tested everything from smartwatches to video games, action cameras and more, but it’s smartphones that make up the bulk of his coverage.
