title: How to turn leftover roast chicken into a brilliant midweek meal – recipe | Chicken | The Guardian
description: Whip up a curry mayonnaise and turn your leftovers into a semi-instant classic
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Whip up a curry mayonnaise and turn your leftovers into a semi-instant classic
Content: Tom Hunt’s leftover roast chicken coronation chicken.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s leftover roast chicken coronation chicken.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian.Waste notChickenHow to turn leftover roast chicken into a brilliant midweek meal – recipeWhip up a curry mayonnaise and turn your leftovers into a semi-instant classicTom HuntWed 23 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was my gran’s funeral a few weeks ago, so today’s recipe seems rather fitting, because coronation chicken was one of the few savoury dishes she cooked, and also one I loved. This homage to her glorious personality and astonishingly sweet tooth (add extra mango chutney for sweetness) is a wonderful way to use up leftover chicken from a roast, barbecue or whatever. I make the mayo from scratch, because I don’t keep mayonnaise in my larder, but I do have eggs and extra-virgin olive oil.Leftover roast coronation chickenCoronation chicken was a genius solution to a common caterers’ conundrum, and was created by Rosemary Hume and Constance Spry fora 350-person banquetat Westminster school to mark Queen Elizabeth’s coronation. I take a similar approach, whether I’m cooking a dinner party for five or feeding 500 at a festival, and generally go for simple recipes that can be finished with little effort (and have mymise en placeready, of course). This dish is a brilliant use of Sunday’s leftovers, be it as a delicious stand-alone supper or a superior sandwich filling. Don’t be precious about which bits of leftover chicken you use: thigh meat, wing meat, the oysters, skin, and any last scraps clinging to the carcass – all of it goes in.Serves21egg1 heaped tsp wholegrain mustard, or to tasteFlaky sea salt and black pepperJuice of ¼ lemon, plus the finely grated zest if the fruit is organic and unwaxedAbout 150ml extra-virgin olive oil, or enough to emulsify and thicken the mayoFinely grated zest and juice of ¼ unwaxed lemonA few coriander sprigs, stalks finely chopped, leaves left whole1 tbsp mango chutney1 tsp mild curry powder, or a pinch each of a few warm spices such as turmeric, cinnamon, cumin, fenugreek, mustard seed, ginger, black pepper and nigella seeds – whatever you have to hand300g cooked chicken or turkey scraps, pulled off a roast1 handful flaked almonds, toasted, to serveTo make the dressing, crack the egg into an immersion blender jug and add the mustard, a pinch of sea salt, the lemon juice (and zest, if using), the finely chopped coriander stalks, the chutney and the curry powder. With the motor going, slowly pour in the oil and blend until the mixture emulsifies into a thick mayonnaise, then taste and adjust the seasoning. The curried mayo will now keep in the fridge for up to four days.To make the coronation chicken, pull any leftover chicken or turkey scraps – 200-300g should feed two generously – into rough pieces, then mix in a bowl with enough mayonnaise to coat the meat well. Serve topped with toasted flaked almonds and the coriander leaves.Explore more on these topicsChickenWaste notFoodFood wasteSauces and graviesMeatMain courseHerbs and spicesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kenji Morimoto’s gochujang corn fritters and oyster mushrooms with butter bean mash – recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Snacks never tasted so good: spicy corn fritters with a lime pickle-spiked yoghurt, and king oyster mushrooms laced with blackberries, pomegranate molasses and soy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Snacks never tasted so good: spicy corn fritters with a lime pickle-spiked yoghurt, and king oyster mushrooms laced with blackberries, pomegranate molasses and soy
Content: Kenji Morimoto's gochujang corn fritters with lime pickle yoghurt.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenKenji Morimoto's gochujang corn fritters with lime pickle yoghurt.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.FoodKenji Morimoto’s gochujang corn fritters and oyster mushrooms with butter bean mash – recipesSnacks never tasted so good: spicy corn fritters with a lime pickle-spiked yoghurt, and king oyster mushrooms laced with blackberries, pomegranate molasses and soyKenji MorimotoWed 23 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing oyster mushrooms are quite the centrepiece: relatively meaty and receptive to big flavours. Paired with a vibrant glaze spiked with sweet blackberries, tart pomegranate molasses and savoury soy sauce, every bite balances the richness with sharp, fruity acidity. But first some tangy, fresh fritters, celebrating fresh corn with an earthy base of gochujang, which works brilliantly against the lime pickle yoghurt. Creamy, crisp and the perfect treat.Gochujang corn fritters with lime pickle yoghurtThese can be made vegan by swapping the yoghurt for a plant-based alternative. Don’t have access to fresh corn? Use tinned, making this a true pantry rustle-up.Prep15 minCook15 minServes3-4as alight lunch2corn on the cob, kernels stripped off, or 1 standard 198g tin sweetcorn, thoroughly drained and patted dry3 spring onions, trimmed and finely sliced (about 40g net)20g fresh coriander, roughly sliced, plus extra to garnishSalt60g plain flour20g cornflour1 tsp baking powder2 tbsp gochujangNeutral oil,for fryingFor the lime pickle yoghurt200g full-fat Greek yoghurt1-2 tbspIndian lime pickle, roughly chopped1 lime,half juiced, the other half cut into segments to servePut the corn, spring onions and coriander in a large bowl with a pinch of salt and, using the back of a wooden spoon, roughly crush some of the kernels.In a second bowl, whisk the flour, cornflour and baking powder, then add the gochujang and 100ml cold water, and whisk until smooth and slightly thick. Add this to the corn bowl and fold in, until the corn is well coated; if the mixture seems a bit too thick, add an additional 10-20ml water to loosen.To make the lime pickle yoghurt, gently mix the yoghurt, chopped lime pickle and lime juice, then adjust the seasoning, if need be.Pour a couple of centimetres of neutral oil into a large frying pan on a medium-high heat. Test the oil’s temperature by dropping a little bit of the corn batter: it should sizzle and bubble immediately. Drop spoonful-sized dollops of the batter into the oil – they will naturally spread a bit, so try not to poke them too much – and cook for one to two minutes on each side, until deeply golden. They may look a bit overcooked, but remember the dark colour is also coming from the gochujang. Drain the fritters on kitchen paper and salt immediately while still hot.Serve on top of the lime pickle yoghurt, garnished with the lime segments and remaining coriander leaves.King oyster mushrooms with a blackberry, pomegranate and soy glaze and a chive and butter bean mashView image in fullscreenKenji Morimoto’s king oyster mushrooms with a blackberry, pomegranate and soy glaze and a chive and butter bean mash.The velvety bean mash and golden pangrattato can be made up to two days in advance, turning this into a fast, stress-free weeknight dinner. To make this vegan, simply swap the butter and soured cream for plant-based alternatives.Prep15 minCook20 minServes23-4 large king oyster mushrooms2 tbsp neutral oil30g unsalted butter2-3 garlic cloves, peeled and smashed with a knife1rosemary sprig150gblackberries2 tbsp pomegranate molasses1 tbsp soy sauceFor the pangrattato1 slice stale sourdough1 tbsp olive oil4-5thyme sprigs, leaves pickedFlaky sea saltFor the butter bean mash2400g tinsbutter beans, drained, reserving 30-40ml of the liquid30g unsalted butter50gsoured cream, or full-fat greek yoghurt20g fresh chives, finely choppedTo make the pangrattato, tear up the sourdough and pulse to crumbs in a food processor. In a small pan, heat the olive oil, add the crumbs and fry, stirring, for two to three minutes, until golden brown. Turn off the heat and toss in the thyme leaves and a pinch of flaky salt. This will now keep in an airtight container at room temperature for a few days.Cut the mushrooms in half lengthwise, then, using a small, sharp knife, lightly score the flat surface of each one in a crosshatch pattern.Put the butter beans, reserved bean stock and butter in a small saucepan, and cook for three to five minutes, until hot. Add the soured cream, blend with a stick blender to your desired consistency – I like a slightly chunkier mash– then fold in the chopped chives and season. Cover and keep warm.Put two tablespoons of neutral oil in a large frying pan on a medium-high heat. Lay in the mushrooms cut side down and leave to cook undisturbed for three to four minutes, until there’s a golden crust on the scored surface. Flip over, add the butter, smashed garlic and rosemary sprig, then tilt the pan and baste the mushrooms with the foaming butter for a few minutes. Transfer the cooked mushrooms to a plate, and discard the aromatics.Turn down the heat to medium and add the blackberries, soy sauce and 50ml water to the pan. Use the back of a spoon to gently crush the berries, then leave to bubble for a few minutes. Stir in the pomegranate molasses and cook for one to two minutes longer on a low heat, until very syrupy.Spoon a generous amount of butter bean mash on to two plates, followed by the mushrooms. Spoon the blackberry sauce on top and garnish generously with the pangrattato. Serve with a rocket, watercress and lemon salad, if you like.Explore more on these topicsFoodAutumn food and drinkVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkHerbs and spicesFruitSnacksrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Unhappy couples staying put due to cost of living crisis, say divorce lawyers | Divorce | The Guardian
description: Financial pressures suspected to be behind figures showing failed marriages are lasting longer in England and Wales
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Financial pressures suspected to be behind figures showing failed marriages are lasting longer in England and Wales
Content: ‘As a result, some couples remain in unhappy or hostile environments, which can be detrimental to everyone involved,’ one lawyer said.Photograph: Andor Bujdoso/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘As a result, some couples remain in unhappy or hostile environments, which can be detrimental to everyone involved,’ one lawyer said.Photograph: Andor Bujdoso/AlamyDivorceUnhappy couples staying put due to cost of living crisis, say divorce lawyersFinancial pressures suspected to be behind figures showing failed marriages are lasting longer in England and WalesHelena HortonWed 23 Sep 2026 11.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCouples are putting off divorce because of the cost of living crisis, lawyers have said, after figures showed the average length of a marriage ending in divorce in England and Wales reached a record high last year.The Office of National Statistics (ONS) released figures on Wednesday showing that the average marriage ending in divorce in 2025 lasted for 13 years. This is the longest since records began in 1963 and up from a record low of 8.9 years in 1985.Rebecca Aston‑Jones, a senior associate at Clarke Willmott, a top law firm that specialises in divorce, said the rising cost of living was keeping unhappy couples together.“One of the main factors discouraging people from pursuing a divorce is the significant financial pressure that comes with establishing and maintaining two separate households,” she said.Inflation, which is rising as a result of the escalation of conflict in the Middle East, has pushed up the cost of rent, mortgages and childcare. “It is unsurprising that many people find the prospect of separation financially daunting,” Aston-Jones said.The ONS figures show there are fewer divorces now than at their peak in the 1980s-2000s, when they reached 150,000 a year.There were 105,002 divorces in England and Wales in 2025, made up of 102,879 opposite-sex couples and 2,123 same-sex couples. The latter figure was the highest since same-sex marriage was legalised in 2014. There were also 959 civil partnership dissolutions involving 270 opposite-sex couples and 689 same-sex couples.The head of population life events at the ONS, Greg Ceely, said: “Divorce rates have remained stable over the past few years, but are lower than the peak levels in the 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s. Our latest findings show that people who divorce or dissolve a partnership are staying in the relationship for longer before it ends.”That marriages were lasting longer before failing was partly down to people waiting longer before they divorced, lawyers suggested.“As a result, some couples remain in unhappy or hostile living environments, which can be detrimental to everyone involved,” Aston-Jones said. “We are increasingly seeing couples who have separated but continue to live under the same roof so they can retain the benefit of shared assets and continue to split household expenses.“This arrangement can often exacerbate tensions and create a more volatile home environment. We are also witnessing a growing prevalence of financial abuse within relationships, which can prevent individuals from taking the step to end their marriage because they are concerned about their ability to manage financially on their own.”Lisa Pepper, a partner and specialist divorce lawyer at Osbornes Law, said: “Divorce is now more accessible than it ever has been in the past 60 years yet these incredible figures show that couples are staying together for a record amount of time.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe suggested that one “less romantic reason” for marriages lasting longer was likely to be that couples were unable to afford to divorce.“Couples are more hesitant to get divorced and trying things like mediation or couples therapy before going for the nuclear option as the consequences are often perceived as worse than continuing with their marriage,” she said.Aston-Jones said there were cheaper ways to get divorced and that seeking advice early could help.“There are a number of effective alternatives that can help parties reach a resolution outside of court, including mediation and arbitration,” she said. “These methods often provide quicker, more cost-effective, and practical outcomes, enabling families to move forward more amicably, which is particularly beneficial where children are involved.”Explore more on these topicsDivorceMarriageUK cost of living crisisFamilyFamily financesRelationshipsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mum’s Alzheimer’s has trapped the kids’ NatWest cash | Money | The Guardian
description: A First Saver account was set up by my mother when the children were born which we planned to use to fund them through university
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: A First Saver account was set up by my mother when the children were born which we planned to use to fund them through university
Content: Investing in a NatWest child’s account was an investment in the future… only when it came to accessing the the rewards, it proved impossible.Photograph: Chris Dorney/AlamyView image in fullscreenInvesting in a NatWest child’s account was an investment in the future… only when it came to accessing the the rewards, it proved impossible.Photograph: Chris Dorney/AlamyConsumer championsMoneyMum’s Alzheimer’s has trapped the kids’ NatWest cashA First Saver account was set up by my mother when the children were born which we planned to use to fund them through universityAnna TimsWed 23 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy mother set up NatWest First Saver accounts for my children when they were born. The accounts are held in trust for when they turn 18 and my parents have paid into them monthly to help fund them through university.My mother is now in the final stages of Alzheimer’s and I have registered financial power of attorney for her.My daughter began university last year and my son starts this month, but I have been unable to access the £20,000 in their respective accounts. I was told my mother has to give consent for the children to access them, but she’s not in a position to do so.I’ve been variously advised to set up online banking in my mother’s name without her consent, to request a one-off payment of less than £1,000 and, upsettingly, that it would be easier if my mother were dead.As a consequence, we’ve had to take out a bank loan to cover my daughter’s expenses.SW,WorcestershireI nearly lost my new home because of a NatWest banking errorRead moreNatWest blames “lack of colleague awareness” of a “complex process”. We’re talking here of numerous colleagues in call centres and in branches who, over the best part of a year, have been unable to fathom what should be a standard procedure.This appears to be a training issue and it’s hardly reassuring that “learning from your experience” will be used to “inform future improvements”.Your children now have access to their funds and compensation has been paid to reflect the delays.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsMoneyConsumer championsConsumer affairsConsumer rightsNatWest GroupSavingsBanks and building societiesFamily financesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My body is on fire!’: my perilous, painful, perfect month of pilates | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: A growing number of men, including singers Shaggy and Harry Styles, are taking up pilates. When I realised I could no longer touch my toes, I decided to try it out
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: A growing number of men, including singers Shaggy and Harry Styles, are taking up pilates. When I realised I could no longer touch my toes, I decided to try it out
Content: ‘It’s all a bit of a blur’ … Sammy Gecsoyler tries out a pilates class.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s all a bit of a blur’ … Sammy Gecsoyler tries out a pilates class.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianHealth & wellbeing‘My body is on fire!’: my perilous, painful, perfect month of pilatesA growing number of men, including singers Shaggy and Harry Styles, are taking up pilates. When I realised I could no longer touch my toes, I decided to try it outSammy GecsoylerWed 23 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIrealised something needed to change when I nearly toppled over trying to tie my shoelaces. I was on a busy high street, with people rushing past holding shopping bags, when I saw my open shoelace spooled on the ground. I bent down to deal with it and felt gravity move against me. Only a quick flail of my arms stopped me from faceplanting. When I raised myself back upright, I felt a sharp pain in my lower back. This can’t be right, I thought.Bracing my foot on a bin to finally fix my shoelace, it dawned on me. I’d become rusty. My core strength was nonexistent, as was my flexibility. Years behind a desk had taken a toll, not helped by an after-work routine of watching TV or playing video games on the sofa. But after getting home and doing some research (yes, from my sofa), I found a potential remedy: pilates.Originally known as contrology, this so-called “mind-body exercise” was created by a former boxer roughly a century ago. JosephPilates, a German national, came up with the series of exercises while detained as an “enemy alien” on the Isle of Man during the first world war. In the 1920s, he moved to New York City and set up a studio near a dance school, where it was discovered by ballerinas seeking to soothe their overworked joints.As well as boosting flexibility, I read that pilates could help with injury recovery. I’ve had shoulder pain since the start of the year, so this seemed another reason to give it a try.I’m late to the party, though. The UK pilates and yogamarket is now worth a reported £1.1bn, and although the practice has long been dominated by women, men are increasingly taking notice. Asthe Wall Street Journal reportedthis week, “Gym bros are going to pilates – and leaving shaking like a chihuahua.”Sports stars including LeBron James, Cristiano Ronaldo and David Beckham have sung pilates’ praises, alongside the actorGlen Powelland the singerHarry Styles. The reggae star Shaggy has become so fond of reformer pilates, with its bed-like exercise machines, that he is considering buying some for his homes in Florida and Jamaica. “You’re touching muscles you didn’t know you had,”he told the New Yorkermid-exercise. “Jesus Christ!” His praise (or warning) is ringing in my head as I venture to my first class.But before heading off, I have to sort out my attire. Pilates may once have been “more of a male discipline”, in the words of Hernan Castro-Vidal, who runs the Pilates Nutrition studio in south London, but it’s become associated with images of impeccably groomed “pilates princesses”, showcasing their carefully chosen, colour-coordinated outfits on social media. My wardrobe is much less stylish. When it comes to the gym, I usually throw on an old T-shirt – but this won’t do if I’m to become a “pilates prince”.I manage to dig out a wrinkled gym vest, but, despite numerous attempts, it appears resistant to my iron: perhaps I should just embrace the term “pilates pauper”.Week one: ‘After 20 minutes, I am pleading for the class to be over’I start with reformer, not just the most fashionable form of pilates, but also the easiest-looking. As far as I can see, you just strap your hands and legs into some felt hoops and let the machine do the work. Walking into a mid-afternoon class at my local gym, however, I still feel intimidated. There are more than a dozen machines in the room, looking more intricate than I expected now I can see them close up. And my classmates – about 50/50 men and women – appear to know them inside out.View image in fullscreenHernan Castro-Vidal helps Sammy with the exercises.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianBefore getting strapped in, we are told to touch our toes while maintaining a steady balance. I falter a few times, getting flashbacks to my shoelace mishap, but eventually get the hang of it. Then the fun part begins. We are told to lie on the machine, remove some coloured springs to adjust the resistance, place our toes on the foot bar (a horizontal pole at the end of the contraption) and push, lengthening our bodies. Not too difficult, I think, but things are just getting started. After doing the same movement with both heels, we are told to raise one leg into the air, bent at the knee, and push the foot bar again. We look like a roomful of half-arsed ballerinas, but I can feel a burn starting. Swapping legs, we do the other side before things ramp up.The next 40 minutes are a bit of a blur, though the most traumatic exercises I recall include the hundred, where we place our hands in the hoops and, keeping our legs in the air, pump our arms up and down, which leaves my core burning, and leg circles, where we place our feet in the hoops and raise them towards the ceiling before lowering them and widening to make a circle. It looks simple but, after the fifth circle, every bit of my lower body is on fire. I struggle to keep up and the instructor comes over repeatedly to correct my form. After 20 minutes, I am pleading for the class to be over.The next day is where things really come into focus. I struggle to stand and parts of my body I never knew could be targeted are burning. It may have looked easy – but far from it.Week two: ‘The appeal is starting to dawn on me’After my large class, it’s time for something more intimate. At Castro-Vidal’s studio, I join a session with three others, one woman and two men. I arrive after work, with the aches from last week’s class just about subsiding and, to be honest, I’m dreading it.Castro-Vidal says he has seen a sharp rise in men signing up for pilates, with many influenced by “celebrities and footballers”. Most are nervous about diving head-first into a group class, and opt for private sessions at first. Out of the 15 clients he sees for private classes, 12 are men. “They’re a little bit shy and they don’t want to join a group session yet,” he says. I, however, am thrown into the deep end and plonked on to a reformer machine after a brief warmup. The exercises are similar to the previous class, but Castro-Vidal corrects my form throughout, pressing down on my stomach while angling my body on the machine to ensure my core is correctly engaged, and holding my feet down when they are on the verge of slipping off the foot bar. It makes a world of difference. In the larger class, keeping pace with everyone else was top of my mind.Today, the pace is slower, but every movement feels like it’s hitting the right place. That’s not to say it isn’t utterly exhausting. Halfway through, I feel myself buckling, but with Castro-Vidal’s keen eye on me, I persist. I stretch my body out on the machine, and this time the hundred isn’t the ordeal it was before. I even raise my legs towards the ceiling with ease.At the end of the session, I’m beat, but I’m able to move my bad shoulder with much less pain. The appeal of pilates is starting to dawn on me. “We need to differentiate between workout classes and the true essence of pilates,” Castro-Vidal tells me. For him, classes with dozens of people might be a good taster for reformer pilates, but they’re not the real deal. “It’s not just a workout – it’s a discipline. It can even become a way of life,” he says. He believes “six people is the maximum number to be able to provide attention to everyone”.View image in fullscreen‘My body aches but not nearly as much as before.’Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianAlongside me in the class is Divanka Wijendra, a 43-year-old GP. He used to attend Hiit (high-intensity interval training) classes and did CrossFit, but as age crept up on him, he thought: “I don’t think I can keep up with the intensity.” This is a trend he has observed among his male friends. “People are enjoying the slightly slow pace of it compared with the intense Hiit style of training,” he says.This shift is industry-wide. In 2018, about 14,000 gyms around the world were affiliated with CrossFit. In 2025, this figure haddroppedto less than 10,000. At the same time, pilates, especially reformer, is booming. In the UK, the business insurance provider Protectivity reporteda rise of more than 900%in applications from reformer instructors between 2024 and 2025.Wijendra’s interest was piqued by social media. “On Instagram, it was always popping up on the algorithm and I started to see a lot more people doing it. There were a lot of funny videos of men trying to do it and getting it a bit wrong.”His first session with Castro-Vidal left him feeling achey and stretched. “I was thinking: ‘Oh, my God, this is quite tough” – but he persisted because he “enjoys a challenge”. Six months on, his core is stronger and his posture has improved. “I can definitely bend down and touch my toes,” he says. I’ve still got some work to do to match him.Week three: ‘My body is once again on fire’After two high-octane weeks, I book a machine-free mat pilates class and hope for some respite. Oh, how wrong I am. I join a class of eight, including one other man, lying on the mat, placing a ball between my shoulder blades and doing what feel like crunches on overdrive. I’m familiar with most of the exercises that follow, but without the machine, I’m relying on my own balance, strength and flexibility. I topple to my side many times. After 40 minutes of gut-busting stretches, arduous leg raises and (I never thought I’d say this) some mercifully tame planks, the class is over. It’s far harder than reformer and my body is, once again, on fire. But if I’d done my research, this wouldn’t have come as a surprise.“We recommend reformer to people who struggle to do mat to help them to get stronger,” says Stephanie Tam, a pilates instructor at Third Space. She has been an instructor for eight years and teaches only mat pilates.“Mat is the original. It’s what pilates started as,” Tam says, calling it the “best form of exercise for everyone”. When she started teaching, she didn’t see men very often, but now they are a common sight in her classes. “I love it when men come,” she says. “I think a lot of them expect it to be really easy and then they try it and see how challenging it really is.”Despite the shared exercises, the two variants of pilates feel distinct. Reformer is great for feeling flexible, but mat feels like a true test of my abilities. I enjoy the challenge and I can see myself doing both in the future.Week four: ‘I am beginning to feel at one with the machine’After three weeks, have I graduated to a “pilates prince”? I look more like one, having treated myself to a trio of fancy workout vests. But it’s time to test myself with a final session. I return to the reformer class I joined in my first week, in a conquering mood. Like the others in my class, I am beginning to feel at one with the machine.Before getting started, it’s time to warm up. I bend down and manage to touch my toes without toppling over. Hurdle one complete. Now the hard graft. We begin with pushing ourselves up with our toes and heels on the foot bar. Easy! Then some leg raises. My confidence falters a bit here and I fail to keep a fixed position, but I bounce back after readjusting and taking things at my own pace, ignoring the veterans around me. Next up is the hundred. It’s tough, but nowhere near as arduous as the first time around.Before I know it, the 40 minutes are almost over. My body aches, but not nearly as much as before: it seems I’m getting used to it. We finish with “hunchbacks”, our hands sprawled against the ground touching our toes before rolling our spines upwards until we’re standing. Class is over.Did a month of pilates change me? My stomach certainly feels firmer. I can also bend down and touch my toes with good balance: an untied shoelace will take me down no longer. Doing the splits is a long way off but my morning stretches feel more elongated and my posture is slightly improved, though my spine is hardly ruler-straight. And what about my shoulder? I didn’t expect pilates to be a magic bullet, but there’s less pain.Will I be posting my #pilatesprince snaps on social media? I’ll hold off for now. I haven’t transformed into a pilates obsessive – but I can see myself taking a class every few weeks.Explore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingPilatesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Italian pop legend takes the lead in Maria Grazia Chiuri’s Fendi collection | Milan fashion week | The Guardian
description: Milan show full of diaphanous dresses and visible bras celebrates ‘incredible feminist’ of the 1970s, Raffaella Carrà
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Milan show full of diaphanous dresses and visible bras celebrates ‘incredible feminist’ of the 1970s, Raffaella Carrà
Content: A model in Fendi in Milan. Designer Maria Grazia Chiuri often uses her collections as a platform to celebrate women’s creativity.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA model in Fendi in Milan. Designer Maria Grazia Chiuri often uses her collections as a platform to celebrate women’s creativity.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty ImagesMilan fashion weekItalian pop legend takes the lead in Maria Grazia Chiuri’s Fendi collectionMilan show full of diaphanous dresses and visible bras celebrates ‘incredible feminist’ of the 1970s, Raffaella CarràJess Cartner-Morleyin MilanWed 23 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaria Grazia Chiuri has been having more fun with clothes since she decamped from Paris back to her native Rome to work at Fendi. “I have less of a uniform these days. I think it is because being back here makes me feel young again. I’m not sure my daughter appreciates [this attitude]! But I don’t care,” she said at a preview before her Milan fashion week show.Not that Chiuri doesn’t approach her work as a designer seriously. She described her second ready-to-wear season at Fendi not as a show, or a collection, but as “the second part of the project I am working on for them”.She is continuing the protocol she developed as the designer ofDiorof using each event as a platform to celebrate women’s creativity. But instead of a ceramicist or a philosopher, her muse for this season is the Italian pop legend Raffaella Carrà.Carrà, once described as a “one-womanAbba”, had a Lady Gaga bob and a taste for sequined catsuits. She caused a sensation with her raunchy outfits – the first bare midriff ever seen on Italian TV, in 1970 – and her sex-positive lyrics (her song A Far L’Amore Comincia Tu translates as “Take the lead when making love”).View image in fullscreenRaffaella Carrà, performing on Italian TV in the late 1970s.Photograph: Giorgio Ambrosi/Mondadori/Getty Images“She was an incredible feminist, and her relationship with her clothes was so free,” said Chiuri of Carrà, who died aged 78 in 2021.On the catwalk, Carrà’s influence became diaphanous 1970s dresses with trailing hems, visible lace bras, embroidered waistcoats and vintage fur stoles, while men’s shirts were unbuttoned to the navel.The biggest and starriest show of thisMilan fashion weekbelonged not to any designer, but to Vogue. Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, Milan’s glass-domed cathedral to retail, became a catwalk for a line-up that included Jennifer Lopez in Dolce & Gabbana and Cardi B in vintage Versace, with the singer Alicia Keys and the ballet dancer Roberto Bolle performing live.Vogue is leaning into live events to amplify its brand and strengthen its coffers as print income declines. Vogue World Milano follows last year’s Vogue World: Hollywood in LA, which generated $30m (£23m) in revenue.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenVisible bras and vintage fur stoles featured heavily in Maria Grazia Chiuri’s Fendi collection at Milan fashion week.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesBilled as a celebration of Italian craftsmanship and the human touch in fashion, the event highlighted the stark reality of an increasing dependence on benefactors from Silicon Valley.Sponsors of the event included Meta Glasses and OpenAI, and the finale included two dancing robots, who were greeted with notably less enthusiasm by the stellar line-up of Italian designers in the front row than the rest of the show.“The landlords have entered the chat,” read one comment beneath a video of the robots circulating on social media.Explore more on these topicsMilan fashion weekFashion weeksMaria Grazia ChiuriItalynewsShareReuse this content

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: if you can’t use retinoids, these proven anti-ageing formulas are the next best thing | Beauty | The Guardian
description: Stop ‘pushing through the pain’ or ceaselessly searching for the ‘right retinol’ – there are some great alternatives
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: Stop ‘pushing through the pain’ or ceaselessly searching for the ‘right retinol’ – there are some great alternatives
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Sali Hughes on beautyBeautySali Hughes on beauty: if you can’t use retinoids, these proven anti-ageing formulas are the next best thingStop ‘pushing through the pain’ or ceaselessly searching for the ‘right retinol’ – there are some great alternativesSali HughesWed 23 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnyone with an internet connection will no doubt have heard that retinoids – a group of vitamin A-based compounds – are the most evidenced and effective ingredients in treating the visible signs of skin ageing. Message received loud and clear. But what often goes unheard are the voices of many beauty consumers who have found that they simply cannot use them. All too often, I see experts online telling those complaining of discomfort, unremitting dryness, persistent redness, stinging or angry reactions that they just need to “find the right retinol” or simply “push through” the pain barrier. But I will die on this hill: not everyone can use retinoids, and they can still achieve great results without them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: a shortcut to glass skin? Try these one-step moisturisersRead moreIf I don’t convince you, believe my esteemed consultant, dermatologistDr Justine Hextall(a woman I respect and trust so completely that I have entrusted her with my children’s skin health), because she agrees. While Hextall, as any good derm would, prescribes retinoids on a daily basis, she also sees patients for whom there is a more appropriate, kinder pathway. “While retinoids are effective, they can be difficult to tolerate and may not be used consistently in those with sensitive skin,” she says. “Consistency is the key in skincare.”double quotation markIf your skin won't tolerate retinol every day, it may be better to use a group of other well-evidenced ingredientsEssentially, she believes that if skin is not robust enough to tolerate one ingredient every day, it may be better to use a group of other well-evidenced ingredients it can cope with. In such cases, she recommends a combination of peptides, like Matrixyl 3000 (a key inclusion in The Ordinary’sMulti-Peptide + Copper Peptides 1%Serum, £28.90), for supporting collagen, and a neuropeptide, like Argireline (present in Skinceuticals’P-TioxSerum, £135, and Naturium’sMulti-Peptide Advanced Serum, £27), to help smooth fine lines. If the idea of multiple serums turns you off – it does me –Asterwoodmakes one that combines both, for a reasonable £26.99. Beauty Pie’sSuperdrops Flash Face Lift Intense Serum(£45; £24 for members) is another good Matrixyl/Argireline combo.Hextall also recommends the use of azelaic acid and alpha hydroxy acids to brighten dull skin. I use AHAs 2-4 times a week after cleansing, and it’s worth the minimal effort. Any that your skin tolerates well will be fine. Finally, Hextall suggests a good antioxidant, like Cetaphil’sAdvanced Defence Serum(£26.50), and, of course, sunscreen. Without adequate sun protection, any penny spent on the above is as good as down the drain.Explore more on these topicsBeautySali Hughes on beautySkincarefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From 50p gold hot pants to Paul Smith suits: how Kylie Minogue became one of pop’s ultimate chameleons | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The star’s rise from Ramsay Street to global superstar is the subject of a new book. It’s a journey that has cleverly harnessed the power of fashion to transform, subvert – and shock
Author: Michael Cragg
Headline: The star’s rise from Ramsay Street to global superstar is the subject of a new book. It’s a journey that has cleverly harnessed the power of fashion to transform, subvert – and shock
Content: Spinning Around … Minogue in her famous gold hot pants.Photograph: Channel 5View image in fullscreenSpinning Around … Minogue in her famous gold hot pants.Photograph: Channel 5FashionFrom 50p gold hot pants to Paul Smith suits: how Kylie Minogue became one of pop’s ultimate chameleonsThe star’s rise from Ramsay Street to global superstar is the subject of a new book. It’s a journey that has cleverly harnessed the power of fashion to transform, subvert – and shockMichael CraggWed 23 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 20 December 1989,Kylie Minoguefirst harnessed the power of fashion. Attending the Australian premiere of her film The Delinquents, she wore a custom sequined noughts-and-crosses minidress by Australian designers Morrissey Edmiston and a cropped blond wig. She also arrived with a new accessory: a rock star boyfriend in the shape of Michael Hutchence from INXS.Before then, there’d been her Neighbours character Charlene’s peak-80s silk taffeta and lace wedding dress, and Kylie the pop star on the cover of her first album, in 1988, wearing a topless hat showing off cascading curls. But that had been fashion forced on her, at a time when she had no say in her image.View image in fullscreenBreakout moment … with Michael Hutchence at the premiere of The Delinquents.Photograph: Mick Hutson/RedfernsFrom that moment, Kylie, or the public-facing version at least, took control. She used fashion as a reflection of her desire and need to evolve. Forever the pop chameleon, she anchored each new era via deliberate fashion choices that communicated where she was at in her life and career. As Jean Paul Gaultier wrote in the foreword to her 2012 photo-book Kylie/Fashion: “You change, you transform yourself, you adapt with the evolution of times, fashions, desires … and still stay yourself.”View image in fullscreenEspecially for you … inthatwedding dress with Jason Donovan in Neighbours.Photograph: Fremantle Ltd/RexWhile shapeshifting and defining distinct eras via fashion is a classic pop star move, Kylie’s early evolutions had to be more extreme. Madonna – the queen of reinvention, whose influence can be traced to Lady Gaga and Addison Rae – arrived fresh from the streets of New York and a friendship group that included Keith Haring and Jean-Michel Basquiat. Her 80s look of fishnets, gloves and copious amounts of bangles felt cool. The wide-eyed Kylie, meanwhile, had to take bigger risks; she had to shake off Neighbours, Jason Donovan and the sense of playing dress-up in a box marked “cringe”.This need manifested itself in her 1991 Let’s Get to It tour. The singer, keen to bury her Smiley Kylie persona, turned to the then relatively unknown John Galliano. “I just love dressing up and anyone who enjoys dressing up,”said Galliano at the time. The looks included corsets, stockings and suspenders and, most controversially, revealing underwear that showed off her buttocks. It created a tabloid scandal. NME accused Kylie of sending out a “dangerous message” to her young fans, which was sort of the point. She was using fashion to signal a move away from the old version of herself. “Those outfits weren’t a mistake,” she told Big! magazine that year. “I didn’t employ John Galliano to make me neck-to-toe cover-ups.”By the early 90s, Kylie had become a mainstay on the covers of style magazines such as the Face and i-D. For the latter she worked with fashion alchemist Judy Blame, whose outfits for Neneh Cherry helped define the look of the 80s, before teaming up with Katie Grand, considered one of the most powerful stylists in fashion. Grand would work on the cover shoot for 1994’s album, Kylie Minogue – her first for dance label Deconstruction. The choice of a black-and-white shot of a bare-footed and bespectacled Kylie in a Paul Smith suit was a more androgynous and interesting look for a pop star famed for pearly white teeth and vibrant colour. The image would help set the template for the new Cool Kylie era, anchored by songs such as Confide in Me.This more daring and intuitive approach to fashion would bleed into the next phase, Indie Kylie. Via her new stylist and so-called “gay husband” William Baker, Kylie would be introduced to new, edgier designers such as Owen Gaster, Antonio Berardi and Véronique Leroy. The feel was more stripped back, almost grunge-adjacent, but with a flash of the pop star peaking through.View image in fullscreenWearing a costume designed by John Galliano on her Showgirl: The Greatest Hits Tour in 2005.Photograph: Maurice McDonald/PAThe new millennium, however, would see Kylie ditch any indie overtones, chiefly thanks to a pair of now incredibly famous 50p gold hot pants found in a charity shop. They weren’t bought specifically for the Spinning Around video – Kylie had previously worn them in 1996 for a “nerds, tarts and tourists” party hosted by a friend – but they quickly became the video’s star. They perfectly encapsulated her return to pop and, via the tanned and carefree video, the optimism of a new millennium.The hot pants, alongside the majority of Kylie’s most stunning outfits, were donated by the lady herself to the Arts Centre Melbourne, occasionally being put on display in glass cabinets like the work of art that they’ve become.View image in fullscreenWearing a Gareth Pugh costume on the Showgirl Homecoming tour at Wembley Arena in 2007.Photograph: Pete Still/RedfernsAnother striking fashion moment would arrive a year later via Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s white hooded jumpsuit, complete with navel-scraping neckline. Designed by Mrs Jones, AKA the London designer Fee Doran, and with a nod to Grace Jones, it was a sign of Kylie’s style becoming more ambitious and future-facing – the perfect accompaniment to that era’s sleek Fever album.Kylie’s ability to signal personal and professional changes via her clothes is what anchors her as one of pop’s best chameleons. It’s there in the body-hugging, less obviously suggestive sexiness of the blue Balenciaga dress from 2003’s sultry Slow video, or the armour of English designer Gareth Pugh’s futuristic designs, which captured the resilience of 2007’s X era after Kylie returned to pop after being diagnosed with cancer. She is able to wear the gothic beauty of the Vampire’s Wife one minute and Dolce & Gabbana’s silver and gold miniskirts on stage the next.She even made a cameo appearance in Chanel’s recent handbag campaign, with the advert a homage to Kylie’s Michel Gondry-directed Come Into My World video from 2002.Kylie is not just one thing. Via her various musical eras throughout a near four-decade career, she’s moved across fashion with a nimbleness that only people with taste can. No one designer has ever “owned” her, and no stylist has locked her into a specific style. Kylie uses fashion like she uses her musical collaborators: to help colour in the various aspects of who she is.Can’t Get You Out of My Head: In Search of Kylie by Michael Cragg is published on 24 September by Faber (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFashionKylie MinoguePop and rockJohn GallianofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bolognina: make tracks for Bologna’s bustling former rail workers’ quarter | Italy holidays | The Guardian
description: This once industrial area has been transformed into a vibrant artistic hub with a thriving food and drink scene
Author: John Brunton
Headline: This once industrial area has been transformed into a vibrant artistic hub with a thriving food and drink scene
Content: Bollore is a cool vermouth bar in the Mercato Albani  that also organises concerts, art exhibitions and cultural events.Photograph: John BruntonView image in fullscreenBollore is a cool vermouth bar in the Mercato Albani  that also organises concerts, art exhibitions and cultural events.Photograph: John BruntonZoning inItaly holidaysBolognina: make tracks for Bologna’s bustling former rail workers’ quarterThis once industrial area has been transformed into a vibrant artistic hub with a thriving food and drink sceneJohn BruntonWed 23 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 02.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy go now?Located just north of the Centrale train station, Bolognina neighbourhood is more than just a Little Bologna. It is a completely different world from the medieval maze of palaces, churches and towers that define the city’s “Centro Storico”, which is increasingly filled with crowds of tourists as Bologna joins the big league of Italian getaway destinations.There is an immediate visual difference as narrow cobbled lanes give way to wide, tree-lined avenues, pastel-coloured low-rise apartment blocks, spacious parks and piazzas. Bolognina sprang up at the beginning of the 20th century, initially to house families of workers from the railway, then from nearby manufacturing industries.Today, the quarter is home to a diverse multi-ethnic population and remains a stronghold for militant leftwing politics, with the local community committed to avoiding gentrification. Tourists are certainly made welcome, and it is a delight to feel part of genuine local life.Where to eat and drinkView image in fullscreenTrattoria di via Serra chef Tommaso Maio.Photograph: John BruntonEating out here makes a refreshing change from the city centre. Of course there are still spots serving traditional freshly made tagliatelle al ragù such as the atmospheric old-school trattoriaLa Golosità di Nonna Aurora. But you can also sample Georgian cuisine atPane Georgiana, a sharing plate of Ethiopian and Eritrean dishes atRistorante Africano Adal, spicy Sichuan cooking atBa Hot Pot, or handmade tortellini and tortelloni stuffed with halal meat at the innovativeBrodellini.For vegetarians, the perfect spot isPiazza Martino, a cantina and deli owned by a nearby farm in the Bolognesi Hills that practises a “first we grow, then we eat” philosophy, transforming their organic produce into delicious aubergine parmigiana, vegan pepperoni lasagne, and courgette and potato polpette (balls).Bolognina’s prime foodie street is Via Luigi Serra, symbolised by the fiercely independentTrattoria di Via Serra. The restaurant’s three small, rustic salons are always packed and getting a reservation isn’t easy as they don’t take bookings through social platforms and rarely answer the phone or emails. Chef Tommaso Maio and co-owner Flavio Benassi used to have a restaurant up in the hills nearby, but 13 years ago decided to come to the city, choosing Bolognina rather than the city centre for their new venture. “Our aim then, and still today, is to offer the locals here an old-fashioned neighbourhood trattoria where they can still order a comforting bowl of tortellini in capon broth, lasagne and freshly baked crescenti biscuits,” they explain.View image in fullscreenA mural of local hero Lucio Dalla, an iconic Italian singer-songwriter.Photograph: John BruntonIf there is no free table at the Trattoria, then the street offers plenty of options, from hearty plates of cold cuts and cheeses at the deli-dinerLa Vecchia Bottega, cocktails, spritz and craft beers at the hipFermentobar, or local wines atLa Petite Enoteca. To finish the evening, there is often live music at the bars in Piazza Lucio Dalla, named after Bologna’s local hero, an iconic Italian singer-songwriter.Cultural experiencesView image in fullscreenThe monumental Holocaust memorial is one of the first things you see on arriving in the quarter.Photograph: Riccardo Bianchini/AlamyLeave historic Bologna behind by walking from the central train station across the Matteotti bridge and you immediately come face to face with a strikingHolocaust memorial, an austere, minimalist monument of two narrowly separated 10-metre high steel walls. Just opposite stands the massive Chiesa del Sacro Cuore di Gesù, dating back to 1912 when Bolognina was first being built. It is worth visiting just to marvel at the soaring 60-metre-high dome.Hidden away in the backstreets in a former tram shed,La Memoria di Ustica Museumis a unique homage to a commercial flight between Bologna and Palermo that was mysteriously shot down in 1980 with no survivors. French artist Christian Boltanski has meticulously reconstructed the wreckage of the downed airliner and assembled the personal items belonging to the victims, creating an immense, intensely moving installation.View image in fullscreenThe impressive dome of Chiesa del Sacro Cuore di Gesù.Photograph: John BruntonCheckpoint Charlyis a thriving alternative art and artisan cooperative occupying a former lingerie warehouse. Workshops include ceramics, printmaking, photography, graphics and music, with a dozen cultural events presented each year. TheDLF– Dopo Lavoro Ferroviario – is a sprawling park behind the station originally created in the 1920s for after-work activities for railway workers. This green lung has been saved from abandonment and now houses the laid-back all-dayKinotto Bar, theVecchia Orsa DLFcraft brewery and beer garden, apizzeria, thePuccini concert arenaand theLocomotiv Club, a live indie music venue.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhere to shopView image in fullscreenIlario di Lorenzis in his workshop with one of his hand-crafted bags.Photograph: John BruntonAlthough this essentially residential neighbourhood may not be a shopping paradise, bargain hunters should plan to visit on the first Sunday of the month when the Piazza Lucio Dalla is transformed into a huge flea market. Over in the daily Mercato Albani, Ilario di Lorenzis has recently openedIntelligenza Artigianale, an atelier showcasing his funky hand-crafted bags, T-shirts and caps, while cycling fans should head forBolognina Bike Shop, whose friendly owner, Dario Brunetto, repairs bikes and recycles vinyls, retro decor and collectible vintage cycling jerseys.Don’t missView image in fullscreenA food stall in Mercato Abani.Photograph: John BruntonSince opening in 1934,Mercato Albanihas been the beating heart of Bolognina. Running down the middle of a shady tree-lined avenue, locals gather each morning for their daily shopping from bustling stalls selling Bologna’s speciality mortadella (pork salami) and prosciutto, fish, cheese and organic veggies. Then there is a complete change of personality from 5pm till around midnight when shuttered stands open up as lively cocktail and craft beer bars, the natural wineenoteca,Vineria Punk, plus casual diners serving pizza and pasta, vegan dishes and Greek cuisine. Giuseppe Agrello the owner ofBollore, a cool vermouth bar, explains that “when we were invited to open in the mercato, we insisted that during the day it should stay as it is and not become just another tourist food court. So we only begin in the evening and also organise concerts, art exhibitions and cultural events for the community.”Where to stayView image in fullscreenThe eclectic Hotel Il Guercino.Photograph: John BruntonHotel Il Guercinois a delightfully quirky, family-owned hotel, extravagantly decorated with a mix of baroque and Asian influences, with a spa featuring sauna, hot tub and steam bath. Doubles from €150.This trip wasprovided byBologna WelcomeandEmilia Romagna TurismoExplore more on these topicsItaly holidaysZoning inCity breaksBologna holidaysEurope holidaysFood and drinkCultural tripsRestaurantsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI | Technology | The Guardian
description: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting
Content: Google's AI mode is advertised on 30 October 2025 in London, United Kingdom.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGoogle's AI mode is advertised on 30 October 2025 in London, United Kingdom.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesTechnology‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AIA feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shiftingBlake MontgomeryWed 23 Sep 2026 15.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a featureGooglecalls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting.“AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search,last August. In May, the company saidmore AI is coming.As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Academic studies are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Media outlets and website owners are enduring a sustained traffic decline. Large US media companiesare suingGoogle, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue.Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume fromGoogleSearch to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.”The Guardian asked readers whether Google has improved or worsened in the age of AI and how their habits of searching the internet have changed.‘Google is better now’Better, mainly because it leads you in your quest rather than you having to search on yourself. I am happy to have the AI lead me to an answer but the mega caution is that Google AI or any of them are not at all trustworthy. I have had it admit that it was lying to me and apologise!Sionn Achog, retired teacher 76, DublinI find that AI responses are more informative than previously, which simply referred the user to other relevant websites.Peter Warb, 75, UKAI has made Google better. I use AI mode for all my searches.Jose Garcia Jr, 40, recovery coach, Dallas, TexasView image in fullscreenJose GarciaAI has improved Google search. The analysis and chat functions are so much more useful than a ranked list of websites that still need to be explored by the user. Reviewing a list of websites is still an option but is very time consuming, and frustrating.Alan Caruana, consultant, 62, MaltaFar more better, faster and real. I search now with confidence, complete assurance and a high degree of accuracy.Eleazar Eke, electrical engineer, 67, Onitsha, NigeriaMuch better. It hasn’t changed my behavior, just getting better and more focused results.Catherine Weber, former political analyst, 57, OregonIt’s made Google search much better, I find that I rarely actually click on the website links any more. I find information I want much faster and have a deeper understanding of any topic as I can ask questions about it and drill into the areas I’m interested in.Mark Johnson, 52, software engineer, LondonGreatly improved it by getting at more arcane info regarding subject matter. Juxtaposition has improved with AI and abstruse knowledge of subjects becomes more accessible to layman. Wonderful tool with power to extend mind through sensing connections and very akin to human thinking.Samuel Lieberstein, 90, retired teacher, Cherry Hill, New Jersey‘Search has gotten worse’Search has become worse. Google AI obscures sources and tries to claim information it did not create while diverting traffic from the sources it steals from.Sean Peters, document processor, 41, Portland, Oregonskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSean Peters.Every time I search I have to scroll down to find an actual real website to find a full article or discussion or to confirm that the AI summary isn’t making things up. Occasionally when I am feeling particularly bitter, I remember to add the ““-ai”” tag to my search.Ewan Herbert, English teacher, 33, JapanWorse. I have disabled AI overviews using an extension.Chris Gibson, DundeeAbsolutely worse. I want to be able to decide for myself which results are the most useful and relevant, and we’re no longer able to turn off the AI summary results.Jon Wilkinson, personal trainer, 43, Manchester, UKView image in fullscreenJon Wilkinson.‘It’s so bad I quit Google’Google has been enshittified … I do miss old Google Search and I really hope something of equal capabilities eventually comes to replace it.The search engine I currently use is good for a lot of things, but if I need to look for something in languages other than English, the quality of the results is much lower. Image search is also not as good as that of Google used to be.Sofia, postdoctoral physics researcher, 30, Lausanne, SwitzerlandMy first stop now is Duck Duck Go, a pale imitation of Google’s search engine at the height of its powers. Unfortunately, the top results often include Grokipedia entries and other garbage.Craig Garrett, book editor, 52, New York CityView image in fullscreenCraig Garrett.I have stopped using Google. I now use another search engine with no AI overviews.Guy Arthur Simpson, writer 66, SpainI’ve made a conscious effort to find a browser which does not lead with the AI results. Mine is now Ecosia.Dan Jennings, IT, 54, Southampton, UKI do a lot of research for my studies, and the AI features are a nightmare! I’m still scouring for a decent search engine without any of these ‘AI features’, the last thing i want is to accidentally utilise a water-wasting AI behemoth datacentre when I forget that crucial suffix. I’ve even resorted to using my local library’s resource of legal cases for my work, at least it is trustworthy.Catherine O’Leary,student studyinglaw,politics andsociology, 17, Newcastle Upon TyneGoogle has become almost useless, searches I’ve made in the past which yielded specific results, (news articles, local information, historical references) no longer appear. I no longer submit to Google search first, I go directly to Wikipedia as my first source, then to DuckDuckGo, (with AI disabled) then to Reddit and only to Google as a last resort.Pedro Reyes, 61, Galicia, SpainExplore more on these topicsTechnologyGoogleSearch enginesAI (artificial intelligence)News websitesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: my brother gave me an unexpected gift – and a whole new life at sea | Disability | The Guardian
description: The water was my childhood playground but, as I grew up, my health left me landbound. Then my brother found a way to launch me back into the waves ...
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The water was my childhood playground but, as I grew up, my health left me landbound. Then my brother found a way to launch me back into the waves ...
Content: Bethany Handley.Photograph: Courtesy of Bethany HandleyView image in fullscreenBethany Handley.Photograph: Courtesy of Bethany HandleyA moment that changed meDisabilityA moment that changed me: my brother gave me an unexpected gift – and a whole new life at seaThe water was my childhood playground but, as I grew up, my health left me landbound. Then my brother found a way to launch me back into the waves ...Bethany HandleyWed 23 Sep 2026 01.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy brother and I grew up surfing at Porthcawl in south Wales. My earliest memories are of playing in the waves and I learned to bodyboard not long after I learned to walk. When I lost the use of my legs, I felt as if I had lost the sea – and a part of who I was.I was in my teens when I started to develop chronic illnesses, including endometriosis. At first, I was still able to surf – I just needed to rest afterwards. Then, in my early 20s, I developed further chronic conditions, including a connective tissue disorder that affected my joints and muscle strength. I could stand just for a few seconds and was able to walk only a few metres. At 23, an acute infection led to complications, including the loss of the use of my legs. Later, my stomach became paralysed; I’m now fed via a tube that runs down my oesophagus, through my stomach and into my intestines.When I was 24, one year after becoming a full-time wheelchair user, my brother, Leon, gave me an unexpected birthday gift: a battered, pink and yellow surfboard to which he had fitted shower handles either side of where my chest would rest. He was training as an adaptive surf coach, he explained, so that he could teach me.Wheeling over to the board, all I could think was, how on earth would I possibly surf? I didn’t know adaptive surfing existed. I couldn’t even move around my house because my wheelchair was so wide and heavy.I couldn’t use my legs, and my core muscles had turned gelatinous. I hadn’t been able to get to a coffee shop with friends, let alone return to the sea. On my phone, I had watched with envy as Leon chased swells in Sri Lanka, Indonesia and New Zealand. Eventually, I had vowed to stop pining for a lifestyle that was no longer attainable – my limited energy was too precious. I had sold my surfboard and resigned myself to the fact that beach wheelchairs are hard to come by (beach access is rarely considered a priority) and the sand was hostile to my current set of wheels.View image in fullscreenGetting a piggyback … Bethany Handley with her brother, Leon, in Bude in June 2026.Photograph: Courtesy of Bethany HandleyAt a time when every day seemed like a riptide threatening to drag me into another hospital admission, the new surfboard felt like an ambitious gift. But it also sparked a desire to adapt and take risks again. It was crying out for the sea.I decided to head to Bude, Cornwall, a place where I had spent holidays as a kid. Leon gave me a piggyback down to the beach while my partner, Harris, strode behind, carrying our boards. We wrapped the end of my feeding tube in a plastic sandwich bag while my parents watched on, nervously.View image in fullscreenHandley on the beach in Bude.Photograph: Courtesy of Bethany HandleyLeon waded in up to his knees with me on his back before placing me on my board as Harris straightened out my legs for balance. The waves that day were messy and unpredictable, crumbling under an onshore wind before we could catch them. Holding the back of my board, Leon paddled us over the breaking waves, each one launching us towards the sky before we crashed back down. Then a large wave rolled slowly towards us, building, becoming steeper. Leon launched me on to it, shouting: “Paddle, paddle, paddle!” Without having to haul the heavy, ill-fitting wheelchair around with me, I instantly felt stronger. Muscle memory kicked in as I used my arms to part the water as quickly as I could.Far up the beach, waiting expectantly, was my wheelchair. Harris grinned from the shallows as I hurtled towards him. I felt light and physically powerful. In the brief respite from pain, I whooped with unrivalled joy, my grin so broad I almost swallowed an ocean’s worth of water.Adaptive surfing hasn’t returned me to my old life – it’s given me a new one. I wish I could visit my bedbound, newly disabled self and tell her of the radical hope I have been given by this unexpected gift. One of the handles fell off after our Bude trip, but it hasn’t stopped me getting out on the waves; I just have to cling on harder. Returning to the place that had shaped me made me see how the limits placed on my freedoms could be removed, and I’m for ever grateful to my brother for giving me back the sea.My Body is a Meadow: Finding Freedom in the Outdoors by Bethany Handley is out now (Headline Press, £20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
