title: Country diary: An autumn bounty of fruits is well on its way | Environment | The Guardian
description: Cardigan: Taking a walk beside the River Teifi, I encounter trees beginning to fade into new season colour, and the low blur of a weasel
Author: John Gilbey
Headline: Cardigan: Taking a walk beside the River Teifi, I encounter trees beginning to fade into new season colour, and the low blur of a weasel
Content: ‘The sloes are plump and mature with the promise of a warming winter spirit to come.’Photograph: John GilbeyView image in fullscreen‘The sloes are plump and mature with the promise of a warming winter spirit to come.’Photograph: John GilbeyCountry diaryEnvironmentCountry diary: An autumn bounty of fruits is well on its wayCardigan:Taking a walk beside the River Teifi, I encounter trees beginning to fade into new season colour, and the low blur of a weaselJohn GilbeyWed 23 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 02.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is rare for me to visit the same place twice within a couple of weeks, but my walk in the Teifi Marshes recently was curtailed by heavy rain, and I feel that I have unfinished business. Last time I started from the Cilgerran end of the marsh, so today begin at the seaward side – crossing the bridge over the Teifi and heading upstream past the site of the old, sadly long-departedCardigan railway station.My route follows the former course of the railway line, but I briefly divert along a boardwalk into the broad reedbeds at the heart of the marsh. Here, I am surrounded by the ambient sound of the wind in the reeds, which ebbs and flows with an almost animate organic static – pushing back the distant sounds of traffic on the main road. Scrub and small trees interact with the reeds at the margins, their autumn bounty of fruits already well advanced. The blackberries are almost over, but the sloes are plump and mature with the promise of a warming winter spirit to come.Back on the main trail, a weasel, a low blur of fur and legs, dashes across the path in front of me just as the sun emerges from banks of grey cloud. The new shadows make me look up. Beyond the mile or so of reedbed, the valley side is wooded with deciduous trees just beginning to fade into autumn colours. Among them, a few bare crowns of what I take to be dead ash trees stand skeletal, awaiting the winter stormView image in fullscreenReedbeds at the margin of the Afon Teifi.Photograph: John GilbeyThe Afon Teifi is tidal here, and it is about an hour after high water. The level in the creek off the main channel is starting to fall, exposing freshly wetted mud. Along the edge of the water, a pair of dunlin explore what the receding tide has left on offer, hunting with their short bills and jerky movements, while nearby ducks take a more leisurely approach. On my last visit, I caught a glimpse of a kingfisher from this spot, but today it is absent – as is the heron I had hoped to get a better picture of. Next time, perhaps. Next time.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentCountry diaryRural affairsPlantsRiversAnimalsTrees and forestsBirdsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: London buses in decline? Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised | Transport | The Guardian
description: As experts fear for future of UK capital’s bus network, some commuters are giving up entirely. London is not alone – with worrying implications for poorest in society
Author: Ed Gargan
Headline: As experts fear for future of UK capital’s bus network, some commuters are giving up entirely. London is not alone – with worrying implications for poorest in society
Content:
TransportLondon buses in decline? Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualisedAs experts fear for future of UK capital’s bus network, some commuters are giving up entirely. London is not alone – with worrying implications for the poorest in societyEd Gargan,Gwyn Topham,Prina Shah,Scarlet PestellandAshley KirkWed 23 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareFew things say London more than a red double-decker. But the capital’s
        buses have a problem: they are getting slower.In congested streets, services are being squeezed. And for the millions
        of people who rely on buses, more than any other form of London
        transport, journeys are ever longer.On the22, a route through some of the
        busiest streets in the capital towards Oxford Circus, it’s easy to see
        why.Buses regularly get stuck in stop-start traffic…Strings of red lights frequently slow buses down…And roadworks restrict the space in which buses can operate.…In 2025, the22was the second slowest bus
        in London, averaging just under 6mph.This is16% slowerthan its average speed a decade ago. Back
        then, today’s hour-long journey would have taken 51 minutes.When the Guardian sent a reporter on the bus on a June morning, the bus
        was stationary for40out of the108 minutesit took to reach Oxford Circus.This is a pattern seen across the UK capital.In the west, the207 to White Cityis14% slowerthan a decade ago, with an average speed of 7.4mph
        in 2025.That’s slower than the average beginner cyclist.The243 to Waterloo, connecting north
        London to the city centre,slowed down by 5%.One of the city’s most popular routes, these slower journeys were taken
        by 9.8 million passengers in 2025.These routes are three examples of wider, continuing trend across London
        – and indeed, other cities across the world.Buses are slow, and they’re getting slower.Percentage change in average speed in 2025 versus 2015.This map shows how578of the700London
        bus routes have seen their average speed reduced in the past decade.20% slowerNo change20% fasterChange in average speed between 2015–2025, for routes in continuous service
    for this period. Changes in route are not accounted for. Where routes overlap,
    a weighted average of all speed changes is shown.Experts warn that slower buses risk driving passengers away:research cited by Transport for London (TfL)suggests a 10% fall in speed leads to a 6% drop in demand.Passenger journeys in London have already fallen by more than 300m a year, or 16%, since 2013, despite the city’s population growing by almost a million people.The city’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, does not play down the issue. “We’re really concerned about bus usage. One of the reasons, when you speak to commuters, is a lack of reliability. And why is it they lack reliability? Because of bus speed.”A congested city, with ever more demands on road space, has left London facing difficult choices over which modes of transport to prioritise. But when passengers turn away from slower buses, the service frequencies and even routes are liable to be cut.The fear is, as one industry figure puts it, “a vicious circle of decline”: slower buses; fewer passengers; and increasing pressure on services.Recent research has also pointed to this trend being recorded in other global cities such as Paris, Brussels, Lisbon and beyond.The growing wait for the London bus – in dataGuardian analysis ofdatafrom TfL, which runs London’s road and rail public transport network, reveals several indicators that the capital’s bus services have slowed, become truncated or less reliable. The Covid-19 pandemic had a sharp and obvious impact on the data, but there are clear downwards trends cutting through that period.Across the network as a whole, the average speed in 2025-26 stood at 9.18mph – the lowest speed since comparable records began in 2013-14, and a 4.8% drop over this period.Chart showing how bus speed has dropped from 9.6mph in 2013 to 9.2mph 2025, spiking to 10.3mph in 2020Bus timetables have long been adjusted to reflect London’s traffic. A snapshot of routes analysed by the economist Alexander Jan, a veteran of transport planning in the capital, found scheduled journey times are now, on average, 30% longer than they were 50 years ago.Yet even with that extra time built in, buses are increasingly failing to meet expectations. Delays have worsened: on high-frequency routes – those running more than five buses an hour – passengers now wait 22% longer than expected, up from 18% in 2018.Chart showing how passengers are waiting at bus stops for longerIf unreliability is, as Khan argues, deterring passengers, the latest ridership figures are concerning.Last year saw the first fall in bus journeys since the post-pandemic recovery. Between 2010 and 2019, annual passenger numbers consistently exceeded 2 billion; in 2024, they fell to 1.8 billion.Chart showing how ridership has not recovered after Covid-19 and is falling againAt the same time, the size of London’s bus network has shrunk. Between 2010 and 2019, TfL buses travelled an average of 487m km (303m miles) a year. Over the past three years, that figure has fallen to about 460m.Chart showing how buses are covering less distanceAcross the network buses are slower, passenger numbers are falling, services cover fewer miles and waiting times are rising.Those slower journeys come with a financial cost. Because drivers’ wages account for the largest share of operating costs, slower buses mean more vehicles and more staff are needed to provide the same level of service.According toanalysis by the Confederation of Passenger Transport, making London’s buses 10% faster would bring in an extra £70m a year in fares and cut operating costs by £214m.Delays and cuts also hit the poorest in society, who are more likely to rely on buses for shift work, lower costs or lack of a car. In London, a bus into the centre costs less than half the peak tube fare, and housing costs increase with proximity to underground stations.A global trendLondon is far from the only city whose buses are slowing down.A 2026 report by the Transport Strategy Centre (TSC)at Imperial College London found a “persistent decline in bus speeds” in the past decade in 15 networks in Europe, Asia and North America.Chart showing how declining bus speed is a global problemLondon’s slowdown is modest compared with other cities: in Paris, Istanbul, Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, bus travel is more than 10% slower than before the pandemic.Local factors vary, but the TSC report identifies a pattern: growing traffic and congestion and less space for buses, “diminished in part to the expansion of road space for cycling and walking”.In Barcelona, the redevelopment of Plaça de les Glòries Catalanes pushed traffic on to surrounding roads, at lower speed limits, with no priority for buses. Journey times rose by more than 25%.In New York, widening the protected cycle lane on Sixth Avenue reduced general traffic lanes from four to three; morning-peak bus speeds fell by 8% over the following year.When buses are fast and reliable, as the TSC report concludes, passengers “respond with increased use, strengthening the viability of the system; when speeds decline, ridership suffers, undermining sustainability goals”. In other words, making buses better is, the TSC says, “a primary lever for achieving equitable, low-carbon, and resilient cities”.Why are London buses getting slower?In London, the persistent slowdown comes despite successive London mayors championing buses and bringing in better technology and vehicles. There was a great leap forward in bus performance in the early 2000s through Ken Livingstone’s congestion charge and investment in infrastructure such as GPS tracking, which massively improved reliability.Livingstone’s fleets of new bendy buses were phased out by his immediate successor, Boris Johnson, a self-professed enthusiast – even if his signature New Routemasters proved controversial.Since then Khan, famously the son of a bus driver, has brought in the Hopper fare, allowing multiple bus connections for the price of one journey, and is aiming for a fully electric bus fleet by 2030. Passengers on many routes now enjoy cleaner, quieter, cheaper buses, not least on the electric doubledeckers pioneered on the 63 route with better seats, skylights, wood-effect flooring and charging points – a nicer environment, at least, to wait in traffic.Again Khan does not play down the issues: “We’re really concerned about bus usage. I’m fully aware that it’s poorer Londoners that rely on buses because they’re cheaper.”Geoff Hobbs, TfL’s director of public transport service planning, says travel patterns have changed since Covid, with more home working, fewer trips to high streets and shifting demographics reducing demand in some areas. The growth of online shopping has also brought more delivery vans on to London’s streets, adding to congestion.“School rolls in some parts of London are getting smaller and some schools are even closing. And it’s youngsters that make heaviest use of buses,” he says.There is also “the double whammy of many more deliveries and delivery vans: you make less trips to town centres; and those same vans stop at places we’d rather they didn’t, blocking traffic”, Hobbs adds.Commuters on the 22 and 14 share their frustrations about bus travel in LondonA Guardian reporter’s journey on the 22 bus was slowed – and often stopped – by many of these obstructions. On the 1 hour 47 minute journey, long single-lane queues around Putney and various lane and road closures from roadworks in Mayfair kept the bus still for 40 minutes in total.But TfL and operators identify two factors above all others: growing pressure on road space and the sheer volume of roadworks.Graham Vidler, the chief executive of the Confederation of PassengerTransport, says: “There are too many vehicles wanting to use the roads at popular times. You can account for that in timetabling.“But what you can’t account for are unplanned and uncoordinated roadworks. And that’s probably the biggest thing that’s moved the dial. The number of roadworks seems to be mushrooming.”Seb Dance, London’s deputy mayor for transport, agrees: “The biggest impact is roadworks and particularly unplanned roadworks. We’ve got a problem in London where we’ve got old infrastructure, whether it’s sewage, water, electricity, gas.”A post-pandemic rebound in utility works, alongside road redesign projects and repairs to weather-damaged roads, has left more than 1,000 roadworks obstructing London’s streets on an average day.Roadworks chartRoadworks impinge on an increasingly limited road space, with five times as much of London now covered by cycleways as a decade ago – 450km compared with 90km. The conversion itself has meant lengthy works to build separate lanes – as well as move pavements and relocate bus stops – for surging cycling and e-bike use.Hobbs says bus performances has had to come second to other considerations, including safety and the general city environment: “There are trade-offs to be done … London has become a more walkable city. There are more cycle lanes. There have been all sorts of schemes that make London, a better place to live. You go back far enough, Trafalgar Square was a sort of giant roundabout.”Pedestrianisation of that square, once a key bus interchange, will be followed at Oxford Street, another important bus route.Operators believe buses are at the raw end of such trade-offs. Vidler says the cycle lanes built in recent years “serve a really important purpose – but if the politicians decide to give more space to one mode it follows that others will get less. And if you’re putting in more cycle lanes, it means it’s harder for bus passengers to travel.”Dance resists this interpretation. “Mainly there are just too many cars. So moving people out of cars to more efficient spaces such as public transport, buses and bikes is part of that solution,” he says.Demand from other types of vehicles is growing, whether Lime bikes, e-scooters or the embryonic robotaxi fleets from the likes of Uber. But technology can also help buses find a way through. The next wave of TfL’s Fusion programme – “basically computers on all the traffic lights across London”, says Dance – will link the capital’s thousands of signals to speed up flow and give more buses priority where possible.A lane rental scheme, charging companies by the day for the roadworks they carry out, was pioneered on TfL’s roads and is being extended to boroughs, incentivising work to be coordinated and completed quicker.“We’ve got to make our buses more reliable,” says Khan. “Which means them going faster.”The hot summer of 2026 is likely to have further affected bus performance. The mayor told bus drivers to take breaks and even to stay in the depot rather than operate a vehicle without functioning air-cooling systems. Contractual penalties for poor performance will be suspended during extreme heat, which is likely to be more common.And for speed as heat, safety remains priority. Road speed limits across London are decreasing, with more 20mph routes and the 50mph on major suburban roads planned to be cut to 40mph before 2030 – potentially affecting even the express Superloop buses established by Khan.For now, those orbital bus routes in the outer boroughs, rebranded and remapped under Khan, are seen as a success story. Instead of a doom loop of slower buses and fewer passengers, he says, “the Superloop has shown we can increase bus usage. If you provide a good product, people will use it.”Claire Wright, TfL’s head of streets performance, says that despite the “marginal decline” in speeds, the bus network remains the most popular form of public transport in the capital, “helping people get around affordably while also delivering public health and air quality benefits from fewer people driving”.She adds: “We’ll continue to closely monitor network performance to ensure the bus network serves Londoners as effectively as possible.”

title: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years | London Stock Exchange | The Guardian
description: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market
Content: Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but it wants Airtel Money to be listed separately.Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/ReutersView image in fullscreenAirtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but it wants Airtel Money to be listed separately.Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/ReutersLondon Stock ExchangeIndian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in yearsSunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock marketNils Pratley: Does this mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yetJoanna PartridgeWed 23 Sep 2026 07.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the strugglingLondon Stock Exchange.Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that hasfaced a string of recent departures.The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-SaharanAfrica, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.View image in fullscreenSunil Bharti Mittal controls Bharti Enterprises.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesIt operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 butdelayed itto the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAirtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result ofoverseas takeovers of UK companies.Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wisefloated in 2021with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from Londonto New York.Explore more on these topicsLondon Stock ExchangeIPOsEmerging marketsStock marketsAfricaIndiaLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl | South Africa | The Guardian
description: Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality
Content: A vigil at the University of Cape Town last week for the nine women whose bodies were found across Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg. In a separate case, a police officer has been charged with rape, people trafficking and grooming.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA vigil at the University of Cape Town last week for the nine women whose bodies were found across Ekurhuleni, east of Johannesburg. In a separate case, a police officer has been charged with rape, people trafficking and grooming.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesSouth AfricaTop South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girlArrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminalityRachel Savagein JohannesburgWed 23 Sep 2026 05.38 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls.Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child.Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk.South Africa is reeling after the discovery ofnine women’s bodiesacross Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year.Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.”Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet.The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him.Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according toNews24.Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct.“Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.”When Sibiyaappeared before the Madlanga Commissionin February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation.Sibiya also denied that he hadreceived a gift of 20 impalasfrom Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift.Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering,declined to commenton the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaRape and sexual assaultAfricaViolence against women and girlsFemicideWomennewsShareReuse this content

title: Milei threatens at UN that Argentina will take ‘matters into our own hands’ on Falklands | Falkland Islands | The Guardian
description: Argentinian president accuses United Nations of being filled with ‘parasites’ in bellicose general assembly speech
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Argentinian president accuses United Nations of being filled with ‘parasites’ in bellicose general assembly speech
Content: Javier Milei accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the Falklands.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/CNP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJavier Milei accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the Falklands.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/CNP/ShutterstockFalkland IslandsMilei threatens at UN that Argentina will take ‘matters into our own hands’ on FalklandsArgentinian president accuses United Nations of being filled with ‘parasites’ in bellicose general assembly speechDaniel BoffeyChief reporterWed 23 Sep 2026 14.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJavier Milei has condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of theFalkland Islands.In a caustic speech at the general assembly in New York, the Argentinian president criticised the UN for being ineffective when it came to the long-running tensions over the British overseas territory in the south Atlantic known inArgentinaas the Malvinas.“An organisation that set out to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way regarding the situation of the Malvinas Islands,” Milei said of the UN, adding that Argentina was willing to act unilaterally over recent oil exploration near the territory.Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talkRead moreThe president criticised the Sea Lion project, a major offshore oil development located in the North Falkland Basin, describing exploitation of the territory’s resources as an “unlawful act”.The president told the assembly that Argentina would “not remain indifferent to those who exploit resources under illegal foreign occupation”.“Argentina is not going to sit around waiting for the UN and the international community to live up to their own mandate,” he said. “We’re going to take matters into our own hands.”Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands. Milei’s government began sanctions proceedings this month against more than 60 companies and people linked to the oil drilling project.The Falkland Islands government had approved the field development and production plans for the project, which is a joint venture between an Israel-based energy company and a London-listed oil and gas exploration company.The UN does not officially recognise either British or Argentine sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentine forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and 3 Falkland Islanders.“For us, the Malvinas are a national cause,” Milei told the general assembly. The UN, he said, was a “useless organisation whose only purpose is to sustain a cast of faintly arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“That’s why the Malvinas are not merely an issue between Argentina and the United Kingdom,” he said. “They also raise a question regarding the ability of this organisation to enforce its own resolutions.”Areferendum on the political status of the archipelagowas held in the Falkland Islands in 2013. On a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, withonly three votes against.Milei told the UN delegates that the principle of self-determination should not apply for the Falkland Islands as “the population was implanted by the occupying power on a territory whose sovereignty is in dispute”. “We call on the United Kingdom to resume negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute as required by international law,” he said.Last month, Donald Trump said he was ​reviewing the US’s neutral position on ​the Falklands. The issue was a topic of discussion this week in afirst meeting between Trump and the UK’s prime minister, Andy Burnham.“The ‌clear ⁠position is: we will stand firm in the face of any threats,” Burnham said. “We will defend the ​right of ​the ⁠Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British. I just ​wanted ⁠the president to know directly from me, that’s the clear British ⁠position, ​and he very ​much understood what I was saying.”Explore more on these topicsFalkland IslandsAmericasJavier MileiArgentinaUnited NationsForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Delcy Rodríguez poses with Trump in New York as Maduro languishes in jail nearby | Delcy Rodríguez | The Guardian
description: Venezuela’s interim president hails ‘historic meeting’ and does not say whether she will visit snatched predecessor
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Venezuela’s interim president hails ‘historic meeting’ and does not say whether she will visit snatched predecessor
Content: Delcy Rodríguez and Donald Trump pose for a picture together on Tuesday.Photograph: Venezuelan presidency/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDelcy Rodríguez and Donald Trump pose for a picture together on Tuesday.Photograph: Venezuelan presidency/AFP/Getty ImagesDelcy RodríguezDelcy Rodríguez poses with Trump in New York as Maduro languishes in jail nearbyVenezuela’s interim president hails ‘historic meeting’ and does not say whether she will visit snatched predecessorTom PhillipsLatin America correspondentWed 23 Sep 2026 08.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVenezuela’s interim president,Delcy Rodríguez, has celebrated a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with the US president, less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro.The former foes met at a five-star hotel a few blocks from Trump Tower in Manhattan late on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN general assembly. The hotel is about 7 miles from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas in January.From socialist student to Trump proxy: the 25-year rise of Venezuela’s Delcy RodríguezRead moreOn the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, an American reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro, under whom she served as vice-president, during her stay in New York. She did not reply.But she did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of Venezuela’s diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. On Wednesday she is expected to address the annual UN assembly.“We held a historic meeting with … Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on Instagram, ina 133-word statementthat made no mention of her incarcerated ally.Oliver Blanco, one of Rodríguez’s top diplomats, claimed the meeting marked “a new stage of dialogue and understanding between both countries” and was “an important step toward new opportunities for our country and our people”. Blanco also posted a cheery photo in which he and Trump smiled and gave the thumbs up to the camera.A White House aide said the meeting was also attended by top US officials including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller.“It was a short meeting but it was an important meeting,” Rubio said on Wednesday, telling reporters it had focused on Venezuela’s economic recovery and political transition.Hours earlier, Rodríguez had sat in the general assembly hall watching Trumpcelebrate the “massive military operation”during which Maduro – whom he called an “outlaw dictator” and “a real criminal” – was captured. “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils,” Trump bragged of the recent oil deal between the US and Venezuela, as Rodríguez appeared to wince.View image in fullscreenObservers suggested Delcy Rodríguez’s clenched left hand signified her discomfort around Donald Trump.Photograph: Venezuelan presidency/AFP/Getty ImagesSome observers also detected signs of discomfort in the body language captured in the photo of Trump and Rodríguez, who appeared to be clenching her left fist.Some of Rodríguez’s critics in Venezuela called her treatment by Trump an unmitigated humiliation for a socialist party politician who has spent years railing against American imperialism.After Maduro’s capture, Trump warned that Rodríguez would “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” if she did not toe the US line. Since then, Rodríguez has made a series of concessions, including ceding control of Venezuela’s oil revenues to Washington and agreeing to a controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal that Trump on Tuesday called “the largest oil deal in history”.One opposition figure denounced the Rodríguez-Trump meeting as an encounter between a“shameless puppet and her unscrupulous puppeteer”.But Rodríguez has succeeded in consolidating power, with Trump seemingly more focused on gaining access to Venezuela’s natural resources than pushing for a fresh presidential election that would move the South American country back towards democracy.Trump has repeatedly praised Rodríguez’s “fantastic” and “terrific” leadership whilesidelining her main rival,the opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado, who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel peace prize in Oslo, has been unable to return and is exiled in Panama. She reportedly made three attempts to return to Venezuela this week but failed.​Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, rejected the idea that Rodríguez had been humiliated by her meeting with Trump. “It’s a huge triumph [for her]. She got the photo op she wanted. I frankly don’t think you can overestimate how important the photo op was for her,” said Pérez, who believed the image legitimised Rodríguez’s position as president and signalled that Washington was happy to keep working with her and for other leaders to engage with her.For Trump, meeting Rodríguez was a way to show Maga voters he had “won Venezuela” by commandeering its massive oil reserves with January’s invasion. “So that picture was a win-win for Delcy and for Trump,”Pérez added.Before Tuesday’s tête-à-tête, the presidents of the US and Venezuela had last met in 2015, when Barack Obama and Maduro spoke briefly during a regional summit in Panama. In the decade that followed, Maduro became an international pariah as he led his country into economic chaos and increasingly authoritarian rule, and Venezuela was hit by punishing international sanctions.At the 2015 summit, Obama conceded that the days in which“the US could meddle with impunity”in Latin America were over. But Trump has dramatically different ideas and has been forging ahead with attempts to reassert US dominance in a region it has long considered its back yard.As well as capturing Venezuela’s government and trying to topple Cuba’s communist government by strangling its economy, Trump’s push for hegemony has also seen the USaccused of trying to swing Brazil’s presidential electionin favour of the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro through diplomatic and economic pressure.Addressing the UN assembly on Tuesday, the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, hit back at such efforts, without directly citing the US. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians,” said Lula who is facing a tough battle to win re-election in October’s vote.“Brazil doesn’t fit into anyone’s back yard,” added Lula, who also called for elections in Venezuela. He did not meet Rodríguez during her visit to New York but said the “people of Venezuela deserve to decide their own future”.Explore more on these topicsDelcy RodríguezVenezuelaDonald TrumpTrump administrationNicolás MaduroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jamaica hails King’s decision to refer slavery reparations petition to privy council as ‘really big deal’ | Jamaica | The Guardian
description: The move comes after Jamaica’s culture minister Olivia Grange travelled to the UK earlier this month to lodge the historic petition
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: The move comes after Jamaica’s culture minister Olivia Grange travelled to the UK earlier this month to lodge the historic petition
Content: Olivia Grange, Jamaica’s minister of culture, has hailed the King’s decision to refer her slavery reparations petition to the privy council.Photograph: Jess Hurd/PAView image in fullscreenOlivia Grange, Jamaica’s minister of culture, has hailed the King’s decision to refer her slavery reparations petition to the privy council.Photograph: Jess Hurd/PAJamaicaJamaica hails King’s decision to refer slavery reparations petition to privy council as ‘really big deal’The move comes after Jamaica’s culture minister Olivia Grange travelled to the UK earlier this month to lodge the historic petitionNatricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentTue 22 Sep 2026 21.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing Charles has referred a landmark slavery reparations petition fromJamaicato a high-level UK appeals court for legal advice, Jamaica’s culture minister announced in parliament on Tuesday.Referring to the move as a “really big deal”,Olivia Grangetold Jamaica’s MPs the monarch had confirmed that their legal questions have been passed on to the London-based privy council – the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.The petition seeks guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans toJamaicawas lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.Jamaica’s plea to the king: use your authority to ensure colonial slavery is examined | Olivia GrangeRead more“Indeed we went fearless and boldly into this chapter when wepetitioned the king on Monday, September 7, 2026– one day after the 245th anniversary of the commemoration of the Zong massacre, an event that captures the barbarity of chattel enslavement,” Grange said in parliament.“The king could have ignored us. The king could have delayed responding to us. The king could have made a decision not to refer the questions to the privy council, or he could make a decision to refer the questions,” she said, before adding “King Charles has referred the petition filed on the 7th of September, 2026, on behalf of the people of Jamaica to the Judicial Committee of the privy council.”Jamaica had activated a rarely used mechanism in theJudicial Committee Act 1833, which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts, according to the country’s legal counsels.The minister said that taking the matter to the International Court of Justice, was not an option for Jamaica.“The United Kingdom has placed specific reservations on the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ which prevent the Court from adjudicating on disputes between the United Kingdom and the government of any other country which is or has been a Member of the Commonwealth”.A privy council opinion would not compel the UK government to pay reparations, but Jamaican officials believe it could shape negotiations and legal options and set a precedent for other Commonwealth nations seeking reparations.Earlier this month, Grange led a Jamaican delegation to Londonto officially lodge the petition. While in the UK, the group, lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparation met diaspora communities, MPs, church leaders and cultural institutions – among them the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts taken during colonial rule.Tuesday’s announcement follows theCaricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place in Barbados last week. Officials at the conference said that Caribbean nations aredrawing up a multi-pronged “action plan”with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal.Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options.Speaking at the conference, Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today.He said: “When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?”Earlier this month, a spokesperson forAndy Burnhamreiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.Grange told parliament that the country is “awaiting directions from the Judicial Committee of the privy council as to the next steps to be taken in the case. And the attorney general is preparing to deal with the case”.Explore more on these topicsJamaicaReparations and reparative justiceSlaveryAmericasCaribbeanColonialismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump greets Xi Jinping at plane as Chinese leader arrives for state visit | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president to give red-carpet treatment to Chinese counterpart despite tensions over AI development
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: US president to give red-carpet treatment to Chinese counterpart despite tensions over AI development
Content: Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan arrive at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, to be greeted by Donald and Melania Trump.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenXi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan arrive at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, to be greeted by Donald and Melania Trump.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersDonald TrumpTrump greets Xi Jinping at plane as Chinese leader arrives for state visitUS president to give red-carpet treatment to Chinese counterpart despite tensions over AI developmentTrump greets Xi – live updatesAI, trade, Taiwan and climate: what will and won’t be on agenda at Trump-Xi summitAriana Baioin WashingtonWed 23 Sep 2026 19.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping on Wednesday evening, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to kick off his state visit to Washington.Xi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 100ft long red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries. US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and first lady Melania Trump traveled to the the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan’s hands upon their arrival in the US.AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and ChinaRead moreIt came as Scott ⁠Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced that the US ⁠and ​China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called “Busan ⁠agreement” – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies.Bessent, who met Chinese ‌vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months after it was due to expire.View image in fullscreenDonald and Melania Trump welcome China’s leader Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersThe pageantry will continue with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events.The simmering trade war is one of many thorny issues Trump and Xi must confront during the visit, includingthe race in artificial intelligencedevelopment and geopolitical instability during the two-day visit.On Thursday, the White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi.View image in fullscreenXi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 100ft long red carpetPhotograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesThere was one discordant note in the carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony, when Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet, listening to the US national anthem. Video of the momentshowedthat while Trump recoiled from the sound of the flyover, Xi remained impassive, as did the wives of both men.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump winced at a loud US military flyover during an arrival ceremony for China’s president, Xi Jinping, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Wednesday.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersThe moment, which was widely mocked online, was captured on a White House livestream but not included in the edited highlights of the ceremony released by Trump’s aides later.The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.Trump hasdismissed concerns that AIdevelopment could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race.“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China.Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honor Xi.“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit toFox & Friendson Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”Robert Mackey contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpChinaAsia PacificUS politicsXi JinpingUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My friend’: Anthony Albanese announces $60m more for Ukraine at Zelenskyy meeting | Australian foreign policy | The Guardian
description: An emotional prime minister says that Kyiv’s cause is ‘an issue for the world’ as he also sets out his vision for a new world order
Author: Martin Farrer
Headline: An emotional prime minister says that Kyiv’s cause is ‘an issue for the world’ as he also sets out his vision for a new world order
Content: Anthony Albanese embraces Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese embraces Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian foreign policy‘My friend’: Anthony Albanese announces $60m more for Ukraine at Zelenskyy meetingAn emotional prime minister says that Kyiv’s cause is ‘an issue for the world’ as he also sets out the need for a new global orderMartin FarrerWed 23 Sep 2026 15.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Albanese has announced Australia will provide $60m more in support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s invasion during an emotional meeting with Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the UN meeting in New York.With the prime minister planning to use a key speech in New York to warn that the international world order was “no longer fit for purpose”, he hugged the Ukrainian president as the latter thanked Australia for its support.‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf clubRead moreAlbanese became emotional as he paid tribute to his “friend” Zelenskyy in his fight against Russian aggression.“[His] leadership has been, I think, quite extraordinary, leading people in circumstances which are extraordinarily difficult,” he said.“Russia thought it could just steamroll through in a matter of weeks, and what we have found is that the people ofUkrainewere underestimated.”The two leaders signed a 10-year bilateral security agreement which will lead to an extra $45m in Australian Defence Force equipment for Ukraine.A further $10m will go to Ukraine’s energy support fund, while $5m will be spent on humanitarian assistance.The $60m fund will bring Australia’s total contribution to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in 2022 to $1.9bn.As part of the agreement, Australia will also step up training to help Ukrainian forces deter and repel any future Russian attacks. It will also look to explore co-operation for training centres and jointly produce air-defence measures, missiles and drones.The prime minister said the agreement was a proud day for Australians in seeking to uphold international laws.“This is an issue not just for Europe, this is an issue for the world,” Albanese told reporters in New York upon signing the agreement.“If a large, more powerful country in Russia is allowed to profit from breaking the international rules of law with its illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine, then that sets a bad precedent for the entire world.”Albanese said the bilateral agreement would be in place not only during the war in Ukraine, but during peacetime once the conflict concludes.Zelenskyy said the agreement was the “strongest document between our countries”, and would increase trade and security.“It’s all for our people, for the security,” he said.It was a busy day of diplomacy for Albanese, who was addressing the Atlantic Council with a major speech on foreign policy and also signed a new strategic partnership with the Netherlands, seeking to boost defence ties and secure justice for the victims of MH17.In his speech, the prime minister was expected to say that the international world order set up following the second world war was no longer fit for purpose and that institutions that were necessary post-1945 were not enough to meet present-day challenges.The prime minister will use the speech on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York to argue partnerships with alliances remain crucial in a rapidly changing global environment.“Since the end of the cold war, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security, efficiency mattered more than resilience and international rules would be observed,” he will say.“Those assumptions rested on the expectation that the influence of the major democratic powers would remain largely unchallenged.“The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.”Australian Associated Press also contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsAustralian foreign policyUkraineAnthony AlbanesenewsShareReuse this content

title: How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair | Cyberwar | The Guardian
description: Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are being used to spread deceitful narratives
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are being used to spread deceitful narratives
Content: Deepfake image from the fake documentary Olympics Has Fallen, produced by Russia-affiliated influence actor Storm-1679. It advanced pro-Kremlin disinformation and used the image and likeness of Tom Cruise, who did not participate in any such documentary.Illustration: Storm-1679/Microsoft Threat Analysis CenterView image in fullscreenDeepfake image from the fake documentary Olympics Has Fallen, produced by Russia-affiliated influence actor Storm-1679. It advanced pro-Kremlin disinformation and used the image and likeness of Tom Cruise, who did not participate in any such documentary.Illustration: Storm-1679/Microsoft Threat Analysis CenterDisinfo black opsCyberwarAnalysisHow the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despairDan MilmoandRobert BoothWhether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are pushing multiple false narrativesWed 23 Sep 2026 15.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 17.53 EDTShareRussian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies.The narratives range froma deepfake Tom Cruise criticising the Paris Olympicsto portrayinga recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland borderas a false-flag operation.Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo ona video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorskfour years ago.New UK agency to fight ‘information warfare’ from likes of Russia, Burnham tells UNRead moreThe tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots.It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough,announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence.“We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said.Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”.Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research atAlliance4Europe,a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats.“You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says.Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”.Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks”, this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning.It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption.The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says.It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both useddeepfake newscasterstoadvance their goals.Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguardsRead moreOne recent study, conducted mostly in February by theSocial Market Foundation, a British thinktank, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic.The UK governmentdefines misinformationas the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect.Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”.Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service.Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest bylaunching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unitafter the Southport disturbances in 2024. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”.The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns.One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News.Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accountsOne of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024.The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity | EditorialRead moreRobert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them.He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather, he said, Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it.“What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka.AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns.The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models.The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.Explore more on these topicsCyberwarDisinfo black opsDeepfakeAI (artificial intelligence)InternetTechnology policyRussiaChatbotsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Germany pledges to phase out fossil fuels for first time with target of 2045 | Greenhouse gas emissions | The Guardian
description: Campaigners say plan marks notable shift away from oil and gas as previously pledges were only for carbon neutrality
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Campaigners say plan marks notable shift away from oil and gas as previously pledges were only for carbon neutrality
Content: Solar station near Munich, Germany, which has set a target of generating an additional 215GW of solar energy by 2030.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenSolar station near Munich, Germany, which has set a target of generating an additional 215GW of solar energy by 2030.Photograph: AlamyGreenhouse gas emissionsGermany pledges to phase out fossil fuels for first time with target of 2045Campaigners say plan marks notable shift away from oil and gas as previously pledges were only for carbon neutralityFiona HarveyEnvironment editorWed 23 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope’s biggest economy,Germany, has committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045, despite fierce debate about its green policies.In aroadmap published on Wednesday, the German government set out for the first time an explicit promise of “transitioning away” from fossil fuels. Previous pledges were only for “carbon neutrality”.The plans include ramping up renewable energy from 55% to 80% of electricity generation by 2030, with an additional 12GW of onshore wind, and a target of 215GW of solar energy by 2030. The previously stated target ofwinding down coal usein the next decade, with a view to anexit from coal in 2038, was also reaffirmed, with the potential for an earlier target of 2035.Emissions of methane, agreenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, will be cut by 30% by 2030, in accordance with aglobal methane pledge signed in 2021.Andreas Sieber, head of global political strategy at 350.org, said the plan marked a “notable shift” in making the phaseout of fossil fuels an explicit policy goal. But he warned that Germany’s ministry for economic affairs and energy was also pushing intensely for greater use of gas.“The economic ministry keeps sabotaging the transition away from fossil fuels,” he said. “This year has shown in the starkest terms that fossil-fuel dependence is a risk for everyone as it exposes households and businesses in Germany and around the world to price shocks, volatility and geopolitical insecurity.”Germany’s former climate envoy Jennifer Morgan said the government must put more effort into electrifying transport and heating. “Accelerating the shift from coal, oil and gas to clean renewables will bolster energy independence and insulate consumers from price shocks at a critical moment,” she said. “However, a roadmap is only the starting line.”She said the strategy must be paired with a faster, more deliberate rollout of green electrification.The push for heat pumps to replace gas boilers came under attack from the far-right wing of German politics after aheating law was passed in 2023that would have banned the installation of most oil and gas heating. Alternative für Deutschland made the issue a key campaigning point andforced a watering down of the rules earlier this year, while the party’s co-leader Alice Weidel hasdescribed wind turbines as “windmills of shame”. Heat pumps now make up about half of all new domestic heating systems.Germany is the third major developed economy to publish such a roadmap, after France and the Netherlands, after amajor international conferencein Colombia in April at which all participants promised to set out plans for a full phaseout of fossil fuels.It comes afternations debated how to expand their currently inadequate efforts to tackle the climate crisisat the UN general assembly in New York. António Guterres, the UN secretary-general, has been astrong advocate of climate action for his 10 years in office, but the end of his term this December has raisedfears that his successor may be less firm.The UK has still not published its pledge to phase out fossil fuels, and will take up the presidency of the G20 group of developed and developing economies in December, for which the climate and thesoaring costs of oil and gasare expected to be key issues.Explore more on these topicsGreenhouse gas emissionsGermanyRenewable energyEuropeEnergyFossil fuelsClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: The EU’s Canada offer is more mood than reality but it could hint at a future geometry for the bloc  | World news | The Guardian
description: While Brussels and Ottawa desire a deeper partnership born of Trump-era volatility, ​the EU has no legal framework to accommodate it
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: While Brussels and Ottawa desire a deeper partnership born of Trump-era volatility, ​the EU has no legal framework to accommodate it
Content: Mark Carney and Ursula von der Leyen are like-minded on many important global issues.Photograph: Pascal Bastien/APView image in fullscreenMark Carney and Ursula von der Leyen are like-minded on many important global issues.Photograph: Pascal Bastien/APThis Is EuropeWorld newsThe EU’s Canada offer is more mood than reality but it could hint at a future geometry for the blocWhile Brussels and Ottawa desire a deeper partnership born of Trump-era volatility, ​the EU has no legal framework to accommodate itDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereJon Henley, Europe correspondentWed 23 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU and Canada,Ursula von der Leyen saidlast week, “see the world with the same eyes”, with shared stances on everything from AI to the climate crisis, the Ukraine war and the unholy chaos unleashed by the current occupant of the White House (OK, she didn’t actually say that last bit. But I like to think she almost certainly thought it.)So, the European Commission president went on, Canada should become “the first associate member of the EU”. In the audience, Mark Carney beamed with delight. The next day, Canada’s prime ministerenthusiastically embraced the ideaof an “alliance for the future”, to build “collective resilience” through “deep cooperation”.Cue standing ovations, warm handshakes – and agreat deal of head-scratchingin Brussels and assorted EU capitals. Because “associate membership” of the EU is not, in fact, a thing. Nor,as a Guardian editorial pointed out, is there “any blueprint for what such a thing might involve”.The term was, the editorial argued, “a political hypothesis”, describing “a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined”. So what exactly are the commission andCanadaplaying at here, and where might it lead?You can see where they’re coming from. On paper, in a world of unpredictable and increasingly aggressive great powers, it makes perfect sense. For Canada – which already has theCeta free trade agreementwith the EU – the catalyst for even closer cooperation is clearly Donald Trump:incessant tariff threats, an escalating trade war, bullying talk of Canada as the “51st state”, therenaming of Lake Ontario– all have left Ottawa eager to diversify its relations.Aligning with European industrial strategy, working together on defence and AI, and joining EU scientific research and student exchange programmes would offer Canada a reliable counterweight to its all-too-unreliable southern neighbour. (Unsurprisingly, Trump called the tie-up“laughable”, and threatened more tariffs.)For the EU, meanwhile, Canada is a dream partner: a stable, like-minded “middle power” rich in critical minerals, rare earths and – as Carney couldn’t resist noting – good manners. Plus, Canada’s unbridled EU-enthusiasm is a pleasing boost to the bloc’s bruised ego afterIceland’s recent rejectionof more EU accession negotiations.There’s only one problem:“associate membership”is not a status in the EU treaties, and creating such a status would mean treaty reform, which member states won’t contemplate. There are things called “association agreements”,such as with Ukraine, Moldova or Georgia, but those are essentially stepping stones to full membership – which Canada can’t aspire to, for the very good reason that it isn’t in Europe.But if “associate member” sounds vaguely familiar, that’s because the EU has been talking about a “second circle” since the days ofJacques Delors: an outer ring of countries bound by shared values, free trade and security cooperation to an inner core of members, but without full voting rights or complete regulatory integration.Emmanuel Macron’sEuropean Political Communityis a variation on this theme, and Germany’s chancellor,Friedrich Merz, recently floated “associate member” status for Ukraine. Indeed, non-EU nations in the European Economic Area (EEA) and European Free Trade Association, such as Norway, Iceland or Switzerland, already function as quasi-associate members, enjoying single-market access while being largely “rule-takers”: adopting EU rules without having a vote in Brussels.Writing in the Guardian, Fabian Zuleeg suggested that Canada and Europe actually need more of an“integrated partnership”– a model that leaves single market access to one side, focusing instead on concrete collaboration in areas such as defence, supply chains and EU programmes like Horizon and Erasmus+.Alberto Alemanno, a professor of EU law,noted thata realistic EU-Canada landing zone would have to go further than Ceta and might more resemble the kind of tailored framework of the EU-Swiss relationship. But the real significance of any formal new status, he said, was that it could make the EU “an institutional hub around which other democracies organise strategic autonomy – but without joining the union”.What that might actually look like is anyone’s guess: visa-free work access, shared military procurement, Canadian seats on EU regulatory committees? For the moment, Canada’s hypothetical “associate membership” is more of a mood than a reality: the expressed intent of a democratic bloc and a middle power to deepen ties in the face of mounting global uncertainty.Does it, all the same, hold any hope forBrexit-regretting Britain? As Jill Rutter of the Institute for Government highlighted, the EU’s sudden willingness to display“institutional imagination”at least shows that the bloc is willing to think about adapting when geopolitical pressures demand.But a new deal for Canada won’t automatically fix the UK’s issues. As Joël Reland of UK in a Changing Europe pointed out,the vagueness of the EU offer to Canadamight look promising for the UK. But Canada wants “deep cooperation” without touching single-market rules, and the UK’s main problem is that it is now shut out of that same market. Whatever Canada eventually gets, it’s unlikely to work for the UK.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA miserable time for MerzView image in fullscreenFriedrich Merz needs to rethink policy in order to stay on top.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersFriedrich Merz is in trouble. A fortnight after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept toa crushing victoryin one state election in Saxony-Anhalt, the German chancellor’s centre-right CDUfailed to clear the 5% thresholdneeded to enter the state parliament in another, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.It fared a little better in Berlin, where it was the incumbent, but was still beaten – by a clear five-point margin – by the far-left Die Linke. And the AfDmade headwayin the capital, too, surging to a double-digit result. Theembattled chancellor has vowed to fight on, but faces an uncomfortable choice: revise the unpopular economic reforms he insists are essential, or risk oblivion defending them.Meanwhile, as long as he refuses to step aside and no one is actively seeking to replace him,a volatile and damaging deadlock will reignin Europe’s biggest economy. After 16 months in office, it is becoming increasingly clear –as a Guardian editorial noted– that Merz is “ill-suited for the job” of defending Germany’s democratic future against the far right.To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeMark CarneyCanadaEuropean UnionFriedrich MerzGermanynewslettersShareReuse this content

title: UK to join EU ocean science scheme to better predict extreme weather events | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Cooperation on OceanEye, which aims to better anticipate climate events, comes amid efforts to boost ties with bloc
Author: Karen McVeigh
Headline: Cooperation on OceanEye, which aims to better anticipate climate events, comes amid efforts to boost ties with bloc
Content: Melting sea ice in the Arctic Ocean at Svalbard in Norway.Photograph: Lisi Niesner/ReutersView image in fullscreenMelting sea ice in the Arctic Ocean at Svalbard in Norway.Photograph: Lisi Niesner/ReutersClimate crisisUK to join EU ocean science scheme to better predict extreme weather eventsCooperation on OceanEye, which aims to create ‘real-time’ model of world’s oceans, comes amid efforts to boost EU tiesKaren McVeighWed 23 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain is to join a major new ocean science programme, led by the EU, to better forecast extreme weather and climate events, the environment secretary is to announce in New York.The announcement on Wednesday will come as Andy Burnham’s government aims to rebuild the UK’s relationship with Europe, and follows warnings this year’s“supersized” El Niño, tracked in the Pacific Ocean, will fuel more extreme weather globally.Scientists have warned that the global marine monitoring system, which is vital to predict extreme weather events and ultimately to save lives, is under strain afterthreats by the US administration this yearto dismantle its substantial share of global ocean observations.In June,the EU launched a €92m (£78m) initiative called OceanEye, to boost its role in ocean observation and to provide data-backed marine intelligence to deepen understanding and management of the ocean. It plans to create a digital “real time” replica model of the ocean, collected by satellites, sensors and other models by 2030, to help decisions on ocean protection and security. The EU introduced aninternational alliance with Canadaas part of OceanEye, to address critical gaps in under-monitored regions and strengthen cooperation between nations.In addition to weather and climate predictions, ocean observations also underpin national security, global trade and marine protections.Angela Eagle will announce the UK is to join the scheme at a meeting attended by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, at the UN headquarters in New York.Britain will share more data from the Met Office and other agencies with the EU and Canada than before.The environment secretary will tell the event: “As an island nation and a global leader in climate science, we know that data from ocean monitoring is essential to our ability to protect and restore our oceans, and anticipate and respond to the huge threats they face, because we cannot save our oceans if we do not understand them.”“Changing weather patterns and currents are fuelling the extreme weather which is already impacting all of our nations – through floods, droughts, storms and extreme heat.
