That’s why the UK is so committed to maintaining our vital global network of observation systems, which span coastal waters, shelf seas and the open ocean, including some of the longest-running observations in the world.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJoining the alliance to support and provide data to the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) would help better protect Britain from the impacts of climate change, said the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Currently, the global ocean observing capacity has significant gaps, at the poles, the deep ocean and of biological measurements.The US, which provides over half the ocean observing platforms and much of the technology, has reversed a proposal to scrap its$368m (£275m) funding for its Ocean Observatories Initiativeafter a backlash from scientists. However, moves to cut funding for US ocean agencies have left GOOS vulnerable to changing priorities of the US administration.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisOceansEuropean UnionForeign policyBrexitEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Save the Children officially warned by regulator over staff put at risk in Yemen | Charities | The Guardian
description: Warning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Warning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023
Content: Children displaced by war wait to collect food aid at a camp for internally displaced people near Aden, Yemen, on 23 September 2026.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenChildren displaced by war wait to collect food aid at a camp for internally displaced people near Aden, Yemen, on 23 September 2026.Photograph: ReutersCharitiesSave the Children officially warned by regulator over staff put at risk in YemenWarning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023Patrick ButlerSocial policy editorWed 23 Sep 2026 14.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe international aid charity Save the Children has been issued with an official regulatory warning over management failures and misconduct that put staff at itsYemenoffice at serious risk.Thewarningconcluded a two-year investigation by the Charity Commission for England and Wales into the running of the office after the death of its safety and security director, Hisham Al-Hakimi, in October 2023 after he was detained by the Yemeni authorities.The commission said weak governance meant staff at the Yemen office were not properly safeguarded in response to what it called a “live security concern”, and incidents of poor conduct by staff were not addressed.The warning letter refers to “substantial policy breaches and a lack of accountability” at the office, and said local charity bosses failed to adequately assess and escalate complaints and reports made by whistleblowers.An internal Save the Children investigation in 2024 after the death of Al-Hakimi found a “negative working culture” in the Yemen office had left staff “disillusioned and marginalised”.It apologised to staff after admitting it had let them down by failing to properly appreciate the risks facing them amid the deteriorating security situation in the country.In a statement to the Guardian, Save the Children International said that since 2024 it had made significant changes under new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve support for staff and rebuild trust. The charity has closed its north Yemen office because of security concerns.It said despite its best efforts to understand the circumstances around Al-Hakimi’s detention and his death the challenges in Yemen meant it may never know what happened and why. Another Save the Children member of staff is understood to currently be in detention.The commission’s warning comes amid a growing humanitarian crisis in Yemen, where the charity has been providing emergency medical help, shelter and drinking water to displaced families.Official warningsare relatively rare, and are issued when the commission decides breaches of trust or mismanagement in a charity put its staff or beneficiaries at risk. They can be issued where charity trustees are deemed to have acted recklessly or without proper care.The commission ordered Save the Children International to ensure sufficient resources are in place to safeguard and protect staff and other individuals working with the charity.Stephen Roake, assistant director for high-risk compliance at the commission, said: “It can be incredibly difficult for charities operating in high-risk, volatile environments and we know that circumstances can change rapidly. However, it is for this very reason that trustees must ensure they have sufficient oversight of their overseas operations.”In a statement, Save the Children International said it had accepted the commission’s findings of serious shortcomings in governance, management, oversight and compliance with policies and procedures in the Yemen office at the time.Since 2024, it had installed new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve staff support and rebuild trust. It had also introduced detention risk assessments, taken steps to improve incident management procedures and strengthened crisis management.It said: “We remain committed to learning from this tragedy and ensuring a safe, supportive environment for our colleagues.“We will continue to work closely with the Charity Commission to address any outstanding matters, while continuing to support our colleagues in Yemen and deliver for children in extremely challenging contexts.”Save the Children’s Yemen officewarned last weekthat the country faced a “catastrophic humanitarian situation” as a result of escalating conflict, collapsing health services and outbreaks of disease.More than 1,000 people have been killed or wounded, and tens of thousands displaced byfighting in recent weeksbetween the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.Explore more on these topicsCharitiesYemenVoluntary sectorMiddle East and north AfricaAidHumanitarian responsenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk | Iran | The Guardian
description: Masoud Pezeshkian says Tehran is ready for dialogue and diplomacy ‘but without the language of force’
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Masoud Pezeshkian says Tehran is ready for dialogue and diplomacy ‘but without the language of force’
Content: Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, addressing the UN general assembly in New York on Wednesday.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, addressing the UN general assembly in New York on Wednesday.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesIranIran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talkMasoud Pezeshkian says Tehran is ready for dialogue and diplomacy ‘but without the language of force’Patrick Wintourin New YorkWed 23 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting thatIranhad always shown a commitment to the negotiating table.In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US.But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.”On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators.Asurprise three-hour meetingbetween Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech.US delegation walks out during Iranian president’s UNGA speechThe Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for thefuture of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar.He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently.Iran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New YorkRead morePezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” forassassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khameneiat the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war.“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.”He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons.He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added.Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war.0:48Donald Trump says he could ‘annihilate Iran’ if no deal is reached – videoInsisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.”Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.”He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”.Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage.In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position.He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.”Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest publishedfigures suggestthe number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day.The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing.Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.Explore more on these topicsIranUnited NationsUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New York | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Trump says further talks possible as barrel of Brent crude falls to below $100 for first time in two weeks
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Trump says further talks possible as barrel of Brent crude falls to below $100 for first time in two weeks
Content: Tehran set seven preconditions before returning to talks and said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAView image in fullscreenTehran set seven preconditions before returning to talks and said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAUS-Israel war on IranIran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New YorkTrump says further talks possible as barrel of Brent crude falls to below $100 for first time in two weeksUnited Nations general assembly – latest updatesPatrick Wintourin New YorkWed 23 Sep 2026 06.41 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 06.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has pushed back on claims that it dropped former preconditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz in surprise talks held in New York under the mediation of Qatar between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.Trump said the three-hour talks held in a room at the UN headquarters had gone very well and been very productive. He suggested further talks were possible imminently, which led to the price of a barrel of Brent crude to fall to below $100 (£75) for the first time in two weeks. Witkoff said the talks had been “encouraging, constructive and successful”.In his speech to the UN general assembly, Trump said he had a decision to make very soon on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” or help turn it into one of the great countries of the Middle East, the kind of bombastic threat Trump often deploys during talks withIran.OECD: global economy more resilient to Iran war than expectedRead moreIn Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed the talks had occurred, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed.Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the crucial strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met.It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz – a key waterway for transporting oil – that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control.The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. Latest publishedfigures suggestthe number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day, but estimates of the US navy are much higher.The blockage in the strait is made worse by the uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis’ (the Iranian-backed Yemeni paramilitaries) of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean.There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran or indeed with the Houthis as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular war that the Americans think they are losing.Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for Iran to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet.Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday after arriving in New York on a flight from Tehran as talks were under way.Pezeshkian is an advocate of negotiations with the US but has not played a direct role in the talks. He has said thememorandum of understanding(MoU), agreed with the US on 17 June, remained the starting point.Implementation of the MoU fell apart after the two sides accused one another of breaching its terms by trying to take control of the strait. Iran said the MoU clearly left Iran in control of the strait for an interim period before a long-term agreement on its management was reached, including the possibility of Oman and Iran charging fees for navigational services.Pezeshkian is expected to condemn western double standards over what he regards as an illegal US assault on Iran that has left schoolchildren dead and infrastructure ravaged. Europe’s preparedness to call out Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, and its reticence in criticising the attack on Iran, or Israel’s treatment of Palestinians in Gaza, has been a constant theme of Pezeshkian’s remarks.Many of the most powerful speeches on Tuesday at the UN general assembly came from European and Arab politicians who decried the inability of the west to enforce peace. In his farewell speech to the UN, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, criticised the attempt to overthrow the Iranian government by the US and Israel, arguing: “Every time a few states, sometimes even in the name of international order, have tried to replace the people in order to change a regime or a system, they have plunged those states into even greater chaos.”He also said that the west had not imposed a peace in Gaza. “Some boast of a supposed peace. But this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second. Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never!”Macron landed himself in hot water with Israel when he suggested Hamas was not present in the West Bank, as opposed to Gaza.Netanyahu’s office responded, using the biblical name for the West Bank: “Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria.”Jordan’s King Abdullah II attacked the Israeli government for “moving the goalposts”, for continuing attacks and the destruction of civilian infrastructure in Gaza, and for refusing to withdraw from the war-torn Palestinian territory. This has forced the Palestinian population in Gaza into barely one-third of the territory, he said.Observers must no longer treat Israeli policies as “temporary military measures” or a “consequence of war”, he said.“Accountability begins when we call things what they are: an attempt to erase Palestinian life and impose a new territorial reality in Gaza,” he added.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranDonald TrumpIranUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricaOilStrait of HormuznewsShareReuse this content

title: Sri Lanka Easter bombings: 15 sentenced to hundreds of years in prison each over deadly terror attacks | Sri Lanka | The Guardian
description: Islamic State-inspired bombings of churches and hotels in 2019 was one of the country’s worst ever attacks
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Islamic State-inspired bombings of churches and hotels in 2019 was one of the country’s worst ever attacks
Content: Catholic nuns carry portraits of the  victims of the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attack through Colombo, Sri Lanka, in April 2025. Fifteen people have been sentenced over the series of terror attacks.Photograph: Chamila Karunarathne/EPAView image in fullscreenCatholic nuns carry portraits of the  victims of the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attack through Colombo, Sri Lanka, in April 2025. Fifteen people have been sentenced over the series of terror attacks.Photograph: Chamila Karunarathne/EPASri LankaSri Lanka Easter bombings: 15 sentenced to hundreds of years in prison each over deadly terror attacksIslamic State-inspired bombings of churches and hotels in 2019 was one of the country’s worst ever attacksHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiTue 22 Sep 2026 20.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA court in Sri Lanka has convicted 15 men on terrorist charges for their involvement in the deadly2019 Easter bombingsand sentenced them each to at least 220 years in prison.The terror attacks, which targeted luxury hotels and churches as they held Easter services, left 267 people dead and wounded almost 600. The bombings, which were inspired by Islamic State (IS), were among the deadliest terror attacks in Sri Lanka’s history and sent shockwaves through the country.Two Sri Lanka-based Islamist militant groups were believed to have orchestrated the attacks. A video, recorded by the suicide bombers the day before the bombings, showed the attackers with their faces covered, armed with rifles and swords and pledging allegiance to the then-IS leader Abu Bakhr al-Baghdadi to make Sri Lanka an Islamic nation and wage war.The attacks were carried out by nine suicide bombers who died in the blasts. None of those who directly participated survived.Those on trial were accused of conspiring and aiding the bombings, which had deliberately targeted the minority Christian community and foreign tourists. The proceedings had spanned nearly five years, with the slow pace of justice frustrating victims and their families.Sri Lanka’s Easter Bombings review – startling and deeply disturbing viewingRead moreIn 2021, authorities filed 23,270 charges against 25 suspects whom they accused of planning or inspiring the attacks: three at churches, three at tourist hotels, one at a motel where an attacker killed himself, and two others after aborting a plan to attack a fourth hotel. The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism, and firearms and explosives offences under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.The verdict was finally delivered on Tuesday by a three-judge high court amid tight security, with hundreds of police deployed around the courthouse.In total, 15 defendants, who were all from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community, were sentenced to more than 200 years each. The judges also ordered the property of the defendants to be confiscated.Nine defendants were freed after the court found that the charges against them were not proven. One other died before their case reached trial.View image in fullscreenSecurity personnel inspect St Sebastian’s church in Negombo on 22 April 2019, a day after the church was hit in series of bomb blasts targeting churches and luxury hotels in Sri Lanka.Photograph: Ishara S Kodikara/AFP/Getty Images“Finally, we have justice,” said Catholic priest Jude Fernando. “It has taken a long time to get to this point.”However, the completion of the trial is unlikely to offer full closure for some. Sri Lanka’s Catholic church has long alleged that perpetrators put on trial were not the masterminds behind the bombings.Since Sri Lanka’s new government was elected in late 2024, there have been renewed investigations into allegations that elements within the Sri Lankan state – tied to former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa and his powerful family dynasty – may have had links to those responsible for the attacks.Investigators have alleged the Easter bombings were part of a conspiracy to manufacture a security threat, that would create chaos and help bring Rajapaksa, a former defence chief, to power.Rajapaksa was elected as president just a few months after the attack, on the back of a campaign that portrayed him as a strongman leader who was tough on terror.A parliamentary committee found that police andintelligence officials failed to acton repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks. In July, a former police chief and a former senior defence ministry official were sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.Earlier this year, police also arrested Suresh Salley, a former intelligence chief and retired army major general, alleging he had prior knowledge of the attacks and worked with Islamist extremists before the bombings were carried out. He remains in custody but denies the charges.The country’s defence ministry and the Rajapaksa family have denied any involvement in the attacks.Explore more on these topicsSri LankaSri Lanka attacksSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Tony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 years | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chances
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Andy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chances
Content: A YouGov poll conducted in June found Labour vowing to seek membership of the EU would help unite progressive voters behind the party.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA YouGov poll conducted in June found Labour vowing to seek membership of the EU would help unite progressive voters behind the party.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press/ShutterstockBrexitTony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 yearsAndy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chancesKiran StaceyPolicy editorWed 23 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain should work towards rejoining the EU in the next decade, Tony Blair has said, adding to growing pressure onAndy Burnhamto abandon Labour’s reluctance to revisit the 2016 referendum.The former prime minister has urged Burnham to use his 10-year plan in November to put the country’s membership of the union back on the table, a decade after it voted to leave.In a paper entitled A Path to Rejoining a Reformed Europe, theTony BlairInstitute (TBI) calls for the UK to accept free movement of people and make a financial contribution as the price of entry.The intervention comes after Burnhamdeclined to rule outpromising to rejoin the EU in the next Labour manifesto, though it also threatens to reopen the deep rifts caused by the vote 10 years ago.In a foreword to the paper, Blair argues: “Britain should signal an intention if the terms are right to enter into a structured formal relationship with Europe and initiate a process of negotiation where everything is on the table but nothing agreed until everything is agreed.”TBI researchers say in the paper itself: “Over the next decade, Britain should work towards the ambition of rejoining a significantly reformed EU.”View image in fullscreenTony Blair speaking at a Board of Peace conference in New York on Wednesday.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty ImagesBlair is the latest in a series of Labour figures to back rejoining the EU. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary,has calledthe Brexit vote a “catastrophic mistake” and said the party should aim to rejoin the bloc, while Burnham himselftold the Guardianlast year: “I hope in my lifetime I see this country rejoin the European Union.”But Burnham has said he does not wish to pursue membership of the union in the near term. When asked by reporters this week if it could be in the next election manifesto, he said it was a question “for another day”.Others are sceptical of the electoral wisdom of giving the appearance that the party wants to undo the result of the 2016 referendum, especially in areas of the country where Reform UK has made inroads in recent years.Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary,dismissed the ideaearlier this year as she warned against “reopening the circular arguments that we ended up in as a country”.However, pollsters suggestLabourcould benefit electorally by promising to rejoin. A new megapoll conducted by YouGov on behalf of the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain suggests the party could more than double its seat total if it goes into the next election promising to rejoin.The survey of more than 13,000 people, undertaken in June before Burnham became prime minister, found that a pledge to seek membership would help unite progressive voters behind Labour while doing nothing to boost Reform’s vote.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe results suggested the move could take Labour from a projected 136 seats to 321 – though those totals will have changed since Burnham came to office, which has given the party a poll lead for the first time in months.The TBI paper calls for Britain to try to accelerate European market reforms using possible re-entry as leverage. It argues that pro-reformers in Brussels would have a significant incentive to work with Britain on a project to make the EU more economically liberal and to reform its regulations on energy and technology.It adds that Burnham should scrap the government’s red lines of not rejoining, not allowing free movement and not entering the single market or a customs union. The paper argues that the prime minister should replace them with a single promise only to sign up to rules and initiatives that prove of economic or strategic benefit to the UK.TBI has advocated in recent years for the UK to slow down its push to achieve net zero carbon emissions and is a heavy backer of increased use of artificial intelligence in government.Its policy positionshave brought scrutinyon some of the institute’s most high-profile funders, who include the technology billionaire Larry Ellison, and its clients, which include the government of Saudi Arabia.Explore more on these topicsBrexitTony BlairAndy BurnhamLabourForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Three charged with assault after anti-migration protests in Hampshire | UK news | The Guardian
description: Hundreds gathered on Tuesday night in anticipation of a small boat arriving in Gosport
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Hundreds gathered on Tuesday night in anticipation of a small boat arriving in Gosport
Content: Police faced protesters in Gosport on Tuesday night.Photograph: Lab Mo/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice faced protesters in Gosport on Tuesday night.Photograph: Lab Mo/SOPA Images/ShutterstockUK newsThree charged with assault after anti-migration protests in HampshireHundreds gathered on Tuesday night in anticipation of a small boat arriving in GosportHarry CockburnWed 23 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 17.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree people have been charged in connection with anti-migrant protests that drew hundreds of demonstrators to a marina in Hampshire on Tuesday night.Six people were arrested by police, as anti-migrant activists who mistakenly believed a small boat was due to arrive at Gosport gathered in an attempt to disrupt the arrival of any asylum seekers.Those charged are Shannon Dodds, 32, of Leonard Road in Gosport, who has been charged with two counts of assault by beating of an emergency worker, Sally Pearson, 31, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with assault by beating of an emergency worker and a racially aggravated public order offence, and Toby Matthews, 33, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with common assault of an emergency worker.Dodds and Pearson have been remanded in custody and will appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on Thursday 24 September.Matthews was bailed but must appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 9 November.Hampshire police said in addition to these charges, a 19-year-old man and a 36-year-old man from Salisbury who were arrested on suspicion of aggravated trespass had been bailed with conditions until 22 December while inquiries continued.They added: “A 67-year-old man from Gosport was also given a fixed-penalty notice for driving without due care and attention. He was also arrested on suspicion of assaulting an emergency worker and has been bailed with conditions until 22 December while enquiries continue.”The protests in Gosport followed a social media push by far-right activist Daniel Thomas, who styles himself Danny Tommo, who called for action to disrupt the potential arrival of asylum seekers as he livestreamed efforts to apprehend small boats crossing the channel to more than 100,000 followers on Tuesday afternoon.He is also now facing a police inquiry after he used a knife to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard.His livestream showed him approaching an empty dinghy which had contained about 50 migrants who had reportedly left from a beach in Normandy. They had been picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area, but a French official then got on to the craft.The footage showed Thomas taking out a knife and slashing at the vessel in the channel, shouting at the French rescue worker: “Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more.”“Traitor,” Thomas shouted as his boat motored away.The protesters in Gosport, many of whom wore black clothing and face coverings, chanted “send them back”, wrongly assuming the boat would arrive on the Hampshire coast.Instead of heading for Gosport, the RNLI transferred the asylum seekers to a Border Force vessel which landed in Dover early on Wednesday.Hampshire police said they had deployed officers to the town on Tuesday evening “to help facilitate peaceful protest, ensure the safety of the local community and support partners in the event of any emergency at sea”.A Home Office spokesperson said: “We have been clear that groups creating fear and intimidating communities cannot be allowed to operate with impunity.“Police should make full use of the powers available to them to deal robustly with criminality and ensure communities, staff and those in their care are protected.”Campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the incident as “disgusting” ina post on X, and said Thomas’s supporters in Gosport had blocked ambulances during the protests.The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, was forced to order an urgent security review after the failure by the Border Force to intercept two other migrant boats in two days before they reached the Kentish coast this week.She said on Wednesday: “This was not acceptable. Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare. But even one is one too many.“The new tactics adopted by the smugglers, like launches from much further west in France, are a reminder of two things. Firstly, these gangs have no regard for human life. They are putting people on increasingly long and dangerous crossings.“Secondly, our efforts are having an impact. We are making it much harder for gangs to launch vessels, forcing them to change their approach, and as a result we are significantly reducing the numbers coming here by small boat.”The total number of migrants who have crossed the Channel by boat so far this year is 17,784, according to the government – a figure 45% lower than at the same point last year.The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Tuesday’s “chaos” showed the UK was seeing “illegal immigrants crossing at will over ever larger distances and in ever larger boats”.“This latest fiasco shows that the French are not even trying to stop the illegal immigrants’ boats,” he added.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Millions in England unaware they have ‘silent killer’ condition, research reveals | High blood pressure | The Guardian
description: Approach to treating high blood pressure ‘not fit for purpose’, say researchers, with 59% of cases undiagnosed
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Approach to treating high blood pressure ‘not fit for purpose’, say researchers, with 59% of cases undiagnosed
Content: According to a new study by Oxford University, only half of people being treated by their GP for high blood pressure have it under control.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PAView image in fullscreenAccording to a new study by Oxford University, only half of people being treated by their GP for high blood pressure have it under control.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/PAHigh blood pressureMillions in England unaware they have ‘silent killer’ condition, research revealsApproach to treating high blood pressure ‘not fit for purpose’, say researchers, with 59% of cases undiagnosedAndrew GregoryandWill ParmanWed 23 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnly half of people being treated by a GP for high blood pressure in England have it under control, and millions more are completely unaware they have the “silent killer” condition, research reveals.Most people with hypertension (59%) are in the dark and undiagnosed, raising their risk of stroke, heart attack and early death, according to the largest ever study of its kind.Even among those who are diagnosed and receiving medication via their family doctor, in 50% of cases their blood pressure is out of control, the Oxford University study of 1.4 million adults suggests.Researchers said the findings,published in journal BMJ Public Health, suggested the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure in England was “not fit for purpose”.The study used data from theOur Future Health programmeand looked at people enrolled between 2022 and 2025 with high blood pressure, defined as 140/90 mmHg or higher.‘People should not feel guilty’: weekend lie-in may be good for you, experts sayRead moreResearchers calculated that more than a third of adults (37%) had high blood pressure, with six in 10 of these oblivious to their condition.Hypertension was almost 50% more common in men than women (42% compared with 29% across all ages), and more common in older people, according to the research.Despite substantial improvements in high blood pressure detection and control during the 2000s, progress had plateaued since about 2011, the researchers said.There were also “indications of worsening trends following the Covid-19 pandemic, possibly because disruptions to healthcare delivery may have had lasting effects”.Wenyu Liu, a medical statistician at Oxford PopulationHealthand lead author of the study, said: “While hypertension is largely a ‘silent killer’, the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure is not fit for purpose.“Our study highlights the prevalence of hypertension across demographics. This underscores the need for population-wide prevention strategies alongside targeted treatment for people at high cardiovascular risk.”The researchers said “the most striking finding” of the study was the high absolute number and the high proportion of people with undiagnosed hypertension. It also found only half of adults with high blood pressure treated by a GP were adequately controlled.Dr Iain Turnbull, a GP, deputy chief medical officer at Our Future Health and a clinical research fellow at Oxford Population Health, said it was not clear why 50% of patients who said they were taking blood pressure-lowering drugs had uncontrolled hypertension.“Blood pressure varies considerably between people, and some people need changes in dose or two or more different medicines before it is brought under control. Other health conditions and medications can affect blood pressure, too.AI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggestsRead more“There are also practical and social factors: side effects, complicated treatment regimens and competing health or life pressures can make medicines difficult to take consistently. Weight, diet, salt intake, alcohol and physical activity can also influence blood pressure.“So a high reading can have many explanations and shouldn’t be seen simply as a reflection of what an individual patient or healthcare professional has done.“There are also some important caveats … we did not have prescribing records available to independently confirm medication use, and a blood pressure measurement on one day does not necessarily represent someone’s usual blood pressure.“Even with those caveats, I wouldn’t regard 50% as a satisfactory figure. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of stroke and heart disease, and bringing it under control reduces that risk.”Prof Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, said the study “paints a concerning picture of the scale of undetected high blood pressure in the UK, and the challenges of keeping blood pressure under control in those already receiving treatment”.“Better detection and treatment could help tens of thousands of people to avoid a preventable heart attack and stroke,” he added. “But to achieve this, we will need to rethink how we identify, treat and support those at risk so that blood pressure checks and effective treatment can benefit everyone.”Explore more on these topicsHigh blood pressureStrokeHeart attackHeart diseaseHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tories target universal credit claimants in plan condemned as ‘fast track to poverty’ | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Proposals aim to push people into work, but charities say families are still paying price of austerity cuts and rise in cost of living
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Proposals aim to push people into work, but charities say families are still paying price of austerity cuts and rise in cost of living
Content: Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said welfare had to be a safety net, ‘not a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered’.Photograph: Jacob King/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said welfare had to be a safety net, ‘not a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered’.Photograph: Jacob King/PAConservativesTories target universal credit claimants in plan condemned as ‘fast track to poverty’Proposals aim to push people into work, but charities say families are still paying price of austerity cuts and rise in cost of livingPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentWed 23 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople claiming universal credit (UC) would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan condemned by one charity as “a fast track to increased poverty”.Under the proposals, those who receive this “subsistence allowance” would have it paid into a dedicated debit card that would prevent from them buying alcohol or tobacco, based on an Australian system that was scrappedafter trials foundlimited evidence it changed behaviour.While the proposals are billed by theConservativesas a way to push people into work, the poverty charity Trussell said trimming incomes so that people struggled with rent and transport was likely to make it even harder for them to find and keep a job.Pay rent, eat or keep warm? Growing numbers face hard choices as housing benefit gap growsRead moreUnder the plan, UC claimants would receive the full amount to which they are entitled for six months, but after this point the sum would be tied to how long they have worked at a level that triggers national insurance payments.This would have to happen for at least twice as long as the claimant period, meaning someone who has amassed two years of NI payments would qualify for another 12 months of full UC, before falling to the lower rate.Set at 70% of the standard amount, this would leave a single claimant aged under 25 living on £237 a month, or just over £7.50 a day. For a couple aged 25 or over, under the plan they would lose £200 a month, falling to £466 in total.Anyone placed on the reduced level would have their UC payments put on to a “back to work card”, which would block purchases of alcohol, tobacco and gambling, or cash withdrawals.The plan would exclude those already in work – about a third of UC claimants have jobs – and those who are assessed as having what is called limited capability for work and work-related activity, because of a health condition or disability. Separate payments connected to housing or dependant children would be unaffected.The Conservatives said the plan would affect about 350,000 people in England, Scotland and Wales and save £538m a year.Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the aim was to be “tough on those who exploit the system”, adding: “Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered.”The party argues that in some countries such as Germany and the Netherlands, unemployment payments are contingent on sufficient contributions having been made and can be time-limited.Those payments, however, are notably more generous and can be between 60% and 70% of someone’s previous monthly wage. There is also separate support for those who have not paid in sufficiently, with single people in Germany receiving about £480 a month.Sara Ogilvie, the director of policy at ChildPovertyAction Group, said: “The reality is that families are still paying the price of austerity cuts to our social security safety net. With living costs continuing to rise, these proposals are a fast track to increased poverty and are the last thing people need as they try to get back on their feet.”Helen Barnard, the head of policy at Trussell, called the idea “deeply misguided”, saying UC already had strong conditions to ensure people seek work.She said: “If you’re struggling to afford food and rent, childcare or the bus fare to an interview, then finding and keeping a job becomes harder not easier. Cutting support would only make things worse.”Explore more on these topicsConservativesUniversal creditWelfareBenefitsPovertynewsShareReuse this content

title: Pupils to be offered vocational GCSEs in radical shake-up of system in England | GCSEs | The Guardian
description: Courses such as finance and construction form part of PM’s push for education ‘that offers a path for everybody’
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Courses such as finance and construction form part of PM’s push for education ‘that offers a path for everybody’
Content: The new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England.Photograph: Peter Muller/Getty Images/Image SourceView image in fullscreenThe new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England.Photograph: Peter Muller/Getty Images/Image SourceGCSEsPupils to be offered vocational GCSEs in radical shake-up of system in EnglandCourses such as finance and construction form part of PM’s push for education ‘that offers a path for everybody’Richard AdamsandSally WealeWed 23 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeenagers are to be offered a range of new vocational GCSEs under a radical shake-up of the school system inEnglanddesigned to tackle a crisis that has left nearly a million young people out of work or training.From 2029, pupils will be able to supplement compulsory GCSE subjects such as English, maths and sciences with courses such as construction, creative media production and child development, marking the biggest changes to the qualification for more than a decade.The Department for Education (DfE) said the newGCSEswould be two-year courses taken in year 10 and 11, “with nationally set content, grading and assessment” and regulated by Ofqual, England’s qualifications watchdog, to the same standards as academic GCSEs.England’s teenagers outperform peers in most countries in maths, reading and scienceRead moreThe courses are part of an effort by Andy Burnham to fulfil his pledge of “an education system that offers a path for everybody, academic and technical, in equal balance”, madethe day after his electionas MP for Makerfield.Announcing the new courses, the prime minister said: “We’ve all heard someone say ‘school wasn’t really for me’ because they were not given the chance to study vocational courses as well as traditional subjects.“That one-size-fits-all approach isn’t working, so we’re building an education system that values both academic and technical paths. I want to give all young people across Britain the hope that their future will be brighter, whether it starts at university or not.”Whitehall sources said the courses were expected to be offered from September 2029 but that the education secretary, Lucy Powell, wanted to move more quickly if possible, with schools given the option to add vocational GCSEs to their existing subjects.Powell said: “Time and again young people, parents and employers tell me they want schools to do more to help them understand and prepare for the jobs of the future. Our new vocational GCSEs will give young people a stronger connection to the careers and industries shaping our economy, helping them discover and develop their talents while maintaining high standards across our education system.“This is not about creating different routes for different children. It is about ensuring every child has access to a rich and ambitious education that opens doors, creates opportunity and prepares them for life beyond the classroom.”View image in fullscreenThe new courses would be designed to lead into further study including A-levels.Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesThe change is part of a range of measures that Burnham has announced since coming to power to tackle the Neets crisis, with a call to “value the hard hat as much as the graduation cap”. It follows plans togive local businesses a rolein setting curriculums in their areas.In a review published in May, Alan Milburn said that without significant change the number of young people not in work or education couldgrow by 25%by the early 2030s, opening up a “generational fault line” between the young and old.Critics, however, say the focus on technical education risks widening the gap between richer and poorer children. Sam Freedman, a policy adviser to Michael Gove when he was education secretary,wrote last month: “The more we ration a full set of academic GCSEs to children from better-off families, the more we will bake in existing inequalities.”The shadow education secretary, Laura Trott, said the courses would mean lowered expectations for disadvantaged children who had benefited most from high standards.“Labour are sabotaging young people’s futures,” she said. “Just weeks after thelatest Pisa resultsshowed England’s pupils climbing into the world’s top 10 for reading, maths and science, they want to rip up the system and review existing GCSEs.“Soaring up international league tables didn’t happen by accident. It followed years of evidence-led reform built around knowledge, rigour and high expectations.Labourrisks throwing that progress away and if English, maths and science become merely a ‘common entitlement’, not a requirement for new qualifications, we risk repeating the mistakes of the past.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe DfE said the subjects offered could include management and finance, creative media production, digital technology and building and construction, and would be designed to lead into further study including A-levels.The new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England, with travel and tourism and health and care courses among the most popular. About 350,000 technical awards and certificates were issued this year, compared with more than 5m GCSEs.Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needsRead moreSchool leaders said the success of the new courses would depend on having the resources and staffing to teach specialist subjects.The general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, Pepe Di’Iasio, said: “Reshaping and rebadging vocational and technical qualifications is well intentioned but will not in itself address the barriers to more young people taking these subjects. Reform needs to be accompanied by a strategy to ensure that schools have the staffing and resources to deliver them, and a campaign to raise public awareness of vocational and technical routes.”The general secretary of the National Education Union, Daniel Kebede, agreed. “These proposed changes will fall at the first hurdle unless there is sufficient investment in schools and the workforce,” he said.The general secretary of the NAHT school leaders’ union, Paul Whiteman, said: “In recent years, the content behind too many GCSEs became unwieldy and the over-reliance on final exams did not play to the strengths of all students.“It will be crucial these pitfalls are avoided in developing these qualifications and that the government works closely with educators, local leaders and employers to ensure they offer high-quality learning which sets young people up for future training, education or employment.”The government has also said it will launch a “national mission” by calling on employers to provide an additional 200,000 work experience placements to give young people exposure to the workplace by age 16. No 10 North will offer work experience for students aged 14 to 16 this academic year.Explore more on these topicsGCSEsVocational educationEducation policyLabourSecondary schoolsSchoolsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Texas executes death-row prisoner over 2005 triple killing | Texas | The Guardian
description: Ker’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection, the sixth person to be executed by Texas officials this year
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ker’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection, the sixth person to be executed by Texas officials this year
Content: The Texas execution chamber in Huntsville.Photograph: Pat Sullivan/APView image in fullscreenThe Texas execution chamber in Huntsville.Photograph: Pat Sullivan/APTexasTexas executes death-row prisoner over 2005 triple killingKer’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection, the sixth person to be executed by Texas officials this yearAssociated PressWed 23 Sep 2026 19.52 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man found guilty of fatally shooting three people during a 2005 attempted robbery at a ruralTexashome was executed Wednesday, a week after the other man convicted in the killings was put to death.Ker’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection at the state penitentiary in Huntsville. He isthe sixth person executed so far this year in Texas, with three more people scheduled over the next two months.A jury convicted Ramey of capital murder and sentenced him to death over the shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, in the home they shared in the small city of Edna, about 100 miles (160km) south-west of Houston.Ramey and LeJames Norman believed there was cocaine in the house and hoped to steal it, according to court records. They found none and killed the three victims, who lived across the street from Norman.View image in fullscreenKer-Sean Ramey in 2022.Photograph: Texas department of criminal justice/APNorman was put to death on 16 September, also in Huntsville. He had no last words, and no relatives or friends of the victims witnessed that execution.The US supreme court rejected a final appeal from Ramey hours before Wednesday’s execution.Ramey’s attorneys had argued that jurors never heard about how he suffered physical abuse as a child and grew up in poverty. State prosecutors told the court the appeal was “meritless” and argued that evidence showed Ramey had “an escalating pattern of criminal behavior”.Norman testified at Ramey’s trial nearly two years before being sentenced to death by a jury after pleading guilty to capital murder. He testified that he and Ramey shot the victims. Ramey’s attorneys blamed the shootings on Norman.Ramey’s former girlfriend testified that she was with him when he threw two pistols into a lake after the killings, and that he told her in detail about his involvement.Lopez was shot four times, including in the back of the head; Peacock was shot twice in the head; and Roberts was shot five times in the chest, neck and head.Explore more on these topicsTexasCapital punishmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Justin Bieber performs surprise acoustic gig in beleaguered Los Angeles park | Justin Bieber | The Guardian
description: Small crowd enjoys singer’s free concert in MacArthur Park, which has often drawn headlines for less cheery reasons
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Small crowd enjoys singer’s free concert in MacArthur Park, which has often drawn headlines for less cheery reasons
Content: Justin Bieber performs at this year’s Coachella festival in southern California.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for CoachellaView image in fullscreenJustin Bieber performs at this year’s Coachella festival in southern California.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for CoachellaJustin BieberJustin Bieber performs surprise acoustic gig in beleaguered Los Angeles parkSmall crowd enjoys singer’s free concert in MacArthur Park, which has often drawn headlines for less cheery reasonsUwa Ede-OsifoWed 23 Sep 2026 19.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith no announcement and little fanfare, Justin Bieberperformeda free acoustic set on Monday at a Los Angeles park often in local headlines for less cheery reasons.Invideosthat surfaced online, four musicians flanked the global phenom, who wore a plain T-shirt and shorts as he sang hits including Daisies and Yukon. The low-key affair with a small crowd stood in stark contrast to Bieber’s recent blockbuster World Cup and Coachella performances.Some online users expressed surprise at the venue choice. A spokesperson for Bieber could not be immediately reached for comment about what spurred the show.MacArthur Park, located west of downtownLos Angeles, is often described in ominous terms. The area has been plagued by gang activity and rampant drug use. Homeless encampments have also cropped up around the park in recent years.View image in fullscreenA jacaranda tree in MacArthur Park in May.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesEarlier this year, federal authorities condemned the park as an “open-air drug market” afterarresting several individualswho they accused of trafficking meth and fentanyl on to its grounds.The park also became a flashpoint in the Los Angeles mayoral race, with mayor Karen Bass’s challengers using it as a benchmark for her progress on public safety.In June, Bassdisavowedcrime in the park, saying the Los Angeles police were employing every resource to curtail illicit activity. Bass said the state and county had a role to play in the solution. “They must increase funding for treatment facilities and recovery services to stop the revolving door between jail and our parks,” she said.Bieber’s performance comes after Los Angeles district attorney Nathan Hochman hosted apicnicat the park, following up on an earlier pledge to make the park family-friendly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“He’s definitely on the invite list for next year’s Labor Day weekend picnic!” Hochmanwroteon X of Bieber.“Bieber in MacArthur park. That’s progress,” first assistant US attorney Bill Essaylipostedon X. “Amazing what can happen when criminals and drug dealers are removed from public spaces.”Explore more on these topicsJustin BieberCaliforniaWest CoastLos AngelesnewsShareReuse this content

title: RFK Jr received $4m in book advances from Maha allies over past year | Robert F Kennedy Jr | The Guardian
description: In 2024 ethics filing, US health secretary pledged to ‘not engage in writing, editing, marketing or promotional services for any of these books during government service’
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: In 2024 ethics filing, US health secretary pledged to ‘not engage in writing, editing, marketing or promotional services for any of these books during government service’
Content: Robert F Kennedy Jr in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington DC on 18 September.Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy Jr in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington DC on 18 September.Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/APRobert F Kennedy JrRFK Jr received $4m in book advances from Maha allies over past yearIn 2024 ethics filing, US health secretary pledged to ‘not engage in writing, editing, marketing or promotional services for any of these books during government service’Maya YangWed 23 Sep 2026 18.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, received $4m over the last year in book advances from allies within the Make America Healthy Again movement, according to a new report.The advances were for upcoming books by Skyhorse Publishing, a publishing house belonging to Tony Lyons, a friend of Kennedy Jr who is also president of Maha Center, a non-profit that describes itself as “tackling America’s health crisis through education, investigation, innovation and action”.The advances werefirst reportedby the New York Times on Wednesday.According toa 2024 ethics filing, Kennedy Jr pledged: “I will not engage in writing, editing, marketing or promotional services for any of these books during government service.”Kennedy Jr has written several books with Skyhorse Publishing, including The Real Anthony Fauci and The Wuhan Cover-Up.According to Kennedy Jr’s 2026 financial disclosure forms, also reviewed by the Guardian, he accepted $126,500 worth of housing in Washington DC, at a “vacation home” owned by Gavin de Becker.De Becker is a security consultant and Kennedy Jr ally who also provided the secretary with gifts including nearly $45,000 in roundtrip airfare to Greece and nearly $97,000 in roundtrip airfare to Fiji, where the Wall Street Journalreportsde Becker owns a compound.RFK Jr lied in Senate confirmation hearings, newly revealed documents indicateRead moreIn addition to donating at least $10m to Kennedy Jr’s Super Pac in 2024, with $9.65m being returned,according toPolitico, de Becker has published a book with Skyhorse Publishing titled Forbidden Facts: Government Deceit and Suppression About Brain Damage From Childhood Vaccines.In astatementto the New York Times, an HHS spokesperson said that Kennedy Jr “complies with all applicable federal ethics laws, regulations and financial disclosure requirements”.“The secretary works with HHS, career ethics officials to ensure that his financial interests, gifts, outside activities and other reportable matters are appropriately disclosed and handled consistent with those requirements,” the spokesperson added.Meanwhile, de Becker told the outlet: “Bobby is among my closest friends in the world for many years, and I’m grateful to be able to host him anytime … He has hosted my family at his homes, he’s stayed at my homes, we take family vacations together every year, and did so for years before he was in his current job.”The Guardian has reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services, de Becker and Lyons for additional comment.The financial disclosures also noted that Kennedy Jr’s wife, Cheryl Hines, accepted $210,000 in consultation fees from the non-profit advocacy group Maha Action, which Lyons also leads.Speaking to the New York Times, Kedric Payne, a senior ethics counsel at the Campaign Legal Center said: “Lavish gifts to an official from major political donors don’t get the same benefit of the doubt as dinner from a former classmate … The public deserves full transparency about the nature of these gifts and any interests the donor has before the government.”Explore more on these topicsRobert F Kennedy JrUS press and publishingTrump administrationUS politicsNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stung by Trump, machinists union campaigns for affordability in midterms | US unions | The Guardian
description: One of the largest labor unions in the US targets eight battleground states in ‘workers v billionaires’ campaign
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: One of the largest labor unions in the US targets eight battleground states in ‘workers v billionaires’ campaign
Content: Members of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers hold a rally on 5 May 2026.Photograph: Ross Olson/IAMAWView image in fullscreenMembers of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers hold a rally on 5 May 2026.Photograph: Ross Olson/IAMAWUS unionsStung by Trump, machinists union campaigns for affordability in midtermsOne of the largest labor unions in the US targets eight battleground states in ‘workers v billionaires’ campaignMichael SainatoWed 23 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM), one of the largest labor unions in the US, haslauncheda “workers v billionaires” political campaign tour targeting members in eight battleground states and encouraging them to support pro-worker candidates in the midterms.IAM hasnearly 700,000 active and retired membersin North America, covering workers at corporations that include Boeing, Lockheed Martin, United Airlines and Harley-Davidson. The union is targeting members and voters in Maine, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Arizona, Nevada and Illinois.“We made a strategic commitment that we’re going to be the most engaged that we have ever been in the history of our union in working,” said Brian Bryant, international president of IAM. “We’re living in an economy that only favors billionaires and does not favor working people, and it’s time that Congress and this administration realize who they should be looking out for.”Bryant emphasized thatseveral union members, including those with IAM, voted for Trump in 2024 because of promises that he would fix the economy and make things more affordable. Throughout his 2024 presidential campaign, Trumprepeatedly claimed: “When I win, I will immediately bring prices down, starting on day one.”Yet since Trump took office, inflation has increased from 3.0% in January 2025 to3.4%in August 2026, health insurance costs aresoaringdue to the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies andgas pricesare on average $1 a gallon higher due to Trump’s war with Iran.‘The most anti-union president’: how Trump turned his back on US workersRead moreThe union will “send a message to this administration that what the status quo is right now is not acceptable, and they’re going to have to stand up and pay attention to working people”, Bryant said.Jason Gayler, president of IAM local 776A in Fort Worth, Texas, said his state “is more purple than what people put out to be”. As Democrats are seeking to flip several seats,pollsare showing that races are the most competitive they’ve been in decades.“The price of just the cost of living in north Texas now has absolutely skyrocketed, and it’s starting to really affect a lot of our members, which is motivating them to back candidates that focus primarily on the working class,” Gayler said.He also noted that the machinists recently elected their first rank-and-file member to the Texas senate; Taylor Rehmet, president of the IAM’s Texas state council, won a special election in January, flipping a state senatedistrict that Trump wonin 2024 by 17%.Shay Blodgett, an Alaska Airlines worker in Phoenix who is helping to lead IAM’s political program in Arizona, said the union has worked toopposeRepublican-led state legislation that would have restricted public sector workers’ ability to organize and supported theArizona AFL-CIO “labor 2026 blitz” campaign.“We’ve been conducting member-to-member engagement this summer, reaching out, asking members what matters to them,” Blodgett said. “We heard them loud and clear. The No 1 thing was the economy, cost of living, fuel prices, healthcare and food costs.”Co-workers have expressed regret over voting for Republicans in the last election, especially since transportation workers areexemptfrom the temporary no-tax-on-overtime deduction that was passed as part of Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was passed last summer.“The majority of our airline workers in the state will be entering contract negotiations in early 2027, and we need elected officials that will fix the economy and allow airline workers to fulfill the American dream of home ownership and raising families in Arizona,” Blodgett said.Rich Howell, former president of IAM local 1776, a longtime member of the union and worker at Philadelphia international airport, said the union is supporting Democrats in Pennsylvania who are trying to flip four congressional districts and the state senate while maintaining control of the governorship and statehouse.Trump “said he was going to bring down the prices a year and a half ago. That was his campaign message. If you go back and see all the promises, there wasn’t one that he held,” Howell said.He noted this is a difficult election year due to the amount of money billionaires are pouring into politics –more than $1.6bnin the 2026 midterm elections so far – but noted that “money doesn’t buy a race”.“Trump put the tariffs on, cutting more jobs, hurting more people in our industry,” Howell added. “It’s billionaires versus the workers, and that’s the stance we’re making. They are getting rich and we’re paying for it. We’re paying for it out of our pockets.”This article was amended on 23 September 2026 to clarify that more than $1.6bn has been poured into the 2026 midterm elections so far. An earlier version incorrectly stated it was $1.6tn.Explore more on these topicsUS unionsUS midterm elections 2026Donald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsAerospace industryShareReuse this content

title: McDonald’s to take on KFC and rivals as Gen Z flock to fried chicken | McDonald's | The Guardian
description: Fast food giant aiming to increase share of global chicken market as rising cost of beef hits profits
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Fast food giant aiming to increase share of global chicken market as rising cost of beef hits profits
Content: The fast food chain’s CEO, Chris Kempczinski, said McDonald’s current share of the chicken market was ‘high teens’, but that it was bigger and growing at twice the pace of beef.Photograph: Steve Parsons/PAView image in fullscreenThe fast food chain’s CEO, Chris Kempczinski, said McDonald’s current share of the chicken market was ‘high teens’, but that it was bigger and growing at twice the pace of beef.Photograph: Steve Parsons/PAMcDonald'sMcDonald’s to take on KFC and rivals as Gen Z flock to fried chickenFast food giant aiming to increase share of global chicken market as rising cost of beef hits profitsSarah ButlerWed 23 Sep 2026 13.38 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMcDonald’s is betting on fried chicken as health concerns and the rising price of beef shift dining habits.The company said that it aimed to take an extra 1.5 percentage point-share of the global chicken market by 2030, with an aim to increase its share of drinks by the same proportion. McDonald’s said the growth in chicken, a lower-priced protein, would not come at the expense of beef burger sales, saying it aimed maintain its “leadership position in beef”.Chris Kempczinski, McDonald’s chair and chief executive, told investors in May that the chain’s share of the chicken market was in the “high teens”, compared with about 45% in beef, but the chicken market was bigger and growing at twice the pace of its red meat counterpart.From McDonald’s to Congress: can a former fry cook flip a key district for Democrats?Read moreMcDonald’s has warned that the rising cost of beef, as well as energy, was hitting profits for its franchisees. The chain also faces heavy competition from the rapid rise of chicken shop chains including Popeyes and Wingstop as well as expansion by the more established player KFC, driven particularly by the popularity of fried chicken among younger Gen Z consumers.“McDonald’s has the unmatched scale, customer insights, brand loyalty and operational capabilities to not only adapt to the next wave of change in our industry, but to turn it into an advantage,” said Kempczinski.The chain also said it would spend about $8.5bn (£6.4bn) to help franchisees with rent and improve their restaurants.The change comes amid the rapid rise in chicken shops and sales of chicken and the surging price of beef, which has risen by more than 20% in the past two years in the US and the UK, according to figures from the UK’s Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board.Peter Backman, an independent food service industry analyst, said “chicken is cheaper and perceived as healthier”.He said the rising price of beef was likely to be a “drag on the market” for burgers and offering more chicken would enable McDonald’s to sell more to its fans and “steal a bit of market share from other quick service operators”. He said higher drinks sales were probably attractive as beverages tended to be more profitable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the UK, 39% of consumers used chicken shops in 2025 compared with 37% in 2023, according to market research firm Mintel, with Gen Z usage hitting 52%, almost matching pizza outlets at 56%. A plethora of other options, including Asian-inspired chains such as Wagamama, are also eating into the market share of burgers and pizza.Late last year Domino’s Pizza Group announced that its chief executive of two years had stepped down with immediate effect, less than two weeks after he appeared to suggest theUK may be approaching “peak pizza”and that the chain should try to broaden its menu to sell more chicken.Explore more on these topicsMcDonald'sFood & drink industryChickenFoodFast foodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years | London Stock Exchange | The Guardian
description: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market
Content: Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but it wants Airtel Money to be listed separately.Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/ReutersView image in fullscreenAirtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but it wants Airtel Money to be listed separately.Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/ReutersLondon Stock ExchangeIndian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in yearsSunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock marketNils Pratley: Does this mark the end of London’s listing drought?
