Not yetJoanna PartridgeWed 23 Sep 2026 07.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the strugglingLondon Stock Exchange.Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that hasfaced a string of recent departures.The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-SaharanAfrica, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.View image in fullscreenSunil Bharti Mittal controls Bharti Enterprises.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesIt operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 butdelayed itto the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAirtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result ofoverseas takeovers of UK companies.Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wisefloated in 2021with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from Londonto New York.Explore more on these topicsLondon Stock ExchangeIPOsEmerging marketsStock marketsAfricaIndiaLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former NFL star Antonio Brown to avoid possibility of 30 years in prison with plea deal | NFL | The Guardian
description: Former NFL star Antonio Brown plans to accept a plea deal on an attempted murder charge in Miami, his lawyer said Wednesday
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Former NFL star Antonio Brown plans to accept a plea deal on an attempted murder charge in Miami, his lawyer said Wednesday
Content: Antonio Brown played in the NFL for 12 seasons.Photograph: Corey Sipkin/APView image in fullscreenAntonio Brown played in the NFL for 12 seasons.Photograph: Corey Sipkin/APNFLFormer NFL star Antonio Brown to avoid possibility of 30 years in prison with plea deal38-year-old had been facing attempted murder chargeFormer player will accept aggravated assault chargeGuardian sportand agenciesWed 23 Sep 2026 15.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer NFL star Antonio Brown plans to accept a plea dealon an attempted murder chargein Miami, his lawyer said Wednesday. Doing so will mean the former wide receiver avoids prison.Brown is scheduled to appear in court next Wednesday to make the deal final. He could face up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the current attempted murder charge.“They made [Brown] an offer he couldn’t refuse,” Brown’s attorney, Mark Eiglarsh, said in a statement. “There is a profound difference between believing you can win a case and deciding that you and your family cannot afford to spend another year, or potentially several years, wearing an ankle monitor and fighting it.”Brown is accusedof grabbing a handgun from a member of security after a celebrity boxing match in Miami in May 2025. The 38-year-old is then alleged to have fired two shots at a man he had gotten into a fistfight with earlier, according to an arrest warrant. Zul-Qarnain Kwame Nantambu told investigators that one of the bullets grazed his neck.Nantaumbu’s attorney, Richard L Cooper, said this month that his client has forgiven Brown and would no longer take part in the case against the former player.“We believe that the ends of justice are accomplished with this plea deal, and my client wishes Mr Brown good health,” Cooper told ESPN on Wednesday.Eiglarsh said Brown would accept a charge of aggravated assault as part of the plea deal.“There’s no prison, there’s no jail, there’s no house arrest. There’s only straight probation,” Eiglarsh told ESPN. “And no alcohol or drug evaluation, no psychological evaluation, no letter of apology, no community service hours, no fines. Just stay away from the victim.”TheMiaminative played 12 NFL seasons for the Pittsburgh Steelers, New England Patriots and Tampa Bay Buccaneers, becoming one of the most prolific receivers of his era. He caught 928 passes for 12,291 yards and 83 touchdowns over 146 career games and was named to the Pro Bowl seven times, earning first-team All-Pro honors in four consecutive seasons from 2014 to 2017.Brownwon a Super Bowl with Tampa Bayin the 2020 season, catching a touchdown pass from Tom Brady in the game. His career ended in 2021 after hedramatically exited a game mid-play, removing his jersey and jogging off the field.Explore more on these topicsNFLMiamiUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Giants’ Jaxson Dart set for season-ending surgery after serious knee injury | New York Giants | The Guardian
description: The quarterback’s knee injury, suffered in New York’s loss to the Rams, is said to be more severe than anticipated and will keep him out for an extended time
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The quarterback’s knee injury, suffered in New York’s loss to the Rams, is said to be more severe than anticipated and will keep him out for an extended time
Content: Jaxson Dart walks off the field Monday night with teammate Abdul Carter after the Giants’ loss.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/APView image in fullscreenJaxson Dart walks off the field Monday night with teammate Abdul Carter after the Giants’ loss.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/APNew York GiantsGiants’ Jaxson Dart set for season-ending surgery after serious knee injuryQB suffered MCL, PCL and meniscus damageSurgery expected to result in full recoveryDart injured on opening drive of Rams defeatGuardian sportWed 23 Sep 2026 12.10 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart is expected to undergo knee surgery that will end his 2026 season after suffering damage to his MCL, PCL and meniscus in Monday night’s loss to the Los Angeles Rams, according to reports Wednesday.NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafoloreportedthat the surgery is expected to lead to a full recovery. ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported that the damage to Dart’s left knee included his MCL, PCL and meniscus, with the meniscus considered the main issue.Rams crush Giants but Jaxson Dart escapes ‘devastating outcome’ after knee injuryRead moreThe second-year quarterback was hurt on the opening possession of the Giants’ 28-6 defeat to the Rams. Initial reports said that Dart sprained his MCL and avoided broken bones, with an MRI set for Tuesday. Head coach John Harbaugh said Monday that he believed a “devastating outcome” had been avoided and that he did not expect Dart to be out long-term without giving a further recovery timeline.The 23-year-old started the season strong in New York’s Week 1 win over Dallas but left the field after taking a huge hit from Byron Young and Josaiah Stewart on the Giants’ seventh play Monday night. Dart watched the second half in a track suit on the sidelines. Jameis Winston could not get much going after Dart’s exit, throwing an end-zone interception as New York got all of their points from field goals.Dart was one of several quarterbacks injured around the league in Week 2.Caleb Williamsof the Chicago Bears is week-to-week and will miss some time with a hamstring injury suffered against the Vikings, while the Washington Commanders’ Jayden Daniels dislocated his left elbow in a defeat to the Cowboys and has no timeline for return.Explore more on these topicsNew York GiantsUS sportsNFLnewsShareReuse this content

title: Harry Kane admits England’s World Cup 2026 exit ‘hurt more than any other’ | England | The Guardian
description: The striker, who will lead England against Spain in the Nations League, said World Cup defeat hurt ‘even more than when I missed the penalty in Qatar’
Author: David Hytner
Headline: The striker, who will lead England against Spain in the Nations League, said World Cup defeat hurt ‘even more than when I missed the penalty in Qatar’
Content: Harry Kane and England are preparing for four Nations League matches in 11 days.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenHarry Kane and England are preparing for four Nations League matches in 11 days.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAEnglandHarry Kane admits England’s World Cup 2026 exit ‘hurt more than any other’‘It wasn’t the team that we wanted and said we’d be’England host Spain in Nations League on SaturdayDavid HytnerWed 23 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Kane has described England’sWorld Cup semi-final defeatagainst Argentina as his most painful tournament exit because of how the team lost sight of who they were.The captain is determined to move on as quickly as possible and is chasing a statement performance against Spain at Wembley on Saturday night in theNations League. But he admits he is yet to get over the Argentina game and knows it is something he and his England teammates must work to process.Branthwaite reveals brain study helped him conquer injuries and earn England callRead more“It felt like it wasn’t us as a team,” Kane said, as he reflected on howEnglandlost their way in the 2-1 defeat, barely touching the ball after they went ahead in the 55th minute. “It wasn’t the team that we wanted to be and said we’d be. When you maybe go against your beliefs and you lose, it feels 10 times worse than just losing in a way where … if we lose doing it our way you accept it, take it on the chin and move on. It’s tough and it will still be tough.“I’m so passionate about England and especially because I’ve been on this journey … been to finals, semi‑finals and been so close. Each one hurts in a different way and this one hurt, for sure, more than any other one. I’d say even more than when I missed the penalty in Qatar [in the2-1 defeat by Francein the 2022 World Cup quarter-finals] because of just the manner that it happened.”It was put to Kane that it was a healing process. “It kind of is,” he replied. “But you have to heal while getting on with it. In football, you don’t have time. Before you know it’s the next one. It’s a hard balance because you’re trying to get over it and learn from it but also we play the world champions on Saturday and it’s a big, important game.”Kane knows England must identify why they have repeatedly fallen short against the toughest teams when it matters most. “How can we be better in those moments? How can we be ourselves more in those moments? Through qualifying campaigns and a lot of games in tournaments, we play with a certain intensity, we play in a good way. It’s something that we haven’t quite been able to do in latter stages of tournaments against the bigger and better nations.“It may be a mixture of things. It may be personalities, mentality. It may be just the direction and how we want to play in those games. It’s conversations that we need to have as a group.”Kane accepts it was not only against Argentina that England were not at their best. “Taking away the big loss at the end, there were still games at theWorld Cupwhere we didn’t quite reach our potential, the way that we train,” he said.But the message – as articulated by Thomas Tuchel when he addressed the squad at St George’s Park on Tuesday – was of the need to fine-tune. “The general messaging is that we continue what we’ve been building,” Kane said. “Sometimes after a tournament, it’s easy to say it’s a new start but I don’t think it is that. It’s a continuation because we have done a lot of good things.”View image in fullscreenHarry Kane asked: ‘How can we be better in those moments? How can we be ourselves more?’ after England’s World Cup heartbreak.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersTuchel has beenrocked by the withdrawalsof Declan Rice, Cole Palmer, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento for the upcoming Nations League fixtures; after Spain, England play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia. Rice’s absence has attracted attention because it is for load-management reasons rather than an injury that would immediately rule him out. Kane understands the move, given Rice’s well-documented problems with nerve pain in a hamstring.“I spoke to Dec,” Kane said. “I know Dec goes far and beyond for the club and country. I know he’s been struggling for a while with his issues. Dec reached out to me, he voice-noted me. Everyone has to look after themselves and I trust all the boys.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is a seismic time for Kane. He is four caps shy of Peter Shilton’s all‑time England record of 125; he could be level with him by the end of this international window. Kane is also tipped to win the Ballon d’Or on 26 October and is poised to extend his contract at Bayern Munich. “We’re fairly close,” he said. “I’m happy there. It won’t be too long before there’s some sort of announcement.”The 33-year-old allowed his thoughts to drift to the longer term and as he mused about his ambition to become an NFL kicker, there was a clear hint he saw himself finishing his football career in Major League Soccer.“I take penalties and it [being an NFL kicker] is a very similar pressure and technique. If I was to do it, it is something I would take seriously. I would take six months to a year to try and practise before. Maybe if I am in the MLS in the future or somewhere like that, it might be a thing where you could connect the two maybe with the seasons.”Kane has previously said he would be interested in becoming a professional golfer. He loves to play and revealed he did not watch the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina because he went for a round of golf in New York.“I watch golf and think: ‘I could be there.’ Then I go out and play and I am like: ‘There’s no way.’ I play off two. But I am a member at Wentworth and I shoot 10 over. Then I watch the pros, who played there last week, and 20 under wins it. I think I’ll stick to football.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandHarry KaneWorld Cup 2026World CupNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Jack Dempsey v Gene Tunney at 100: when a great champion met his greatest inquisitor | Boxing | The Guardian
description: On 23 September 1926, two of the best heavyweights in American history met in front of 120,000 fans in Philadelphia. The fight drew in a nation
Author: Thomas Hauser
Headline: On 23 September 1926, two of the best heavyweights in American history met in front of 120,000 fans in Philadelphia. The fight drew in a nation
Content: Gene Tunney (right) and Jack Dempsey clash during their 1926 fight.Photograph: The Stanley Weston Archive/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGene Tunney (right) and Jack Dempsey clash during their 1926 fight.Photograph: The Stanley Weston Archive/Getty ImagesBoxingJack Dempsey v Gene Tunney at 100: when a great champion met his greatest inquisitorOn 23 September 1926, two of the best heavyweights in American history met in front of 120,000 fans in Philadelphia. The fight drew in a nationThomas HauserWed 23 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 12.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe two fights between Jack Dempsey and Gene Tunney rank with boxing’s most-storied championship bouts and are among the greatest sports spectacles ever seen in America. Wednesday marks the one hundredth anniversary of their first encounter.Dempsey bridged boxing’s old and modern eras and was one of the most charismatic fighters in history. When Dempsey was young, biographer Randy Roberts recounts, “he lived in mining camps and hobo jungles, rode the rods, and more than once begged for food. What separated him was his willingness, even eagerness, to work. He accepted any type of employment from washing dishes, cutting lawns, and scrubbing floors to the harder work of coal-mining, digging ditches, and picking fruit.”Dempsey had his own thoughts on his origin story: “I was a hobo,” Dempsey said. “But I was never a bum.”Fighting under the name “Kid Blackie”, Dempsey had roughly 100 fights in Colorado, Utah, and Nevada from 1911, when he turned 16, through 1914.“When you’re fighting, you’re fighting for one thing,” he later recalled. “To get money. When I was a young fellow, I was knocked down plenty. I wanted to stay down. I couldn’t. I had to collect that $2 for winning or go hungry. I had one fight when I was knocked down 11 times before I got up to win. I had to get up. I was a hungry fighter. When you haven’t eaten for two days, you’ll understand.”In the ring, Dempsey attacked with unrelenting ferocity. Trainer Ray Arcel likened him to “a saloon fighter” and observed, “With Dempsey, every part of your body was a legal target.”Sportswriter Paul Gallico echoed that theme, writing, “Dempsey seemed to have a constant bottomless well of cold fury somewhere close to his throat. He had tremendous courage, speed and determination, and good hitting powers. He was never a good boxer and had little or no defense. His protection was aggression. Dempsey never boxed anybody. When the bell rang, he ran out and began to attack his opponent, and he never stopped attacking him, trying to batter him to the floor until the bell ended the round. He had a smoldering truculence on his face and hatred in his eyes. He was utterly without mercy or pity, asked no quarter, gave none.”Dempsey said: “To be a good fighter, you have to have three things. You’ve got to be able to give it. You’ve got to be able to take it. And you’ve got to have a fighting heart.”Boxing was at low tide as America neared the “Roaring Twenties”. There hadn’t been a popular heavyweight champion since James Jeffries retired in 1904. Moral “reformers” were attacking the sport as sinful. And their efforts to abolish boxing gathered steam after Jack Johnson emerged as champion in 1908.I rewatched the Thrilla in Manila with Muhammad Ali. He still winced at the blows years laterRead moreOn 5 April 1915, Jess Willard defeated Johnson in Havana. The new champion was poised for stardom. But after winning the title, Willard went on tour with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West Show and other theatrical companies, and defended his title only once in four years.Finally, in 1919, Tex Rickard, America’s premier boxing promoter, lured Willard back to the ring with a $100,000 guarantee to fight Dempsey in Toledo, Ohio on 4 July. It was the first major outdoor prizefight in the United States since Jeffries had come out of retirement and been battered into submission by Johnson on 4 July 1910. Willard weighed 245 lbs; Dempsey just 187. After three rounds, Willard’s jaw and nose were broken. Six teeth had been knocked out. There were cuts above and below his eyes. He could fight no more. Jack Dempsey was heavyweight champion of the world.View image in fullscreenA publicity poster for the motion picture of the Jack Dempsey v Gene Tunney fight.Photograph: Screen Archives/Getty ImagesRickard wanted to make boxing a respectable sport that appealed to all classes. Dempsey’s exciting fighting style and charisma made him an ideal instrument to achieve that goal. Meanwhile, more and more states were legalizing boxing, and religious reform movements had begun to weaken. Dempsey versus Georges Carpentier followed and brought the sweet science to new heights.Dempsey-Carpentier was contested on 2 July 1921, in a temporary arena at Boyle’s Thirty Acres on the outskirts of Jersey City. More than 80,000 spectators (the largest crowd to witness a sporting event in America up until that time) attended. The live gate was $1,789,238 (more than double the previous record for a fight and equivalent to more than $32.5m today). The fight was also the first world championship bout to be broadcast live on radio, blow-by-blow.Carpentier was hailed as a man of destiny, not just in his French homeland but throughout Europe. He was the reigning world light-heavyweight champion. But more important to his image, he’d served in the military as a pilot during the first world war and been decorated twice for heroism. He was handsome, graceful, intelligent, debonair, spoke reasonably good English, and was regarded by many as the most glamorous fighter ever to step into a boxing ring.Dempsey was viewed as Carpentier’s opposite. He’d been indicted and tried (although acquitted) of fraudulently evading the draft during war. “He was dark complexioned,” Roberts notes. “His beard was coarse; his eyebrows were thick; and his face seemed cast in a permanent iron scowl. In the latter part of his career, Dempsey’s reserve in public would be recognized for what it was; basic shyness. But in 1921, his reserve and awkwardness around people were interpreted as the characteristics of a mean conceited man.”In other words, Dempsey-Carpentier was hero versus villain with the foreigner in the preferred role. “The Frenchman was the hero,” Dempsey later said. “I was the flat-nosed bum.”“The Fight of the Century” captured attention worldwide. On the morning of the bout, legendary sportswriter Grantland Rice wrote, “The greatest single day in the ancient history of an ancient sport has come at last; a day that has caught the imagination of more people from crowded centers to remote off-lying places than any single contest since the world’s dim dawn.”Vanderbilts, Rockefellers, Whitneys, and Astors were seated at ringside. The United States Senate and House of Representatives had adjourned in anticipation of the event because 12 senators and 90 congressmen had tickets. The fight was also attended by a significant number of women. Ladies had been present at Willard-Dempsey but were confined to a special section. At Dempsey-Carpentier, they mingled freely with the men.As was the custom of the day, the champion was introduced first.Dempsey later recalled, “Joe Humphreys picked up his megaphone and bawled, ‘In this corner, weighing 188lbs, from Salt Lake City, Utah, the heavyweight champion of the world, Jack Dempsey.’ The only response from 80,000 Americans was a little applause and a low murmur. ‘And in this corner, weighing 172lbs, the challenger from Paris, France, Georges Carpentier.’ The people went wild. It was deafening. It hurt; believe me.”The bell for round one rang at 3.16pm. At 3.30, it was over.“Carpentier had more charm, more good manners, and more class in his dress than anybody I had ever met,” Dempsey said years later. “But it was probably the worst mismatch in the history of the heavyweight division.”View image in fullscreenFans in Boston fans gather to listen to the fight. The Boston Globe’s special radio bulletin broadcast was almost simultaneous with the action in the ring.Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty ImagesThe New York Times devoted multiple pages to the fight and announced the result with a large-type, three-line headline that ran the full width of page one.“I read the stories about the fight in the next day’s papers,” Dempsey said later. “Carpentier was the hero of the hour. Never before had anybody seen such courage. I was just a butcher who happened to win. I was a pretty bitter fellow. No matter what you’ve got, you want them to like you.”Dempsey v Luis Firpo – Argentina’s “Wild Bull of The Pampas” – was the next building block for the Dempsey legend. On 14 September 1923, more than 88,000 fans filled the Polo Grounds in New York. An estimated 35,000 more were turned away. Once again, America’s blue-blood aristocracy was at ringside, joined this time by Babe Ruth.Ten seconds into round one, a left uppercut from Firpo dropped Dempsey to his knees. The champion rose and floored Firpo seven times. Then Firpo launched a series of blows punctuated by a monstrous right hand that knocked Dempsey out of the ring. That moment,recreated on canvas by artist George Bellows, is one of the most famous sports images of all time. Dempsey landed in the press section; cut his lower back on a typewriter; and with the aid of one or more writers, was pushed back into the ring before the count of 10.“It was pitch dark for a few seconds,” he said later. “Then I managed to focus on Firpo’s fuzzy form. I don’t remember climbing back in the ring, but I remember seeing 20 Firpos standing in front of me.”In round two, Dempsey knocked Firpo down twice more. The Argentinian was counted out at 57 seconds of the round.View image in fullscreenJack Dempsey and Gene Tunney in the run-up to their first fight.Photograph: Keystone-France/Gamma-Keystone/Getty ImagesThen, like Willard before him, Dempsey put the title on ice, refusing to fight for three years. Finally, on 23 September 1926, he returned to the ring against Gene Tunney.Tunney was a brilliant tactician. The only defeat in his 67-bout career was a loss by decision to the great Harry Greb, who he fought five times. As a young man, Tunney had knocked out Soldier Jones on the undercard of Dempsey v Carpentier. Then, instead of going to his dressing room, he’d stayed at ringside and, still in his robe, watched the main event. Over the years, he’d studied films of Dempsey countless times.Tunney was complicated. He hadn’t graduated from high school but read prolifically as a road to self-improvement. That led to ridicule by some members of the press who treated his interest in books as a joke. During the build-up to Dempsey-Tunney, Paul Gallico wrote, “I think Tunney has hurt his own game with his cultural nonsense. It is a fine thing that he has educated himself to the point where he no longer says ‘dese’ and ‘dem’ and ‘dose’ and where he can tell one book from another and indicate some familiarity with their contents. But the man who steps into the ring with Dempsey with nothing but his hands as weapons needs to be a fighter and nothing but. He will have to have a natural viciousness and nastiness well up in him that will transcend rules and reason, that will make him want to commit murder with his two hands. I don’t think that Master Tunney, who likes first editions and works of art, has it in him.”That earned a rejoinder from Tunney, who declared, “It never occurred to me that a habit of reading could be seen as a stunt or a joke. Wasn’t reading something we wanted to champion?”A staggering total of 120,757 fans jammed Sesquicentennial Stadium in Philadelphia to witness Tunney challenge Dempsey for the heavyweight crown. That number and the $1,895,733 they paid in gate receipts (more than $36m in today’s dollars) were records for the time. An estimated 39 million more people listened to the fight on radio.The bout was scheduled for 10 rounds; a distance approved by both the champion, who was giving away youth, and the challenger, who thought that 10 rounds with Dempsey would be enough. At 29, Tunney was only two years younger than the champion. But Dempsey had lived a hard life. His body had absorbed the blows of hundreds of fights. And he’d been out of the ring for three years. It was a classic confrontation between a puncher who was past his prime and a boxer who was in it.“From the time the bout started,” Dempsey acknowledged later, “I was aware that my body and brain weren’t communicating properly. I was slower than I thought, or Gene was faster. He glided around the ring like he was on ice. Wherever I went looking for him, he stuck that left of his in my face, keeping me off balance, piling up points. Now and then, he’d stop me with a stiff right. There seemed to be nothing I could do, though I tried. Tunney was so scientific a boxer that all I seemed to be able to do was to take his punishment.”Tunney won every round. He cut Dempsey over the right eye and jabbed his left eye shut. By the end of the bout, the champion’s jaw was swollen and he was bleeding from the mouth.“I have no alibis to offer,” Dempsey said. “I lost to a good man.” Years later, he reflected back on that night and noted, “It’s sad to hear the fellow with the microphone yell: ‘The winner andnewheavyweight champion of the world’ when you’re the old one.”But there was another memory of that day that the fallen champion carried with him. Late in life, he reminisced, “I was booed when I fought Willard, though he seemed twice my size. I fought a Frenchman before an American audience and was booed. I fought an Argentinian before my countrymen, and I was booed. It always dug deep and hurt terribly. But when I started to leave the ring [after losing to Tunney], something happened that had never happened to me before. To my surprise, I was loudly cheered; more than I had ever been cheered before. The people were cheering for me, clapping for me, calling out my name. I never realized how much I had hungered for a sound like that.”One year later, Dempsey and Tunney fought again. Tunney-Dempsey II unfolded before 104,843 fans at Soldiers Field in Chicago and generated boxing’s first $2m gate (the total was $2.7m). That encounter, which Tunney also won by decision, is best remembered for the “long count” controversy when referee Dave Barry refused to start counting until Dempsey went to a neutral corner after knocking Tunney down in round seven (the only time in Tunney’s career that he was on the canvas).But that’s a story for next September.Thomas Hauser’s email address is thomashauserwriter@gmail.com. His most recent book – a classic detective tale titledSherlock Holmes and Mrs Rutledge– is available now. In 2019, Hauser was selected for boxing’s highest honor – induction into the International Boxing Hall of Fame.Explore more on these topicsBoxingUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea have entered the realm of late-stage American sports capitalism | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: The Blues’ lack of success was no impediment to Todd Boehly and Mark Walter recouping profits from the club’s sale. That’s how things work in the US
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The Blues’ lack of success was no impediment to Todd Boehly and Mark Walter recouping profits from the club’s sale. That’s how things work in the US
Content: Chelsea fans protested against Todd Boehly’s ownership in 2024.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenChelsea fans protested against Todd Boehly’s ownership in 2024.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAChelseaAnalysisChelsea have entered the realm of late-stage American sports capitalismLeander SchaerlaeckensThe Blues’ lack of success was no impediment to Todd Boehly and Mark Walter recouping profits from the club’s sale. That’s how things work in the USWed 23 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.20 EDTShareHere follows a list of the things accomplished atChelseaFootball Club during a time that historians may choose to grandly term the First Clearlake Era, or perhaps the Boehly Bungle.Since the May 2022 purchase of the club from the sanctioned Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich, when Todd Boehly took over the club’s daily operations, Chelsea –Premier Leaguechampions as recently as 2017 and 2015, and Champions League winners in 2021 – have placed 12th, sixth, fourth and 10th in the league.After the sacking of Thomas Tuchel, the incumbent upon the takeover, five permanent and four interim managers were installed. They employfivesporting directors.Todd Boehly exits Chelsea diminished after having his fingers burnedRead moreAbout $2.37bn (£1.78bn) –with a B!– was spent on 60 new players, per Transfermarkt. The same source values Chelsea’s current first team at just $1.23bn (£920m). And when, to put it in ProfessionalBusinessGuy speak, your entire trading strategy rests on buying young players you plan to profit from later, it doesn’t seem great when you’ve spent twice as much on your portfolio of assets as it is now worth.Those signings included at least one of the Premier League’s all-time busts (Mykhailo Mudryk) and one of its worst contracts (Raheem Sterling).Chelsea set a new Premier League record for the biggest pre-tax loss.And, infamously, the clubsold its women’s team to itselfas part of some accounting shenanigans to stay on the right side of financial regulations.And now let us go through the things that were not achieved:A credible title challenge.Qualifying for European competition in two of four seasons, which ought to be the rock-bottom minimum for a club of Chelsea’s means.Building a new and larger stadium, even thoughone was mooted.All the same, Boehly will walk away after four years as chair of Chelsea – althoughhis influence had recently waned– with a profit in his bank account, or wherever it is that money men of his kind stash their cash. So too will his fellow American and minority stakeholder Mark Walter, after both mensold their 12.8% shares to Clearlake Capitallast week.Welcome to the final stage of the American ownership model, which has now enveloped most of the Premier League. At this stage, members of the billionaire class just pass stakes in teams around among themselves, always for at least a bit more than they paid. They are not stewards of their clubs and don’t see themselves as such. They feel no obvious alliance or allegiance to the fans, acting only as the current holders of the paperwork that confers financial control over a valuable asset.Come back soon Premier League, the endlessly moreish mega-product | Barney RonayRead moreAs part of the Clearlake takeover group, Boehly and Walter each bought their stakes with the club at a $3.3bn (£2.5bn) valuation and have now sold at $6.7bn (£5bn), doubling its supposed value after four chaotic years. The exiting owners made a “modest profit”, per the Financial Times. That would probably be explained by the $2.3bn (£1.75bn) investment that Boehly, Walter and the other new owners committed to when they took over the club.That they should get to exit with more money than they spent at all is instructive in a way that the exact figures involved here are not.The dirty little secret of the way American sports functions at the highest levels is that the season-to-season balance sheet is sort of immaterial. So is being competitive (unless you care about fan sentiment). The ownership class makes its money by buying a club and then holding on to it; by possessing a ultra-scarce asset for a spell, until someone else is willing to pay more for it. They may move the furniture around in the name of optimization, but the house largely remains unaltered. If the team makes a bit of money – although nothing like the sort of profit that would justify its valuation – or breaks even, then that’s dandy. If it suffers losses, that’s probably fine, too, as they will be offset, and then some, in profit from the sale.There is no correlation between price point and how well or poorly these teams have actually been run – all that matters is the premium someone else is willing to pay for an institution that has historically been as safe a bet as any. It is virtually impossible to lose money by parking it in a beloved sports team over the long term. All you have to do is not get relegated (if such a thing is even possible in your league). And so clubs, or chunks of them, are now picked up and dumped as easily as Normals like you and me might grab and ditch a stock in an online brokerage account. And with little more ceremony than anearnest press release.That’s the game England’s many legacy clubs find themselves in now. The game the Glazer family kicked off when they bought Manchester United mostly with borrowed money in 2005 for $1.47bn (£800m at the time) and then, in 2023,sold Sir Jim Ratcliffe a quarter of the clubfor about $1.6bn (£1.3bn) in cash and infrastructure investment. Which is to say that the Glazers recouped more or less the entirety of the investment they made with the money of others – even though much of it still sits on the club’s books as debt – and retained three-quarters of one of the planet’s most valuable sporting brands.This is the game Mark Walter mastered when he bought the Los Angeles Lakers for $10bn and flipped them on for $12.5bn just 14 months later, as he liquidates some of his vast sporting portfolio in the face of a federal investigation into fraud.This summer, a consortium including Amazon founder Jeff Bezosbought 30% of Liverpoolfor $2.2bn (£1.65bn) from Fenway Sports Group, which had acquired the club outright for $464m (then £300m) in 2010. That represents a 1,580% profit , in case you’re keeping score. In that light, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola really don’t sound all that expensive.That’s how things have been done stateside for decades. It is now also how things are done in England. It doesn’t drive sporting excellence or foster deeper connections with the fans that bring the club its value in the first place. The clubs now exist to make rich people richer. There’s little anyone can do about it. It sucks.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.Explore more on these topicsChelseaPremier LeagueBusinessanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Lynx clinch WNBA No 1 seed despite ‘embarrassing’ loss to Fever and Olivia Miles injury | Minnesota Lynx | The Guardian
description: Caitlin Clark had 27 points, nine assists and seven rebounds, and Kelsey Mitchell added 20 points to her WNBA single-season scoring record
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Caitlin Clark had 27 points, nine assists and seven rebounds, and Kelsey Mitchell added 20 points to her WNBA single-season scoring record
Content: Antonia Delaere and Caitlin Clark compete for the ball on Tuesday night.Photograph: Michael Conroy/APView image in fullscreenAntonia Delaere and Caitlin Clark compete for the ball on Tuesday night.Photograph: Michael Conroy/APMinnesota LynxLynx clinch WNBA No 1 seed despite ‘embarrassing’ loss to Fever and Olivia Miles injuryPortland Fire’s win hands Lynx top seed for playoffsOlivia Miles held out of lineup due to calf injuryGuardian sportand agenciesWed 23 Sep 2026 07.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCaitlin Clark had 27 points, nine assists and seven rebounds, and Kelsey Mitchell added 20 points to her WNBA single-season scoring record as the Indiana Fever beat theMinnesota Lynx96-77 on Tuesday night.It was a mixed night for the Lynx. The Portland Fire’s victory over the Golden State Valkyries later in the evening meant Minnesota have clinched the No 1 seed for the playoffs, which start Sunday. However, the Lynx were without Olivia Miles. Therecord-breaking rookiewas a late scratch because of an injured left calf, and her absence clearly had an impact. Miles broke Clark’s single-season scoring recordby a rookie against Connecticut last Sunday. Minnesota coach Cheryl Reeve said she almost held Miles out for that game and that the team would take the injury day by day as the playoffs approach.‘It’s payback time’: the WNBA-leading Lynx are on the hunt for title redemptionRead moreIndiana took control with a 14-2 run to close the first quarter while opening up a 31-16 lead. The Fever extended the margin to 38-18 quickly in the second quarter and led by as much as 57-28 the first half. That led Reeve to pull most of her starters for the second half and Minnesota forward Napheesa Collier said she was unhappy with her team’s performance on the night.“It’s embarrassing,”Collier told ESPN. “We should be disappointed and embarrassed about the product that we put on the floor tonight. Not proud of what we did.”The Fever have already clinched their place in the playoffs, and Tuesday’s win kept alive their faint hopes of earning the No 4 seed and home-court advantage in the first round for at least one more day.“We’re scary when we’re clicking,” Clark said. “Like, we’re the best offensive team in the league, and we’ve shown moments where we can be really good defensively. I feel very confident in everything and everybody that we have in this locker room, and I think for us it’s just finding a level of consistency.”Reeve had called for her team to aim at “ripping people’s hearts out, and taking momentum back”. However, after the loss to Fever, Reeve said she hoped her team would find that mindset when the team meet again on Thursday.“Well, that’s not my version of ‘F you,’” Reeve said. “So, we’ll maybe discuss that. Like, what does that mean to you? And so that would be great that maybe that might exist on Thursday.”Reeve also said that clinching home-court advantage for the playoffs did not matter to her because the Lynx are a “damn good road team”.Explore more on these topicsMinnesota LynxIndiana FeverWNBAUS sportsGolden State ValkyriesnewsShareReuse this content

title: LA 2028 triathlon course will see athletes race from Venice Beach into Pacific | LA Olympic Games 2028 | The Guardian
description: The first medals of the Los Angeles Games will be decided at Venice Beach, with triathletes racing from the sand into the Pacific Ocean
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: The first medals of the Los Angeles Games will be decided at Venice Beach, with triathletes racing from the sand into the Pacific Ocean
Content: Venice Beach will host the triathlon and road cycling events and the start of the marathon during the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Photograph: Xavier Arnau/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVenice Beach will host the triathlon and road cycling events and the start of the marathon during the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Photograph: Xavier Arnau/Getty ImagesLA Olympic Games 2028LA 2028 triathlon course will see athletes race from Venice Beach into PacificWomen’s triathlon will award first medals of GamesBeach start only second in Olympic triathlon historyBryan Armen GrahamWed 23 Sep 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first medals of the 2028Los AngelesOlympics will be doled out on the eclectic confines of Venice Beach, where organizers have unveiled a triathlon course that will send athletes racing from the sand into the Pacific Ocean.LA28 unveiled initial details of the Olympic and Paralympic triathlon routes on Wednesday, laying out a compact course through Venice that takes in the beachfront bike path, neighboring streets and the Venice Canals before finishing overlooking the coastline.The women’s individual triathlon on 15 July 2028 will produce the first medals of the Games, one day after theunprecedented dual-venue opening ceremonyat the the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum and SoFi Stadium in Inglewood. The men’s race follows on 16 July, with the mixed relay on 20 July.In a departure from the usual Olympic setup, the individual races will begin on the beach rather than from a pontoon. It will be only the second beach start in Olympic triathlon history, following the 2016 events at Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach, with athletes sprinting from the sand directly into the Pacific. They will complete a two-lap 1,500m swim – an opening 1,000m circuit followed by a 25m run along the beach and a second 500m swim.View image in fullscreenVenice Beach will host the triathlon and road cycling events and the start of the marathon during the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Photograph: Frederic J Brown/AFP/Getty ImagesFrom there, competitors will move to a largely flat 40km cycling course consisting of eight 5km laps along the Venice bike path and surrounding streets, including two technical turnaround points. Riders will pass beneath the neighborhood’s famous Venice sign before returning to the central transition area. Organizers said the course’s forgiving topography is intended to encourage fast racing.The concluding 10km run will be comprised of four 2.5km laps, again using portions of the bike path and nearby streets and taking competitors over bridges spanning the Venice Canals before a finish overlooking the Pacific.All three disciplines will revolve around a single transition and finish area where Venice Boulevard meets the sand, a configuration organizers say will allow spectators to see athletes repeatedly during the multi-lap contests.View image in fullscreenA map of the Venice Beach course for the women’s and men’s individual triathlon events at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The course features a 1,500m swim, 40km bike ride and 10km run.Illustration: LA28“With less than two years until we host the Games, we’re excited to share more with athletes, fans and our local communities about the dynamic events they will experience in the Venice Beach Zone,” said Shana Ferguson, LA28’s chief of sport and Games delivery officer.“This iconic neighborhood will add another meaningful chapter to its storied history as the first LA28 medals of the 2028 Games are awarded here.”The mixed relay will use a shorter version of the course, with each member of the four-person team completing a 350m swim, 6.6km bike ride and 1.6km run.View image in fullscreenThe 2016 Olympic triathlon gets under way from Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro. LA28 will feature only the second beach start in Olympic triathlon history.Photograph: Adam Pretty/Getty ImagesVenice will return to the spotlight a month later for the Paralympics. Para triathletes will start from a barge beyond the breakwater rather than the beach, completing a 750m swim followed by a 20km bike leg and 5km run on 18 and 19 August.The triathlon course adds to Venice’s prominent role in the 2028 Games, with the famously countercultural beachfront neighborhood also hosting the starts of the Olympic marathon and cycling road races and the Paralympic marathon.Triathlon has a particular connection to southern California. The modern version of the sport emerged in the region during the 1970s before making its Olympic debut at Sydney 2000.The Venice courses are set to receive a full-scale test next summer when a World Triathlon event will be staged there from 16-18 July, giving organizers an opportunity to assess the routes and operations a year before the Games.Explore more on these topicsLA Olympic Games 2028LA Paralympic Games 2028TriathlonAthleticsLos AngelesWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I want to go’: Lewis Hamilton hopes F1 is able to end season in Middle East | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The seven-time F1 world champion said of the proposed final two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi: ‘I personally want to go. I love going to the Middle East’
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The seven-time F1 world champion said of the proposed final two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi: ‘I personally want to go. I love going to the Middle East’
Content: Lewis Hamilton spoke to the media before the Azerbaijan Grand Prix this weekend.Photograph: Michael Potts/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton spoke to the media before the Azerbaijan Grand Prix this weekend.Photograph: Michael Potts/ShutterstockFormula One 2026‘I want to go’: Lewis Hamilton hopes F1 is able to end season in Middle East‘I love going to the Middle East,’ says Ferrari driverQatar and Abu Dhabi races could still be cancelledGiles RichardsWed 23 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton said he hopes the Formula One season can still end at the two scheduled rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, with the finale still in doubt because of the war in the Middle East.Formula One is pressing ahead with its original plan, although a contingency is understood to be in place to host a final round in Imola if the volatile situation means both meetings have to be cancelled.Speaking before this weekend’s grand prix in Azerbaijan, which borders Iran, Hamilton said he trusted the sport to make the right decision, given the unease among many in the paddock of racing in the region while the conflict continues.Spanish GP plans to change Madring after fierce criticism from F1 driversRead more“I personally want to go. I love going to the Middle East,” he said. “From what I have read, things seem OK out there, but I don’t have all the information and I don’t know what the risk levels are. I trust in Stefano [Domenicali, F1’s chief executive] to make the right decision for the sport. And I do hope we get to go there.”Whether the races take place or not could affect the world championship.Kimi Antonelli leadshis Mercedes teammate George Russell by 81 points with nine meetings remaining. If that number was reduced to eight the Italian could close it out even sooner than might be expected. As things stand a lead of 100 points after Mexico, in five races time, or 75 after Brazill would suffice.A decision is unlikely to be forthcoming until after Antonelli has the championship won, however, at the very least to keep the title fight alive as long as possible.In March the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian grands prixwere called offbecause of the ongoing US-Iran conflict. The Bahrain race has been moved to next weekend at Sepang in Malaysia and it is believed F1 must deliver at least 23 races to meet its commitments to broadcasters, meaning the cancellation of Qatar and Abu Dhabi would make a finale at Imola imperative.The promoters of the races are bullish that they will go ahead but are always reluctant to cancel as they would still be liable for the race fee payable to F1. If the sport cancels, the fees do not have to be paid.Abu Dhabi organisers have gone as far as confirming musical acts set to perform including Zara Larsson, the Script, Imagine Dragons and Lewis Capaldi. However, that the situation was far from settled was illustrated this week when Larsson said she would not be performing.Responding to a post on social media asking her: “Please read about what UAE is doing to Sudan then cancel your Abu Dhabi show,” the Swedish singer posted: “I will not be going to Abu Dhabi.”This was later deleted but Larsson did go on to confirm she would not perform at the meeting. “Maybe it came off as a impulsive response to a comment,” she said. “But I have spent some time thinking about everything and decided that to not do the show aligns with me the most right now, for many different personal reasons beyond politics.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Lewis HamiltonFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cristiano Ronaldo vows to play on for Portugal and targets 1,000 career goals | Portugal | The Guardian
description: Cristiano Ronaldo said he considered quitting international football after the World Cup, but did not and now aims to reach 1,000 goals for club and country
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Cristiano Ronaldo said he considered quitting international football after the World Cup, but did not and now aims to reach 1,000 goals for club and country
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo said: ‘The Portuguese count on me. That’s why I’m still here … Just look at the numbers.’Photograph: Antonio Pedro Santos/EPAView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo said: ‘The Portuguese count on me. That’s why I’m still here … Just look at the numbers.’Photograph: Antonio Pedro Santos/EPAPortugalCristiano Ronaldo vows to play on for Portugal and targets 1,000 career goalsPlayer reflects on critics, says ‘they’ve tried to kill me’Jorge Jesus launches passionate defence of 41-year-oldBen Fisherin LisbonWed 23 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 16.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo said heconsidered quitting international footballafter the World Cup, but confirmed he plans to play on for Portugal and hopes to reach 1,000 goals for club and country. Ronaldo, who is 21 goals shy of the milestone, accepted some critics are trying to “kill” him but is determined to carry on.Ronaldo, who has won 233 caps for his country, captainedPortugalin the summer at the World Cup, where they exited to Spain in the last 16. Asked if he considered walking away from international duty, he replied: “Yes, I did. Of course, I’m always thinking about my decisions, my future, the present also. I’m a thinker; you have to think. This is why you see me here now, it means I will continue.‘Have some humanity’: Diogo Jota chants at Rúben Neves a wake-up call for Saudi ArabiaRead more“I had a conversation with our president [Pedro Proença], with our coach. I still believe that I’m able to help the national team to reach what they want. I think I can give the national team my support, not only through the goals, but also outside of football. There is a new young generation, but for me the basic point is to be able on the pitch to score the goals and to help the team win games.“Whenever they say they don’t want me in the national team, I will be the first one to go. When I think I am not adding anything to the team, or that I create an atmosphere, I will be the first to go. I will take my suitcase and leave. The Portuguese count on me. That’s why I’m still here … Just look at the numbers, I’m sure you can make some calculations, I’m still doing well. The day they don’t count on me, no problemo, I will leave. I will always be the No 1 fan of this federation.”Jorge Jesus, the Portugal head coach who managed Ronaldo at Al-Nassr, said the 41-year-old would start in his first game in charge, against Wales in theNations Leagueon Thursday. Jesus, who has succeeded Roberto Martínez, also launched a passionate defence of Ronaldo, drawing applause from many in attendance at Portugal’s City of Football complex in Lisbon.Quick GuideBellamy remembers 'president' Ronaldo's arrivalShowCraig Bellamy said Wales must enjoy facing “heavyweight” opposition in Portugal on Thursday and colourfully recalled being stuck at Lisbon airport because it was on lockdown to ensure Cristiano Ronaldo a “president-like” arrival.Bellamy (pictured) twice visited the city on pre-season camps with Burnley, where he worked as assistant to Vincent Kompany for two years. “He is beyond a superstar,” the Wales manager said of the Portugal captain, whom he shared a pitch with in the Premier League almost 18 years ago, when Ronaldo, who turns 42 in February, scored twice in a 2-0 win for Manchester United at home to West Ham.“There were rows of police cars everywhere,” Bellamy said of the moment he realised the airport was on lockdown. “We were like: ‘Something’s happened. We thought it was a security breach. We were stuck on the coach for about 10, 15 minutes. ‘When are we going to get off the coach?’ Suddenly this car turns up – I’ll be doing it a disservice but it was a Bentley or something like that – and parks in this parking slot, this guy walks out the front, goes to the boot, grabs this rucksack, and this other kid comes out the front, puts the rucksack on. Who is it? Ronaldo.“Even the police are like [trying to look at Ronaldo] but no one could bother him. It was the coolest walk I’ve ever watched. For a minute, we were on the coach just jaws dropped. ‘Everyone who is moaning? Shut up.’ We don’t mind. We’re watching this … it was like president stuff. How can you lock off a whole airport? I won’t even be able to get my computer through customs at Cardiff. What have I just seen?”Bellamy was effusive in his praise for Portugal’s all-time record goalscorer, who is closing on 1,000 goals for club and country. “Who gets 1,000 goals?” the 47-year-old said. “Seriously? It’s just silly, eh? I hope he gets it – but I hope he gets nothing on Thursday. We’re talking about one of the greatest players of all generations – his name will go down in history for hundreds and hundreds of years.”Ben FisherPhotograph: José Sena Goulão/LUSAWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“Cristiano is a symbol of Portugal and the national team,” said Jesus, sitting alongside Ronaldo at the Portugal federation’s campus. “If he will play the games, he is not entitled to that, it is up to the manager to decide.”Ronaldo cut a relaxed figure on stage alongside Jesus. “For me the most important thing is I know what I am,” he said. “I know what I do to be here, I know what I have done to have the success that I have had. I know why young kids love Cristiano, because they see me as an example, and I will continue to do that. Even when I am retired … in 10 years.“I’m happy with myself. It doesn’t matter if I play tomorrow, if I’m rested for the next game, for me the most important thing is that I feel good. The people around me, they trust in my work. Focus on the people who love Cristiano, not the people who criticise me, so I am a happy person.”Asked directly about the criticism, Ronaldo triggered laughter from many in the room by replying: “I cannot be 100% honest, sometimes I have to be politically correct.” He added: “I do understand that some TV channels like to criticise me, they’ve tried to kill me – with a shotgun – but I can still move away from it. Anyway, I am used to it. I have been doing this for more than 20 years, I’m quite used to it. What I can control, I will. What I can’t, I won’t.”View image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo attends a training session before the Nations League group stage match against Wales.Photograph: Rodrigo Antunes/EPAOn Thursday Ronaldo will return to the Estadio José Alvalade, where he began his career with Sporting, before joining Manchester United in 2003. It is Portugal’s first game in Lisbon since beating the Republic of Ireland in a World Cup qualifier last October.“It’s a special feeling because it was there where my beautiful history started,” Ronaldo said. “I’m very proud about that, to play for the national team after so many years, playing where I practically was opened to the world … It was a beautiful moment.“It is always a pleasure to play for the national team, to wear the colours of Portugal. After so many years, it is [still always] like the first time. I will step on to the pitch with passion, emotion. I hope we can get off on the right foot. Because it’s at Sporting, it does feel a bit more special.“It would be the cherry on the top of the cake to score my 1,000th goal with the national team. It would be the culmination of a beautiful story. I said I wanted to reach that target and I will reach that target. But I don’t have an obsession. If you are obsessed with something, you won’t get it … Just enjoy. Carpe diem, enjoy the day.”Explore more on these topicsPortugalCristiano RonaldoWalesNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham signals he may lift ban on alcohol in football stands | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Prime minister says measure is discriminatory when fans of other sports are not similarly restricted
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Prime minister says measure is discriminatory when fans of other sports are not similarly restricted
Content: Andy Burnham with Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, at Everton’s stadium last week.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, at Everton’s stadium last week.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesSoccerAndy Burnham signals he may lift ban on alcohol in football standsPrime minister says measure is discriminatory when fans of other sports are not similarly restrictedPippa CrerarandTom GarryWed 23 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has signalled he may lift the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, suggesting it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports.The prime minister, a committedEverton fanwho still attends matches, said there was a case for trialling an end to the ban to bring football in line with rugby and cricket.The move was welcomed by the Football Supporters’ Association and the English Football League, but police warned it would be “incredibly rash” to make changes without considering their impact on safety.Burnham has long opposed the ban, saying it is discriminatory and out of date, harking back to an era when football violence was fuelled by drinking within view of the pitch.Asked by reporters on the planeto New Yorkabout lifting a ban, Burnham said: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination.“There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”The Sporting Events (Control ofAlcoholetc) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales.The fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the ban to be re-examined and suggested piloting the sale of alcohol within sight of the pitch in lower-tier English football.A spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit, which coordinates football policing policy in England and Wales, said: “The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.“Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor report [of 1990 into the causes of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster] for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster. It would be incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area.”A spokesperson for the English Football League said it would be “receptive” to a review of legislation that “was introduced more than 40 years ago and has not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding”.Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters’ Association, said: “The FSA has always argued that it’s unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We welcome the prime minister’s comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed. We look forward to being part of that consultation.”Supporters at Women’s Super League and WSL2 matches have been permitted to drink alcohol in view of the pitch since the start of this season, after a successful 18-month trial period led to a change to the WSL’s regulations this summer, allowing clubs – but not obliging them – to give fans that option.Since that rule change, 25 of the 26 clubs across the two divisions of English women’s football have decided to take up the option at all of their home games. The only exception is Brighton & Hove Albion’s home matches at Crawley’s Broadfield Stadium, but Brighton have permitted fans to drink in view of the pitch when the team play their home matches at the Amex Stadium, such as last Sunday when they hosted Aston Villa. Women’s matches have typically seen fewer incidents of crowd trouble.Explore more on these topicsFootballAlcoholPoliceAndy BurnhamLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Kaptein fantastic strikes as Chelsea battle to WCL win over Austria Vienna | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Wieke Kaptein’s goal after 11 minutes was enough to secure victory for Chelsea in their league-phase opener, with Keira Walsh’s early withdrawal a concern
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Wieke Kaptein’s goal after 11 minutes was enough to secure victory for Chelsea in their league-phase opener, with Keira Walsh’s early withdrawal a concern
Content: Wieke Kaptein (left) and Veerle Buurman celebrate after the former’s decisive goal.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenWieke Kaptein (left) and Veerle Buurman celebrate after the former’s decisive goal.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersWomen's Champions LeagueKaptein fantastic strikes as Chelsea battle to WCL win over Austria ViennaSuzanne Wrackat the Cherry Red Records StadiumWed 23 Sep 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWieke Kaptein’s early goal gave Chelsea a winning start to their Champions League campaign proper against Austria Vienna, but it was a far from comfortable evening for them.“Probably the performance is not the one we wanted to have,” Chelsea’s manager, Sonia Bompastor, said. “We could have controlled the game a little bit better in terms of scoring a second goal to kill the opposition’s hope, but sometimes you need to focus on what is most important and tonight that was to win and to take the three points from the game.”Caldentey’s late penalty provides WCL relief for struggling Arsenal against KøgeRead moreA David v Goliath endeavour welcomed the visiting team at the Cherry Red Records Stadium and they rose to the challenge. The mammoth financial gulf between the two teams was highlighted in the buildup by the Austrian broadcaster ORF, which reported: “Chelsea Women’s personnel costs alone for the 2024-25 season, at a cool €17m, were higher than those of the entire Austria club (€14.9m) – including the men’s department, by far the largest item.” Meanwhile, Uefa noted that the manager, Stefan Kenesei, has a full-time job in state pensions insurance.Ultimately, the gap in quality on the pitch looked far smaller than the finances suggested. Aware of that possibility, Bompastor did not take any risks and made only three changes to the team that secured a 2-0 win against Birmingham on Saturday, despite Arsenal up next on Sunday at Stamford Bridge.It was a statement of intent from a team desperate to get their hands on the only club trophy to elude them and they were right to be cautious. As the Danish side HB Køge showed against Arsenal on Tuesday night, Champions League minnows can cause big problems.“The physicality from those [lower-ranked] teams is good,” Bompastor said. “The players are able to match the intensity of the Champions League games from the beginning of the game until the end, as you could see tonight. I also think the coaches who are coaching those teams are good in terms of the tactical aspects. When they come into this game, they are really well prepared and they have a good game plan. So, nothing is easy.”A moment of magic from the Dutch midfielder Kaptein gave the host side the breathing space of an early lead 11 minutes in. The 21-year-old was quickest to the loose ball after a slick sliding tackle from Katharina Schiechtl dispossessed Melvine Malard and she sent a rising strike in off the underside of the bar from 25 yards.View image in fullscreenSonia Bompastor, the Chelsea manager, shouts instructions from the sidelines.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAAustria Vienna responded rather than folding, threatening until the final whistle while supported vocally by the small block of travelling fans who appreciated the efforts of the underdogs. Set pieces and the forward Modesta Uka were their best outlets. Uka’s close control provided both an attacking threat and gave her teammates a reprieve from chasing.The threat from Uka had been evident in the Austrian side’s qualifying campaign. The Kosovan scored in their 3-2 win against Hajduk Split and scored another two in their 5-0 victory against Farul Constanta in the second qualifying round, before grabbing a hat-trick in a 4-0 win against the Norwegian side Brann to overturn a 2-1 away defeat in the third round and secure their place in the league phase.“She’s a great player and she deserves to play at this level, just as the whole team does,” Kenesei said. “She deserves to play in the Champions League and we’ve seen today how much potential there is.”The longer the game went without Bompastor’s side building on their lead, the more confident the players in white became. Just shy of the 70th minute there was another tense moment for the host side, when pressure from the ever-bright Uka forced Veerle Buurman into an error. Katie McCabe looked to have clipped the Austria Vienna player, who seemed to have beaten her to the ball, but a pause after the ball went out of play did not lead to an intervention from the video assistant referee.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrustrations boiled over a little at the close, when Almedina Sisic re‑entered the field without waiting a minute after receiving some treatment, with Bompastor forced to hold back her enraged assistant, Camille Abily, before giving the fourth official a piece of her mind.Quick GuideRoundup: Lyon hit eight, Barça rally past Paris FCShowMarie-Antoinette Katoto [pictured] scored a hat-trick asLyonnesthrashedServette8-0 in their opening league phase game of the Women’s Champions League. Katoto’s treble, Melchie Dumornay’s double and two own goals from the Swiss hosts saw Lyonnes go top of the early standings with a crushing display.The eight-times winners went ahead eight minutes in through Laia Balleste’s own goal before Katoto took control. The France striker bagged her first of the night in the 28th minute and added a second 12 minutes later. Dumornay’s chipped finish gave Lyon a four-goal advantage at the break and just two minutes after the restart, Katoto completed her treble from Lily Yohanes' backheeled pass.Dumornay added her second in the 54th minute and Laura Strik’s own goal piled more misery on Swiss champions Servette, who conceded again in the 89th minute when Ines Benyahia struck. In Wednesday's other early kick-off,Romasubstitute Marta Pandini hit the post with a stoppage-time penalty as they were held to a 0-0 draw atOH Leuven.Ewa Pajor’s double helped holdersBarcelonaget off to a winning start as they came back from behind to beatParis FC5-2. Barça were handed an initial scare when Evelyne Viens put Paris in front only five minutes in, but Kerolin replied for the hosts with a tidy finish in the 18th minute.Clara Serrajordi put Barca ahead 10 minutes later, kicking off a destructive 15 minute-period for the hosts, which saw Pajor and Caroline Graham Hansen strike.Pajor struck again in the 70th minute, before the visitors pulled one back through Clara Mateo as Barça comfortably saw out the win.Lyonnes host Chelsea next Wednesday in their second league-phase game, while Barcelona visit Roma and Paris FC welcome Arsenal.PA MediaPhotograph: Pierre Albouy/REUTERSWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.In the end, it is a testament to the visiting team that they will leave London extremely disappointed not to have taken anything from a game that gave them opportunity after opportunity to do so.“Yes, we’re proud,” Kenesei said. “We were brave as we’d planned, really, but to be honest I’m also disappointed that we didn’t get at least one point. We saw what you all saw today, that we performed at almost the same level as Chelsea.”Chelsea can breathe easy, although Keira Walsh’s precautionary early withdrawal with a quad issue will be a concern, but they have a job to do to snuff out those chances before they face teams that will capitalise and punish them.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueChelsea WomenAustria Vienna WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Netherlands v Germany: Klopp and Xavi begin revival projects with derby | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Jürgen Klopp and Xavi Hernández face each other in Nations League as they take the reins following disappointing World Cups
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Jürgen Klopp and Xavi Hernández face each other in Nations League as they take the reins following disappointing World Cups
Content: Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp (left) and Netherlands head coach Xavi Hernandez.Composite: Getty Images; EPAView image in fullscreenGermany head coach Jürgen Klopp (left) and Netherlands head coach Xavi Hernandez.Composite: Getty Images; EPANations LeagueNetherlands v Germany: Klopp and Xavi begin revival projects with derbyJürgen Klopp and Xavi Hernández face each other in Nations League as they take the reins following disappointing World CupsNick AmesWed 23 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore the latest instalment of a time-honoured international rivalry gearing up for two distinct new beginnings,Jürgen Kloppcould not resist sprinkling a little of the old mischief. “The good thing is that we both have the exact same situation,” he said of Xavi Hernández, his counterpart when Germany visit the Netherlands on Thursday night. “We met on Monday and play on Thursday. And the coach knows the players from television. I actually know more of the Dutch players personally than Xavi does. Whether that’s an advantage, I don’t know, but it’s still a fact.”Jürgen Klopp vows to change Germany but threatens to quit if family hounded by mediaRead moreIn his public appearances Klopp has been on irrepressible form since taking the role in July. The task of whippingGermanyback into shape has visibly and audibly topped up the energy levels that had drained by the time he departed Liverpool. Klopp, his wit sharp and appetite piqued, looks a far cry from the character who, to most trained eyes, was going through the motions upon his unveiling as Red Bull’s head of global soccer early last year.Securing Klopp was a coup for the German football federation even if it came with a caveat, issued within seconds of his introduction to the media, that he would not be seen for dust if his family were hounded by the media. Xavi’s arrival in Amsterdam is no less fascinating even if, in the Dutch way, no bones were made by his employers about the fact Pep Guardiola and Arne Slot had been higher in their sightsafter Ronald Koeman’s departure. He is the Netherlands’ first foreign manager since Ernst Happel’s 10-month stint ended in 1978 but the fit is instinctively pleasing. Even if Guardiola was out of reach, they could land upon another product of the Johan Cruyff school that created modern-day Barcelona.View image in fullscreenXavi’s captain is Virgil van Dijk, who considered international retirement after the World Cup.Photograph: Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP/Getty ImagesIf Xavi is to take theNetherlands, occasionally exciting but frequently unstable during a World Cup run that shuddered to a halt in the last 32, back to their roots it will require a measure of patience. The pool of players does not allow much else; the recall of Borussia Dortmund’s Joey Veerman, who has not played international football for more than two years, speaks of the need for a technically adept midfield fulcrum but otherwise Xavi has scant scope for surprises. Virgil van Dijk will continue as captain despite considering international retirement during the summer; the head coach’s options may feel more complete when Frenkie de Jong and Donyell Malen have returned from injury.Xavi has resisted any temptation to engage in analysis of the Netherlands’ performance in the United States. “I don’t talk about the past,” is the standard line, ironically an easier one to roll out if theNations Leagueopener in Amsterdam brings a performance redolent of headier times. The revolution may have to be conducted with minimal effusive pronouncements from the coach. It is certainly a less dramatic shake-up than the one Klopp, acting like a man licensed to break a few moulds, has enacted before the next fortnight’s four-game baptism.It raised eyebrows when Klopp named a squad of 44 players for the matches against the Netherlands, Serbia and, home and away, Greece. The expanded unit will be split into two: half will play on Thursday and in Germany’s next game, at home against the Greeks, and the remainder will be involved in the second two games. Only Finn Dahmen, the Augsburg goalkeeper, will be required across the set.“I want to get to know as many players as possible,” Klopp said. “There is no A or B team. The squads are put together in a way that makes sense on the pitch and in terms of character and experience.”View image in fullscreenThe goalkeeper Finn Dahmen (centre) is the only player on call for all four Germany matches.Photograph: Federico Gambarini/DPA/APClub managers feeling squeamish at their players’ workloads during this expanded break will immediately have warmed to Klopp’s split selection. But the priority is to discover who best fits his vision for an intensely committed, front-footed, enthusiasticNationalmannschaftthat places round pegs, even unexpected ones, in round holes. Four players from Freiburg have made his sprawling selection; so has Felix Keidel from promoted Elversberg. Mika Baur of Celtic and the Hoffenheim winger Bambasé Conté were both stunned to receive first call-ups. The Brentford midfielder Vitaly Janelt joins his teammate Kevin Schade in the fray.
