Sixteen are uncapped.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCanale and Gill the heroes as Paraguay hand Germany first World Cup shootout defeatRead moreLast weekend Klopp and his coaching staff convened at their headquarters in Herzogenaurach to watch as many of their charges’ domestic games as possible in one go. Freiburg’s Max Rosenfelder, one of the new brood, acknowledged the aura surrounding Klopp and described him as “a very, very special person”. Even if the mixed lineups prove to lack experience and cohesion, Klopp hopes his charges’ sheer thirst for the task will lift Germany from the doldrums of their most recent World Cup flop.If he can unite 44 players, why not a whole country? Among Klopp’s many recent pronouncements was the timely intervention in favour of “positive patriotism” that followed an election victory by the anti‑immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party in Saxony‑Anhalt. If it is some time since Germany’s football team have been at their best, perhaps the same may be said for the nation too.In the Dutch capital, two big‑name managers will take their first steps towards bringing the good times back. “It could be a bit wild, but I accept that, it just has to be lively,” Klopp said. That comes with something approaching a cast‑iron guarantee.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueNetherlandsGermanyJürgen KloppfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Christian Eriksen leaves Wolfsburg by mutual consent after on-pitch collapse in June | Christian Eriksen | The Guardian
description: Christian Eriksen and VfL Wolfsburg have ended his contract by mutual consent after the 34-year-old collapsed during a Denmark friendly in June
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Christian Eriksen and VfL Wolfsburg have ended his contract by mutual consent after the 34-year-old collapsed during a Denmark friendly in June
Content: Christian Eriksen playing for Wolfsburg in March.Photograph: Andreas Gora/APView image in fullscreenChristian Eriksen playing for Wolfsburg in March.Photograph: Andreas Gora/APChristian EriksenChristian Eriksen leaves Wolfsburg by mutual consent after on-pitch collapse in JuneDanish midfielder has been recuperating in homelandEriksen: ‘I’m pleased we were able to find a solution’Reuters andGuardian sportWed 23 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristian Eriksen and the German side VfL Wolfsburg have agreed to terminate ⁠his contract by mutual consent, the club announced on Wednesday.The 34-year-oldcollapsed during a Denmark friendly ⁠against Ukrainein June. Eriksen said in July he would ​return to his homeland to undergo a ‌rehabilitation programme. He previously suffered a cardiac arrest during Denmark’s opening Euro 2020 group match ⁠against Finland in Copenhagen in 2021.Florian Wirtz does not look like a £116m player but it is early to write him offRead moreThe decision brings ⁠an early end ⁠to ​Eriksen’s contract, which was set to run until June 2027. The midfielder joinedWolfsburgas a free agent a year ago, making 34 appearances across all competitions. Eriksen scored three goals and provided 10 assists for the Wolves, but could not prevent their relegation from the Bundesliga.“At the moment, it is important for me to ‌be close to my family inDenmark. I’m pleased that we were able to find a solution together,” Eriksen said in a statement. “My time in Wolfsburg was marked by many highs and lows,” he added. “I know that the club is now ‌in good hands as it aims to make its way back to the Bundesliga, and I am convinced ​that a successful future lies ahead for VfL.”The Wolfsburg ⁠managing director of sport, Dieter Hecking, said the second-tier club granted ​Eriksen’s request to ​cancel the agreement. His last appearance for the team came in May’s promotion/relegation playoff defeat by Paderborn.“He has already ​experienced and achieved a great deal during his ​extraordinary career,” ‌Hecking said. “Despite his ​short time ​here, he has left a lasting impression on his teammates, our staff and the fans.”Eriksen played for Ajax, Tottenham and Inter before his on-pitch collapse in 2021. He was fitted with an implantable cardioverter-­defibrillator (ICD) device, but had to leave Inter because Serie A rules prohibit playing with a pacemaker.View image in fullscreenDenmark and Ukraine players gather around Christian Eriksen after his collapse in June.Photograph: Bo Amstrup/Ritzau Scanpix Foto/APAfter joining Brentford in 2022, Eriksen spent three years at Manchester United before joining Wolfsburg last summer.He said in Junethat his ICD device “did what it was designed to do” after he collapsed on the pitch for a second time.“Receiving a shock from my ICD has had a major impact on both me and my family, but I want to reassure everyone that this was a different situation from what happened in 2021,” Eriksen posted on social media.“I am feeling good, and my recovery has already started. I am incredibly grateful to the doctors who have cared for me and my heart over the years. Thanks to their expertise, my ICD did exactly what it was designed to do: protect me when I needed it.”Explore more on these topicsChristian EriksenWolfsburgEuropean club footballDenmarknewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United report seventh straight annual loss and sell fans £125 grass clumps | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Manchester United reported their seventh straight annual ⁠loss but ⁠forecast record revenue of between £740m and £760m for the next financial year
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Manchester United reported their seventh straight annual ⁠loss but ⁠forecast record revenue of between £740m and £760m for the next financial year
Content: Manchester United’s wage bill was down £11.3m, or 3.6%, on the previous year.Photograph: Paul Currie/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenManchester United’s wage bill was down £11.3m, or 3.6%, on the previous year.Photograph: Paul Currie/ShutterstockManchester UnitedManchester United report seventh straight annual loss and sell fans £125 grass clumpsNet loss of £43m for year ended 30 June 2026Revenue hits record £677.6m and forecast to growMatt HughesWed 23 Sep 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United have reported an annual loss for the seventh ­successive year, taking the club’s combined losses to £444m since 2019.The financial results were released as it emerged United are raising revenue by selling small clumps of grass from the Old Trafford pitch to supporters. United relaid the playing surface for the first time in 14 years this summer,and an email to fans has offered them the chance to buy 7cm x 7cm clumps of turf for £125.The £43m net loss for 2025-26 is a significant increase on the £33m for the previous 12 months, with compensation paid to the sacked manager Ruben Amorim a contributory factor along with the decision to increase the club’s borrowing facility by £93m to help fund the redevelopment of Old Trafford.Slip sliding away: football season-ticket holders fear falling down pecking orderRead moreUnited’s continued losses come despite record revenue of £677.6m – up 1.7% on the previous 12 months – and the implementation of a major cost-cutting regime by Sir Jim Ratcliffe under which hundreds of staff have lost their jobs.In discussing United’s results on an investor call, the chief executive, Omar Berrada, said the club’s summer transfer window, during which they spent £155m on three players, had been planned with “financial sustainability in mind” in an indication that the budget will continue to be tight for newthe manager, Michael Carrick.That is underlined by the fact that United’s wage bill dropped to £301m, down 3.6% on the previous year, more than £100m lower than Manchester City’s.While United reported operating profits of £22.6m for the 12 months to 30 June 2026 the increase in revenue was more than offset by the cost of financing the club. Net finance costs more than tripled to £69.2m from £21.2m in the previous year, partly owing to foreign-exchange ­movements, and the club refinanced several loans, increasing their net debt from £471.9m to £577.6m.United sources have said the refinancing provided funding for the £63.5m purchase of a plot of land next to Old Trafford required to build their proposed new 100,000 capacity stadium, the first major investment in a complex project that could end up costing more than £2bn.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBerrada said the results demonstrated “the underlying strength of our business, particularly in a season without European football” and said: “This shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years. It also proves Manchester United’s enduring popularity and commercial strength. While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.”United are confident their financial outlook will improve over the next 12 months owing to the club’s return to the Champions League and the start of increased sponsorship deals with the training-kit partner Betway and shirt-sleeve partner SumUp, which will bring in £20m and £22m a year respectively. The club is forecasting revenue of between £740m and £760m for 2026-27.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedFinancesBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ireland manager gets prime minister Martin’s backing in row with Israel over ‘genocide’ | Republic of Ireland | The Guardian
description: Micheál Martin has backed his country’s football manager, Heimir Hallgrimsson, who was accused by Israel’s football federation of ‘stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Micheál Martin has backed his country’s football manager, Heimir Hallgrimsson, who was accused by Israel’s football federation of ‘stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy’
Content: Heimir Hallgrímsson addresses the media on Wednesday.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHeimir Hallgrímsson addresses the media on Wednesday.Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesRepublic of IrelandIreland manager gets prime minister Martin’s backing in row with Israel over ‘genocide’Heimir Hallgrímsson accused of ‘stupidity’ by Israel’s FAMicheál Martin says IFA’s response is ‘unacceptable’Agence France-PresseWed 23 Sep 2026 05.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 07.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIreland’s prime minister, Micheál Martin, backed his country’s football manager, Heimir Hallgrímsson, after Israel’s football federation accused Hallgrimsson of “stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy” over comments about the war in Gaza.“I think those are unacceptable remarks; they should be withdrawn,” Martin told reporters in New York, where he is attending the UN general assembly. “Israel can’t keep denying what the world knows, and what the world understands.”Hallgrímsson sparked the row after saying before twoNations Leaguefixtures against Israel: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide. We’re playing against Israel, we’re not playing with Israel.”Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Martin said Hallgrímsson’s comments reflected concerns about the scale of death and destruction inGaza, also citing remarks by the UN secretary general, António Guterres.On Wednesday Hallgrímsson, preparing for Thursday’s game in Kosovo, expressed gratitude for Martin’s backing. “What I said at the last press meeting has taken the attention away from maybe what’s most important; we are playing an important game against Kosovo,” Hallgrimsson said.“Maybe, from a ‌leadership point of view, not clever for me to take the attention like this. But to answer the question, we are thankful for all the support we get. It’s a tricky time for ​us.“The dispute comes amid mounting controversy in the Republic over the fixtures, scheduled for 27 September and 4 October. More than 160 Irish sportspeople have signed an open letter calling on the national team to boycott the matches, and protesters gathered outside the team’s Dublin hotel on Monday. Further protests are planned around the country in the run-up to the games.The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) passed a motion last November requesting that European football governing body, Uefa, suspend Israel from international competition. The FAI has said it has little choice but to fulfil the fixtures or risk sporting and financial sanctions.Ireland’s designated home match on 4 October was moved from Dublin’s Aviva Stadium to Backa Topola, Serbia, after concerns over disruption and security. The 27 September match, officially Israel’s home fixture, will also be played at a neutral venue, in Debrecen, Hungary.Israel strongly rejects allegations that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide. Hamas led the deadliest attack against Israel on 7 October 2023 when militants killed 1,221 people and dragged into Gaza 251 hostages, 44 of them already dead, according to Israeli official figures.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsrael launched a massive retaliatory offensive that has displaced virtually the entire population at least once and has killed 73,919 people, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are generally considered reliable.Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause, with sympathy for Palestinians often linked to the country’s history of British rule. Dublin formally recognised a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway and has repeatedly criticised Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsRepublic of IrelandIsrael (Football)Israel (World news)GazaNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Florian Wirtz does not look like a £116m player but it’s too early to write him off | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: The 23-year-old playmaker has been disappointing for Liverpool but has he really been that bad?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 23-year-old playmaker has been disappointing for Liverpool but has he really been that bad?
Content: The numbers show that fans and pundits should give Florian Wirtz more time.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe numbers show that fans and pundits should give Florian Wirtz more time.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesGuardian Sport NetworkLiverpoolFlorian Wirtz does not look like a £116m player but it’s too early to write him offThe 23-year-old playmaker has been disappointing for Liverpool but has he really been that bad?ByOpta AnalystDavid SegarWed 23 Sep 2026 09.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 16.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenFlorian Wirtz signed for Liverpoolin the summer of 2025, there was only one logical assumption. The Premier League champions at the time had recruited one of the hottest young talents in world football – a key player in the Bayer Leverkusen team that had won the double in 2023-24 and a star in the Germany team. An exciting and productive young attacking midfielder being added to the best team in England? How could this notwork?Football has a habit of flipping the script, though. Last season was difficult forLiverpoolfor several reasons, and Wirtz, along with other new arrivals, struggled to make the impact expected of a player costing up to £116m. There were conversations among fans this summer about how long he and his fellow nine-figure signing Alexander Isak should be given before difficult questions needed be asked. The consensus was until Christmas.As it turned out, the real answer was after the opening game as Wirtz and Isak laboured inLiverpool’s 2-2 draw at Newcastleand loud doubts began to surface. Jamie Carragher spoke on the first Monday Night Football of the season about Wirtz’s signing in 2025 potentially being part of the “worst transfer window in Premier League history”.The former Liverpool defender was criticising a few players – and Isak has since gone on to score four times in hislast four league appearancesto quieten his doubters – but Carragher focused his ire on Wirtz again on Sunday in a new podcast for Sky Sports.“The reason I worry is, I don’t think Wirtz is in poor form since he came to Liverpool. I think what we’re seeing is what he is,” he said. “The worry for Wirtz now is that what he’s given Liverpool is so low. Where we were expecting him was to take Liverpool to another league title, to take Liverpool to a Champions League. The gap he’s got to close to justify what people were expecting I almost think is too big. You can’t get there. Even if he improves a bit, it’s still not what Liverpool thought they were getting. AndoniIraola’s got a decision to make here. Wirtz would not be in my Liverpool team.”Carragher derided Wirtz – who has just one assist in six games this season – for his performance in the team’s1-0 win at Bournemouth, calling it “one of the poorest I’ve ever seen him in a Liverpool shirt”. Iraola was more generous, though, and accepted that the German had struggled in the first half. “He started the game slowly,” Iraola said. “After that first phase, we improved. Florian has helped us also to improve. Second half he was playing much better, he was finding better spots to receive and turn. I’m much more happy with his second half.”Wirtz’s numbers from the game were not that bad. He created three chances, the joint-most of any Liverpool player along with Cody Gakpo; he won six of his eight duels; and he won possession four times: only Alexis Mac Allister (seven), Ronald Araújo (six), and Jérémy Jacquet (six) won the ball more often for the visitors.Perhaps we should not be saying this, being Opta and all, but data does not always tell the whole story. Anyone watching the game could see a player struggling to impose himself, with several passes not finding the target. Only 26 of Wirtz’s 37 attempted passes reached a teammate (70.3%). That is not unusual for a creative midfielder but there were too many simple balls sloppily overhit or played too close to Bournemouth defenders.View image in fullscreenWirtz received a lot of criticism for giving the ball away; he lost possession 15 times before leaving the pitch in the 71st minute. Only Araújo (24) and Gakpo (16) did so more often, though they both played the whole game. That said, “possession lost” is a tricky statistic to hang your hat on, as creative players who play risky passes in the busiest areas of the pitch often find themselves losing the ball the most.He also made a near-post run in the second half that led to the ball dropping kindly for Isak to score the winner. It did not go down as an assist as it touched a defender on the way to Isak but, without Wirtz’s run, the goal would not have happened. He also showed some nice moments, even in the first half. He drifted through defenders before winning a free-kick on the edge of the Bournemouth penalty area early on, while a classy one-touch layoff to Isak could have been a nice assist if the striker hadn’t sent his shot high and wide.Expectations were greater for Wirtz, though. He was meant to take games by the scruff of the neck and decide them with moments of brilliance like he did at Leverkusen. Suggestions that Wirtz maybe just isn’t good enough to be the player he was expected to be in the Premier League seem harsh, though. There was hype around his arrival for very good reason.View image in fullscreenAfter joining Leverkusen from Cologne at the age of 16, he recorded 18 goals and 21 assists in 69 games in his first two full seasons. Wirtz tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his left knee in March 2022, though, and missed 10 months of action.He showed no ill effects on his return, playing a central role in one of the most incredible campaigns by a team in recent years. Leverkusen won their first Bundesliga title, becoming the first team to go unbeaten over a league season in the German top flight. They also won the DFB-Pokal, and reached the Europa League final, where adefeat to Atalantawas their only loss in any competition across the entire campaign.Wirtz recorded 18 goals and 19 assists in 47 games that season; the only player from Europe’s top five leagues to record at least 16 goals and 16 assists in all competitions. He produced 16 goals and 14 assists in his final season before heading to England, with only Mohamed Salah (18) and Lamine Yamal (13) getting more than his 12 assists from open play among players from Europe’s top five leagues.However, he recorded only seven goals and eight assists in 49 games in his first season at Liverpool, and it took until late December to register his first league goal as the champions struggled, ultimately limping home in fifth place and ending the campaign without a trophy. To be fair, it was a hard environment to come into. The death of Diogo Jota cast a dark cloud over the club and Arne Slot struggled to get his team playing anywhere near as coherently as they had the previous year.View image in fullscreenWirtz was far from terrible, though. He was by some considerable distance Liverpool’s most creative outlet in open play, which helped after the loss of Trent Alexander-Arnold. He created 95 chances from open play in all competitions, at least 27 more than any other Liverpool player. But there was no denying that it was a disappointing debut season for him.The World Cup was a chance to show he could do it on the big stage and he managed three assists in four games for Germany before they wereeliminated on penalties by Paraguay in the last 32. Only two players at the tournament had more assists at the end of that round, and only five players created more chances from open play than his nine. Despite that, he still bore the brunt of criticism from many in Germany for their underwhelming showing, such are the standards expected of him.View image in fullscreenWith a pre-season under Iraola, though, there was hope that a new system and a fresh start would help. You could argue he has played pretty well in at least two of his six appearances so far this season. Liverpool were not great in the2-2 home draw with Nottingham Forest, but Wirtz was their main threat, denied what would have been a well-taken goal by an offside call against Jeremie Frimpong, and playing a neat pass into Víctor Muñoz for their second equaliser.He was also impressive in the2-1 home win over Atlético Madridin the Champions League, and would have had another assist had Bradley Barcola not dragged his shot wide when sent through on goal by some sharp play by Wirtz.While he struggled to make much of an impact in games against Newcastle, Ipswich Town and Fulham, those “what if” moments have been a theme. Wirtz was not great in the 2-0 win at Ipswich, but he did produce a fine turn and cross for Isak to score what would have been his hat-trick goal, only for the flag to deny him by the narrowest of margins.Wirtz has at least been trying to make a difference in possession. He has made 19 progressive passes in the league this season (joint 16th), level with Martin Ødegaard and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. He has also made 43 line-breaking passes at a rate of 9.6 per 90, almost double his 5.2 per 90 in the Premier League last season.Another area where there has been an increase, numbers-wise, from Wirtz this season is off the ball. He has won possession in the opposition’s final third six times in the Premier League; only five players have done so more often, while only five have applied more pressures than him (419) and only six have received more pressures (260), showing that he is doing his work out of possession and is occupying defenders in possession. He ranked joint 12th, 21st and 27th in the Premier League for each metric, respectively, last season.Wirtz has also covered the most distance of Liverpool players in three of his five Premier League games, but it is his lack of impact on the ball that seems to have most people taking aim. He has been underwhelming, but six appearances into a new season seems early to be making damning conclusions. Things have barely got going under Iraola, and Liverpool as a team are clearly still several rungs below their potential.Slip sliding away: football season-ticket holders fear falling down pecking orderRead moreWirtz is a 23-year-old trying to find his feet in the strongest league in the world and, while there is no denying that he’s far from his best, that doesn’t mean improvement is impossible, or even unlikely.The eye-watering fee is undoubtedly a factor for the critics. Whether fair or not, players are judged against how much they cost. Paul Pogba was hardly a success story at Manchester United, but the criticism often felt over the top, mostly because of his £93m fee and the hype that followed his return to Old Trafford in 2016.The big question is can Wirtz ever show more in England? Undeniably world-class players have failed to do so in the past, including another highly rated former Bayer Leverkusen midfielder in Michael Ballack, who never really found his best form in a Chelsea shirt after his move from Bayern Munich in 2006. Patience has been shown, and more is required for now. It still feels too soon for sweeping statements and loud conclusions.This is an article byOpta AnalystExplore more on these topicsLiverpoolGuardian Sport NetworkAndoni IraolaJamie CarragherEuropean club footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I had a headache for days’: Hrgovic reveals brutal toll of Itauma world title fight | Boxing | The Guardian
description: The Croat, who shocked Moses Itauma to win the IBF heavyweight title last month, said: ‘I didn’t celebrate. I went home to rest. It was such a hard fight’
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: The Croat, who shocked Moses Itauma to win the IBF heavyweight title last month, said: ‘I didn’t celebrate. I went home to rest. It was such a hard fight’
Content: Filip Hrgovic said he ‘received a lot of shots and was bruised’ during his win against Moses Itauma.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenFilip Hrgovic said he ‘received a lot of shots and was bruised’ during his win against Moses Itauma.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersBoxing‘I had a headache for days’: Hrgovic reveals brutal toll of Itauma world title fight‘I didn’t celebrate. I went home to rest. It was a hard fight’Hrgovic stopped Briton to win the IBF heavyweight titleDonald McRaeWed 23 Sep 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilip Hrgovic, the new IBF world heavyweight champion, has offered a candid insight into the ordeal he endured beforebeating Moses Itaumain a shock stoppage victory last month, revealing he absorbed so many heavy punches in the first eight rounds that he felt headaches for a number of days afterwards.“I felt fucked up,” said the 34-year-old Croat. “I received a lot of shots and I was bruised. I had a bit of a headache for a few days. On the Wednesday after the fight I was back in the gym, working out already, but for a few days I felt really tired and bruised, with some headaches.”Jack Dempsey v Gene Tunney at 100: when a great champion met his greatest inquisitorRead moreHrgovic, who aims to unify the heavyweight division, said there was a chance he would faceRico Verhoeven, the Dutch fighterwho used to be a world kickboxing champion, on the undercard to the much-delayed bout between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury that is expected to finally take place in Cardiff on 11 December.But revisiting the aftermath of the brutal Itauma bout which changed his life, Hrgovic said: “I didn’t celebrate. I just went home to rest. It was such a hard fight I didn’t even do my tradition after I win, when I go to McDonald’s. I didn’t have the strength.”Hrgovic believes Itauma is so skilful that, if he learns from his painful defeat, the 21-year-old British prodigy can become unbeatable: “He’s really good. He’s special. Very fast, very talented and he countered whatever I tried with his speed and timing. I never was in the ring before with such a talented kid, with such a fast guy. You have some fast guys but they’re small heavyweights. You can handle them with your power but this kid is fast and big. He’s got great IQ and great talent. If he recovers from this loss, mentally, it will be hard for anyone to ever beat him again.”View image in fullscreenFilip Hrgovic said ‘it will be hard for anyone to ever beat him [Moses Itauma] again’ if he recovers from his first defeat.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersItauma is a complex character and Hrgovic suggested that doubts remain about his mentality. “We’ll see. It was a big shock for him, a big humiliation, so maybe it’s the end of his career if he’s not mentally tough.“A lot of people, after that kind of loss, never come back. It will be a hard journey for him to come back but if he recovers and he does not lose his confidence then, with this experience, I think no one will ever beat him again.”Since his shattering defeat, attention has focused on a comment Itauma made before the fight which implied that he has never sparred for 12 successive rounds. Hrgovic said: “It’s not about physical preparation. It’s about experience and mentality. If we go for a run now, or we’re in the gym together, he’s in tremendous shape. He will beat me in every exercise, running, hitting the heavy bag. I think he was physically ready but it’s the mental part. It’s experience.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHrgovic, however, compared his own preparation with the less hard-edged approach of Itauma. “You have to go through a ruthless, hard training camp. You need to go through hell to be mentally ready for this shit. Old school is the best school. I told Itauma this before the fight. He’s drinking water, hugging trees in the morning, saying hello to the sun. He does a lot of this bullshit. He’s surrounded by 10,000 yes-men, nutritionists and a coach for sleeping. You can’t get ready for a war this way.”An exhausted Itauma ran out of energy, after setting a blistering pace, and he was overwhelmed in the ninth round. But the new champion said: “I’m still kind of angry because he outboxed me. In my whole career, in 20 years of boxing, I was never outboxed in any sparring or any fight. I was always competitive. But this kid outboxed me. On that night, I think he will beat anyone apart from myself. But that night I refused to lose.”Hrgovic is relishing his rise to world champion: “If I knew it would be so good I would have won the championship before. It’s amazing to be world champion. I want to unify the division and stay here as long as possible. I feel great.”Explore more on these topicsBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Prem agrees to revamp refereeing in boost for England’s Rugby World Cup hopes | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: Steve Borthwick has secured a boost for the World Cup next year, with an overhaul in the refereeing of Prem matches for the coming season designed to help England’s hopes
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Steve Borthwick has secured a boost for the World Cup next year, with an overhaul in the refereeing of Prem matches for the coming season designed to help England’s hopes
Content: Steve Borthwick is seeking to mount a challenge to the supremacy of South Africa at the World Cup in Australia.Photograph: Alex Livesey/The RFU Collection/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSteve Borthwick is seeking to mount a challenge to the supremacy of South Africa at the World Cup in Australia.Photograph: Alex Livesey/The RFU Collection/Getty ImagesRugby unionPrem agrees to revamp refereeing in boost for England’s Rugby World Cup hopesLeague agrees new interpretations to help BorthwickScrum and breakdown targeted as areas of inconsistencyExclusive byGerard MeagherWed 23 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSteve Borthwick has secured a boost to his preparations for the World Cup next year, with an overhaul in the refereeing of Prem matches for the coming season designed to help England’s hopes in Australia.The Guardian understands that in the formal absence of relegation from the Prem for the first time this season, agreement has been reached over a number of law interpretations that will better align officiating in club matches with the international game.Prem Rugby 2026-27: the essential club-by-club guide to the new seasonRead moreThe areas that will be policed differently include the offside line as well as the scrum – specifically the brake-foot law – as England’s head coach seeks to mount a challenge to the supremacy of South Africa at the World Cup in Australia next year. Borthwick has also previously lamented how differently the breakdown is refereed in the Prem – in which there tends to be less of a contest – than the international stage. Indeed, the breakdown was a frequent problem during England’s miserable Six Nations campaign, whilethe four-Test series between South Africa and New Zealandover the summer highlighted the ferocity with which elite nations are contesting that area of the game.It is understood that Borthwick met the directors of rugby last month and a presentation was given by the Rugby Football Union’s refereeing team on the intended law interpretations. England’s scrum has markedly improved since the appointment of Borthwick, under the guidance of the assistant coach Tom Harrison.Borthwick, however, will be mindful of how dominant South Africa, who have won the past two World Cup tournaments, are in that facet of the game and how influential it was in their series win against New Zealand.Interestingly it was Karl Dickson, one of the RFU’s professional officials, who twice penalised the All Blacks hooker Codie Taylor for brake‑foot infringements in the fourth Test in Baltimore. The brake-foot law was introduced in 2022 as a safety measure and requires the hooker to position one foot forward before engagement at the scrum. The New Zealand assistant coach Neil Barnes said afterwards that it is a law “which no one really gives a shit about, but the referees are concentrating on”.View image in fullscreenNew law interpretations around the breakdown and scrum will aid England players such as Northampton’s Henry Pollock.Photograph: Garry Bowden/ShutterstockIn February it was announced that the coming season, which begins on Friday with Northampton hosting Newcastle and Harlequins facing Bath, would bethe first in which the Prem is formally a closed league. It is understood that the absence of the jeopardy of relegation has been a significant factor in allowing for the aligned law interpretations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Prem director of rugby told the Guardian: “The standard and the intensity of the Prem has increased. At international level the speed is quicker than it is in the Prem. The physicality is more intense and then there’s the nature and style and strategy of the game. That comes down in part to how it’s refereed and we had a conversation around the product we want to get out there and the nuances and interpretations of the laws. Can we align that with international refereeing?”Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSteve BorthwickEngland rugby union teamPrem RugbynewsShareReuse this content

title: New UK agency to fight ‘information warfare’ from likes of Russia, Burnham tells UN | Cyberwar | The Guardian
description: PM aims to ‘stem poisonous tide’ of disinformation and deepfakes with National Centre for Information Defence
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: PM aims to ‘stem poisonous tide’ of disinformation and deepfakes with National Centre for Information Defence
Content: 2:18Andy Burnham calls out Russia as a hostile actor in misinformation war during UN address – videoCyberwarNew UK agency to fight ‘information warfare’ from likes of Russia, Burnham tells UNPM aims to ‘stem poisonous tide’ of disinformation and deepfakes with National Centre for Information DefencePippa Crerarin New YorkWed 23 Sep 2026 03.52 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecurity chiefs will set up a new national centre to tackle disinformation and deepfakes from hostile states such as Russia, Andy Burnham has announced, saying the government had a duty to “stem the poisonous tide” from damaging British interests.The National Centre for Information Defence will “detect, attribute and disrupt” information attacks by foreign powers, many of which are enabled byAI, bringing together the intelligence agencies, law enforcement and social media companies.It will be tasked with making sure the UK has the defensive capability necessary to combatinformation warfareand build national resilience by helping communities to identify and combat disinformation, preventing a “distorted and untrue” narrative about the UK.Burnham said the country would have to go into the next decade “eyes wide open” about “insidious” campaigns, many of which had been orchestrated by Russia, which “twisted” what people at home felt about their own country and community.In eye-catching remarks, the prime minister suggested that Britons who were struggling with the cost of living and young people not in education, training or employment may be particularly susceptible to foreign influence online, underlining how inequality further undermined society.11:31Has Burnham proved he can handle Trump? - The LatestIn his speech to the UN in New York on Tuesday night, Burnham said: “We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair.“On top of that, we have seencyber-attacks on our companies and institutions. We know that AI will multiply the threat. We have tiptoed around this for too long. Over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality. Well, no more.“We are going to face the new decade in a different way – with our eyes wide open. We are going to be much prouder in standing up for our values and the rule of law. And we are going to help our people to strengthen their resilience – because, faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home.”Burnham’s speech came after Donald Trump – during a press conference at the UN with Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy – said that Keir Starmer’s rhetoric had been“too tough” towards Moscowand that London “needs to be a little bit careful”.Downing Street pushed back on the US president’s remarks, saying that every UK prime minister – up to and including Burnham – had been consistent in the view that Russia’s threats, whether hybrid attacks or rhetoric, were “egregious and unacceptable”.“The UK is united with our allies on the importance of defending ourselves, and Russia’s aggression will not deter us from supporting Ukraine,” the prime minister’s official spokesperson added.View image in fullscreenDowning Street pushed back on comments by Donald Trump, who met Andy Burnham on Tuesday, that previous UK government rhetoric had been ‘too tough’ towards Moscow.Photograph: Toby Melville/Pool Reuters/APIn his speech, Burnham singled out Russia, saying the Kremlin spent around £1.3bn each year on manipulating information.“Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears. They’ve used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles,” he said.“Forged the branding of 28 British organisations – including universities and the BBC. They’ve amplified far-right narratives. And we have evidence that they tried tointerfere with the 2019 general election.Russia-linked accounts spread far-right narrative online during Ceuta migration crisis, analysis findsRead more“We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events. The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive – but it is what they do.”The prime minister suggested that certain groups of people who felt their own lives were not improving may be more vulnerable to disinformation and deepfakes.“If you’re struggling with the cost of living and your life is not improving – or if you’re a young person not in employment, education or training – then you are going to be much more vulnerable to this kind of influence,” he said.“So part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need. When inequalities grow too wide, our societies are at greater risk. So we will work to make life more affordable. And we will put in place the architecture we need to stem this poisonous tide.”The UK plans to share its experience of being on the receiving end of information attack with other countries, and has already supported Moldova, for example, to protect its elections from Russian interference.“As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues – some for the first time. So we’re ready to share our understanding of how these actors work, and how we can respond – because this is vital for our collective security and resilience,” Burnham added.Emily Thornberry, the chair of the foreign affairs select committee, said: “I’m absolutely delighted the prime minister has announced a new centre to tackle the threat of disinformation, which was the major recommendation of the foreign affairs committee’s March 2026 disinformation diplomacy report.“For too long, the approach of successive governments to disinformation has been disjointed and without organisation, allowing states like Russia to amplify lies about this country, to sow division and stoke tensions. This new National Centre for Information Defence is an opportunity to finally take on this very serious threat.”Explore more on these topicsCyberwarDeepfakeAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI | Technology | The Guardian
description: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting
Content: Google's AI mode is advertised on 30 October 2025 in London, United Kingdom.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGoogle's AI mode is advertised on 30 October 2025 in London, United Kingdom.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesTechnology‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AIA feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shiftingBlake MontgomeryWed 23 Sep 2026 15.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 15.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a featureGooglecalls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting.“AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search,last August. In May, the company saidmore AI is coming.As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Academic studies are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Media outlets and website owners are enduring a sustained traffic decline. Large US media companiesare suingGoogle, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue.Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume fromGoogleSearch to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.”The Guardian asked readers whether Google has improved or worsened in the age of AI and how their habits of searching the internet have changed.‘Google is better now’Better, mainly because it leads you in your quest rather than you having to search on yourself. I am happy to have the AI lead me to an answer but the mega caution is that Google AI or any of them are not at all trustworthy. I have had it admit that it was lying to me and apologise!Sionn Achog, retired teacher 76, DublinI find that AI responses are more informative than previously, which simply referred the user to other relevant websites.Peter Warb, 75, UKAI has made Google better. I use AI mode for all my searches.Jose Garcia Jr, 40, recovery coach, Dallas, TexasView image in fullscreenJose GarciaAI has improved Google search. The analysis and chat functions are so much more useful than a ranked list of websites that still need to be explored by the user. Reviewing a list of websites is still an option but is very time consuming, and frustrating.Alan Caruana, consultant, 62, MaltaFar more better, faster and real. I search now with confidence, complete assurance and a high degree of accuracy.Eleazar Eke, electrical engineer, 67, Onitsha, NigeriaMuch better. It hasn’t changed my behavior, just getting better and more focused results.Catherine Weber, former political analyst, 57, OregonIt’s made Google search much better, I find that I rarely actually click on the website links any more. I find information I want much faster and have a deeper understanding of any topic as I can ask questions about it and drill into the areas I’m interested in.Mark Johnson, 52, software engineer, LondonGreatly improved it by getting at more arcane info regarding subject matter. Juxtaposition has improved with AI and abstruse knowledge of subjects becomes more accessible to layman. Wonderful tool with power to extend mind through sensing connections and very akin to human thinking.Samuel Lieberstein, 90, retired teacher, Cherry Hill, New Jersey‘Search has gotten worse’Search has become worse. Google AI obscures sources and tries to claim information it did not create while diverting traffic from the sources it steals from.Sean Peters, document processor, 41, Portland, Oregonskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSean Peters.Every time I search I have to scroll down to find an actual real website to find a full article or discussion or to confirm that the AI summary isn’t making things up. Occasionally when I am feeling particularly bitter, I remember to add the ““-ai”” tag to my search.Ewan Herbert, English teacher, 33, JapanWorse. I have disabled AI overviews using an extension.Chris Gibson, DundeeAbsolutely worse. I want to be able to decide for myself which results are the most useful and relevant, and we’re no longer able to turn off the AI summary results.Jon Wilkinson, personal trainer, 43, Manchester, UKView image in fullscreenJon Wilkinson.‘It’s so bad I quit Google’Google has been enshittified … I do miss old Google Search and I really hope something of equal capabilities eventually comes to replace it.The search engine I currently use is good for a lot of things, but if I need to look for something in languages other than English, the quality of the results is much lower. Image search is also not as good as that of Google used to be.Sofia, postdoctoral physics researcher, 30, Lausanne, SwitzerlandMy first stop now is Duck Duck Go, a pale imitation of Google’s search engine at the height of its powers. Unfortunately, the top results often include Grokipedia entries and other garbage.Craig Garrett, book editor, 52, New York CityView image in fullscreenCraig Garrett.I have stopped using Google. I now use another search engine with no AI overviews.Guy Arthur Simpson, writer 66, SpainI’ve made a conscious effort to find a browser which does not lead with the AI results. Mine is now Ecosia.Dan Jennings, IT, 54, Southampton, UKI do a lot of research for my studies, and the AI features are a nightmare! I’m still scouring for a decent search engine without any of these ‘AI features’, the last thing i want is to accidentally utilise a water-wasting AI behemoth datacentre when I forget that crucial suffix. I’ve even resorted to using my local library’s resource of legal cases for my work, at least it is trustworthy.Catherine O’Leary,student studyinglaw,politics andsociology, 17, Newcastle Upon TyneGoogle has become almost useless, searches I’ve made in the past which yielded specific results, (news articles, local information, historical references) no longer appear. I no longer submit to Google search first, I go directly to Wikipedia as my first source, then to DuckDuckGo, (with AI disabled) then to Reddit and only to Google as a last resort.Pedro Reyes, 61, Galicia, SpainExplore more on these topicsTechnologyGoogleSearch enginesAI (artificial intelligence)News websitesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplay | Games | The Guardian
description: From highlighted ledges to characters telling you what to do, blockbuster games are increasingly taking the challenge out of playing – and players are pushing back
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: From highlighted ledges to characters telling you what to do, blockbuster games are increasingly taking the challenge out of playing – and players are pushing back
Content: No friction … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyView image in fullscreenNo friction … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWhy fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplayFrom highlighted ledges to characters telling you what to do, blockbuster games are increasingly taking the challenge out of playing – and players are pushing backDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 23 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarvel’s Wolverine, the latest action game from Sony’s stable of expensive blockbuster-factory studios, has had an unfortunate launch.Reviews were decent, if not stellar, but a series of viral video clips from reviewers and streamers have made it the scapegoat for a patronising flavour of game design that gamers have hated for decades.This clip, from Skill Up’s review, shows the player entering a beautiful wintry landscape before being overwhelmed by visual cues telling them what they’re supposed to be doing there. Sonar pulses point you in the direction of objectives. Targets – which, it bears emphasising, areshaped like targets– get an extra reflective visual effect so you know you’re supposed to pay attention to them. A trail shows you not just where to go, but where the level’s sole hidden collectible is.It is hand-holding to the point of parody. Indeed, it reminded me of the sniggersomeMario in Unreal Enginesatiricalvideosthat makes the social media rounds every few months (“A mushroom? I should take a look at this”). Skill Up’s clip has been followed by hundreds of others, gleefully ripping into Wolverine with ironic savagery. In one much-copied clip, a streamer simply lays down his controller during a motorbike chase sequence and watches as Wolverine speeds on regardless, bouncing off the scenery as the game plays itself.People really detest this kind of thing. It’s impossible to pinpoint exactly when big-budget games started assuming that players were irredeemably stupid, but throughout the late 00s and 2010s it became more and more common to see obvious GPS trails showing you where to go, and for characters to talk to themselves to remind you what to do. At the same time, there’s been a cyclical discussion over the difficulty of games: every time a notably challenging game comes out, we rehash the same talking points about whether all games should have easy modes. Is it acceptable for games to shut players out if they aren’t prepared to “git gud”?I am not a game designer, but as a critic wholoves challenging gamesand has thought a lot about them, for me there is a difference between a game’s difficulty and its friction. A game might be difficult for all kinds of reasons, intentional or otherwise: perhaps the controls or camera aren’t great; perhaps there’s a mid-game boss with a bafflingly massive health bar and one devastating unblockable attack; perhaps the balancing is off. But a game’s friction is always an intentional part of its design. Friction is about how much a game helps you achieve its tasks. Games with perfect friction are clear about showing you what to do, but not overbearing about helping you do it: there is intentional distance, distance that you must broach with agency, strategy and skill. Friction leaves space for frustration and learning, and a sense of achievement.View image in fullscreen‘A game is only fun if you have to do something’ … 007 First Light.Photograph: IO Interactive A/SA lot of modern blockbuster game design seems hellbent on removing this friction. Not sure where to go? Here – follow this brightly coloured trail of fart gas. Not sure how to climb that building? We’ve helpfully painted the ledges yellow. Have you stood still for 30 seconds? We’ll have another character talk in your ear and tell you exactly what you need to do. Playing through the opening hours of007 First Lightrecently, I was dismayed when Bond inevitably acquired a watch that magically highlights important things in his vicinity with the press of a button.At its best, game design like this helps players avoid becoming irrevocably stuck. At its worst, it totally removes agency and challenge – you know, the reasons that many of us play games in the first place. Fundamentally, a game is only fun if you have to do something. I don’t play games for passive entertainment. That’s what binge-watching Netflix is for. If you don’t have to invest anything to reap the rewards, the experience just washes over you.Games can be difficult and have high friction. InHollow Knight: Silksong, you are constantly figuring out what to do, where the next boss might be, how to open that tantalisingly blocked path. Achieving those goals is then also very challenging, requiring practice and mastery of whip-fast fighting and precise jumping. Or they can be high-friction, low-difficulty:Blue Princetells you literally nothing about how to make your way to its mansion’s secret 46th room, but it’s not difficult to walk around and try out ideas. An example of a low-friction, high-difficulty game, meanwhile, would be a combat-focused one likeDevil May Cry(or most shooters), where the aim is always “kill all the guys to open the next area” but actually killing all those guys is majorly demanding.Low-friction, low-difficulty games hold very little interest. Many mobile games fall into this category, where you barely have to do anything save prod the screen to provoke a dopamine-shower of flashy visual effects (I’m looking at you, Monopoly Go). It’s unfair to lump Wolverine in with these almost entirely valueless games – but it is instructive that it has been subjected to such ridicule.The infamously challengingDark Souls, a dramatically influential game that turned 15 years old this week, seemed to remind the entire games industry that you canactually trust players: that they won’t drop the controller and storm off as soon as they get skewered by a skeleton. That there’s immense and unique pleasure in participatingin a game, unravelling it, conquering it little by little with skill and understanding. I hope that the reaction to Wolverine will serve as another reminder of that fact, for any executives who need to hear it.What to playView image in fullscreenPsychosocial dread … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnKonami’s horror series is on a roll lately. The Silent Hill 2 remake was very well received (with a few exceptions,including our critic), last year’s feminist, small-town Japanese horror story Silent Hill: f was excellent, and nowSilent Hill: Townfallhas succeeded in sending the series to a new setting: an island off the Scottish coast. Per our reviewerLewis Gordon: “This is a taut, smart tale, less about psychosexual terror than psychosocial dread… Townfall seems to understand that some things should remain shrouded in fog. The fate of St Amelia naturally festers in our imagination. How very Silent Hill.”Available on:PS5, Xbox, PCEstimated playtime:12-15 hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenPikachu in spaaaaaace … a toy Pikachu floats inside the International Space Station.Photograph: S Adenot/ESA/NASA/SWNSPikachuisnow an astronaut, thanks to a collaboration between Pokémon and the European Space Agency as part of the franchise’s seemingly endless series of 30th birthday celebrations. Human astronaut Sophie Adenaut brought a Pikachu plush up to the International Space Station, where it spent 67 days in orbit.According to Sonic Team boss Takashi Iizuka, Sega was once poised to kill off the wholeSonicfranchise. It was the success of 2020’s live-action Sonic movie that saved it. “I had to fight within the organization to keep the franchise as long as possible,” he toldOne More Game.The newResident Evil movieis out, and it’sgoing down well. Aftermathdescribesit as like watching your inept stoner roommate play the games; certified horror-game enjoyer Keith Stuart says it’s one of the best video game adaptations he’s seen.The Tokyo Game Showhad to wrap up one day early last week due to an incoming typhoon. Gamesindustry.biz has a slightly depressingrundownof the show, which was heavily dominated by AI.There have been yet moredramatic changesat Microsoft’sXboxdivision. The company is all but closing Halo Studios and moving Halo’s development to Activision, which will also now be in charge of storied British studio Rare. Multi-BAFTA-winning studio Ninja Theory is starting consultations on a proposed closure, having failed to find a funding deal to return itself to independence.What to clickSilent Hill: Townfall – shame and suffering on the Scottish coast | ★★★★☆Resident Evil – Zach Cregger’s rebooted action horror is a wild rollercoaster ride | ★★★★☆Control Resonant – save New York from paranormal phenomena | ★★★☆☆Roman Sands RE:Build – marooned in a crumbling vaporwave dream | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenSurreally European … Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.Photograph: Kepler InteractiveReaderMikeasks:“I just finished reading your article about the GameCube, which ironically got me thinking about the PS1 & 2, marvellous machines which I remember fondly. The game I got bundled with my PS2 was ‘Shadow of Memories’ which sticks with me to this day, the story was magnificent and also beautifully rendered, with multiple endings. Are there any similar ‘timeywimey’ games set in beautiful European villages, evoking memories of this game, out there today? Either on Android or PS5?”This question unearthed a bunch of half-remembered fragments from the early days of the PS2 – I definitely played Shadow of Memories as well. It’s a Konami game about a young German travelling through time, trying to solve his own murder. You mentioned games available on PS5, so here are a few that have some of the same elements. TheLife is Strangeseries is set in the US but has a similar time-travel and murder-solving premise;Clair Obscuris a very different kind of game but is as uniquely and surreally European; this year’s Japanese RPGThe Adventures of Elliotinvolves travelling through different eras to prevent a catastrophe. None of these have the same strange adventure-game atmosphere as Shadow of Memories, though – that’s something that felt really specific to the PS2 era. Readers, have you any more suggestions for Mike?If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter –email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterMarvelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Andy Burnham’s accusation against the Kremlin tells half the story. Domestic extremists amplified by US big tech are part of the same problem
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Andy Burnham’s accusation against the Kremlin tells half the story. Domestic extremists amplified by US big tech are part of the same problem
Content: Elon Musk addressing crowds at a rally organised By the far-right activist Tommy Robinson in London in 2025.Photograph: Grant Rooney Premium/AlamyView image in fullscreenElon Musk addressing crowds at a rally organised By the far-right activist Tommy Robinson in London in 2025.Photograph: Grant Rooney Premium/AlamyOpinionCyberwarThe Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicityEditorialAndy Burnham’s accusation against the Kremlin tells half the story. Domestic extremists amplified by US big tech are part of the same problemWed 23 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareIn November 2020, Barack Obama warned of an “epistemological crisis” facing western democracies. Polarisation and radicalisation were corroding trust in established information sources. “If we do not have the capacity to distinguish what’s true from what’s false, then by definition the marketplace of ideas doesn’t work,” the former US president said.That vulnerability has grown since then. Democracy’s enemies have become more determined to exploit it. This is the threat that Andy Burnham highlighted in a speech at the United Nations this week. The prime ministeraccused Russiaof waging an “industrial-scale assault” on the UK’s information environment using bot armies and fake websites to spread falsehoods, interfere in elections, foment discord and poison inter-community relations.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetThe prime minister announced the creation of a National Centre for Information Defence to thwart campaigns of epistemological sabotage by hostile actors. It is an overdue enhancement of Britain’s civil defence capabilities.Mr Burnham is right to highlight the threat, but he told only part of the story. The Kremlin would be wasting its money pumping out disinformation if large US tech platforms didn’t provide convenient channels for the toxin to spread, if there weren’t a complicit audience in Britain sharing the offending material and if the market for spreading pernicious propaganda weren’t so lucrative. Information warfare is only effective when it exploits structural vulnerabilities in the target society. Far-right material sowing hatred against migrants is most fruitful where the terrain has been fertilised by domestic politics.Earlier this year,analysis by the Guardianfound that more than half of accounts on X that were posting about racially aggravated riots in Belfast and civil disorder in Southampton were based outside the UK. Seven of the most-read tweets originated in the US, including one posted by X’s proprietor, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man.Mr Musk has been assiduous in promoting a warped, dystopian idea of Britain as a failed state whose culture is being corroded by mass migration. His platform has been invaluable to far-right activists who have mustered gangs of masked men into mobs that obstruct roads, intimidate people and threaten asylum claimants at British ports. Last year, Mr Muskaddressed a rallyorganised by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, where he called for the Labour government to be removed. Earlier this year, Mr Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon,travelled to Moscowon a trip funded by the Musk Foundation. He said the purpose of the trip was to “see the beauty of a civilised society”.Mr Burnham did not address that side of the anti‑democracy equation in his speech, perhaps because he felt that it would be impolitic to impugn US big tech under the president’s nose. Mr Trump is also an originator and disseminator of falsehoods online, but the nature of transatlantic diplomacy prevents a UK prime minister confronting him with that record.Under the circumstances, it made sense for Mr Burnham to concentrate his remarks on the threat from the Kremlin, but that must not signal the limit of his policy focus. British democracy is indeed under attack fromRussia, but an effective campaign to build resilience has to recognise also the complicity of domestic extremists and the digital privileges they enjoy thanks to US technology companies.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the future of the UN: more embattled, but more necessary, than ever | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: As the secretary general, António Guterres, prepares to step down, the general assembly is highlighting the scale of the organisation’s challenges
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: As the secretary general, António Guterres, prepares to step down, the general assembly is highlighting the scale of the organisation’s challenges
Content: The UN headquarters in New York City, US. ‘It remains an essential forum, not least for smaller countries to coordinate and campaign.’Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UN headquarters in New York City, US. ‘It remains an essential forum, not least for smaller countries to coordinate and campaign.’Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesOpinionUnited NationsThe Guardian view on the future of the UN: more embattled, but more necessary, than everEditorialAs the secretary general, António Guterres, prepares to step down, the general assembly is highlighting the scale of the organisation’s challengesWed 23 Sep 2026 13.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareThe United Nations was created,its charter states, to “save succeeding generations from the scourge of war”. Donald Trump used his address to the general assembly tothreaten Iran, another member state, with annihilation again. The charter also speaks of the obligations of international law. On Venezuela, Mr Trumpgloatedthat “to the victor belong the spoils”. His speech in New York on Tuesday might be regarded as an improvement onlast year’sonly in that it was not an explicit, full-scale attack on the UN itself, merely on its founding principles.The absences this year are perhaps as telling as the US president’s hostile presence. Vladimir Putin has not attended for more than a decade. Nor has Xi Jinping – but the snub is more striking ashe is in Washingtonto meet the US president. India’s Narendra Modi is not present; nor are Cyril Ramaphosa, Bola Tinubu or Abdel Fatah al-Sisi – the leaders of Africa’s three giants, South Africa, Nigeria and Egypt. While their reasons are various, the gaps speak collectively to Mr Trump’s wrecking capability and the broader challenges faced by the UN.View image in fullscreenAntónio Guterres.Photograph: Bianca Otero/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockIn a world where “cracks have become canyons”,to quote António Guterres, the body is more necessary than ever, and under greater strain. The outgoing secretary general has struggled with a “might is right” world: an authoritarian resurgence, the rising tide of conflict and a deadlocked security council. Mr Trump sought to supplant the UN with his “Board of Peace” for Gaza before largely losing interest. Even the biggest champions of multilateralism, such as Canada’s Mark Carney, are looking primarily to other mechanisms rather than UN reform.With extremely limited powers, secretary generals usually fall into mediator or activist roles. Critics argue that Mr Guterres should have beenmore hands-onin diplomacy, in conflicts such as Sudan, as he was in brokering aBlack Sea grain dealin 2022. But he has been a powerful voice of conscience: early to raise the threats posed by AI, passionate in calling for climate action and heartfelt on the suffering in Gaza, Ukraine and beyond. He has also kept the organisation on its feet – no mean feat given the disappearance of essential US funding (though Washington is nowpaying some of its debt).The first female secretary general is long overdue and the informalregional rotationwould suggest that a Latin American or Caribbean figuremay succeed him; Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana have been frontrunners. But major powers may be biding their time, with serious contenders still to emerge. Observers think that there is a real possibility that a successor may not be agreed before Mr Guterres’s departure date of 31 December, underlining the UN’s challenges.Yet it remains an essential forum, not least for smaller countries to coordinate and campaign – resulting in important action on issues from landmines to global heating and its consequences. And major powers will eventually have to recognise that the case for security council reform, stressed again by Mr Guterres, cannot be ignored for ever. The charter reminds us that the UN was born from the desperation engendered by two world wars rather than a utopian dream. It endures not because of glorious successes, nor because it has avoided glaring failures, but because a world without it would be far worse. The troubles it faces are all the more reason to defend it.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous  | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like Trump
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like Trump
Content: ‘Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment.’Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment.’Photograph: David Dee Delgado/ReutersOpinionUS newsTrump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerousKenneth RothIt is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like TrumpWed 23 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 13.33 EDTShareDonald Trump’sspeechon Tuesday to the United Nations general assembly was an object lesson in his lawless rule and remarkable capacity for self-delusion. Disregarding the UNcharter’semphasis on the peaceful resolution of disputes, he doubled down on his violent unilateralism while denigrating the global issues that the UN is designed to address.For many, the headline remark was his musing about whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” ofIran. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”But it was probably less a genuine threat than a clumsy effort to influencenegotiationswhere he has little leverage. Trump is in desperate quest of some face-saving gesture that will allow him to feign “victory” and extract himself from his disastrous war of choice.He spoke of destroying the “Islamic Republic”, which might imply the Iranian military, a legitimate military target. But his reference to precluding future generations suggests he meant to threaten the Iranian people. Attacking them would be a blatant war crime.In July, he alreadyvowedto destroy Iran’s bridges or power plants – itself athreatto commit war crimes. The international criminal court (ICC) has charged four Russianmilitarycommandersfor doing precisely that in Ukraine.Trump didn’t even bother to offer a coherent rationale for his threat. Once more, he proclaimed: “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” But Tehran has long disavowed that goal.He claimed that other American presidents “just wanted to ignore” the issue. But Barack Obama negotiated adealto constrain Iran’s ability to build a nuclear weapon. Trumprippedit up, preferring his utterly counterproductive military solution, which has brought Iran farcloserto a nuclear weapon than ever before.Preposterously, Trump claimed, “when it comes to Iran,” the midterm election “doesn’t even enter my mind.” No one believes that. If the Republicans face the disastrous showing that the polls nowpredict, he knows the election will be seen as a repudiation of his arbitrary tariffs and Iran war which have fueled inflation and aggravated the affordability crisis that hebelittles.Trump also spotlighted his other acts of aggression. He celebrated the seizure of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro, emphasizing how some political prisoners have now been freed, althoughhundredsremain. But while Trump lauded his coerced deal with Venezuela’s remaining autocratic leaders to take a large chunk of the country’s oil, he said nothing about a democratic future. Instead, touting hismight-makes-rightbeliefs, he proclaimed: “To the victor belong the spoils.”He noted the newagreementon Greenland without mentioning his earlier threat to seize the territory by force even though it has long been administered by Denmark, a fellow Nato member.He raved about slaughtering drug suspects at sea, claiming they are “at war with civilization” and “should be killed … as enemy combatants”. But there isnoreal war, only a rhetorical one.Drug traffickers form a criminal cartel, not an organized force in armed conflict with the United States. They should be arrested and prosecuted, not summarily executed by drone. The killings are murders and arguablycrimes against humanity.Many of the victims were on boats registered in Columbia or Venezuela – both at the time members of the ICC. That would give the court jurisdiction over these crimes, which may bewhyTrump reprised his attack on this important institution of justice. Trump wants to be restrained only by his own warped “morality”.It has beenreportedthat Trump may soon supplement his sanctions against 13 ICC personnel – judges and prosecutors – with sanctions against the court as a whole. But that would only compound the criminality of his conduct, because retaliation against court personnel for the performance of their official duties is obstructing justice under article 70 of the court’sstatute.Trump emphasized his role as a peacemaker. “I have made peace,” he declared, as he claimed to have “settle[d] eight wars”. Yet the reality is more complicated.He said he had “ended the war in Gaza”. In fact, despite the “ceasefire”, Israel’s continuing attacks continue to raise thedeath toll. Trump mentioned his 20-point peace plan for Gaza without noting that virtually none of it has been implemented. Israel continues tokillPalestinians andblockneeded supplies, while Hamas has notdisarmed. He didn’t even bother to mouth the word “Palestinian”.Indeed, the Trump administration hasrejecteda leading candidate for the next UN secretary general because she has publicly recognized that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, suggesting that Trump will accept only future UN leaders who are willing to deny thisreality.He claimed to have “contribute[d] to peace” between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, without noting that Rwanda’s M23 militia continues tooccupylarge swathes of eastern DRC. Trump seems fine with that, so long as the murderous M23 brings the region’smineralriches to the western market.He claimed to be making progress in securing peace in Ukraine, without acknowledging his prior suggestion to reward Vladimir Putin’s aggression by having Ukraine not only cede territory already illegally occupied by Russia but tohand overadditional chunks of its territory as well.Meanwhile, Trump belittled the problems that the UN, able to convene the world’s nations, is ideally suited to address. He called the existential threat of climate change a “hoax”. Ignoring the enormousrisksposed by artificial intelligence, he attempted to relabel AI as “superintelligence” and derided efforts to regulate it as “globalist.”This week Trump meets with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Yet rather than outline the important issues to be addressed, Trump chose to self-promote: “We’re leading now over China by a lot”.Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment. It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president who excels mainly in disseminating self-promoting fantasies while flouting the most basic rules of decency. His UN speech put that all on painful display.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionUS politicsDonald TrumpUnited NationsUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyIrancommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham survived his first Trump meeting. His nice hair may have had something to do with it | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: The PM’s shiny newness could explain the easy ride he got this time. But who would dare predict the ever-shifting weather in the president’s head? asks Guardian columnist, Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The PM’s shiny newness could explain the easy ride he got this time. But who would dare predict the ever-shifting weather in the president’s head? asks Guardian columnist, Emma Brockes
