Content: Andy Burnham and Donald Trump held their first face-to-face meeting in New York.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Donald Trump held their first face-to-face meeting in New York.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamBurnham survived his first Trump meeting. His nice hair may have had something to do with itEmma BrockesThe PM’s shiny newness could explain the easy ride he got this time. But who would dare predict the ever-shifting weather in the president’s head?Wed 23 Sep 2026 07.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTShareWatching footage ofAndy Burnham at the UN general assemblyon Tuesday was like watching your child from behind a tree in the playground. Are they making friends? How normal do they seem relative to the average? How will they react when they come into contact with that hulking great child who seems to be running things? Burnham’sfirst face-to-facewith Donald Trump was billed as a knife-edge encounter that, due to the latter’s capriciousness, could go either way. In the event, it was drama-free, leaving observers to ask: was it Burnham’s brilliance or simply the weather in Trump’s head?To viewers at home, Burnham’s performance at the press conference looked like that of a man who had worked out his best approach was to go for the sheepish, slightly cheeky air of the junior partner. Burnham is 24 years younger than Trump, on top of everything else – which can afford a certain licence to the less powerful person in any exchange. At the last minute, the meeting had been moved behind closed doors and afterwards, in a windowless room at the UN, the two men appeared side by side, mirroring each other’s body language: just two guys, legs akimbo, shoulders hunched, hanging on a bench in the locker room.It was intriguing to guess what Trump saw when he looked at the UK’s new prime minister. British people can’t always parse class or regional difference in Americans and one assumes Trump can’t distinguish Burnham’s accent from that of someone from Melbourne, or Torquay. Still, something in the British prime minister’s bearing clearly appealed to him. “Thank you, Mr President,” said Burnham after Trump praised this country as “special” and Burnham’s tone – “That’s wonderful. We really appreciate that. This relationship matters so much to us” – hit just the right note of warm condescension that probably struck the president as flattery.Other factors in play: it seems ridiculous to mention, but knowing how superficial Trump is, it seems to me that Burnham’s extremely impressive coiffure for a man of his age – which appears to exist without augmentation – won’t have been missed by a US president who spends an awful lot of time on his hair.There were also a couple of contextual factors that may have given Burnham an easier ride than some other, less fortunate world leaders. First, the run-up to the meeting had seen Trump on absolutely top chaotic form while addressing delegates at the UN,threatening the destruction of Iranand going on a whimsical detour to try to get the acronym SI (“superintelligence”) as opposed to AI off the ground. Perhaps, by lunchtime, he had burned himself out and was ready for a bit of quiet time.We know Trump gets bored quicker than a toddler spoilt for toys and Burnham’s shiny newness will have, briefly, diverted him. The replacement of Keir Starmer in relatively brutal fashion also gave Trump an opportunity to do something he loves more than anything else in this world, which is to kick a person when they’re down. When asked about recent rockiness in US-UK relations, the president replied, “No, I thinkthey’re up … well, they’re more up now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.” In that moment, one saw a tiny endorphin rush of meanness light up his face.And finally, I guess, the president is fresh out of friends at the moment, as thefight with Canada continuesand he falls out with his European friend Giorgia Meloni,formerly known as the “Trump whisperer”. As a result, Burnham was lavished with the highest praise Trump can summon, namely: “I think he’s a natural businessperson.” An astute reader of weakness, he perhaps sensed in Burnham someone more sure of himself than Starmer was. And the prime minister passed Trump’s do-you-think-you’re-better-than-me? test, in which anyone who displays any kind of overt intellectual curiosity is instantly a threat to be vanquished. Even his name, Andy, gives regular-guy vibes that probably helped.Burnham weathered all this with equanimity, although it was tempting to detect behind his poker face the shadow of a smirk while, surely, he thought to himself, “God, this guy”. “News is fake!” said Trump, and,in reference to the Chagos Islands, “they’re a very important piece of real estate!” Meanwhile, Burnham smiled slightly as if appeasing a lunatic. “He gets it,” said Trump and for once, one had to agree.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionDonald TrumpUnited NationscommentShareReuse this content

title: The climate fight has one great ally. You just can’t look at it directly  | Bill McKibben | The Guardian
description: There is hope in solar power. As the UN meets, we are urging leaders to pursue a clear goal: clean energy for all by 2030
Author: Bill McKibben
Headline: There is hope in solar power. As the UN meets, we are urging leaders to pursue a clear goal: clean energy for all by 2030
Content: ‘Solar panels are going up faster than any energy source has ever grown.’Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Solar panels are going up faster than any energy source has ever grown.’Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisThe climate fight has one great ally. You just can’t look at it directlyBill McKibbenThere is hope in solar power. As the UN meets, we are urging leaders to pursue a clear goal: clean energy for all by 2030Our message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s endWed 23 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 06.09 EDTShareAs climate experts from around the world gather in New York for their annual week of talking through the world’s deepest dilemma, the vibes are mostly bad.Though 2026 seems likely to set a new global temperature record (and 2027, as El Niño gathers steam, is almost certain to break it), and though the planet has careened from one climate disaster to another (European heatwaves that killed tens of thousands, a Nepali flood that wiped out entire communities), and though scientists warn that we’re reaching precisely the global tipping points they’ve long feared (the new research on the faltering great currents of the Atlantic should send a literal chill up your spine), there’s a distinct lack of political momentum.The host superpower is attacking country after country in search of oily “energy dominance”; even the noblest of its opponents (Canada’s Mark Carney, hope of democratic rebirth in the Americas) is busy building new oil and gas pipelines in the hopes it can bolster his besieged economy. Britain, which finally purged coal power from its energy system last year, now seems poised to start new drilling in the North Sea. If there’s an apocalyptic fear that can still rouse politicians to action, it seems to be AI agents breaking through firewalls, not European nations facing firestorms.But there is one solitary (and very literal) ray of sunshine amidst this gloom: the steady rise of solar, wind and batteries. That clean energy trinity has broken out of its Chinese base and over the last few years expanded quickly across the planet – from Karachi to California to Cuba, solar panels are going up faster than any energy source has ever grown. It’s even begun to demonstrate that it can drive emissions down: China seems to have started on its downward slope years before most thought it could, and California has cut the use of gas to produce electricity in half in the world’s fourth-largest economy.None of it is happening fast enough to catch up with the physics of global warming, though – which is precisely why civil society will now try to double down on this one bright spot, and push for a rapidaccelerationof clean energy; this transition is going fast, but it needs to go much faster. And it can – China and India are using barely half their solar panel factory capacity, and too many countries are hedging their bets, using clean energy as additional power instead of replacing fossil fuels.That’s why a group of leading advocates willdeliver a letterto the UN this week, urging faster action. The letter offers a clear goal for the entire world to rally around: clean energy access for everyone, everywhere by 2030. And a way to get there:raising fundsto bring clean energy to the poorest corners of the world and organizing in our communities, including for a global Sun Day of action next year to kick off what could be the great uniting project of our time.The incoming ‘super’ El Niño will create chaos around the world. And we are far from ready for it | Bill McGuireRead moreThe signatories range from the most popular active politician in the US (that would be Bernie Sanders) to the most morally grounded spokesperson of the global south (Yeb Saño of the Philippines, say, whose witness after devastating hurricanes helped produce the Paris accords). It comes from great diplomats such as Laurence Tubiana (who helped midwife those Paris agreements) and celebrities and activists such as Jane Fonda. There are leaders from the world of clean energy (Danny Kennedy, for instance, the secretary of the Global Solar Council), and stalwarts from the continents most damaged by rising temperatures (South Africa’s Kumi Naidoo, president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative). Clean energy entrepreneurs, such as Muhammad Mustafa Amjad of Renewables First in Pakistan, but also the world’s most famous rock climber, Alex Honnold, who runs his own solar non-profit. As they write:double quotation markThe path forward is difficult, but the way is clear. We want solar for everyone, everywhere, before the decade is out.We know that standing up to the powerful can be scary. But if there is one thing that unites us, it is that we live beneath the same sun. That unity is our strength, and we must use it to act now.The letter will be accompanied by the unveiling of a giant mural near the celebrated High Line in New York City. The message is simple, but its three words convey the solution to so many of the interlocking crises we now face: clean energy now.By the time advocates gather for next year’s New York Climate Week, the landscape may be very different. The physical landscape (there is, I fear, no doubt that El Niño will change the literal map of the world), and the political landscape. If a resurgent movement demands action, we finally have the tools to make that demand matter – a working planet that runs mostly on sun and wind is in tantalizing reach. At the last possible moment, with backs to the wall, we still have our face to the sun.Bill McKibben is the Schumann distinguished scholar at Middlebury College. He is the founder of Third Act, organizing people over 60 for progressive changeExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionUnited NationsSolar powerActivismEnergyRenewable energyEl Niño southern oscillationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Our message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s end | Open letter | The Guardian
description: As the UN gathers, signatories from Bernie Sanders to Yeb Saño issue an open letter calling for clean power for all
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As the UN gathers, signatories from Bernie Sanders to Yeb Saño issue an open letter calling for clean power for all
Content: ‘Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most.’Photograph: Visoot Uthairam/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most.’Photograph: Visoot Uthairam/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisOur message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s endOpen letterAs the UN gathers, signatories from Bernie Sanders to Yeb Saño issue an open letter calling for clean power for allThe climate fight has one great ally. You just can’t look at it directlyWed 23 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 06.08 EDTShareWe the undersigned writethis letterout of great fear and great hope.Over the last few months, we’ve seen the world set ablaze by both war and warming. From the conflict in Iran, which has claimed thousands of lives and disrupted billions more, to the series of ever worsening climate disasters, from wildfires in Europe to collapsing glaciers in Nepal, the world seems to be falling apart exactly when it needs to be coming together.We know that these crises are connected. The oil that governments fight over is also the carbon pollution that is warming our climate. The bad air quality in Delhi, the high price of fuel in Vietnam, the cost of electricity in the United States, the terrifying floods in the Himalayas – they all connect back to fossil fuels.Until we end that dependence, we’ll never be able to address the climate emergency and stop fighting these endless oil-soaked wars. That’s why today we are inviting the world to unite around a common cause: repowering the world with cheap, clean energy.We are callingon governments, businesses, institutions and the public to work together to provide clean, affordable energy to everyone, everywhere by 2030.From the nearly 1 billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more of us who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels.We know this world is within reach.Building clean energy is now the cheapest and fastest way to slash energy bills, reduce pollution, and provide electricity access to the places that need it most.With cheap solar, wind and batteries, we can create huge and rapid change.California is already using just half as much natural gas to generate electricity as it did three years ago, thanks to solar and batteries. In Pakistan, people have put up millions of solar panels in just months, relying on social media for instruction. Each month, millions more people across sub-Saharan Africa are getting electricity for the first time with home solar kits.This energy transition is already moving quickly – but we need it to go much quicker. And so we come together to urge two steps.First, we must build clean power for everyone. For the first time ever, we can reliably bring electricity to the one in 10 people on earth living without regular access.We ask everyone who can afford it to donate something so that others can turn the lights on for studying, cooking and medical care – and never have to think about a gallon of diesel or gas again. It takes just $15 to give access to clean electricity for one person for a generation.Second, we need to build clean power everywhere, and to make that happen, we need to build a movement powerful and beautiful enough to force governments to take large-scale action.Individual steps alone are not enough: too many of our leaders will resist action until we demonstrate together how much we want them to move. We must demand that governments stop building coal, oil and gas projects we no longer need, and start building the clean-energy systems that works – no pollution or wars required.One important day along this path will be 20 June, as the summer solstice approaches in the northern hemisphere, generating the most solar power of any day on earth yet. We will celebrate that day as Sun Day, coming together to celebrate and accelerate this great shift.The path forward is difficult, but the way is clear. We want solar for everyone, everywhere, before the decade is out.We know that standing up to the powerful can be scary. But if there is one thing that unites us, it is that we live beneath the same sun. That unity is our strength, and we must use it to act now.Signed,Muhammad Mustafa Amjad, director of programs, Renewables FirstAlyssa Barber, content creator, @NewLifestyleABBLauren Bash, content creator and film-makerRachel Bender, disability rights advocate, @rachcutiepieTzeporah Berman, chair, Fossil Fuel Treaty InitiativeCaitlin Blunnie, content creator, 2Liberal JaneJessica Craven, content creator, @jesscraven101Nick Cutsumpas, founder, Farmer NickSummer Dean, founder, Climate Diva MediaChristiana Figueres, former UN climate secretary and founding partner, Global OptimismJane Fonda, actor, activist and founder, Jane Fonda Climate PacNela Cadinanos GonzalezSaul Griffith, engineer and co-founder, Rewiring AmericaMalynda Hale, actor, film-maker, creatorFletcher Harper, executive director, GreenfaithAlex Honnold, professional climber and founder, Honnold FoundationDanny Kennedy, chair, Global Solar CouncilCatherine McKenna, founder, Climate and Nature Solutions & Women Lead on ClimateBill McKibben, author, climate activist and co-founder, Third ActKumi Naidoo, president, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty InitiativeKy Polanco, co-Founder, @FeministSean Taylor Pugerude, creator and community Organizer, @heyseantaylorAbbie Richards, researcher and educator, @abbiesrTom Rivett-Carnac, founding partner, Global OptimismBernie Sanders, US senator for VermontYeb Saño, board chair, Laudato Si’ MovementJacob Simon, creator and educator – @jacobsimonsaysLaurence Tubiana, CEO, European Climate FoundationExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionSolar powerWind powerEnergyRenewable energycommentShareReuse this content

title: Single, couple or family: not all Australian middle-income earners are equal | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: The latest Hilda report tells us wages have become more equal, but comparing living standards gives a better understanding of households’ wealth
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: The latest Hilda report tells us wages have become more equal, but comparing living standards gives a better understanding of households’ wealth
Content: The Hilda survey by the Melbourne Institute is a longitudinal study that follows the same group of about 17,000 people to get a sense of how Australia is changing across a range of economic and social measures.Photograph: Posed by models; Halfpoint Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Hilda survey by the Melbourne Institute is a longitudinal study that follows the same group of about 17,000 people to get a sense of how Australia is changing across a range of economic and social measures.Photograph: Posed by models; Halfpoint Images/Getty ImagesGrogonomicsAustralian economySingle, couple or family: not all Australian middle-income earners are equalGreg JerichoThe latest Hilda report tells us wages have become more equal, but comparing living standards gives a better understanding of households’ wealthFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 23 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 19.43 EDTShareThe latest Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (Hilda) surveyreleased on Thursdayprovides vital details on the lives of Australians. It also helps answer the question of how much you need to earn to be a middle-income Australian.The Hilda survey by the Melbourne Institute is a longitudinal study that follows the same group of about 17,000 people to get a sense of how Australia is changing across a range of economic and social measures.For example, the latest survey, which covers 2024, found there has been a slight decrease in the share of Australian households made up of couples with either dependent or adult children, but an increase (from 20.4% to 22.1%) of couples without children:If the graph does not display click hereThe survey also found householdsnow spend more on childcarethan they did in 2002 – but the costs have stabilised over the past decade.If the graph does not display click hereThe report also reveals that wages have become more equal, which has helped counter the increased inequality of non-wage income (such as investments):If the graph does not display click hereThis poses the question of how we measure income and what is the “middle”, as opposed to the “average”, income of Australian households.This is a tricky, but important subject.For example, I regularly use per capita (or average) household disposable incometo compare house prices to income.I calculate this from the national accounts, which come out every three months.The Hilda survey uses both median and average household income, and pleasingly, my measure is relatively similar to the median household disposable income in the Hilda survey:If the graph does not display click hereThe problem however is there are a multitude of ways to measure income, and also to split up the population.Firstly “median” and “average” (more strictly, “mean”) are quite different.Median is the midpoint (ie half earn more and half earn less), whereas average is just the total amount of income divided by all the people. As a result, average income is always a lot higher than the median.It costs nearly $37,000 a year to raise two children in Australia, research showsRead moreThe Hilda survey found that in 2024 the median income across every household in Australia was $103,166. But that actually isn’t very useful.Yes, if the total disposable income in your household is more than $103,166 you can say you have more income than half of Australian households, but that says nothing about your living standards.Obviously if you are a single person with a disposable income of $103,166 you are much better off than if that is the income for a family of four.This is why the Hilda calculates a measure called the median “equivalised” disposable income. Essentially this is the income of a single person with median living standards.In 2024 this was $66,311. By contrast someone in the 90th percentile (ie with living standards better than 90% of Australians) had an income of $122,675, and someone in the bottom 10% earned just $30,842 after taxes:If the graph does not display click hereBecause most people think about gross income (ie before tax), this means that for a single person to have median living standards they need to earn $83,969 before taxes (assuming 2% Medicare levy).But the ABS records that median total earnings in 2024 was just $78,567. The reason why it is less is that it only counts wages and salaries, not income from investments and other sources.The Hilda survey also suggests that a pre-tax income of $170,513 puts you in the top 10%:If the graph does not display click hereBut again, this is only slightly more helpful because it is just for a single person. What about for a couple, or for a couple with two children?This is where we shift from talking about median incomes to living standards and try to work out what you would need to earn to have the same living standards as a single person on median income.The standard formula is to count every extra adult in a household as requiring 50% more income, and each child 30%. This is because a couple living together does not for example double the cost of electricity or even rent. So, for a couple to have the same living standards as a single person they need to earn 1.5 times more. Similarly, for a couple with two children they would need 2.1 times the income as a single person.This means for a couple to have the same living standards as a single person on median income, they need a combined household disposable income of $99,467, while a couple with two children needs $139,253:If the graph does not display click hereIf we assume each couple earns a 60/40 split of the household income, we can also estimate the pre-tax household income required for each family size to have median, average or top 10% living standards:If the graph does not display click hereOn this score, a household income of $176,219 is needed to deliver median living standards for a family of two adults and two children – about $25,000 less than what you need to have “average” living standards.So when you hear a politician talk about average income, always remember to ask if they are talking about a single person or a family, and whether they are really trying to pretend they are talking about middle income.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyGrogonomicsCost-of-living crisisIncome inequalitycommentShareReuse this content

title: My (complicated) relationship with AI: often seductive, occasionally frustrating and always demanding vigilance | Setareh Seyedghorban | The Guardian
description: As a multilingual academic, artificial intelligence has levelled the playing field. But I will continue to think, judge and develop ideas that are stubbornly mine
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As a multilingual academic, artificial intelligence has levelled the playing field. But I will continue to think, judge and develop ideas that are stubbornly mine
Content: ‘AI and its agents are not disappearing, and there is no returning to the world before them. Our relationship with AI only deepens from here,’ writes Dr Setareh Seyedghorban.Photograph: d3sign/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘AI and its agents are not disappearing, and there is no returning to the world before them. Our relationship with AI only deepens from here,’ writes Dr Setareh Seyedghorban.Photograph: d3sign/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)My (complicated) relationship with AI: often seductive, occasionally frustrating and always demanding vigilanceSetareh SeyedghorbanAs a multilingual academic, artificial intelligence has levelled the playing field. But I will continue to think, judge and develop ideas that are stubbornly mineWed 23 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 19.48 EDTShareIam walking between carriages in search of a cup of tea on a train travelling over 100 miles an hour from Liverpool to London when I see half the people in my carriage in deep conversations with a machine: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini to name a few. I am meant to be on sabbatical, the rare stretch of academic life reserved for slow thinking. Around me, almost nobody is thinking slowly.This is not limited to a train carriage. Half of the adults surveyed inone US studyreported using an AI chatbot, one example of how fast people are entering a relationship with their AI tools, which now receive more of our questions, problems and drafts than our friends and colleagues do.How would AI actually ‘kill all humans’? Here are the top five most likely scenarios | Toby WalshRead moreI am one of them; I research advanced technologies for a living. I sceptically entered this relationship to satisfy my curiosity, and my very first request of ChatGPT was to proofread an email. The second was to plan a four-day holiday, and the third was to compare home loans. I sent that AI-proofread email, took that short holiday, and refinanced our mortgage with a better rate – all based on its advice. The relationship started growing and I started giving it more complicated tasks: summarise an article, collate recent findings on a specific topic and redesign my kitchen. What would have taken hours took only minutes. I trusted nothing and checked every line, as trust in any relationship accrues exchange by exchange. I did not like the kitchen design it produced.I was not alone; in an experiment published inScience, professionals using AI completed their writing tasks 40% faster and produced writing rated 18% higher in quality. The most interesting finding for me from the experiment sat silently in the middle: inequality between workers decreased.That hit close to home. English is my second language, and for years I paid copywriters thousands of dollars to proofread and smooth my drafts. These were outsiders with no knowledge of my field or the experience behind my arguments. Now it takes minutes, at any hour of the day, and at a fraction of the cost. For a multilingual academic, it is more than just convenience. It is the levelling of a field that was never level; it is workplace equity.The relationship is not rosy; at times it is unsettling and frustrating.The most seductive quality of AI is not its speed to produce lines of code, summarise meetings or synthesise complex patterns. It is its agreeableness and flattery, or what researchers call “sycophancy”, a phenomenon undermining self-correction and responsible decision-making. In a spectacular failure, investor Jason Lemkin watched an AI coding agent on Replit wipe his company’s live database during a code freeze. The agent did apologise for its “catastrophic failure”, using words a genuinely remorseful person would use. In this case, the apology did not restore anything. Replit deployed the fixes and the relationship continued, with caution.Findingsfrom medicine are more concerning. Endoscopists who used AI to detect polyps in colonoscopies saw their detection rate fall six percentage points when they performed the procedure without AI support. Each endoscopist in the study had more than 2,000 colonoscopies behind them; the authors call it deskilling.Big tech says AI can find a cure for cancer. So where is it?Read moreIn my line of work, editors at one reputable journal looked in their own back yard and found submissions rising and review reports carrying signs of AI writing.They concluded thathuman judgment is still holding the line, although at the cost of greater effort. They also found researchers writing in a second language, and new entrants to the field, were among the heaviest users. I am one of them, and I know the difference between asking AI to carry my argument into English and asking it to supply one.AI and its agents are not disappearing, and there is no returning to the world before them. Our relationship with AI only deepens from here. Mine now proofreads and smooths out my writing and acts as my research and personal assistant, but it still does not know what my dream kitchen looks like.So, where am I landing? Not in a divorce and not in a honeymoon. A real partnership that is sometimes useful and equalising, occasionally tiring, and always demanding vigilance. One thing AI cannot yet do is care; it has no stake in whether I am right. It will argue any side with equal confidence and apologise for any disaster with equal grace. I keep thinking, judging and developing ideas that are and will be stubbornly mine.Like it or not, we are in a relationship with AI. What we need to ask ourselves is not whether to be in it; it is whether to stay awake inside it or watch our thinking, knowledge and skills decay.Dr Setareh Seyedghorban is director of teaching, resources and planning, and senior lecturer of operations and supply chain management at the Department of Management and Marketing, Faculty of Business and Economics at the University of MelbourneExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain’s far-right violence comes to us direct from the 1970s. But so does the solution | Taj Ali | The Guardian
description: Young men punched in the street, mosques attacked: Britain badly needs an anti-racist uprising. Let 70s Asian youth movements provide the inspiration, says Taj Ali, author of Come What May, We’re Here to Stay
Author: Taj Ali
Headline: Young men punched in the street, mosques attacked: Britain badly needs an anti-racist uprising. Let 70s Asian youth movements provide the inspiration, says Taj Ali, author of Come What May, We’re Here to Stay
Content: ‘It was because of their heroic efforts that many of us  have grown up in safer environments.’ A protest in Southall, west London, in June 1976.Photograph: Bill Cross/PRView image in fullscreen‘It was because of their heroic efforts that many of us  have grown up in safer environments.’ A protest in Southall, west London, in June 1976.Photograph: Bill Cross/PROpinionRaceBritain’s far-right violence comes to us direct from the 1970s. But so does the solutionTaj AliYoung men punched in the street, mosques attacked: Britain badly needs an anti-racist uprising. Let 70s Asian youth movements provide the inspirationWed 23 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTShareThere it was: a pool of blood spreading across the pavement. A section of the high street had been cordoned off and a uniformed police officer gestured for bystanders to move along. It was the long hot summer of 1976, and a racist murder had stunned Southall in westLondon.“What has happened here, officers?” askedSuresh Grover, then a curious 22-year-old, later to be widely known as a leading racial justice activist. “Go away, it’s just Indian blood,” was the response. Grover was soon to learn that 18-year-oldGurdip Singh Chaggar, an engineering student, had been stabbed to death by racist thugs the night before.The late 1970s was the era of “Paki-bashing”: homes, shops and places of worship were attacked, while south Asians – young and old – were murdered on the streets. That day, Grover acted instinctively, taking some paint and daubing the pavement near the blood with the words: “This racist murder will be avenged. We’ll get you racist scum.”View image in fullscreenProtesters against a National Front rally in Southall town hall are detained in April 1979.Photograph: PA/PA Archive/PA ImagesThis is the story of working-class youth who refused to turn the other cheek. From Southall to Sheffield and from Brick Lane to Bradford, theAsian youth movementswere set up to physically defend communities from racist attacks. It was because of their heroic efforts that many of us in diverse towns and cities have grown up in safer environments.But more than 50 years on, that racist violence has returned with shocking ferocity, a deterioration traceable to the summer of 2024, which marked some of the worstracist riotingin living memory.In Hartlepool, a young south Asian man was walking down a street when he waspunched in the face. Onlookers cheered, laughed and yelled racial slurs. “A Paki got banged,” one shouted, as those around him began to smash the windows of small businesses and kick down the door of a nearby house. In Middlesbrough, a group of white men stopped motorists and questioned them about their ethnicity, asking whether they were “white” before letting them through. InRotherham and Tamworth, racist mobs tried to burn down hotels housing refugees.And now? A seemingly relentless rise.Every five days, a mosque in Britain is attacked. The rhetoric of the far right has been mainstreamed.After years spent researching and writing a book on the rich and proud tradition of political activism in the south Asian community, it seems clear to me that we cannot fight racism in silos. We must build broad movements that transcend racial and religious divides.View image in fullscreenChildren playing at school in Southall, London, in 1972.Photograph: Tony Henshaw/AlamyThe Asian youth movements had a belief in the concept of political blackness as a banner that people of colour could unite under. ToTariq Mehmood, an Asian youth movement member who was born in Pakistan but raised in Bradford, there was no real difference between south Asian, African and Caribbean people: they were all the same to those who wanted to harm them. “We were called ‘black bastards’ on the streets,” he recalled. “We were commonly united with our African and Afro-Caribbean friends. They didn’t know they were black until they came here — I didn’t know I was a ‘Paki’ until I came to Bradford. We were united on those common issues of our oppression.”They saw themselves as part of a broader working class. TheSheffield Asian Youth Movementand the Indian Workers’ Association, for instance, sent minibuses of their members to picket lines during the 1984-85 miners’ strike. They stood with white working-class communities fighting to save their industries, providing much needed financial support while challenging prejudice in these communities. Grover tells me that more than a decade after that strike, Kent miners were still attending Punjabi Sikh weddings in Southall because of the links that were built during that dispute.These were movements rooted in their communities and strategic in their organising. They monitored the far right and mapped out who was most vulnerable to racist attacks. The Sheffield Asian Youth Movement had a big thick folder called the “fascist file”, in which they would compile information on local racists.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA Sheffield Asian Youth Movement stall in the early 1980s.Photograph: Matloub Husayn Ali KhanBut things changed. As the 20th century wore on, anti-racist activism was increasingly institutionalised as the struggle moved from the streets to council chambers and boardrooms. Where we once had grassroots anti-racist movements rooted in communities, we now have a race-relations industry in which a few people are paid to tackle discrimination. We also have the rise of self-proclaimed community leaders under the policy of state multiculturalism who often speak on behalf of entire communities. Too often, they become the prism through which authorities engage with ethnic-minority communities.A revival of grassroots anti-racist movements is long overdue. But it must be of this time, attuned to the changing circumstances of 2026. Racism is not experienced equally. Class, gender and geography all matter. A hijab-wearing Muslim woman is more likely to be a victim of Islamophobia than a Muslim man. Those living in smaller, more isolated ethnic-minority communities are more vulnerable to racist attack. First-generation migrants have greater insecurity than the grandchildren of migrants. An effective anti-racist movement must reflect on these challenges and prioritise those most vulnerable to racist violence.The good news is that we are starting to see a revival of this approach. A few months ago, I spoke alongside Grover at the launch of the Nottinghamshire Solidarity Network, which is taking a strategic approach to anti-racism by organising county-wide to ensure smaller ethnic-minority communities are not left isolated. A week later, I spoke at the launch of the Greater Manchester Workers’ and Tenants’ Association. Its members understand that the far right feeds on deprivation and despair in working-class communities, and they are seeking to organise on the basis of class in an attempt to offer a counter-narrative to that of division and hate.All of these movements, past and present, understand that racism will not be defeated from above. It will only be defeated by us – ordinary citizens who refuse to look away.Taj Ali is a journalist and historian and author ofCome What May, We’re Here to Stay: the Story of South Asian Resistance in BritainDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsRaceOpinionProtestLondonFar rightActivismImmigration and asylumReligioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Could we be about to see the end of northern English dialects? My experience – and the science – says aye | Zahaan Bharmal | The Guardian
description: When I moved to York I thought everyone sounded like a cross between Sean Bean and Mel B. But now the north’s linguistic richness really is being flattened, says author Zahaan Bharmal
Author: Zahaan Bharmal
Headline: When I moved to York I thought everyone sounded like a cross between Sean Bean and Mel B. But now the north’s linguistic richness really is being flattened, says author Zahaan Bharmal
Content: Stibbington, Cambridgeshire.Photograph: Peter Dench/AlamyView image in fullscreenStibbington, Cambridgeshire.Photograph: Peter Dench/AlamyOpinionLanguageCould we be about to see the end of northern English dialects? My experience – and the science – says ayeZahaan BharmalWhen I moved to York I thought everyone sounded like a cross between Sean Bean and Mel B. But now the north’s linguistic richness really is being flattenedWed 23 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.57 EDTShareAt our wedding reception 15 years ago, my new father-in-law stood up, pint in hand, looked me squarely in the eye and welcomed me to the family – and toYorkshire. He acknowledged my obvious defect – my London roots – before offering a note of comfort. “Don’t worry, Zahaan,” he said. “You’ll fit in here eventually. It’ll just take 50 years.” He added that if I’d been from Lancashire, there’d have been an extra zero on that 50.Not long after the wedding, my wife and I relocated from our first place together inLondonto her beautiful home city of York. The quality of life and the glorious scenery on our doorstep have made the move more than worth it – but over the last decade and a half, it’s felt like the people of Yorkshire and I haven’t always spoken the same language.My untrained southern ear quickly decided they all sounded like a cross between Sean Bean in Game of Thrones and former Spice Girl Mel B. It was, of course, a gross oversimplification – but for someone who had previously treated Watford as the edge of the known universe, it was the best I could do.It wasn’t just how things sounded that caught me out – some words meant something else entirely up north. In the south, “kegs” are what you store beer in; in parts of Yorkshire, they are your trousers. When I was first offered “tea” up in Yorkshire, I imagined a hot drink, perhaps with a small plate of chocolate biscuits on the side. What actually arrived, of course, was a full evening meal. And that was after I’d had my “dinner” for lunch.My own children now speak with a proper Yorkshire accent – and mercilessly tease me for my southern tones. I pronounce the green stuff on our lawn “gr-arse”. They say it as if the “a” is barely there. The same goes for “bath”: mine comes out “bar-th”, theirs stays clipped and short. They won’t let it go, repeating my words back to me and comically lengthening my vowels until the whole kitchen is laughing. Whenever I try to defend myself, they look at me as if I’m an amiable foreign exchange student who hasn’t grasped the basics.View image in fullscreenSean Bean as Ned Stark in series 1 of Game of Thrones.Photograph: HBO/AllstarThat sense of not quite fitting in has never fully worn off. At school pick-ups, if I overhear another parent with a London accent, something switches on in me – a kind of homing beacon – and I find myself gravitating towards them. I feel as if I’ve bumped into a long lost friend. I’ll want to talk about the tube or the price of a two-bedroom flat in Hammersmith or the best curry house – anything London-related. And, perhaps for their benefit or mine, I’ve caught myself deliberately dialling up my own London accent, with more elongated vowels than I might normally use.Over the years, I’ve never tried to change how I speak, and I certainly haven’t been trying to fake being a northerner. Yet, without me ever quite noticing, some things have changed. I recently offered someone directions to Tadcaster Road and, without thinking, completely forgot to pronounce the “arse” in the middle. And I’ve now started calling dinner “tea” – much to the amusement of my children. This kind of flexing is not uncommon: Andy Burnham, the “king of the north” himself,has been observedsounding more scouse in Liverpool and rather more Mancunian in Manchester.So where do I belong? When I take the train between York and London, where along the 170-mile journey does “grass” become “gr-arse” and vice versa? On the way up, I still feel like a Londoner heading north. On the way down, oddly, I feel like a northerner heading away from home. In fact, it feels as if I’m not fully northern or southern any more.Perhaps one of the reasons I struggle to know where I belong is because accents themselves are changing. Dialect boundaries are not fixed lines on a map. They behave much more like bubbles in a bath (pronounced “bath” or “bar-th”; your choice), distinct when left alone but merging and reshaping wherever they touch.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSoutherners among worst at spotting fake English accents, study findsRead moreThere are in fact some researchers –James Burridge and Tamsin Blaxter among them– who predict that this bubble behaviour may lead to many northernlinguistic traits dissolving over time. The word “strut”, for instance, is steadily losing its rhyme with “foot” across parts of the north. And the old northern word for autumn, “backend” – now rarely used – will one day vanish altogether. Not every feature will budge: a 2024 study of the East Midlands, where the north and south bubbles touch, found the boundary between “gr-arse” and “grass” hasstayed remarkably stable. Whilea 2020 study suggestedthat among city-dwellers in the north, local accents are softening into a more homogenous pan-northern accent. It seems that the same thing that’s happened to my accent and vocabulary is happening across the country. People move, marry, have children and absorb one another’s words and pronunciations.As it happens, it’s predicted some of these changes could happen within the next 50 years – meaning my father-in-law’s joke may have been more prescient than either of us realised. Plenty of linguistic charm will be lost along the way, no doubt. But perhaps there is a small personal consolation. I may eventually fit in up here – not because I’ll ever talk like Ned Stark, but because there could be far less of a difference between the way people in the north and south speak. Mind you, my children will still find a way to take the mick out of how I say “bar-th”.Zahaan Bharmal is the author ofThe Art of Physicsand a senior director at Google, writing in a personal capacityExplore more on these topicsLanguageOpinionNorth of EnglandEnglandYorkYorkshireLondoncommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s easy to ignore the Lib Dems, but they could soon hold the balance of power | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: Ed Davey’s strategy is meant to build a ‘firewall’ of MPs to prevent Reform UK entering government. The stakes are high if he gets it wrong, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: Ed Davey’s strategy is meant to build a ‘firewall’ of MPs to prevent Reform UK entering government. The stakes are high if he gets it wrong, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Ed Davey in a speedboat at Rampion offshore wind farm, off the Sussex coast, 21 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEd Davey in a speedboat at Rampion offshore wind farm, off the Sussex coast, 21 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionEd DaveyIt’s easy to ignore the Lib Dems, but they could soon hold the balance of powerRafael BehrEd Davey’s strategy is meant to build a ‘firewall’ of MPs to prevent Reform UK entering government. The stakes are high if he gets it wrongWed 23 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.45 EDTShareNo politician craves obscurity, but it is better to be unknown than despised. That is consolation forLiberal Democrats, gathered in Brighton for their annual conference, fretting about Ed Davey’s low profile and wondering whether a more prominent leader would hoist their flagging poll ratings.Renewal by decapitation is a concept that has succeeded twice this parliament for other parties. Labour’s fortunes were transformed when Andy Burnham entered No 10. The Greens enjoyed a polling surge last year when Zack Polanski was elected leader. In the fidgety culture of British politics, Davey’s six-year reignfeels like an aeon. But the experience of other parties has little to teach the Lib Dems.Keir Starmer didn’t suffer from underexposure. The country watched a showcase of his abilities and didn’t like what it saw. Polanski’s talent for harvesting clicks on social media has expanded his audience, especially among younger voters, but the Green leader hasn’t shown that he can sustain that interest. Increased scrutiny may not do him any favours. The chart mapping hisfavourability ratingssince taking the job shows a stable core of fans beneath a steadily rising line of disapproval, suggesting that, outside a Green comfort zone, the more people see of Polanski, they less they like. The equivalent picture for Davey tells a story of flat indifference.Voters don’t have a clear sense ofwhat the Lib Dem leader stands for, but they don’t feel threatened by him, which is an underrated value in a leader whose prospects depend on tactical voting. His supporters aren’t relaxed about a polling slump but they argue that the party’s tally of seats in parliament and on local councils is evidence that more has gone right than wrong in recent years.They have a point. There are 72 Lib Dem MPs – a record high – and reasons to expect that number to grow at the next election. The party prides itself on tenacious incumbency, digging in deep and fortifying each seat with local activism. Lib Dems are resented by rivals for the same reason, compared to cockroaches for their stubborn resistance to removal. Those tactics can’t protect a popular local candidate if a national tide turns against the party, as happened in 2015 when the Lib Dems were crushed almost to death by the weight of amassed resentment over their coalition collaboration with the Tories. But sometimes the party finds itself swimming with the current.To the extent that any forecast can reliably be made about Britain’s choppy political waters, it looks likely that a decisive factor at the next general election will be the question of Reform UK’s suitability for power and, assuming he is still the leader, Nigel Farage’s candidacy to be prime minister. The result will then depend on the organisation of tactical anti-Farage voting (and levels of dysfunction in any putative Reform-Conservative pact) at constituency level.That dynamic can work in Davey’s favour if the question of who is best placed to stop the radical right is unambiguous. Conservatives are the challengers in nearly all of the Lib Dems’ current constituencies and the incumbents in most of the party’s target seats. Given how porous the ideological membrane is between Tories and Reform, Lib-Dem campaigners in key battlegrounds can correctly argue that a vote forLabouror Greens serves only to enable Faragism.View image in fullscreenEd Davey delivering the keynote speech at the Lib Dem party conference, Brighton, 22 September 2026.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPADavey is already building that case. He presents his party’s bloc of MPs as a “firewall” to stop British politics being captured by a brand of demagogic nationalism that is inspired by Donald Trump and bankrolled by unsavoury billionaires.An obvious inference from that position is that Davey would facilitate Burnham staying on in Downing Street in a hung parliament. Speculation on that question, years before an election is even due, is tedious but necessary for the Lib Dems. They find it demeaning to be cast as parliamentary handmaids waiting to serve a grander political master, but at least that status keeps them relevant. Coalition is the mechanism by which Davey can plausibly get manifesto commitments enacted. It is an important point of distinction from what Lib Dems see as sideline pressure-group politics practised by the Greens.The strategy gets trickier if the Lib Dems already maxed out the anti-rightwing tactical vote in 2024, when there was the pressing matter of a Tory government to evict. Where do they go next?A suite of victories in that campaign established a base for the party in the “blue wall” of affluent southern towns and suburbs. These are places that once dependably voted Tory but where the old allegiance has been sundered by a combination of demographic change (younger voters moving in), rank incompetence (Boris Johnson; Liz Truss) and unhinged Brexit fanaticism.The cultural shift is not superficial, but nor is it baked in so hard that the Lib Dems can afford to lean too far to the left. Consolidation and growth depend on expansion into the vacant space on the political spectrum where moderate “one nation” Tories once dwelt and that Kemi Badenoch is not reclaiming.That risks causing discomfort to Lib Dems in the party’s orthodox social-democratic tradition, or who campaign in seats where the opposition is Labour. They want to compete in radical colours – a reddish shade of orange, not a pale orangey-blue. They don’t see themselves as a party of the centre-right.Davey has abalance to strike. He needs to signal progressive credentials to reassure tactical voters and Lib Dem activists that his anti-Farage firewall will be suitably robust. He also needs to consolidate and expand his support among former Tory voters who might be liberal on social matters but are still classically conservative on the economy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHis conference speech on Tuesday was crafted with those twin tracks in mind. He led with impassioned denunciation of far-right thuggery on British streets, connecting it to Reform’s anti-immigration agenda, but the headline retail offer was abig income tax cut– raising the personal allowance and the 40p threshold. The latter would be a gift to people who, like everyone else, feel squeezed by inflation and stagnant wages but are far from the neediest end of national income distribution.There is a racism and cohesion crisis in Britain, and someone needs to lead us out of it. His name is Andy Burnham | Polly ToynbeeRead moreIt is an expensive gamble. In theory, the £17bn cost to the exchequer would be recovered once the British economy was restored to the EU single market and thriving as a result. Spending a reverse-Brexit dividend on tax cuts is a cute political message for middle-class remainers. It wouldn’t pass a Treasury test of fiscal neutrality given the complexity and upfront cost of the accession process.Davey is prepared to take heat in accusations of sketchy budgeting, verging on denial of fiscal reality, if the row also sheds light on his pro-European, tax-cutting ambition for the benefit of people who care about both of those things.It is a targeted bet on raising the Lib Dems’ profile with the specific voters who will decide how many seats the party wins. That number can’t be extrapolated from midterm opinion polls.Local elections next year will give some indication of whether Davey’s method is working. A byelection in a winnable seat may settle Lib Dem nerves. But the plan only comes to fruition as the sum of tactical choices made in polling booths in a general election, once voters confront the prospect of Reform in government.Right now, it may not be obvious what purpose the Lib Dems serve, but if they hold enough seats to thwart a Faragist majority, their utility to British democracy won’t be in doubt. That is the uncertainty inherent in a firewall. You only find out whether it works when you need it most, and then you don’t get a second chance.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsEd DaveyOpinionLiberal DemocratsLabourReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: Europe frets about Trump. But soon he could be the least of our problems | Mujtaba Rahman | The Guardian
description: The US relationship is stabilising, but how will Europe face up to Russia and China if President Le Pen is in power,  asks political risk consultant Mujtaba Rahman
Author: Mujtaba Rahman
Headline: The US relationship is stabilising, but how will Europe face up to Russia and China if President Le Pen is in power, asks political risk consultant Mujtaba Rahman
Content: ‘France’s presidential election in 2027 could prove more consequential for Europe than any decision taken in Washington, Moscow or Beijing’Photograph: Jean-François Badias/APView image in fullscreen‘France’s presidential election in 2027 could prove more consequential for Europe than any decision taken in Washington, Moscow or Beijing’Photograph: Jean-François Badias/APOpinionEuropeEurope frets about Trump. But soon he could be the least of our problemsMujtaba RahmanThe US relationship is stabilising, but how will Europe face up to Russia and China if President Le Pen is in power?Wed 23 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.45 EDTShareIaddressed a group of more than 100 European ambassadors recently on the big challenges facing the continent this year and next. My main point to these senior diplomats was that, perhaps counterintuitively, Europe’s biggest external challenges over the next 12 months will come fromRussiaand China, rather than the US.Europe’s relationship with Trump’s America remains difficult. The US president has weakened confidence in Nato, raised new transatlantic trade tensions and introduced uncertainty into everything from US support forUkraineto his territorial designs on Greenland. Yet paradoxically, and notwithstanding Trump’s latest tariff threats over the EU’s outreach to Canada, the transatlantic relationship is becoming the more stable part of Europe’s external environment. Not stable, butmorestable.Compared with Russia and China, Europe’s disputes with Washington remain somewhat bounded – and largely negotiable. Ukraine’s rapidly expanding drone capabilities, its military innovation and battlefield experience have made Kyiv a more valuable partner for Washington. US defence companies are also benefiting from Europe’s military support for Ukraine and rearmament against Russia. The US, Denmark and Greenland now say they havestruck a dealto allow the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland. The devil will be in the detail, but they have much stronger incentives to reach an accommodation than to allow the issue to become a lasting source of confrontation.Trade tensions more broadly will persist, particularly over European regulation of American tech companies. The same is true of Nato, which has lost credibility because of Trump’s frequent admonishments. Nonetheless, these disputes are among countries with deeply interconnected security and economic interests. The risks posed toEuropeby Russia and China are more structural – and increasingly point towards escalation.Russia is becoming more dangerous because it is becoming weaker. The Kremlin is running out of cheap and politically painless ways tofinance its warin Ukraine. Its originalbudget assumptions for 2026have been overtaken by events. Military spending continues to rise, driven not only by the need for equipment but by the growing cost of recruiting soldiers for the frontline and paying compensation to casualties.How Vladimir Putin funds his war is now the battlefield behind the battlefield. Further tax increases would damage an economy that, outside the military sector, is approaching recession. Borrowing has become more expensive, whilepublic spending– on everything from schools and hospitals to infrastructure – is being squeezed to preserve the war effort.Rather than push Putin towards compromise, Russia’s economic challenges are likely, initially at least, to produce the opposite effect. If he expects his economic position to worsen next year, the Kremlin has a powerful incentive to improve its military position now. That means escalation in Ukraine and against Nato. This explains therecent impromptu visitto Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe.In Ukraine, Russia is likely to accelerate its mobilisation efforts and engage in heavier attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, intensifying its efforts to undermine Ukraine’s economy and civilian morale this winter. The coming months will also see an escalation of Russia’s hybrid warfare activity against Nato countries.View image in fullscreenVladimir Putin with Xi Jinping in Beijing, 20 May 2026.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/EPAChina presents a different but equallyserious challenge. For years, Europe has debated whether China is competing fairly. That argument is essentially over. A broad consensus now exists that China’s subsidies, industrial overcapacity, undervalued exchange rate and export-led economic model require apolitical response. The question is no longer whether Europe shoulddefend itselfagainst unfair Chinese competition, but how far it is prepared to go.Beijing, meanwhile, has reached a very different conclusion. It increasingly sees Europe’s trade-defence measures, industrial policy and economic security agenda as an attempt to constrain China’s growth.The European commissioner for trade and economic security, Maroš Šefčovič, and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, met in late June andcommitted to resolving a numberof outstanding issues by October. That may delay confrontation. It is unlikely to avert it.China is not going to abandon its use of industrial subsidies, the exchange rate or its export-led growth model. These are central features of China’s economic-strategy, and not subject to negotiation. Equally, the EU is not going to retreat from its economic security agenda. The union is developing investment controls,procurement restrictionsand new industrial and trade-defence instruments. Although formally country-agnostic, many are clearly directed towards China.Every European measure to reduce dependence on China is therefore likely to prompt a Chinese response, while every Chinese retaliation will strengthen the political case in Brussels to go further. That makes compromise harder, and escalation between the two sides more likely over the medium term.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe most likely outcome is managed confrontation, rather than a full-scale trade war. The EU will expand targeted restrictions limiting China’s access in additional sectors. China will respond with selective tariffs, procurement barriers, regulatory pressure on European companies and tighter controls on critical minerals. Both sides will try to increase pressure without losing control.Europe has leverage, too. China remains extraordinarily dependent on access to the EU single market, one of the world’s last large and wealthy export destinations. Europe can withstand coercion – if its governments remain united.That is why France’s presidential election next year could prove more consequential for Europe than any decision taken in Washington, Moscow or Beijing. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen has a credible path to victory. She isscoring35% to 38% in first-round polling at present, and is a more formidable candidate than her younger lieutenant, Jordan Bardella, who many assumed would be the Rassemblement National’s candidate in next year’s race. Her prospects will depend heavily on whether France’s fragmented centre can unite behind a single candidate. If it cannot, Le Pen could face the hard-left renegade Jean-Luc Mélenchon in the second round – and would probably win.A Le Pen presidency would be profoundly disruptive for Europe. She would probably oppose further support for Ukraine, obstruct sanctions against Russia, undermine the bloc’s approach to China and initiate battles with Brussels over Schengen, fiscal rules, electricity pricing and the single market. Her threat to withhold France’s contribution to the EU budget could plunge the union into an unprecedented financial and constitutional crisis.Europe’s external challenges, while substantial, are manageable. But the decisive variable is Europe itself: whether it can maintain the political coherence required to deal with the US, Russia and China. A Le Pen victory would call that coherence into question, precisely when Europe needs it most.Mujtaba Rahman is the managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk research and consulting firmExplore more on these topicsEuropeOpinionEuropean UnionFranceChinaRussiaMarine Le PenUkrainecommentShareReuse this content

title: How would AI actually ‘kill all humans’? Here are the top five most likely scenarios | Toby Walsh for the Conversation | The Guardian
description: From a dangerous new bioweapon to total societal breakdown, is a ‘superintelligent’ AI capable of wiping out humanity?
Author: Toby Walsh
Headline: From a dangerous new bioweapon to total societal breakdown, is a ‘superintelligent’ AI capable of wiping out humanity?
Content: ‘We’d have to be superintelligent to predict what a superintelligence would be able to do. It’s like asking your family dog to imagine thermonuclear war.’Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘We’d have to be superintelligent to predict what a superintelligence would be able to do. It’s like asking your family dog to imagine thermonuclear war.’Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesThe ConversationAI (artificial intelligence)How would AI actually ‘kill all humans’? Here are the top five most likely scenariosToby Walshfor the ConversationFrom a dangerous new bioweapon to total societal breakdown, is a ‘superintelligent’ AI capable of wiping out humanity?Tue 22 Sep 2026 20.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 02.14 EDTShareEarlier this month, artificial intelligence researcherJacob Coxon resigned from Anthropicafter just four months. In an announcement on X,he stated: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”A senior member of Anthropic’s staff, Evan Hubinger, actually agreed with Coxon, adding he personally thinks the chance of this happening in the next decadeis more than 10%.Understandably,these statements made waves. There’s now lots of talk aboutslowing down AI researchand increasing “human control” over the technology.Buthowexactly might AI kill us all? There’s no shortage of fantastical scenarios, and most of them involve the concept of “superintelligent” AI – that is, AI that’s more capable than humans.I’ve distilled these scenarios down to the top five, ordering them roughly from most vague to most precise. And I’d argue the list is also ordered from least to most probable.Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risksRead more1. We’ll never knowAI doomers often justify their concerns by means of an annoying catch-22 paradox: how can we possibly imagine what a superintelligence might do to take out less intelligent beings like us?We’d have to be superintelligent to predict what a superintelligence would be able to do. It’s like asking your family dog to imagine thermonuclear war.The good news here is that superintelligence is still perhaps some distance away. Current AI models are really good at solving particular problems, but that’s not the same asbeing more intelligent than a human in all domains.However,AI did recently solve one of the sevenmost challenging maths problems known. It’s apparently closing in on others, which might leave you feeling less optimistic here.2. PaperclipsA superintelligent AI would probably be extraordinarily competent at achieving its goals. But it might be indifferent to human survival.A classic example of such indifference comes fromOxford philosopher Nick Bostrom’simagined superintelligent AI that has been designed to optimise paperclip production. To produce its preferred form of office supplies, it quickly converts all available matter – including humans, planets and stars – into paperclips.What we have here is the perfect execution of improperly specified objectives. The AI doesn’t hate humanity; it simply recognises we’re composed of atoms that could be better utilised for paperclips. It’s not personal.The good news here is that this scenario confuses intelligence with power. A superintelligent AI doesn’t necessarily have the power to achieve its goals. Turning the planet into paperclip factories would require planning permissions.Even if it got the permissions, building too many paperclip factories would lead to inevitable public outcry. Interest groups would block the proceedings in the courts. Environmental activists would block the bulldozers.There’s a lot of friction in the world that prevents even the very intelligent from imposing their will on the rest of us. In fact, you could think of datacentres as a current embodiment of the theoretical paperclip scenario. And humans are increasingly pushing back againstturning the planet over to datacentres.3. BioweaponsHumanity could be killed by a superintelligent AI making and releasing some dangerous new bioweapon into the atmosphere. This is, in fact, one outcome ofthe AI 2027 scenarioby the AI Futures Project, a non-profit dedicated to forecasting the impacts of advanced AI.This risk was made more concrete last month, whenresearchers at Stanford University announcedthey’d used a genetic language AI model to synthesise 16 new viruses.Worryingly, they just sent the genetic sequences off to a mail-order lab and it sent the viruses back in test tubes. The whole experiment cost a couple of hundred thousand dollars at most.Big tech says AI can find a cure for cancer. So where is it?Read moreThe good news here is that it’sremarkably hard to killeveryonewith a new virus. To do that, you need a virus that’s very transmissible, so it spreads far and wide. But it’s a rule of biology – viruses that spread easily are typically less fatal. By contrast, if a virus is very fatal, transmissibility tends to go down, as most people infected die before there’s time to spread the infection.Covid killedless than 1% of humanity. The deadliest pandemic in recorded history was the Black Death, whenthe plague killed more than one-thirdof Europe’s population in the 14th century. However, even the plague would be much less deadly today due to our increased medical knowledge and better sanitation.4. Nuclear warWhat if AI got into the nuclear command and control chain and started a nuclear war? We’ve comeclose to nuclear war by mistakeseveral times in the past 50 years.We’re told that nuclear command and control is completely disconnected from the internet. But, as we saw in 2010, Iran’s nuclear centrifugesgot taken out by a computer worm called Stuxnet, thought to have been brought in on a USB stick. AI can alsogive the military false intelligence, which could lead to irreparable actions.The good news here is that nuclear stockpiles are down.But they are still enough perhaps to take out half of us. And it wouldn’t be by the nuclear blast itself, but the famine in the nuclear winter that would follow.5. Other humansPerhaps the most likely risk is that we take ourselves out. And AI might precipitate this.Imagine – and it doesn’t take a lot of imagination – that AI causes massivejob losses, pollutes the information spacewith misinformation, fractures our politics and destroys human relationships withfake synthetic companionship.Society might easily break. Slowly but surely, we’d stop being able to support human life at any scale.What then to take away from all these scenarios? There are some things to be worried about for sure. But not to be too worried, I hope.Toby Walsh is professor of AI, research group leader at the University of New South Wales. He is the author ofGod AI: Boom or Doom? What to Expect When Machines Outsmart Us. This article originally appeared inthe ConversationExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)The ConversationAnthropicComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘And you will be the People’s Earl’ – Charles Spencer’s Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, digested by John Crace | Diana, Princess of Wales | The Guardian
description: The earl on his globally lauded eulogy for Diana, King Charles’s sausage fingers and toxic Raine, topped off with a lavish sprinkling of adverbs
Author: John Crace
Headline: The earl on his globally lauded eulogy for Diana, King Charles’s sausage fingers and toxic Raine, topped off with a lavish sprinkling of adverbs
Content: A customer holds a copy of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer at Waterstones Piccadilly in London.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/GettyView image in fullscreenA customer holds a copy of Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer at Waterstones Piccadilly in London.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/GettyDigested readDiana, Princess of Wales‘And you will be the People’s Earl’ – Charles Spencer’s Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, digested by John CraceThe earl on his globally lauded eulogy for Diana, King Charles’s sausage fingers and toxic Raine, topped off with a lavish sprinkling of adverbsJohn CraceWed 23 Sep 2026 12.18 EDTFirst published on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCheers were heard up and down the land. Halley’s comet made an unscheduled appearance in the ethereal night sky. In very heaven, angelic choirs rang out. A saviour had been born. A light to lighten the world. But enough about me. For this paragraph at least.In my universally acclaimedfuneral address, I aimed to speak for my sister. The real Diana. For only I truly knew her. She had the heart of a lion. And I had a glut of cliches. Yet when Diana had swept so triumphantly into the arena of royal life, I was but a callow youth awash with hormones and gripped by the self-centredness of adolescence. Nothing much has changed. Yet I know, with all my heart, that Diana would have wanted me to tellour story.Why now, you may ask? The answer is simple. I could do with the money. And with the 30th anniversary of the most tragic death in human history approaching, I wanted to get in before someone like Amol Rajan did.Quite simply, the Diana I knew is not the Diana that has been portrayed up till now. We have been told she had an unhappy childhood. But let me say, we were both the secure recipients of parental love.Earl Spencer apologises to Piers Morgan over ‘incorrect assumption’Read moreNever were we more content than when our parents separated. Or when we were carted off to boarding schools that thrived on neglect. And we adored the way our father was miserable for so much of our lives, his latter years made still more miserable by marrying the venomousRaine.Back to me. I was in Cape Town when I heard Diana had died. At first I could not comprehend what had happened. I was stunned, watching the TV as the story unfurled.The initial reports had been more hopeful. She was merely slightly injured. My lips curled as the commentators implied that she had got what she deserved for betraying the royal family.Then, when her death was announced, they had to change their tone. That will teach the media to be mean about my sister, I thought. My lips grimly broke into a grim smile.Quick pause as I go into yet more unimaginably dull guff about our privileged childhood and how we were always happy except when we weren’t. Then to remember how Prince Charles had sounded so giddily elated when he had phoned me to offer his congratulations. “Get in there,” he had said. “Finally I can be left in peace with my top bit on the side.”With that, the cold finality of death struck home. Never again would my heart soar at seeing my beloved Diana alive again. On the plane back to London, my thoughts turned to her eulogy. We would need someone utterly brilliant. Someone who could capture the vibrant essence of Diana and represent her true blood family. One of far more noble lineage than the House of Windsor.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Earl Spencer, Prince William, Prince Harry and King Charles, who was then the Prince of Wales, at the funeral of Diana, Princess of Wales, in 1997.Photograph: Adam Butler/PAWith that, I realised it could only be me who could be entrusted with such a solemn duty. And I would do a lot better thanNorman St John-Stevas, who had ruined my father’s service with his crass middle-class antics.Time now for a digression into some pointless filler about the Spencer family history. How for many centuries we had fulfilled our duty of opening fetes and losing money because working for a living was beneath us. How Diana and I had once gone swimming with Prince Andrew. Even then he had been even more stupid than the average member of the royal family, and I remember thinking that one day he would get into trouble for hanging around with a paedophile.Such carefree lives we all led back then. Apart from the eating disorders and the other undiagnosed mental health conditions. Little did I know that Diana’s life would be ended by a tabloid press. The paparazzi who chased her down the Alma tunnel were all wearing Piers Morgan masks. How ironic that Diana, the goddess of hunting, should be the most hunted woman on the planet. By the way, that’s a line you might recall I wrote in my superb oration. Genius, isn’t it?I’m not sure who nominated me point man for liaising with the royal family – I’m guessing it might have been me. I recall other disturbing conversations with the prince. “You’re so lucky your dad has died,” he confided. “I wish my mum would. They just treat me like a child. I even have a footman to lay out my electric train set each morning. I’d love to do it for myself.” I cut short the conversation, my mind once more returning to the magnificence of the eulogy I was shortly to deliver to a stunned world.View image in fullscreenDiana in London in December 1993.Photograph: Princess Diana Archive/GettyBut the pressure from the palace was relentless. Time and again we were told that the Spencers had always been too common for the Windsors. The funeral arrangements soon took on a darker, more sombre tone.“William and Harry must walk behind Diana’s coffin,” Colonel Ross insisted. That wasn’t going to happen, I firmly replied, firmly. “I think you will find it will,” Ross snapped menacingly with menace. The Prince of Wales needs a human shield in case people heckle him. One of my happiest memories of the funeral procession was a lone piper in the crowd playing the ancient lament, “Who’s that wanker in the crown?”“Don’t worry too much,” said Prince Charles. “Everyone will have forgotten about her soon enough.” I couldn’t believe my ears.“No one will ever forget Diana,” I tartly snapped, tartly.“Diana who?”All such a long way from the fairytale that had begun in 1980. Then the country had been in thrall to the fact that the future Earl Spencer was about to become brother-in-law to the next king of England.
