Diana, though, was already a broken butterfly, crushed by a man who had told her he would never love her but would marry her because he couldn’t really get out of it. “Thing is,” he said. “Not only do I adore Camilla with all my heart but you’re actually a bit podgy.” How I wish I had been there to say: “You’re no oil painting yourself, sausage fingers.”Diana later told me she had sobbed, sobbingly to my father that she could never marry a man who didn’t love her. But my father wouldn’t countenance such a thing. The Spencers always do their duty dutifully. Till death us do part.And so the inevitable train of events that would lead to her death were put in train. She was to be the royal family’s sacrifice to an insatiably, ravenous tabloid press who would not relent until she lay dying in the back of a car in Paris.“Oh Carlos,” Diana said to me.“Oh Duch,” I replied, replyingly“Oh Carlos.”“Oh Duch.”I find it almost too unbearably unbearable to recall some of the all too fleeting moments we had together. Though I sincerely believe that Diana was always at her happiest when she was with me. And we were so in tune with each other that silently we often didn’t need to talk.Only once did I try to dissuade her from getting a divorce, but she quickly shut me up. I like to think that Diana, like me, would be on to her fourth marriage by now, had she lived. Then we could have had a good old moan about our exes. And how expensive they are.View image in fullscreenElton John, ‘the warm-up act’, plays a specially rewritten version of Candle in the Wind at Diana’s funeral service.Photograph: Paul Hackett/APNow we get to the most solemn moment of the entire book. I find it incredible that no one in all these years has stopped to enquire how I felt when making the most celebrated eulogy in the history of mankind. Do I not count for something?Only Tony Blair fleetingly acknowledged the nation’s debt of gratitude to me. “Diana will always be the People’s Princess.” He paused, for effect. Clearly he had learned from my oratorical oratory. “And you will be the People’s Earl.”My years as a journalist for NBC filing meaningless stories that no one had ever watched was the perfect training for someone about to write a eulogy to end all eulogies. Have I mentioned that I was writing the eulogy?Once I was satisfied that I had achieved perfection, a car drove me to the chapel where Diana’s coffin was resting. It was almost as if she was tired of life. There I read her my eulogy. And at that moment, the sun shone through the stained glass and crowds bowed down in the streets, and from the coffin came Diana’s disembodied voice: “You’re a leg, Carlos.”The funeral passed almost in a daze. I remember Elton John singing Candle in the Wind and thinking: “Who is this idiot who has been brought in as my warm-up act?” After all, this was a day for me as much as for her. As for the eulogy? Let’s just say that the whole world bowed down to remember both me and Diana. Though let’s be clear, I was doing this for William and Harry. In the same way that this book is dedicated to them too.And so we come to the end of this book. Who knows what lies ahead for me? More divorces probably. But I can face the world knowing I have done right by my sister. Her memory will live for ever. Who knows what she might have become? The first lady of the US? Nelson Mandela’s wife? But at least she can rest in peace knowing that in death, at least, she had my eulogy. The eulogy which is mine.AAAGH. MAKE THIS STOP.Digested read, digested: Swanning AroundSwan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer is published by Michael Joseph (£28). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsDiana, Princess of WalesDigested readKing Charles IIIMonarchyPrince WilliamPrince HarryAristocracyAutobiography and memoirfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A blood-splattered surgeon after an emergency horse op: Andrea Modica’s best photograph | Photography | The Guardian
description: ‘You’d have to be out of your mind not to want to photograph this incredible woman. And I only realised afterwards that she looks like a medieval statue, a madonna’
Author: Amy Fleming
Headline: ‘You’d have to be out of your mind not to want to photograph this incredible woman. And I only realised afterwards that she looks like a medieval statue, a madonna’
Content: ‘The floor was covered in the contents of the horse’s intestines. We went outside’ … Modica’s shot taken at the horse hospital.View image in fullscreen‘The floor was covered in the contents of the horse’s intestines. We went outside’ … Modica’s shot taken at the horse hospital.My best shotPhotographyA blood-splattered surgeon after an emergency horse op: Andrea Modica’s best photograph‘You’d have to be out of your mind not to want to photograph this incredible woman. And it was only afterwards that I realised she looks like a medieval statue, a madonna’Interview byAmy FlemingWed 23 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter my first job in the 80s, I had a little money and set off for Italy with my camera and a backpack. I had grown up hearing about Italy, where my family is from, and so began 40 years of travelling back and forth – at times to teach photography, or for a relationship, and always to make photographs with no real agenda, just being in the moment.My new book and the show that this image appears in spans my many visits. It was taken about six years ago. I becamevery interested in a horse hospital outside Bologna.I made a large body of work there and this first appeared in a book called Theatrum Equorum, Latin for Horse Theatre, all caught on an old-style large-format 8x10 camera.I photographed horses that had been taken out of surgery, and put into these wonderful recovery boxes filled with shredded paper and beautiful light. To give you a sense of the size of the camera, it takes 8x10 inch negatives – a lot bigger than the tiny negatives from 35mm cameras. The large format meant I couldn’t photograph a horse galloping across a field.double quotation markEveryone in my work is posing – but hopefully not appearing to be posing. That is where the skill comes inIn my work everybody knows they’re being photographed. They are reacting to me and the camera, and in a sense posing, but hopefully notappearingto be posing, which is where my skill comes in. With the horses in recovery, I had a few minutes before they came to. I also made pictures of the surgical tools, before and after surgery. Then I focused on the devices that stud horses mount to have sperm collected – that’s big business. The device is a stand-in for a female horse, but first the male smells an actual horse which they keep in heat for 365 days a year. Then there were some one-off images, and this is one of them.Two people operated there: a head surgeon(the owner), and this woman,who I liked very much and connected with. In this image, she had just done emergency surgery on a horse with an obstruction in its gastrointestinal tract. The floor was covered in blood and the contents of the intestines. Many of the procedures I photographed were keyhole surgeries and the tools were very tidy, whereas this was really dramatic.She came out of surgery looking like this. I asked if I could make her portrait – you’d have to be out of your mind not to want to photograph this incredible woman. We went outside into the shade where I knew the detail would showin all its glory,as opposed to in the sun.Where punk meets Catholicism: Andrea Modica’s portraits of 1980s schoolgirlsRead moreI didn’t do it on purpose, but I like that her feet are covered so she looks like a column, and I think her hands resemble those I often saw on medieval wooden statues of saints and madonnas. This was all very unconscious, but I could see after that she looks like a statue, and I also think a very beautiful and very powerful woman. I like the picture for so many reasons that maybe somebody else wouldn’t consciously notice. But photographs can work on viewers without them knowing why.I don’t title my work.Photographyis so tied to the facts. The way the blood drips down from each one of the folds, each one becomes its own little painting. Those are facts that really existed. What we do with the facts can create an interesting story, which the viewer can ideally interpret for themself. Of course the photographer has to make the image seductive, so that a viewer actually wants to get to that point. I think this picture is at once elegant and yet has elements of horror. She’s powerful but she’s also covered in blood. There’s conflict.Andrea Modica: Italian Story is atAlice Austen House, Staten Island, New York, until 20 FebruaryAndrea Modica’s CVView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jerry SpagnoliBorn:Manhattan, 1960High point:I don’t look back and think something’s higher than what I’m doing now, even though it may have been a bigger accomplishment. I’m shooting a portrait today at 3 o’clock – that’s what I’m excited about right nowTop tip:The best work can be made if you disregard audience completely – an important message now, with people shooting and posting on social media directly. title: Why fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplay | Games | The Guardian
description: From highlighted ledges to characters telling you what to do, blockbuster games are increasingly taking the challenge out of playing – and players are pushing back
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: From highlighted ledges to characters telling you what to do, blockbuster games are increasingly taking the challenge out of playing – and players are pushing back
Content: No friction … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyView image in fullscreenNo friction … Marvel's Wolverine.Photograph: SonyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesWhy fans are digging their claws into Wolverine over its patronising gameplayFrom highlighted ledges to characters telling you what to do, blockbuster games are increasingly taking the challenge out of playing – and players are pushing backDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 23 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarvel’s Wolverine, the latest action game from Sony’s stable of expensive blockbuster-factory studios, has had an unfortunate launch.Reviews were decent, if not stellar, but a series of viral video clips from reviewers and streamers have made it the scapegoat for a patronising flavour of game design that gamers have hated for decades.This clip, from Skill Up’s review, shows the player entering a beautiful wintry landscape before being overwhelmed by visual cues telling them what they’re supposed to be doing there. Sonar pulses point you in the direction of objectives. Targets – which, it bears emphasising, areshaped like targets– get an extra reflective visual effect so you know you’re supposed to pay attention to them. A trail shows you not just where to go, but where the level’s sole hidden collectible is.It is hand-holding to the point of parody. Indeed, it reminded me of the sniggersomeMario in Unreal Enginesatiricalvideosthat makes the social media rounds every few months (“A mushroom? I should take a look at this”). Skill Up’s clip has been followed by hundreds of others, gleefully ripping into Wolverine with ironic savagery. In one much-copied clip, a streamer simply lays down his controller during a motorbike chase sequence and watches as Wolverine speeds on regardless, bouncing off the scenery as the game plays itself.People really detest this kind of thing. It’s impossible to pinpoint exactly when big-budget games started assuming that players were irredeemably stupid, but throughout the late 00s and 2010s it became more and more common to see obvious GPS trails showing you where to go, and for characters to talk to themselves to remind you what to do. At the same time, there’s been a cyclical discussion over the difficulty of games: every time a notably challenging game comes out, we rehash the same talking points about whether all games should have easy modes. Is it acceptable for games to shut players out if they aren’t prepared to “git gud”?I am not a game designer, but as a critic wholoves challenging gamesand has thought a lot about them, for me there is a difference between a game’s difficulty and its friction. A game might be difficult for all kinds of reasons, intentional or otherwise: perhaps the controls or camera aren’t great; perhaps there’s a mid-game boss with a bafflingly massive health bar and one devastating unblockable attack; perhaps the balancing is off. But a game’s friction is always an intentional part of its design. Friction is about how much a game helps you achieve its tasks. Games with perfect friction are clear about showing you what to do, but not overbearing about helping you do it: there is intentional distance, distance that you must broach with agency, strategy and skill. Friction leaves space for frustration and learning, and a sense of achievement.View image in fullscreen‘A game is only fun if you have to do something’ … 007 First Light.Photograph: IO Interactive A/SA lot of modern blockbuster game design seems hellbent on removing this friction. Not sure where to go? Here – follow this brightly coloured trail of fart gas. Not sure how to climb that building? We’ve helpfully painted the ledges yellow. Have you stood still for 30 seconds? We’ll have another character talk in your ear and tell you exactly what you need to do. Playing through the opening hours of007 First Lightrecently, I was dismayed when Bond inevitably acquired a watch that magically highlights important things in his vicinity with the press of a button.At its best, game design like this helps players avoid becoming irrevocably stuck. At its worst, it totally removes agency and challenge – you know, the reasons that many of us play games in the first place. Fundamentally, a game is only fun if you have to do something. I don’t play games for passive entertainment. That’s what binge-watching Netflix is for. If you don’t have to invest anything to reap the rewards, the experience just washes over you.Games can be difficult and have high friction. InHollow Knight: Silksong, you are constantly figuring out what to do, where the next boss might be, how to open that tantalisingly blocked path. Achieving those goals is then also very challenging, requiring practice and mastery of whip-fast fighting and precise jumping. Or they can be high-friction, low-difficulty:Blue Princetells you literally nothing about how to make your way to its mansion’s secret 46th room, but it’s not difficult to walk around and try out ideas. An example of a low-friction, high-difficulty game, meanwhile, would be a combat-focused one likeDevil May Cry(or most shooters), where the aim is always “kill all the guys to open the next area” but actually killing all those guys is majorly demanding.Low-friction, low-difficulty games hold very little interest. Many mobile games fall into this category, where you barely have to do anything save prod the screen to provoke a dopamine-shower of flashy visual effects (I’m looking at you, Monopoly Go). It’s unfair to lump Wolverine in with these almost entirely valueless games – but it is instructive that it has been subjected to such ridicule.The infamously challengingDark Souls, a dramatically influential game that turned 15 years old this week, seemed to remind the entire games industry that you canactually trust players: that they won’t drop the controller and storm off as soon as they get skewered by a skeleton. That there’s immense and unique pleasure in participatingin a game, unravelling it, conquering it little by little with skill and understanding. I hope that the reaction to Wolverine will serve as another reminder of that fact, for any executives who need to hear it.What to playView image in fullscreenPsychosocial dread … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnKonami’s horror series is on a roll lately. The Silent Hill 2 remake was very well received (with a few exceptions,including our critic), last year’s feminist, small-town Japanese horror story Silent Hill: f was excellent, and nowSilent Hill: Townfallhas succeeded in sending the series to a new setting: an island off the Scottish coast. Per our reviewerLewis Gordon: “This is a taut, smart tale, less about psychosexual terror than psychosocial dread… Townfall seems to understand that some things should remain shrouded in fog. The fate of St Amelia naturally festers in our imagination. How very Silent Hill.”Available on:PS5, Xbox, PCEstimated playtime:12-15 hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenPikachu in spaaaaaace … a toy Pikachu floats inside the International Space Station.Photograph: S Adenot/ESA/NASA/SWNSPikachuisnow an astronaut, thanks to a collaboration between Pokémon and the European Space Agency as part of the franchise’s seemingly endless series of 30th birthday celebrations. Human astronaut Sophie Adenaut brought a Pikachu plush up to the International Space Station, where it spent 67 days in orbit.According to Sonic Team boss Takashi Iizuka, Sega was once poised to kill off the wholeSonicfranchise. It was the success of 2020’s live-action Sonic movie that saved it. “I had to fight within the organization to keep the franchise as long as possible,” he toldOne More Game.The newResident Evil movieis out, and it’sgoing down well. Aftermathdescribesit as like watching your inept stoner roommate play the games; certified horror-game enjoyer Keith Stuart says it’s one of the best video game adaptations he’s seen.The Tokyo Game Showhad to wrap up one day early last week due to an incoming typhoon. Gamesindustry.biz has a slightly depressingrundownof the show, which was heavily dominated by AI.There have been yet moredramatic changesat Microsoft’sXboxdivision. The company is all but closing Halo Studios and moving Halo’s development to Activision, which will also now be in charge of storied British studio Rare. Multi-BAFTA-winning studio Ninja Theory is starting consultations on a proposed closure, having failed to find a funding deal to return itself to independence.What to clickSilent Hill: Townfall – shame and suffering on the Scottish coast | ★★★★☆Resident Evil – Zach Cregger’s rebooted action horror is a wild rollercoaster ride | ★★★★☆Control Resonant – save New York from paranormal phenomena | ★★★☆☆Roman Sands RE:Build – marooned in a crumbling vaporwave dream | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenSurreally European … Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.Photograph: Kepler InteractiveReaderMikeasks:“I just finished reading your article about the GameCube, which ironically got me thinking about the PS1 & 2, marvellous machines which I remember fondly. The game I got bundled with my PS2 was ‘Shadow of Memories’ which sticks with me to this day, the story was magnificent and also beautifully rendered, with multiple endings. Are there any similar ‘timeywimey’ games set in beautiful European villages, evoking memories of this game, out there today? Either on Android or PS5?”This question unearthed a bunch of half-remembered fragments from the early days of the PS2 – I definitely played Shadow of Memories as well. It’s a Konami game about a young German travelling through time, trying to solve his own murder. You mentioned games available on PS5, so here are a few that have some of the same elements. TheLife is Strangeseries is set in the US but has a similar time-travel and murder-solving premise;Clair Obscuris a very different kind of game but is as uniquely and surreally European; this year’s Japanese RPGThe Adventures of Elliotinvolves travelling through different eras to prevent a catastrophe. None of these have the same strange adventure-game atmosphere as Shadow of Memories, though – that’s something that felt really specific to the PS2 era. Readers, have you any more suggestions for Mike?If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter –email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterMarvelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sindhu Vee: ‘Makeup, music to feel reckless, two pieces of milk chocolate – and then I go on’ | Stage | The Guardian
description: The banker turned standup turned actor shares her preshow rituals, what’s behind her ‘very swanky hairstyle’ and her joke about Indian Santa Claus
Author: Liam Pape
Headline: The banker turned standup turned actor shares her preshow rituals, what’s behind her ‘very swanky hairstyle’ and her joke about Indian Santa Claus
Content: ‘One day I may get a facelift because never say never’ … Sindhu Vee.Photograph: Matt CrockettView image in fullscreen‘One day I may get a facelift because never say never’ … Sindhu Vee.Photograph: Matt CrockettComedy Q&AStageSindhu Vee: ‘Makeup, music to feel reckless, two pieces of milk chocolate – and then I go on’The banker turned standup turned actor shares her preshow rituals, what’s behind her ‘very swanky hairstyle’ and her joke about Indian Santa ClausInterview byLiam PapeWed 23 Sep 2026 09.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow did you go from investment banker to standup comedian?I didn’t go on purpose from one to the other. I transitioned from banking to stay-at-home mother to standup comedian. There was absolutely no previous thought process. I got on stage almost by chance, and a lot of alcohol was involved. Standup found me, and I’ve never left it alone.What inspired your latest show, Swanky?It’s just the continuing story of Sindhu Vee! The trials and tribulations, the victories and losses. My parents passed away in quick succession recently and, in their absence, I realised I had to champion myself. I took a long hard look at my life and I thought: actually it’s not going that badly. A word my father used for things that were good but kind of like mysterious and cool was swanky. I suppose one could say that my life is swanky. Why not? Then I got a very swanky hairstyle and a dress for the poster. In the absence of my parents, I had to do it. They were big champions of me.Do you have any preshow rituals?I don’t typically wear a lot of makeup, but for shows I have a very small, neat makeup routine. I listen to a playlist which is made up of primarily old music that I’ve always loved, nothing new. It’s music that makes me feel reckless. I’ll always have two pieces of milk chocolate before going on. That’s it.Did you decide to become an actor, or did it happen to you?I think a lot of standups will tell you, as you start becoming known, sooner or later your agent will get a call and say: “Would you like to read for this part?” That’s how I got everything from Sex Education to Matilda to Feel Good to Starstruck. I didn’t think I was an actor. I genuinely thought, “This is a diversity casting issue.” It turns out I can act, and a number of people who have absolutely no upside in lying to me about it have said, “No, no, you can act.” So that’s been fantastic.Standup now is very familiar. I understand it. Acting is like being in some seductive foreign country where you want to try the food and wear the clothes. It’s all very cool, but you don’t really know what’s going on. So I’ve been lucky to have directors who have been very generous.View image in fullscreen‘You can be funny without punching down’ … Sindhu Vee.Photograph: Matt CrockettWhat’s one of the strangest fan encounters you’ve had?One happened a couple of weeks ago in an airport lounge. We were all getting in the lift to go to our flight and suddenly someone said, “Oh no. Really?”, then started sobbing. We all turned to this woman. She was staring at me, so everyone then turned to stare at me. Because it was in America, I thought, “Have I said something and she’s offended?” She was crying and she said, “It’s you and I have been trying to see your shows.” Then she asked, “Can I give you a hug?” And I could not, in front of 30 people, be like: maybe that’s a step too far. So she walked across the hallway and hugged me and sobbed. I told her it was fine, wished her well, and she calmed down. I would be nowhere without fans and without my audience, but I find this a little disconcerting.Whatwas one of your all-time favourite gigs?There was a gig in a big marquee in St Albans one Christmas many years ago. We got there and it was cosy but gross because everyone had been stuffed in. It didn’t have glass windows, but if it did, they’d have fogged up from everyone’s breath. I remember I was trying out a joke about Santa Claus. I was sort of commenting on poverty in India and how that made Indian Santa Claus very skinny, so it was difficult for children to believe in him. It was a little bit tricky because I think it’s not easy to make fun of poverty. But again, as a comic, I think: this could be funny. It went down really well, and that’s when I realised how you can bring people into seeing that something is funny without punching down.Can you recall a gig so badit’s now funny?I gigged in Delhi early on in my career. I had to do 20 minutes and for some reason the MC brought me on and said, “Here’s Sindhu, who left India to go to the UK and become a comic there.” It really alienated me and everyone was furious. I started some of my best material and someone said, “Why don’t you fuck off back where you come from?” I was like, “Bro, I’m from Delhi.” Everyone hated me. People jumped on stage, stood in front of me, and said, “Look, we can tell jokes better than her.” I went home and drank half a bottle of whiskey.What have you learned from standup?If you can make people laugh, no matter how divided they are, they will feel all part of the same humanity while they’re laughing. Human beings have a capacity for that. I’ve always known it, but now I’ve experienced it. My audiences are from 20 to 80 years old. Politically, I think, they’re quite varied. But they can all laugh at the same thing. I think that means I’ll never be cynical about what human beings are capable of.What’s next for you?There’s this skin treatment called XERF. It’s a kind of a radio frequency thing on your face. One day I may get a facelift because never say never. But before that, you can try this and see what it does to your face. I’m going to try it – I’m so excited. So if you see me in the papers with a super sharp jawline, it’s because I’ve done XERF. And I’m in The Split Up, coming out on the BBC.Sindhu Vee: Swanky is on tour in the UK until 17 AprilExplore more on these topicsStageComedy Q&AComedy (Stage)Sindhu VeeComedy (Culture)featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘We live in a world of extreme consumption and waste’: Magali Reus, the artist reimagining rubbish | Art | The Guardian
description: Making vast versions of sardine tins and fishing lures, the Dutch sculptor explains how she imbues disposable objects with autonomy and meaning
Author: Sam Moore
Headline: Making vast versions of sardine tins and fishing lures, the Dutch sculptor explains how she imbues disposable objects with autonomy and meaning
Content: ‘Our understanding of objects is one of a quick transaction’ … Magali Reus with her works.Photograph: Gerrit Schreurs/ BaZView image in fullscreen‘Our understanding of objects is one of a quick transaction’ … Magali Reus with her works.Photograph: Gerrit Schreurs/ BaZArtInterview‘We live in a world of extreme consumption and waste’: Magali Reus, the artist reimagining rubbishSam MooreMaking vast versions of sardine tins and fishing lures, the Dutch sculptor explains how she imbues disposable objects with autonomy and meaningWed 23 Sep 2026 09.03 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMidway through my conversation with Magali Reus, we are interrupted by a courier. They’ve arrived at the artist’s studio to deliver an important package – one of the final components of a sculpture being finalised for Reus’s show Swimming By Night at the Perimeter in London.The studio is filled with such sculptures, all in various stages of completion. Reus likes to take everyday, often disposable, items – pizza boxes and sardine tins among them – and recreate them on a larger-than-life scale. One of them – vast looming fish hook lures made to look like uncanny cupcake cases or severed skeletal limbs – looms nearby, resting against a studio wall.View image in fullscreen‘Let’s Hang’ … Rig (All Eyes On), 2025.Photograph: Courtesy of the Artist and Mai 36 Galerie, ZurichBorn in the Netherlands and now based in London, Reus has shown in institutions across Europe and the US over the last few years, with her sculptures often responding to the specific details of buildings such as the Kunstverein Freiburg in Freiburg im Breisgau, Germany, and Kunsthalle Wien in Vienna, Austria. Her practice comments on our world of overconsumption and the fast disposing of objects that have served their purpose. “Our understanding of objects is one of a quick transaction,” she says.Reus tells me that when someone is first confronted by her sculptures, her hope is that they will seem simultaneously familiar and alien. Often, her work takes objects that would normally be briefly used then thrown away, and turns them into something more physically robust and imposing.At first glance, works from her series Subs are made to look like discarded pizza boxes – but their aluminium construction and meticulously ripped and hand-hammered edges reveal something much less disposable. “We live in a world of extreme overproduction, consumption and waste,” Reus says. Inside the “pizza boxes” that make upSubs are images of discarded Christmas trees, objects that have a brief, but meaningful, space in our lives.“In December, we gather around it, decorate it and sing beside it,” says Reus. “For a brief period of time it is a totemic, almost monumental presence in our home. By January, it lies forlorn in the street or has been thrust headfirst into a bin.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStreamers (Sprout), 2025.Photograph: Courtesy of the Artist and Mai 36 Galerie, ZurichEven when she’s describing these objects, Reus imbues them with a sense of humanity that is at odds with their disposable nature. There’s a deliberateness in the way that the work is slowly made: sheet metal is bashed into shape; multiple layers of paint are applied to resin. “The transformation,” Reus says, “changes the way that people relate to the object or the image.”Reus tells me that her aim is to give them “autonomy as objects”, allowing these things to occupy a new space, serving a purpose other than the one that might be foisted on them. These objects then become, to borrow the artist’s phrasing, “active agents,” rather than passive things to be manipulated or cast aside by people. At the centre of Rig (All Eyes On) is a recreation of a candy heart, blown up in size, with the words “Let’s Hang” emblazoned across it. This object, in its normal context, would be smaller and much more fleeting, dissolving on the tongue of whoever might consume it.View image in fullscreenFamiliar and alien … Merlin (The Tide), 2024.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Galerie Greta Meert, BrusselsReus wants these objects to “refuse to serve us, [establishing] their own parameters”. She tells me that people don’t often clock the fact that her pizza boxes are made from aluminium rather than cardboard. “I like listening to and allowing the material to dictate how things come together,” she says.Reus’s world might seem surreal, sharp and dangerous around the edges. But the more time you spend surrounded by it, the more the artist’s real aim comes into focus: allowing people to slow down and reimagine the world around them.Magali Reus: Swimming by Night is at the Perimeter, London, 25 September to 16 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArtSculptureExhibitionsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The living dead: we can watch ‘Janis Joplin’ perform or reunite the Beatles, but who are the real winners here? | Music | The Guardian
description: Advances in digital technology mean that avatars are ever more realistic, and zombie concerts are coming our way. Exciting as it might be to witness the Fab Four, or Maria Callas on stage, I’d rather have flesh and blood live experiences any day.
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Advances in digital technology mean that avatars are ever more realistic, and zombie concerts are coming our way. Exciting as it might be to witness the Fab Four, or Maria Callas on stage, I’d rather have flesh and blood live experiences any day.
Content: A trick of the light … you think you’re seeing Abba in 3D but you’re not.Photograph: Johan Persson/Abba Voyage/PAView image in fullscreenA trick of the light … you think you’re seeing Abba in 3D but you’re not.Photograph: Johan Persson/Abba Voyage/PATom Service on musicMusicThe living dead: we can watch ‘Janis Joplin’ perform or reunite the Beatles, but who are the real winners here?Tom ServiceAdvances in digital technology mean that avatars are ever more realistic, and zombie concerts are coming our way. Exciting as it might be to witness the Fab Four, or Maria Calla on stage, I’d rather have flesh and blood live experiences any day.Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.01 EDTShareIt seems that AI’s powers – terrifyingly – know no bounds. But can it raise the dead? Here’s what Avatar concert producer Unit1 Studio’s CEO Barney Wragg said in a recent interview. “We [are] talk[ing] aboutusing AI to simulate the way that tears evaporate in your eye between blinks, or subcutaneous blood flow, so that when one of our [digital] characters laughs or opens their mouth or smiles, areas of their flesh will change colour as it would do in a real human”. Digital avatars are already part of our entertainment landscape – fromTupacandAbbatoMaria Callas– but now that an avatar’s cheeks can change colour mid-set, is it game over for humans?double quotation markIn the 21st century’s equivalent of the magic lantern,  audiences will pay to witness a very expensive LED screen showing phantom musiciansWragg last week reported a massive investment in his company to makehyper-realistic avatar-entertainment.Unit1 plans to roll out avatars of musicians living – and dead – so that the success ofAbba Voyageis just the start of a slew of “hybrid” concerts. In other words, flesh-and-blood audiences paying massive amounts of human money to witness a very expensive LED screen showing phantom musicians in the 21st century’s equivalent of the magic lantern. (The tech is a 2D illusion: you think you’re seeing Abba’s Agnetha in 3D, but you’re not; it’s all just a new-fangled but fundamentally old-fashioned trick of the light.)And the frontiers for Wragg and his team are endless: recreating Live Aid, Hendrix at Woodstock, the Beatles at the Cavern Club, and doing so in multiple locations simultaneously.View image in fullscreenPart of our entertainment landscape … Snoop Dogg performs at Coachella in 2012 with a digital avatar of Tupac.Photograph: Christopher Polk/Getty ImagesIt’s the logical endpoint of a culture of nostalgia epitomised for Wragg byhis teenage nephew, who, having discovered and fallen in love with Janis Joplin’s music, wanted to see her live, but the unfortunate fact of her death in 1970 meant that this was impossible. But why should that tiny hiccup be an impediment? Unit1 can bring her back, potentially resurrecting all your other favourites of yesteryear in what Wragg calls “time-travel tourism” – assuming that they receive permission from the musicians’ estates.Wragg talks about the tech not in terms of its creative use, but its documentary capacity: “We are re-engineering a moment in time, absolutely to fidelity. It’s not a case of interpreting what somebody said, it’s just representing exactly what they said.” Unit1’s vision goes far beyond any of classical music’s attempts to recreate the musical cultures of the past withhistorically informed performance practice. Wragg talks in terms of absolute fidelity to what happened, a perfect simulacrum not of a song, a symphony, or an aria, but of an actual “moment in time”, rendered as precisely as possible, to be repeated indefinitely.double quotation markIsn’t fiction the whole point of the technology? Why not have Mozart in a keyboard battle with Beethoven?Wragg admits there are limits: “We have been approached where people say, ‘What about if this person met this star?’ We’ve said, ‘Look, you’re straying into a world of fiction.’” But surely, seeing Joplin’s avatar perform as if she were still alive today is the height of science fiction. Isn’t fiction the whole point of the technology? Why not imagine Freddie Mercury singing with Ella Fitzgerald, Nat King Cole with Marlene Dietrich, or how about Mozart in a keyboard battle with Beethoven?The problem with Mozart, Beethoven or Bach, say, is that they didn’t, alas, leave much of a digital record to work with to make their avatars, unlike Abba or Joplin. As opposed to recreating, faithfully, actual moments in time, this seems to actually be about making advanced-level digital exhibits that people will pay to see every night in spaces once reserved for human musicians to perform in but that will now be consecrated to these digital homunculi: zombie concerts, opiates for an apocalyptically nostalgic age. Try throwing an apple at the stage; try interrupting the setlist; try making them perform an encore; try to get their autographs; try to find empathy and connection with this digital playback.View image in fullscreenA hologram of Maria Callas (1923-1977) performs during a concert at the National Auditorium of Mexico City in April 2019.Photograph: José Méndez/EPAOr maybe I should get with the programme and embrace the theme-park immersion of this wondrous age of technology that helps keep us stuck in a permanently perfected past. But if Unit1 could find enough digital traces out there in the ether, I’d love to have been there for the premiere of Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro in Vienna in 1786; to have witnessed Louise Bertin’s Fausto in Paris in 1831; to be overwhelmed by Mahler’s Eighth Symphony when it was first performed in Munich in 1910; or to have been in the crowd for the premiere of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring in Paris in 1913 to find out if there really was a riot at the ballet.But here’s the thing. Even if Unit1 could accurately represent not only the performers but every detail of these events, it would still be meaningless as a creative project.Classical music, at least, is all about interpreting what somebody wrote in the context of our times, not recreating the same thing night after night. That’s true time travel, and there’s no AI required.This week Tom has been listening to:Keir GoGwilt and friends’The Zarabanda Variations, which takes a simple question – what are the origins of the dance known as the sarabande in European repertoires? – anddiscovers and unearthsa network of stories that connect Africa to the Caribbean, European salons to the realities of colonialism, and turns all of those histories into a teeming, thrumming, retuned present tense.Explore more on these topicsMusicTom Service on musicClassical musiccommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I find myself weeping after almost every scene’: how seminal show 7 Up has touched your lives | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s inspired careers, moved you deeply and helped you reevaluate your own journeys. As the series that began in 1964 comes to an end with 70 Up, Guardian readers explain the impact of the decades-spanning tale
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: It’s inspired careers, moved you deeply and helped you reevaluate your own journeys. As the series that began in 1964 comes to an end with 70 Up, Guardian readers explain the impact of the decades-spanning tale
Content: ‘Changed my life’ … The participants gather for 7 Up’s final season, 70 Up.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Changed my life’ … The participants gather for 7 Up’s final season, 70 Up.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockTelevision‘I find myself weeping after almost every scene’: how seminal show 7 Up has touched your livesIt’s inspired careers, moved you deeply and helped you reevaluate your own journeys. As the series that began in 1964 comes to an end with 70 Up, Guardian readers explain the impact of the decades-spanning taleGuardian readersandAlfie PackhamWed 23 Sep 2026 05.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 07.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleITV’s landmark 7 Up documentary series has launched its final outing after 63 years. The show started following the lives of 10 boys and four girls in England when they were seven years old, and has returned every seven years since.‘It’s the Bayeux tapestry of TV!’ After six decades, the seminal series bows out with 70 UpRead moreAs the final season 70 Up reaches its conclusion, seven people tell us what it has meant to them over the decades – along with pictures of themselves contrasting their appearance now with their childhood selves.‘Life is a sum of experience, even if seemingly mundane’View image in fullscreenJudith Barton.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenJudith Barton, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityThe sadness of Suzy as a teenager and seeing her become more content and confident was a standout moment. As was Bruce becoming a “missionary” in his own way by teaching. And, of course, Neil, whose life has often been troubled but is probably the most interesting. It has been a privilege to be able to compare myself with the participants and look at my own journey. It has made me realise that life, whether you’re rich or poor, is a sum of experience, even if seemingly mundane. In many ways, it’s not education or privilege that makes life interesting, but what you do with opportunities as they present themselves. The most engaging characters have been those who have challenged themselves, pursued an ambition or who have had difficulties to overcome.Judith Barton, 69, Surrey‘Deeply moving’View image in fullscreenSheila Lambe.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenSheila Lambe, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityThat Neil, who was the most adorable, magical-thinking seven-year-old, would have mental health crises had a deeply moving effect on me. His challenge was one that could have affected any of the participants, regardless of class and background. And Nick achieved so much despite relatively humble beginnings but gave one of the most impactful statements – that the birth of his son was his greatest moment. As the series progressed, it seemed that the real measure of success was not academic or material achievements after all, but familial love and finding peace.Sheila Lambe, 63, Scotland‘The series fired my imagination’View image in fullscreenMartin Forsey.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenMartin Forsey on his first day of school.Photograph: Guardian CommunityIt was Bruce I related to most. His disposition, his search for meaning. I was an overseas volunteer and related strongly to his search for local connections later in his life. Different, but the same. The series changed my life. I first encountered it through a sociology of education class, as part of a graduate diploma I was studying part-time in the evenings, while working as a science teacher. I was from a working-class background and had no idea what sociology was when I left school. The Up series fired my sociological imagination; I retrained and became a sociologist and anthropologist because of it. It was exciting in the ways it helped explain myself to myself, as well as the broader world in which I lived. My research focused on education and I have written a number of papers focused on the structural and cultural effects of class on life trajectories and the choices people make.Martin Forsey, 65, Fremantle, Western Australia‘The best TV series ever’View image in fullscreenShirley.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenShirley, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityI’ve watched the whole series. It resonated with me because I am of a similar age. I was not surprised to see that the girls seem to have a lesser part, with emphasis during interviews on their roles as wives and mothers, rather than their careers. I experienced the same kind of thing. I think the teenage years showed a lot of vulnerability in girls who wanted to appear grown up to the world. I believe it is the best TV series ever, showing how times have changed from the 60s to the present and the progression through a person’s life. I think perhaps every seven years it should be repeated in its entirety, with tributes to those involved who have passed.Shirley, 68, London‘Unexpectedly overwhelming’Lyle JacksonPhotograph: Caitlin Steva/Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenLyle Jackson, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityWatching 70 Up has been unexpectedly overwhelming. I have found myself weeping after almost every scene. Over the past three years, I have lost several close friends and family members, so grief is always near the surface. The series brings back not only the years that have passed, but also what was lost, what endured and what was learned along the way. When I started watching in 1975, documentaries were almost absent from commercial television in the US. It was intimate, patient and honest about ordinary lives. It showed that a person’s story could unfold slowly, with all its disappointments, contradictions, resilience and surprise.That recognition changed the arc of my life. I became a documentary photographer and producer, winning 18 regional Emmys. My work has often focused on people who were overlooked, marginalised or simply not often given the space to be seen.Documentarywork kept me grounded through hard periods in my own life. I will always be grateful for what the series gave me: a belief that ordinary lives are never ordinary when someone has the patience and compassion to keep looking.Lyle Jackson, 72, Nashville, Tennessee‘As I grow older, I identify with the participants more and more’View image in fullscreenKhalid Dajani.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenKhalid Dajani, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityI most identify with Paul, who is first seen at the foster home and establishes a family of his own with his lovely wife in sunny Australia while remaining the sensitive, gentle and intelligent boy he was when we first saw him in 1964. He struggled with his self-confidence, even though there was no apparent reason for that, and bravely acknowledged it as an ongoing issue. I would have liked to have been his friend, had I been a seven-year-old there with him back in 1964.I first heard of the series about eight years ago, through a Roger Ebert book where he marked it out as the best documentary he had ever seen. I watched all the episodes on YouTube over two weeks just in time for the 2019 release and it was amazing to see the children grow into middle age. By pure luck, I also got a chance to see [the now late director] Michael Apted and his wife in Dubai who were here for a movie showing at that time. As I grow older, I identify with the participants more and more while also noticing what different lives we all lead but with the same, shared core of wanting to spend our limited time as best as we can. If only we knew how.Khalid Dajani, 54, Dubai‘I became a documentary film-maker in my 20s and the 7 Up films set a gold standard’View image in fullscreenAlan Reich.Photograph: Guardian CommunityView image in fullscreenAlan Reich, aged seven.Photograph: Guardian CommunityIn 1970, when I was seven, my brother and I went to a Jewish summer camp. I cried for the first few nights missing my parents and home. In the first week, the original 7 Up film was shown on a noisy film projector and I sat transfixed, watching these other seven-year-olds from such a different world to my sheltered religious Jewish bubble. I continued to seek out the following films wherever I lived and catch up with these familiar children, who were like friends that were always seven years ahead of me in my own life journey. With the edit back to their younger selves, I could understand how the little boy and girl can still be seen in that grown up. I became a documentary film-maker in my 20s and the 7 Up films set a gold standard for me to have a deeper connection with interviewees, and where possible maintain contact with them.In 2018, at the Sheffield documentary festival, I met Michael Apted and told him that the 7 Up films had influenced me to become a documentary film-maker. In his intense, inquiring questioning style that I recognised from all those films, he flashed back: “And how is that going for you?” The truth is that by then my career in films had petered out and I had retrained as a psychotherapist. I am now 63 and I still enjoy the deeper connection with people, helping them to explore and shine a light on how our past still plays out in our adult lives.Alan Reich, 63, LondonExplore more on these topicsTelevisionDocumentaryFactual TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threats | Dolly Parton | The Guardian
description: Star’s estate granted restraining order against Bryan Seaver, who publicly announced Parton’s death, over alleged intimidation that he denies
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Star’s estate granted restraining order against Bryan Seaver, who publicly announced Parton’s death, over alleged intimidation that he denies
Content: Dolly Parton performing at Glastonbury festival in England in 2014.Photograph: Ian Gavan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDolly Parton performing at Glastonbury festival in England in 2014.Photograph: Ian Gavan/Getty ImagesDolly PartonDolly Parton estate in feud with nephew over alleged ‘warfare’ threatsStar’s estate granted restraining order against Bryan Seaver, who publicly announced Parton’s death, over alleged intimidation that he deniesBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 23 Sep 2026 06.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 18.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe estate of the lateDolly Partonis involved in a dispute with the country music star’s nephew and former head of security, and was granted a restraining order against him and his private security company amid allegations of threats.Bryan Seaver was responsible for Parton’s security, and was tasked with announcing herdeath on 25 Augustwith a video, “something Dolly asked of me years ago”, he said.But since the singer died, her estate, which is run by Parton’s manager Danny Nozell, has reportedly fired Seaver from his security job, and has now alleged that he made “relentless” threats against Nozell and others.According toBillboard, the lawsuit filed in aTennesseecourt reads: “These were not ordinary workplace disputes or heated words; they were deliberate threats from a self-proclaimed heavily armed, former security operative with a military-contractor background. Many of [Parton’s staff members] are now afraid to come to work or have resigned entirely because they do not feel safe.”Wednesday’s restraining order says theTennesseejudge took into account the repeated threats cited in the complaint, as well as the alleged demands for payment and Seaver’s “claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate”.As part of the order, Seaver and his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, must refrain from talking with or being within 1,000ft (300 meters) of employees, attorneys and business partners of She’s Alive, the entity founded to manage Parton’s estate. The order is also meant to keep Seaver from interfering with its business relationships.A hearing is scheduled for 7 October.Seaver is alleged to have written to a lawyer for Parton, “I’m a killer”, and separately told Nozell: “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” He is also alleged to have claimed that he made a $27m arms and ammunition deal with Haiti.He allegedly claimed he would “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or fucking pay me.”Seaver repeated some of those claims in comments to TMZ while defending his actions, saying: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.”Regarding the messages to Nozell, Seaver said: “I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster. A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.”In another message, Seaver reportedly said: “I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratfucking anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”Speaking to TMZ, Seaver said of that comment: “I was talking about people that have done bad to Dolly in business – a specific company that scared her and intimated her. Those comments were about specific, horrible business partners that have done wrong to her and I stand by that.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeaver’s security contract was terminated on 15 September, with a leaked termination letter saying the decision was made “for the protection of the trust and beneficiaries as a whole”, though it reassured Seaver it was “not a termination of your personal interest in the trust”.Seaver put out a statement after the termination, saying: “We remain unshakably resolved to fulfil her final directive to protect her family, and we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much.”The Guardian has contacted Seaver and lawyers for Parton’s estate for further comment.Parton left behind considerable financial assets: not only her songbook featuring hits such as 9 to 5, but also a broad business empire including the entertainment resort Dollywood in Tennessee.She had no children, and her husband, Carl, died in 2025, but she is survived by other family members including six siblings and an uncle. Seaver is the son of her sister Cassie.Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsDolly PartonCountryLaw (US)CelebrityTennesseenewsShareReuse this content

title: Angry Anderson dies aged 79: Rose Tattoo frontman was a ferocious rock’n’roll singer and youth advocate | Australian music | The Guardian
description: The singer, songwriter, actor and advocate, who has died after a cardiac arrest while touring in Europe, kept his band’s flame burning until the end
Author: Andrew Stafford
Headline: The singer, songwriter, actor and advocate, who has died after a cardiac arrest while touring in Europe, kept his band’s flame burning until the end
Content: Angry Anderson performs on stage at Mornington Racecourse, Melbourne, in April 2025. Anderson has died aged 79 after he was hospitalised in Germany on tour with band Rose Tattoo in September.Photograph: Martin Philbey/WireImageView image in fullscreenAngry Anderson performs on stage at Mornington Racecourse, Melbourne, in April 2025. Anderson has died aged 79 after he was hospitalised in Germany on tour with band Rose Tattoo in September.Photograph: Martin Philbey/WireImageAustralian musicAngry Anderson dies aged 79: Rose Tattoo frontman was a ferocious rock’n’roll singer and youth advocateThe singer, songwriter, actor and advocate, who has died after a cardiac arrest while touring in Europe, kept his band’s flame burning until the endAndrew StaffordWed 23 Sep 2026 02.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGary “Angry” Anderson – who has died aged 79 after he was hospitalised following a cardiac arrest while on tour in Germany with the band Rose Tattoo, the balls-out band he fronted for 50 years – was not a nice boy growing up. As one of the founding members of Melbourne motorcycle club the Vigilanties, Gary Anderson initially earned the sobriquet Mouse, on account of his diminutive stature.Determined to prove himself a man, he developed a penchant for taking on blokes twice his size. It earned him a new nickname: the Angry Ant. “Angry” – shortened for impact – suited him better. An accomplished rabble-rouser and ferocious rock’n’roll singer, Angry Anderson ended up channelling his energy into a variety of causes.By Anderson’s own admission, the Angry persona was akin to a cartoon character; Buster Brown – his band before Rose Tattoo, with AC/DC’s Phil Rudd on drums – was actually named after one. In 1974 they cut an album for Mushroom, Something to Say, and built a loyal following among the local sharpies in Melbourne. But that was a mere dress rehearsal.Rose Tattoo, formed in Sydney in 1976, were a far meaner proposition. Slide guitarist Peter Wells gave their sound much of its switchblade menace and brain-busting volume, but it was Anderson’s voice that cut through everything. In Buster Brown, he had proved himself a capable blues singer. In Rose Tattoo, he rarely bothered with such niceties;nice boys don’t play rock’n’roll.Then there was the small matter of Anderson’s appearance. Tiny, bald and nearly fully illustrated (his upset mother told him he wasscarred for life), with mirrored aviator shades and kicked-in teeth, Angry was flanked by much bigger hooligans on stage. But there was no doubting who the leader of the gang was.The first self-titled Rose Tattoo album, released in 1978 – the same year as AC/DC’s Powerage and the Angels’ Face to Face – appeared at the height of the blood-and-thunder Alberts sound defined by producers and former Easybeats Harry Vanda and George Young. Featuring the enduring singles Bad Boy for Love and Rock ’n’ Roll Outlaw, it is a stone classic of the genre.But mainstream Australia was nowhere near ready for the Tatts. The butchest of bands, who looked as if they’d just busted out of Pentridge, managed to get temporarilybanned from Countdownafter Anderson exchanged chewing gum in a kiss with guitarist Mick Cocks. Radio ignored them, crowds thinned, and the band lost momentum.Overseas, however, it was a different story. Rose Tattoo’s fortunes changed in 1981 when their self-titled debut and its follow-up, Assault and Battery, both reached No 1 on the British heavy metal charts. At Reading festival in the UK, Anderson’s physicality was terrifying, head-butting the amplifier stacks until blood streamed down his face.Welcomed home as conquering heroes, the band’s third album Scarred for Life yielded an Australian hit with We Can’t Be Beaten before the lineup split. What happened after that was one of Oz rock’s most unlikely transformations as Anderson slowly ingratiated himself into the nation’s heart as a youth advocate and all-round rough diamond.There were forays into acting – a 1985 appearance asIronbar Basseyin Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome was fully on brand – and social justice; soon he was making surprise appearances on the Midday Show with Ray Martin, then more regular ones on A Current Affair. But the biggest curveball of Anderson’s career was yet to come.View image in fullscreenAnderson and mother Marie at the 2006 Aria Hall of Fame presentation in Melbourne.Photograph: Kristian Dowling/Getty ImagesBy 1987, Anderson was the sole remaining member from the classic Rose Tattoo lineup. The power ballad Suddenly, a world away from their earlier hellraising sound, was released as a solo single and became a smash when it was used to soundtrack – of all things! –thewedding of Scott and Charlene(Jason Donovan and Kylie Minogue) on Neighbours.Suddenly went to No 2 nationally, ironically kept from top spot by Minogue’s debut single Locomotion. It also went to No 3 in the UK. For a while, Angry was everywhere – even headlining the half-time entertainment at the 1991 AFL grand final, arriving in what looked like a Batmobile to sing Bound for Glory in alegendarily off-key performance.But by then, Anderson’s legacy was secure. Guns N’ Roses – havingcovered Nice Boyson their Live ?!*@ Like a Suicide EP – recruited the band to support them on their Use Your Illusion tour in 1993; the same year, Anderson was awarded an Order of Australia. In 2006, after two strong comeback albums, Rose Tattoo were inducted into the Aria Hall of Fame.Indeed, Rose Tattoo’s imprint on Australian music has never been more obvious. You can trace their lineage through a slew of punk and hard rock bands, from the Cosmic Psychos to Amyl and the Sniffers (even the Veronicasinvited Angry on stage to do Nice Boys). Their impact on the 80s new wave of British heavy metal, as well as the Gunners, was decisive.In later life, Anderson blended charity, television and music with hard-right politics. After expressing anti-immigrant views, he appeared in SBS’s Go Back to Where You Came From in 2012. In the 2013 federal election, he stood for the electorate of Throsby in New South Wales for the National party, switching to the Australian Liberty Alliance in 2016.Anderson also suffered significant tragedy in his life. His work with troubled youth stemmed from his own experience of child abuse; later, he stumped for men’s health after five of his early Rose Tattoo comrades succumbed to cancer. The cruellest loss of all was that of his son Liam, killed in 2018 in a case that made national headlines.It is both true and a cliche to say Angry Anderson was a survivor. He was also a more complex, talented and three-dimensional figure than he was often given credit for. And he kept the Rose Tattoo flame burning until the end, to huge and appreciative crowds – one of the last great true believers in theremedy they call rock’n’roll.Explore more on these topicsAustralian musicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content
