title: Brothers review – Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey’s super-fun sitcom about the chance they’re related | Television | The Guardian
description: The actors co-star in a lightly fictionalised meta-comedy about their real-life bromance – and possible sharing of parents. It’s a tasty little treat
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: The actors co-star in a lightly fictionalised meta-comedy about their real-life bromance – and possible sharing of parents. It’s a tasty little treat
Content: Play it again … Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson in Brothers.Photograph: Ryan Green/Courtesy of AppleView image in fullscreenPlay it again … Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson in Brothers.Photograph: Ryan Green/Courtesy of AppleTV reviewTelevisionReviewBrothers review – Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey’s super-fun sitcom about the chance they’re relatedThe actors co-star in a lightly fictionalised meta-comedy about their real-life bromance – and possible sharing of parents. It’s a tasty little treatJack SealeWed 23 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cheek! The indulgence! The privilege! Did anyone, anywhere in 2026, look up from news of a world in flames and say, what we really need now is a meta-comedy where two actors play gently self-satirising fictional versions of themselves?They did not, and yet here are Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson. They once co-starred in thefirst season of True Detective, one of TV’s darkest and best crime dramas, but otherwise their personae have them as lifelong besties who are both free spirits, unencumbered by the rules of the fame game – not the sort of chaps who would stop and think about how their self-referential comedy bagatelle might be received. In Brothers, they portray themselves as blokes who don’t stop and think, full stop.We begin in Malibu at Harrelson’s sea-view mansion, where we see him army-crawling past the infinity pool in an effort not to be seen by his wife and daughters, because he has detected the sound of the thing he fears most, raw female feelings. Sure enough, once he’s been spotted and captured, it turns out that his elder daughter Olive (Highdee Kuan) has suffered a collapsed engagement and the family is in crisis. So he implements the only solution he can come up with given his lack of emotional intelligence, which is to bundle his women into his converted bus and road-trip to the Texas hilltop homestead of his old buddy,Matthew McConaughey. The wide plains and wide-armed Texas welcome will heal all.When he gets there, though, he finds McConaughey agonising over a speech he’s giving at an event commemorating his venerated late father. The introspection, and the possibility of showing himself to be an inspiring orator sparks a midlife-crisis plan to run for election as state governor. The presence of Harrelson, a house guest who has arrived unbidden and does not know when to leave, is a complication, even before Harrelson has a bomb dropped on him in a private conversation with McConaughey’s mother: she used to know Harrelson’s dad, and that’s “know” in the sense that he might also have been McConaughey’s father.The two pals reconnect over such staples of Texas life as huntin’, fishin’, rodeo-ridin’ and returning from a car journey with the bloody corpse of the deer you ran over strapped to the roof. The mild culture clash between the straight-talking Texan McConaugheys and the angsty Californian Harrelsons causes beef that’s easily sorted with huggin’ and learnin’ at the episode’s end – albeit with the potentially cow-sized beef of the two men’s secret genetic link rumbling through the season.It sounds inessential, and it is, but hock-bobbit and skippity-breakfast if this pair of toot-scootin’ Hollywood butt-nuts haven’t hit upon a tasty little comedy dynamic. Their screen personalities are different but the same in ways that can never be resolved, which is just what a comedy wants. McConaughey is a man of faith, in God and “the universe”, whose conservative ways are at odds with Harrelson’s west-coast liberalism, but Harrelson’s environmental awareness and animal-rights principles are also articles of blind faith. Harrelson seems selfish and insensitive compared with McConaughey’s convivial mateyness, but his bluntness often shakes his friend out of the fantasy world he lives in. Both are all hat and no cattle, but each can only see that in the other, not in themselves.The fake screen Harrelson and the exaggerated fictional McConaughey are, in other words, strong sitcom protagonists. Even better, though, are the supporting players, starting with Holland Taylor as the aforementioned loose-lipped matriarch, Ma Mac, a self-described “woman of quality” who occasionally has a shotgun in one hand and always has a drink in the other. “This isn’t adraaaaaank,” she tells Harrelson: “This is my mornin’ coffee ‘n Kahlúa! There’s barely any vodka in here!”Fiercely competing with Taylor for the show’s best scene-stealer is Lisa Gilroy as McConaughey’s campaign manager, a power-suited dispenser of unvarnished honesty. “I love the folksy spirit of this!” she says, waving a hand at her client, as he rambles on about his down-home family values. “Not personally. Personally I find it repulsive. But for the campaign? It’s gold!” Or to McConaughey’s patient wife Valentina (a somewhat thankless role for Natalie Martinez): “I love you playing the role of this cool, level-headed spouse, it really works for you. I am going to get you a stylist though, because the dress you’re wearing? It’s made of jeans. And I’m going to get you a good hairbrush. Hey Siri! Remind me to get the wife a good hairbrush!”Such fine creations further down the cast show that Brothers is a bit more than two famous guys blithely horsing around, even if that’s what it ultimately boils down to. It’s a fun little trip.Brothers is on Apple TVExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewWoody HarrelsonMatthew McConaugheyTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Martin Compston’s guide to Las Vegas, his bizarre second home | Television | The Guardian
description: The actor, whose wife is from Vegas, finds a hotel room with a basketball court and loses big at blackjack. Plus: Not Going Out turns 20. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The actor, whose wife is from Vegas, finds a hotel room with a basketball court and loses big at blackjack. Plus: Not Going Out turns 20. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Riding with the King … Martin Compston: Living Las Vegas.Photograph: Tern Television Productions LtdView image in fullscreenRiding with the King … Martin Compston: Living Las Vegas.Photograph: Tern Television Productions LtdTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Martin Compston’s guide to Las Vegas, his bizarre second homeThe actor, whose wife is from Vegas,  finds a hotel room with a basketball court and loses big at blackjack. Plus: Not Going Out turns 20. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Ali Catterall,Graeme Virtue,Hollie RichardsonandSimon WardellWed 23 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMartin Compston: Living Las Vegas10pm, Channel 4Actor Compston is married to a woman from Vegas; this three-part documentary sees him trying to get a handle on a place that has never quite felt like home. He’s a cheerful guide to this bizarre city of hype, neon and casinos, checking out a hotel room with its own basketball court and blowing a hypothetical $20k on four hands of blackjack. Eventually, you understand both the excitement and the reservations engendered by the place.Phil HarrisonThe Secrets of Your Phone: They Don’t Want You to Know7pm, Channel 5Are smartphones snooping on us? Because increasingly, it feels as if we’re all buckling under an avalanche of personalised ads. The truth may be more disturbing: for all the hoo-ha, we’re still supremely relaxed about handing over our “digital profiles”. But we can, at least, erect some guardrails, as Alexis Conran discovers.Ali CatterallShakespeare & Hathaway: Private Investigators8pm, U&AlibiLove looks not with the eyes but with the mind. Will that help Stratford private eye duo Lu (Jo Joyner) and Frank (Mark Benton) when a heartsick client hires them to infiltrate a sensory-based matchmaking service? Judging by this opener, series six of the cosy crime drama is as fun as ever.Graeme Virtue20 Years of Not Going Out9pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenModern yet traditional … Not Going Out, which is turning 20.Photograph: Perou/BBC/AvalonLee Mack’s domestic sitcom is turning 20 – a feat that seemed unlikely when it was cancelled in 2009. It was given a stay of execution thanks to audience pressure and has thrived ever since: according to this breezy documentary, the secret is its clever balance between modernity and tradition. Season 15 begins immediately after.PHGrand Designs9pm, Channel 4Emily and Peter have a bold rebuild plan that will replace their London home with a pair of three-storey “cloud houses” inspired by the pastel colours and art deco curves of 1930s Miami architecture. But will they pass muster as McCloud houses? Kevin monitors a typically tumultuous project.GVSam Smith: Live at the London Coliseum10.40pm, BBC OneThe Grammy/Oscar/Brit winner is on a stripped-back “intimate” tour with a new album,Hazel Eyes, where their gorgeous vocals are front and centre. This specially recorded night at the London Coliseum also closes with their greatest hit, Stay With Me.Hollie RichardsonFilm choiceToy Story 5 (McKenna Harris and Andrew Stanton, 2026),Disney+View image in fullscreenA new sheriff in the bedroom … Bullseye (left) and Jessie, voiced by Joan Cusack, in Toy Story 5.Photograph: Pixar/Lucasfilm/Disney/APNot particularly hot off the production line – Toy Story 4 was seven years ago – Woody, Buzz and their boxful of plastic friends are back, but WALL-E director Andrew Stanton maintains the franchise’s beguiling focus on the joys and pitfalls of childhood. With the retired Woody (Tom Hanks) absent, Joan Cusack’s Jessie is the new sheriff in town/bedroom. But she faces an existential threat when her owner, Bonnie, ostracised by her tech-savvy peers, gets a tablet – the superior Lilypad “Lily” (Greta Lee) – and loses all interest in play. While having a dig at society’s digital obsessions, it’s also a nostalgic eulogy to a world where pure imagination and the capacity to be silly are cherished.Simon WardellThe Love Hypothesis(Claire Scanlon, 2026),Prime VideoWeirdly, the bestselling novel on which Claire Scanlon’s campus romance is based started life as Star Wars fan fiction about Rey and Kylo Ren. Not that you’d know it, save for the involvement in this film of Tom Bateman, Daisy Ridley’s husband, who stars as Adam, AKA “Dr Evil”, a loathed Stanford biology lecturer. He is persuaded by doctoral student Olive (Lili Reinhart) to pose as her boyfriend, so her best pal, Anh (Rachel Marsh), will date a boy Anh thinks Olive still fancies. In return, he will look more committed to the university and have his funding renewed. Love among the lab coats ensues.SWExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our job was not to attack’: how do you make a documentary about America’s culture wars? | Documentary | The Guardian
description: Oscar-winning film-maker Barry Levinson’s docuseries Bucks County, USA examines the political divide in one town in a revealing and infuriating manner
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Oscar-winning film-maker Barry Levinson’s docuseries Bucks County, USA examines the political divide in one town in a revealing and infuriating manner
Content: ‘We’re looking into what happened in an area that was almost idyllic, that threw us out that far out of whack?’Photograph: SenArt Films & Baltimore PicturesView image in fullscreen‘We’re looking into what happened in an area that was almost idyllic, that threw us out that far out of whack?’Photograph: SenArt Films & Baltimore PicturesDocumentary‘Our job was not to attack’: how do you make a documentary about America’s culture wars?Oscar-winning film-maker Barry Levinson’s docuseries Bucks County, USA examines the political divide in one town in a revealing and infuriating mannerAdrian HortonTue 22 Sep 2026 20.41 EDTFirst published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike many teenage best friends, Evi and Vanessa have a penchant for finishing each other’s sentences. Whether enmeshed on a couch or telling a story, one, a red-headed musical theater nerd with a personality nearly as boisterous as her signature puffy skirts, collides with the other, darker in hair and disposition, their speech bubbling with indecipherable affirmations and giggles. In a heady chorus of “duuude” and “no, you!”, it can be difficult to tell where one girl ends and the other begins.‘Who do you really believe?’: the true crime fans who became a part of the storyRead moreExcept, that is, at their respective homes. Evi’s mother, Lela, who like her daughter, espouses views considered left of liberal in the US context, speaks in support of LGBTQ+ students at local school board meetings and advocates for fact-based history lessons. Vanessa’s father, Paul Martino, is a right-leaning venture capitalist who likes to brag about installing school board members by spending $500,000 on local campaigns, an effort triggered by what he saw as unjustified school closures in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic.That their parents do not see eye to eye is an understatement; both are actively involved – on social media, on Zoom and in the meeting room – in lobbying their local school district board, and frequently call out the other by name. Like many towns across the US, the girls’ home in Doylestown, Pennsylvania, an affluent district north of Philadelphia, has been roiled by the political and cultural currents triggered by upheaval of Covid-19. Seemingly overnight, concerns that simmered in various social media forums and side chats – the legality of masking, critical race theory, DEI, slavery, election conspiracy theories and viral fixations over transgender students and bathrooms – concentrated in perhaps the one unifying place in town: the school, and in particular its governing board, whose public meetings frequently ended in ugly shouting matches. Evi and Vanessa may open each episode of Bucks County, USA, a new five-partPBSdocuseries embedded in one emblematically polarized town, in unison, but the adults, it seems, could not stop fighting.The series, directed by Robert May and Oscar-winning film-maker Barry Levinson, of Rain Man glory, and filmed over four highly contentious years, plays out a roving gallery of 2020s US politics in miniature – a “microcosm for communities around the country”, said May, where concern for one’s children morphs and mutates into hardline stances. Good intentions and, at times, bad information collide with pride in familiar, if fascinating and infuriating, stalemates. “We’re not trying to be political, to point fingers about this and that,” Levinson said of the dispassionate series, which gives many town-members free range to express their views. “We’re looking into what happened in an area that was almost idyllic – what threw us that far out of whack?”By the time the film-makers arrived in town in late 2021, inspired by a two-partepisodefrom the New York Times’ The Daily podcast, the Central Bucks school board was already riven with conflict. Pushback to the district’s mask policy and Covid closures, along with Martino’s money via a Pac, fueled previously inconceivable attack ads and fake fliers. A new conservative majority on the board had turned their attention to certain books, which were either “grooming” children or LGBTQ-positive, depending on who was doing the talking. And talk people did, from parents to students to former teachers, from board members with pride bumper stickers on their cars to a parent speaker affiliated with Moms for Liberty, the Florida-based rightwing group that built anoutsized influenceon school boards across the country primarily viabook ban campaigns.“We wanted to talk to people from both sides that really had a point of view,” May explained, letting curiosity be their guide to a true cross-section of the town’s ideological landscape. Interviews often began with personal questions and with promises to not interrupt, which were greeted warmly, particularly by conservative townspeople more skittish about a film crew. “It’s a rarity for someone to be able to speak for 30 seconds without someone firing back a counterpoint, and neither one of them then are listening to one another,” said May. “Our job was not to attack the person that’s sharing their opinion, but allowing them to share their opinion, to allow multiple sides to share an opinion and let the audience decide.“We know that there will be critics that will see this series, looking at someone that they don’t like, and they will say: ‘Well, they were lying, and we should have told them that or called them out on it,’” he added when I noted the potential for false equivalencies. “And of course, if you have that point of view about it, you missed the whole point of the series.”View image in fullscreen‘We wanted to talk to people from both sides that really had a point of view.’Photograph: SenArt Films & Baltimore PicturesThe team spent hundreds of hours filming in the town, anchored by Evi and Vanessa, who remained close even as Evi campaigned against the school board’s proposed ban of classroom pride flags, while Vanessa assisted her mother Aarati Martino, on the campaign trail for school board as an Indian-American former tech worker who viewed DEI as, in her opinion, a self-limiting mindset. “The idea here is to let people see these people as human, and then they can go out and determine what they know or don’t know about any particular issue that may be presented in the series,” May said of the long-term investment in listening and observing as views shift in real time.In its five hours, Bucks County, USA presents numerous avenues into the predominant culture wars of the decade’s first half, from book bans and transgender healthcare to DEI and vaccines. But though it is long on the many, many ways personal experience and emotions can crystallize into one’s politics, how baffling and contradictory and at times hypocritical all of us can be, it is short on compromise. What, after all, is the middle ground between a trans student fighting for acceptance, and a mother who believes said acceptance is “grooming” children? Or Martino, who argues “equity is not a fundamentally American principle”, and a Black parent who recognizes that “for someone to say they don’t want diversity, equity and inclusion … then to me, you’re saying you don’t want my family here.”There isn’t, really, though May and Levinson remain hopeful through the effort of trying. “We didn’t necessarily witness folks that changed their political persuasion or changed their political view, but we did witness people that agreed to figure out how to talk to one another and come together,” said May, particularly in a final series roundtable, after the first two episodes’ 2025 Sundance premiere, where both conversation and tensions flare. “You see it throughout the series – there’s an effort,” said May. “It doesn’t all get wrapped up in a bow by any means. But you can see the respect level go up.”“The idea is to be able to approach somebody and say, ‘I love you and I respect you. And I am curious about why you think a certain way,’” he added. Evi and Vanessa, now out of high school, suggest perhaps the only way forward: reciprocation. “We ought to be able to hear something and respond in kind and not try to accelerate it into left and right,” said Levinson. “Once you do that, you can’t work things out.”Bucks County, USA is available on PBS and to watch on the PBS appExplore more on these topicsDocumentaryUS televisionTelevisionFactual TVPolitics TVPBSfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: John Green got an astronomical following from his books. What came next? ‘I’m still competing for clicks’ | John Green | The Guardian
description: Returning with his first-ever adult novel, the bestselling author reflects on fame, YouTube and his brother’s AI controversy
Author: Carter Sherman
Headline: Returning with his first-ever adult novel, the bestselling author reflects on fame, YouTube and his brother’s AI controversy
Content: John Green: ‘I suspect that young people want to be famous for the same reason I wanted public attention, which is that I thought it would fill a hole inside of me.’Photograph: Marina WaterView image in fullscreenJohn Green: ‘I suspect that young people want to be famous for the same reason I wanted public attention, which is that I thought it would fill a hole inside of me.’Photograph: Marina WaterJohn GreenJohn Green got an astronomical following from his books. What came next? ‘I’m still competing for clicks’Returning with his first-ever adult novel, the bestselling author reflects on fame, YouTube and his brother’s AI controversyCarter ShermanWed 23 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.28 EDTShareBy his mid-30s,John Greenhad done pretty well for himself. His debut novel, Looking for Alaska, had won a prestigious award for young adult literature. He and his brother, Hank, had launched a popular YouTube channel, where they regularly posted videos about their lives. With their combined incomes, Green and his wife were able to cobble together a living, buying a house and starting a family in Indianapolis.And then, in 2012, he published The Fault in Our Stars.“The week that book came out, it sold more copies than all of my previous books had sold in hardcover combined,” Green recalled in a recent interview with the Guardian podcastStateside with Kai and Carter. “Up until that moment, I’d been very cavalier about sharing my life online and offline, and it was only in the wake of that that I started to realize the cost of that. People started coming to our house, sometimes quite late at night. We had young kids – babies – back then. People don’t always have the best boundaries.”The Fault in Our Stars follows the story of Hazel, a 16-year-old living with cancer, who falls in love with a fellow cancer patient. Powered in part by Green’s online fandom, the book sold more than 20m copies – enough for every person in the state of New York to have a copy, and then some. In 2014, Hollywood adapted it into a movie starring Shailene Woodley and Ansel Elgort. After the film became a blockbuster, raking in more than $300m at the global box office, Hollywood started adapting Green’s other books, too.double quotation markYou have a choice about how public to make your life. You don’t really have a choice about the public’s response to thatJohn GreenToday, Green is as famous as an author can probably get. He has published another young adult novel and two nonfiction books – all of which also became bestsellers. HisYouTubechannel with Hank, Vlogbrothers, now has north of 4 million subscribers. The brothers have posted about practically every topic imaginable, from giraffe mating to presidential tax platforms to what it feels like to spend 15 hours in a Target.But he remains decidedly ambivalent about his popularity. It doesn’t feel nourishing, he said. It feels like empty calories.“It was uncomfortable to talk about, because how do you not be grateful for this overwhelmingly wonderful thing in your life?” Green said. “I have a friend who’s a very successful author, and I remember she said to me once: ‘Of all the good things that ever happened to me, fame was the worst.’ I think that’s a pretty good way to think about it.”View image in fullscreenHollywood, Ending by John Green.Green decided to work through his mixed feelings in his new book, Hollywood, Ending. Released this week, the book follows two young actors who make a movie about Andy Warhol, fall in love, and try to stay sane as they sell pieces of themselves to the internet and the Hollywood publicity machine. It’s Green’s first novel in nearly a decade, and his first-ever for adults. But it still feels like a classic John Green book – thanks, predominantly, to its ardent belief that art, and other people, can help us survive anything. In an era in which more and more people must market themselves on social media, courting the dizzying highs and crushing lows of fame, Green still hopes we’ll find something better.I spoke with Green about the moral complexity of the attention economy, what he wishes he had done differently as a pioneering YouTuber and his brother Hank’s recent AI controversy.This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. Watch the Stateside podcast episode in fullhere.CS:This book is so much about fame and the various machines that create and perpetuate celebrity culture: journalists, social media, movie studios. Why was this something you wanted to write about?JG: It used to be that this was a question mostly for celebrities, mostly for actors and to a lesser extent novelists. Now, it is a question for everyone because we all participate in this attention economy. We all transform our private lives into publicly consumable goods, whether that’s posting about our dog’s death on Facebook or our marriage on Reddit or whatever. These questions about how best to handle the publicization of one’s private life are no longer rarefied.I guess the overriding question was: is it worth it to make art in an age where art will inevitably be so commodified and will cost us so much in the making?I feel like the moment your fame really kicked into a different gear was with the publication of The Fault in Our Stars in 2012. When did you realize:“Wow, I have really hit something new here?”I remember I was on the road for about a month touring. I got home, and I called my agent and I said: “When does this end?”And she said: “You don’t really choose.”How did you feel in that moment?Both excited and trapped, which I think is the nature of celebrity a little bit – that it’s exciting and also claustrophobic. You have a choice about how public to make your life. You don’t really have a choice about the public’s response to that.View image in fullscreenAnsel Elgort (left) and Shailene Woodley in the film adaptation of The Fault in Our Stars (2014).Photograph: 20th Century Fox/Sportsphoto/AllstarOn the other hand, it was wonderful to have the book reaching so many millions of people. Living with all that at the same time was both exciting and challenging, like it is for the young people in Hollywood, Ending.It’s much harder for them because I was 35 years old and married and had kids and the foundational relationships in my life were pretty set. When this happens when you’re 22, as it happens to a lot of people, whether they’re influencers or actors, you often don’t have those relationships. It can be really disorienting.It sounds to me like you’re saying:“This thing that was happening around my house, around my family, that was more real.” Why did the excitement around the book feel unreal?I don’t think it ever feels real, to be honest with you. I think it always feels like that’s happening to someone else. One of the things that [Andy] Warhol saw coming is that people don’t really see famous people as people. They see them as both more than people and less than people. They objectify them in every imaginable way. They feel free to comment on their bodies, they feel free to comment on their work as if they weren’t people, and so on.The other thing is that I wanted really badly to be successful. I think I wanted much more than would be healthy to be successful. I had no concept of what it would actually feel like. It was really rewarding to have so many people respond to the books and the story so generously. But the fame part of fame was quite empty.Why did you want fame in the first place?I don’t think I was liked very much in middle school. I really struggled with making friends. I thought that if I was famous, then everyone would be my friend and like me. That turns out to be a little bit of an oversimplification.A lot of people don’t like you, right? The nature of being famous is that everybody has an opinion about you, but not everybody has a positive opinion about you. That’s one thing that I hadn’t really thought very hard about.The other thing is that compliments simply don’t penetrate. I believe people in the abstract when they say that my work has been helpful to them or that it has been meaningful for them, and I’m extremely grateful for that. I don’t want to disbelieve them because that would dishonor the gift that they’ve given me by investing in my work and by bringing their deepest selves to it.But the criticism just penetrates in a different way. I believe it, because deep down there’s something about me that believes I don’t deserve any of this and I’m an impostor and I’m not a very good writer.47:50John Green wanted to be famous. Now what? – Stateside with Kai and CarterYou and your brother Hank have been creating videos for YouTube since 2007. How do you feel about your legacy as a pioneer of the social internet?Hank and I try really hard to do interesting, useful, fun, meaningful stuff in online spaces that build community and also make the world suck less. I hope that we’ve been able to do some of that. But there’s no question that just participating in an algorithmically generated internet is morally complex.You’re competing with Mr Beast for clicks. Even if I’m making an educational video that’s intended for high school students to be able to understand US history or physics or organic chemistry or whatever, I’m still competing for clicks with people who will do or say literally anything for clicks.Do you think, feeling the way you feel now about the social internet, you would have started making YouTube videos if you had to do it all over again?I’d do it again because it’s been an amazing experience and it’s been such a gift in my life.I might do it without my face in the videos, to be honest with you. That’s the big difference. A lot of my educational video friends don’t have their faces in their videos, and I find that admirable.But so much of the community you build is, frankly, parasocial.Yeah, it is. It is face-based. It’s hard to imagine not doing it that way.Actually, the time when Hank and I both realized that we weren’t actually in control of what we share was when Hank got cancer a couple years ago. We realized one of two things was gonna happen.One: Hank was going to, for the first time in 20 years, take eight months away from making Vlogbrothers videos without an explanation. Or, two: he was going to be forced to talk about having cancer in public.Hank ended up dealing with it beautifully by not just talking about having cancer, but by sort of science-communicating his way through cancer treatment, which is a very Hank Green thing to do.What do you make of the fact that in the age of the social internet, so many people, particularly young people, really just wanna be famous? The fame itself is a goal.Not only is the fame itself a goal, fame has become so decoupled from wealth that no longer is fame a guarantee of financial security. I have a friend, for example, who was a famous TikToker and also worked at the Gap. People would come to the Gap where they worked and be like: “Why are you working?” They would be like: “For money. Because this is where I work.”double quotation markI do think we have to build meaningful relationships with each other in meat space, as they say onlineJohn GreenI suspect that young people want to be famous for the same reason I wanted public attention, which is that I thought it would fill a hole inside of me. What fills the hole is real connection, which is the relationships that are gonna sustain you through everything you have to survive.It’s interesting that you’re saying this. In an interviewyou did last year with the New York Times, you talked about feeling like people believe the internet fills a hole – but then, you didn’t really want to tell young people not to try to use the internet to heal themselves. I’m wondering if you have different advice for young people now.It’s so hard. I’m going through this now with one of my godchildren, where when you don’t have the relationships that you want to have in your community because you’re different – as I was – or because your interests are too niche or whatever it is, you find connection online. I was part of the first generation of people who found that, in 1993 on CompuServe. It was revelatory, to be able to not be stuck inside of a body that was frail and embarrassing and full of failure, and instead to be this creature online where I could really connect with people. Some of the people I connected with, I’m still connected to. I’m so grateful for that.Yet at the same time, it can’t replace what we experience with real life connection. I do feel a little differently than I did a year or two ago. I do think we have to build meaningful relationships with each other in meat space, as they say online.I think it’s very helpful to be reminded that my body is made out of meat, that even the thinking parts are made out of meat. It’s very easy online to lose track of the fact that you’re a mammal. You’re much, much, much closer to being a squirrel than you are to being an artificial intelligence.I feel like in the book and in this conversation, you are suggesting that fame is corrosive to us and that the online attention economy is not good for us. But having a social media platform, having a personal brand, being on camera – that is all stuff that more and more people just have to engage with, not in order to necessarily be famous,but to have a professional life. How are we supposed to move forward?What the book concludes, I hope, is that we have to seize the reins of power and understand that we have more power than we think we have as internet citizens, as creators online.I remember suddenly becoming conscious on the set of The Fault in Our Stars that everyone cared what I thought. The reason they cared what I thought was not because I’m an incredibly compelling person, but because I had millions of followers on Twitter and at any moment I could blow up the movie. Understanding that with the sacrifices involved in participating in the social internet – there is also an exchange of power. Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk don’t have all the power, as evidenced by the declining role of X in society. They have a lot of power. They have too much power. Way, way, way too much power. But, combined, we have more.View image in fullscreenJohn Green (left) and Hank Green speak at VidCon at the Anaheim convention center on 23 July 2015 in Anaheim, California.Photograph: FilmMagicHollywood, Ending is to some extent about how much you have to feed the content beasts in order to succeed. So I did want to ask about a recent dust-up that Hank was involved in, where he was accused of using AI to write part of a script for a video. He addressed the controversy. He said that AI did not write the script but admitted to relying on AI more and more to research his work. That’s honestly understandable to me, because he really produces a lot. Hank suggested that you and he had spoken and that you had some criticism of his AI use. Are you comfortable telling me about those criticisms?Yeah, it’s more than being critical of his AI use in particular. I have my own opinions. I don’t use LLMs and don’t see a need to use them in my work.It was more about the fact of what you just said, which is Hank makes a lot of stuff. I think especially in the last couple of years, Hank has been obsessively trying to get everything in his head out into the world and I think that is not healthy. We’ve had that conversation and that’s part of being a brother. Hank’s had those conversations with me many times before.Hank Green: ‘I used all my power to make YouTube powerful, good and strong’Read moreTrying to get everything out of your head seems like a pretty reasonable response to a bad health scare.Yeah, I think it is a reasonable response to mortality. I think the more reasonable response – not that I’m here to lecture my brother – is to invest in your core relationships.You have expressed mixed feelings about people seeing too much of you in the art you make. I have spent this interview very much reading you into Hollywood, Ending. How do you feel about that?You haven’t read into it in a way that makes me uncomfortable, so I feel fine about it. There are other things you could have read into it that would have bothered me.It’s uncomfortable to be read into the book because I don’t want to be a character in the book. I have written two nonfiction books now and six novels, and writing fiction is so much more vulnerable and intimate than writing nonfiction.Why is it more vulnerable?It just is. Because I have to go to deeper places within me. I have to go to places that nobody else knows about, not even the people closest to me. That’s really hard work, but it’s good work because I’m asking the reader to do the same. I’m asking them to bring their deepest selves to the story, to bring their own particular traumas and fears and loves and losses to the story in a way that no one else can. That’s asking a lot. So I have to do the work on the other side to make that worth it. Hopefully.Hollywood, Endingby John Green is out now via Dutton Books

title: The Complex by Karan Mahajan review – a superb family saga set in Delhi  | Fiction | The Guardian
description: At once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty squabbles, this tale of corruption and betrayal is packed with drama
Author: James Smart
Headline: At once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty squabbles, this tale of corruption and betrayal is packed with drama
Content: Karan Mahajan.Photograph: Briscoe SavoyView image in fullscreenKaran Mahajan.Photograph: Briscoe SavoyFictionReviewThe Complex by Karan Mahajan review – a superb family saga set in DelhiAt once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty differences, this tale of corruption and betrayal is packed with dramaJames SmartWed 23 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe learn about the murder of the Chopra clan’s shifty, crude, charismatic patriarch Laxman in the opening pages of The Complex. Twenty-five years have passed, but the stain on this once-respectable Punjabi family remains. The man who did it, Laxman’s nephew Brij, has served his jail time and is about to be released. Some relatives think Brij is too dangerous, too shameful to return to the family home, but his son Mohit decides the pair will live together – and rewinds the clock to tell the story of the decades leading up to the crime.Karan Mahajan’s warmly received first two works, Family Planning andThe Association of Small Bombs, explored individual lives alongside larger forces – urban development in the former, a car bomb’s traumatic aftermath in the latter. His excellent third novel has Delhi at its heart, but also visits Indian villages and cities, the American midwest and London, its short chapters flitting between different members of the Chopra family. You start by nodding in appreciation at Mahajan’s observant character portraits; before you know it you’re waist-deep in frustration, corruption and betrayal, as the book ranges through politics, faith, migration, infidelity and entrepreneurship.The main stage for Mahajan’s epic yet grubby tale is the residential compound that gives the novel its name. This sun-eaten collection of flats and bungalows in the Delhi suburbs became the family’s base in the post-independence glory days of SP Chopra, a freedom fighter turned politician and businessman. Since his death from a boardroom heart attack, his nine children and their descendants have never quite lived up to his reputation, and the complex has become the increasingly ramshackle home of several couples and their offspring. Family members swap gossip, chide their servants and tussle for the best apartments, flouting building regulations and each other’s wishes as they go.double quotation markMahajan’s skill at getting into his characters’ heads means The Complex is a wonderfully immersive and in-the-moment workSP’s elder children are mostly distant figures, and instead we follow the youngest, Laxman, who half-heartedly runs a bobby pin factory and a local temple; Brij, a military pilot turned paper-mill manager; and Brij’s younger brother Sachin, who moves to Michigan to develop squeezable plastic sauce bottles. Around these would-be giants of industry, women find what power and release they can. Laxman’s wife Archana sneaks on to the complex roof for cigarettes and privacy, while Brij’s wife Karishma walks the weedy garden. In the US, Sachin and his wife, Gita, have both more space and more isolation, but the rest of the Chopras are never far away: on visits they demand tea at all hours and comment on the pair’s problems conceiving. The swaggering, entitled Laxman makes grim lunges at both Gita and Karishma.As the 70s become the 80s, Sachin and Gita return to Delhi while Laxman, Karishma and Brij join forces to produce a line of ayurvedic balms. Children cram for exams and play cricket; adults bicker, hatch plans and do their best to ignore the increasingly blatant infidelity in their midst. Outside the complex, socialist governments become increasingly pro-business, Indira Gandhi is assassinated and Hindu nationalism rises. Laxman at first tries to mollify tensions, before becoming a vital player in a fledgling party that seeks to inflame them: the BJP.This is a novel at a constant simmer, packed with characters who are all deeply flawed and often deeply awful. Everyone plays the game to one degree or other, confident problems can be solved by money, force of personality or the right favour from the right person. But the Chopras are fraying, and the Complex is at once a palace and prison, with its “glum black water tankies; the clotheslines savagely crossing the roofs; everything sloping toward death”.Mahajan’s skill at getting into his characters’ heads means The Complex doesn’t feel as bleak as that image might suggest: it’s a wonderfully immersive and in-the-moment work. There’s beauty here, in marble temple floors “the colour of a thunderstorm”, or the image of Gita tightening her shawl to protect her “inky Banarasi silk sari from the cinders whizzing like miniature glowing kites” – as well as kindness, particularly in the sweet relationship between Gita and her nephews.But the darkness is rendered just as vividly: cruel conversations around the snack table, vengeful nationalism, caste snobbery, the almost surreal horror of communal violence, Laxman’s grasping hands. This is a fine piece of work, at once a grand sweep through history and a domestic novel of petty squabbles. Mahajan drops enough breadcrumbs as he goes that the Chopras’ journey towards murder and radicalism feels less like a twist and more like a procession – but one packed with drama and life.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Boorman and the Devil review – enjoyable re-evaluation of the disaster that was Exorcist II: The Heretic | Movies | The Guardian
description: John Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly panned
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: John Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly panned
Content: Oh the horror … John Boorman in Boorman and the DevilView image in fullscreenOh the horror … John Boorman in Boorman and the DevilMoviesReviewBoorman and the Devil review – enjoyable re-evaluation of the disaster that was Exorcist II: The HereticJohn Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly pannedPeter BradshawWed 23 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Kittredge gives us a thoroughly enjoyable, detailed account of the catastrophe that was John Boorman’s 1977 film Exorcist II: The Heretic, the deeply ill-conceived and widely derided follow-up to The Exorcist, a bizarre but ambitious fantasy supernatural rhapsody, brimming with unintentional comedy. Yet it was visually bold and even brilliant, pioneering in its use of Steadicam; Linda Blair and Max von Sydow were persuaded to return; Richard Burton was cast as a troubled priest, and Louise Fletcher as a psychiatrist whose weird “mind-reader” contraption was entirely ridiculous. At the first film, people screamed. Now they screamed with laughter.According to an apocryphal tale gleefully repeated by William Friedkin, director of the first film, the sequel resulted in an enraged audience one night turning round and booing Warner Brothers executives in the back row of the cinema, and then chasing them out of the building and down the street. Boorman desperately recut the film with the sillier bits removed. But the damage was done.Boorman is interviewed here and generously goes into great detail about his painful and mortifying experience with the film, how he had originally been offered the first Exorcist, disliked the story and turned it down, but was induced to take on the sequel. Perhaps Kittredge could have made it clearer how risky it was for Boorman to have taken on a project which he fundamentally didn’t believe in and was somehow creatively working against. He hired a kind of script-and-direction consultant, his friend Rospo Pallenberg, whose influence with Boorman annoyed the cast.This, after all, was the era of sequels, and Coppola’s Godfather II had shown that they could be as good or better than the original. It was also an era when brilliant directors were trusted by studios to follow their instincts, cushioned from risk by something called “blind bidding” from movie theatre chains who would pay upfront for films on the basis of known quantities like stars, story and director, a practice which this disastrous film ended. But it was also an era when, after Mel Brooks’s The Producers, the media’s chattering classes were alive to the hilarity of so-bad-it’s-good. There was something else, too, something rarely acknowledged by reviewers: the pressure to follow extravagant praise with disparagement, so that the critical-superlative economy does not go bankrupt. And finally, like William Friedkin’s Sorcerer that same year, like all films good and bad of the time, Exorcist II: The Heretic had to go up against Star Wars, which blew everything else out of the water.It’s another proof of William Goldman’s maxim that nobody knows anything. If people had laughed at the spinning head in the first Exorcist, industry sages would have shrugged and said: yes, of course, obviously, it’s absurd. But the stars were aligned for that one. Now in retrospect we can make a case for Exorcist II: The Heretic being an interesting and misunderstood film. Kittredge quotes some mean reviews but doesn’t mention that the New Yorker’s Pauline Kaelactually made a contrarian case for it at the time, on the basis of its delirious experimental visuals. Perhaps the truth is that Heretic was, like Boorman’s sci-fi adventure Zardoz with Sean Connery in the crazy red mankini: weird, surreal, challenging, a shapeshifting creature vulnerable to mockery, at once monstrous and terribly fragile.Boorman and the Devil is in UK and Irish cinemas from 25 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsHorror filmsThe ExorcistJohn BoormanFilm industryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: North Sea, Nature Untamed review – stunning footage finds the beauty and splendour under the water | Movies | The Guardian
description: Diver Peter van Rodijnen’s footage of basking whales, plankton blooms and fatherly fish disputes the idea that the North Sea is a bleak wilderness
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Diver Peter van Rodijnen’s footage of basking whales, plankton blooms and fatherly fish disputes the idea that the North Sea is a bleak wilderness
Content: No fillings … a still from North Sea, Nature Untamed.Photograph: Joost van Uffelen/©Dutch Maritime ProductionsView image in fullscreenNo fillings … a still from North Sea, Nature Untamed.Photograph: Joost van Uffelen/©Dutch Maritime ProductionsMoviesReviewNorth Sea, Nature Untamed review – stunning footage finds the beauty and splendour under the waterDiver Peter van Rodijnen’s footage of basking whales, plankton blooms and fatherly fish disputes the idea that the North Sea is a bleak wildernessCath ClarkeWed 23 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 04.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe North Sea, with its cold grey waters, is the world’s drabbest. Or so you might have thought, but this documentary featuring the Dutch diver and underwater cinematographer Peter van Rodijnen sets out to tackle the misconceptions. His stunning footage puts all the splendours of this stormy stretch of water on show, and his voiceover gives it an endearing eccentric charm.First, the greyness. Van Rodijnen films the North Sea’s waves sparkling with the cosmic blue light of bioluminescent algae, and lit up with the disco colours of coral and plankton blooms. He also brings us cute, coo-worthy stories from the depths; take the male shorthorn sculpin fish (no looker, it must be said) who spends the winter looking after his eggs, cleaning and blowing fresh water over them. Van Rodijnen’s camera is there for the baby fish hatching – pop, pop, pop out of their pearly plump pink eggs. There are some quirky stories, too, including a barnacle with a superlong penis.‘Sharks are my film stars’: how the Jacques Cousteau of the North Sea finally unlocked its beautyRead moreOther moments are pure spectacle. A teeming school of mackerel puts on an Olympic show of synchronised swimming, and Rodijnen’s patience as a film-maker pays off with jaw-dropping footage, literally in the case of a basking shark filmed off the coast of Scotland. Swimming with its mouth open, feeding on plankton, it’s “the big friendly giant of the seas”, says Van Rodijnen. But it can’t be a nature documentary unless there is an environmental catastrophe on the horizon. In Scotland, numbers of a puffin breeding colony are down by 30% due to overfishing. But there are eco wins, too. The Atlantic bluefin tuna, which vanished from the North Sea in the 1960s,is back, and it’s a brute – it can grow heavier than a grand piano. What the film lacks in slickness, it makes up for with enthusiasm.North Sea, Nature Untamed is in UK cinemas from 25 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMarine lifeNetherlandsEuropeWildlifereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Manhunter review – Michael Mann serves up a bold and queasy starter to the serial killer spectacle | Movies | The Guardian
description: Before Anthony Hopkins’ Dr Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, Brian Cox played a cannibalistic killer in Mann’s pioneering Red Dragon adaptation
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Before Anthony Hopkins’ Dr Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, Brian Cox played a cannibalistic killer in Mann’s pioneering Red Dragon adaptation
Content: Downbeat and deadly … Brian Cox as Dr Hannibal Lecktor in Manhunter.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenDownbeat and deadly … Brian Cox as Dr Hannibal Lecktor in Manhunter.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMoviesReviewManhunter review – Michael Mann serves up a bold and queasy starter to the serial killer spectacleBefore Anthony Hopkins’ Dr Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, Brian Cox played a cannibalistic killer in Mann’s pioneering Red Dragon adaptationPeter BradshawWed 23 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFive years before The Silence of the Lambs, there was writer-director Michael Mann’s pioneeringThomas Harrisadaptation Manhunter, now on re-release in a director’s “final cut” for its 40th anniversary. It was his version of Harris’s 1981 novel Red Dragon, a movie which features Dr Hannibal Lecter (here spelt Lecktor) in a relatively minor part, and played in a much more coolly matter-of-fact and downbeat way by Brian Cox, who is first discovered in his cell lying down with his back to the camera.It has long been a haughty, hipster film-bro affectation to claim that Cox is better in the role than Anthony Hopkins. (Lecktor’s early acoustic stuff was great, you see, before he went electric as Lecter.) I think that’s a bit obtuse, for all that Cox is of course very good. Hopkins in The Silence of the Lambs is the definitive version: face it. But I will concede that Cox is more interesting than Hopkins by the time the latter came to make the 2002 adaptation of Red Dragon, at which stage the franchise had become a bit tired. Manhunter itself is a very interesting and watchable movie, but feels a little unevolved compared to Jonathan Demme’s masterly guignol spectacle, although Demme clearly inhaled Mann’s excitement at jets, ’copters and military hardware deployed at speed to bring down just one man.As in Lambs, the idea is that Dr Lecktor has to be creepily consulted in prison by a law enforcement officer who needs his help bringing down another serial killer, in this case the Tooth Fairy. (Unlike that monster or Lambs’ Buffalo Bill, Lecktor himself does not suffer the vulgar indignity of a nickname, and is always respectfully addressed by his name and academic title.) But there is an interestingly hostile charge in the fact that the person coming to see Lecktor is not a demurely polite young woman, but the guy who actually brought him down in the first place: careworn but brilliantly intuitive FBI profiler Will Graham (William Petersen). The cold dislike in Cox’s face, and his subsequent evil plan, is a marvel.After the trauma and burnout of tracking down Lecktor, Graham has been persuaded back on to the job by FBI chief Jack Crawford (Dennis Farina), desperate for his expert help; this has obvious implications for what no one in 1986 called Graham’s “mental health”. Graham is brilliant at the job because he can think his way into the serial killer’s twisted mind, and doing this all over again could send him over the edge. Right now, he has a very 80s-looking luxury sunkissed beachfront home in Florida in which to spend his retirement.The Tooth Fairy himself is Francis Dollarhyde (Tom Noonan) who has a Frankenstein’s-monster type tendresse with a blind co-worker called Reba, played byJoan Allen. It is with her that the film has the strange and rather amazing, if preposterous, scene; somehow Dollarhyde has connections at the zoo which lets him get Reba in behind the scenes to stroke a sedated tiger in one of the most startling “first date” scenes in cinema.The film also features an obnoxious tabloid journalist, Freddy Lounds (Stephen Lang), whose terrible fate at the hands of the Tooth Fairy is pretty plain from the outset: we see how creepy loser Lounds in his way has something in common with serial killers: pathetic, inadequate and predatory, projecting his failings into compulsive behaviour, but evidently without the satanic glamour and imagination of the alpha-male psycho murderers. Manhunter is a brash, queasy, bold thriller; yet for me, it is a curtain-raiser for the main event.Manhunter is in UK and Irish cinemas from 25 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmThrillersMichael MannJoan AllenBrian CoxFilm adaptationsThomas HarrisreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Remake review – Ross McElwee’s magnificent and moving tribute to a tragic loss and the art it inspired | Movies | The Guardian
description: Celebrated documentary maker Ross McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this profoundly moving tribute and meditation on making art
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Celebrated documentary maker Ross McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this profoundly moving tribute and meditation on making art
Content: A film that works on  many levels … Adrian McElwee in Remake.Photograph: PR ImageView image in fullscreenA film that works on  many levels … Adrian McElwee in Remake.Photograph: PR ImageMoviesReviewRemake review – Ross McElwee’s magnificent and moving tribute to a tragic loss and the art it inspiredSherman’s March director McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this magnificently affecting film and meditation on making artLeslie FelperinWed 23 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 04.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis new film from revered documentary-maker Ross McElwee is an extraordinary work, arguably his most audacious use yet of autobiographical material while at the same time being a coruscating self-criticism of that same technique. Think of it as an artistic ouroboros (a snake eating its own tail). Remake is all at once about creativity, shame, love and loss, revelling in the way film can capture a moment of truth and honesty, but tempered by the knowledge that once a subject knows they’re being filmed everything becomes a kind of performance. It’s a film that works on so many levels and at the same time is so simple and direct.On that very simplest level, Remake starts out as a documentation of how Hollywood got in touch with McElwee and told him they wanted to make a fictionalised remake ofhis best-known film, Sherman’s March. Made in 1985 with a one-man crew (McElwee himself), Sherman’s March recorded the McElwee’s trip back to South Carolina where he grew up; there he films his family, old friends, and himself as he continually fails to establish romantic relationships with various women, all of it lavishly slathered with his own warm, softly southern-accented voiceover.But a lot happened after McElwee made that film. He did eventually get into a lasting relationship and had a son, Adrian; later the couple adopted a baby girl in Paraguay. All that becomes grist for the feature at hand, as we learn quite early on that Adrian died relatively recently as an adult and so every shot of him – a cute chatty little kid, fishing off a pier, pretending to run a restaurant, and slowly getting older and bigger – becomes painfully charged. It’s not just that the little kid is gone; Adrian himself is entirely gone and all that’s left is the material his father shot of him, as well as the film clips Adrian made himself when at one point he wanted to become a film-maker too. Adrian’s craving to be seen and his willingness to let his father film him starts to feel troublesome to McElwee – especially when you consider that others started to push the camera away.Remake slowly reveals what it was that led to Adrian’s death – not in order to create any kind of salacious mystery, but because it only makes sense, as much as something so senseless ever will, after we’ve got to know Adrian better: his aspirations and his troubles, a bipolar diagnosis, the deep wells of self-doubt that are not unlike his father’s. The end result is a profoundly moving work, one that will resonate with anyone who is a parent or close to a troubled kid, but one that has so much more about the making of art, its joys and its dishonesties. It lingers in the mind long after the tears have dried.Remake is in UK and Irish cinemas from 25 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsFamilyBipolar disorderreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Love Hypothesis review – hit BookTok romcom lacks spark on screen  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Riverdale’s Lili Reinhart does some heavy lifting in adaptation of Ali Hazelwood’s hit book, but it’s not quite enough
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Riverdale’s Lili Reinhart does some heavy lifting in adaptation of Ali Hazelwood’s hit book, but it’s not quite enough
Content: A still from The Love Hypothesis.Photograph: Philippe Bossé/PRView image in fullscreenA still from The Love Hypothesis.Photograph: Philippe Bossé/PRMoviesReviewThe Love Hypothesis review – hit BookTok romcom lacks spark on screenRiverdale’s Lili Reinhart does some heavy lifting in adaptation of Ali Hazelwood’s hit book, but it’s not quite enoughAdrian HortonWed 23 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFans of the dearly departed Riverdale – or, moreover, admirers of all the batshit things the CW comic soap could make its bright young actors say with straining sincerity – have long rooted for Lili Reinhart. The Betty Cooper of yore was the best of that talented crop (Charles Melton and Camila Mendes among them) at rising above her subpar surroundings, her impressively expressive eyes able to sell the unsellable with complete conviction. She is the type of helplessly endearing performer suited to roles of naivety who masks surprise steeliness, as in her notable turn in 2019’s Hustlers or, better yet, romcoms, though there remains a dearth of worthy material. (A dual role in 2022’sLook Both Ways, a Netflix homage to Sliding Doors, didn’t cut it.)Heart of the Beast review – Brad Pitt survivalist dogmance serves up wilderness with side of cheeseRead moreAt least on paper, The Love Hypothesis, a new romcom fromAmazon Prime Video, should be that material. The BookTok sensation by neuroscientist turned author Ali Hazelwood presents an ideal Reinhart protagonist: extremely nerdy, in a periodic table way, yet conventionally beautiful, awkward and self-deprecating yet cutting when it counts, the type of sweet-presenting young woman who will shout “fuck” repeatedly in private. Which Reinhart’s Olive Smith, a young biology PhD student at Stanford, winsomely does in the film’s unsettlingly cold open, as a bleary-eyed Olive, blind from expired contacts, freaking out before her grad school interview and then boldly stating her cancer-solving intentions to a brusque, handsome professor in a lab bathroom.That Olive and said professor, haltingly played as a robot-cum-dreamboat by Tom Bateman, will fall in love is of course a given; The Love Hypothesis arrives amid a wave of BookTok adaptations that largely tinker with the genre formula, with mixed results, from the hit-and-miss CoHo movies (Regretting You,Reminders of Himand, most notoriously and successfully,It Ends With Us) to the YA smashThe Summer I Turned Prettyand this summer’s hit Off Campus, itself riding the cultural tidal wave that wasHeated Rivalry. In that long shadow, The Love Hypothesis, directed by Claire Scanlon, a veteran of Netflix’s 2018 romcom wave (Set It Up), from a screenplay by Sarah Rothschild, comes off as artlessly, almost lazily by the numbers, a faltering chain of tropes (enemies to lovers) and stock characters (the unavailable man, the gay best friend) to a jaunty string score.It does not help that The Love Hypothesis possesses one of the flimsiest fake-dating plots in a deluge of fake-dating plots. The setup is a bit convoluted, and perhaps necessarily rushed through: Olive, an orphan whose mother’s death inspired her apparently pioneering research into pancreatic cancer detection (this, I believe!), bonds quickly at Stanford with Anh (Rachel Marsh), a fellow grad student whose bold personality is signified by her “feminism” T-shirts. When Anh turns down a date with Jeremy (Nicholas Duvernay) because she knows Olive has feelings for him, Olive scurries like a lab mouse to find a reason to convince her otherwise. Cue a sudden kiss, in between lab tests, with the first man she can find, who happens to be Dr Adam Carlsen, that handsome scientist all the students call Dr Evil … and who also needs a girlfriend to prove to administrators that he’s staying put, lest they cancel his grant funding.Again, Reinhart can sell many imperfections – a mousy shade of brunette, a wardrobe more 2016 than 2026, a very inconsistent voiceover, clunker lines like: “My dopamine is surging!” or: “Your work on circulating tumor cells is groundbreaking!” – but a choppily edited fake-dating plot this thin proves especially challenging. Still, she is admirably game for the task, as Olive and Adam, both extremely task-oriented and possibly (though never explicitly) neurodivergent, awkwardly try to convince others of their attraction while continually hashing out the terms of their “experiment” with all the control/variable terminology you’d expect. At her best, Reinhart invokes the near-hammy but impossibly charming comedic timing of Big Fat Liar-era Amanda Bynes, particularly in a scene in which the couple must sell their relationship to Dr Tom Benson (Arty Froushan), the suave Harvard lab director of Olive’s dreams who also happens to be Adam’s best friend.Reinhart remains the film’s ace through its many tonal stops and starts, from relatively molehill-sized conflicts to an abrupt swing toward the comically evil (perhaps a holdover from the novel’s roots as Star Wars fan fiction). That inconsistency is reflected in Bateman’s performance, which jerks between unfeeling automaton and swoonworthy romantic hero too readily; there is only so much he can do to mask his ability to play tall, dark and handsome leading man, though one unexpectedly sensitive, female gaze-y sex scene – let’s just say that a line reading I have to imagine was supposed to be “you’re incredible” lands as “you’re edible” – does a lot to boost the film’s flagging heat. Still, you don’t have to be a scientist to be left wanting for more chemistry. The Love Hypothesis demonstrates that you can have all the right ingredients for a romcom, but movie magic has never been a science.The Love Hypothesis is available on Amazon Prime nowExplore more on these topicsFilmRomance filmsComedy filmsAmazon Prime VideoComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Romeo and Juliet review – Russell Kane and Natalie Casey turn love’s young dream into a midlife fling | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Cacophonous and comedic staging sees an experienced, older duo engage in an enthusiastic liaison rather than a rebellious first romance
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Cacophonous and comedic staging sees an experienced, older duo engage in an enthusiastic liaison rather than a rebellious first romance
Content: Certain in her desires … Russell Kane and Natalie Casey in Romeo and Juliet at the New Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme.Photograph: Patch DolanView image in fullscreenCertain in her desires … Russell Kane and Natalie Casey in Romeo and Juliet at the New Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme.Photograph: Patch DolanTheatreReviewRomeo and Juliet review – Russell Kane and Natalie Casey turn love’s young dream into a midlife flingNew Vic, Newcastle-under-LymeCacophonous and comedic staging sees an experienced, older duo engage in an enthusiastic liaison rather than a rebellious first romanceMark FisherWed 23 Sep 2026 06.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs in any production of Shakespeare’s tragedy of star-crossed lovers, the nurse can tell Juliet’s age “unto an hour”. In this collaboration between the New Vic and Not Too Tame, however, that age is older than most. The Capulets’ upcoming party – a barrage of Balearic beats around a swimming pool with Tybalt (Patrick Knowles) on the decks – will mark her 40th birthday.Played by Natalie Casey, Juliet gets ready to the sounds of a chamber orchestra playing Like a Virgin. If you believe the nurse (Louise Haggerty), she is anything but.This Juliet is no innocent girl waking up to the possibility of love, but an assertive woman, certain in her desires. She has her adult insecurities, but she knows what she wants and argues forcibly to get it. Not so mature that she won’t do the splits or dance on the spot, she is as impulsive and lovable as anyone.That suits the similarly seasoned Romeo, played by comedian turned actorRussell Kane, dressed as a scaffolder in hi-vis jacket and shorts, his belt stuffed with spanners and wrenches. With impressive command of the language, he is no headstrong youth but just as lovestruck.View image in fullscreenTweakments … Lizzie Hopley as Lady Capulet, right, with Natalie Casey as Juliet.Photograph: Patch DolanIn all the cacophony of Jimmy Fairhurst’s staging, their relationship feels more like an enthusiastic fling than a meeting of soulmates. You miss a sense of profundity even as you will them on.Age in itself, however, is not an impediment to the story. What is lost is the sense of the new order trying to overthrow the old, a young generation recognising the folly of family feuds and the old generation closing ranks. For all its passion, this love is not rebellious. The tragedy is more private than political.And while there is a lot to enjoy in Fairhurst’s production, with its Botox injections for Lady Capulet (Lizzie Hopley), updated gags and chirpy audience interaction, it also strains too hard to persuade us we are enjoying ourselves. The extraneous business accounts for a longer-than-average running time and, for all the ebullience and heart of the cast, a little more trust in the play would be no bad thing.AtNew Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreRomeo and JulietRussell KanereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s about being loudly visible’: Ahadadream, the British-Pakistani dance star defanging racist slurs | Dance music | The Guardian
description: Like many south Asians in the UK, he kept creativity separate from a corporate career. But after co-signs from dance music’s A-list, he’s releasing a defiant – and daringly titled – debut album
Author: Tara Joshi
Headline: Like many south Asians in the UK, he kept creativity separate from a corporate career. But after co-signs from dance music’s A-list, he’s releasing a defiant – and daringly titled – debut album
Content: ‘The intention is pride, confidence, and self-love’ … Ahadadream photographed this month in Lahore, Pakistan.Photograph: Marshall LawrenceView image in fullscreen‘The intention is pride, confidence, and self-love’ … Ahadadream photographed this month in Lahore, Pakistan.Photograph: Marshall LawrenceDance musicInterview‘It’s about being loudly visible’: Ahadadream, the British-Pakistani dance star defanging racist slursTara JoshiLike many south Asians in the UK, he kept creativity separate from a corporate career. But after co-signs from dance music’s A-list, he’s releasing a defiant – and daringly titled – debut albumWed 23 Sep 2026 08.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Ahad Elley was 12, his family moved from Karachi to the UK. Quickly, he discovered his Pakistani identity was the basis of a slur. “Growing up inPakistan, I never knew that was a bad word, because why would it be? The word ‘pak’ means clean, it has no negative connotations.” Elley’s childhood response was to disconnect from his heritage, and what followed was “potentially shrinking or hiding parts of myself to fit into society”. It’s likely a familiar story for many diasporic south Asians who, at some point, have felt the call to assimilate.Twenty years later, Elley is better known as Ahadadream, an integral architect of the current British south Asian music scene, as well as a DJ, producer, label head, A&R and promoter shining a light on dance music from around the world. His tracks are favourites in sets by A-list dance artists such as Fred Again, Caribou, Peggy Gou and Four Tet, and with the release of his debut album, P★KI (pronounced “pee-star-kay-eye”) Elley’s star is set to rise further.The album’s title has caused some upset, given the word is laced with hurt and histories of racist violence, but Elley wants to reframe a slur used against him. “The intention is pride, confidence, and self-love,” he explains over video call from his home in east London. “There’s no intention to cause anyone any hurt or pain. But I totally understand everyone’s perspectives, and it’s also about sharing perspectives with each other, which I think is your responsibility as an artist.”Music wasn’t always an obvious journey for Elley. Like many desis, he thought of creativity as a hobby. “Music had always been drilled into me as something you did on the side,” he says. It was dance producer Skrillex who, in 2023, encouraged Elley to pursue his dreams. “He said to me: ‘No, you’ve got to quit your job. If you can’t make enough money, you can come and sleep on my sofa.’”Elley had spent a decade working full-time corporate jobs while establishing himself at the forefront of British underground dance music in his spare time. While studying chemistry at university, Elley had discovered club culture: attending Elijah and Skilliam’s infamous grime raves, Butterz; listening to Mini Mixes on Annie Mac’s Radio 1 show; running his own nights. He felt the pull of percussion early on, he says: “Rhythmic music has probably always been in my blood, going to weddings and being exposed to the dhol [drums]. Maybe I was drawn to UK funky because it’s more rhythmic, and that was almost a gateway to discovering things like gqom from South Africa, [Brazilian] baile funk, [Angolan] kuduro … I don’t understand why those sounds aren’t given as much importance as house and techno.”View image in fullscreen‘Rhythmic music has probably always been in my blood’ … Ahadadream.Photograph: Marshall LawrenceAnd so his own sets and productions began weaving together kinetic global polyrhythms. In 2017, he co-founded the label More Time, releasing tracks by artists from Trinidad to Taiwan. Simultaneously, he worked behind the scenes at DJ livestreaming company Boiler Room, all while making space for south Asian DJs who couldn’t easily be categorised: whether at his club night No ID, or Dialled In, the platform he co-founded. Though it started as a London-based festival, Dialled In has scaled up, with parties across the Indian subcontinent, international shows for south Asian artists, mentoring and, most recently, a record label – through which Elley is releasing P★KI.Capturing the bold energy of his DJ sets, with drums leading the melody throughout, P★KI is a thrilling love letter to Elley’s constituent parts, marrying a bright, borderless mesh of sounds that feel like being free. There’s a euphoric shout-out to inclusive clubbing on Make Space, alongside dark, boisterous nods to grime, slinky UK funky, skittering bass. The album’s visual identity, created with Elley’s wife, architect Esha Sikander, is a nod to the Radio Pakistan logo, with Elley dressed in brash colour combinations to embody his journey. He grins: “It’s about being loudly visible.”It’s fitting, then, that P★KI opens with Elley’s edit of transcendent qawwali singer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, arguably the greatest icon of Pakistani music. Tere Bin is a gleaming rework that’s become a fan favourite – at least one couple have played it down the aisle at their wedding and, at Dialled In’s fifth birthday in London this summer, a rapturous, misty-eyed crowd sang along.“It’s always so emotional,” says Elley. “Sometimes I question where those emotions come from: like, why are there tears on the dancefloor when we’re all singing Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan at the highest possible volume we can? There’s some sense of healing, and part of that is because in our day to day lives we are maybe a little bit disconnected from our heritage or identity.”On P★KI, Ahadadream is proudly facilitating that healing for a new generation, rejecting the urge to shrink away.P★KI is out now via Dialled In/Island. Ahadadream plays Electric Brixton, London, on 27 NovemberExplore more on these topicsDance musicClub cultureFolk musicPakistanElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From 50p gold hot pants to Paul Smith suits: how Kylie Minogue became one of pop’s ultimate chameleons | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The star’s rise from Ramsay Street to global superstar is the subject of a new book. It’s a journey that has cleverly harnessed the power of fashion to transform, subvert – and shock
Author: Michael Cragg
Headline: The star’s rise from Ramsay Street to global superstar is the subject of a new book. It’s a journey that has cleverly harnessed the power of fashion to transform, subvert – and shock
Content: Spinning Around … Minogue in her famous gold hot pants.Photograph: Channel 5View image in fullscreenSpinning Around … Minogue in her famous gold hot pants.Photograph: Channel 5FashionFrom 50p gold hot pants to Paul Smith suits: how Kylie Minogue became one of pop’s ultimate chameleonsThe star’s rise from Ramsay Street to global superstar is the subject of a new book. It’s a journey that has cleverly harnessed the power of fashion to transform, subvert – and shockMichael CraggWed 23 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 20 December 1989,Kylie Minoguefirst harnessed the power of fashion. Attending the Australian premiere of her film The Delinquents, she wore a custom sequined noughts-and-crosses minidress by Australian designers Morrissey Edmiston and a cropped blond wig. She also arrived with a new accessory: a rock star boyfriend in the shape of Michael Hutchence from INXS.Before then, there’d been her Neighbours character Charlene’s peak-80s silk taffeta and lace wedding dress, and Kylie the pop star on the cover of her first album, in 1988, wearing a topless hat showing off cascading curls. But that had been fashion forced on her, at a time when she had no say in her image.View image in fullscreenBreakout moment … with Michael Hutchence at the premiere of The Delinquents.Photograph: Mick Hutson/RedfernsFrom that moment, Kylie, or the public-facing version at least, took control. She used fashion as a reflection of her desire and need to evolve. Forever the pop chameleon, she anchored each new era via deliberate fashion choices that communicated where she was at in her life and career. As Jean Paul Gaultier wrote in the foreword to her 2012 photo-book Kylie/Fashion: “You change, you transform yourself, you adapt with the evolution of times, fashions, desires … and still stay yourself.”View image in fullscreenEspecially for you … inthatwedding dress with Jason Donovan in Neighbours.Photograph: Fremantle Ltd/RexWhile shapeshifting and defining distinct eras via fashion is a classic pop star move, Kylie’s early evolutions had to be more extreme. Madonna – the queen of reinvention, whose influence can be traced to Lady Gaga and Addison Rae – arrived fresh from the streets of New York and a friendship group that included Keith Haring and Jean-Michel Basquiat. Her 80s look of fishnets, gloves and copious amounts of bangles felt cool. The wide-eyed Kylie, meanwhile, had to take bigger risks; she had to shake off Neighbours, Jason Donovan and the sense of playing dress-up in a box marked “cringe”.This need manifested itself in her 1991 Let’s Get to It tour. The singer, keen to bury her Smiley Kylie persona, turned to the then relatively unknown John Galliano. “I just love dressing up and anyone who enjoys dressing up,”said Galliano at the time. The looks included corsets, stockings and suspenders and, most controversially, revealing underwear that showed off her buttocks. It created a tabloid scandal. NME accused Kylie of sending out a “dangerous message” to her young fans, which was sort of the point.
