She was using fashion to signal a move away from the old version of herself. “Those outfits weren’t a mistake,” she told Big! magazine that year. “I didn’t employ John Galliano to make me neck-to-toe cover-ups.”By the early 90s, Kylie had become a mainstay on the covers of style magazines such as the Face and i-D. For the latter she worked with fashion alchemist Judy Blame, whose outfits for Neneh Cherry helped define the look of the 80s, before teaming up with Katie Grand, considered one of the most powerful stylists in fashion. Grand would work on the cover shoot for 1994’s album, Kylie Minogue – her first for dance label Deconstruction. The choice of a black-and-white shot of a bare-footed and bespectacled Kylie in a Paul Smith suit was a more androgynous and interesting look for a pop star famed for pearly white teeth and vibrant colour. The image would help set the template for the new Cool Kylie era, anchored by songs such as Confide in Me.This more daring and intuitive approach to fashion would bleed into the next phase, Indie Kylie. Via her new stylist and so-called “gay husband” William Baker, Kylie would be introduced to new, edgier designers such as Owen Gaster, Antonio Berardi and Véronique Leroy. The feel was more stripped back, almost grunge-adjacent, but with a flash of the pop star peaking through.View image in fullscreenWearing a costume designed by John Galliano on her Showgirl: The Greatest Hits Tour in 2005.Photograph: Maurice McDonald/PAThe new millennium, however, would see Kylie ditch any indie overtones, chiefly thanks to a pair of now incredibly famous 50p gold hot pants found in a charity shop. They weren’t bought specifically for the Spinning Around video – Kylie had previously worn them in 1996 for a “nerds, tarts and tourists” party hosted by a friend – but they quickly became the video’s star. They perfectly encapsulated her return to pop and, via the tanned and carefree video, the optimism of a new millennium.The hot pants, alongside the majority of Kylie’s most stunning outfits, were donated by the lady herself to the Arts Centre Melbourne, occasionally being put on display in glass cabinets like the work of art that they’ve become.View image in fullscreenWearing a Gareth Pugh costume on the Showgirl Homecoming tour at Wembley Arena in 2007.Photograph: Pete Still/RedfernsAnother striking fashion moment would arrive a year later via Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s white hooded jumpsuit, complete with navel-scraping neckline. Designed by Mrs Jones, AKA the London designer Fee Doran, and with a nod to Grace Jones, it was a sign of Kylie’s style becoming more ambitious and future-facing – the perfect accompaniment to that era’s sleek Fever album.Kylie’s ability to signal personal and professional changes via her clothes is what anchors her as one of pop’s best chameleons. It’s there in the body-hugging, less obviously suggestive sexiness of the blue Balenciaga dress from 2003’s sultry Slow video, or the armour of English designer Gareth Pugh’s futuristic designs, which captured the resilience of 2007’s X era after Kylie returned to pop after being diagnosed with cancer. She is able to wear the gothic beauty of the Vampire’s Wife one minute and Dolce & Gabbana’s silver and gold miniskirts on stage the next.She even made a cameo appearance in Chanel’s recent handbag campaign, with the advert a homage to Kylie’s Michel Gondry-directed Come Into My World video from 2002.Kylie is not just one thing. Via her various musical eras throughout a near four-decade career, she’s moved across fashion with a nimbleness that only people with taste can. No one designer has ever “owned” her, and no stylist has locked her into a specific style. Kylie uses fashion like she uses her musical collaborators: to help colour in the various aspects of who she is.Can’t Get You Out of My Head: In Search of Kylie by Michael Cragg is published on 24 September by Faber (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFashionKylie MinoguePop and rockJohn GallianofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fire in My Mouth review – Wolfe’s multimedia oratorio tells its tragic story with focus and power | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Marin Alsop, the Philharmonia and three outstanding choirs gave the London premiere of Wolfe’s work about the deaths of 146 workers in a New York garment factory fire in 1911
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: Marin Alsop, the Philharmonia and three outstanding choirs gave the London premiere of Wolfe’s work about the deaths of 146 workers in a New York garment factory fire in 1911
Content: Scissors snapped shut in unison with metallic bite … Fire in My Mouth at Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Pete WoodheadView image in fullscreenScissors snapped shut in unison with metallic bite … Fire in My Mouth at Royal Festival Hall, London.Photograph: Pete WoodheadClassical musicReviewFire in My Mouth review – Wolfe’s multimedia oratorio tells its tragic story with focus and powerRoyal Festival Hall, LondonMarin Alsop, the Philharmonia and three outstanding choirs gave the London premiere of Wolfe’s work about the deaths of 146 workers in a New York garment factory fire in 1911Alexandra CoghlanWed 23 Sep 2026 08.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 08.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Saturday 25 March, 1911, Greenwich Village’s Triangle Shirtwaist Factory caught fire. One hundred and forty-six garment workers – mostly recent Jewish and Italian immigrant women – died, many prevented from escaping the flames by stairwells and exits locked by the management.The disaster is the catalyst for Pulitzer-winning composer Julia Wolfe’s 2019 multimedia oratorioFire in My Mouth: the third in her series of large-scale works drawing on the history of the American worker, and a punchy opener to the Southbank Centre’s autumn season.This isn’t the first protest-work we’ve seen from Wolfe in London this year; 2026 opened withunEarth at the Barbican– an earnest homily on the climate emergency. But where the latter preached, Fire in My Mouth dramatises. Succinct and direct, told largely in verbatim words from survivors and contemporaries, the piece’s strength is its refusal to widen the lens, to turn a tragedy into a touchstone or individuals into everywomen.View image in fullscreenMassed protest song … the Philharmonia, London Voices, the RSNO Youth Chorus and Farnham Youth Choir perform Fire in My Mouth.Photograph: Pete WoodheadThe score churns and whirs with kinetic energy: the clack of the sewing machines or the swell of the ocean we first meet the women crossing “without passports or anything”. Text is fragmented and superimposed, layered in motoric patterns until consonants become verbal pistons and levers. Underneath, a large orchestra (here a keenly expressive Philharmonia conducted by Marin Alsop) shapes more sustained soundscapes, occasionally fascinatingly alien: the pitchless grind of bows into strings creating a flickering Geiger counter effect, or the scissors raised high above the chorus’s heads, snapped shut in unison with metallic bite.With so many moving parts – an all-female professional chamber choir and youth chorus; a slow-strafing slideshow of black and white photographs and archive film footage created by Jeff Sugg; ritual gestures and movements by director Anne Kauffman – it would be easy for the music to turn into a soundtrack. The distilled clarity of Wolfe’s score ensures it doesn’t, aided here by outstanding performances fromLondon Voicesas well as theRSNO Youth ChorusandFarnham Youth Choir– all crisply and undemonstratively marshalled by Alsop.The work ends (echoes of John Adams’ 9/11 homage On the Transmigration of Souls) with a litany of the names of the dead. It’s a statement that would have been impossible until 2011, when the final victims were at last identified, just a year before a fire in a Bangladesh garment factory killed 124.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicThe Philharmonia OrchestrareviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sometimes I do cruel things – and it’s worth it’: the fabulous shameless art of the great Sophie Calle | Sophie Calle | The Guardian
description: The French artist has stalked people, posed as a hotel maid to get into rooms, and filmed her mother’s last breath. Has she any regrets? Non! As a major UK show opens, she recalls her career highs
Author: Chloë Ashby
Headline: The French artist has stalked people, posed as a hotel maid to get into rooms, and filmed her mother’s last breath. Has she any regrets? Non! As a major UK show opens, she recalls her career highs
Content: ‘I don’t always tell the truth’ … Sophie Calle in her studio in Paris.Photograph: Rasmus Quistgaard / Louisiana ChannelView image in fullscreen‘I don’t always tell the truth’ … Sophie Calle in her studio in Paris.Photograph: Rasmus Quistgaard / Louisiana ChannelSophie CalleInterview‘Sometimes I do cruel things – and it’s worth it’: the fabulous shameless art of the great Sophie CalleChloë AshbyThe French artist has stalked people, posed as a hotel maid to get into rooms, and filmed her mother’s last breath. Has she any regrets? Non! As a major UK show opens, she recalls her career highsWed 23 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve read enough interviews withSophie Calleto know that the conversation ahead could be tricky. France’s most famous conceptual artist can be a touch evasive. Which is why I’m so surprised by the woman before me, who is friendly and seemingly open, all smiles. She’s wearing big tinted glasses, and behind them I picture her eyes twinkling. Then, 10 minutes in, she tells me she is obsessed with absence. When I ask why, she says: “Why do you live in England? Why are you wearing that sweater? I am not here to do therapy with you.”She is talking to me from the same Paris apartment she has been living in for almost 50 years. Hanging from the ceiling is a disco ball, and, alongside pictures and books, there are boxes that I imagine are filled with the innermost thoughts and feelings of her subjects. Since the early 1980s, Calle has made a name for herself with art that is at once intimate and detached, morbid and playful, immersing us in the lives of others – and in her own life, too. With a camera and a notebook in hand, she has invited strangers to sleep in her bed, posed as a hotel maid to document the belongings of guests, and called everyone in a lost address book to build a peculiarly tender portrait of its owner. Now, at 72, she is about to open her first big show in the UK for nearly two decades.double quotation markI didn’t know what to do with my days. So I followed people to see what they did with theirs“I became an artist to seduce my father,” she tells me, matter of fact. He was a doctor and a collector of pop and conceptual art. She was 26 and “very lost”. He wasn’t happy with how she’d been spending her time, hitch-hiking around the world with no money or sense of purpose. When she returned to Paris and peered at the works on his walls, she thought it might please him if she made art too. “I could not paint,” she says, “but I enjoyed writing, and taking photos seemed possible. I did not know what I was doing or where it was going, but I was confident.”View image in fullscreenWater therapy … a Turkish man sees the sea for the first time in 2011’s Voir la Mer .Photograph: © Sophie Calle / DACS, London, 2026 Courtesy of the artist and PerrotinRight away, she started following people. “I did not know what to do with my days,” she explains. “So I thought, ‘Let’s see what other people do with theirs.’ Immediately, I liked the feeling of not having to decide; it was both restful and active.” In 1980, she stalked a man she’d met at a party from Paris to Venice, tracing his movements in time-stamped entries and photographing him in his raincoat as he passed through the twisting city streets, unaware of the woman in the blond wig following just a few steps behind.Her new exhibition, Something Missing?at Turner Contemporary in Margate, brings together photographs, videos and installations from 1986 to 2024. It is about absence: Calle’s late parents, a former lover, discarded ideas. When her mother was dying in her bed in 2006, the artist made a film about it, apparently so she wouldn’t miss her last breath. Turning it into a project helped her emotionally, she says. “When I am in a difficult or sad situation, I need to create some distance so that I am not swallowed by the event.”When her father died in 2015, she decided to stop making art, because she thought it would be nice “for sentimental reasons” if he’d seen everything she’d done. “I went travelling,” says Calle. “Then I got bored and started again.”As well as absence, Calle tells me she is obsessed with death: “I speak of it more and more because I am getting closer and closer.” She has already commissioned her headstone, and she once commissioned an obituary, which (of course) she then edited. In 2023, she compiled a new series of unfinished works. These will feature in the Margate show, to give them life while she’s still here. She says that some ideas are abandoned because they’re not good enough or would be impossible to pull off. And some require too much time and money. “Sometimes I think an idea is too cruel and not worth that cruelty,” she says, before smiling and adding: “Sometimes I do cruel things and it is worth it.”View image in fullscreen‘I like the feeling that no one depends on me’ … Danger from 2018.Photograph: © Sophie Calle / DACS, London, 2026 Courtesy of the artist and PerrotinBefore making one of her most moving series,1986’s The Blind, Calle worried that the project might be cruel. It involved asking people born without sight to describe their image of beauty. But then the first man she approached answered her simply and clearly. “In a way, he gave me permission.” Black-and-white portraits of the participants are paired with their responses, which include the colour green, the actor Alain Delon, and sheep. Twenty-five years later, she invited people living in Istanbul to see the sea for the first time: Voir la Mercaptures Turkish men, women and children on film, first from behind, then as they turn to face the camera, their eyes bright with emotion.Calle doesn’t do regrets: “There are projects I would like to have done, but I did others instead.” While she remains preoccupied with seeing and being seen, she is no longer interested in the same things that stirred her imagination as a young artist. “I would not follow somebody I do not know for days and days, partly because I do not have the energy,” she says. “You know, I have concerns now that I did not have when I was 26.” She is well aware that she has detractors as well as admirers; that some see her work as inventive, others as invasive. She used to be afraid of running out of ideas, but not any more. “If they stop coming, it won’t be a big deal. I have plenty to do. I will enjoy life.”Which isn’t to say that she’s fearless. When Calle was first invited to do a show at the Picasso Museum in Paris, she refused because she was worried about being crushed by the modernist master, and it was only after seeing his paintings covered up during the pandemic that the prospect of exhibiting alongside him seemed manageable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWrong Turn, 2023, from the series Catalogue Raisonné of the Unfinished,Photograph: Claire Dorn/© Sophie Calle / DACS, London, 2026 Courtesy of the artist and PerrotinHastily hidden to protect them from dust and light, his greatest works became less awe-inspiring, more amusing, like lovers the morning after, self-consciously hunched beneath rumpled sheets. “I was afraid of being crushed by Picasso, but I wasn’t afraid of his absence – that gave me a new direction.” In 2023, she took over four floors of the museum and moved in her personal belongings. “Everything that’s here was there,” she says, gesturing around her apartment. “I lived in the show.”Aside from her spell bunking with Picasso, Calle has always lived alone. “I don’t really like couples,” she tells me, adding in the same breath that she’s been seeing the same man for the past 25 years. “I think most of the time people whoarein a couple are much more fun when they go out by themselves.” She’s never made work about her partner, who convinced her to sign an agreement stating that, if she ever does create art about him, he has to leave her. “So, it is an easy out if ever I want to be single again,” she says, with a laugh.In the past, she has spoken about feeling sorry for people who have children. Does she still feel that way? “It is not a reasonable thing to say, but it is how I feel. I am sure some people are incredibly happy and were not before. And maybe I am being defensive because I can’t change my mind now, so I may as well stick to it and keep pretending even to myself that I made the right decision.” Not the answer I was expecting from a woman with no regrets. She smiles as if she can read my mind. “But I do think I made the right decision. I like the feeling that nobody depends on me.”Which brings us back to her obsession. Could it be, I ask, preparing myself for another rebuttal, that she is drawn to absence because, as with the lack of dependents, it leaves ample time and space for her to create? She nods, sort of, before going off on a curious and revealing tangent. “I don’t tell the truth,” she says, referring back to the film she made about her mother, and how she plugged the gap she deliberately carved out between them. “I tell what has happened, but what has happened is not the truth. The truth has a before, an after, context.” I search her shaded eyes for a sign, but she is poker-faced.Something Missing? is atTurner Contemporary, Margate, from 3 October to 24 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsSophie CalleArtPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Another taste of honey: Shelagh Delaney’s long-lost play about a teenage truant is a little gem | Audio drama | The Guardian
description: The playwright’s daughter found Catch Me Who Can after her mother’s death. Now it has become a compelling audio drama with Toby Jones and Rita Tushingham
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: The playwright’s daughter found Catch Me Who Can after her mother’s death. Now it has become a compelling audio drama with Toby Jones and Rita Tushingham
Content: A remarkable gift for dialogue … Shelagh Delaney pictured in 1960.Photograph: Tom Stuttard/the GuardianView image in fullscreenA remarkable gift for dialogue … Shelagh Delaney pictured in 1960.Photograph: Tom Stuttard/the GuardianAudio dramaAnother taste of honey: Shelagh Delaney’s long-lost play about a teenage truant is a little gemThe playwright’s daughter found Catch Me Who Can after her mother’s death. Now it has become a compelling audio drama with Toby Jones and Rita TushinghamMichael BillingtonWed 23 Sep 2026 04.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 04.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWas Shelagh Delaney a one-hit wonder? Absolutely not. Aside from A Taste of Honey which, in the words of Dominic Dromgoole, “has a rock-solid heart and the gleam of the natural”, she wrote the screenplays for the films Charlie Bubbles and Dance With a Stranger, TV series including The House That Jack Built and several radio plays. But now a 30-minute piece,Catch Me Who Can, has come to light, been released as an audio drama and turns out to be a little gem.Its origins are fascinating. It deals with a teenage truant and was discovered by Delaney’s daughter, Charlotte, after her mother’s death in 2011. But why did it lay hidden for so long? According to Charlotte, who has adapted it for audio: “It imagines my last few hours on the lam having run away from home and school when I was 14 in 1978. I was gone for three days and two nights. I’d suggest it’s a racing certainty that the reason nothing has ever been heard of it is that it’s about me and my mum had rules about that kind of thing.”The bulk of the play consists of a testy confrontation between the runaway Hattie (Ivy Sheehan) and her maths teacher (Toby Jones) who tries to persuade her to return home. Although the teacher is only out jogging in a park because he is on strike, he stands for a world of order, discipline and control; Hattie, on the other hand, embodies the need for freedom, anarchy and self-expression. But Delaney imbues the situation with its own ironies. The teacher argues for the sanctity of family life but is himself a conspicuous loner; Hattie’s urge for self-discovery conceals a total disregard for other people including her anxious parents.View image in fullscreenRita Tushingham, far left, with Robert Stephens, Murray Melvin and Dora Bryan in the 1961 film version of A Taste of Honey.Photograph: Ronald GrantSeveral things make the play worth listening to. One is the ease and naturalness of the dialogue. Hattie, not unlike the teenage Jo in A Taste of Honey, asks endless questions. At one point she taxes the teacher as to whether he ever did anything to find out what it was like just for the sake of it since “you once told us curiosity was divine”. Delaney also introduces an itinerant bag lady – played by none other than Rita Tushingham who was Jo in Tony Richardson’s film of A Taste of Honey – who says of a relative: “They took him into hospital and took his leg off – just like President Tito.”The best theatre to stream this month: Bryan Cranston cranks up the tension in All My SonsRead moreAs well as a collision between self-restraint and teenage truancy, the play offers – in Charlotte Delaney’s words – a snapshot of London life in 1978, with oblique references to the IRA, the Vietnamese “boat people” and Rock Against Racism: a reminder of the turbulence of the times.Deftly produced by Polly Thomas, the piece is very well acted by Jones as the audibly repressed teacher and by Sheehan as the experience-hungry Hattie. What you come away with is a reminder of Delaney’s remarkable gift for dialogue and her equal understanding of the value of education and the exuberance of youth.Catch Me Who Can is on SpotifyExplore more on these topicsAudio dramaTheatreShelagh DelaneyToby JonesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bolognina: make tracks for Bologna’s bustling former rail workers’ quarter | Italy holidays | The Guardian
description: This once industrial area has been transformed into a vibrant artistic hub with a thriving food and drink scene
Author: John Brunton
Headline: This once industrial area has been transformed into a vibrant artistic hub with a thriving food and drink scene
Content: Bollore is a cool vermouth bar in the Mercato Albani  that also organises concerts, art exhibitions and cultural events.Photograph: John BruntonView image in fullscreenBollore is a cool vermouth bar in the Mercato Albani  that also organises concerts, art exhibitions and cultural events.Photograph: John BruntonZoning inItaly holidaysBolognina: make tracks for Bologna’s bustling former rail workers’ quarterThis once industrial area has been transformed into a vibrant artistic hub with a thriving food and drink sceneJohn BruntonWed 23 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 02.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhy go now?Located just north of the Centrale train station, Bolognina neighbourhood is more than just a Little Bologna. It is a completely different world from the medieval maze of palaces, churches and towers that define the city’s “Centro Storico”, which is increasingly filled with crowds of tourists as Bologna joins the big league of Italian getaway destinations.There is an immediate visual difference as narrow cobbled lanes give way to wide, tree-lined avenues, pastel-coloured low-rise apartment blocks, spacious parks and piazzas. Bolognina sprang up at the beginning of the 20th century, initially to house families of workers from the railway, then from nearby manufacturing industries.Today, the quarter is home to a diverse multi-ethnic population and remains a stronghold for militant leftwing politics, with the local community committed to avoiding gentrification. Tourists are certainly made welcome, and it is a delight to feel part of genuine local life.Where to eat and drinkView image in fullscreenTrattoria di via Serra chef Tommaso Maio.Photograph: John BruntonEating out here makes a refreshing change from the city centre. Of course there are still spots serving traditional freshly made tagliatelle al ragù such as the atmospheric old-school trattoriaLa Golosità di Nonna Aurora. But you can also sample Georgian cuisine atPane Georgiana, a sharing plate of Ethiopian and Eritrean dishes atRistorante Africano Adal, spicy Sichuan cooking atBa Hot Pot, or handmade tortellini and tortelloni stuffed with halal meat at the innovativeBrodellini.For vegetarians, the perfect spot isPiazza Martino, a cantina and deli owned by a nearby farm in the Bolognesi Hills that practises a “first we grow, then we eat” philosophy, transforming their organic produce into delicious aubergine parmigiana, vegan pepperoni lasagne, and courgette and potato polpette (balls).Bolognina’s prime foodie street is Via Luigi Serra, symbolised by the fiercely independentTrattoria di Via Serra. The restaurant’s three small, rustic salons are always packed and getting a reservation isn’t easy as they don’t take bookings through social platforms and rarely answer the phone or emails. Chef Tommaso Maio and co-owner Flavio Benassi used to have a restaurant up in the hills nearby, but 13 years ago decided to come to the city, choosing Bolognina rather than the city centre for their new venture. “Our aim then, and still today, is to offer the locals here an old-fashioned neighbourhood trattoria where they can still order a comforting bowl of tortellini in capon broth, lasagne and freshly baked crescenti biscuits,” they explain.View image in fullscreenA mural of local hero Lucio Dalla, an iconic Italian singer-songwriter.Photograph: John BruntonIf there is no free table at the Trattoria, then the street offers plenty of options, from hearty plates of cold cuts and cheeses at the deli-dinerLa Vecchia Bottega, cocktails, spritz and craft beers at the hipFermentobar, or local wines atLa Petite Enoteca. To finish the evening, there is often live music at the bars in Piazza Lucio Dalla, named after Bologna’s local hero, an iconic Italian singer-songwriter.Cultural experiencesView image in fullscreenThe monumental Holocaust memorial is one of the first things you see on arriving in the quarter.Photograph: Riccardo Bianchini/AlamyLeave historic Bologna behind by walking from the central train station across the Matteotti bridge and you immediately come face to face with a strikingHolocaust memorial, an austere, minimalist monument of two narrowly separated 10-metre high steel walls. Just opposite stands the massive Chiesa del Sacro Cuore di Gesù, dating back to 1912 when Bolognina was first being built. It is worth visiting just to marvel at the soaring 60-metre-high dome.Hidden away in the backstreets in a former tram shed,La Memoria di Ustica Museumis a unique homage to a commercial flight between Bologna and Palermo that was mysteriously shot down in 1980 with no survivors. French artist Christian Boltanski has meticulously reconstructed the wreckage of the downed airliner and assembled the personal items belonging to the victims, creating an immense, intensely moving installation.View image in fullscreenThe impressive dome of Chiesa del Sacro Cuore di Gesù.Photograph: John BruntonCheckpoint Charlyis a thriving alternative art and artisan cooperative occupying a former lingerie warehouse. Workshops include ceramics, printmaking, photography, graphics and music, with a dozen cultural events presented each year. TheDLF– Dopo Lavoro Ferroviario – is a sprawling park behind the station originally created in the 1920s for after-work activities for railway workers. This green lung has been saved from abandonment and now houses the laid-back all-dayKinotto Bar, theVecchia Orsa DLFcraft brewery and beer garden, apizzeria, thePuccini concert arenaand theLocomotiv Club, a live indie music venue.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhere to shopView image in fullscreenIlario di Lorenzis in his workshop with one of his hand-crafted bags.Photograph: John BruntonAlthough this essentially residential neighbourhood may not be a shopping paradise, bargain hunters should plan to visit on the first Sunday of the month when the Piazza Lucio Dalla is transformed into a huge flea market. Over in the daily Mercato Albani, Ilario di Lorenzis has recently openedIntelligenza Artigianale, an atelier showcasing his funky hand-crafted bags, T-shirts and caps, while cycling fans should head forBolognina Bike Shop, whose friendly owner, Dario Brunetto, repairs bikes and recycles vinyls, retro decor and collectible vintage cycling jerseys.Don’t missView image in fullscreenA food stall in Mercato Abani.Photograph: John BruntonSince opening in 1934,Mercato Albanihas been the beating heart of Bolognina. Running down the middle of a shady tree-lined avenue, locals gather each morning for their daily shopping from bustling stalls selling Bologna’s speciality mortadella (pork salami) and prosciutto, fish, cheese and organic veggies. Then there is a complete change of personality from 5pm till around midnight when shuttered stands open up as lively cocktail and craft beer bars, the natural wineenoteca,Vineria Punk, plus casual diners serving pizza and pasta, vegan dishes and Greek cuisine. Giuseppe Agrello the owner ofBollore, a cool vermouth bar, explains that “when we were invited to open in the mercato, we insisted that during the day it should stay as it is and not become just another tourist food court. So we only begin in the evening and also organise concerts, art exhibitions and cultural events for the community.”Where to stayView image in fullscreenThe eclectic Hotel Il Guercino.Photograph: John BruntonHotel Il Guercinois a delightfully quirky, family-owned hotel, extravagantly decorated with a mix of baroque and Asian influences, with a spa featuring sauna, hot tub and steam bath. Doubles from €150.This trip wasprovided byBologna WelcomeandEmilia Romagna TurismoExplore more on these topicsItaly holidaysZoning inCity breaksBologna holidaysEurope holidaysFood and drinkCultural tripsRestaurantsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Byron Bay’s ‘daggier neighbour’ named in Lonely Planet’s 2027 Best in Travel list | Australia holidays | The Guardian
description: The Tweed region is easily as beautiful as nearby Byron, but without the glamour and crowds. For locals, the biggest drawcard is the community
Author: Susan Chenery
Headline: The Tweed region is easily as beautiful as nearby Byron, but without the glamour and crowds. For locals, the biggest drawcard is the community
Content: Tumbulgum, a town in the Tweed Shire in New South Wales. The Tweed region is named in Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel list for 2027.Photograph: Luke MarsdenView image in fullscreenTumbulgum, a town in the Tweed Shire in New South Wales. The Tweed region is named in Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel list for 2027.Photograph: Luke MarsdenAustralia holidaysByron Bay’s ‘daggier neighbour’ named in Lonely Planet’s 2027 Best in Travel listThe Tweed region is easily as beautiful as nearby Byron, but without the glamour and crowds. For locals, the biggest drawcard is the communitySusan CheneryWed 23 Sep 2026 01.38 EDTLast modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 01.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLocals in the Tweed region already knew we were a bit special, obviously. The sheer beauty of the place routinely stops you in your tracks. It turns out we are also having a moment on the world stage. Along with the Red Centre in the Northern Territory, the Tweed is one of only two Australian destinations named in Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel 2027, the travel publication’s annual list of 50 standout holiday spots and experiences, announced on Wednesday.Now those who came here to escape the world may find it is coming to them.“Bloody hell,” says a fellow resident Sarah Killington, whose verandah overlooks the wide, flat Tweed Valley. “We don’t want to turn into another Gold Coast.”Jessica Lockhard, Lonely Planet’s destination editor for Oceania, says that the Tweed was chosen because: “What we’re really looking for is places that feel less crowded, that are offering a deeper and more meaningful experience, or are really inviting travellers to slow down.” We can definitely do slow.Tweed Shire is Byron Shire adjacent, easily as beautiful but without the glamour. There are fewer “healers” and drum circles, less tourist overcrowding and recently arrived wealth. We are traditionally the poorer, daggier neighbour. And we like it that way. A place that people usually drive past on their way from the Gold Coast toByron Bay. You can almost feel the atmosphere change when you enter Byron.View image in fullscreenWaves roll in at Cabarita beach on the Tweed coast.Photograph: Luke MarsdenFlora grows madly in the volcanic soil and artisan producers abound, alongside generational cattle and cane farmers. There is, says Phillip Hepburn, co-owner of the restaurant Tweed River House, “an incredibly diverse agricultural and primary production sector”. Buying food from local producers becomes a mantra. Everyone goes to the Wednesday farmers’ market at the showground in Murwillumbah.The town of Murwillumbah seems to have rebranded itself as an artist colony, dominated by M’Arts, a vast building in the centre of town, which functions as a performance space and where artists produce their work from studios. Once a service town for the agricultural industry, it has now evolved, says Troy Stanley, the owner of the M’Arts cafe and bar, into “a town where people are supportive of the arts and everything creative”.Sunburnt surrealism: Gerwyn Davies’ love letter to kitschy, coastal Australiana – in picturesRead moreStill, those who came here, like myself, because it was spectacular but cheap, now face skyrocketing rents and house prices. Since 2019, house prices have nearly doubled as city dwellers descended with their city money.The Northern Rivers Rail Trail, which opened in 2023, filled the region with Lycra-clad bulging thigh muscles.Scenery aside, for the people who live here it is all about community. Even if locals argue ferociously about One Nation and chemtrails on the community Facebook pages, this is a community that pulled each other through the floods of 2017 and 2022. “Watching the way this community does community … There’s nothing like it,” says Stanley.And even with all the inevitable attention as a tourist destination, it is unlikely that the character of the place will wholly change.“It is a very strong community with a genuine cultural and creative identity,” says Hepburn. Geoff Anstee, the chef-owner of the recently opened Sayu Japanese restaurant, puts it more succinctly: “They are beautiful working-class people, hard working, salt of the Earth.”Just so you know.Explore more on these topicsAustralia holidaysAustralian lifestyleNew South Wales holidaysByron BayNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kenji Morimoto’s gochujang corn fritters and oyster mushrooms with butter bean mash – recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Snacks never tasted so good: spicy corn fritters with a lime pickle-spiked yoghurt, and king oyster mushrooms laced with blackberries, pomegranate molasses and soy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Snacks never tasted so good: spicy corn fritters with a lime pickle-spiked yoghurt, and king oyster mushrooms laced with blackberries, pomegranate molasses and soy
Content: Kenji Morimoto's gochujang corn fritters with lime pickle yoghurt.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenKenji Morimoto's gochujang corn fritters with lime pickle yoghurt.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.FoodKenji Morimoto’s gochujang corn fritters and oyster mushrooms with butter bean mash – recipesSnacks never tasted so good: spicy corn fritters with a lime pickle-spiked yoghurt, and king oyster mushrooms laced with blackberries, pomegranate molasses and soyKenji MorimotoWed 23 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing oyster mushrooms are quite the centrepiece: relatively meaty and receptive to big flavours. Paired with a vibrant glaze spiked with sweet blackberries, tart pomegranate molasses and savoury soy sauce, every bite balances the richness with sharp, fruity acidity. But first some tangy, fresh fritters, celebrating fresh corn with an earthy base of gochujang, which works brilliantly against the lime pickle yoghurt. Creamy, crisp and the perfect treat.Gochujang corn fritters with lime pickle yoghurtThese can be made vegan by swapping the yoghurt for a plant-based alternative. Don’t have access to fresh corn? Use tinned, making this a true pantry rustle-up.Prep15 minCook15 minServes3-4as alight lunch2corn on the cob, kernels stripped off, or 1 standard 198g tin sweetcorn, thoroughly drained and patted dry3 spring onions, trimmed and finely sliced (about 40g net)20g fresh coriander, roughly sliced, plus extra to garnishSalt60g plain flour20g cornflour1 tsp baking powder2 tbsp gochujangNeutral oil,for fryingFor the lime pickle yoghurt200g full-fat Greek yoghurt1-2 tbspIndian lime pickle, roughly chopped1 lime,half juiced, the other half cut into segments to servePut the corn, spring onions and coriander in a large bowl with a pinch of salt and, using the back of a wooden spoon, roughly crush some of the kernels.In a second bowl, whisk the flour, cornflour and baking powder, then add the gochujang and 100ml cold water, and whisk until smooth and slightly thick. Add this to the corn bowl and fold in, until the corn is well coated; if the mixture seems a bit too thick, add an additional 10-20ml water to loosen.To make the lime pickle yoghurt, gently mix the yoghurt, chopped lime pickle and lime juice, then adjust the seasoning, if need be.Pour a couple of centimetres of neutral oil into a large frying pan on a medium-high heat. Test the oil’s temperature by dropping a little bit of the corn batter: it should sizzle and bubble immediately. Drop spoonful-sized dollops of the batter into the oil – they will naturally spread a bit, so try not to poke them too much – and cook for one to two minutes on each side, until deeply golden. They may look a bit overcooked, but remember the dark colour is also coming from the gochujang. Drain the fritters on kitchen paper and salt immediately while still hot.Serve on top of the lime pickle yoghurt, garnished with the lime segments and remaining coriander leaves.King oyster mushrooms with a blackberry, pomegranate and soy glaze and a chive and butter bean mashView image in fullscreenKenji Morimoto’s king oyster mushrooms with a blackberry, pomegranate and soy glaze and a chive and butter bean mash.The velvety bean mash and golden pangrattato can be made up to two days in advance, turning this into a fast, stress-free weeknight dinner. To make this vegan, simply swap the butter and soured cream for plant-based alternatives.Prep15 minCook20 minServes23-4 large king oyster mushrooms2 tbsp neutral oil30g unsalted butter2-3 garlic cloves, peeled and smashed with a knife1rosemary sprig150gblackberries2 tbsp pomegranate molasses1 tbsp soy sauceFor the pangrattato1 slice stale sourdough1 tbsp olive oil4-5thyme sprigs, leaves pickedFlaky sea saltFor the butter bean mash2400g tinsbutter beans, drained, reserving 30-40ml of the liquid30g unsalted butter50gsoured cream, or full-fat greek yoghurt20g fresh chives, finely choppedTo make the pangrattato, tear up the sourdough and pulse to crumbs in a food processor. In a small pan, heat the olive oil, add the crumbs and fry, stirring, for two to three minutes, until golden brown. Turn off the heat and toss in the thyme leaves and a pinch of flaky salt. This will now keep in an airtight container at room temperature for a few days.Cut the mushrooms in half lengthwise, then, using a small, sharp knife, lightly score the flat surface of each one in a crosshatch pattern.Put the butter beans, reserved bean stock and butter in a small saucepan, and cook for three to five minutes, until hot. Add the soured cream, blend with a stick blender to your desired consistency – I like a slightly chunkier mash– then fold in the chopped chives and season. Cover and keep warm.Put two tablespoons of neutral oil in a large frying pan on a medium-high heat. Lay in the mushrooms cut side down and leave to cook undisturbed for three to four minutes, until there’s a golden crust on the scored surface. Flip over, add the butter, smashed garlic and rosemary sprig, then tilt the pan and baste the mushrooms with the foaming butter for a few minutes. Transfer the cooked mushrooms to a plate, and discard the aromatics.Turn down the heat to medium and add the blackberries, soy sauce and 50ml water to the pan. Use the back of a spoon to gently crush the berries, then leave to bubble for a few minutes. Stir in the pomegranate molasses and cook for one to two minutes longer on a low heat, until very syrupy.Spoon a generous amount of butter bean mash on to two plates, followed by the mushrooms. Spoon the blackberry sauce on top and garnish generously with the pangrattato. Serve with a rocket, watercress and lemon salad, if you like.Explore more on these topicsFoodAutumn food and drinkVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkHerbs and spicesFruitSnacksrecipesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn leftover roast chicken into a brilliant midweek meal – recipe | Chicken | The Guardian
description: Whip up a curry mayonnaise and turn your leftovers into a semi-instant classic
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Whip up a curry mayonnaise and turn your leftovers into a semi-instant classic
Content: Tom Hunt’s leftover roast chicken coronation chicken.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s leftover roast chicken coronation chicken.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian.Waste notChickenHow to turn leftover roast chicken into a brilliant midweek meal – recipeWhip up a curry mayonnaise and turn your leftovers into a semi-instant classicTom HuntWed 23 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was my gran’s funeral a few weeks ago, so today’s recipe seems rather fitting, because coronation chicken was one of the few savoury dishes she cooked, and also one I loved. This homage to her glorious personality and astonishingly sweet tooth (add extra mango chutney for sweetness) is a wonderful way to use up leftover chicken from a roast, barbecue or whatever. I make the mayo from scratch, because I don’t keep mayonnaise in my larder, but I do have eggs and extra-virgin olive oil.Leftover roast coronation chickenCoronation chicken was a genius solution to a common caterers’ conundrum, and was created by Rosemary Hume and Constance Spry fora 350-person banquetat Westminster school to mark Queen Elizabeth’s coronation. I take a similar approach, whether I’m cooking a dinner party for five or feeding 500 at a festival, and generally go for simple recipes that can be finished with little effort (and have mymise en placeready, of course). This dish is a brilliant use of Sunday’s leftovers, be it as a delicious stand-alone supper or a superior sandwich filling. Don’t be precious about which bits of leftover chicken you use: thigh meat, wing meat, the oysters, skin, and any last scraps clinging to the carcass – all of it goes in.Serves21egg1 heaped tsp wholegrain mustard, or to tasteFlaky sea salt and black pepperJuice of ¼ lemon, plus the finely grated zest if the fruit is organic and unwaxedAbout 150ml extra-virgin olive oil, or enough to emulsify and thicken the mayoFinely grated zest and juice of ¼ unwaxed lemonA few coriander sprigs, stalks finely chopped, leaves left whole1 tbsp mango chutney1 tsp mild curry powder, or a pinch each of a few warm spices such as turmeric, cinnamon, cumin, fenugreek, mustard seed, ginger, black pepper and nigella seeds – whatever you have to hand300g cooked chicken or turkey scraps, pulled off a roast1 handful flaked almonds, toasted, to serveTo make the dressing, crack the egg into an immersion blender jug and add the mustard, a pinch of sea salt, the lemon juice (and zest, if using), the finely chopped coriander stalks, the chutney and the curry powder. With the motor going, slowly pour in the oil and blend until the mixture emulsifies into a thick mayonnaise, then taste and adjust the seasoning. The curried mayo will now keep in the fridge for up to four days.To make the coronation chicken, pull any leftover chicken or turkey scraps – 200-300g should feed two generously – into rough pieces, then mix in a bowl with enough mayonnaise to coat the meat well. Serve topped with toasted flaked almonds and the coriander leaves.Explore more on these topicsChickenWaste notFoodFood wasteSauces and graviesMeatMain courseHerbs and spicesfeaturesShareReuse this content
